items.title: Most of What You’re Building Doesn’t Matter － Brandon Fuhrmann － AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
Brandon Fuhrmann argues most sellers waste time building AI tools that already exist as paid software, and proposes a "skip, buy, or build" framework, then walks through the few dashboards he actually built himself, including an inventory pipeline with seasonality projections and a week over week SQP tracker.

 

TOPICS:

  1. A skip, buy, or build framework for deciding what's actually worth building with AI
  2. Underused report automation features already built into tools like Sellerboard and Data Rova
  3. Three homegrown dashboards worth building: seasonal inventory, an SQP week over week tracker, and an "attack chase defend" keyword prioritizer

cliff_notes:
Brandon Fuhrmann warns that most AI enthusiasm in the room is going toward rebuilding things that already exist as reliable paid software, and lays out a framework for deciding what's genuinely worth building versus skipping or buying.

 

THE SKIP, BUY, OR BUILD FRAMEWORK

  • Skip: if the excitement to build something is mostly vanity ("because you can"), if you'll rarely use it, or if you won't notice when the underlying data goes wrong, it isn't worth building or maintaining.
  • Buy: if reliable software already exists and someone else maintains it against Amazon's constantly shifting fee structures and calculations, pay for it rather than rebuilding it yourself; treats data as something to source from a trusted, maintained provider rather than home-build.
  • Build: only when the tool would give a real edge, needs your own proprietary data, will be used constantly enough that you'd immediately notice if it broke, and doesn't already exist reliably in the market.
  • Warns that AI will confidently insist inflated or wrong data is correct ("gaslighting" behavior), so any home built pipeline needs to be used often enough that errors get caught quickly.

 

UNDERUSED BUILT-IN TOOLS PEOPLE OVERLOOK

  • Sellerboard has built-in report automation that generates a live link, which can be pasted directly into Google Sheets to auto-populate and refresh reports daily, a feature most users don't know exists.
  • Data Rova similarly exports directly into Google Sheets, making custom-built rank trackers largely redundant.
  • Keepa already provides verified price history, sales rank, and demand data that doesn't need to be rebuilt from scratch.
  • Recommends a trusted freelance developer (found via referral) who specializes in pulling data from various software sources directly into Google Sheets for further automation, rather than building custom scraping or API integrations personally.

 

WHAT HE ACTUALLY BUILT HIMSELF

  • A custom inventory pipeline spanning AWD, multiple marketplaces, and multiple suppliers, projecting seasonal demand using the prior year's actual sales data adjusted with safety stock and multipliers per SKU, producing weekly action items; acknowledges the model isn't perfect for products that suddenly go viral but is "repeatable" and good enough for most SKUs.
  • A supplier order consolidation tool that shows total units needed across multiple marketplaces for the same supplier in one screen, so smaller-market orders (e.g., Canada, UK) can be tacked onto a larger US order to help hit MOQ.
  • An FBA shipment lookup tool: uploading a sourcing team's shipment table automatically returns direct links and details for each shipment, replacing manual searching in Seller Central.
  • An SQP week-over-week comparison dashboard, automatically populated via MCP, letting him compare current data against 1, 2, 4, 8, or custom week windows to see which keywords are trending up or down, pulling rank data from Data Rova as well.
  • An "Attack, Chase, Defend" dashboard comparing click-through rate, conversion rate, and add-to-cart rate against market benchmarks: keywords beating the market on all three but with weak rank are attack opportunities; two of three signals warrant a closer look; strong on all three plus good rank just need defensive monitoring against competitors.
  • Admits some of his own built tools (an AI image prompt generator, storage fee and profit analytics dashboards) turned out not to be worth the effort and go largely unused, reinforcing his own framework's lesson.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid corrective to AI tool-building enthusiasm, arguing that most sellers should buy or use already-maintained data sources rather than reinventing dashboards that exist, and should reserve actual building effort for the small number of genuinely proprietary, frequently used tools that provide real competitive edge.

cliff_notes:
Tracy Lin, who sells birthstone themed fashion jewelry, follows up on an earlier presentation about using Open Claw as a non-technical seller by describing the jump from uploading files for AI analysis to directly connecting Amazon via MCP, which she calls a genuine game changer.

 

BIRTHSTONE INVENTORY DASHBOARD

  • Standard inventory tools (cited: SoStocked) use flat 90-day averages and can't reflect the monthly birthstone color peaks unique to her 12-color product family, requiring only manual mapping of SKUs to their birthstone month as the one recurring manual input.
  • Tracks multiple distinct Amazon shipment timestamps in the forecasting logic: created but not yet shipped, inbound to FBA (air or ocean), FC transfer (not immediately available, roughly a 1-2 week lag), and pending/reserved orders (which clear within 1-2 days), each weighted differently in the forecast.
  • Pulls ledger report data by region (splitting inventory distribution across East, Central, and West warehouse groupings, since that's the finest granularity Amazon allows when creating a shipment) to recommend which region a new shipment should replenish to keep inventory balanced nationally.
  • Final output is a shipment recommendation sheet showing peak month mapping, days of coverage remaining, units to ship, air vs. ocean, target region, and long term storage fee risk, exportable as a flat file ready to hand to a VA for upload.

 

MCP CONNECTION SETUP AND SECURITY

  • Uses Agent Central (built by MDS member Christian/"Thor Dynatrace"), read-only permissions enabled with all write permissions unchecked, describing it as an accessible, non-technical way to connect to Amazon's API.
  • Notes Agent Central is query based (you ask a question and it fetches data on demand) rather than a continuously live feed; another attendee recommended a different, more expensive (~$100-120/month) real time data feed service (referred to as "Sarah's"/SARS) for continuous rather than on-request data.
  • In audience Q&A on security: acknowledged her dashboards are hosted as public HTML with masked sales figures and no built-in authentication; another attendee recommended asking Claude directly to add page authentication and session timeouts as a simple security fix.

 

PPC EXPANSION DASHBOARD (SIMILAR TO PRIOR SESSION)

  • Since her account ranks strongly on necklaces but weaker on earrings and bracelets, built a dashboard checking whether the same generic keywords (e.g., "emerald jewelry") that rank well for necklaces show any organic or paid visibility for earrings and bracelets, treating that as a signal worth pushing PPC spend behind.
  • Includes deduplication logic to avoid overlapping ad spend with existing PPC on the same term, and surfaces current CPC for terms already being advertised by other categories to gauge competitiveness before entering.
  • Applies different confidence thresholds by keyword type: for Prime Day and seasonal keyword groups, will push earrings/bracelets even with zero prior ranking; for regular evergreen terms, requires necklace to already rank in the top 50 and earrings/bracelets to show at least some organic or sponsored visibility first.
  • Dashboard organizes keywords into tagged groups (Prime Day winners, Mother's Day, generic high volume evergreens, long tail evergreens, birthstone-specific seasonal prep) with a filter button to surface "strong opportunity" keywords for export.

 

In conclusion, this session reinforces that moving from manual file uploads to a direct Amazon MCP connection meaningfully upgrades what a non-technical seller can build, letting Tracy encode business-specific logic (birthstone seasonality, multi-warehouse balancing, cross-category keyword expansion) into dashboards that would otherwise require a much more technical setup.

cliff_notes:
Charles Chakkalo, half his Amazon business in resale and half in private label, shares the deliberately incremental path he took from an unused Mac Mini to a working AI chief of staff, aimed specifically at people intimidated by code or command line tools.

 

STEP ONE: CLAUDE DISPATCH FOR MOBILE TASK EXECUTION

  • Set up an always on computer (a Mac Mini, or a cheaper ~$200 Beelink alternative) running Claude Desktop with Cowork, accessible remotely via Dispatch in the Claude mobile app; requires only the $20 Pro plan.
  • Real examples with no prior training: sent a customer service message and resolved a spam case through Amazon buyer-seller messaging from his phone on a Saturday night, and pulled Walmart ACOS data remotely at a conference, self-correcting after Dispatch initially logged into the wrong Walmart Ads dashboard (API vs. self-service) using only conversational back and forth.
  • Also used it to check whether a specific order was fulfilled by merchant or by Amazon before deciding if a customer inquiry was even his responsibility to handle.
  • A fellow attendee raised a caution about browser based agents interacting with Amazon's backend at inhuman (millisecond) speed, warning this pattern (not scraping itself, but rapid automated clicking) is the kind of behavior that has led to account suspensions in other cases; Charles maintains his usage has not caused issues.

 

STEP TWO: BUILDING "DONNA," A TRAINED CLAUDE CODE CHIEF OF STAFF

  • Used a paid five day course (by Jay Margolis, an MDS discount code available) to build a Claude Code connected local folder system, not a true autonomous agent, that integrates Obsidian, Gmail, calendar, and other connectors.
  • The course provided a blank slate "Donna" folder (personality and skills only, no business knowledge); Charles then spent the five days manually teaching Donna his org chart, shipping/inventory workflows, ordering processes, active projects, and quarterly goals.
  • Is now duplicating the same blank folder template to build a second agent, "Sally," a sales analyst trained on manually imported Seller Board, COGS, and PO data (not yet connected to SP API).
  • Acknowledges a current usability gap: reports and briefings from Donna currently require being physically at the server computer to access, though cloud-based workarounds (like having Donna email reports) are possible once email send permissions are granted, which he has not yet done.

 

SECURITY RECOMMENDATIONS FOR RUNNING AN ALWAYS ON AGENT MACHINE

  • A fellow attendee recommended running a virtual Mac OS server inside the physical Mac Mini (a "Mac inside a Mac") to sandbox the agent with its own IP and network access, protecting the host machine and any stored credentials or passwords if the agent behaves unexpectedly.
  • Charles confirmed he already runs his Mac Mini on its own isolated network as a baseline security measure, with information deliberately structured to stay contained to that machine.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a low intimidation, staged onboarding path into AI agents for non-coders, starting with mobile controlled Cowork tasks via Dispatch and progressing to a locally trained, business specific Claude Code chief of staff, while flagging real security and platform risk considerations along the way.

cliff_notes:
Hymie Zebede runs a boutique agency managing 20 Amazon brands (plus two personal brands) with a 17 person VA team, and built a Claude connected system that pulls together ClickUp tasks, Fireflies meeting transcripts, Outlook email, and daily Amazon SP API data so he can ask natural language questions across his entire operation.

 

THE CORE SYSTEM: EVERYTHING WRITTEN DOWN, EVERYTHING CONNECTED

  • Enforces a strict team rule: no WhatsApp or verbal updates are acceptable, all task related communication must be logged in ClickUp under the specific task, including detailed forms for weekly Monday briefs (plan for the week) and Friday recaps (what got done, what didn't).
  • PPC team members fill out structured weekly forms with auto-populated data (7-day sales, ad spend, ACOS, organic units) alongside written summaries of issues like inventory concerns or suppressed listings, giving Claude rich qualitative context alongside raw numbers.
  • Daily SP API data (sales, search terms, keyword performance) is pulled into Google BigQuery rather than queried live, avoiding API latency and building a persistent, queryable historical dataset.
  • Fireflies records and transcribes every meeting (internal and with clients), which Claude can search across dozens of past sessions to identify recurring unresolved issues or disconnects between what a client is told and what the internal team is actually reporting.

 

SURFACING DISCONNECTS AND ENCODING PERSONAL RULES

  • Can ask Claude about a specific product or account and get a synthesized answer citing the last several weekly reports, flagging issues repeatedly mentioned without resolution (e.g., a stock issue unresolved for three straight weeks) and comparing that against what was told to the client via Outlook.
  • Had Claude review roughly 70 of his own past meeting transcripts to extract standing rules he had repeatedly stated verbally but never formally documented, for example, automatically reducing ad spend whenever stock falls below 30 days of coverage, building a database of his own decision making logic without him having to write it out explicitly.
  • Automated recurring reports (days of supply, sales velocity by 7/30/90 day windows, long term storage fee exposure) that auto-populate into Google Sheets and post directly to ClickUp channels with a natural language summary and recommendation (e.g., which SKUs should be discontinued or price-reduced due to poor sell-through and low ad spend).
  • Customizes report formats per team member's stated preference, since different staff like to view the same underlying data differently.

 

ACCOUNTABILITY AND CULTURE SHIFT

  • Established a firm standard: if Claude can't read ClickUp and produce a full, accurate status update on a given task, the team member effectively didn't do their job, regardless of any verbal explanation given in a meeting or call.
  • Reports having fired several long tenured employees specifically for failing to properly document their work once this standard was in place, treating AI queryability as the actual measure of whether work was done.

 

In conclusion, this session shows how enforcing rigorous, structured documentation across an entire team, then connecting that documentation (ClickUp, Fireflies, Outlook, SP API data) into a single AI queryable system, can surface both operational blind spots and a leader's own undocumented decision rules, turning "if it's not written down, it didn't happen" into an actual accountability standard.

cliff_notes:
Abraham Wercberger manages three pharmaceutical Amazon brands and built two internal tools with Claude Code, an FBA reorder report and a deeper inventory forecaster, to solve chronic over- and under-stocking caused by a 4 to 5 month raw material lead time.

 

WHY HE BUILT THIS

  • Needed to maintain 30 days of FBA inventory and 30 days of warehouse inventory while accounting for 4 to 5 months of raw material lead time, a mismatch that repeatedly caused either excess or insufficient stock.
  • Started by copying his existing spreadsheet columns (inventory, SKU, velocity, pricing) directly into Claude Code and asking for an automated dashboard version; got a working first version in under a minute.
  • Split the original combined report into two separate tools (an FBA reorder report and a standalone inventory forecaster) once the single tool became too elaborate to use cleanly.

 

THE INVENTORY FORECASTER

  • Core question it answers: what to order, how much, and when, and which SKUs are at risk of stockout, based on manually or CSV imported SKU velocity and current on-hand inventory (no live Amazon API connection currently).
  • Projects a full six month forward view combining open POs and FBA inventory, color coding SKUs by stock health and flagging specific items on track to stock out under current flow.
  • Includes adjustable default assumptions (under a settings panel) that recalculate the entire forecast when changed, and supports loading sample data to demo or test the tool without live business data.
  • Built to run entirely as a local HTML file, not hosted online, explicitly built for desktop use only (not optimized for mobile).

 

BUILD PHILOSOPHY AND COMMON MISTAKES

  • Recommends documenting the workflow first (inputs, process, outputs on paper) rather than trying to automate everything at once; his forecaster grew incrementally, feature by feature, rather than being planned in full up front.
  • Warns against treating Claude like a generic chatbot rather than a tool being fed real, structured business data and expertise.
  • Recommended next step for others: identify one repeatable decision in the business, write out its inputs/process/outputs, build a first version with Claude, and test it against real data before expanding scope.

 

AUDIENCE PUSHBACK AND NUANCE

  • In Q&A, another attendee (running a more complex, developer built forecasting system) noted that a good forecast needs more than SKU velocity and current inventory, since factors like halved keyword search volume year over year or a 40 percent jump in CPCs materially change true demand, distinguishing simple replenishment math from genuine long range forecasting.
  • Abraham acknowledged the tool currently pulls flexible lookback windows (30, 60, or 180 day velocity) but is more of a replenishment and stockout warning tool than a fully demand-adjusted forecast; another attendee described a similar homemade approach using month by month multipliers applied to prior year order data as a lighter weight forecasting alternative.

 

In conclusion, this session is a concrete, incremental example of converting a documented spreadsheet process into working internal software using Claude Code alone, showing real inventory forecasting output while candidly acknowledging its current limits compared to more sophisticated, multi-factor demand forecasting approaches.

cliff_notes:
Dimitri Vorona, a serial entrepreneur with four prior exits, walks through a custom internal web application he vibe coded with Claude Code to replace the spreadsheets his team previously used to run Amazon operations.

 

WHY BUILD ONE CUSTOM APP

  • Built a single, browser based, permission controlled internal app hosted on his own domain and server, covering five functions: purchase orders and labels, inventory management, launch and performance tracking, Instagram/influencer outreach, and user admin.
  • Motivation: spreadsheets didn't talk to each other, and he wanted one fast, shared system the whole team could use, with AI layered on top to surface things humans wouldn't otherwise notice (a good or bad sales day, a keyword rank shift, a competitor price change).
  • Deliberately splits the system into two zones: low risk operational data (POs, labels, suppliers) that he plans to eventually hand fully to an AI agent to replace VA staff, versus live sales/ranking/ad data that AI can flag and suggest on, but where he insists a human still makes the final decision.

 

KEY BUILD LESSONS

  • Strongly recommends paying for a third party Amazon data wrapper/connector (rather than building a direct Amazon API integration yourself) since Amazon changes its API frequently and unpredictably; his own prior software company suffered from this exact pain, and $100-400/month to offload that risk is, in his view, some of the best money a seller can spend.
  • Recommends writing pseudocode (a plain English, step by step logic description) via ChatGPT first, then feeding that pseudocode to Claude Code, which he says dramatically reduces bugs compared to prompting the coding agent directly.
  • Describes Claude Code as behaving like "a junior developer" that will take shortcuts unless explicitly instructed: it initially built flat files instead of a real database, left data unprotected without being told to add security, and didn't include a mobile version until specifically asked.
  • Built in CSV import/export from day one for backup and migration safety, and added automatic data backups before any bulk data overwrite, after learning the hard way that a system like this can break.
  • Uses event triggered (not scheduled) data refresh, only pulling new data when someone actually logs in, to control token and API costs rather than refreshing on a fixed schedule nobody needs.

 

SPECIFIC MODULES DEMOED

  • PO and label tracking: auto generates purchase orders and PDFs per supplier, tracks label inventory against POs, and flags reorder points; currently POs are entered manually into the system as a deliberate "walk before automate" step while staff and the tool build trust together.
  • Launch tracker: standardizes and logs every product launch (giveaways, PPC, keyword targeting, add-to-cart data) against a defined launch plan, arguing that most sellers assume they're following a consistent launch process but usually aren't, and that standardizing improves outcomes over time.
  • Compliant influencer outreach: requires staff to log outbound Instagram/social messages into the system before sending, allowing automatic flagging of risky phrasing (e.g., soliciting reviews) to stay within platform terms of service, with a full historical record if a staff member needs to be replaced.
  • SQP and keyword performance dashboards: surfaces search query performance data (click-through rate, conversion rate, keywords outperforming category/market averages) to help concentrate ad spend on proven winners rather than spreading it thin.
  • All data currently requires human approval before action; Dimitri acknowledges he's still in an "everything gets approved" MVP phase rather than moving to autonomous execution.

 

In conclusion, this session is a practical, still evolving blueprint for replacing scattered spreadsheets with one custom internal Amazon operations app, emphasizing that outsourcing the fragile Amazon API connection to a third party wrapper, and treating Claude Code like a junior developer that needs explicit guardrails, are the two biggest lessons for anyone attempting something similar.

cliff_notes:
Sam Haddad, co-founder of Greenhouse (a brand acquisition holding company) and operator of the boat cleaning brand Bo Choose, presents a structured method for feeding Claude persistent business context via knowledge documents inside a Claude project, rather than re-explaining the business in every chat.

 

WHY GENERIC AI OUTPUT FAILS WITHOUT CONTEXT

  • Identifies three failure modes without dedicated context: wrong voice (doesn't match how the brand actually talks to customers), wrong customer (writes generically instead of to a specific ideal customer profile), and wrong strategy (doesn't understand the business's actual goals and plan).

 

THE LAYERED KNOWLEDGE DOCUMENT STRUCTURE

  • Layer one, Identity: about us, founder story, mission and values, org chart.
  • Layer two, Market: ideal customer profile (considered the single most important document), full product/offer catalog (individual items, kits, bundles), competitive differentiation, and customer FAQs.
  • Layer three, Proof: testimonials and reviews scraped from every sales channel (Amazon, TikTok, brand website) to ground claims in real customer language.
  • Recommends building one Claude project ("brain") per department (marketing, sales, operations, customer service, finance, HR), each pulling in the same core knowledge documents but built and used separately so the relevant context loads without unnecessary bloat.
  • Clarifies the relationship between "skills" (repeatable, specific tasks) and "brains" (Claude projects providing brand context): a skill executed inside a brain-equipped project produces much stronger output than the same skill run without that context.

 

REAL BEFORE/AFTER EXAMPLE AND COMMON MISTAKES

  • Demoed a landing page copywriting prompt targeting a "wake boat owner" ICP: without the business brain, Claude made generic, thin assumptions about the product and audience; with the brain loaded, output pulled in detailed, accurate ICP and product context automatically.
  • Common mistakes to avoid: dumping everything into one giant file (Claude loses signal), using the wrong file format (recommends Markdown or plain text over PDF or Word docs for reliable readability), and treating the setup as "set and forget" rather than updating knowledge files quarterly or monthly as the business and personas evolve; also notes that connected Google Drive files don't auto refresh when the source is updated.
  • Used Claude's Deep Research feature to generate an initial ideal customer profile by having it scan the broader internet (including Reddit) for real pain points and personas related to the brand, taking about 20-25 minutes, though he stresses the output still needs human validation.
  • In Q&A, clarifies that scheduling or automating tasks isn't possible from within a Claude Chat project directly; it requires bringing that project's context into Claude Cowork to automate and schedule recurring tasks.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a practical, beginner accessible framework, four to ten structured knowledge documents inside department specific Claude projects, for eliminating repetitive re-explanation and generic output by giving Claude persistent, accurate context about a brand's identity, customers, and proof points.

cliff_notes:
Shawn Kolodny runs Big Shiny Balls (giant inflatables) and Colossal Arts (large scale event installations for clients like Taylor Swift and Kendrick Lamar), and demos two low cost methods for generating short form AI video content.

 

METHOD ONE: STORYBOARDING A BRANDED MINI MOVIE

  • Brainstorms concepts with Claude first (batting around silly scenarios for the brand's inflatable ball characters), then has Claude or Nano Banana turn the chosen concept into an actual visual storyboard, specifying style (claymation, sketch, photoreal) and camera direction.
  • Feeds the finished storyboard into Higgsfield (an aggregator of nearly every video model, including Seedance and Kling) to generate the final video, calling out Higgsfield's built in Marketing Studio tool, which can auto generate ad units from a single product photo and description.
  • Cost per short video clip: roughly $2 to $3, making rapid, cheap experimentation feasible; is building out a "Big Shiny Balls Creative Universe" (BSBCU) with different stylistic universes (film noir, etc.) as an ongoing top of funnel content experiment.

 

METHOD TWO: ANIMATING A SINGLE STILL PHOTO

  • Takes an existing still photo (even a low quality one, like a phone snapshot from an event) and feeds it into a video generator, directing camera movement (pan, subject motion) via text prompts to turn it into moving video content.
  • Can also feed a series of stills as start and end frames into tools like Seedance, letting the model infer the motion needed to connect them, effectively turning any photo library into raw video material.
  • Argues planning is the biggest lever for quality: more upfront specification produces better final output, and a weak source still image will produce weak, flawed motion when animated.

 

PRACTICAL LESSONS AND CAVEATS

  • Reports early signs of TikTok flagging and removing AI generated videos, but doesn't hide the AI origin since this content is explicitly experimental, low stakes, top of funnel material rather than direct ad units.
  • A fellow attendee shared a contrasting real result: AI generated people used in Meta ads caused engagement to collapse (with audience comments calling it out as fake), and performance recovered only after switching back to real UGC, suggesting AI actors currently underperform for direct response ad contexts specifically.
  • Uses AI generated product photography extensively on the brand's own website (placing one physical product into many colors, venues, and backgrounds) since it's dramatically cheaper and faster than reordering and reshooting physical variants, and reports customers have referenced these AI images back to the brand as inspiration, unaware they aren't real installations.
  • Character consistency is improving across tools; locking a defined character (including a personal AI avatar of yourself, built from reference photos and video) helps maintain the same "actor" across multiple generated clips.
  • Audience Q&A add-on: another attendee described a related but distinct practice, recording extensive spoken brainstorming and decision making, transcribing it, and feeding it into AI over months to build a personal "AI clone" capable of replicating one's own creative decision making and content style, kept as a private local agent rather than shared publicly.

 

In conclusion, this session shows that AI video generation has collapsed the cost and time barrier to producing short form branded content to a few dollars and under an hour, while candidly noting that AI generated people still underperform real UGC in direct response ad testing even as AI generated product photography and stylized brand content clearly work.

cliff_notes:
Shan Shan Fu, an apparel and accessories seller, shares her practical workflow for converting product photography entirely to AI generated images, based on live conversion testing across multiple listings.

 

WHY AI PHOTOS OUTPERFORMED THE ORIGINALS

  • Ran a live audience poll on several images; most attendees couldn't reliably tell AI generated photos from real photography.
  • Reports that in her own testing, AI generated versions outperformed the original photography on conversion rate across every example she tested, including a heavily Photoshopped self portrait run through Nano Banana.

 

SOLVING PRODUCTS AI CAN'T IMAGINE CORRECTLY

  • For products like belts where factory photos only show the front, no AI image tool could correctly generate a plausible back view from scratch.
  • Solution: pulled a competitor's product photo showing the needed angle, cut it out, and fed both her own product image and the competitor's reference image into Nano Banana with a prompt asking it to update her product into the same format as the reference, framing this as legally defensible since many sellers source from the same Chinese factories.
  • Uses the same two-reference-image technique for lifestyle photography, editing factory photos to swap styling elements (e.g., changing a skirt and shoes to a "goth" aesthetic) to better match US shopper expectations, and for seasonal edits (adding Christmas ribbon and candy cane props to an existing product photo in minutes).
  • AI generated infographics and size charts (via ChatGPT) also converted well when given precise product parameters as input.

 

FULL TOOL STACK

  • Prompting: uses ChatGPT to write detailed image generation prompts before passing them to an image tool.
  • Image generation: primarily Nano Banana; also uses Savannah AI, a fashion-specific platform, for patterned items (florals, prints) where Nano Banana underperforms.
  • Video: uses a startup called Ad Glow to convert static product photos into short video ads; also flagged Google's new "Omni" model (soon expected on Higgsfield) as an emerging option for changing a subject's outfit or pose directly from a single video.
  • Upscaling: uses Pixart (referred to informally as "Pixar") to upscale small, blurry factory images to sharp 2000x4000+ pixel resolution, free of charge.
  • Editing: uses Photoroom for final photo editing.
  • Testing: uses PickFu to run reviewer panels on finished images, valuing the qualitative feedback (e.g., a reviewer citing an image as "too provocative") as much as the pick itself; does not currently run formal Amazon experiments but plans to start.

 

LIMITATIONS AND VARIATION HANDLING

  • Reports Nano Banana performs poorly on jewelry, belts, and complex fabric patterns when generating from scratch, but works well for small angle adjustments (roughly 20 degrees) to an existing reference image.
  • For color variations across a listing, Nano Banana handles most color swaps reasonably well, though light-to-dark or dark-to-light swaps are less reliable.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a concrete, tested AI photography workflow for apparel sellers, showing that AI generated images can outconvert traditional photography, while candidly acknowledging the gray area of using competitor reference photos to solve angles AI genuinely cannot generate on its own.

cliff_notes:
This is an open hot seat discussion where a member with a 30 person team asks the room how to scale AI tool adoption company wide without costs spiraling, since a mix of shared accounts, hit usage limits, and overlapping tools had pushed the software bill to roughly $15,000-$20,000 a month.

 

THE CORE PROBLEM

  • Started with a shared team account for tools like Claude, which worked initially but quickly hit usage limits as more people built and shared projects (e.g., a graphic design project one person created that the rest of the team then used).
  • Team was fragmented across Claude, ChatGPT, multiple note taking tools (Fireflies, Superhuman, and others), plus separate automation platforms (n8n, Zapier, Make) and Airtable, all billed separately and stacking up.
  • Landed on CircleBack over Fireflies specifically because CircleBack has a native MCP connection into Claude (Fireflies requires more manual setup to achieve similar context sharing), letting meeting content feed directly into company AI context.

 

MODEL ROUTING AS THE COST FIX

  • Key point from the group: most day to day e-commerce tasks (including a lot of coding) don't require top tier models like Opus; cheaper or open weight models handle the bulk of routine work adequately.
  • Recommends Open Router as an account layer that automatically routes each task to the most cost appropriate model (including free or near-free Chinese models like Kimi or Qwen) rather than defaulting everyone to premium subscriptions; shows real time usage and cost tracking per model.
  • For image and video generation and ad creative specifically, recommends Higgsfield, an aggregator with its own MCP that connects directly to Claude and can generate full ad units from a single product photo, described as cheaper and comparable in quality to Claude's native image tools.

 

DEPLOYMENT: VS CODE OVER DESKTOP APPS FOR NON-TECHNICAL TEAMS

  • One member shares switching the entire team to VS Code as the interface (rather than Claude Desktop or a command line terminal), expecting resistance but finding onboarding was actually fast and smooth even for non-technical staff.
  • Advantages cited: quick account/login switching when usage limits are hit, centrally added MCPs propagate automatically to every team member's VS Code instance, and personal skill files stay synced locally via Dropbox or Git so updates push out company-wide without manual redistribution.
  • Pushback from another member questioning whether VS Code still feels too "command line" for average staff; the original presenter maintains it functions as a simple desktop app launch for end users, not a raw terminal experience.

 

SIDE DISCUSSION: WILL AI COMPUTE GET CHEAPER OR MORE EXPENSIVE

  • One view: frontier model costs (top tier, "Mythos" class models) will likely rise as companies pass through real infrastructure costs.
  • Counter view: for the vast majority (cited as ~90%) of typical business tasks, free or near-free open weight Chinese models are already good enough, meaning effective average costs per business could collapse even as frontier pricing rises, similar to how enterprises eventually adopt cheaper "good enough" alternatives at scale.

 

In conclusion, this hot seat surfaces a common scaling pain point, AI tool sprawl driving costs up without a proportional gain in team productivity, and converges on two practical fixes: consolidating around tools with native MCP integration to reduce duplicate context work, and using a model router (Open Router) plus a lightweight, syncable interface (VS Code) to match task complexity to model cost rather than defaulting everyone to the most expensive option.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788307763789-Transcript - Leverage Your Working Geniuses, to Get AI to Handle Your Frustrations － Daniel Meredith － AI Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
Daniel Meredith, a hardware and electronics seller and MDS member since 2017, presents on combining the Six Types of Working Genius framework (from author Patrick Lencioni) with AI tool design to close the gap between what people love doing and what they're forced to do.

 

THE SIX WORKING GENIUS FRAMEWORK

  • Six types: Wonder (spotting undiscovered problems/opportunities), Invention (creating new solutions), Discernment (judging if it's a good idea), Galvanizing (getting others on board), Enabling (getting the work started amid ambiguity), and Tenacity (pushing through to actual completion).
  • Everyone has two genius types they love, two they're neutral on, and two they genuinely hate doing; a $25 online assessment identifies which is which for each person.
  • Restructured his own hiring funnel around core values, core competency, and working genius fit; credits this with helping shrink his team from 31 to 9 people while increasing output, and with three years of zero voluntary turnover.
  • Notes he no longer promotes purely up a traditional leadership ladder, since someone skilled at execution may hate Discernment or Galvanizing, the genius types most associated with management.

 

WHY AI ROLLOUT FAILED UNTIL HE MATCHED IT TO GENIUS TYPES

  • Initial company-wide AI rollout struggled because he built automations around tasks he personally hated doing, which happened to be tasks his team actually loved, so they saw the AI as taking away enjoyable work rather than reducing frustration.
  • Audited roughly 3,200 of his own AI sessions over 60 days and had AI itself run tests to see which genius-type tasks different models handled well; found AI is strong at Enabling (getting ambiguous tasks started) and Tenacity (finishing/deploying), weaker at Invention, and generally poor at Wonder, Discernment, and Galvanizing.
  • Recommends matching AI usage to what a given person or team member actually hates doing, not what the AI's own strengths are in the abstract, since a team dominated by Enabling/Tenacity types (finishers) will resist AI tools built around those same genius types.

 

PUTTING IT INTO PRACTICE

  • Added his own working genius profile directly into his core Claude/agents memory file (loaded at the start of every session); this changed the AI's behavior noticeably, for example it stopped over-explaining or trying to "convince" him of ideas (Galvanizing, one of his most hated types) and moved straight to action.
  • Recommends this as a concrete first step: pick one task you hate, identify which genius type it falls under, confirm your own assessment result, and hand that specific task to AI.
  • Closes by noting the presentation slides themselves were finished by AI after he brain-dumped content for the genius types he enjoys and got fatigued partway through, offering it as live proof that AI reliably picked up the remaining "finishing" work he didn't want to do.

 

In conclusion, this session argues that successful AI adoption, for a founder or an entire team, depends less on the AI's raw capability and more on matching automation to the specific tasks each person is wired to dislike, using an existing psychometric framework as the shared language for making that match explicit.

cliff_notes:
Lee Assoulin runs an agency managing multiple Amazon accounts and, despite agreeing with an earlier "don't over-build" presentation, built his own custom dashboard with Claude Code because paying for Sellerboard, Sellerize, and similar tools separately across many client accounts didn't let him get granular or customize enough.

 

HOW HE BUILT IT

  • Took screenshots of Sellerboard, Sellerize, and Expandly and fed them directly into Claude Code, asking it to replicate each feature, despite having no prior coding experience; spent about 20 hours initially, now spends 2-3 hours a day refining it.
  • Already had a long-running SQL database pulling Amazon data before starting this project, making the AI layer a relatively simple plug-in on top of existing infrastructure rather than a from-scratch build.
  • Recommends Supabase for anyone attempting something similar without pre-existing database infrastructure.
  • Hired a dedicated AI engineer specifically to verify data accuracy and confirm which database tables each dashboard number was actually pulling from, since he doesn't fully understand the technical layer himself.

 

KEY FEATURES BUILT

  • Product level urgency rules: customizable if-then logic per brand or SKU (e.g., if a product exceeds a revenue threshold and its ACOS crosses a set level, flag it as urgent) letting him surface true priority products instead of relying on broad, generic performance categorization.
  • A "second brain" briefing tool: feeds all Fireflies call transcripts, Slack messages, and emails into a vector database, so a generated briefing explains not just that sales dropped (e.g., 93 percent) but why, pulling in the actual documented reason (e.g., a shipment stuck in transit) rather than presenting a raw number in isolation.
  • An SQP-to-campaign workflow: clicking a button on a tracked keyword automatically adds it to a keyword tracker and flows it into a single keyword campaign structure.
  • A subscribe and save dashboard replicating Expandify style metrics (active subscribers, etc.), acknowledging LTV tracking specifically is still a work in progress.
  • Deliberately keeps humans in the loop rather than fully automating everything (only buy box related features are automated so far), preferring to manually refine a process before automating it rather than letting AI define the process itself.

 

PRACTICAL FEEDBACK FROM THE ROOM

  • A fellow attendee diagnosed a live data loading delay as likely caused by the database running multiple separate queries instead of one consolidated query, and recommended giving the AI explicit database optimization instructions to fix it.
  • General framing: this level of custom building only makes sense for someone managing many accounts (like an agency) who needs deeper customization and cross-tool integration (keyword ranking, SQP, and other data combined) rather than a single brand for whom an off the shelf tool like Sellerboard is sufficient.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a candid, self-taught account of building a genuinely useful custom Amazon operations dashboard from scratch using Claude Code and screenshots of existing SaaS tools, emphasizing that the value came from combining scattered data sources and context (not just raw numbers) into one system, rather than from technical sophistication.

In conclusion, this is a short, practical share pointing to a specific AI training resource and two niche talent sourcing channels (Ecom Talent and Work.ua), with the standout insight being that drop shipping and content clipping backgrounds can translate surprisingly well into strong content strategist hires.

Brandon Himmel runs a live, collaborative TikTok Shop mastermind session with roughly 60 MDS brands, sharing real account data and fielding direct questions from peer sellers across every GMV tier.

 

THE FOUR TIER FRAMEWORK

  • Tier one (34 brands, under 10k GMV): still getting started; Brandon points them to his Inspire talk covering the full 90 day cold start playbook.
  • Tier two (13 brands, testing phase, roughly 10k to 70k-100k GMV): still figuring out outreach consistency and affiliate retention.
  • Tier three (12 brands, scaling, 100k+ GMV): commission economics finally work because there's enough payout to motivate serious affiliate commitment; recommends starting with aggressive commissions (20% organic, 10% GMV Max) since raising them later is much harder than lowering them.
  • Outlier tier: one brand doing over $1M GMV in the last 30 days, largely live stream driven; the top 12 brands account for 77% of the room's total GMV.
  • Clarifies GMV vs. gross revenue: GMV is what the customer actually paid after TikTok promotions/discounts; gross revenue (what the brand receives) can be higher if TikTok subsidizes part of a discount itself.

 

CONTENT MECHANICS THAT ACTUALLY WORK

  • Core hook formula: always combine a text hook, a visual hook (constant movement, camera angle changes every 2-2.5 seconds), and an audio hook; keep animated subtitles that change color per spoken word for extra visual stimulation.
  • Once a video format proves it can go viral (Brandon cites an 11-second Joe Rogan audio clip reused across product colors, generating 600K then 900K views), aggressively harvest and repeat that exact format rather than always testing new ideas; recommends a 70/30 split between repeating proven formats and experimenting.
  • Consistent camera framing (keeping eyes in the same screen position across cuts, as TV productions do) improves subconscious viewer comfort.
  • Founder/vulnerable storytelling content (not product pitching) tends to outperform product focused content; Brandon's most viral video was about his parents' passing, not the product itself.
  • A guest (Valentino) shares an alternative in-house AI-animation content model (20+ videos/day scaling to 100+/day) built around obsessively reusing viral scripts with slight variations rather than affiliate outreach, suited to storytelling-driven products like books.

 

COMMUNITY, PRICING, AND OPERATIONAL DETAILS

  • Discord vs. WhatsApp: both work; the key is giving affiliates a reason to join (video ideas, feedback, exclusivity) rather than starting a community before there's momentum to sustain it.
  • VIP retainer programs gate access behind Discord membership plus a video quota, creating a feedback loop where affiliates get personal video critiques, driving measurable improvement.
  • Recommends pricing parity between Amazon and TikTok Shop, warning that a TikTok account manager confirmed TikTok will penalize listings priced higher than Amazon; flash sales/coupons are commonly used to appear discounted without actually lowering list price long term.
  • Smart Promotion fees (an additional 3-4.5% on top of affiliate commissions) are widely underappreciated and often invisible unless sellers dig into TikTok payout statements directly; some brands only enable it selectively during major deal events (Black Friday, Prime Day competitors).
  • Product card ads (not just video content) can drive meaningful GMV (one brand reported a third of sales from product cards) by feeding a full catalog into GMV Max with even a single mediocre video, letting the algorithm surface which products actually convert.
  • Agency vs. in-house consensus: multiple operators (David, Brandon, Elias-style guests) argue in-house is almost always better since agencies can't care about the brand relationship as much as the founder, though agencies can be useful narrowly for GMV Max media buying specifically.
  • Halo effect on Amazon is real and significant: Brandon's branded search now makes up 33% of Amazon sales and rising, with contribution margin improving from 24% to 28%+ even while investing heavily (and unprofitably in the short term) in TikTok growth.

 

In conclusion, this mastermind format surfaces concrete, field tested tactics across every stage of TikTok Shop growth, converging on a few repeated principles: commit fully and quickly rather than dabbling, keep pricing consistent with Amazon, build affiliate community around real value rather than money alone, and relentlessly harvest whatever content format is already proven to work.

cliff_notes:
Joe Cowling runs a roughly 1,000 SKU catalog with about 40 percent of sales coming from Amazon B2B, and shares a short, informal update on a custom catalog monitoring tool built after existing tools failed to catch real problems.

 

WHY HE BUILT A CUSTOM CATALOG MONITOR

  • Struggled with automated strike-through pricing across the catalog and frequent Amazon-side variation breaks, but found no SaaS tool that could reliably monitor the catalog without generating excessive noise, describing getting around 40 alerts a day for a single ASIN from existing tools.
  • Built his own system defining a "source of truth" for what each parent/child listing should look like (target price, copy, images), connected to his PIM and DAM, so any copy or image change that doesn't match the defined source of truth gets automatically flagged.
  • Pulls data from Amazon and Keepa, but runs it on a staggered, roughly three-hour cycle rather than real-time/on-demand, since his use case doesn't require instant data, keeping the total cost to about $50 a month.

 

OPEN PROBLEMS STILL BEING WORKED ON

  • PPC and keyword research: most sales come from long tail keywords, but most spend currently goes to broad match; is trying to figure out how to better organize and manage keyword clusters, complicated by having many product variations (pack sizes, actual sizes) across labels, bags, and shipping supplies.
  • Supply chain: previously believed supply chain was fully under control, then swung from 0 percent to 8 percent of the catalog out of stock within a single week, prompting a new focus on building a solution for this specific gap, an effort still in early stages.

 

In conclusion, this is a brief, still-developing update showing a practical, low-cost custom catalog monitoring build that solved a real alerting problem, alongside two open, unresolved challenges (PPC keyword clustering and a supply chain blind spot) the presenter plans to address next.

TOPICS:

  1. APIs versus MCPs explained, and why owning your own data warehouse beats relying on vendor MCPs alone
  2. A seasonal inventory dashboard predicting exact stockout windows and recommending PPC pullback or price increases
  3. A simple launch tracker and a keyword-based PPC expansion tool for cross-category growth

cliff_notes:
William Langford opens with foundational context on APIs and MCPs then Tracy Lin of Lilafil (birthstone jewelry, highly seasonal with 12 monthly color peaks plus holiday spikes) demos three AI powered dashboards built to manage that complexity.

 

APIS VERSUS MCPS: THE INFRASTRUCTURE PRIMER

  • API (application programming interface): direct, full control, universal support, less overhead, but requires understanding the endpoint documentation yourself.
  • MCP (model context protocol): a self-describing wrapper around APIs that lets AI models talk to tools conversationally without needing to understand raw documentation, but it is "wiring, not functionality" and mostly limited to whatever data the vendor chose to expose.
  • Recommends the stack: pull data via API into your own database (Postgres, Sheets, etc.), build AI dashboards on top of your own tables (not a vendor's limited view), then layer an MCP on top for conversational access, arguing owned historical data survives cancellations and enables joins no single vendor will provide.
  • Warns that MCPs require someone to build and maintain them, and using an MCP for something simple wastes tokens when a direct API call would be faster.

 

TRACY'S MCP SETUP AND WHAT TO ASK VENDORS

  • Uses a commercial, turnkey MCP connector called Agent Central (built by an MDS member) since she lacks a technical background; runs it via a cloud hosted VPS with granular Amazon scope permissions, initially read-only, later adding write access for PPC bid edits.
  • Advises asking any MCP vendor exactly what endpoints exist before assuming capability; discovered no endpoint exists for pulling all ASINs with future scheduled deals via Amazon's API, but found an unexpected endpoint tracking every listing edit (images, titles, bullets).

 

INVENTORY DASHBOARD: PREDICTING EXACT STOCKOUT WINDOWS

  • Goal isn't just preventing stockouts but maximizing profit around them: if a stockout is unavoidable, the dashboard recommends pulling back PPC or raising price ahead of time rather than continuing to spend into a dead window.
  • Flags ASINs under 60 days of coverage, calculates whether air freight can still arrive in time, and if not, surfaces PPC pullback and price increase as the fallback actions, with downloadable action sheets (units to ship, region, shipping mode).
  • Combines three growth signals (7-day real time growth, dynamic year-to-date growth, and the seasonal curve) to distinguish short-term spikes/dips from real prolonged shifts, with any deviation greater than 15 points routed to human review; newer products under 10 units/day use only year-to-date growth to avoid noisy forecasts.
  • Built a custom model (since no Amazon API endpoint tracks fulfillment center transfer timing directly) by pulling and pattern-matching roughly 2,000 historical FC transfers, finding 64 percent of shipments land locally (1-3 days) versus 36 percent cross-region (8-14 days), which was critical after a costly 24-hour stockout during a past Valentine's Day caused by assuming on-hand inventory covered a gap that FC transfer delays actually created.

 

LAUNCH TRACKER AND PPC KEYWORD EXPANSION

  • A simple launch tracking spreadsheet logs pricing, PPC spend, listing edits, coupons, and inventory sent as "levers," pulled via API twice weekly to correlate each lever change against resulting rank and key metric movement, replacing what was previously manual VA data entry.
  • PPC expansion concept: since her account is dominated by strong necklace rankings, checks whether the same generic keywords (e.g., "emerald jewelry") that rank well for necklaces are also showing early positive signal for weaker categories like earrings or bracelets (e.g., necklace ranked #4, earrings ranked #47 but still generating organic sales), then tiers keywords into higher or lower bid opportunities to intentionally cross-sell PPC investment into underdeveloped categories.

 

In conclusion, this session pairs a technical foundation for building owned data infrastructure with concrete, seasonally tuned dashboards showing how a small, non-technical team can use commercial MCP tools and custom forecasting models to predict exact stockout windows and make more precise pricing, shipping, and PPC decisions than on-hand inventory numbers alone would suggest.

items.title: Product Research Through Social Listening Automation － Danson Hui － AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
Danson Hui shares an in-progress pivot from traditional Helium 10 style product research toward scanning TikTok, Facebook, and Twitter for early trend signals and social listening, using browser automation to work around scraping tool limitations, while candidly admitting he doesn't yet trust the AI's conclusions enough to commit real inventory spend.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why TikTok trends often precede Amazon sales spikes, making early social signal more valuable than reactive Amazon scanning
  2. Using browser automation (a Hermes agent on a Mac Mini) to work around Apify's limitations on nested Facebook comments
  3. The core unresolved problem: not trusting whether AI's aggregated social listening conclusions are accurate enough to act on

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788476359454-Transcript － Danson Hui － AI Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
Danson Hui, a seller in the durable baby products space looking to expand into consumables like supplements and beauty, shares an early stage pivot in his product research process toward social listening rather than traditional keyword and competitor scraping.

 

WHY HE MOVED FROM AMAZON-FIRST TO SOCIAL-FIRST RESEARCH

  • Spent months building product research automation around Helium 10 style scraping and his "classic" research method, but concluded it was less effective than scanning TikTok (including Kalodata) and other social channels for trending products and shops.
  • Key observation driving the shift: Amazon trend spikes that look like they came from nowhere usually had visible growth signals on TikTok and other platforms first, meaning the real opportunity window is earlier, upstream on social media, not on Amazon itself.
  • Layers in social listening, analyzing comment sentiment much the way one would analyze Amazon reviews, as a way to validate whether a trending product has real, sustained demand versus a passing spike.

 

TECHNICAL WORKAROUNDS FOR SCRAPING LIMITATIONS

  • Uses Apify for TikTok data with good results, but found it inadequate for Facebook, since it only captures top-level comments and misses nested replies, losing significant information.
  • Solved this by setting up a dedicated Mac Mini running a "Hermes" agent that acts as a human-like browser user, automatically clicking through and expanding every nested comment thread rather than relying on Apify's limited API-based scrape.
  • Plans to apply the same approach to Twitter/X: searching a keyword, navigating into relevant groups or threads on a given topic, and having the agent read through and summarize hours of comment threads that would otherwise take him hours to read manually.

 

THE CORE UNRESOLVED PROBLEM: TRUST IN AI CONCLUSIONS

  • States plainly that his biggest current obstacle isn't technical, it's trusting whether the AI's aggregated conclusions from comments and social data are accurate or fabricated ("didn't make shit up").
  • Describes roughly half of the AI's output as feeling legitimate and half as something he remains skeptical of, which is directly blocking him from committing real capital (cited figures of $50,000-$100,000) to launch a product based on this research alone.
  • Frames this as a genuine open problem rather than a solved workflow, closing by saying he hopes to have something more concrete to report in a future session.

 

In conclusion, this is an honest, still unresolved account of shifting product research upstream to social platforms where trends actually originate, showing real technical workarounds for scraping limitations while candidly flagging that AI output trust, not tooling, is the actual bottleneck preventing him from acting on the research.

  2. Turning product returns into a self-funding affiliate gifting engine
  3. An annual instructor certification event that compounds affiliate recruitment organically

cliff_notes:
Tamkin Collins, a former aerospace defense contractor, founded Cakes Concealed Carry (luxury gun bags for women) in October 2024 and grew it to $1M in year one and a $2.5M current ARR using zero ad spend, zero Amazon, and zero TikTok Shop, entirely through Shopify and affiliate driven community building.

 

BUILDING AROUND IDENTITY, NOT DEMOGRAPHIC

  • Positioned the brand around an identity ("hot girl carry," a woman refusing to look frumpy or masculine while carrying a firearm) rather than a broad demographic, drawn directly from her own experience as one of two women in a concealed carry class.
  • Argues this identity-driven, authority-seeking approach fits emotionally dense, higher stakes purchases (firearms, pregnancy products, hernia recovery products) better than the high-volume, low-emotion affiliate spray approach other brands described earlier in the summit.

 

FINDING AND ACTIVATING CATEGORY AUTHORITY FIGURES

  • Identified firearms instructors as the trusted authority in her category, since students in her own class bought everything the instructor recommended without question.
  • Recruits instructors as affiliates by simply asking for their opinion on the product, since instructors already create content and want to help their students; pays only a 5 percent commission plus a 10 percent customer discount code, deliberately keeping incentives modest and framing the relationship as mission driven rather than money driven.
  • Allows a single level of affiliate-recruits-affiliate (a discounted 2.5 percent override), explicitly capping the tree at one level to avoid resembling MLM.

 

RETURNS AS A SELF-FUNDING GIFTING ENGINE

  • Inspects and repurposes returned bags (rather than restocking them) into free product for affiliate requests, meaning the gifting program's cost scales naturally with sales volume and returns rate (currently 3.9 percent).
  • Uses Up-Promote on Shopify to automate affiliate applications, W9 collection, and one-level downline tracking, and a Gorgias rule to auto-route incoming free-product requests into the affiliate application flow.
  • Invites affiliates to Instagram collaborations (their posts appear on the brand's own page) instead of paying for content, generating 20 to 50 organic content pieces per affiliate at no direct cost.

 

COMMUNITY DEPTH: SUPPORT ROUTING AND A CERTIFICATION EVENT

  • Routes untrained customers who call in confused about their firearm to affiliate instructors for real training, which drives leads back to instructors and deepens their loyalty to the brand.
  • Runs an annual "Cakes certified" training event for instructors, which compounds recruitment organically as certified instructors return home and run their own local classes and events.
  • Highlighted that follower count is a poor predictor of value: her top affiliate (265K in attributed sales) had only 4,000 Instagram followers at the time of seeding.

 

RESULTS AND ATTRIBUTION

  • Achieved $1M in the 12 months prior to any paid spend (March 2025 to March 2026), 100 percent organic and Shopify-only, with 200 affiliates recruited over 20 months, most now self-recruiting through the referral tree.
  • Uses discount codes for 100 percent manual attribution (a customer typing in "Katrina10" proves the referral) rather than relying on platform-based attribution tools.
  • Since starting Meta ads in April 2026 (using a verified sensitive-item ad account to show firearms), reports a roughly 35 ROAS and about $7 CAC against a roughly $200 AOV, crediting the pre-built affiliate and community foundation for the paid channel's early performance.

 

In conclusion, this session shows that for emotionally dense, identity driven categories, building trust through category authority figures and community depth can outperform volume-based affiliate strategies, and that a disciplined, low-incentive affiliate structure fed by returns can scale to seven figures without any paid acquisition.

items.description:

TOPICS:

  1. A beauty brand testing three bundle offers with 15 total ad creatives at $200 to $700 daily spend per bundle
  2. A sunglasses brand redesigning a buy-more-get-more offer after feedback that "buy two get one free" outperforms "buy one get two free"
  3. A bird feeder brand using a loss leader gear product to fund a private label seed subscription

cliff_notes:
This session is a live workshop where members apply Corey Smith's acquisition cost reverse engineering framework to their own products, presenting offers to the room for direct critique.

 

BEAUTY BRAND: THREE BUNDLE TEST

  • Victor's team is testing three bundles of five creatives each (15 total), spending $200 to $300 per bundle per day (up to $700 if scaling), each using top-performing TikTok Shop UGC video content reused as Meta creative.
  • Bundles combine three face care products plus a free digital product at 40 percent off, targeting a landing price around $70 against a stated acquisition cost cap of $70, meaning the offer currently breaks even at best and needs further tightening.

 

SUNGLASSES BRAND: REFRAMING THE BUNDLE OFFER

  • Tacredi (Grinder Patch) proposed a buy-one-get-two-free sunglasses bundle funnel styled as an unlockable game on the checkout page, mirroring the brand's Amazon positioning around losing/replacing sunglasses cheaply.
  • Table feedback: reframe as "buy two, get one free" instead of "buy one, get two free," since giving away two free units cheapens perceived value while the reworded offer feels more special despite similar economics.
  • Proposed three tiers: $39 single pair (acknowledged unprofitable against a $15 COGS and $40 to $50 acquisition cost, but included to build brand trust with hesitant buyers), $78 buy-two-get-one-free with free shipping ($13 margin per unit), and $99 for six pairs (three sender's choice plus three of the customer's choice) with free shipping, plus an optional $20 to $30 lifetime warranty/insurance add-on.
  • Corey's direct pushback: even the best $99 offer only nets about $28 in margin against a roughly $50 acquisition cost, a $22 gap with no defined plan yet to close it; recommended not launching until every tier has a credible path to covering acquisition cost, citing his own rule of never testing an offer he wasn't confident would clear his target margin.

 

BIRD PRODUCTS BRAND: LOSS LEADER GEAR FUNDING A SUBSCRIPTION

  • Chris proposed using a bird feeder (low margin, low price point) as an explicit loss leader to acquire customers who then subscribe to higher margin bird seed bags.
  • Offer structure: one 5-pound bag alone at $40 (low expected take rate, roughly 5 percent), three bags plus a free feeder at $120 (expected roughly 70 percent take rate, positioned as the anchor offer), and six bags plus a free feeder and free shipping at $240 for a smaller "crazy bird person" niche.
  • A 5-pound bag lasts roughly one month for typical customers, though some buyers already subscribe to 40-pound bags every two weeks, informing the subscription cadence.
  • Corey's guidance: the specific bundle size or price point matters less than confidence that it clears acquisition cost; recommended testing even an unusually large or high priced bundle rather than assuming customers won't pay for it, drawing a parallel to his own team's success testing high-priced bucket bundles that customers did in fact buy.

 

In conclusion, this workshop shows Corey's acquisition cost framework applied live: several offers looked appealing on paper but didn't yet clear the target margin, reinforcing that every tier needs an explicit, tested path to profitability before scaling spend behind it.

  1. Using Vibe.co to buy affordable, aggregated connected TV ad inventory across 50+ streaming channels
  2. Real ROAS results from a $8,000 commercial shoot across top of funnel and retargeting campaigns

cliff_notes:
Gary Kane runs a DTC flag brand (90 percent of ad spend previously on Meta no Amazon presence) and shares his first four months running connected TV (CTV) ads through Vibe.co as a way to diversify away from Meta dependency.

 

WHY AND HOW HE GOT INTO CTV ADVERTISING

  • Wanted to diversify after Meta's Andromeda algorithm update repeatedly cratered performance on a budget where 90 percent of daily spend went to one platform.
  • Shot a professional, TV-ready 30 second commercial (1920x1080, 16:9, broadcast quality) for about $8,000 through a small agency, though he now believes it could have been done far cheaper with tools like Higgsfield.
  • Vibe.co acts as a broker aggregating ad inventory across roughly 50+ streaming apps and channels (Hulu, Roku, Disney Plus, Paramount, NBC, Peacock, Tubi) into a single bundled buy, accessible to small brands in a way traditional CPG-scale TV advertising never was.
  • Each commercial includes a QR code and strong call to action driving directly to his Shopify website (not applicable for Amazon sellers, though he believes Amazon-linked CTV ads are possible), tracked via Pixel and Google Analytics.

 

RESULTS AND ATTRIBUTION APPROACH

  • Achieved a 2.7x blended ROAS and $25.34 CAC over a 30 day window, with retargeting campaigns hitting 3.6x ROAS and top of funnel campaigns at 1.9x, split roughly 70/30 retargeting to top of funnel; now spending about $1,000/day and scaling.
  • Deliberately focuses only on blended ROAS across all channels rather than isolating exact attribution per platform, reasoning that a coordinated Google/Meta/CTV effort makes precise single-channel attribution unreliable and less useful than the combined result.
  • Uses a 30-day attribution window (adjustable) and relies on post-purchase surveys for directional signal, without dedicated landing pages or channel-specific coupon codes yet.
  • No clicks or cost-per-click tracking exist in this ad format; available metrics include cost of acquisition, web page views/impressions, and frequency, though he currently prioritizes ROAS above all else.
  • Group discussion confirmed CTV/Vibe advertising has driven real Amazon halo effect for other brands even without direct Amazon integration, and that geographic, interest-based, and even political-leaning targeting are available through the platform.

 

CREATIVE LESSONS AND AI VS. REAL PEOPLE

  • Shot two additional commercials the week of this presentation, both using real human actors (produced by a small Pittsburgh based agency, not a dedicated TV commercial specialist), and plans to repurpose the same creative for Google TV in addition to Hulu/Fox-style inventory.
  • Tested AI generated people in Meta ads and saw performance collapse; reverting to real human actors immediately restored performance, reinforcing his decision to stick with real actors for both Meta and TV commercials going forward.
  • Views quarterly (possibly monthly) creative refreshes as sufficient for CTV given the platform's much lower frequency exposure compared to constant-scroll platforms like Meta or TikTok, where creative fatigue sets in far faster.

 

In conclusion, this session shows a small DTC brand successfully entering a channel once reserved for major CPG advertisers, using an aggregated CTV ad broker to achieve a consistently profitable blended ROAS while validating that real human actors, not AI generated ones, currently perform better across both streaming and social ad formats.

cliff_notes:
Matt Demirel runs a home office supplies business combining resale and private label and gives a short, informal recap of his team's early shift from ChatGPT to Claude following MDS Inspire.

 

SWITCHING TO CLAUDE AND WORKING WITH QUARTILE

  • After hearing about Claude at MDS Inspire roughly three months ago, moved the team off ChatGPT and onto a Claude team plan (around 125 seats), seeing quick improvements specifically in listings, keyword work, and PPC.
  • Has cycled through multiple PPC agencies (including ones referred to as Lucas and George from London) before settling back on Quartile, now paired with an in-house manager who reviews Quartile's reports pulled through Claude to keep visibility into agency spend, which he notes tends to run higher than expected.
  • Has not yet connected Claude directly to the Amazon API, but plans to after a fellow attendee (Tracy) recommended it during the session.

 

AN UNEXPECTED CROSS-TEAM VISIBILITY ISSUE

  • Noticed that when asking Claude to generate a PowerPoint using specific information he provided, it appeared to pull in additional context or insight that seemed to come from other team members' work, more than he expected it to know.
  • Flags this as something worth understanding and controlling, since shared projects are useful but he wants clearer boundaries on what Claude surfaces across different team members' sessions.
  • Mentions wanting to try Sam Haddad's "business brain" approach (from an earlier session) as a next step to make this shared context more structured and intentional rather than an accidental crossover.

 

In conclusion, this is an early stage, still forming account of a smaller team's shift from ChatGPT to Claude, showing real but modest gains on listings and PPC through an agency partnership, while surfacing a genuine open question about how much context Claude should share across team members by default.

cliff_notes:
Justin Cao founder of the sunglasses brand Sohos (a 10 year Amazon business that grew out of prior OEM manufacturing for European brands), shares an informal, self described secret approach to sourcing and vetting influencers with AI, communicated through mixed English and help from other attendees translating.

 

SOURCING AND SCREENING INFLUENCERS WITH AI

  • Describes running a large scale outreach program targeting a wide range of influencer tiers, from major celebrities down to ordinary customers who receive product for free rather than payment.
  • Uses Bright Data, a US based data provider, to pull candidate influencer profiles and information rather than manually searching for them.
  • Feeds resulting photos and videos into Google Gemini to analyze and determine whether a given influencer is genuinely a fit for the brand (young, fashion focused audience) before pursuing outreach, avoiding mismatched creators.
  • Sends outreach via bulk/group email to identified candidates rather than one by one manual messaging.

 

UNPAID AMAZON INFLUENCER PROGRAM SEEDING

  • Has participated in Amazon's official Influencer Program (organized through Amazon's Fashion department) for about three years; these influencers are not paid directly by the brand and instead earn commission through Amazon's own program structure.
  • Core tactic: recruits influencers and everyday customers to purchase the product themselves and post a video directly under the Amazon listing, which he describes as significantly boosting listing ranking, distinct from and more important to him than typical review generation.
  • Deliberately avoids influencers with mismatched or unwanted audiences (jokingly citing recruiting a grandmother by mistake through a Vine style campaign) since brand fit matters more than raw follower count or willingness to participate.

 

CONNECTING TO DSP TARGETING

  • Once the right influencer content and audience signal exists on the listing, uses that data to inform Amazon DSP targeting, helping the algorithm (and by extension, Rufus/Alexa) correctly understand the brand's target customer (young, fashion-oriented) rather than a mismatched demographic.
  • Frames the overall funnel as sequential: identify the right influencers with AI screening, seed real listing engagement through them, then let that signal sharpen DSP audience targeting downstream.

 

In conclusion, despite a genuinely difficult live presentation due to a language barrier, this session outlines a real, functioning AI assisted influencer sourcing and vetting pipeline, using Bright Data and Gemini to filter for brand fit before investing outreach effort, then leveraging that curated influencer activity to strengthen both organic listing ranking and DSP targeting precision.

items.title: Hot Seat Using AI to Increase Exit Value － Eric Hulli － AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
Eric Hulli, an eight figure mostly Amazon seller planning a sale roughly three years out, opens a hot seat asking whether and how AI adoption actually increases exit multiple, and the group pushes back on vague answers with real, current data from another member mid-way through an active sale process with strategic buyers.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Whether AI adoption itself moves the needle on exit multiple, or just efficiency
  2. What acquirers actually reward: sales growth and profitability, not tooling
  3. A live case study where key man risk from AI heavy operations scared off buyers during real due diligence

TOPICS: Whether AI adoption itself moves the needle on exit multiple, or just efficiency What acquirers actually reward: sales growth and profitability, not tooling A live case study where key man risk from AI heavy operations scared off buyers during real due diligence

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788386019459-Transcript - Hot Seat Using AI to Increase Exit Value － Eric Hulli － AI Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
Eric Hulli running an eight figure, mostly Amazon business with plans to potentially sell in about three years, opens a hot seat asking how AI adoption specifically affects acquisition value, since his lean eight person team already runs efficiently and he's unsure what deploying more AI (including a proposed team of consultants) would actually change for a buyer.

 

WHAT ACTUALLY DRIVES MULTIPLE

  • A member with M&A experience states plainly that sales growth (historic and, more importantly, credible future opportunity) is by far the strongest driver of a premium multiple, followed by improving gross and net margins.
  • AI's value to a valuation only matters through those two levers: either it demonstrably helps grow the business (better targeting, better ROAS) or it demonstrably improves profitability/efficiency; simply stating "we use AI" carries no value on its own.

 

A LIVE CASE STUDY: KEY MAN RISK FROM AI HEAVY OPERATIONS

  • Another attendee, actively selling his own fast growing (multiple hundred percent growth) business and nine months into conversations with 15 potential strategic and fund buyers via an investment bank, shares real, current buyer feedback.
  • Buyers are impressed by the growth rate and EBITDA but expressed real concern (and some walked away) over "key man risk": heavy reliance on AI systems that only the founder/team fully understands, with buyers uncertain how they'd operate the business if that person left.
  • Buyers separately flagged discomfort with how the business individually branded products rather than building one unified brand, forcing the seller to address that structural issue before returning to market.
  • The group's takeaway: current AI heavy operations can scare off buyers today specifically because of poor documentation and personal dependency, but as more strategic buyers adopt AI themselves over the next 12-24 months, that same AI dependent efficiency is expected to become a genuine value driver rather than a red flag, once buyers understand it's transferable, not personality dependent.

 

FRAMING THE BUSINESS FOR A SALE

  • Group pushback on Eric's framing: even sophisticated AI tooling doesn't matter if it isn't transferable and documented in a way a new owner (with their own software stack) could take over without the seller present.
  • Consensus: build and document AI driven processes as replicable systems (not personal know-how locked in the founder's head) if the goal is to actually increase exit value, since an acquirer's own tech stack will likely replace bespoke tools anyway.

 

In conclusion, this hot seat surfaces a timely, unresolved tension in exit planning: AI adoption is currently more likely to raise key man risk concerns with buyers than to directly boost multiple, though the group expects this to shift as buyers themselves become more AI fluent, making documentation and transferability the real determinant of whether AI investment helps or hurts a coming sale.
