cliff_notes:
Alec Celini runs an agency managing multiple Amazon accounts and despite agreeing with an earlier "don't over-build" presentation built his own custom dashboard with Claude Code because paying for Sellerboard, Sellerize, and similar tools separately across many client accounts didn't let him get granular or customize enough.

 

HOW HE BUILT IT

  • Took screenshots of Sellerboard, Sellerize, and Expandly and fed them directly into Claude Code, asking it to replicate each feature, despite having no prior coding experience; spent about 20 hours initially, now spends 2-3 hours a day refining it.
  • Already had a long-running SQL database pulling Amazon data before starting this project, making the AI layer a relatively simple plug-in on top of existing infrastructure rather than a from-scratch build.
  • Recommends Supabase for anyone attempting something similar without pre-existing database infrastructure.
  • Hired a dedicated AI engineer specifically to verify data accuracy and confirm which database tables each dashboard number was actually pulling from, since he doesn't fully understand the technical layer himself.

 

KEY FEATURES BUILT

  • Product level urgency rules: customizable if-then logic per brand or SKU (e.g., if a product exceeds a revenue threshold and its ACOS crosses a set level, flag it as urgent) letting him surface true priority products instead of relying on broad, generic performance categorization.
  • A "second brain" briefing tool: feeds all Fireflies call transcripts, Slack messages, and emails into a vector database, so a generated briefing explains not just that sales dropped (e.g., 93 percent) but why, pulling in the actual documented reason (e.g., a shipment stuck in transit) rather than presenting a raw number in isolation.
  • An SQP-to-campaign workflow: clicking a button on a tracked keyword automatically adds it to a keyword tracker and flows it into a single keyword campaign structure.
  • A subscribe and save dashboard replicating Expandify style metrics (active subscribers, etc.), acknowledging LTV tracking specifically is still a work in progress.
  • Deliberately keeps humans in the loop rather than fully automating everything (only buy box related features are automated so far), preferring to manually refine a process before automating it rather than letting AI define the process itself.

 

PRACTICAL FEEDBACK FROM THE ROOM

  • A fellow attendee diagnosed a live data loading delay as likely caused by the database running multiple separate queries instead of one consolidated query, and recommended giving the AI explicit database optimization instructions to fix it.
  • General framing: this level of custom building only makes sense for someone managing many accounts (like an agency) who needs deeper customization and cross-tool integration (keyword ranking, SQP, and other data combined) rather than a single brand for whom an off the shelf tool like Sellerboard is sufficient.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a candid, self-taught account of building a genuinely useful custom Amazon operations dashboard from scratch using Claude Code and screenshots of existing SaaS tools, emphasizing that the value came from combining scattered data sources and context (not just raw numbers) into one system, rather than from technical sophistication.

items.title: Build a Brand Customers Actually Care About - Josh Hadley - Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Josh Hadley shares a practical framework for transforming Amazon-focused businesses into real, durable e‑commerce brands. 

TOPICS:

  1. How to define a real brand vs. an Amazon arbitrage business
  2. The 16-step framework: association, proof, repetition, and experience
  3. Practical examples of brand building, customer journeys, and influencer partnerships
items.description_text: In this session, Josh Hadley shares a practical framework for transforming Amazon-focused businesses into real, durable e‑commerce brands. TOPICS: How to define a real brand vs. an Amazon arbitrage business The 16-step framework: association, proof, repetition, and experience Practical examples of brand building, customer journeys, and influencer partnerships
cliff_notes:
In this session, Josh Hadley discussed a 16-step framework for building a strong e-commerce brand, emphasizing the importance of creating a cohesive brand playbook.

He highlighted the need for a clear brand promise, consistent messaging, and a customer-centric approach. 


Josh stressed the significance of proof, repetition, and experience in building trust. He provided examples like Boom Beauty and Liquid Death, which successfully integrated their brand promises into every customer touchpoint.

He also introduced various trust models, such as creator endorsements and co-branding partnerships, to enhance brand credibility and loyalty.



Josh Hadley's Introduction and Brand Building Framework

 

  • Josh Hadley introduces himself and outlines the focus of the session: building a brand with raving fans.
  • Josh mentions his 16-step framework, which he and his team have been implementing.
  • He emphasizes the importance of building a cohesive brand playbook, not just having trademarks or A+ content.
  • Josh highlights the goal of higher conversion rates, repeat purchases, and lower CAC over time.
  • He discusses the issue of margin compression on Amazon and the need to command a premium price.



The Importance of Building a Real E-commerce Brand

  • Josh explains that most Amazon sellers are in the arbitrage business, not true brand building.
  • He stresses the need for a lasting brand that can outlive the founder and make a difference.
  • Josh introduces the brand weakness test: if customers don't recognize the brand without the logo, or if they don't search for the product if it falls off the first page, the brand is weak.
  • He outlines the formula for brand strength: association, proof, repetition, and experience.
  • Josh invites questions and feedback from the participants, encouraging a productive conversation.



Building Association: Defining Customer and Brand Positioning

  • Josh discusses the importance of defining what customers should remember the brand for.
  • He suggests running surveys to audit what the brand currently means to customers.
  • Josh emphasizes the need to choose a single idea to own in the customer's mind.
  • He provides examples of strong brand positioning, such as Boom Beauty targeting women aged 50+ and Liquid Death targeting rebellious water drinkers.
  • Josh explains the importance of defining the customer tension and choosing the enemy the brand is against.



Proving the Association: Product Messaging and Customer Outcome

  • Josh highlights the need to write the brand promise and ensure it is consistent across all touchpoints.
  • He advises building a product world that customers can understand, organized by customer use case, progress, and moment.
  • Josh discusses the importance of designing the first win to make the brand promise feel real immediately.
  • He emphasizes the need to build proof into every major claim, using reviews, customer stories, and expert validation.
  • Josh provides examples of how brands like Boom Beauty and AG One build proof through customer testimonials and influencer partnerships.



Repetition: Creating a Memory System and Consistent Brand Language

  • Josh explains the importance of creating a memory system, such as a brand style guide, to ensure consistency.
  • He advises creating repeated brand language and using it everywhere without exception.
  • Josh emphasizes the need to turn content into a trust machine, making it repeat the brand idea while making customers more capable.
  • He discusses the importance of aligning performance marketing with the brand to avoid destroying the brand memory.
  • Josh highlights the need for a cohesive message across all ads, emails, product packaging, and social content.



Experience: Designing the Customer Journey and Service

  • Josh discusses the importance of designing the customer journey so that people actually feel the brand.
  • He advises creating a full customer touchpoint map, including the waiting period between purchase and unboxing.
  • Josh emphasizes the need to design customer service as a brand experience, not just a transactional process.
  • He suggests building retention around customer progress and community around shared identity.
  • Josh recommends making the brand guide a company decision and running a monthly brand review.



Compounding the Brand: Influencer Partnerships and Trust Models

  • Josh introduces the concept of compounding the brand through various trust models.
  • He explains the different models: paid creator endorsements, longer-term ambassadors, creator ownership or equity partnerships, product collaborations, expert partnerships, co-branding partnerships, and community and lifestyle associations.
  • Josh provides examples of each model, such as Nike and Michael Jordan, Logan Paul and KSI, and Crocs and Post Malone.
  • He emphasizes the importance of borrowing trust from influencers and experts to build a strong brand.
  • Josh concludes by encouraging participants to adopt a mindset shift towards building a true e-commerce brand.

items.title: AI That Acts. Not Just Advises － Shaurya Ithikkat － AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
Shaurya Ithikkat of Hector shows a three part Claude framework, skills, live artifacts, and scheduled tasks, designed to close the gap between AI generated analysis and actual execution, arguing most AI use stops at producing dashboards that still depend on a human to act on them.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why most AI adoption stalls at analysis instead of action, citing a McKinsey stat on executive AI ROI
  2. Three Claude building blocks: skills (saved logic), artifacts (live dashboards), and scheduled tasks (automated triggers)
  3. A closed loop framework chaining artifacts, thresholds, and skills into autonomous execution

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788476812726-Transcript - AI That Acts. Not Just Advises － Shaurya Ithikkat － AI Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
Shaurya Ithikkat of Hector, an Amazon MCP and ads platform, argues that most AI adoption fails to deliver real value because it stops at analysis and dashboards, still leaving execution to a human who can be slow, inconsistent, or simply forget.

 

WHY MOST AI USE STALLS AT ANALYSIS

  • Cites a McKinsey figure that only 1 percent of executives report measurable value from AI, with the rest treating it as a support layer rather than a true operational driver.
  • Argues that whether someone manually uploads spreadsheets or uses a live MCP connection, both hit the same bottleneck: a human still has to execute the recommendation, and execution quality degrades over time due to inconsistency ("laziness") in daily habits like media buying.

 

THREE BUILDING BLOCKS FOR MAKING AI ACT

  • Skills: saved, reusable logic files (MD files in Claude) that standardize decisions across an entire team, for example a "bleeding" skill that automatically flags and negates a search term once it crosses a defined wasted-spend threshold, or a "headroom" skill surfacing profitable search terms with strong impression share that aren't getting enough spend. Skills require customizing brand specific thresholds but then apply consistently across an organization without variation in interpretation.
  • Artifacts: live, real time dashboards built through Claude Cowork on desktop (not the Chrome extension) that refresh data without manual Excel uploads, for example an account health dashboard blending COGS data via MCP to show true profit, or separate function specific dashboards for inventory (SKU consumption) and content (conversion rate by listing).
  • Scheduled tasks: automated triggers set inside Claude Cowork that can post recurring reports to Slack, execute a skill automatically once a defined metric crosses its threshold (rather than waiting for a human to notice and act), or run detailed analysis on a recurring schedule.

 

THE CLOSED LOOP FRAMEWORK

  • Recommended architecture: an artifact (live dashboard) sits on top, continuously monitored; a scheduled task watches for a defined threshold breach; when triggered, it automatically activates the relevant skill to execute the fix; results feed back into the artifact, closing the loop without requiring a human to notice, decide, and manually act each time.
  • Frames this three part structure (artifact, task, skill) as generalizable beyond Amazon ads to any function or platform (cites Meta creative performance as another applicable use case).

 

HECTOR'S OFFER AND CAVEATS

  • Hector's MCP is positioned as currently the only MCP offering pre-built skill templates specifically for Amazon ads; skills still require the user to input their own brand specific guardrails (e.g., bleeding threshold, target margin).
  • Artifacts must be built individually per brand since dashboard design is inherently a matter of each founder's own visual and functional preference, though Hector can build custom versions on request.
  • Offers a flat monthly fee (roughly $1,000, scaling with number of brands managed) rather than a percentage of ad spend, with a 50 percent discount for the first three months for new signups.

 

In conclusion, this session's core argument is that dashboards and AI generated recommendations alone don't create business value: real ROI comes from chaining live monitoring, defined thresholds, and pre-built execution logic together so that routine decisions get acted on automatically rather than depending on a human to notice and follow through every time.

cliff_notes:
Teresa Widodo, TikTok's head of brand partnerships for commerce, presents a suite of AI tools built around TikTok's "watch it, love it, want it" framework, spanning creative generation, funnel analytics, and automated ad buying.

 

WHY TIKTOK POSITIONS ITSELF AS A FULL FUNNEL PLATFORM

  • Argues today's purchase journey (discovery across multiple shopping apps, AI trip/product planning tools, validation with friends) is fragmented, and TikTok combines social discovery and e-commerce checkout into one app.
  • Cites Nielsen study data showing TikTok delivers 2x ROAS in paid media compared to other platform averages, and notes growing on-platform search behavior (including AI generated sentiment summaries of search results) as a differentiator.

 

CONTENT: TIKTOK ONE AND TIKTOK SYMPHONY

  • TikTok One connects brands to creators at scale and provides a traffic boost for creator content sourced through the platform, framed as making human creativity easier to access rather than replacing it.
  • TikTok Symphony, powered by TikTok's in-house "Seedance 2.0" video model, generates content via image-to-video, reference-video-to-new-video (using a viral video as a style template), text-to-video, TikTok-style auto editing (text overlays, remixing multiple creator/product videos into permutations), AI generated brand avatars, and inspiration pulled directly from top performing TikTok ads.

 

FUNNEL ANALYTICS: MARKET SCOPE

  • A new first-party data tool segmenting a brand's entire audience into awareness, consideration, and conversion stages via an "audience assets" feature, with segments exportable directly into TikTok Ads Manager for targeting.
  • Provides benchmarking across eight engagement metrics against competitors (paid and organic), plus a merchandise feature surfacing category best sellers and competitive pricing insights, and a consolidated post-campaign attribution report.

 

AUTOMATED ADS AND NEW CHECKOUT TOOLS

  • Smart Plus: automated ad buying based on a set target ROI/CPA and budget, using all available creative assets and machine learning that improves with campaign duration.
  • GMV Max: the TikTok Shop equivalent, automatically optimizing ad spend across owned and affiliate content toward a revenue (GMV) target.
  • Shopping Assistant: an in-feed AI chat (accessible from ad placements) that answers shopper questions about a brand or product and surfaces relevant reviews.
  • Buy Direct from Brand (newly launched, allowlist only): preloads a brand's own website (e.g., Shopify or brand.com) inside TikTok so ads lead directly to a fully functional product page with add to cart, coupons, and order tracking, without leaving the app; AI chat/DM based shopping and TikTok search based product surfacing are described as in progress.

 

CASE STUDIES

  • MOOM (Southeast Asia supplement brand): shifted from a pure lower funnel strategy to an upper funnel Top View placement campaign for its 5th anniversary, driving a 20x GMV increase versus normal days along with higher order value and ROI.
  • Liquid IV (US): ran a halo impact study comparing brand.com and TikTok Shop performance, finding TikTok Shop drove 90 percent incremental conversion and a combined 71 percent ROAS across both web and shop ads, showing the two channels reinforcing rather than cannibalizing each other.

 

In conclusion, this session is a vendor presentation positioning TikTok as an end to end commerce platform, pairing new AI creative and analytics tools with automated ad products and a limited time ad credit matching offer to encourage brands to deepen their TikTok investment.

items.description:
Nate Taminger, director of e-commerce at Native Pet, walks through three beginner-friendly Claude Cowork workflows built from scratch, a daily to-do list tracker pulling from Slack, email, ClickUp, and meeting notes, a weekly team goal tracker, and a quarterly performance review builder, aimed at people just past the basic chatbot stage.

 

TOPICS:

  1. A daily to-do list tracker that pulls tasks from four sources and labels how much AI can handle
  2. A weekly team goal ("MITs") tracker that ends recency bias in setting priorities
  3. A quarterly performance review builder that pulls real evidence instead of relying on memory

cliff_notes:
Nate Taminger runs e-commerce (Amazon and TikTok Shop) at Native Pet and shares three Claude Cowork based workflows built specifically for people moving from basic chatbot use toward simple, standing AI delegation.

 

DAILY WORKFLOW: THE TO-DO LIST TRACKER

  • Built a Claude Cowork artifact that pulls tasks from four scattered sources: Fellow AI meeting notes, Slack (including a personal "Nate's List" channel for late night task capture), ClickUp, and email.
  • A companion skill sorts every task into five buckets based on how much AI can handle: fully autopilot ("do it all"), heavy lifting (AI drafts, human finishes), accelerating (research/prep support), building a tool, and in-person only tasks AI can't touch.
  • Currently manages 38 live tasks this way; acknowledges the tool's time-saved estimates are often optimistic (claiming 20 minutes saved on a task that really took about 4) but still meaningfully clears backlog built up from meetings that would otherwise be forgotten.

 

WEEKLY WORKFLOW: THE "MITs" ENGINE

  • Automates the team's existing "Most Important Things" (3 to 7 priorities per person per week) system, which previously suffered from recency bias (priorities reflected whatever was top of mind Sunday night) and invisible progress (no one knew a MIT had slipped until the following Monday).
  • Pulls evidence from the same four sources (Slack, ClickUp, meeting notes, email) to mark each prior week's MITs as done, slipped, or not started, then proposes next week's MITs tied back to quarterly "rocks," cross referencing employee self-proposed MITs so Nate edits rather than drafts from scratch.
  • Key guardrail: every proposed MIT must map to one of three defined Amazon focused pillars (visibility, conversion/new launches, efficiency), which were explicitly given to the AI as fixed categories.

 

QUARTERLY WORKFLOW: THE FEEDBACK BUILDER

  • Addresses three recurring problems with manual quarterly reviews: evidence scattered across tools, unconscious recency bias favoring recent performance over the full quarter, and no easy way to compare self ratings against manager ratings.
  • Gathers a full quarter of evidence across ClickUp, Slack, email, and meeting notes, scores each direct report 1-5 against defined core values plus quality, productivity, and results, and cites specific concrete examples (e.g., "13 out of 13 weeks of MITs on time") rather than vague impressions.
  • Produces three sections: what's going well (where self rating and manager rating agree), where perceptions differ (often revealing recency bias or a misunderstood core value), and what needs work.
  • Hard guardrail: the tool only ever produces a draft; Nate edits scores and content before any review happens, and the tool is instructed not to argue with or overwrite his edits, since feedback authorship must remain human. Reports unanimous positive feedback from direct reports calling it the most substantive review process they've received.

 

HOW TO BUILD THESE YOURSELF (AND WHAT WENT WRONG FIRST)

  • Recommended process: do the task manually and narrate it out loud first, write the steps in plain English, hand them to Claude Cowork, then run the tool alongside your own manual process for a few weeks before trusting it alone.
  • Admits early mistakes: giving the AI too much freedom to guess at judgment calls (should only automate the typing/execution, not the judgment itself), and skipping guardrails on the first feedback tool version, which produced confident but factually unreliable content.
  • Closing exercise: write down one repetitive task, name where its source information lives (Slack, email, spreadsheet), and define what "done" looks like, as a concrete first step to try the following Monday.

 

In conclusion, this session offers an accessible, guardrail focused entry point into AI delegation for people earlier in their AI journey, showing three concrete, still human edited workflows built from ordinary business tools rather than a fully autonomous setup.

items.title: Is Your PPC Building Organic Rank... or Just Renting Traffic － Luke Lim － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Luke Lim, CEO of Scale Insights, breaks down proprietary data from analyzing thousands of Amazon accounts into four milestones for knowing whether PPC spend is genuinely building organic rank or just renting temporary traffic, culminating in an MCP that automates the entire analysis.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Calculating the dollar value of hitting 50 percent query share before chasing any keyword
  2. Using conversion delta to separate keywords you can actually win from ones you can only rent
  3. Break-even CPC zones and why bigger markets cost more to move

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788211289832-Is Your PPC Building Organic Rank... or Just Renting Traffic － Luke Lim － AI Scaling Live Singapore.pdf

cliff_notes:
Luke Lim, CEO of Scale Insights, shares data aggregated across thousands of Amazon seller accounts to lay out four milestones for determining whether PPC spend actually builds sustainable organic rank.

 

MILESTONE ONE: SIZE THE OPPORTUNITY BEFORE CHASING IT

  • Aggregated account data shows organic rank position 17 captures roughly 7x the click share of the bottom of page one, making it a realistic, less competitive target rather than aiming straight for rank 1.
  • Introduces "query share" (ASIN impressions divided by total query search volume) with roughly 50 percent as the target where meaningful organic traction begins.
  • Demonstrates calculating the dollar value of closing a query share gap (e.g., an insulated water bottle keyword needing 30,000 more impressions to hit 50 percent share, worth over $5,000 based on historical click-through and conversion rates), arguing you must know the size of the prize before deciding whether to chase it.

 

MILESTONE TWO: FIND KEYWORDS YOU CAN ACTUALLY WIN

  • Introduces "conversion delta": the ASIN's own conversion rate minus the market's conversion rate for that search term.
  • A positive conversion delta (converting better than market) correlates strongly with rank climbing and sticking; a negative delta makes rank very hard to sustain even with heavy spend.

 

MILESTONE THREE: KNOW HOW HARD YOU CAN PUSH WITHOUT LOSING MONEY

  • Shows two real (anonymized) account examples: one keyword where modest PPC spend steadily grew both query share and organic rank (positive conversion delta, manageable market size), versus another where heavy spend never moved query share past 1 percent and rank reverted the moment spend stopped, meaning the brand was just renting traffic.
  • Market size determines difficulty: the same visibility gain costs far more CPC in a huge market (e.g., "water bottle") than a smaller, more specific one (e.g., "insulated water bottle"), because a fixed ad budget represents a smaller share of a bigger total query volume.
  • Defines break-even CPC from profit per order and conversion rate, then three zones: sustainable (below break-even, can run indefinitely), push zone (losing money short term to buy rank, requires close P&L monitoring), and out of limit (unsustainable, requires campaign restructuring).
  • Warns against trusting small sample "strong signals," citing an example where an apparent 33 percent conversion rate came from just 3 orders out of 33 unseen clicks, one of which was a competitor purchase later refunded; recommends anchoring to product or market level conversion data until click and order volume provide real statistical confidence.

 

MILESTONE FOUR: CONCENTRATE SPEND TO ACTUALLY MOVE RANK

  • Recommends isolating a target query into its own single keyword exact match campaign, pausing overlapping keywords elsewhere, and adding negative exact matches to prevent cannibalization from broad and phrase campaigns.
  • Suggests using a high top-of-search placement modifier (e.g., 100 percent) with a reduced base bid to effectively cap CPC at break-even while concentrating spend on the specific placement that moves rank.
  • Recommends verifying weekly that organic rank actually follows query share improvement; if it doesn't after concentrated, top-of-search spend, the keyword likely isn't rankable at a sustainable cost and further spend should stop.

 

THE MCP AUTOMATING THIS ANALYSIS

  • Scale Insights' MCP runs this full opportunity sizing, conversion delta, and break-even analysis automatically across an entire account's SQP data, sorting keywords into optimize, reduce, or scale queues with dollar-ranked priority.
  • Conversion modeling deliberately defers to more reliable data sources when session/click counts are low (ASIN's own conversion above 100 sessions, otherwise falling back to market level conversion), weighting confidence by data volume.
  • Two additional MCP reports (SI Analyst and SI NextMove) surface account-wide changes ranked by dollar impact and generate prioritized, ASIN-level action plans; the full toolset currently spans more than 40 commands.

 

In conclusion, this session provides a data driven framework for distinguishing PPC spend that builds durable organic rank from spend that merely rents temporary visibility, centered on sizing opportunities in dollars, requiring a positive conversion delta, respecting break-even economics, and concentrating spend rather than spreading it thin.

items.title: Putting an Al Agent to Work on Amazon PPC － Kevan Soh － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Kevan Soh, founder of an eight figure Amazon brand, breaks down three Claude and Scale Insights MCP driven PPC skills, listing re-optimization, an SKC (single keyword campaign) audit, and weekly negation, built around comparing his own conversion data against market conversion data six months into a product's life.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Re-optimizing listings months post launch using real search query performance data instead of pre-launch guesses
  2. An SKC audit that splits keywords into offense, defense, testing, and rank push buckets
  3. A weekly negation skill that also surfaces overly aggressive blacklist terms to move back into the whitelist

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788211188250-Transcript - Putting an Al Agent to Work on Amazon PPC － Kevan Soh － AI Scaling Live Singapore.pdf

cliff_notes:
Kevan Soh runs an eight figure Amazon brand plus a seven figure Singapore home appliances brand, and shares three repeatable PPC skills built on the Scale Insights MCP, which gives Claude direct access to Amazon's search query performance (SQP) and search term report data.

 

WHY POST LAUNCH LISTING OPTIMIZATION BEATS PRE LAUNCH GUESSING

  • Initial listing optimization (using tools like DataDive) at launch is inherently a guess, since no real search term or SQP data exists yet for a brand new ASIN.
  • After a minimum of 90 days, real SQP data becomes available; the skill uses 90 day data as the backbone and overlays more recent 30 day data (capturing current reviews, velocity, and market conversion rate) to prioritize what to feature.
  • Calculates an "index" (equivalent to what Scale Insights calls conversion delta) by comparing the ASIN's own conversion rate against market conversion rate for each search term, then multiplies by search volume to rank keyword opportunity for title, bullets, and highlights placement, deduplicating overlapping terms.
  • Automatically adapts to platform constraints like Amazon's newer 75 character title limit.

 

THE SKC AUDIT: OFFENSE, DEFENSE, TEST, AND RANK PUSH

  • Offense: unpauses and builds dedicated SKC (single keyword campaign) structures for high opportunity terms already converting above market rate, and calculates a break even CPC automatically.
  • Test: assigns promising but currently low performing terms (high click count, low actual conversion, meaning likely competitor clicks) into a shared multi keyword test campcampaign (up to 8 keywords) to validate before committing to a dedicated SKC.
  • Defense: identifies search terms with substantial spend and clicks that convert well below market rate, flagging them for a stop advertising decision (left to human management approval rather than automated).
  • Rank push: separately targets terms with strong conversion but low impression share (below roughly 20 percent), applying top of search bid adjustments specifically to close that visibility gap rather than to defend already well ranked terms.

 

WEEKLY NEGATION AND THE WHITELIST DISCOVERY

  • The skill studies the product directly (using a browser automation tool) before recommending negations, reducing the human error of negating a term based on a misunderstanding of what the product actually is.
  • The most valuable discovery: cross-checking existing blacklisted terms against currently prioritized, high opportunity keywords and surfacing accidental overlaps for management to move back into an active whitelist, since terms auto negated early in an ASIN's life (e.g., after 15 clicks with no sales) may deserve reconsideration a year later with hundreds of reviews behind the product.
  • Warns that a search term showing zero conversions in a report may simply mean it was never advertised, not that it can't convert, and should be tested rather than dismissed.

 

RESULTS AND LESSONS FROM TESTING ACROSS ASINS

  • Testing across evergreen ASINs since around July showed rising organic revenue and improved conversion rate, attributed to advertising more heavily on terms already converting well rather than spreading spend broadly.
  • Realized the team had been unknowingly blocking some of its best converting search terms via the blacklist, and separately found some products were priced too low to leave enough margin for meaningful ad spend, prompting a pricing process change.
  • In Q&A, on category critical keywords that convert below market: advises that spending more will not fix a real conversion problem, and instead recommends improving secondary images, offer, and overall listing presentation rather than assuming ad placement alone can compensate; also notes the "rank push" bucket already addresses low impression share terms without needing a separate manual top of search override.

 

In conclusion, this session shows how connecting Claude to real Amazon search query data via MCP turns PPC optimization into an evidence based, repeatable process built around comparing actual versus market conversion rates, correcting both hypothesis driven pre launch keyword choices and unintentional over negation built up over a product's lifecycle.

items.title: Operator Panel － Leslie Chang & Ivan Ong & Viktor Villand & Elias Tiong － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Three operators, Ivan Ong (baby brand, $100M+), Viktor Villand (Amazon seller and developer), and Elias Tiong (matcha brand), field moderator Leslie Chang's questions on how AI actually fits into scaling their businesses, converging on the same core message: AI should help humans think and execute faster, not replace judgment or headcount.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Where each operator draws the line between automating with AI, software, or hiring a low cost VA
  2. Real examples of AI surfacing insights across combined data sources, including halo effect tracking
  3. Team adoption challenges and how each operator trains or manages resistant employees

TOPICS: Where each operator draws the line between automating with AI, software, or hiring a low cost VA Real examples of AI surfacing insights across combined data sources, including halo effect tracking Team adoption challenges and how each operator trains or manages resistant employees

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788211083642-Transcript - Operator Panel － Leslie Chang & Ivan Ong & Viktor Villand & Elias Tiong － AI Scaling Live Singapore.pdf

cliff_notes:
Moderator Leslie Chang leads a panel with Ivan Ong (baby brand scaling past $100M), Viktor Villand (a 12 year Amazon seller now running a lean two person brand with his wife), and Elias Tiong (a matcha brand using what he calls an "AI co-founder"), on how AI actually changes day to day operating decisions.

 

WHEN TO AUTOMATE WITH AI VERSUS HIRE A VA

  • Ivan's rule: only build AI automation for high level, high paid manager work; simple tasks a $300 to $400 a month Philippines based VA can do are left to a VA, since maintaining AI long term can cost more than low level human labor.
  • Ivan frames AI explicitly as an enabler, not a replacement, telling staff the company will invest in whatever AI tools help them hit their KPIs, partly to avoid a culture where AI adoption feels threatening.
  • Viktor built his own Python program with direct Amazon API access to manage listings, profit allocation (profit first system), and supplier communication with a much smaller team than his prior 60 person operation, arguing the core job is protecting and growing existing SKUs rather than chasing new product ideas.
  • Elias describes an "AI co-founder," really a shared AI workspace with separate folder based context for him and his human co-founder, running on a hosted virtual private server that continuously pulls data from every connected API overnight.

 

WHERE AI GENUINELY MOVED THE NEEDLE

  • Elias combines Scale Insights MCP branded search data with Meta ad spend, Meta impressions, and TikTok impressions on a week by week graph to test for real halo effect correlation across channels, something manual tracking couldn't easily surface.
  • Viktor used Scale Insights MCP to cluster his PPC keywords into buyer intent families and discovered he was spreading spend across underperforming clusters instead of concentrating on the highest converting ones first, a change he credits as his single biggest PPC money saver despite 12 years of PPC experience.
  • Ivan cites an inventory analysis dashboard that surfaced locked up cash during a cash flow crunch as a concrete example of AI directly driving a decision, framing the highest value use case as whatever the business's current constraint happens to be.
  • All three agree: AI should help humans think faster and execute recurring, repetitive work, but forward looking strategic decisions still require human judgment; asking AI what to do next just returns generic, non differentiated answers.

 

TEAM ADOPTION AND DATA ACCURACY

  • Ivan holds firm that employees unwilling to adapt to an AI enabled workflow will naturally become misaligned with the company's culture over time, citing "Good to Great" data that top performing companies fire faster than mediocre ones.
  • Ivan's team is piloting an internal "AI enabler" role who works directly with department heads to find pain points and build automations for them, rather than expecting managers to self teach AI on top of their existing workload.
  • Ivan avoids adoption as its own KPI, instead holding departments to the same output targets regardless of how much AI they use, arguing outcomes matter more than tool usage; Elias agrees, rejecting token usage style KPIs used at some larger companies.
  • On data accuracy, Viktor cross checks Amazon SP API data against Scale Insights MCP data as a sanity check; both Viktor and Elias admit there's no fully solved method beyond periodic manual spot checks, since AI can confidently present inaccurate underlying data as correct.

 

In conclusion, this panel converges on a consistent operating philosophy across three very differently sized businesses: AI is a tool to accelerate execution and surface data faster, but strategic thinking, adoption culture, and data verification still require deliberate human ownership.

items.title: 3 Weeks to 6 Hours 1 － Damon Sununtnasuk － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Damon Sununtnasuk lays out a three tier framework for AI workflows (read, draft, act), walks through seven live examples from his supplement brand covering morning briefs to autonomous demand planning, then adds a bonus workflow that autonomously fixes website ADA compliance issues.

 

TOPICS:

  1. A three tier framework (read, draft, act) for classifying AI workflow risk and value
  2. Seven live AI workflow examples spanning dashboards, content, listings, and inventory
  3. A bonus workflow that autonomously monitors and fixes ADA website compliance

cliff_notes:
Damon Sununtnasuk, a dietary supplement seller who joined MDS one year ago, argues that businesses adopting AI early gain a compounding advantage, then walks through the tiered framework and specific workflows behind his own 26 agentic systems.

 

THE THREE TIER FRAMEWORK

  • Read: AI reads data and surfaces it for a human to act on, lowest risk and lowest barrier to entry.
  • Draft: AI reads data and produces work (an email, a piece of content) for human review and approval before sending.
  • Act: AI is given a goal, tests hypotheses, and acts autonomously without a human in the loop, highest risk but highest reward.
  • Cites a Harvard Business School and BCG study showing companies adopting ChatGPT 4 saw a 12 percent increase in tasks completed, 25 percent faster outcomes, and 43 percent higher quality work, with those gains compounding under a quarterly rollout cadence.

 

TIER ONE: READ ONLY WORKFLOWS

  • A 6am morning brief pulling calendar, email, and cash position data via Claude Code, saving about 30 minutes a day and an estimated $12,000 a year.
  • A daily transcript summarizer that publishes to an internal company wiki and sends a weekly to-do recap, saving about 8 hours a month, roughly $10,000 a year.
  • A custom AEO (answer engine optimization) tracker querying ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude with 10 brand and competitor prompts twice a day, replacing a $350 a month off the shelf tool and saving an estimated $6,000 a year and 300 hours of manual work.

 

TIER TWO: DRAFTING WORKFLOWS

  • A TikTok creator feedback tool that transcribes creator videos, checks compliance, hooks, and calls to action, then drafts ready to send creator feedback, saving at least two hours a day and about $25,000 a year.
  • An Amazon research and listing builder that automates competitor research, contract manufacturer quoting, and full A plus listing creation, cutting six weeks of agency work and $3,000 to $5,000 in fees down to a couple hours on a $20 subscription, with a 7 to 14 percent conversion uplift worth an estimated $100,000 to $130,000 in added profit per SKU.

 

TIER THREE: FULLY AUTONOMOUS WORKFLOWS

  • A blog agent that scrapes Reddit and Quora for topical insights, then writes and publishes roughly 60 SEO/AEO focused articles a month directly to WordPress and Shopify with no human review, replacing an agency writing team entirely.
  • A demand planning and PO generator, built after a $500,000 stockout, that combines sales velocity, multi warehouse storage data, supplier lead times, and cash position to auto generate and send purchase orders, preventing two to three stockouts since launch.

 

CHOOSING WHAT TO AUTOMATE, AND WHAT WENT WRONG

  • Filters for automation candidates: does it save meaningful time, are the input rules stable even if inputs vary, and does someone genuinely hate doing it.
  • Warns against over automating, citing a failed internal attempt to fully automate PO generation that took 20 hours to build and saved only 15 to 20 minutes on a task done twice a month.
  • A transcript summarization workflow once leaked sensitive salary discussion data in a company wide recap; fixed by adding sensitive data filters and failure alerts.
  • Recommends picking one AI platform and sticking with it, starting with a single simple connector based workflow, and naming an explicit owner for every workflow's upkeep.

 

BONUS: AUTONOMOUS ADA COMPLIANCE WORKFLOW

  • After being sued over website accessibility (ADA/WCAG) despite having no knowledge of the requirement, built a Claude and Shopify connected workflow that scans the site monthly, auto fixes compliance issues across all pages, and emails a report of fixes made and manual follow ups needed.
  • Estimates this saves around $20,000 in legal exposure and per page compliance vendor fees, and shared a public GitHub template of the tool with attendees.

 

In conclusion, this session offers both an aspirational and practical map for adopting AI workflows, arguing that a disciplined tiered approach, clear ownership, and caution against over automating routine but low value tasks are what actually make AI adoption pay off.

items.title: Rolling Out an Internal Al Layer to a Team That Didn't Ask for It － Khalid Abdulla － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Khalid Abdulla breaks down why he failed seven senior hires in 14 months at a cost of about $62,000, then walks through the AI assisted, gated hiring system he built afterward to filter scammers and double jobbers before they ever reach a live team.

 

TOPICS:

  1. The seven failed senior hires and what actually went wrong in each case
  2. A gated, AI assisted hiring system built to catch fraud and low performers early
  3. Onboarding tools and accountability structures used once someone is hired

cliff_notes:
Khalid Abdulla, a former Amazon hiring manager who has run thousands of interviews, opens by admitting that despite strong hiring credentials, he failed seven senior hires over 14 months, with none reducing his workload and two turning out to be outright fraud.

 

WHAT WENT WRONG WITH SEVEN SENIOR HIRES

  • A PPC and listing director was a strong individual contributor but could not lead others or delegate.
  • A chief of staff and a GM both built process and reporting but never actually solved problems.
  • A senior brand manager was caught logging in from three different devices in three different cities within two weeks, indicating someone else was doing the real work.
  • A supply chain manager with ex Thrasio credentials interviewed well but had no real skill underneath.
  • One hire quit within a month once the workload expectations became clear.
  • Core lesson: 80 to 90 percent of take home assessment candidates are now leaning on AI, so polished answers no longer signal real ability.

 

THE REBUILT, AI ASSISTED HIRING SYSTEM

  • Pulls a candidate's full interview transcript history and uses it to generate a customized, AI resistant skill assessment for that specific person and role, rather than a generic test.
  • Adds a live, screen shared "cold work session" before any offer, watching for AI usage, hesitation, or shady behavior in real time.
  • Requires proof of resignation from a prior job by day 14 to catch double jobbing, a common practice among some offshore hiring pools.
  • Uses Time Doctor tracking for the first three months as a non negotiable filter that scares off scammers early.
  • Runs background checks via Google Workspace login monitoring, which is how the multi device brand manager fraud was caught.
  • Gives every new hire a personal "how to work with me" document built with AI from his own communication patterns and expectations.

 

ACCOUNTABILITY AND CULTURE STRUCTURE

  • Uses a 30, 60, 90 day plan with explicit deliverables, but shortens the real trial window to 30 days rather than 90, holding himself to grading it honestly.
  • The single metric he now uses to judge a senior hire: does his own operational and cognitive load actually go down.
  • Hires almost entirely outside the US (Pakistan, Ukraine, South America, Eastern Europe), reasoning that under $200,000 a year, US hires rarely clear the bar he needs.
  • Group discussion adds supporting color: MDS is building a shared blacklist of scam candidates into its Millie AI assistant, and multiple members have separately caught the same repeat offender working several MDS brands simultaneously.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid postmortem on repeated senior hiring failures, turned into a concrete, AI supported screening and accountability system built to catch fraud and low performers before they ever cost real operational time.

items.title: How I Run Our Ecom Engine with Al － Lee Lim － AI Scaling Live Singapore
items.description:
Lee Lim, co-CEO of a pet care brand on Amazon and Shopify, runs his entire e-commerce operation through a single 24/7 Claude Code agent hosted on a Mac Mini and controlled via Telegram voice notes, covering executive assistant tasks, payroll verification, customs validation, and Amazon listing monitoring, with no developers or agencies.

TOPICS:

  1. Why business processes should never be templated, even across seemingly identical brands

cliff_notes:
Lee Lim, former Amazon aggregator operator and IBM/NEC technology strategy consultant, now runs his pet care brand's entire operational engine through one always-on AI agent, with no developers, agencies, or written scripts.

 

WHY BUSINESSES CAN'T BE TEMPLATED

  • Draws on his aggregator experience: brands looked identical on paper (same platform, same FBA setup) but fell apart on integration because supplier terms, shipping incoterms, compliance requirements, and branding playbooks were all genuinely different.
  • Argues the AI framework has three layers: AI reasoning (judgment and edge cases), scripts (consistent, repeatable execution), and plain language SOPs (the actual playbook that makes the system uniquely yours and cannot be copied).
  • Says business goals should shape SOP design: a lifestyle business owner should automate admin to reclaim personal time, while an exit focused owner should prioritize reporting, templating, and clean books for buyer diligence.

 

THE SETUP: ONE AGENT, TELEGRAM, AND VOICE NOTES

  • Runs a single Mac Mini based agent (in Taiwan) using Claude Code with Claude Fable 5, controlled entirely through Telegram for text, voice, and file input, connected to ClickUp, Gmail, Xero, Airwallex, Amazon, and Shopify.
  • Writes no code or scripts personally; simply tells the AI what he needs and it writes them, and dictates SOPs via a voice to text tool (WhisperFlow) rather than typing them.
  • Total cost is about $100 a month (Claude subscription plus Mac Mini hardware), with no developers or agencies involved.
  • Uses voice notes to offload tasks into ClickUp within about 30-45 seconds, citing the Zeigarnik effect (unresolved thoughts consume mental focus) as the psychological reason this reduces mental load, not just saves time.
  • Cites a real example where a customs delayed shipment stuck in New York was resolved via a single voice note dictated over dinner, with the agent drafting the full customs compliance email response.

 

FOUR COMPLIANCE AND MONITORING WORKFLOWS

  • Payroll verification: cross checks payroll against Airwallex bank account data to catch missed payments or changed bank details without manually reviewing every line.
  • GST and customs reconciliation: automatically reconciles quarterly GST filings against accountant records, replacing manual reconciliation work previously done with a finance controller.
  • Customs entry validation: cross checks customs broker entries against the correct information after discovering brokers were entering wrong tariff percentages despite having correct codes, catching real financial leakage.
  • Amazon listing monitoring: runs a daily baseline check across listings, catching real issues like an unauthorized review split and a missing 50 percent coupon on a top selling product.

 

GETTING STARTED AND MANAGING MEMORY

  • Recommends starting by listing 10 recurring weekly tasks, picking the most time consuming one as the first workflow, dictating the SOP by voice, and granting AI tools read-only access first rather than read-write.
  • Says the system broke constantly in the first month of building it and treats ongoing tuning as a normal, expected part of the process rather than a sign of failure.
  • In Q&A: chose a dedicated Mac Mini over the Claude app specifically for persistent long-term memory (via an Obsidian database) and to avoid context rot by spawning fresh sub-agent contexts for deep research tasks.
  • Runs a monthly memory audit to prune outdated or irrelevant learned information so the agent's long-term memory stays accurate and doesn't bias future decisions.
  • Manages token usage by clearing session context at roughly a 40 percent usage threshold and deliberately spawning sub-agents rather than running everything in one long session; is also removing an earlier LightRag based memory triage layer now that newer models like Fable 5 handle raw Obsidian retrieval well enough without it.

 

In conclusion, this session shows a lean, no-code approach to running core e-commerce operations, from executive assistant tasks to customs compliance, through a single voice controlled AI agent, with genuine emphasis on business specific SOPs and careful memory management over any off the shelf tooling.

  • Doug: prompts ChatGPT before a presentation starts to hold and only summarize slide photos at the end, producing an instant business action list without needing to take manual notes during sessions.
  • Chip: built a free, self hosted omni channel dashboard (Claude/Codex, Vercel free tier, Supabase, official Amazon/TikTok/Shopify APIs) that connects to ClickUp SOPs via MCP so Claude understands the business before executing PPC changes, inventory forecasting, or shipment creation.
  • Damon Sununtnasuk: adds one line to Claude's general instructions ("always assess and tell me how we can turn this into a repeat skill") so long chats automatically get flagged for conversion into reusable skills, SOPs, or projects.
  • Khalid Abdulla: simply feeds other presenters' shared files and frameworks directly into Claude to extract what can improve his own systems.
  • Emily (GEO hack): reverse engineers why competitors get recommended in AI answers by analyzing what evidence and sources AI cites, then closes the gap with clearer product entities, evidence backed claims, and outside authority building.
  • Vincent (Yuka): demoed a simple MCP connected prompt asking whether TikTok activity tracked with Amazon sales for a hero ASIN, framing conversational AI queries as a way to run halo effect analysis without a dedicated analyst hire.

 

AMAZON SPECIFIC TACTICS

  • Nate: convinced Amazon to accept Chewy retail purchase order prices as proof of higher COGS (rather than manufacturer invoices) by matching business names and addresses, roughly doubling reimbursement payouts overnight.
  • Matt: detailed Amazon Bulk Services (ABS), which can unlock up to a 25 percent referral fee discount by structuring listings into a case and pallet package hierarchy (minimum 10 units, 1,400 cubic inches, 35+ pounds), applicable to FBA offers as well as FBM.
  • Kim: replaced professional product photography with AI tools (naming Magnific) fed by as few as 15 iPhone photos to generate main and lifestyle images.

 

RELATIONSHIP AND PERSONAL HACKS

  • Victor (joking framing): sends suppliers iPhones as leverage to speed up responsiveness, acknowledging it stops working once the gifts stop.
  • Ryan: sends new customers a free personalized report (mold test product) via a Google Form and ChatGPT template, uncovering unexpected B2B buyers (poultry farms, a commercial kitchen) though only about 1.2 percent of buyers currently respond.
  • Cameron: revealed that a Chinese supplier had been quietly sending his wife annual cash kickbacks to secure continued orders, suggesting other sellers ask their sourcing agents whether similar kickbacks exist that could be redirected back to them.
  • Sean: shared that Chinese facing pricing for common seller software (subscriptions like Helium 10) can be significantly cheaper via WeChat based Chinese sales agents, plus a set of travel points hacks (Google Flights with Point.me, Autopilot fare drop refunds, Award Tool, single passenger searches for better award availability) and mentioned using Kiva for international micro lending.

 

In conclusion, this session is a fast, informal grab bag of real, field tested tactics across AI tooling, Amazon account mechanics, and supplier and personal relationship management, reflecting the kind of tactical peer knowledge sharing MDS events are built around.

  1. Two failed launches and why deal dependent ranking collapsed once promotions stopped
  2. Panel diagnosis: price anchoring, out of stock penalties, and weak main image design
  3. A reworked launch playbook using complementary ASIN targeting and Reddit traffic testing

cliff_notes:
Nathan Ross the Founder of Hiccapop, a $30M a year baby and toddler brand, brings two recent failed launches to a live panel (Eva Maxfield, John Spektor, Hammad Yousaf, plus audience input) for diagnosis before testing a new launch strategy on an upcoming product.

 

TWO FAILED LAUNCHES AND WHAT WENT WRONG

  • A toddler bed rail launched at $40 in a $50 to $75 competitive set relied on long tail PPC, giveaways, lightning deals, and best deals, but sales collapsed every time deals were turned off, meaning organic rank never actually took hold.
  • Panel diagnosis: waited too long to update listing photos, ran an outdated product design against newer competitor designs, and never built organic conversion independent of deals.
  • A premium dual sided foam crib mattress had strong 2024 results (900 units/month) but was forced out of stock for 15 months by a 1,700 percent China tariff; on relaunch at a lower price, it could not recover its prior BSR or rank even after matching review counts.
  • Panel diagnosis: extended out of stock periods cause Amazon's algorithm to permanently penalize ranking recovery; suggested workaround is launching a fresh ASIN and requesting a manual merge with the old listing to retain reviews while starting rank fresh.
  • A separate audience member noted that anchoring too low (e.g., $99) then trying to raise price later signals a different price tier to Amazon and can crater conversion rate and suppress the buy box, urging sellers to anchor at the intended price point from day one and use discounts or coupons instead of literal price increases.

 

KEY TACTICAL FIXES DISCUSSED

  • Complementary product ASIN targeting ("sneak attack"): instead of ASIN targeting direct competitors with far more reviews, a new listing should target adjacent, non competing products bought by the same shopper (a bed rail targeting a crib mattress page) to win frequently bought together placement without losing head to head comparisons.
  • Loss leader hero SKU strategy: in commoditized, factory direct competitive niches, keep the main keyword hero SKU near breakeven and make margin on higher priced variations (bigger size, extra features) instead.
  • Reddit as a cheap main image and creative testing channel: running ads at roughly $0.20 per click to US based, credible Reddit audiences (including niche parenting groups) to test main image variants and Meta creative before committing ad spend, since Reddit signals appear to carry real weight and cost is currently very low.
  • Extending add to cart campaigns from the old standard of two to three weeks to one to two months to solidify ranking, especially once a target price point has been set.
  • Simple main image fixes matter as much as strategy: reviewing camera angle (angled vs. straight on making a product look smaller), photographing safety details competitors get right, and using ChatGPT to reference a bestseller's image composition when redesigning a listing's own images.
  • Prime Exclusive Discounts were suggested as a way to show most Prime shoppers a lower effective price while technically keeping a higher list price visible to the small share of non Prime buyers, avoiding a full price cut signal to Amazon.
  • TikTok organic slideshows (not TikTok Shop) using a "search find in bio" call to action were described as a durable, stockout resistant way to drive external search and branded traffic to Amazon.

 

In conclusion, this session is a live, tactical postmortem showing that the real launch failures were not the PPC or deal mechanics themselves but out of stock penalties, price anchoring mistakes, and weak imagery, with the panel converging on complementary ASIN targeting and cheap external traffic testing as the core fixes to try next.

cliff_notes:
Meher Patel runs Hector AI an Amazon advertising agency turned MCP focused tech platform managing over 60 brands, and demos a Claude plugin bundling their internal ad optimization skills into one runnable workflow.

 

WHY RAW MCP ACCESS FAILS WITHOUT STRUCTURED DATA

  • Argues most MCP implementations fail because advertised ASIN, search term, and placement reports are independent by default, so Claude cannot reliably join them without hallucinating.
  • Hector's backend pre joins campaign ID, ad group ID, and search term data so a query like "which search term converted best" returns an answer in under 30 seconds instead of a guessed one.
  • Stopped building dashboard software entirely once AI made dashboards trivially replicable by anyone with a prompt, pivoting the whole company to building MCPs instead.
  • Built an MCP connecting ad performance data to WhatsApp (using ElevenLabs for translation) about 18 months ago, before Amazon's own MCP launched, winning Amazon's Innovation Challenge award for it last year.

 

THE SIX SKILL ADS OPS PLUGIN

  • Explains a skill as a saved sequence of prompts (for example: find search terms that spent over $500 with zero orders, check if they're already targeted as exact match keywords, then negate them) and a plugin as a bundle of multiple skills.
  • Search term negation: automatically finds high spend, zero order search terms and proposes exact match negation in the correct ad group.
  • Search term harvesting: pulls from both the search term report and the search query performance report to surface search terms converting better than category average that aren't yet targeted or aren't bid high enough.
  • Bid and placement correction: fixes each campaign's three placement bid adjustments first (based on revenue per click), then calculates what they call the "Hector bid" for each keyword, factoring in conversion rate, average order value, and target ACOS, adjusted downward to avoid double counting an already high placement multiplier.
  • Budget pacing loss tracking: uses Amazon's change history data to calculate estimated sales lost every time a campaign went out of budget for more than an hour, and recommends specific budget increases based on that lost revenue.
  • All six skills run together in about 30 minutes, surfacing one approval screen where the user selectively approves changes before anything executes live.
  • The plugin auto updates via a connected GitHub link, so new skills added by Hector appear automatically without users needing to reinstall or be notified.

 

SCOPE AND ROADMAP

  • Currently covers only sponsored products, sponsored brands, and sponsored display; no listing optimization, DSP, AMC, or inventory features yet, though DSP is planned.
  • Organic ranking and organic share data are being added soon to prevent paid cannibalization of keywords already ranking well organically.
  • Total sales and total ACOS (beyond ad attributed sales) are also planned additions to the budget pacing loss calculation.
  • Stresses that a clean one parent ASIN per campaign account structure is a prerequisite for running any of this at scale.

 

In conclusion, this session positions properly pre joined backend data, not raw MCP access alone, as the real unlock for reliable AI driven PPC management, packaged into an approval gated plugin the agency runs on its own 60 plus client accounts.

cliff_notes:
Anjie Liu co-founder and CEO of Fodzyme, an eight figure DTC and Amazon digestive enzyme brand, shares how her team built a clinician referral flywheel that now accounts for over 25 percent of new customers without ever paying clinicians directly.

 

WHO THIS STRATEGY FITS

  • Works best for scientifically defensible products relevant to a clear clinician segment, from early stage brands to eight or nine figure brands looking to diversify.
  • Distinguishes clinician referral (word of mouth, unpaid) from clinician wholesale (clinics stocking and reselling inventory, as Thorne and Nutrafol do), which follows a different playbook she does not claim expertise in.
  • Different clinician types (MDs, registered dietitians, naturopaths, chiropractors) have very different evidence standards, so brands need to know which segment they're targeting.
  • Requires patience: building the flywheel took three to four years to compound, though benefits started earlier, and it takes an average of three months for a new clinician contact to make a first referral, five months to become a repeat referrer.

 

A TIERED APPROACH TO CLINICAL CREDIBILITY

  • Started with a roughly $30,000 in vitro study simulating the human gut, which produced a peer reviewed paper, a conference award, and early clinician trust.
  • Followed with low cost observational surveys of paying customers (a few hundred dollars for IRB ethics approval) run in partnership with academic researchers to ensure rigor and credibility.
  • Only after four years did the brand invest in a full randomized controlled trial, a six figure investment, showing that credibility can be built well before that level of spend.
  • Warns that self run, non academic surveys or borrowed ingredient research alone will not gain traction with allopathic practitioners like MDs and dietitians, though it may serve as a starting point.

 

CONFERENCES AND SAMPLES AS THE ENGAGEMENT ENGINE

  • Attends roughly a dozen conferences a year, including Digestive Disease Week, the American College of Gastroenterology, the National Dietetics Conference, and A4M (functional medicine and longevity), scaling up from just one or two shows initially.
  • Sponsors a small booth, gives out samples relentlessly, and scans attendee badges directly into the CRM; hires registered dietitians to staff the booth since clinicians trust other clinicians more than a sales team.
  • Free sample kits for clinicians include a cover letter, research highlights, and patient handouts, since clinicians frequently hand out educational materials during patient visits.
  • Runs educational webinars offering continuing education credits, a strong goodwill driver since clinicians must renew these credits periodically and most paid alternatives are expensive.

 

TRACKING AND CHANNEL RESILIENCE

  • Uses Fairing, a Shopify connected post purchase survey tool, to ask how customers found the brand and, if clinician referred, which specific clinician, helping identify top evangelists (who often never engage directly with the brand themselves).
  • Attribution stays murky since only about a third of customers complete the survey, and Amazon buyers are essentially untrackable; clinicians frequently ask about Amazon availability at conferences, treating it as a trust signal.
  • Cites a real example where a Meta tracking failure roughly halved paid new customer acquisition while clinician referrals kept flowing steadily, framing this resilience as the channel's core value.

 

GETTING STARTED

  • Recommended first steps: search existing reviews, feedback, and support tickets for mentions of doctors, dietitians, or other clinicians already recommending the product; add a post purchase survey if none exists; and calendar the top two relevant conferences early given long sponsorship lead times.

 

In conclusion, this session lays out a patient, low cost path to building an unpaid clinician referral channel, arguing that graduated investment in credibility (not a large randomized trial from day one) combined with consistent conference and sampling presence can create a durable, ad platform independent growth engine.

cliff_notes:
Douglas Iske runs Jerky.com already established on TikTok Live with a dedicated studio and five hosts, and shares how a near accidental entry into Whatnot revealed a fundamentally different, higher intent sales channel.

 

DISCOVERING A DIFFERENT KIND OF SHOPPER

  • First Whatnot show ran from a stripped down desk with a phone tripod, no studio polish, and drew only 15 to 20 viewers versus the 100 to 200 typical on TikTok Live.
  • Despite the low viewer count, that first show did $200 an hour, better than TikTok Live took a full month to reach.
  • Key insight: TikTok is an entertainment platform where sellers interrupt scrollers to create buying intent, while Whatnot users open the app specifically to shop, so a tenth of the viewers produced multiple bidders per auction versus TikTok's frequent zero or single bid outcomes.

 

GROWTH AND UNIT ECONOMICS

  • Grew from zero followers to $100,000 in the first full month, then to a run rate of $150,000 to $175,000 a month by about the three and a half month mark, becoming the 4th biggest seller in the jerky category.
  • One single day hit $7,000 in sales on $8 bags of jerky, with 159 buyers that day; average order value on Whatnot exceeds the $8.99 single bag price on the brand's own site, and repeat purchases within the same live show are common (one customer spent over $10,000 total).
  • Runs a "buyer's choice" merchandising format across more than 140 jerky flavors, showing three flavor options per auction rather than rotating single SKUs.
  • Currently runs three to four hour shows seven days a week from 10am to 11pm, describing volume as consistent rather than the peak and valley pattern seen on TikTok.

 

FULFILLMENT AS AN UNEXPECTED MOAT

  • Whatnot, not the seller, owns and manages the shipping process: buyers pay calculated shipping per item, labels print automatically after the show, and combined shipping discounts stack across purchases in the same order.
  • This separate, non integrated fulfillment process initially felt like a drawback compared to the brand's automated line, but Douglas now treats the added friction as a barrier keeping most competitors from bothering to join.
  • No current 3PL or ShipStation label integration exists, and there is currently no affiliate/creator selling structure, unlike TikTok Shop.

 

In conclusion, this session argues that Whatnot's shopper first intent, not follower count or production polish, makes it an underused, low competition channel worth testing even for brands like supplements that may assume live auction selling doesn't fit their product.

cliff_notes:
Emily Wang formerly of Amazon presents StoreClaw, an AI platform built by a 12 year e-commerce seller turned co-founder to close the gap between AI tools that only advise and AI that actually executes changes in a seller's store.

 

THE FIVE STEP PLAYBOOK FOR AI EXECUTION

  • Connects to Amazon, Shopify, and TikTok Shop stores, with Walmart support expanding for CPG sellers.
  • Steps: give the AI real business context, train it to act like an experienced operator, run it through repeated feedback loops, set explicit approval boundaries for high risk actions, then execute with API writeback and scheduled result review after a few days to a couple weeks.
  • Emphasizes that humans must approve any high risk change (ad budget changes, pricing changes, public posts) before execution, keeping final say with the seller.

 

SAMPLE WORKFLOWS

  • Conversion drop diagnosis: instead of manually checking buy box status, inventory health, and campaign changes across separate tools and teams, the AI runs the investigation as a single workflow and produces an action list, with a scheduled recheck afterward.
  • Listing optimization: scans a category, narrows to a small set of direct competitors as a benchmark, then produces a specific action list rather than a generic AI chat response to a pasted listing.
  • Multimodal content generation: turns a single product image into A+ style listing images and into six shot AI generated video with music, aiming to avoid the distorted product renders common in other AI video tools.

 

GAPS IN CURRENT AI TOOLING THE PLATFORM TARGETS

  • Most AI tools stop at advice with no closed loop from diagnosis to execution to review.
  • Recommendations improve when the AI has direct, real time access to store data rather than working from manually pasted information.
  • Aims to stay current with Amazon policy and advertising compliance rules, and expects recommendation quality to compound as the AI is used and trained over time.

 

AUDIENCE Q&A

  • On data security: the platform does not store connected store data, comparable to a typical ERP connector; a store agnostic mode is available for sellers uncomfortable connecting APIs, though feature depth is reduced without a live connection.
  • On results: no case studies were shown live, but Emily offered to share real data by email on request.
  • Multi channel inventory forecasting and 3PL/FBA replenishment automation for smaller international markets (Canada, UK, Australia) are on the roadmap but not fully built out yet.
  • Recommended first step for new users is trying the listing optimization or new listing creation skill.
  • MDS members get a two month free trial (versus the standard one month) as a summit offer.

 

In conclusion, this session pitches a closed loop AI operator model for Amazon, Shopify, and TikTok Shop sellers, positioning approval gated execution, not just AI generated advice, as the real gap StoreClaw is trying to close.

Cassidy Clawson, founder of a monthly earring subscription brand doing about $100,000 a month, breaks down a waitlist-based scarcity funnel that turned a $16.77 Meta customer acquisition cost problem into a growth engine by optimizing ad spend for cheap email leads instead of expensive direct conversions.

TOPICS:

  1. A waitlist and personality quiz funnel that filters and hypes leads before a monthly sales window
  2. The five types of scarcity and why the initiation effect drives conversion
  3. Why optimizing Meta ads for cost per lead instead of cost per acquisition cut testing costs dramatically

cliff_notes:
Cassidy Clawson runs a monthly earring subscription brand that grew to about $100000 a month in its first year, spending around $30,000 a month on Meta, built around a deliberately frictional waitlist funnel rather than a standard buy now flow.

 

THE WAITLIST FUNNEL MECHANICS

  • Customers see a Meta ad, land on a page with copy like "apply for waitlist" and "sold out," then take a personality quiz to prove brand fit rather than being able to purchase directly.
  • About 15 percent of quiz takers are screened out and rejected from joining, reinforcing exclusivity rather than diluting it.
  • Qualifying leads go into a Klaviyo waitlist and get hyped for days with countdowns and calendar invites ahead of a single monthly sales window (one Saturday, one hour) that generates about 95 percent of new member revenue.
  • A direct test replacing the waitlist with an immediate "join now" purchase flow cut conversion in half, confirming the added friction itself was driving results, not hurting them.

 

THE PSYCHOLOGY AND FIVE TYPES OF SCARCITY

  • Cites the initiation effect from 1960s social psychology research (harder entry increases loyalty and satisfaction), which she nicknames the "Supreme effect" after the hype drop retail model.
  • Identifies five scarcity levers in play simultaneously: supply, time, access, information, and identity, arguing identity ("we see you, you're our kind of people") is the most important.
  • Warns that supply based scarcity alone risks burning trust if faked and can leave real demand unmet if inventory can't keep pace with cheap lead generation.

 

WHY OPTIMIZING FOR COST PER LEAD BEATS COST PER ACQUISITION

  • Cites Motion Analytics data showing roughly 5 percent of Meta ads now absorb 85 percent of ad spend, meaning most creative tested will fail and only rare "whale" ads drive results.
  • Needing about 50 conversions per ad for statistical significance costs roughly $1,600 per ad test at a $32 CAC, versus about $250 per test when optimizing for an email lead event at $4.79 per lead.
  • Once on the list, a lead has roughly a 20 percent chance of converting in the first monthly window, rising to about 33 percent as ongoing email hype continues to work them over time.
  • Tested and abandoned Facebook Instant Form lead ads (roughly $1 per email or phone number) after finding those leads had extremely low purchase intent.

 

RESULTS AND LIMITS OF THE PLAYBOOK

  • States the scarcity funnel converts roughly 2x better than a standard funnel, with intangible brand energy benefits including customers reselling memberships informally.
  • Never discounts except a standing 10 percent teacher discount, relying on scarcity mechanics rather than price cuts to drive urgency.
  • Acknowledges in Q&A that this model depends on the product not being available on Amazon or another instant gratification channel, since Amazon's one day delivery model works against scarcity based positioning.

 

In conclusion, this session shows how deliberately adding friction and scarcity into a DTC funnel, rather than removing it, can lower blended Meta acquisition costs by making ad testing cheaper and leads more durable over time.

items.title: Run Amazon by Exception. Decide at Scale － Ary Selener － Singapore Summit 2026
items.description:
Ary Selener, head of Amazon and AI at Unibrands (27 brands across eight categories doing over $200M), breaks down a management by exception system that reduces over 200 Amazon KPIs down to four headline numbers and a tiered playbook, letting a small team steer a multi-brand portfolio and pre-plan every major Q4 pricing decision in advance.

TOPICS:

  1. A tiered KPI system reducing 200+ Amazon metrics to four numbers that actually trigger action
  2. Named owners, red lines, and pre-written playbooks for every metric that matters
  3. A Q4 decision calendar built around October cost increases and a "Q5" post-holiday harvesting window
