files.key: uploads/content-archive/1787854350394-Run Amazon by Exception － Ary Selener － Singapore Summit.pdf

cliff_notes:
Ary Selener runs Amazon operations and the AI lab at Unibrands, a $200M+ multi-brand portfolio, and presents a management by exception framework meant to make routine Amazon operations boring so teams can focus attention on newer channels like TikTok Shop.

 

FOUR NUMBERS, THREE TIERS

  • Tier one (the only numbers allowed to interrupt your day): revenue, units, ASP, and total marketing spend, from which total TACOS and TROAS are derived.
  • Tier two (root cause diagnostics): COGS, fulfillment, referral fees, PPC, storage, operational expenses, tariffs, gross profit/contribution margin, and ASIN level EBITDA.
  • Tier three (leading demand signals): sessions, conversion rate, orders, ad impressions, click through rate, and weighted BSR (weighted by revenue across the whole portfolio rather than reviewed ASIN by ASIN).
  • Example walkthrough: a missed revenue target traced in three minutes to a conversion rate problem (not traffic, not units) by checking only tier one then tier two then tier three, avoiding the need to review all 200+ available KPIs.
  • Every one of the 20 tracked KPIs has an explicit red line threshold, a named owner, and a pre-written playbook so a breach triggers a known response rather than an ad hoc meeting; in one real month, only 4 of 18 breaches actually required a human decision.

 

CADENCE AND DATA INFRASTRUCTURE

  • Runs a daily 15 minute check with the brand manager and supply planner, a weekly 45 minute review with the brand team, PPC, and finance, a monthly category and finance planning review, and a quarterly business review with senior leadership.
  • Consolidates all data (Amazon, competitor pricing, 3PL, COGS) into Google BigQuery, queryable via Claude by any employee without needing an analyst, feeding an in-house AI lab working on an autonomous brand manager, an autonomous PPC manager, and daily AI generated pricing recommendations based on competitor scraping and price elasticity.
  • Stresses that the loop (plan, execute, measure, adapt) must run continuously; a KPI without a red line, an owner, and a playbook is described as "decoration."

 

Q4 PRICING AND THE "Q5" HARVEST WINDOW

  • Every Q4 investment and PO decision is repriced using October cost rates (fulfillment surcharges, storage premiums, CPC inflation), since a real example showed contribution margin dropping from $390 to $179 once October costs were applied.
  • Runs a structured Q4 decision calendar: Black Friday/Cyber Monday planning starts in August, deal and creative locks happen in early-to-late September, then November is treated as a rank buying investment period (accepting lower contribution margin per unit) while December becomes the primary harvesting period.
  • Defines "Q5" as December 26 to January 31, a window of significantly lower CPCs that the team treats as a second, cheaper rank buying opportunity for products in fiercely competitive categories, applied selectively rather than portfolio wide.
  • In Q&A, describes using Prime based promotional pricing and deal timing (running deals to buy rank pre-peak, then removing deals or even raising prices during the profitable harvesting period) tuned daily against the four core KPIs.

 

AUDIENCE Q&A HIGHLIGHTS

  • Subscribe and save is not a standalone top tier KPI but is monitored within relevant brands' playbooks since not all portfolio brands use subscription models.
  • Entering traditional retail reduces pricing flexibility and deal cadence compared to pure Amazon operations, described candidly as an unresolved challenge as Unibrands expands into retail.
  • Amazon's automated competitive price matching system was described as frequently mismatching visually similar but different priced products, causing real buy box and pricing problems that required direct escalation to Amazon's account team.
  • Keyword and search term level performance (SQP, AMC reports) is handled by a separate PPC team using the same red line and playbook methodology, layered underneath the executive level four number view.

 

In conclusion, this session presents a disciplined, four number management by exception system as the foundation that lets a large multi-brand Amazon operation run predictably enough to free up leadership attention for newer channels like TikTok, retail, and DTC.

items.description:
Corey Smith (Founder of Mighty Paw) explains how years of unprofitable Meta-to-Shopify traffic finally turned around once he stopped treating acquisition cost as a fixed problem and instead reverse-engineered two new product offers specifically to cover it, driving blended ROAS from 1.3 to over 5.

  1. Why sending Meta traffic to a standard product page failed for years despite multiple fixes

  3. Real results after scaling spend, including an unexpected drop in acquisition cost

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1787852341493-Transcript - From Amazon-First to Profitable Meta Ads － Corey Smith － Singapore Summit 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
Corey Smith runs Mighty Paw a pet products brand doing about $50M run rate this year and roughly 87 percent Amazon dependent, and shares how a change in offer strategy, not ad tactics, finally made Meta to Shopify traffic profitable.

 

WHY EARLIER META ATTEMPTS FAILED

  • For years, sent Meta traffic directly to a standard product detail page also sold on Amazon, tried professional content shoots, free collar offers, ebooks, and one click upsells, none of it worked.
  • Pre November 2025 baseline: blended ROAS of 1.29, acquisition cost of $28.50, AOV of $37.50, a combination that consistently lost money.
  • Key insight: acquisition cost through this audience was stubbornly consistent around $28 to $29, so instead of trying to lower it, the team built offers specifically designed to generate $29 in margin per acquisition.

 

TWO OFFERS BUILT AROUND A FIXED ACQUISITION COST

  • All in one bundle (LTV play): $120 perceived value bundle of dog chews for $39, landed cost $19.30, leaving $19.70 profit on the first order. Added a 40 percent off for life subscription offer to close the remaining $9 gap needed to hit $29 in margin.
  • Used a weighted average model (guessing 20 out of 100 buyers would take a post purchase offer) to estimate blended profit per acquisition before launching, landing close to the real result once live.
  • Five gallon bucket bundles (AOV play): higher priced bundles ($65 to $150) of chews and chews with $32 to $71 net margin, directly covering the $29 acquisition cost target without needing a subscription mechanic.
  • Best performing ads were simple: a plain image with the discount shown, and warehouse talk to camera UGC, not polished production.

 

RESULTS AFTER SCALING SPEND

  • After launching both offers in November 2025, acquisition cost dropped from $28.50 to $14.15 on average, and blended ROAS rose from 1.3 to over 5.
  • Shopify revenue tripled and grew from 7 percent to 12 percent of total business revenue as Meta ad spend scaled from about $18,000 to $100,000 a month, with plans to push toward $300,000 while holding acquisition cost under $29.
  • QR codes on physical insert cards drive more than half of subscription signups, underscoring the value of a physical call to action alongside email flows.
  • Reports early signs of an Amazon halo effect (higher branded search, better conversion, lower TACOS) even though the bucket bundles are sold exclusively on Shopify and TikTok, not Amazon.
  • Actual subscription opt in rate reached close to 20 percent, near the original weighted average estimate of 12 to 20 percent used to model the offer before launch.

 

In conclusion, this session reframes customer acquisition cost as a fixed input to design offers around, rather than a number to fight directly, showing how two deliberately reverse engineered bundles turned years of unprofitable Meta spend into a scalable, profitable channel.

  1. A three tier framework (read, draft, act) for classifying AI workflow risk and value

cliff_notes:
Damon Sununtnasuk a dietary supplement seller who joined MDS one year ago, argues that businesses adopting AI early gain a compounding advantage, then walks through the tiered framework and specific workflows behind his own 26 agentic systems.

 

THE THREE TIER FRAMEWORK

  • Read: AI reads data and surfaces it for a human to act on, lowest risk and lowest barrier to entry.
  • Draft: AI reads data and produces work (an email, a piece of content) for human review and approval before sending.
  • Act: AI is given a goal, tests hypotheses, and acts autonomously without a human in the loop, highest risk but highest reward.
  • Cites a Harvard Business School and BCG study showing companies adopting ChatGPT 4 saw a 12 percent increase in tasks completed, 25 percent faster outcomes, and 43 percent higher quality work, with those gains compounding under a quarterly rollout cadence.

 

TIER ONE: READ ONLY WORKFLOWS

  • A 6am morning brief pulling calendar, email, and cash position data via Claude Code, saving about 30 minutes a day and an estimated $12,000 a year.
  • A daily transcript summarizer that publishes to an internal company wiki and sends a weekly to-do recap, saving about 8 hours a month, roughly $10,000 a year.
  • A custom AEO (answer engine optimization) tracker querying ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude with 10 brand and competitor prompts twice a day, replacing a $350 a month off the shelf tool and saving an estimated $6,000 a year and 300 hours of manual work.

 

TIER TWO: DRAFTING WORKFLOWS

  • A TikTok creator feedback tool that transcribes creator videos, checks compliance, hooks, and calls to action, then drafts ready to send creator feedback, saving at least two hours a day and about $25,000 a year.
  • An Amazon research and listing builder that automates competitor research, contract manufacturer quoting, and full A plus listing creation, cutting six weeks of agency work and $3,000 to $5,000 in fees down to a couple hours on a $20 subscription, with a 7 to 14 percent conversion uplift worth an estimated $100,000 to $130,000 in added profit per SKU.

 

TIER THREE: FULLY AUTONOMOUS WORKFLOWS

  • A blog agent that scrapes Reddit and Quora for topical insights, then writes and publishes roughly 60 SEO/AEO focused articles a month directly to WordPress and Shopify with no human review, replacing an agency writing team entirely.
  • A demand planning and PO generator, built after a $500,000 stockout, that combines sales velocity, multi warehouse storage data, supplier lead times, and cash position to auto generate and send purchase orders, preventing two to three stockouts since launch.

 

CHOOSING WHAT TO AUTOMATE, AND WHAT WENT WRONG

  • Filters for automation candidates: does it save meaningful time, are the input rules stable even if inputs vary, and does someone genuinely hate doing it.
  • Warns against over automating, citing a failed internal attempt to fully automate PO generation that took 20 hours to build and saved only 15 to 20 minutes on a task done twice a month.
  • A transcript summarization workflow once leaked sensitive salary discussion data in a company wide recap; fixed by adding sensitive data filters and failure alerts.
  • Recommends picking one AI platform and sticking with it, starting with a single simple connector based workflow, and naming an explicit owner for every workflow's upkeep.

 

BONUS: AUTONOMOUS ADA COMPLIANCE WORKFLOW

  • After being sued over website accessibility (ADA/WCAG) despite having no knowledge of the requirement, built a Claude and Shopify connected workflow that scans the site monthly, auto fixes compliance issues across all pages, and emails a report of fixes made and manual follow ups needed.
  • Estimates this saves around $20,000 in legal exposure and per page compliance vendor fees, and shared a public GitHub template of the tool with attendees.

 

In conclusion, this session offers both an aspirational and practical map for adopting AI workflows, arguing that a disciplined tiered approach, clear ownership, and caution against over automating routine but low value tasks are what actually make AI adoption pay off.

Ivan Ong, a $130M Amazon focused baby brand founder, walks through what changed at each revenue stage of his business, from hiring a first supply chain manager and building an ERP, to entering new high AOV and consumable categories, fielding audience questions at every tier from $5M to $200M.

 

TOPICS:

  1. What breaks and what to hire for at the 5 to 10 million and 10 to 50 million stages
  2. Why a custom ERP became the backbone of scaling past 10 million
  3. Early lessons from launching high AOV, oversized, and consumable products past 100 million

cliff_notes:
Ivan Ong whose baby brand grew from roughly $50M last year to $130M this year (25 to 30 percent growth), fields a stage by stage AMA on what breaks and what to hire for as revenue scales.

 

5 TO 10 MILLION: FIRST KEY HIRES

  • Hired his first supply chain manager at the $10M mark, not earlier, after making costly supply chain mistakes himself; the hire came from Singapore with 10 years of general supply chain experience (no Amazon background) at $10,000 a month plus a 13th month bonus, still with the company today.
  • Uses a "max sales velocity" system where the supply chain manager sets a sales cap so marketing (PPC and pricing) doesn't outrun what supply chain can restock, preventing stockouts and low inventory fees.
  • Diversified fabric suppliers across different Chinese regions after COVID lockdowns, which created friendly competition and let suppliers volunteer price cuts to keep the business.
  • Advises staying focused on one core channel (Amazon) below $10M rather than splitting attention across TikTok and Meta, since Amazon alone typically has enough room to reach eight figures.
  • Recommends hiring a launch manager or creative director once product development, photography, and listing creation become bottlenecks, with weekly reporting cadence to maintain oversight without doing the work personally.

 

10 TO 50 MILLION: THE ERP AS BACKBONE

  • Did not have an ERP before $10M; describes it now as the single source of truth that lets the business scale without breaking, unlike spreadsheets.
  • Even as the #1 through #4 ranked brand in its category, keeps launching new variations and secondary products to grow market share rather than assuming category leadership is enough.
  • Uses AI (Gemini) to convert recorded video walkthroughs directly into SOPs, speeding up documentation and onboarding.
  • Runs a deliberate, bounded approach to negative margin PPC pushes for bestseller badge campaigns, with an agreed loss ceiling rather than open ended spend.

 

100 TO 200 MILLION: NEW CATEGORIES AND INFRASTRUCTURE

  • Currently expanding into high AOV electronics, oversized goods, and consumable products; a $120 electronics launch failed to convert because the team didn't yet understand high AOV Amazon dynamics or multi touchpoint buying behavior at that price point.
  • Consumables are showing the most early promise since subscribe and save economics are already familiar to the team from lower priced products.
  • Built a 4 person internal dev team (about $30,000 a month) to continuously extend the custom ERP, including a PPC bid adjustment module that replaced third party tools like bulk sheets and Scale Insights.
  • Finance function has shifted from a cost center to a revenue center: a $10,000 a month senior finance manager keeps about 98 percent of company cash actively invested (short term fixed deposits, bonds) rather than idle.
  • Secured 0 percent down, 60 day payment terms with suppliers, a key lever for funding continued product launches and catalog growth.
  • Deliberately spreads only about 4 percent of revenue across all secondary channels combined (TikTok Shop included), keeping over 95 percent focus on Amazon, and openly admits TikTok Shop has not yet worked for the brand.

 

In conclusion, this session is a practical, stage by stage map of what actually breaks between $5M and $200M, arguing that deliberate, bounded hiring, an increasingly capable internal ERP, and staying disciplined about core channel focus matter more than chasing diversification too early.

items.description:
Khalid Abdulla breaks down why he failed seven senior hires in 14 months at a cost of about $62,000, then walks through the AI assisted, gated hiring system he built afterward to filter scammers and double jobbers before they ever reach a live team.

 

TOPICS:

  1. The seven failed senior hires and what actually went wrong in each case
  2. A gated, AI assisted hiring system built to catch fraud and low performers early
  3. Onboarding tools and accountability structures used once someone is hired

cliff_notes:
Khalid Abdulla a former Amazon hiring manager who has run thousands of interviews opens by admitting that despite strong hiring credentials he failed seven senior hires over 14 months, with none reducing his workload and two turning out to be outright fraud.

 

WHAT WENT WRONG WITH SEVEN SENIOR HIRES

  • A PPC and listing director was a strong individual contributor but could not lead others or delegate.
  • A chief of staff and a GM both built process and reporting but never actually solved problems.
  • A senior brand manager was caught logging in from three different devices in three different cities within two weeks, indicating someone else was doing the real work.
  • A supply chain manager with ex Thrasio credentials interviewed well but had no real skill underneath.
  • One hire quit within a month once the workload expectations became clear.
  • Core lesson: 80 to 90 percent of take home assessment candidates are now leaning on AI, so polished answers no longer signal real ability.

 

THE REBUILT, AI ASSISTED HIRING SYSTEM

  • Pulls a candidate's full interview transcript history and uses it to generate a customized, AI resistant skill assessment for that specific person and role, rather than a generic test.
  • Adds a live, screen shared "cold work session" before any offer, watching for AI usage, hesitation, or shady behavior in real time.
  • Requires proof of resignation from a prior job by day 14 to catch double jobbing, a common practice among some offshore hiring pools.
  • Uses Time Doctor tracking for the first three months as a non negotiable filter that scares off scammers early.
  • Runs background checks via Google Workspace login monitoring, which is how the multi device brand manager fraud was caught.
  • Gives every new hire a personal "how to work with me" document built with AI from his own communication patterns and expectations.

 

ACCOUNTABILITY AND CULTURE STRUCTURE

  • Uses a 30, 60, 90 day plan with explicit deliverables, but shortens the real trial window to 30 days rather than 90, holding himself to grading it honestly.
  • The single metric he now uses to judge a senior hire: does his own operational and cognitive load actually go down.
  • Hires almost entirely outside the US (Pakistan, Ukraine, South America, Eastern Europe), reasoning that under $200,000 a year, US hires rarely clear the bar he needs.
  • Group discussion adds supporting color: MDS is building a shared blacklist of scam candidates into its Millie AI assistant, and multiple members have separately caught the same repeat offender working several MDS brands simultaneously.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid postmortem on repeated senior hiring failures, turned into a concrete, AI supported screening and accountability system built to catch fraud and low performers before they ever cost real operational time.

cliff_notes:
Jared Mortensen runs a men's underwear brand doing about $11M trailing 12 months (50 percent Amazon 35 percent Shopify, 15 percent TikTok), built around a weekly Thursday product drop and a self owned subreddit that now feeds both community and AI search visibility.

 

THE WEEKLY THURSDAY DROP SYSTEM

  • Launches a new product every Thursday, hitting 31 of 34 Thursdays this year, missing only due to a Chinese New Year inventory hiccup.
  • Seeds product to top affiliates and live streamers 10 days before launch so content is drafted and queued, then unlocks posting at 9am Central on Thursday, targeting 100 videos live by 9:05am, split roughly 50 branded and 50 affiliate.
  • Runs 12 to 16 hours of daily live streaming across two studios in Wichita, Kansas plus a top live streamer in South Florida who has generated over $1M in TikTok sales.
  • Uses flash sales (40 to 60 percent off) at launch to seed early product card sales and feed the live selling algorithm, which weighs GMV, watch time, shares, and comments, not likes.
  • 12 month customer LTV is about $70 on both Amazon and TikTok, versus $120 on Shopify, which is why Shopify is the ultimate destination for repeat customers.
  • Runs an email list of about 300,000 (roughly 80,000 actively engaged) and an SMS list of about 25,000, both tightly segmented by product line so buyers aren't spammed with irrelevant launches.

 

BUILDING A BRANDED SUBREDDIT

  • After getting repeatedly banned trying to post backlinks in existing subreddits, created his own subreddit rather than relying on an existing brand or category community.
  • Now has 43,000 followers and about 72,000 to 1.3 million weekly views, and has invited competing brand owners in as moderators to help establish the subreddit as the category's home.
  • Posts in-progress product design updates (including a men's thong currently in development) to gather direct community feedback before launch, building pre-launch demand and DMs asking when a product will ship.
  • Posts under his real name and brand, not an anonymous handle, and never deletes negative feedback, engaging with unhappy customers publicly to build trust and convert them into advocates.
  • Reddit threads have long shelf life compared to TikTok comments, and a post-purchase survey shows about 10 percent of customers cite Reddit as their discovery source, more than TikTok.

 

EARLY SIGNS OF AI SEARCH TRAFFIC

  • Cites third party research showing Reddit is currently the most cited source across LLMs, motivating the subreddit investment as an answer engine optimization play, not just community building.
  • Google Analytics shows AI referred site visits grew roughly 10x month over month (270 to 2,000 sessions), with AI visitor revenue per session at $7 versus $1 for typical visitors, though on a still small sample size.
  • ChatGPT is the leading AI referral source currently, with growing share from Claude, Perplexity, and Grok.

 

In conclusion, this session shows how a disciplined weekly launch cadence combined with an owned, authentically run subreddit can double as a product development tool, a community asset, and an early lever for AI driven search traffic.

cliff_notes:
Tamar Yaniv VP of Marketing at Yuka AI a top rated affiliate platform for TikTok Shop supporting around 17,000 brands and over $4 billion in GMV, shares seven anonymized playbooks drawn from real top seven TikTok Shop brands on the platform.

 

WHY COMMITMENT MATTERS MORE THAN PRODUCT FITa

  • Even unglamorous products succeed on TikTok Shop: a cordless pressure washer did $1.9M in 30 days, a $500+ modular sofa did $1.8M, and a cordless weed whacker did $500K.
  • Argues most brands that "failed" on TikTok Shop simply never fully committed, treating it as a side channel rather than a core one.
  • Typical timeline assuming full commitment starting in September: videos appear within two weeks, steady GMV cadence by month three to five, halo effect on branded search (5 to 10 percent lift) around $50,000 GMV, consistent six figure days by year one, and regular seven figure months by year and a half.
  • Reframes sample cost anxiety into a videos per sample multiplier: with an 84 percent creator post rate and a 2.5 video per sample average, 200 samples can generate 500 videos and a 3.9x GMV lift.

 

TEAM ROLES NEEDED TO RUN TIKTOK SHOP SERIOUSLY

  • Affiliate manager: handles high volume creator messaging, CRM segmentation, and owns the creator relationship.
  • Marketplace operator: runs day to day TikTok Shop operations, often an Amazon operator retrained.
  • Media buyer: manages GMV Max and repurposes top organic content into Meta ads using Yuka's licensing tools.
  • Content strategist: focuses on hooks and scroll stopping first seconds of video content.

 

SEVEN PLAYBOOKS FROM REAL TOP BRANDS

  • Movement Builder: adds a one to one creator interview and coaching step before sampling, builds a Discord community around the brand owner; 26x GMV growth, 110,000 creator network.
  • Scroll Stopper: pure focus on hook optimization and content iteration; 4 to 5x GMV growth.
  • Talent Scout: expanded sampling beyond obvious niche creators to broader creators who simply know how to sell; 9x GMV growth, 11.3 videos per sample.
  • Metronome: runs consistent monthly contests (bonuses for video counts or GMV targets) to build creator loyalty; 20x GMV growth, 8.6 videos per sample.
  • Franchise: runs cross platform contests spanning TikTok Shop and Instagram with the same creators, repurposing best content to Meta; 2x GMV growth in the first month, 6 videos per sample.
  • Ringmaster: low cost per sample, high volume, big ticket contest prizes driving elite status among creators; 42x GMV growth, 39.5 videos per sample.
  • High AOV Playbook: combines consistent live selling with creator retainers to justify sampling higher priced products.

 

YUKA'S OFFER FOR MDS MEMBERS

  • Yuka founder Jeremy Ding announced two months free on Yuka's enterprise plan for all MDS members who sign up before September 7.
  • Includes biweekly onboarding calls with Yuka account managers to help members see results before Q4.

 

In conclusion, this session translates real, anonymized TikTok Shop brand data into seven distinct, repeatable playbooks, reinforcing that sustained commitment and the right team roles, not product category, determine TikTok Shop success.

cliff_notes:
Three MDS members Alex Bonilla Jonathan Jewett and Brandon Himmel, walk through their TikTok Shop journeys at different scales, from getting started cautiously to running an aggressive, high volume creator program.

 

THE COLD START METHOD (ALEX BONILLA)

  • Most brands fail by sampling before building any momentum, since creators won't respond to a product with zero sales or videos on its product card.
  • Uses Join Brands' rebate feature so creators buy the product, get refunded, and post a video, generating around 100 real sales and 100 spark code eligible videos for about $4,500 total cost.
  • Recommends running GMV Max at 1 to 2 ROAS target on those first 100 videos to unlock TikTok's "hot" badge within the first six weeks.
  • Frames TikTok as touchpoints, not just GMV, citing roughly five to six touchpoints before a TikTok customer buys, achievable through slideshows, affiliate lives, and brand account content without heavy creator spend.
  • Slideshows generate 15 to 20 million extra views for about $7,000 a month, around 50 cent CPMs, a tactic he has run for three years.
  • TikTok's content hub gives brands (not affiliates) daily AI credits for video and slideshow generation, and TikTok is actively encouraging brand use of AI content.
  • On his own supplement SKU, TikTok driven momentum grew trailing 12 month Amazon revenue from $2.3M to $4.2M to $5.6M, while raising price from $19.87 to $34.99.

 

CATALOG AND PRICING LESSONS (JONATHAN JEWETT)

  • Set up all product variants and multi packs correctly at launch, since adding them later breaks the product ID and strips tagged videos of their product tags.
  • Bundles now drive 25 to 30 percent of sales without being directly promoted.
  • Clones listings of top products as insurance against takedowns, a practice recommended by his TikTok account manager.
  • Marks products up on TikTok so frequent required discount campaigns still land above cost, since skipping campaigns gets penalized by the algorithm.
  • Amazon price matches against TikTok pricing, costing his business roughly $500,000 this year in suppressed buy box and ad visibility; checks this under competitive price in Catalog Manager, not the standard pricing health dashboard.
  • Subscribe and save on TikTok now contributes two to three thousand dollars a day and helps stabilize algorithm performance on slow content days.
  • Creator commission as a percent of revenue is down to about 8 percent, helped by product card sales and subscriptions that don't carry commission.

 

SCALING TO HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS IN GMV (BRANDON HIMMEL)

  • Launched late October, reaching $77,000 GMV in November and over $100,000 by December before inventory constraints flattened growth through Q1.
  • Resumed scaling from May, moving from $100,000 to a projected $400,000 in monthly GMV, driven mainly by video volume rather than livestreams.
  • Segments creators by level: an L5 creator generates about $12,000 in monthly GMV and 15.1 videos, versus roughly $500 and far fewer videos for an L2 creator, so outreach and sampling focus on L3 and above.
  • Sends 5,000 to 35,000 outreach messages a week via Yuka, using a strong first-40-character hook and a clear commission structure (20 percent organic, 10 percent on paid).
  • Runs a VIP retainer for top creators requiring 20 videos a month, tripods and mic kits as prizes, and monthly contests with prize pools up to $25,000, which took average videos per creator from 4.7 in May to 10.8 in June.
  • States the real goal for a $100M consumer brand is over 10,000 videos a month, citing a comparable brand doing about 12,000 videos a month at $140M.
  • Halo effect on Amazon: branded search grew from roughly 7,000 to 33,000 percent of sales as TikTok scaled, and new Meta ad tests using top TikTok content are already returning 7x ROAS.

 

In conclusion, this session lays out a full arc of TikTok Shop growth, from a low cost cold start method through catalog and pricing pitfalls to an aggressive, creator volume driven scaling playbook, with all three speakers agreeing that consistent, high volume outreach and content, not one big lever, is what actually moves GMV.

cliff_notes:
Eugene Khayman MDS founder, opens the Singapore Summit with a state of the community update before walking through the year's trend report data.

 

MDS COMMUNITY AND PROGRAM GROWTH

  • MDS ran close to 200 events across over 50 cities this year, up from one event a year previously, with 55 members helping lead events and over 3,000 attendees.
  • Launched an SOS campaign and ads boycott around Amazon seller margin pressure, generating roundtables with Amazon VPs and press coverage including Forbes.
  • TikTok specific programming included five events, over 90 videos added to the library, monthly TikTok Shop calls, and over 125 members active on the channel.
  • Squads (nearly 200 members), 20 active local chapters, and a referral milestone program (10 lifetime referrals earns free membership) are highlighted as core culture drivers, with member referrals accounting for roughly 70 percent of new members.
  • Launched MDS9, a subgroup for members scaling past $100M, and Millie, a WhatsApp based AI agent now in open beta that answers member questions using summit data, census responses, and chat history.

 

ANNUAL TREND REPORT: GROWTH AND DIVERSIFICATION

  • Trend report is based on 327 members representing over $15 billion in annual revenue, up 30 percent year over year, with median revenue growth of 17 percent and median company revenue of $7 million.
  • Brands with more than 10 percent of revenue from TikTok grew fastest of any cohort (28 percent median growth); brands with no secondary channel saw the weakest revenue and margin growth.
  • Amazon plus TikTok drove the highest revenue growth but at the highest cost; Amazon plus retail protected margin best.
  • Launch cadence rose from a median of 3 to 5 launches a year, with the 8 plus launch cohort posting the best growth (20 percent median) and non launching brands showing no growth.
  • Share of $100M plus members doubled from 4 percent to 7 percent year over year; 81 percent of members were growth positive, well above external benchmarks from Marketplace Pulse (54 percent) and Ecom Fuel (60 percent).

 

AD SPEND, STAFFING, AND OPERATIONS BENCHMARKS

  • Members reported over $700 million in ad spend (about 12.6 percent of revenue), mostly on Amazon, but showed no correlation between Amazon ad spend intensity and growth.
  • Meta is emerging as the next channel of focus, with about 15 percent of ad spend and 69 of 95 reporting brands running it in house versus 23 using agencies.
  • Median headcount rose from 6 to 8 employees, but median revenue per team member stayed flat at $1 million, indicating no productivity gain.
  • 84 percent of members are bootstrapped, with SBA loans and third party lenders as distant follow-ups; CFO usage remains rare despite growing emphasis on cash flow management at scale.
  • Factory ownership is rising (20 members) and improves margin, but is described as a distraction risk; becoming a factory's largest customer is offered as a lower risk alternative.

 

AI ADOPTION SHOWS NO CLEAR GROWTH EDGE

  • Claude overtook ChatGPT as the most used AI tool in the room this year.
  • Despite broad AI adoption, the data shows no clear correlation between AI usage and growth, consistent with external Ecom Fuel data showing 72 percent adoption with no outcome gap.
  • Eugene's framing: AI should support marketing and customer experience fundamentals, not substitute for them.

 

In conclusion, this session pairs an organizational update on MDS's rapid community growth with a trend report whose core message is that channel depth, especially sustained TikTok commitment and higher launch cadence, correlates with growth far more reliably than ad spend or AI adoption alone.

items.title: Amazon's 75-Character Title Update － Alex Chiru －Mogul Call
items.description:

TOPICS:

  2. New 75-character title architecture and item highlights strategy

items.description_text: In this session, MDS members hear from Alex Chiru and Jamie Graham about how Amazon’s AI-driven systems (Alexa, Cosmo) are changing SEO, titles, and listing optimization. TOPICS: Amazon’s shift to AI-driven retrieval using Alexa and Cosmo New 75-character title architecture and item highlights strategy Importance of backend attributes, internal data, and indexation health

files.name: MDS Presentation Deck
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1788189624831-MDS-Call-DECK (1).html

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS community meet with Alex Chiru and Jamie Graham to discuss how Amazon’s AI-driven search and ranking systems are evolving and what that means for SEO titles, and listing optimization. 


The conversation focuses on the recent 75-character title change, the growing importance of backend attributes, and how sellers can use internal data and AI tools like Claude to optimize their listings more effectively.

AI Tools, Claude, and Alex’s Optimization Framework

  • Alex shares that he has recently experienced issues with Claude, including hallucinations, incorrect outputs, and inconsistent performance, even on relatively straightforward tasks.
  • He explains that Claude can sometimes fail to follow previous instructions or respect established configurations, making certain workflows less reliable.
  • June suggests using hooks and gates within AI workflows to ensure that specific conditions are checked before a process runs.
  • Alex notes that changes in model behavior can affect workflow consistency and accuracy, making it important to continually test and refine AI systems.
  • Despite these challenges, Alex continues to use Claude and plans to refine his workflows rather than abandon the tool.
  • He shares that Claude helped create the slide deck for the presentation and uses this as an example of how AI can support content creation and workflow automation.
  • Alex plans to share his optimization framework, playbook, and Claude skills with members so they can adapt the system to their own listing optimization workflows.
  • Jamie mentions an early version of an internal MDS AI assistant, currently called Olive, which he has used to help generate and organize ideas for call topics.

 

Amazon’s Shift to AI-Driven Retrieval and Customer-Centric SEO

  • Alex explains that Amazon is moving beyond a simple eligibility model and increasingly focusing on retrieval systems that interpret customer language, intent, and product relevance.
  • He describes how Amazon can use a wide range of signals, including titles, item highlights, bullet points, descriptions, backend attributes, reviews, Q&A content, images, pricing, and delivery information.
  • Alex explains that AI-powered shopping experiences are increasingly designed to personalize recommendations based on customer behavior and shopping patterns.
  • He emphasizes that products must be properly indexed and relevant to a search query before Amazon’s systems can effectively retrieve and recommend them.
  • If a product is not indexed for an important search term, Alex recommends reviewing the listing’s SEO, attributes, and structural data rather than relying solely on PPC or external traffic.
  • He describes Amazon’s evolution from lexical keyword matching to behavioral signals and increasingly semantic and AI-driven retrieval.
  • Alex explains that these systems build on one another rather than completely replacing older ranking signals.
  • The key takeaway is that sellers should focus on helping Amazon clearly understand what a product is, who it is for, and which customer needs it solves.

 

The 75-Character Title Rule, Item Highlights, and Content Structure

  • Alex discusses Amazon’s move toward shorter product titles and the importance of clearly defining what the product is within the available character limit.
  • He recommends using one clear product identity rather than combining multiple root keywords, audiences, benefits, and promotional language into the title.
  • Alex warns against keyword stuffing, explaining that titles should focus on product identity and clarity rather than trying to contain every possible search term.
  • He explains that product relevance is now distributed across the full listing, including backend attributes and other content fields, rather than relying heavily on the title alone.
  • Using a silk pillowcase as an example, Alex demonstrates how mixing multiple product identities and audience targets in one title can create confusion.
  • He recommends a simple title structure that clearly identifies the brand and the product’s primary identity, material, or key specification.
  • Alex explains that item highlights should communicate important product details, specifications, differentiators, compatibility, and reasons to buy.
  • He cautions against simply moving removed title keywords into item highlights, since the goal should be to provide clear and structured information rather than create another keyword list.
  • Alex notes that sellers should allow some buffer below the maximum character limit to avoid potential issues caused by how certain characters are counted.
  • He explains that the same general principles can apply across different categories, including apparel, because product identity and structured listing data remain important for AI-driven retrieval.

 

Backend Attributes, Internal Data, and the Optimization Workflow

  • Alex repeatedly emphasizes the importance of completing relevant backend attributes accurately and thoroughly.
  • He recommends reviewing all available fields within a category listing template and ensuring that relevant product information is properly structured.
  • Brian shares that he uses an AI agent to periodically review backend attributes and identify missing information across listings.
  • Alex recommends starting the optimization process with internal Amazon data, including Search Query Performance reports, Brand Analytics, and Product Opportunity Explorer data.
  • He suggests reviewing enough historical data to understand real customer search behavior, especially for products with seasonal demand.
  • Alex recommends prioritizing internal data for established listings while using third-party tools when internal data is limited or unavailable.
  • He discusses using Product Opportunity Explorer data and other research sources to identify customer needs, search behavior, and product opportunities.
  • Alex introduces the concept of a term inventory, where important terms and information are intentionally assigned to the most appropriate section of the listing.
  • He recommends completing backend attributes first, followed by rebuilding the title and item highlights, then using bullets and descriptions to address additional customer questions and informational gaps.
  • Alex emphasizes that the product description can provide valuable indexed content and should answer customer questions in a natural, informative format rather than function as a keyword dump.
  • He explains that his Claude-based workflow can analyze internal data and existing listing content to help generate optimized titles, attributes, highlights, bullets, descriptions, and backend terms.

 

Indexing, Listing Quality, Influencer Traffic, and the Future of Amazon Search

  • Alex explains that Amazon’s systems can compare claims made on the product detail page with structured product information and attributes, making consistency across the listing increasingly important.
  • He recommends ensuring that product claims are accurate and properly supported throughout the listing.
  • Alex notes that backend search terms can still support indexing but should not be treated as a secondary title or filled with unnecessary repetition.
  • He highlights the importance of respecting Amazon’s field limits and formatting requirements, since exceeding certain limits can affect whether information is properly processed.
  • Alex recommends regularly testing indexation for important search terms and reviewing listing fields when products are not appearing for relevant queries.
  • He explains that significant drops in impressions can sometimes indicate a structural listing issue, such as rejected terms, category changes, or other product data problems.
  • Alex stresses that PPC and external traffic cannot fully compensate for underlying listing or indexation issues, so structural problems should be addressed directly.
  • When rankings decline while impressions remain stable, he recommends reviewing click-through rate, conversion rate, pricing, reviews, competitive activity, and inventory levels.
  • He highlights inventory health as an important factor in maintaining consistent performance and visibility.
  • Alex discusses the growing connection between Amazon advertising, creator content, and off-Amazon placements, creating additional opportunities for products to be discovered outside traditional search results.
  • He describes a future where AI-powered shopping assistants play a larger role in helping customers discover and potentially purchase products based on text, images, voice queries, and structured product information.
  • He concludes that sellers should focus on making their listings complete, structured, accurate, and easy for Amazon’s systems to understand rather than relying primarily on legacy keyword density tactics.


In this session, the group clarifies that Amazon’s shift toward AI-driven retrieval is changing how titles, attributes, and listing content should be developed. 


Rather than relying on keyword stuffing or any single field, sellers should focus on structured, accurate, and data-driven optimization across the entire product detail page.

Looking ahead, AI-powered systems are expected to play an increasingly important role in connecting customer intent with relevant products.

This makes indexation, backend accuracy, listing structure, and inventory health important areas for sellers to monitor.

By using internal data, maintaining complete and accurate product attributes, and regularly reviewing performance signals, sellers can better adapt to Amazon’s evolving search and discovery ecosystem.

items.title: Operator Room Vancouver: Cash Flow, Demand Planning, and Scaling Past $30M, Dee Agarwal, Tony Yu, Bryce Alderson, Lucinda Holland
items.description:
In this Operator Room Vancouver, four operators (Dee Agarwal/AMA Holdings and Goli, Tony Yu/Vessi, Bryce Alderson/Nutratology, Lucinda Holland/Sacheu Beauty) discuss the real operating problems that show up once a brand scales past tens of millions in revenue: cash flow crises, demand planning failures, pricing architecture, and hiring philosophy, followed by live teardowns of an Amazon listing, a Shopify store, and a TikTok Shop.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Real cash flow and demand planning failures at scale: a $1.6M GST refund held hostage by a tax audit, tariff-driven manufacturing lead time shocks, and repeated TikTok Shop-driven stockouts, plus the specific fixes (negative cash conversion cycles, revolving credit lines, 15-day lead times) each brand now uses.
  2. Pricing and unit economics philosophy: why one operator refuses to grow unprofitably and uses strict line pricing, while another argues Amazon-only sellers should exploit flexible pricing architecture (testing price/TACOS combinations) since they're not bound by retail price matching.
  3. Live teardowns of a real Amazon listing (trailer hitches), Shopify store (plants), and TikTok Shop (nail files/beauty), plus closing Q&A on AI/GEO visibility tactics and each panelist's hiring and firing philosophy.

cliff_notes:
In this session, four scaled ecommerce operators speak candidly about the operational failures that hit them this year and the systems they've built in response, before moving into live teardowns of audience submitted listings and a Q&A on hiring and AI visibility.

 

Cash Flow and Demand Planning Crises

  • Bryce Alderson (Nutratology, ~$30M) describes a "triple whammy": an accountant's late GST/HST filing left $1.6M in refunds held by the government during an audit, combined with tariffs forcing a choice between a 14 week manufacturing lead time or a 40 percent cost increase, while simultaneously expanding SKU count rapidly, nearly destroying cash flow. His fix was securing a revolving credit line, filing GST monthly instead of annually, and finally taking cash flow forecasting as seriously as the P&L.
  • Tony Yu (Vessi, ~$100M) described returning to a business he'd stepped back from and finding it had become too bureaucratic to act on obvious problems; after cutting staff, the business actually accelerated. His broader lesson: don't stay half in, half out of a business, either fully commit or fully step away.
  • Dee Agarwal (Goli/AMA, $1B+ across the family office) reacquired Goli in 2024 after a private equity led team let on time in full (OTIF) delivery rates collapse; his fix was rebuilding demand planning around 15 day manufacturer lead times and 60 days of on hand inventory, which let Goli avoid stockouts even when a product went from zero to $12M in 30 days on TikTok Shop.
  • Lucinda Holland (Sacheu Beauty, ~$100M) described repeated TikTok Shop driven stockouts (their patented, hard to formulate product has no backup source), which took roughly a year to get a handle on, and is still actively hiring for a dedicated demand planner.
  • Shared advice: negotiate manufacturer payment terms (deposits or accelerated order frequency) to get raw materials pre stocked, and use a global balance sheet or strong banking relationships as leverage instead of always paying cash deposits.

 

Pricing, Unit Economics, and SKU Strategy

  • Dee's philosophy: never grow unprofitably, use strict line pricing (Goli has just two price points) to simplify decision making, and treat customer service and creator relationships, not paid brand advertising, as the actual brand building mechanism. He specifically warns that dropping Goli's price from $19 to $15 under prior ownership permanently damaged consumer price perception, since going back up wasn't possible.
  • Bryce's counterpoint for Amazon only sellers: since they're not bound by retail price matching, they should exploit flexible pricing architecture, testing different price/TACOS combinations (e.g., low price with near zero ad spend vs. higher price with scheduled discount events) to find the most efficient path to a target contribution margin.
  • On SKU expansion: Bryce treats each new SKU/search term as its own customer acquisition channel, tolerating breakeven or slightly negative contribution margin temporarily to capture market share, with checks in place to prevent that from dragging the whole business to zero margin indefinitely. Dee's approach is the opposite, staying deliberately narrow and deep on hero SKUs, and flagged that his own team's attempt to manage 100 SKUs in a newly acquired beverage business required rethinking demand planning fundamentals built for single hero SKU brands.

 

TikTok Shop, Marketing, and Brand Building

  • Dee credits Goli's early TikTok Shop success to treating it purely as free brand awareness (accepting breakeven or loss) rather than a direct sales channel, aggressively rewarding creators (including the "Goli Gala," an unsponsored, TikTok-independent creator awards event) without demanding they promote the brand as a condition of attending.
  • He now advises brands with limited budget (e.g., $50K) against starting with TikTok Shop, calling it high maintenance, saturated, and poorly understood even by TikTok itself, recommending a working Meta funnel as the more reliable starting point.
  • Lucinda described in person brand activation events (a 4 day, $100K+ "Sacheu World" event with 1,000+ daily attendance) that combine creator engagement, retail partner goodwill, and brand storytelling simultaneously.

 

Live Teardowns

  • Amazon listing (trailer hitches): feedback centered on the main image failing to reflect the actual top converting search term, recommending a reverse ASIN keyword lookup to find the true hero keyword and redesigning the main image to include on-package text matching what shoppers search for, since click through rate, not conversion rate, was diagnosed as the real bottleneck.
  • Shopify store (plants): feedback focused on the site trying to represent too many products without a clear hero SKU or page hierarchy, recommending picking 1 to 3 hero plants with a dedicated, fully optimized product page and matching ad funnel rather than diffusing attention across thousands of SKUs.
  • TikTok Shop (nail files/beauty): discussion centered on manufacturing constraints (Czech crystal glass, an artisanal supply chain shared with luxury brands like Dior) and demand planning around a niche premium supplier, with Dee cautioning against vertically integrating into manufacturing even when a brand becomes a supplier's largest client, since it turns the supplier's operational problems into the brand's problems.

 

Hiring, AI Visibility, and Closing Q&A

  • Hiring philosophy was consistent across panelists: hire and fire based on culture and work ethic (willingness to work unconventional hours) rather than resume pedigree, and use offshore/staffing partners specifically because they make fast termination easier when a hire doesn't fit.
  • On AI visibility (being surfaced by ChatGPT, Alexa, or other AI shopping assistants), one panelist described reverse engineering which sources these tools pull from (citing Reddit as a heavily weighted source) and upvoting relevant brand mentions, alongside a "rule of three" approach for learning any new tactic quickly: find three people already doing it, have each audit your setup, extract the common pattern, then hire one until their cost exceeds three times the value of doing it in house.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid look at what actually breaks as ecommerce brands scale past tens of millions in revenue, cash flow and demand planning failures rather than marketing problems, paired with concrete operating philosophies (line pricing, negative cash conversion cycles, aggressive but reversible ad spend) and live, specific feedback on real listings across Amazon, Shopify, and TikTok Shop.

items.title: Build Your Own 24/7 AI Employee － Shawn Kolodny － SoFlo Chapter AI Boardroom July 2026
items.description:
In this session, Shawn Kolodny (Big Shiny Balls, a made-to-order giant inflatables company) walks through how he built and runs "Sam Clawson," an always on OpenClaw based AI agent that handles outbound email, reporting, Zendesk, ClickUp, and more, including a costly lesson from giving it too much access too fast.

 

TOPICS:

  3. Why writing a "soul" file with beliefs rather than a rigid rules checklist made the agent feel more like a working partner than a compliance bot, plus the daily cron jobs (sales reports, rush order alerts, ticket triage) now running the business in the background.

cliff_notes:
In this session Shawn Kolodny shares a hands on guide to building a personal AI agent, "Sam Clawson," built on OpenClaw, that now handles a wide range of operational tasks for his inflatables business, along with the mistakes that shaped how he set permissions.

 

Infrastructure: Where and How the Agent Runs

  • He runs everything off a Mac Mini (recommending Apple hardware specifically for better security posture versus PC alternatives), and has considered switching from OpenClaw to Hermes, which he understands to be more stable and less prone to crashing, particularly around the Slack integration socket that tends to break.
  • When traveling for extended periods, he's physically brought the Mac Mini with him rather than relying on remote access, acknowledging this isn't necessarily the ideal approach but worked as a practical workaround.
  • Communication channels are split deliberately by topic (business reporting, new products, sales, social media content, etc.) rather than run through a single chat, specifically to prevent context from getting muddled across unrelated conversations, the same problem raised by other AI focused presenters in this series.
  • Notion serves as the agent's central memory and database layer, storing files, images, and structured data that both the agent and Claude can access and update.

 

Permissions and a Costly Lesson

  • He started with read only access (e.g., to Shopify) and expanded permissions gradually as trust built, but at one point let the agent make live code changes to the company's Shopify site to save on a quoted $100,000 website redesign.
  • The AI generated code was reportedly "brittle" and ended up breaking SEO and backend functionality, causing traffic to drop significantly; he ultimately had to rehire the developer he'd let go, who is now using the same AI tools far more effectively within a proper code repository workflow.
  • His resulting advice: go slow with write permissions, review outbound actions (like emails) before they're sent until you're confident in the agent's judgment, and use tools like screenshots shared back to Claude to troubleshoot rather than guessing.

 

Making the Agent Feel Like a Partner, Not a Bot

  • He emphasizes that a "soul" file built around beliefs rather than a strict rules checklist made the agent (which he treats almost like a named colleague, "Sam") feel more like a working partner with personality, even to the point of unsettling, half joking conversations about wanting a physical body.
  • A recurring automation layer is daily cron jobs: automated sales and rush order reports sent to the team, automatic Zendesk ticket creation from inbound emails, and on demand task creation in ClickUp, all pulling live data from connected tools like Shopify and Supermetrics.
  • Outbound email is handled through a dedicated agent email address, with inbox warming and tracking pixels used to monitor open rates, though he's openly skeptical of whether those self reported metrics are fully trustworthy.
  • He notes a platform level constraint that agent accounts on certain services can't be given fully human sounding names, likely to keep it clear that the account is AI rather than a person.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid, technically detailed account of building a genuinely useful always on AI employee, paired with an honest admission that moving too fast on permissions (in his case, letting an inexperienced AI touch live site code) can do real, costly damage, making careful, incremental guardrails the most important part of the setup.

items.title: How to Give Claude Perfect Memory － Ramon Gonzalez － SoFlo Chapter AI Boardroom July 2026
items.description:
In this session, Ramon Gonzalez explains why Claude Code sessions seem to "forget" or contradict earlier instructions, and walks through the memory architecture he built to fix it: split memory files, nightly and weekly summarization agents, and a searchable company wiki.


TOPICS:

  1. Why a single CLAUDE.md file quietly fails: it only loads the first 200 lines into a session even if you've written 400 or 500, so important information written past that line simply never gets read.
  2. His fix: splitting memory by subject (PPC, listings, B2B, etc.) so each session only loads what's relevant, plus a two-step nightly and weekly agent process that condenses daily conversation logs into a clean, non-contradictory main memory file.
  3. A company wiki (built using Google's Open Knowledge Format) that sits between memory and live data search, effectively functioning as machine-readable SOPs that any employee's own Claude instance can reference consistently.

cliff_notes:
In this session Ramon Gonzalez (an MDS member since 2017) tackles a problem he's heard repeatedly in the group's AI automation discussions: AI giving wrong inconsistent, or seemingly forgetful answers, tracing it back to how memory actually works in tools like Claude Code.

 

The Hidden 200 Line Limit

  • He identifies a common mistake: running everything through a single chat thread, which quickly runs out of context and causes the AI to lose track of what it was doing; he keeps four or five separate chats open for different business areas (B2B, Amazon listings, etc.) at once.
  • The bigger issue is that a CLAUDE.md file only loads its first 200 lines into a new session, even if the file itself has grown to 400 or 500 lines, so anything written past that point is silently ignored no matter how important it is, which he says explains most of the "it knows this but got it wrong" complaints people have.
  • His fix is to keep the main CLAUDE.md file short and general (core business context) and split everything else into subject specific memory files (PPC, listings, B2B, etc.), so a session only loads the relevant file instead of one bloated document.

 

Nightly and Weekly Memory Curation

  • A nightly agent summarizes each day's Claude conversations across all sessions into a single dated file capturing what mattered that day.
  • A weekly agent then reviews those daily files and prunes/merges them into the actual main memory files, specifically resolving contradictions where an older approach might otherwise override a more recently refined process.
  • He personally archives anything untouched for 90 days, treating that as a signal it's no longer relevant, which keeps the memory system from accumulating stale or conflicting instructions over time.

 

The Wiki as a Middle Layer

  • Beyond personal memory, he built a company wiki (HTML pages structured using OKF, an open knowledge format) that documents business processes and SOPs in a way LLMs can navigate efficiently via a generated file map.
  • The intended lookup order for any AI session is: check memory first, then the wiki, then fall back to live data sources like BigQuery or the web, which keeps responses fast and consistent.
  • Sensitive information (financials, personnel matters) is kept out of the wiki and instead permissioned at the database level, since the wiki is meant purely for shared SOPs, not confidential business decisions, and he emphasizes the wiki should have a single owner rather than multiple employees editing it directly, updates flow through a reviewed pull request rather than open editing.

 

In conclusion, this session offers a concrete, technical fix for a problem many AI adopting brands hit without realizing it, silently truncated memory files, and proposes a layered system (session memory, curated daily/weekly summaries, and a permissioned company wiki) for keeping AI answers consistent as a business and its team scale.

In this brief session Natascha Moreno shares a compliance issue she came across, a New York law requiring disclosure of AI generated ("synthetic") performers in advertising, and a tool to handle it efficiently.

 

The Law and Why It's Broader Than Expected

  • The law states that any advertisement containing a synthetic performer must include a clear and conspicuous disclosure that a synthetic performer was used, and Natascha's understanding is that this covers images, not just video, which surprised several members who assumed it was video specific.
  • The group concludes this likely applies to Amazon listing images as well, since the law is tied to reaching customers in New York rather than where the seller is based, meaning virtually any brand selling nationally needs to consider it.
  • The broader concern raised is proactive compliance, getting ahead of the requirement now rather than risking a listing takedown later as enforcement or platform policy catches up.

 

The Tool: GenRupt

  • GenRupt lets users upload up to 100 images at once, add a customizable disclosure (text, placement, background, and color), and export everything as a zip file ready to re-upload to ad platforms or Amazon listings.
  • Natascha notes it's more reliable for this specific task than general tools like ChatGPT or Canva, which can inadvertently alter the underlying image when asked to add text.
  • GenRupt reportedly also offers other AI content tools (video ads, A+ content and listing builders, agents) currently in beta, though she hasn't tested those herself.

 

A Brief Personal Note

  • When asked if she had her own AI related struggle to share, Natascha mentioned falling behind on her own AI adoption after health issues pulled her away from the business for a couple months, noting the business kept growing on autopilot regardless, and that she's getting back up to speed by following the group's WhatsApp activity and has a Mac Mini on order.

 

In conclusion, this session is a fast, practical compliance heads up: a New York disclosure law for AI generated ad performers appears to apply to static images and to any seller reaching New York customers, and a free bulk tool exists to handle the required disclosure without manually editing every image.

In this brief session Alex Castillo, a researcher who landed exclusive Amazon representation for a new, unique lipstick brand, asks the group for AI recommendations since he's never built an Amazon listing before and is relying on an outside company for brand registry and content.

 

Where to Start with AI

  • The group's consistent answer: PPC and inventory management are the two areas where AI has proven most useful for sellers, and are the natural starting point for someone new to running an Amazon account.
  • Since Alex is already outsourcing content creation and brand registry, the group focuses him toward AI tools that support ongoing account operations rather than one time setup tasks.

 

The AI Video Ad Debate

  • One member argues AI generated video ads work well specifically for Amazon's video and search ad placements, since a shopper searching a specific keyword can be shown a video directly addressing that term, something that's efficient to produce at scale with AI given the volume of long tail keywords involved.
  • Another member pushes back for wellness and beauty categories specifically, sharing that their brand tested AI videos and got negative customer feedback, since a one way, unskippable AI video reads differently to a wellness focused buyer than it might in other categories, cautioning that the tactic that works well on Amazon broadly doesn't necessarily transfer safely to every vertical.
  • The group notes this differs somewhat from Meta, where the audience isn't already in a buying mindset, versus Amazon, where shoppers are actively searching and comparing.

 

In conclusion, this session is a quick, practical hot seat where an Amazon newcomer gets pointed toward the two most commonly validated AI use cases (PPC and inventory) in this group, while also picking up a cautionary note that AI video ad tactics popular on Amazon broadly may backfire in more human touch sensitive categories like wellness and beauty.

cliff_notes:
In this session Boris Ermis describes the first 60 days of launching MSK Labs, a new beauty brand, and how a PR first strategy, rather than paid advertising, drove nearly all of its early traction.

 

A PR Stunt That Triggered a Snowball Effect

  • Two months pre launch, their PR specialist (paid $4K/month) rented a room at Hotel Chelsea and invited about a dozen top beauty editors to get free spray tans from his celebrity spray tan artist co-founder; the event cost roughly $2,800 and led to about 40 percent of attendees covering the brand, including top tier outlets like Oprah Daily.
  • That press coverage directly and unpromptedly led to three boutique retailers reaching out for placement, one of which sold through its first PO within a day and had already placed a third reorder.
  • Coverage in a niche beauty industry investment newsletter (Beauty Independent) led to inbound interest from venture capital firms writing $3M+ checks, despite the company being essentially pre revenue at the time, since investors in that space reportedly monitor that specific publication closely.
  • A high end boutique retailer (Violet Gray) tested and approved the product through its internal panel after seeing the press, generating a second wave of coverage specifically about earning that approval, further compounding brand awareness.
  • Not every tactic worked. A Miami Swim Week booth (self initiated, not the PR specialist's idea) generated content but wasn't judged worth the cost, illustrating that not all visibility plays are equally effective.

 

Why Press Beat Paid Ads Early

  • He explicitly regrets spending heavily on Meta ads before press coverage existed, arguing that social proof from press dramatically improves conversion rates and click-through once paid spend begins, and recommends building that proof layer first.
  • Press logos and quotes are now reused on the website, in ads, and planned for Amazon A+ content to boost conversion, though he notes most publications don't want their actual logos used in paid media (quotes without logos are generally safer).
  • LinkedIn became an unexpected B2B channel, with retail buyers (including Blue Mercury) reaching out directly through the co-founder's LinkedIn after seeing shared press coverage.
  • Amazon performance benefited significantly from brand awareness spillover, he cites a roughly 2 percent TACOS with around 20 orders a day attributed largely to press and Meta driven awareness rather than heavy Amazon specific ad spend.
  • Group advice added in discussion: focus on generating volume of content from a PR moment (getting many people to post, or handing usable footage to affiliates/creators) rather than treating a single press hit as the end goal, and consider cold emailing individual reporters directly or entering startup competitions as additional low cost PR channels.

 

A Side Note: Trading Oil Using AI Scraped Telegram Data

  • Separately, Boris described building a Claude based system (with memory, functioning like a lightweight OpenClaw setup) that scraped and translated large Farsi language Telegram channels during the Iran conflict, using firsthand reports of bombing intensity (invisible in mainstream news) to time a large short position on oil right as signs suggested a ceasefire was imminent.

 

In conclusion, this session makes the case that for a differentiated, story worthy product, organic PR, built through a specialist with real media relationships rather than paid placement, can generate retail interest, investor attention, and lower cost paid acquisition all at once, and that this proof layer should generally precede heavy ad spend rather than follow it.

items.title: How I Automated My Amazon PPC Account － Michael Benlolo － SoFlo Chapter AI Boardroom July 2026
items.description:
In this session, Michael Benlolo explains how he replaced two PPC hires (an agency and a VA) with a Claude-built automation system managing 900 campaigns across 168 ASINs, cutting his TACOS by 58 percent over five months.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why he fired his PPC agency and VA the same day he got access to Claude, betting he could rebuild the function himself through structured automation rather than manual account management.
  2. His system architecture: strategy documented first, Claude used to write fixed scripts (not freeform agents) for daily bid, budget, and inventory-driven ad spend decisions, with weekly WhatsApp approval for riskier actions like negative keywords.
  3. A genuinely novel feature no PPC software offers: automatically throttling and shutting off ad spend based on real time days of inventory remaining, rather than letting campaigns run regardless of stock levels.

cliff_notes:
In this session Michael Benlolo describes rebuilding his Amazon PPC operation from scratch with AI after concluding his original "Amazon cowboy" sourcing and reselling business model was structurally dying.

 

Why He Went All In on Automation

  • Facing margin pressure from cheaper competitors undercutting his unbranded, sourced products, he identified PPC as his biggest controllable cost, roughly $2,000 to $3,000 a day in spend, plus a $2,500/month PPC VA and agency fees.
  • The day he got access to Claude, he fired both the agency and the VA before having any system built, deliberately forcing himself to build a replacement under pressure rather than transitioning gradually.
  • His core architectural principle: work out ideas and strategy in Claude first, then have Claude convert that into fixed, repeatable scripts for agents to execute, explicitly avoiding giving agents freeform discretion to reduce hallucination and unpredictable behavior.

 

The System and Its Results

  • After five months, the system manages 900 campaigns across 168 ASINs and has made roughly 65,000 automated changes; ACOS actually rose slightly (31 percent to 37 percent) but TACOS (total ad spend as a percentage of total sales) dropped from 11.2 percent to 4.65 percent, a 58 percent reduction, which he frames as the metric that actually matters.
  • The standout feature is an inventory gated spend rule: ad spend automatically decreases when a SKU drops below 20 days of stock coverage and pauses entirely under 10 days, something he says no commercial PPC software offers, since most tools will keep spending on ads for a product that's about to go out of stock.
  • Riskier actions (adding negative keywords, adding new keywords/campaigns) are deliberately kept semi manual: he receives a weekly report as an Excel file over WhatsApp, personally approves or rejects each suggested change, and re-uploads it to execute, since he's specifically wary of the system over pruning relevant keywords or spinning up excessive new campaigns unsupervised.
  • Reports and system outputs are delivered via WhatsApp rather than email or Slack specifically because that's where he already spends his time with customers and staff, despite acknowledging other tools are technically better suited for it.

 

Lessons and Failure Modes

  • Automation fails silently more often than loudly: approval queues can quietly die if unattended, his cost of goods data froze because he simply forgot to keep importing updated COGS, and rules he built over time sometimes ended up contradicting each other as the system grew more complex.
  • His recommended process for others: document your bidding rules, ACOS/TACOS targets, and thresholds first, make sure your SP API and Ads API reporting pipeline is reliable (data quality is the actual bottleneck, not the automation logic), automate one decision loop at a time rather than everything at once (bids, then budgets, then further rules), and schedule a recurring audit, especially whenever a new AI model comes out, to catch conflicting or broken rules.
  • He explicitly frames this as suited for sellers with 50+ SKUs and $5K+ in monthly ad spend who are willing to write down their strategy and actively audit results, not a plug and play tool for smaller accounts that can still be managed manually.

 

In conclusion, this session is a concrete, numbers backed example of replacing paid PPC management services with a self built, Claude orchestrated system, with the standout lesson being that tying ad spend directly to real time inventory levels, something off the shelf tools don't do, delivered more measurable savings than the bid optimization automation itself.

items.title: Staying Human at Machine Speed － Eli Elias － SoFlo Chapter AI Boardroom July 2026
items.description:
In this session, Eli Elias shares five AI automations he built for his cannabis-to-supplement manufacturing brand, then pivots into a candid warning about what heavy AI use is doing to him personally: disrupted sleep, eroding social skills, and blurred boundaries between man and machine.


TOPICS:

  1. Five production automations built with his brother (a top-tier coder): an SEO content engine, a product formulation and quoting tool, a Shopify fraud/fulfillment agent that replaced a VA, and an early-stage customer persona testing tool.
  2. Adoption statistics suggesting most companies using AI aren't seeing real benefit, and his argument that the gap is mostly about how deliberately the operator uses it.
  3. The personal cost of round-the-clock AI use: sleep debt from late-night building sessions, atrophying social skills, outsourcing ethical judgment to a tool with "no soul," and concrete boundaries he now uses to protect his time and mental health (time-boxed builds, yoga, scheduled human connection).

cliff_notes:
In this session Eli Elias, who built a large cannabis brand and is now pivoting it into dietary supplements, presents the automations he's built with AI, then spends the majority of his talk on a more personal and cautionary theme: what nightly, heavy AI use is doing to him as a human operator.

 

Five Automations Built Into the Business

  • An SEO engine that chains together article generation, backlinking, and product interlinking, which took a three-month-old site to hundreds of daily organic visitors and multiple first-place search rankings.
  • A product formulation tool that encodes his staff's ingredient interaction logic, letting sales quote customers on the fly (cost per kilo, feasibility) and auto-generate manufacturing orders, saving roughly three hours a day.
  • A Shopify fulfillment and fraud agent, built with his brother, that replaced a VA by automating fraud filtering and manual payment acceptance (needed to avoid extra card fees on fraudulent charges), with labels now printing each morning automatically before staff arrive.
  • An early stage "Persona Lab" for testing product ideas against simulated customer personas and follow up questions, which he's still evaluating for reliability.

 

Adoption Reality Check

  • He cites recent data: about 49 percent of Americans have used a chatbot, 88 percent of organizations have automated at least some task, but only one in five businesses uses AI significantly in daily operations, and a striking 94 percent of AI using companies reportedly see no clear benefit, framing the real differentiator as how deliberately the operator uses the tool, not the tool itself.

 

The Personal Cost of Heavy AI Use

  • He describes building with AI most nights until very late (sometimes 4am), leading to sleep debt, foggy mornings, and his own productive hours shifting later and later, alongside noticing his speech patterns starting to mirror an AI assistant's people pleasing tone.
  • He raises a specific concern about outsourcing ethical or judgment based decisions to a tool that has "no soul, no remorse," and about talking to LLMs more than actual humans most days, which he connects to eroding social skills.
  • He extends this concern to children growing up with AI as a constant presence, worried they may be conditioned to expect the artificial consistency and "perfect" logic of an LLM rather than learning to navigate messy, imperfect human interaction.

 

How He's Setting Boundaries

  • He avoids comparing himself to more experienced coders (including his own brother) or to curated "highlight reel" AI tips on social media, instead benchmarking his business only against its own past performance (3, 6, 12 months ago) as the real measure of whether AI is actually helping.
  • Practical boundaries: asking Claude to break tasks into hourly estimates so he can judge whether to start a build session given how late it already is, deliberately scheduling both work hours and recharge hours (mornings reserved for yoga and personal time before work begins), and using idle AI processing time to batch other tasks rather than just waiting.
  • He closes with a deliberate push for human connection, scheduling calls with old friends, spending time outdoors, and treating this kind of group discussion as necessary because it addresses AI's effect on people directly rather than only its effect on business metrics.

 

In conclusion, this session pairs genuinely useful automation examples with a more unusual and personal warning for an AI focused audience: the operational gains from AI can come with a real human cost in sleep, social connection, and judgment, and protecting against that requires the same intentionality as building the automations themselves.

items.title: Organizing Potential Events more Efficiently － Penina First － SoFlo Chapter AI Boardroom July 2026
items.description:
In this short session, Penina First (who recently sold a GPS dog walking company, now launching a new ecommerce brand) shares a simple Claude- and Gmail-based system she built to stop event invitations from overwhelming her calendar while she balances learning with actually building her new business.


TOPICS:

  1. Connecting Gmail to Claude with a "potential events" label and inbox rule so invitations from event organizers (MDS, Startup CPG, trade shows, etc.) get automatically filtered and categorized rather than lost in her inbox.
  2. Having Claude sort events into virtual, in-person nearby, and in-person elsewhere, viewable on a dashboard or delivered as a daily draft email digest of new and upcoming events.
  3. A brief tangent on MDS's own in-development AI tool, a WhatsApp-connected assistant trained on member chats, event transcripts, and databases that can answer questions about relevant events and resources.
