cliff_notes:
In this session Penina First, transitioning from a previous GPS dog walking company into a new, soon-to-launch ecommerce brand, shares a lightweight personal system for managing the sheer volume of business events competing for her time.

 

The Problem: Too Many Events, Not Enough Time to Build

  • She's intentionally spending significant time on business education and networking events (MDS and others like Startup CPG) while also trying to actually build and launch her new brand, and needed a way to decide which events are worth committing to versus skipping.
  • Some events she wants to commit to well in advance, while others she'd rather decide on day by day depending on what else is happening, so she needed a system that could hold both types of decisions without constant manual tracking.

 

The Claude and Gmail-Based Fix

  • She connected her Gmail to Claude and created a "potential events" label, with an inbox rule that automatically filters and categorizes emails from known event organizing senders (like Startup CPG) into that label rather than leaving them scattered across her inbox.
  • Claude then sorts these into categories: virtual events, in-person events nearby, and in-person events elsewhere, viewable on a dashboard organized by day, which is especially useful for things like trade shows where she might only want to attend one or two out of dozens per year.
  • Rather than checking the dashboard constantly, she receives a daily draft email each morning summarizing that day's relevant events, plus another at day's end listing newly added events, letting her passively review and pick rather than actively hunting for opportunities.
  • When asked how she originally finds new events to feed into the system, she notes it's mostly organic; one resource tends to surface others once you're actively looking, and mentions her husband separately built a similar AI-powered aggregator (KidsEvents.com) for local family events.
  • A tangent from another member reveals MDS is separately piloting its own AI assistant, accessible via WhatsApp, trained on member chats, event transcripts, and internal databases, that can answer members' questions about relevant events and resources directly.

 

In conclusion, this session is a small but practical example of using Claude as a personal filtering and triage layer for information overload, turning a flood of event invitations into a simple daily digest so a busy founder can make quick, low-effort decisions about where to spend her time.

items.title: Building Scalable Amazon Operations with Data Automation, Clean Databases, and AI －Dorian Gorski －Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Dorian Gorski discusses the creation of a closed-loop system for business automation using a structured database approach, emphasizing the equal importance of both business and operational data.

TOPICS:

  1. The approach to building reliable business automations using a tiered database structure (bronze, silver, and gold) combined with Python to prevent AI errors.
  2. The distinction and integration between business intelligence (quantitative data) and operational intelligence (qualitative data like SOPs and tasks).
  3. The process of implementing automations with a human-in-the-loop initially, capturing data receipts from decisions, and continuously optimizing workflows through feedback.
items.description_text: In this session, Dorian Gorski discusses the creation of a closed-loop system for business automation using a structured database approach, emphasizing the equal importance of both business and operational data. TOPICS: The approach to building reliable business automations using a tiered database structure (bronze, silver, and gold) combined with Python to prevent AI errors. The distinction and integration between business intelligence (quantitative data) and operational intelligence (qualitative data like SOPs and tasks). The process of implementing automations with a human-in-the-loop initially, capturing data receipts from decisions, and continuously optimizing workflows through feedback.
cliff_notes:
The provided video features a discussion on building scalable trustworthy business automations by leveraging a closed-loop system centered on data integrity and operational intelligence.

Core Principles for Scalable Automations

Dorian emphasizes that successful automation requires a foundation beyond just AI agents or chatbots. 

Key strategies include:

Prioritize Data Structure: Avoid "garbage in, garbage out" scenarios by implementing a three-tier database system.

Bronze: Raw data synced from multiple sources.

Silver: Cleaned and verified data that has passed code checks.

Gold: Verified data specifically structured for AI operational tasks.

Leverage Python and SQL: Use Python to perform deterministic data cleaning, ensuring accuracy that AI LLMs often lack when handling complex calculations.


Segment Data Types: Distinguish between Business Intelligence (quantitative data like profits and ad spend) and Operational Intelligence (qualitative data like SOPs, decision logs, and role responsibilities).


Security and Access: Never expose raw credentials directly to the team. Instead, provide team members with read-only access to the structured database, which ensures everyone uses the same verified data.



Building a Closed-Loop System

Dorian describes a cycle where automations, data, and human feedback continuously improve the system.

Automation Execution: When a business event occurs (e.g., a rank drop), the system automatically creates tasks, populates them with necessary data, and assigns them to the appropriate person based on the operational database.

Feedback Logging: Decisions made by the team, time taken, and the results of those actions are logged back into the database.

Continuous Improvement: This feedback loop allows for the refinement of SOPs, training of the team, and optimization of the automations themselves, making them more autonomous over time.

Implementation and Tools

Human in the Loop: Automations should initially include human oversight to approve risky steps until they earn their autonomy.

Infrastructure: For serious automation, Dorian recommends owning a local GPU and running local models (e.g., Qwen, DeepSeek) to avoid excessive API costs and to run complex processes in parallel.

Integration: Tools like N8N are suggested for visual debugging and consistent, deterministic workflows.

Strategic Hires: When hiring for automation roles, prioritize candidates with strong systems and operational thinking over "AI wizards," as understanding the business logic is the most critical requirement.

items.title: AI Second Brains & Portfolio Automation for Real Estate Operators － Real Estate Channel Call July 2026
items.description:
In this session, members of the MDS Real Estate Channel discuss using AI to streamline real estate and hospitality operations through automation, knowledge management, and custom software.

TOPICS:

  • Building a personal "second brain" with Claude Code connected to Gmail, Notion, ClickUp, Google Drive, and more.
  • Organizing knowledge with Markdown, GitHub, and Obsidian.
  • Creating custom tools for portfolio dashboards, expense tracking, and deal underwriting
items.description_text: In this session, members of the MDS Real Estate Channel discuss using AI to streamline real estate and hospitality operations through automation, knowledge management, and custom software. TOPICS: Building a personal "second brain" with Claude Code connected to Gmail, Notion, ClickUp, Google Drive, and more. Organizing knowledge with Markdown, GitHub, and Obsidian. Creating custom tools for portfolio dashboards, expense tracking, and deal underwriting
cliff_notes:
In this session, participants in the MDS Real Estate Channel Call discuss how they use AI tool stacks, “second brain” systems, and custom software to manage real estate and hospitality portfolios. 


The conversation centers on practical demonstrations from Jacobo and others, highlighting how they operationalize AI for data integration, portfolio management, and workflow automation.

Building a “Second Brain” with Claude Code and Connected Data Sources

  • Jacobo explains that he shifts away from experimenting with many scattered open‑source agents and “rabbit holes” and instead focuses on a stable, centralized workflow built in Claude Code.
  • He describes his “second brain” as a unified knowledge base that he builds by connecting Claude Code to multiple data sources, including Gmail, ClickUp, Notion, Google Drive, his calendar, CRM, and accounting tools.
  • Jacobo sets up connectors in Claude Code so the system continuously reads and indexes all of his emails, documents, SOPs, project boards, investor information, assets, and transactions, creating a deep, persistent understanding of his personal and business life.
  • He explains that the second brain stores content as Markdown (.md) files in a folder (e.g., named Claude.md or “Second Brain”), which lives locally on his machine and syncs to GitHub, so he retains ownership and portability of his data.
  • The second brain automatically identifies gaps and blind spots in his operations, such as noticing that a particular property lacks a pool permit, which enables him to correct issues he might otherwise miss.
  • Jacobo emphasizes that once the second brain is in place, he no longer needs to provide long prompts or background context; instead, he simply issues short, natural-language instructions (e.g., “create a new LOI for the lodge with a 20k deposit”), and the system uses the existing .md files for all necessary context.
  • He notes that this approach allows him to treat the AI as an always‑on admin or operations assistant that can recall people, deals, contracts, investor relationships, and historical decisions on demand.


Data Organization, Visualization, and Workflow Practices

  • Jacobo stresses that organizing all knowledge and work outputs into Markdown files is critical, because this structure allows any LLM or tool to read and reason over consistent, text‑based documents.
  • He maintains a central file (e.g., Claude.md or a main HQ file) that describes who he is, what he owns, his top three priorities, his rules, and where all his data and resources live, which serves as a foundational “profile” for the second brain.
  • He describes how Obsidian acts as a complementary visualization layer for his second brain, since Obsidian can open the same .md files and display them as linked notes and graphs, including on his mobile phone.
  • Jacobo explains that he does not build in Obsidian itself; instead, he uses Claude Code for generating and updating the .md files, then uses Obsidian as a front‑end to navigate, visualize, and access them anywhere.
  • He highlights that using Obsidian and GitHub together ensures durability and flexibility, because if Claude or a particular LLM becomes obsolete, his underlying markdown knowledge base still exists and can migrate to other tools.
  • He mentions that his second brain includes detailed rosters of his team members, including roles, compensation, status (current or former), and contact information, so the AI can execute tasks like emailing specific vendors or employees without re-entering details.
  • Jacobo reports that he uses voice input via Whisper Flow instead of typing, which significantly accelerates his interaction with Claude Code and makes it more natural to continuously update his second brain.


Custom Portfolio & Acquisitions Software Built on Top of AI

  • Jacobo showcases custom software he builds in a few weeks to manage his hotel portfolio, leveraging the same data‑first philosophy underpinning his second brain.
  • The software provides a portfolio‑level dashboard that shows each property’s performance, including revenue, occupancy, average daily rate (ADR), and direct booking share, presented in an EOS‑style scorecard format.
  • For each property, the tool displays key metrics such as revenue for tonight, revenue for the month, flash NOI, debt service, and free cash flow, giving him near real-time financial visibility.
  • He integrates the system with Plaid, which connects directly to his bank accounts, allowing the tool to pull transactions in real time without waiting for monthly P&Ls from accountants.
  • On the backend, he maintains a large database of merchants and how they appear in bank statements, so the software can automatically categorize transactions into buckets like utilities, supplies, CapEx, and other expense types.
  • He explains that the software can detect issues such as under‑collected no‑show fees, over‑paid commissions to OTAs like Expedia and Booking.com, and unusual increases in utilities or labor costs, then flag or alert him.
  • The acquisitions module defines “buy boxes” (e.g., waterfront, historic, specific door price ranges, seller finance, particular markets like Eureka Springs) and then continuously scans listings that match those criteria.
  • When the tool finds viable deals, he can view listings, request financials, or run quick or full underwriting scenarios, specifying assumptions like ADR, occupancy, exit cap rate, and financing type (e.g., SBA vs. bridge), and the tool immediately calculates valuations, value creation, and sensitivity analyses.
  • Jacobo notes that the tool can generate PDFs for sharing underwriting outputs and that he deploys the software to Vercel, which provides stable hosting and environment management for his applications.


Implementation Tactics, Cost Management, and Broader AI Practices

  • Jacobo recommends building durable tools as actual software deployed on platforms like Vercel with proper APIs and environment variables, rather than relying heavily on fragile agent interfaces such as “Open Claude” or similar ecosystems that frequently break after updates.
  • He uses Browserbase to circumvent the common issue of agents being blocked by websites, which allows his acquisitions tool to reliably scrape and pull listing data from online sources back into his internal system.
  • He explains that he operates with multiple LLM accounts and models to manage both cost and performance, for example using Claude Opus 5 for planning architectures and high‑level reasoning and Cursor with Grok 4.5 for faster, cheaper code implementation.
  • He clarifies that he previously overspent (around $4,000) on Fable/Claude tokens when using them for everything, and he now keeps overall spend closer to around $500 per month by segmenting workloads across subsidized plans and different tools.
  • He encourages participants to treat AI systems as collaborative builders: even as a non‑developer, he gradually learns software concepts while AI helps write code, integrate services, and refactor, resulting in production‑grade tools for his specific niche.
  • The group briefly discusses versioning and rollback of core files like Claude.md, and Jacobo confirms that because these are just editable text files under version control (e.g., GitHub), he can easily modify, update, or revert rules and configurations as needed.
  • Throughout the discussion, he emphasizes that the long‑term value lies in owning structured data (Markdown files, Git repositories, connected knowledge bases), not in any one specific LLM vendor, since models can change but the data remains portable.

In conclusion, the session illustrates how a real estate and hospitality operator uses AI not as a novelty, but as core infrastructure for data management, portfolio visibility, and deal execution. 


By centralizing information into a second brain and building targeted software on top of it, the team demonstrates a replicable model for other operators who want to modernize their workflows and make AI a durable, cost‑effective part of their business stack.

items.title: After Prime Day: Your Q4 Deal + AI Playbook － Guido Reyes － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Guido Reyes discusses how to use aggressive deal strategy and SaaS support to win rank on Amazon Prime events, and how to layer in practical AI workflows to optimize ads, inventory, and analytics.

TOPICS:

  1. Deal and SaaS strategy for Prime Day and tentpole events
  2. Brand Tailored Promotions and post-Prime Day revenue lift
  3. Practical AI/LLM setup for Amazon ops (models, data, and daily loops)

cliff_notes:
In this session Guido Reyes shares his Prime Day playbook and his outlook on AI tools for Q3 and Q4 with the MDS group. 


He covers deal strategy, promotional segmentation, the fall event calendar, PPC execution, and how he personally uses AI tools to run his operations.

Deals and Rank Strategy on Amazon

  • Guido states that running deals is the primary way to build and defend keyword rank on Amazon in 2026, and buying traffic through gray hat tactics no longer works.
  • He explains that participating in deals is not optional for serious brands that want to dominate their category.
  • He shares an example where a non-brand keyword jumped from around rank 20 to rank 7 or 9 during Prime Day because of the conversion lift from running a deal.
  • He recommends that brands with tight margins evaluate whether they can absorb deal discounts, and if they cannot, they should still find another way to stay competitive since sitting out entirely widens the gap with competitors over time.
  • He notes that Amazon rewards brands that perform well in deals by offering them more deal opportunities afterward.


SaaS (Strategic Account Services) and Vendor Relationships

  • Guido recommends that brands doing 2 million dollars a year in revenue consider SaaS, and calls it a no brainer for brands doing 5 million or more.
  • He explains that the biggest value of SaaS is the ability to unlock deals that would not otherwise qualify, plus added internal leverage with Amazon.
  • He shares that in one case, SaaS allowed him to get a Prime deal approved for a brand with a sub 4.0 star rating, which alone justified the cost.
  • He advises that if a SaaS representative is underperforming, brands should request to meet with the representative's supervisor rather than assume they are stuck with a bad fit.
  • He estimates the cost of SaaS at roughly 50,000 dollars a year, which he weighs against the value of guaranteed ad spend and access to otherwise unavailable deals.


Promotional Segmentation and the Tentpole Event Calendar

  • Guido describes brand tailored promotions as the lead in and lead out strategy surrounding a tentpole event, with cart abandoners producing the largest share of incremental revenue.
  • He states that one brand generated roughly half a million dollars in 30 days purely from turning on these promotions for the first time.
  • He shares that Amazon has tentatively confirmed the Fall Prime Day event for the first week of October, spanning two days.
  • He advises that inventory should be out of Amazon Warehousing and Distribution by September 2nd for minimal split, and by September 9th for an optimized split.
  • He recommends keeping at least 90 days of stock in fulfillment centers heading into a tentpole event to maintain buy box saturation.
  • He suggests dialing back spend on other platforms such as Meta and TikTok during Amazon tentpole events, since conversion shifts heavily toward Amazon during that window.


PPC Execution During Tentpole Events

  • Guido explains that on day one of a deal event, revenue typically outpaces spend, so he banks that early efficiency rather than pushing harder.
  • He states that he leans into increased spend on day two and day three of a multi day event once he understands the performance trend.
  • He recommends using placement and category modifiers to control spend rather than rigid budget caps, allowing high converting campaigns to spend more freely.
  • He describes segmenting spend by hour of the day, pushing budget into the hours that convert best, which for many brands falls in the early evening.


AI Tools and Daily Workflow

  • Guido frames AI models in three tiers, with frontier models such as Claude Fable and Codex used at maximum effort for the highest level planning and reasoning work.
  • He recommends using the highest available intelligence tier even for simple tasks, since current pricing is heavily subsidized relative to the capability provided.
  • He describes using Hermes paired with Obsidian as an easy way to maintain a living memory of business context that persists across model switches, and says this setup can be established within about an hour.
  • He treats his AI agents as direct reports, reviewing proposed changes before pushing them and maintaining a log of changes through an HTML file or a database for accountability and rollback.
  • He recommends starting with simple exported CSV files from tools such as Amazon reports, Scale Insights, or SellerBoard before building more complex integrations such as the Amazon Ads API, the Amazon SP API, or a custom MCP connection.
  • He advises rethinking data schema whenever there is a meaningful leap in model intelligence, since outdated schema can limit what a more capable model is able to reason about.

In closing, the session lays out a practical loop that connects deal strategy, promotional timing, inventory readiness, and AI assisted execution ahead of the Fall Prime Day event. 


One point worth flagging for your own planning is that most of the deal performance figures, such as the half million dollar promotion result, are described by Guido as approximate since he intentionally obscured exact numbers to protect the brand's identity, so treat them as directional rather than benchmarks to plan against.

items.title: All-in-one DTC: Paid Media, CRO & Community － Nnamdi Ugwu, Alice Li, Karim Dalloul － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Nnamdi, Alice, and Karim share distinct operating playbooks: Nnamdi Ugwu (Black Girl Vitamins) on community-driven ambassador events, Alice Li on building an internal AI system that now touches nearly every marketing function, and Karim Dalloul (Legion) on running a large-scale, tiered influencer content engine.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Alice's "Super Agent" platform, with more than 100 AI agents handling data monitoring, media-buying suggestions, and creative generation, plus her hiring philosophy of requiring every sub-director role to prove it can't be done by AI or offshore talent.
  2. Nnamdi's ambassador-led local events (Black Girl Vitamins) that generate the bulk of the brand's organic paid social content, and how he uses trademark protection and reformulation to manage legal risk around demographic-specific health claims.
  3. Karim's influencer content pipeline at Legion, thousands of tiered creators managed through tools like Archive/Refunnel and Brand Champ, converting raw creator content into a constant stream of testable paid ad creative.

cliff_notes:
In this session three DTC operators present distinct but complementary systems for scaling content, community, and marketing operations without proportionally scaling headcount or spend.

 

Alice Li: Building an Internal AI "Super Agent" System

  • After overhauling nearly her entire marketing team, Alice introduced a "writers' room" format (borrowed partly from TV production and modeled on an agency she considers best in class) for reviewing all content, email, SMS, funnels, creative in a live, direct feedback session; this alone roughly doubled creative win rate and lifted lead capture over 30 percent.
  • She's built out an internal AI platform, over 100 autonomous agents covering data collection, competitor ad monitoring, account performance, copywriting, and media buying suggestions, run by a dedicated head of AI she hired specifically for the role.
  • Roughly 5 percent of ad spend is currently end-to-end AI-generated (strategy through creative), with about 50 percent of ads getting AI support on copywriting; she sees the biggest near-term opportunity in AI-assisted media buying, since agents can monitor and adjust an ad account far more frequently than any human media buyer could.
  • Her hiring philosophy: every role below director level must be justified against the alternative of AI or offshore staffing, and she deliberately uses strong replacement candidates to help managers "self-discover" that an underperforming hire should be replaced, rather than mandating terminations directly.
  • She's explicit that this system took real organizational pain to reach; retention had actually been too good in prior years, leaving a team that couldn't self-manage at the pace the business now required.

 

Nnamdi Ugwu: Community and Ambassador Events at Black Girl Vitamins

  • Black Girl Vitamins grew from a private label supplement brand to roughly $180M this year (about 75 percent DTC, 25 percent Amazon) by finding a specific message: serving a historically low trust audience (Black women) with products addressing deficiencies (vitamin D, iron/anemia) more common in that community, since verified through reformulation rather than just messaging.
  • Their core growth engine is roughly 400+ customer ambassadors who host local events (paint and sips, Zumba classes, etc.) in exchange for event budget (around $800 to $1,500) plus $35/hour, generating a required shot list of interviews and content that gets edited and fed directly into Meta ad sets, some of which drive millions in sales.
  • They're intentionally expanding into underserved "tier three" cities rather than saturating major metros, and use large-scale sponsorship presence at events like Essence Fest and BeautyCon to build community reach.
  • On legal risk, Nnamdi noted they've removed explicit "for Black women" claims from the website and product labels (relying on the trademarked brand name and internal formulation choices instead) after direct warnings from the group that demographic-specific health claims require clinical substantiation that most brands, and retail buyers, will demand before a sale or shelf placement.

 

Karim Dalloul: Influencer Content at Scale (Legion)

  • Legion runs a large, tiered influencer program, thousands of creators (compensated mostly in free product and commission) generating an estimated 40 to 50 million monthly impressions, achieving roughly a 1.5 ROAS on tracked influencer spend alone (likely higher when accounting for untracked halo effects).
  • Within that pool, 50 to 70 "loyal" content creators execute precise creative briefs (scripts, shots) for testing new concepts or duplicating proven "hero" ads with different faces; a separate tool (Brand Champ) handles broader, task based influencer requests (from open-ended creative concepts to specific asks like posting a retail review) and pays out via a points system.
  • They use content tracking software (debated in the room between Archive and the cheaper Refunnel) to source and license tagged influencer content directly into paid ad testing, launching around 100 new ads a week pulled largely from organic influencer posts.
  • Legion secures broad NIL (name, image, likeness) style usage rights upfront in influencer contracts, avoiding ongoing commission payouts on ad usage that competing licensing tools would otherwise require.

In conclusion, this session shows three different paths to the same goal: generating a high volume of authentic, testable content and marketing execution without proportional headcount growth, whether through AI agents automating marketing functions, ambassador-led local events generating organic proof, or a tiered influencer pipeline feeding a constant stream of paid ad creative.

items.title: Amazon Focused #ValueAdd － Chris Kjeldsen －MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Chris Kjeldsen (CGK, Beckham, and other bedding brands doing roughly $475M combined, almost entirely on Amazon) breaks down the specific levers behind his brand's 40 percent year over year growth: product variations, aggressive PPC spend, AI-generated video ads, and a Prime Day pricing tactic.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why adding size, pack count, and color variations to legacy listings (illustrated with a pillowcase listing) was the single biggest driver of growth, more than any new product launch.
  2. His "blast PPC" philosophy, now roughly 60 percent of sales come from PPC versus 40 percent organic, a near total inversion from a few years ago, backed by a large in house team.
  3. A candid look at using near fully AI generated video ads and main images on Amazon (outperforming real video in some tests), plus a Prime Day pricing tactic involving a secondary SKU to inflate the visible discount percentage on the deals page.

cliff_notes:
In this session Chris Kjeldsen walks through the concrete tactics behind scaling CGK, Beckham, and related bedding brands to roughly $475M in combined revenue, almost entirely on Amazon, ranking his growth levers in order of impact.

 

Variations as the Number One Growth Driver

  • Chris ranks variations as the single biggest contributor to 40 percent year over year growth, ahead of new products, PPC, and AI video ads.
  • Using their pillowcase listing as an example, merging separate queen, king, two pack, and four pack listings into one clean listing with a full range of sizes, colors, and pack counts took the product from a BSR of around 1,400 to roughly 50.
  • His core principle: variations should reduce customer confusion, not add clutter, each addition needs to make the listing easier to shop, not just broader.
  • He applies the same lens to other members' listings live in the session, suggesting a beauty/supplement brand simplify a cluttered listing (mixing counts and ounce sizes inconsistently) and suggesting a pet brand consider more flavor variations, drawing a comparison to Poppi's flavor heavy lineup ahead of its $1.2B acquisition.

 

Aggressive PPC and AI Generated Ad Creative

  • Chris describes deliberately "blasting" PPC spend rather than pricing to the bottom and conserving budget, arguing that brands not aggressively growing ad spend year over year are losing ground given Amazon's ad heavy business model; PPC now makes up roughly 60 percent of sales versus 40 percent organic, a near total flip from a few years ago, managed by an approximately seven person in house PPC team.
  • Roughly 95 percent of their Amazon creative, video ads and even main/secondary product images, is now AI generated, produced by two specialists (based in Serbia and Spain) at a combined cost far below traditional video production; this generates over $1M a month in video ad driven revenue.
  • In a direct test, one of four top performing ad videos sent by his team was an actual live action video, the rest were AI generated, suggesting AI creative is now competitive on quality, not just cheaper at volume.

 

A Prime Day Pricing Tactic

  • Chris shares (with a request to keep it private) a tactic used on their newly acquired Beckham pillow brand during Prime Day: creating a secondary SKU priced higher, getting a small number of sales on it, which effectively sets a higher reference "list price" that makes the primary hero SKU's deal discount appear much larger (e.g. 50 to 60 percent off) on Amazon's deals page.
  • Other members add a related, more common tactic: maintaining an inflated strike through reference price on the listing (never actually charged) so that everyday "best deal" promotions still display a meaningful looking discount without needing to actually cut the sale price, while cautioning that inflated strike through pricing carries legal risk, particularly if mirrored on a brand's own website rather than just Amazon.

 

In conclusion, this session is a rapid fire, tactically specific look at how one of the largest bedding sellers on Amazon actually spends its time: obsessively expanding and cleaning up variations, treating PPC as a growth engine rather than a cost to minimize, leaning hard into AI generated ad creative, and exploiting deal page mechanics for outsized visible discounts during major sales events.

items.title: Retail: Shocks, Woes & Omni Effect － Jason Ko, Kevin Gould & Kyle Goguen  － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, 3 MDS Members share retail and wholesale operating knowledge: Kyle Goguen (Carbon Pickleball) on independent retail and ambassador programs, Jason Ko (Only Bean) on why retail velocity beats door count, and Kevin Gould on brand hierarchy decisions and a new AI visual merchandising tool.


TOPICS:

  1. Kyle's automated B2B wholesale stack (Shopify Plus, vetted retailer onboarding, Klaviyo flows) and a tiered, application-gated ambassador program that creates exclusivity and drives near-full conversion at product launches.
  2. Jason's case that retail velocity, not store count, is what actually matters to buyers and acquirers, illustrated by Walmart forcing an unwanted expansion that hurt shrinkage and ACV metrics.
  3. A group debate, sparked by a founder with three separate bedding brands (CGK, Beckham, and a third), over whether to consolidate multiple retail brands under one house name or keep them running as independent, competing brands, plus a live demo of an AI tool for planning and archiving retail shelf merchandising.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1785274849123-Kyle Goguen + Jason Ko + Kevin Gould _ 100M+ Ecom Founder Forum 2026 .pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session three founders present distinct retail focused topics back to back, then open into a broader group discussion about brand strategy and a live tool demo.

 

Kyle Goguen (Carbon): Independent Retail and Ambassador Programs

  • Carbon (pickleball paddles, bags, eyewear) does about $20M overall, with roughly $5M coming from 350 active B2B accounts managed by just two people; Kyle contrasts this favorably with the concentration risk of relying on one big retailer like Walmart, despite the higher volume of small account management.
  • Their B2B stack is deliberately simple: a Shopify Plus B2B storefront with tiered pricing for vetted retailers (screened to avoid resellers who'd dump product on Amazon), Streamline for accounts receivable on approved terms, and Klaviyo (already used for DTC) run the same way for wholesale repurchase flows.
  • They offer Value in Kind sponsorships to pro shops (free product in exchange for on site branding), which carries low actual cost given healthy margins but high perceived value for the retailer.
  • Their ambassador program has 3,000 vetted members across five commission tiers (roughly 5 percent up to 15 percent) driving $2.2M in ambassador generated sales last year, plus about $1M in ambassadors buying at 50 percent off for themselves (quantity capped to prevent resale), both profitable segments.
  • Kyle deliberately makes the ambassador application process feel exclusive (essay questions, skill level vetting) so it feels like a sponsorship rather than a simple discount program, and uses Discord (rather than one to one email) to let ambassadors build community with each other, drive engagement around product launches, and convert at what he describes as close to 100 percent when a new product link drops after an hour long livestream.
  • They're also testing a $35 lifetime membership (10 percent off plus an instant $35 gift card) aimed purely at driving a second purchase and brand loyalty, and are exploring a "professional" discount program for coaches and tournament organizers modeled on what athleisure brands do with yoga instructors.

 

Jason Ko (Only Bean): Why Velocity Beats Door Count

  • Only Bean (a single edamame snack product across various seasonings and pack sizes) is projecting about $80M this year (up from just over $50M last year), split roughly 40 percent Amazon, 25 percent club retail, 20 percent mass (Target, Walmart, grocery), and 10 percent DTC/TikTok.
  • His central argument: sales velocity per store matters far more than total door count, since velocity is cheaper to test, gives leverage with retail buyers (more SKUs, better terms), and is what makes a business attractive to acquirers, whereas being forced into too many doors without proven pull becomes a costly headache.
  • He cites Walmart pushing Only Bean from 400 to 2,000 stores against their wishes as a cautionary example, since it strained shrinkage rates and ACV (a digital penetration style metric) in ways that hurt the retailer relationship rather than helped it.
  • He argues ecommerce native brands have a structural advantage entering retail because they already know how to tie marketing spend to dollars (DTC/TikTok halo effects, influencer activation, packaging as a marketing asset), and are now focused heavily on retail media, aiming to push Target's digital sales penetration for their category from around 20 to 45 percent toward a consistent 50 percent plus.

 

Group Discussion: Brand Hierarchy and Retail Realities

  • A founder with three top ranked Amazon bedding brands (a pillow, a sheet brand, and a mattress protector brand) asks the group whether to unify them under one house brand (e.g. "Beckham Pillow by CGK") as he expands into DTC, TikTok, and bundling.
  • Feedback is split: one member suggests deliberately running the brands as separate, competing entities to A/B test pricing and promotions and then invest behind whichever one gains organic traction, rather than merging them (citing Grōns as a model, though noting they haven't cracked bundling either); another warns that overcomplicating brand structure adds operational headaches and urges him to "stay simple," which has been his core strength to that half billion revenue mark.
  • Jeremy (Kitch) argues that in commoditized categories like hair accessories or bedding basics, retailers primarily buy private label unless a brand has strong social/brand recognition (not just Amazon numbers) or a licensing angle, and warns that Amazon success alone won't convince a Target buyer.
  • Kevin Gould and others generally caution against jumping into retail without brand differentiation, citing margin compression from private label competition and repeated stories of retail relationships going badly (a friend's eyewear business getting crushed by Walmart's race-to-the-bottom pricing).
  • Kevin closes with a live demo of an internal AI powered visual merchandising tool his (Glamedic/DigiByte) team is building: importing full SKU libraries to drag and drop shelf layouts for specific retailer display formats (e.g. Ulta's 3, 4, and 6 foot displays), with plans to layer in sales data per shelf position and build a historical, photographed archive of category shelf sets across retailers and seasons, turning messy raw retailer reports into a visual, searchable planning system.

 

In conclusion, this session strings together three practical retail lessons, build simple but well vetted wholesale and ambassador infrastructure, chase velocity over door count, and think carefully before merging or splitting multiple retail brands, while showing a concrete example of AI being used to solve the very unglamorous, high value problem of managing shelf merchandising across many SKUs and retailers.

items.title: TV & App Shopping － Vineet Ganeriwala － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Vineet Ganeriwala of Shop LC (a vertically integrated, $250M TV home shopping company similar to a smaller QVC) explains how the company buys cheap remnant TV ad inventory to drive web traffic, and shares striking lifetime value differences across its TV, web, and mobile app customer segments.

 

TOPICS:

  1. How Tatari lets brands bid on cheap remnant linear cable and connected TV ad inventory (averaging about $2 per 30-second spot) and measures incremental website traffic in the minutes after an ad airs, since there's no clickable link to track directly.
  2. Why TV customers are dramatically more valuable than web customers (roughly $800 LTV versus $67), and why customers who shop across multiple platforms (web, TV, mobile app) have LTVs several times higher still, topping out around $3,000 for app shoppers.
  3. How Shop LC structures separate email flows by acquisition channel, moving each customer toward trying a second or third platform to compound their lifetime value.

cliff_notes:
In this session Vineet Ganeriwala describes Shop LC's business (19 years running, about $250M in revenue, live 24/7 across major cable and streaming platforms) and shares how the company applies TV industry thinking to paid advertising and customer lifetime value.

 

Buying Remnant TV Ad Inventory Through Tatari

  • Shop LC spends roughly $700 to 800K a year on TV advertising, including about $50K a month through Tatari, a platform that resells unsold ("remnant") linear cable and connected TV inventory cheaply, letting advertisers target by demographic, program, and time slot rather than buying premium spots like the Super Bowl.
  • Average cost is about $2 per 30-second spot; since there's no trackable link from a TV ad, Tatari measures incrementality by comparing website traffic in the five minutes after an ad airs against historical baseline traffic for that time slot.
  • Their blended cost per incremental visitor through Tatari is roughly $2.80 to $2.90, which at an assumed 2.5 to 3 percent conversion rate implies a customer acquisition cost close to $90, comparable to or better than their current Meta CAC.
  • They also tested QR code barcode scanning during ads for direct attribution, but scan volume was very low (262 new users), so incremental traffic modeling remains their primary measurement method.
  • Switching from broad brand awareness TV campaigns to specific product campaigns significantly lowered their cost per visit.

 

Why Lifetime Value Varies So Much by Channel

  • A pure web customer has an LTV of about $67, while a pure TV customer's LTV is around $800, reflecting how much time TV viewers spend engaged with the brand and how many products they buy in that context.
  • Customers who buy both a TV aired product and a separate web-only product (multi-platform customers) have an average order value three times higher than pure TV customers.
  • Mobile app customers have the highest LTV by far, around $3,000, and app revenue now represents more than 40 percent of total website revenue, prompting heavy investment in app download campaigns across Google, Android, and Apple.
  • Shop LC built separate, channel-specific email flows: a customer who first buys via TV gets a coupon nudging them toward the website, a website catalog buyer gets a coupon nudging them toward their auction platform, and so on, each customer exits one flow and enters another once they convert on a new platform.

 

Company Context

  • Shop LC is vertically integrated (manufacturing largely in India) and operates in the US, UK, and Germany, selling jewelry, fashion, beauty, and accessories with a catalog of about 60,000 SKUs and roughly 100 new SKUs added daily.
  • Because TV is an impulse-driven, always-changing catalog, demand forecasting works differently than ecommerce; if a hero product runs out, it's simply replaced with something else on air, and any Meta ad inventory that underperforms can be liquidated on TV instead, giving them a built-in overstock safety valve.
  • They've also built an internal AI tool for demand forecasting, and run a One for One Meal program tied to every unit sold.

 

In conclusion, this session shows how a TV-first retailer applies direct response thinking (incrementality measurement, CAC by channel) to an underused, cheap advertising inventory source, while using genuinely large LTV differences across TV, web, and app to justify pushing customers to engage across as many platforms as possible.

items.title: Building Culture, Decision Making & Exit Valuation － Jeremy Thurswell & David Ghiyam － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Jeremy Thurswell (Kitch) and David Ghiyam share hard-won lessons on why masterminds matter most for the relationships they create, how they think about exit valuation and diversification, and the decision-making and work ethic behind scaling multiple large consumer brands.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why diversified, channel-spread businesses are both more resilient and more attractive to strategic buyers than single-channel ecommerce brands, and why the sweet spot for a consumer brand exit is often before $400M in revenue.
  2. A live coaching example of clarifying a founder's actual exit goal (a specific dollar amount) before deciding on tactical questions like whether to relaunch a discontinued product line.
  3. Their shared philosophy on speed, risk, and intuition, wiring money before contracts are signed, testing new channels early (TikTok, live auction platforms), and building a culture where failure is safe because the business is diversified enough to absorb it.

cliff_notes:
In this session Jeremy Thurswell and David Ghiyam speak candidly about what they've actually gotten out of years in mastermind groups, then move into exit strategy, decision making, and the grinding work ethic behind their businesses.

 

Masterminds Are a Starting Point, Not an Ending Point

  • Jeremy frames the real value of masterminds as the one on one relationships formed outside the formal sessions, crediting an early informal group (Kitch, Mary Ruth's, Dermatology, Physicians' Choice, and others) with transforming all of their businesses.
  • He and David describe a "favor banking" philosophy, doing good for others without expecting anything back, which they say has generated significant goodwill and referrals for their staffing business, Activate Talent.
  • Both stress that trust and depth in these relationships builds over time, and that some information stays private until that trust is established.

 

Exit Valuation and Business Diversification

  • Jeremy argues that highly diversified businesses (multiple product categories, many sales channels, from Amazon to Target to salons to Faire) are both more resilient (losing one channel wouldn't require layoffs or change his quality of life) and more attractive to acquirers like L'Oréal, who he says generally won't buy single channel or accessories only businesses.
  • He suggests $300 to 350M in revenue is often the sweet spot for exiting a consumer brand (potentially a $500M to $800M sale), noting that very few consumer brands have ever sold for over a billion dollars, making the buyer pool at very large scale extremely limited.
  • In a live example, David walks a founder through clarifying his actual goal (a specific after tax dollar target) before answering a narrower question about relaunching a discontinued product line, then works backward to the EBITDA and multiple needed to hit that number, illustrating his broader point that unclear high level goals make every smaller decision confusing.

 

Speed, Risk, and Intuition

  • Both describe a bias toward instant action over process, personally wiring money on the spot rather than waiting on procurement or IT, arguing that speed to execution and willingness to overspend or make mistakes is what lets them capture momentum on emerging channels like TikTok before competitors do.
  • David frames intuition as downstream of goal clarity: once you're truly clear on your long term vision, your gut reliably signals which opportunities to chase, citing his own habit of testing people's responsiveness (texting at odd hours) as a hiring signal.
  • They discuss watching for "whisper" signals of the next big opportunity, citing live shopping/auction platforms (e.g. Whatnot) as a possible next wave, similar to how early TikTok Shop signals were spotted.
  • Jeremy explains that a diversified, well capitalized business creates room to fail safely, launching around 200 new products a year and expecting only 15 to 30 to succeed, which lets them take real chances (including large, fast bets on unproven channels) without threatening cash flow.

 

Culture and Work Ethic

  • Both are explicit that raw grind, not luck, is their core competitive advantage, describing themselves working past midnight regularly and expecting the same from key hires.
  • They pair that intensity with a strong reciprocal commitment to employees, framing loyalty and long term care for staff as essential to sustaining that level of work ethic without becoming an exploitative culture.

 

In conclusion, this session is less a single tactical lesson than a window into how two experienced operators actually think: build relationships before information, get brutally clear on your real goal before making smaller decisions, move fast enough to capture momentum on new channels, and treat diversification and work ethic as the real foundations of both resilience and exit value.

items.title: TikTok at Scale － Jay Hunter & Alex Lomov － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Alex Lomov (Snap Supplements) and Jay Hunter (formerly Mary Ruth's, now at Kylie Jenner's K20) trade detailed, scaled operating knowledge on running TikTok Shop, from creator economics to ad tools that don't work.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why TikTok rewards momentum (sales beget affiliate attention, which begets more sales) and why losing momentum, through stockouts or slowing innovation, is so hard to recover from.
  2. Creator and affiliate strategy at scale: sample volume, tiering creators by GMV level, structured giveaway/contest mechanics, and the risk of coaches poaching affiliates for competitors.
  3. A blunt rundown of which TikTok ad products actually work (GMV Max, creative boost) versus which don't (top feed, video views, consideration ads), plus why both brands treat livestreaming as a separate, highly profitable channel from affiliate video.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1785273615822-Jay Hunter + Alex Lomov _ 100M+ Ecom Founder Forum 2026 .pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Alex Lomov and Jay Hunter compare notes on running TikTok Shop at real scale, Snap Supplements having grown from roughly $35M to $70M partly on TikTok spillover, and Jay's new brand K20 hitting $5M in sales just 95 days after launch.

 

Momentum, Inventory, and the Innovation Treadmill

  • Alex frames TikTok as a "momentum platform" where success compounds (sales attract affiliates, which drives more sales) but the reverse is equally true, a stockout or slow season causes affiliates to drop a product and it's very hard to regain visibility once lost.
  • Both speakers cite inventory as their single biggest operational problem: Jay's 12 week lead time meant he couldn't fully restock after his early spike in sales, and Snap Supplements had to intentionally keep margins modest specifically to protect long term momentum rather than maximize short term profit.
  • Alex notes their old strategy of launching a new product every week (common in 2024) doesn't work as well anymore since TikTok now rewards more selective, higher production launches, meaning brands need meaningfully larger upfront investment to break in today than early movers did.
  • Both raise legal and compliance risk as a growing concern, unauthorized or exaggerated health claims by competitors, and discuss exploring joint legal action against brands making noncompliant claims that TikTok's leadership has strong incentive to ignore given internal GMV pressure.

 

Creator and Affiliate Management at Scale

  • Jay's early momentum at K20 came partly from creators green screening a single Kylie Jenner video to produce content before receiving physical samples, technically against TikTok's terms but not enforced.
  • Both stress that direct, personal relationships with mid to upper tier creators (roughly the "L3+" tier, generating $10,000 to $20,000+ GMV per month) matter more than raw creator count; a healthy mix across creator levels matters because TikTok's algorithm won't meaningfully boost a swarm of low level (L1) creators.
  • Jay described a structured giveaway mechanic that rewards consistent daily posting over 60 days with a guaranteed $1,000 payout (about $20/video) plus a randomly selected $10,000 grand prize, deliberately more achievable than competitors' unattainable "win a Lamborghini" style campaigns, alongside smaller daily $100 giveaways to keep engagement high.
  • Both warn that onboarding a top creator as a paid "coach" for the community carries real risk. Alex described a coach who was secretly hired by a competing brand and used the position to quietly poach Snap's affiliates while appearing loyal.
  • In person events (regional creator meetups, dinners with top creators) are called out as one of the best uses of marketing spend specifically for TikTok, even though events are otherwise seen as low ROI.

 

What Actually Works in TikTok's Ad Tools

  • Alex's blunt assessment after two years of testing: top feed ads are expensive with unclear incremental lift, video view ads produce cheap but low quality traffic, and TikTok's heavily promoted "consideration" ads move people to engage but not to actually buy.
  • Creative Boost gets mixed reviews. It can meaningfully lift underspending organic winners, but any performance gains disappear the moment it's turned off since GMV Max doesn't retain that learning.
  • Their shared long term approach to GMV Max is to set a profit target the business is comfortable with (Snap targets roughly 10%, K20 runs closer to a 3.5 ROAS goal) and leave it largely alone, since pushing the goal too aggressively for more profit risks losing momentum and dropping out of top rankings within a couple months.
  • Both treat livestreaming as a distinct, highly profitable channel run as its own P&L, paying inexpensive hosts (as low as $30/hour) to generate GMV without paying affiliate commissions, which anchors overall channel profitability even when affiliate video spend is less efficient. Snap noted a prior misstep in 2024 overinvesting in lives based on TikTok's (unrealized) prediction that lives would dominate sales, which pulled focus away from affiliate video and hurt performance that year.

 

In conclusion, this session is a candid, tactics heavy comparison between two brands operating TikTok Shop at very different stages, converging on the same core lessons: protect momentum above short term profit, invest personally in your best creators rather than chasing volume, be skeptical of TikTok's paid ad products, and treat livestreaming as a distinct profit engine rather than a video marketing afterthought.

items.title: Protecting Your Brand From Copycats, Counterfeits, & Unauthorized Resellers － Oliver Brocato － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Oliver Brocato (founder of Tabs Chocolate, now running a brand protection service) makes the case that copycats, counterfeits, and unauthorized resellers are quietly draining single to double digit percentages of top line revenue from most brands in the room, and pitches an AI-plus-human enforcement service to fix it.

TOPICS:

  1. The hidden cost of ignoring brand infringement: inflated CPMs and CAC from copycats bidding on your ads and keywords, lost sales to counterfeit sellers, support burden, and safety risk from unverified knockoff products.
  2. Why one-off responses (a single lawyer, a single DMCA notice) don't work at scale, illustrated by Athletic Greens having to pull off Amazon for over a year to fight the problem.
  3. How his service works: AI scrapers and reverse image/keyword/transcript search to find infringers at scale, paired with human identification analysts and enforcement agents who go after the infrastructure (vendors, agencies, tools) supporting bad actors.

In this session Oliver Brocato argues that brand infringement, not ad fatigue, tariffs, or internal theft, is quietly one of the biggest unaddressed revenue leaks for most brands in the room, drawing on his own experience scaling and exiting an eight-figure chocolate brand.

The Hidden Cost of Copycats and Counterfeits

  • He lists the main threats: TikTok Shop clones replicating products, competitors running stolen Meta ad creative (which also drives up CPMs since ads are auction based), lookalike sites bidding on branded keywords to steal search traffic, Chinese counterfeits on Alibaba/Temu/Shein, and unauthorized resellers on eBay, Walmart, and even a brand's own ASIN.
  • A quick show of hands revealed that most brands in the room aren't actively monitoring for this, whether by searching their own brand name and logo, checking the Meta ad library for stolen creative, tracking new domain registrations, or monitoring resellers for MAP violations.
  • Beyond direct revenue loss, he points to CAC inflation, added customer support volume from complaints about products that never actually shipped from the brand, negative reviews caused by counterfeit goods, and real safety concerns, citing an example of a brand whose customers were unknowingly inhaling unregulated Chinese made diffuser vapor.
  • He cites Athletic Greens as a cautionary example of what happens when this is left unaddressed: the problem escalated to the point they had to pull their product off Amazon and spend over a year fighting it.

Why One Off Enforcement Doesn't Scale

  • Most brands react ad hoc, hiring a lawyer occasionally or sending a single DMCA takedown and moving on, which he argues is insufficient given how quickly infringers multiply.
  • He contrasts this with what he calls best in class practice: weekly monitoring, dedicated enforcement headcount, and escalations at the marketplace and registrar level, going after every vendor, agency, and software tool supporting the infringing accounts, not just the accounts themselves.

The AI Plus Human Enforcement Model

  • His service uses AI scrapers to search brand keywords, product titles, logos (via reverse image search), and even transcripts from ad creative to find infringers automatically, at a scale he says would otherwise take thousands of man hours a month.
  • That automated layer is paired with identification analysts who triage and confirm bad actors, and enforcement agents who manually pursue takedowns against the infrastructure enabling them.
  • He shared brand specific threat reports prepared for people in the room (using Mary Ruth's as a live example), showing counts of infringers found and estimated monthly revenue loss, not including reputational damage.
  • The service currently works with 160+ mostly 7 to 9 figure e-commerce brands, handling hundreds of thousands of takedowns across its client portfolio, and is priced at a few thousand dollars a month, including a dedicated Slack channel, client success manager, and analyst team.

In conclusion, this session reframes brand protection as a systemic, ongoing revenue and risk issue rather than an occasional legal chore, arguing that most sellers are underinvesting in monitoring and enforcement relative to how much value copycats and counterfeiters are actively siphoning from them.

items.title: Activate Your Business with Top Global Talent － Jared Orkin － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Jared Orkin of Activate Talent pitches the group on outsourced global staffing, walking through which roles are most in demand right now and fielding pointed questions about retention, poaching, and risk.

TOPICS:

  1. The most in-demand roles agencies are placing right now: AI-focused hires, Discord community managers, financial controllers, and media buyers.
  2. How Activate Talent's model works: fast replacement guarantees, candidate vetting against actual client work samples, and safeguards against team members getting poached.
  3. Why some founders use staffing agencies specifically to reduce legal and tax risk during buyer diligence, since a patchwork of individual consulting contracts across countries can complicate an exit.

cliff_notes:
In this session Jared Orkin pitches Activate Talent's outsourced staffing model to the group, and gets pushed hard on the practical concerns founders actually have about using an agency instead of hiring directly.

The Most In Demand Roles Right Now

  • Based on recent client requests, the top asks are people who can implement AI without necessarily using full autonomous agents, for example querying NetSuite data directly to avoid paying for more seats, plus demand planning, forecasting, pricing and bundle strategy, and retention issue escalation.
  • One cited example (Hexclad) has a single "AI project manager" who runs all automation requests through a ticketing system, verified by the COO, essentially working full time just building internal AI tools.
  • Beyond AI roles, the next most requested hires are Discord community managers and moderators, TikTok affiliate managers, and finance roles like AP/AR and controllers, plus experienced media buyers.
  • For Discord specifically, Activate recruits people with backgrounds moderating large crypto communities and trains them through an internal "Activate Academy" using SOPs pulled from top performing brand Discord managers already on their roster.

How the Model Works and Its Guarantees

  • Jared's pitch centers on speed and risk reduction: interviews within about three days, and a same day or near immediate replacement if a placement doesn't work out.
  • For creative roles, candidates are only brought to interview after they've already completed a paid project using the client's real work materials, so the client sees actual output before committing.
  • On retention, when asked what stops Activate from poaching a strong hire for a different client, Jared and another team member argue it would be reputationally and financially disastrous for the business, and that their core value is a large, constantly refreshed talent pool rather than any single placed employee; they also actively discourage placed staff from updating LinkedIn to reduce direct poaching risk.
  • Activate also acts as a safety net for candidates: if a confirmed hire falls through before the person's start date, Activate reportedly keeps paying them until placing them elsewhere, which several members in the room have directly benefited from.

Why Some Founders Outsource Staffing Instead of Hiring Directly

  • One member connects this back to exit planning: having many individual consulting contracts scattered across different countries creates real risk during buyer diligence, since acquirers scrutinize country by country tax and registration compliance, and a staffing agency consolidates that risk.
  • The group closes with a live look at an actual client org chart, distinguishing offshore (Activate sourced) roles from direct US hires, to illustrate how a brand's team can be structured using this model.

In conclusion, this session is a candid, occasionally combative pitch and Q&A where a staffing founder makes the case that outsourced hiring, especially for fast growing AI, community, and finance roles, can move faster and reduce legal risk than direct hiring, while the room stress tests his retention and poaching safeguards in real time.

items.title: Influencer Selection AI System － Justin Cao － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this hot seat, Justin Cao presents an AI-powered system for discovering and vetting influencers at scale, then the group challenges him hard on whether paying celebrities like Paris Hilton and Bella Hadid for a single photo actually delivers a return.

TOPICS:

  1. Building an AI pipeline that scans an influencer's followers, bio, and recent posts (using tools like Gemini) to score fit and extract contact emails into a usable spreadsheet.
  2. The AIPL framework (awareness, interest, purchase, loyalty) and a mega-to-nano influencer pyramid for allocating budget by tier.
  3. Pushback from the group on the ROI of paying for one-off celebrity photos, and a pointed critique that the brand's marketing may be culturally mismatched with its target US audience.

cliff_notes:
In this session Justin Cao walks through an AI-driven system his team built to identify and manage influencer relationships, then opens himself up to direct group feedback on how he's actually spending that budget.

The AI Influencer Discovery Pipeline

  • The system uses AI to pull an influencer's ID, follower list, and new followers to trace how accounts grow virally, then scans bios and recent posts (using tools like Google Gemini) to gauge fit and tone, described in the room as a kind of "vibe score."
  • It also extracts contact emails from profiles automatically, compiling everything (follower counts, post content, contact info) into an Excel sheet the marketing team can quickly review instead of manually researching each account.
  • Justin frames the goal as saving significant staff time on a process that would otherwise require a lot of manual digging across many creators.
  • He ties this back to a framework he calls AIPL (awareness, interest, purchase, loyalty), stressing that loyalty and lifetime value matter more than a single sale.

The Influencer Pyramid: Mega to Nano

  • He presents a pyramid structure from mega influencers (celebrity tier, e.g. Bella Hadid, Paris Hilton) down through mid tier to nano influencers, who cost almost nothing and are used at high volume.
  • When pressed by the group for hard numbers on how this system translates into revenue, he's unable to give a clear answer on ROI or exact influencer counts on the spot, estimating a very large pool (roughly 500,000) without a clean breakdown by tier.
  • He clarifies that mega influencer costs are typically not a one time photo fee but an ongoing agency relationship (he cites roughly $500,000 a year) covering events and long term brand association, not just single content pieces.

The Celebrity Photo ROI Debate

  • The group zeroes in on a specific practice: paying around $10,000 for a single photo of a celebrity wearing the product, usable only on organic social, not in paid advertising.
  • When asked directly what the return on that spend is, Justin admits it's close to nothing in measurable ROI and frames it instead as a long term brand aspiration tied personally to the business, which he describes as his family's "third baby."
  • One member offers direct, pointed feedback: posting a celebrity like Paris Hilton next to a budget sunglasses brand can read as an obvious paid placement rather than authentic endorsement, and suggests the deeper issue is a cultural mismatch, recommending Justin hire someone from his actual US customer demographic to help align marketing spend with what that audience actually responds to.

In conclusion, this session shows a genuinely useful AI powered influencer research tool getting built and used, alongside a more emotionally driven, harder to justify celebrity marketing spend that the group challenges directly, questioning whether it serves the brand's actual customer or the founder's personal aspiration for the brand.

items.title: Hot Seat: Launch, Retire, or Relaunch － Matt Greene & Michael Corrigan － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Matt Greene & Michael Corrigan bring exit strategy questions to the group: Michael (Turtle, a travel accessories brand) is weighing whether to add a sleep supplement line, and Matt (Happy Innovations) is weighing whether to relaunch a discontinued electric trimmer business, both against the backdrop of eventually selling.

TOPICS:

  1. Why buyers and bankers discount revenue from non-consumable, one-time purchase products, even when they're profitable, and how that shapes what founders should launch.
  2. Michael's case for a magnesium glycinate-based "travel wellness" supplement line, tied to his own sleep experience, versus the risk of confusing a travel accessories buyer pool.
  3. Matt's case for reviving a $10M/year electric trimmer line to boost consumable repurchase and AOV, weighed against feedback that tools businesses get discounted and are prone to low-cost competition.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1785232794956-Michael Corrigan & Matthew Greene _ 50M+ Omnichannel Mastermind 2026 .pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Matt Greene & Michael Corrigan separately pressure test whether adding a new product category to their business helps or hurts their eventual exit, and the group (including people who've been through similar decisions) pushes back hard on both.

Michael's Pitch: A Travel Wellness Supplement Line for Turtle

  • Turtle does about $40M in revenue and 3M+ units sold on its hero product, a travel pillow, but Michael notes it has strong acquisition value and poor LTV/repeat rate, the opposite problem a supplement line could solve.
  • His personal experience with magnesium glycinate improving his sleep (roughly six and a half to seven and a half hours a night) is the seed of the idea; he's considering GABA, apigenin, and ashwagandha for travel anxiety and jet lag, framed as a "travel wellness" positioning rather than a generic supplement.
  • He cites Manscaped's subscription upsell model (a cheaper option that auto enrolls buyers into a recurring razor/oil subscription) as a structure he'd like to emulate at the point of purchase.
  • Supporting signal: of 1,000 emailed to his 300,000 person US list, 40 percent said they'd be interested in a supplement product from Turtle, though the group is careful to note that isn't the same as real buying intent.
  • His long term goal is framed as optionality: he'd keep the business long term unless a strong offer came, and sees the company as a "travel and wellness" brand rather than pure travel accessories.

Group Pushback on Michael's Plan

  • Several members warn that mixing a supplement business with a travel accessories business creates a confusing story for buyers, since supplement buyers and travel product buyers are different buyer pools, and pure play businesses are easier to sell.
  • Magnesium and caffeine style "pick me up" products are called out as extremely saturated categories, making differentiation hard without a very specific, travel tied angle (packaging suggestions include small travel packs or gummies rather than a standard 60 count bottle, positioned as something like "trip comfort" rather than sold as a plain supplement).
  • The group also raises that luggage, a related category Michael considered expanding into instead, currently has weak buyer demand and low multiples (citing Base's reported 7x EBITDA range).

Matt's Pitch: Reviving Happy Innovations' Electric Trimmer Line

  • Happy Innovations sells sweat protection and anti chafing products (men's and women's lines) and says it outsells competitors like Manscaped and Megababe in its category on Amazon and TikTok, despite those competitors having raised significant funding.
  • The company previously did about $10M/year in electric trimmers before battery supplier issues took that to zero two years ago; in the same period, the consumable business roughly tripled, so cash flow isn't the concern, valuation impact is.
  • Matt's stated exit plan is to sell in the $40 to 50 million revenue range at a strong multiple, ideally via an IPO adjacent process; the trimmer relaunch is attractive mainly if it drives more consumable customers and higher AOV, not as a standalone growth line.
  • Feedback from bankers and growth equity firms he's already spoken to was mixed to negative: the category is seen as saturated, prone to margin erosion, and likely to degrade the business's overall multiple since tools are one time purchases.

The Shared Lesson: Consumables Get Valued Differently Than One Time Purchases

  • Multiple members reinforce that acquirers discount non consumable revenue heavily, citing examples like a scaled hard goods brand that got undercut by low cost Chinese competitors, and Instant Pot's post acquisition decline, as cautionary tales for one time purchase products.
  • One member shares a parallel example from their own business: they deliberately shrank a declining lash product line to 3 percent of revenue (from a larger share) specifically to keep their growth story clean for buyers, rather than let a shrinking category dilute an otherwise strong narrative.
  • The consistent advice to both founders: talk to investment bankers now to understand how a category addition would actually be priced, and survey existing customers directly about what they'd actually buy, rather than assuming demand from indirect signals.

In conclusion, this session is less about whether either product idea could work commercially and more about a sharper question facing both founders: does adding this line make the business easier or harder to eventually sell, and in both cases the group's answer leans toward caution unless the new line clearly reinforces the core, recurring revenue story.

items.title: Giveaways That Grow Your List and Your Sales － Yoon Kim － MDS9 Mastermind
items.description:
In this session, Yoon Kim of NutriCost (a roughly $500M Amazon supplement brand) explains how scaled-down, attainable giveaways, not big, flashy prizes, turned a near-nonexistent email list into $3.9M in annual email revenue.

TOPICS:

  1. Why NutriCost's early "go big" giveaway approach (Instagram follower-driven, expensive prizes) failed to convert, and why scaling down to around $1,000 attainable prizes worked instead.
  2. The email flow structure built around each giveaway: winner announcements, consolation offers for non-winners, and welcome sequences.
  3. Company context: an Amazon-first, private label-style vitamin brand (compared to Kirkland) now expanding backward into DTC, retail, and international.

cliff_notes:
In this session Yoon Kim of NutriCost, a roughly $500M Amazon supplement business built mostly as a private label style "Kirkland of Amazon" brand, explains how the company reversed a failed giveaway strategy to build meaningful email revenue from almost nothing.

From Failed Big Prizes to Small, Attainable Ones

  • NutriCost is overwhelmingly Amazon first (roughly 70% of the business) and had almost no owned email list, since nearly all of it flowed through Amazon; the giveaway push was specifically an attempt to grow the DTC side (currently around $5M) from scratch.
  • Their initial approach, pushed by ownership to "go big" with expensive prizes to drive Instagram follows, didn't translate into sign ups that actually retained or purchased afterward.
  • The fix was scaling down to prizes around $1,000 that were desirable but attainable (e.g., a smoker/grill set, a Super Bowl TV plus DoorDash package), which meaningfully improved both retention and repeat purchases among entrants.

The Giveaway to Email Flow

  • Each giveaway campaign runs on a simple funnel: a sign up page, paid ad spend driving traffic, then automated flows that announce and celebrate winners, offer promotions to everyone who didn't win, and welcome new subscribers.
  • They run a giveaway roughly monthly and report a strong ROAS for the ad spend involved relative to the size of the resulting list.
  • Results scaled year over year: email revenue went from a baseline of $300K in 2022, to $775K after five campaigns in 2023, up to $3.91M currently, despite the list itself staying relatively small (around 10,000) because they actively prune it rather than accumulating stale subscribers.
  • Current performance sits around a 13% open rate and 0.5% click through rate on these campaigns, which the group noted has room to improve.

Company Context: An Amazon First Brand Moving Backward into DTC and Retail

  • NutriCost is discussed as one of the largest pure Amazon supplement brands, competing near Pattern owned brands, built on a low recognition, "reliable and cheap" private label style model rather than strong brand equity, in contrast to brands built the opposite way (DTC/brand first, Amazon added later).
  • The company owns its own manufacturing and 3PL (17 buildings, 1.2M+ sq ft of warehousing), which the group discusses as key to surviving COVID era supply constraints and keeping costs low, including manufacturing for other brands.
  • Growth strategy includes launching roughly 4 new SKUs a week (1,500+ SKUs total, now launching at 5,000 units instead of 1,000) to stay positioned ahead of trend spikes (e.g., creatine, methylated vitamins), plus a growing retail/wholesale business (around $100M+ across Walmart, Target, Kroger, iHerb) and early international testing via Amazon's IEB program.

In conclusion, this session is a case study in reversing a common giveaway mistake, chasing scale and vanity followers instead of attainable, repeatable offers, and shows how even a brand with minimal existing DTC infrastructure can build meaningful owned channel revenue by starting small and compounding consistently.

items.title: From $300K to $1.1M/Month: Prue Millsap's TikTok Shop Turnaround — MDS9 Masterminda
items.description:
In this session, Prue Millsap shares how her 13-year-old, one-product beauty brand went from stalling at $300K/month on TikTok Shop for years to hitting $1.1M/month in GMV, and how that success spilled over into a major jump in Amazon profitability.

TOPICS:

  1. Why agencies failed to scale her past $300K, and what changed after bringing TikTok in-house with a dedicated head of growth (seeding volume, pulling winning creatives into paid spend, and a properly built Yooka messaging funnel).
  2. The Amazon spillover effect — branded search volume rivaling the top category keyword, Amazon ad spend cut in half while sales doubled, and net margin jumping from ~16% to a 25% yearly average.
  3. The real costs of scaling fast: chronic stockouts, ~$100K in low-inventory fees, and why she recommends focusing seeding/ad spend on one or two products rather than spreading thin across a catalog.
