cliff_notes:
In this session Prue Millsap (13.5-year Amazon seller, now ~60% Amazon) walks through how her brand broke through a two-year plateau on TikTok Shop and the ripple effects that success had across the rest of the business.

 

Breaking the $300K Plateau

  • After four agencies (each running the standard 15-20 creators on retainer at 20-30 videos/month) failed to push her past $300K/month over roughly two years, she brought TikTok in-house in 2025, hiring a head of growth from Latin America with prior 8-to-9-figure scaling experience plus a VA from Pakistan.
  • The needle moved starting in November, and she hit $1.1M in GMV by mid-May — driven by a "seed at scale" strategy (targeting 30 units/day sent to creators) combined with GMV Max, a playbook she picked up largely from another operator's presentation at an MDS TikTok mastermind.
  • A key tactical shift: rather than relying solely on GMV Max to decide where to spend, she started pulling individual high-performing videos and putting dedicated ad spend behind them.
  • Her team also spent weeks building out Yooka (TikTok's messaging/CRM layer) properly — comparing the complexity to setting up Klaviyo, with fully mapped event-triggered flows — with direct coaching from Yooka's team.

The Amazon Spillover Effect

  • TikTok-driven demand pushed branded search on Amazon up to nearly match the top category keyword — unprecedented in 13 years for the brand — which drove Amazon sales up (~$34M to ~$43M) while ad spend and ACOS dropped sharply, since high-intent branded traffic doesn't need to be paid for.
  • Brand-wide contribution margin jumped from roughly $50-60K/day to $120K/day at peak, and net margin rose from 15.8% in 2025 to a 33% peak month, averaging 25% for the year.
  • She prices products roughly 20% higher on TikTok specifically to protect margin against the platform's constant pressure toward discount promotions.

The Real Costs of Scaling Fast

  • Success brought chronic stockouts — she's paid about $100K in low-inventory fees over three months and had to repeatedly air-freight packaging from China; she operates on a lean ~90-day inventory cycle that wasn't built for this scale of demand.
  • Her advice to sellers newer to TikTok: don't spread thin across many SKUs — focus seeding and spend on one or two products (often, but not always, your existing bestseller), since it takes months from seeding to scaled ad performance.
  • The group separately raised concerns about TikTok Shop's broader growth trajectory — beauty category GMV reportedly grew only ~6% quarter-over-quarter once new-brand growth is excluded, suggesting the platform may be struggling to convert past its early-adopter user base into repeat shop buyers.

In conclusion, this session is a concrete before/after case study showing that a real TikTok Shop strategy — not agency-run, in-house, seeding-heavy, and properly resourced — can meaningfully lift not just its own channel but Amazon profitability too, provided the business can absorb the inventory strain that comes with it.

items.title: Scaling TikTok Shop with Creator Communities, GMV Max, and Fulfillment Strategies － TikTok Channel Call July 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants share practical strategies to scale TikTok Shop by improving affiliate management, tightening communication with TikTok via Lark, and optimizing GMV Max campaigns. 

TOPICS:

  1. Managing TikTok creators and affiliate communities 
  2. Fulfillment and operations setup for TikTok orders 
  3. GMV Max strategy and creator outreach
items.description_text: In this session, participants share practical strategies to scale TikTok Shop by improving affiliate management, tightening communication with TikTok via Lark, and optimizing GMV Max campaigns. TOPICS: Managing TikTok creators and affiliate communities Fulfillment and operations setup for TikTok orders GMV Max strategy and creator outreach
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss tactics, tools, and team structures to scale TikTok Shop performance, with a strong focus on affiliates, community management, and GMV Max optimization. 


They share practical experiences, experiments, and lessons learned on creator management, communication with TikTok, fulfillment setup, and campaign tuning to improve sales efficiency and growth.

Managing TikTok Creators and Affiliates (Compliance, Claims, and Blocking)

  • The group discusses that some skincare creators make outlandish or non-compliant claims about products, which leads to TikTok flagging content as inappropriate and creates brand risk.
  • Participants confirm that TikTok provides ways to blacklist or block creators so they cannot tag a brand’s products, although the exact process is not fully clarified in this call.
  • One participant mentions that a mastermind session with “Hudson” indicates that creators can be blacklisted in TikTok, and that videos can also be excluded from GMV Max campaigns, though that may come too late once a video already gains views.
  • The group highlights that controversial or exaggerated claims often drive more views, which makes it harder for brands to balance performance with compliance.
  • Participants suggest escalating these issues directly with TikTok account managers, ideally through Lark, to understand formal options for blocking or restricting problematic affiliates.

Communication with TikTok via Lark and Community Tools (Lark, WhatsApp, Discord)

  • Multiple participants strongly recommend using Lark as the primary communication channel with TikTok account managers because it receives faster and more proactive support than email.
  • One member explains that when a VA accidentally turns off auto coupons in GMV Max, they message their TikTok account manager via Lark and receive an action plan and guidance to fix the resulting sales dip.
  • Another participant notes that older experiences with Lark feel ineffective because they are placed into large, low-value group chats; however, others insist that Lark now works much better and provides quick, tailored support.
  • The group describes how TikTok managers on Lark help update business documents, scrub negative reviews from subscription customers, and provide listing optimization advice and weekly performance analysis.
  • Participants mention that TikTok is pushing Lark not only for brand–account-manager communication but also as a potential platform for building creator communities, although many currently use Discord or WhatsApp instead.

Building and Managing Creator Communities (Programs, Calls, Contests, and Engagement)

  • Participants describe hiring or considering hiring a TikTok affiliate manager or community manager whose full-time focus is growing the creator community, training affiliates, and managing outreach and engagement flows.
  • One brand outlines a dual structure with an affiliate manager who runs outreach through Yuka and a community manager who runs a WhatsApp group, sends three messages per week, and drives creators into a “creator power hour” call.
  • Another brand uses Discord with VIP channels, general affiliate channels, and content ideas channels, and hosts monthly creator calls that are evolving into more frequent, collaborative sessions.
  • A VIP bonus program is described where selected creators receive an extra $1,000 on top of commissions, get access to special channels, and receive more support and feedback from the brand.
  • The group explains how monthly calls include prize announcements (e.g., tripods, gimbals, Bluetooth microphones, “starter” and “pro” creator kits), contests based on posting volume (e.g., 20 videos per month), and recognition for top performers to gamify engagement.
  • Participants emphasize that using live breakdowns of successful videos (from their own brand or large brands like Comfort, HexClad, or others) in calls helps creators understand hooks, pacing, and formats they can replicate.
  • They discuss using special guest “TikTok Shop coaches” (high-earning creators with $1M+ in TikTok Shop sales) for one-time sessions to both train affiliates and attract large creators into the brand’s ecosystem.
  • One participant shares that a mass-scheduled content calendar in WhatsApp (e.g., Monday/Wednesday/Friday breakdowns) feels like email marketing and performs poorly, teaching them that community posts must feel more organic and less “campaign-like.”
  • Another participant counters that engagement improves when posts are accompanied by polls and questions, prompting creators to interact and share feedback directly in the group.
  • The group agrees that open creator groups inevitably include occasional complaints or negative comments, but the upside of community energy, peer support, and transparency outweighs those risks.

Fulfillment, 3PLs, FBT, and Inventory Routing for TikTok Orders

  • Participants discuss moving TikTok fulfillment to 3PLs and explain that they route TikTok orders through Shopify as a central hub for order and inventory management.
  • One brand describes a setup where Shopify connects to TikTok; the default fulfillment source is a bi-coastal 3PL (East and West Coast), and when 3PL inventory runs out, orders automatically route to MCF (Multi-Channel Fulfillment) via Amazon FBA.
  • They explain that daily operations include checking for sync issues between TikTok and Shopify, especially where tracking data fails to push correctly, to avoid late-shipment penalties.
  • Another brand uses SKUPREM for routing orders primarily to a 3PL called “Tactical” in Los Angeles, and is considering moving to bi-coastal warehousing to improve shipping speed and reliability.
  • Several participants stress that FBT (Fulfilled by TikTok) significantly boosts sales, as moving winning products into FBT nearly doubles sales for some brands, so they prioritize sending inventory into FBT once demand is validated.
  • A recommended pattern is to put the main “zero product” or hero SKU into FBT for creators to tag and then use 3PL fulfillment for multipacks or variants under the same parent product.
  • Some brands do not use FBT because of oversized products or uncertainty about which sizes, variations, or multipacks will perform best, so they start with 3PL-based fulfillment and later move proven SKUs into FBT.
  • A participant raises the idea of shipping inventory directly from China into FBT, but no one on the call reports firsthand experience with that specific logistics flow.



GMV Max Strategy, Campaign Cleanup, Boosting, and Creator Outreach at Scale

  • Participants dig into GMV Max configuration, including ROAS targets, budgets, exploration status labels, boosting logic, and negation of poor-performing videos.
  • They note a newly rolled-out “Exploration Status” column in GMV Max analytics, which labels creatives as “ineligible,” “explored,” and then tags them with badges like “performing” (blue) or “outstanding” (green).
  • The group observes that some creatives with low or even 0.5 ROAS still receive an “outstanding” label, which suggests TikTok values other metrics such as CPM, engagement rate, view-through contribution, and top-of-funnel influence.
  • Participants argue that brands should avoid turning off videos that TikTok labels as “performing” or “outstanding,” even when ROAS appears weak, because these creatives may support strong product-card ROAS through multi-touch attribution.
  • One brand reports that every time they conduct a large cleanup—negating low-ROAS or no-sales videos over a 30–60 day period—sales jump by 15–20% and spend becomes more efficient, suggesting that structured pruning still adds value.
  • Others caution that overly aggressive cleanup may conflict with TikTok’s internal signals, and recommend checking product card ROAS and exploration status before deciding which creatives to kill.
  • On boosting, participants share that boosting well-performing videos often degrades performance and lowers ROAS permanently, so they now primarily boost promising but under-exposed videos or creatives that become ineligible and need to be reactivated.
  • A practical guideline emerges: boost at a minimum of $10/day for three to five days to give TikTok enough data, but avoid boosting content already labeled “outstanding” or “performing.”
  • Some brands set very high budgets (e.g., $100,000) with a strict ROAS target and let GMV Max spend up to what content volume supports; they use ROAS controls and creative volume rather than daily manual tinkering to drive growth.
  • One participant uses a 3.5 ROAS target, accepts modest contribution margin, and favors reinvesting all profit into affiliates, bonuses, samples, and community-building to accelerate overall business growth.
  • Another shares that turning on “accelerated testing” for GMV Max is recommended by TikTok/GMV guidance when too few creatives are being boosted, and they plan to monitor its impact experimentally.
  • On outreach, brands use Yuka’s social intelligence features to build creator lists from top brands’ past 12 months of creator videos, segment creators by GMV (e.g., 25k–100k vs. 100k+), and send highly personalized outreach referencing the exact brand and content they saw.
  • They emphasize that the first 40 characters of the outreach message function as a hook (e.g., “20M+ units sold, your turn to earn”), and that detailed personalization plus a clear “what’s in it for you” section (commissions, bonuses, contests) significantly lifts sample request rates.
  • Brands also incorporate Discord join links and contest details (e.g., 100-video challenges, 10k top-prize contests, 1k retainers for 20+ videos) into outreach emails and messages to convert creators into long-term community members rather than one-off posters.
  • Re-engagement flows—following up multiple times (e.g., at 3-day intervals) and reactivating creators whose old videos performed well months ago—are highlighted as an effective way to revive older products and maintain creator focus.

In conclusion, this session centers on practical, experience-based strategies for growing TikTok Shop through strong creator ecosystems, effective communication with TikTok via Lark, and thoughtful use of GMV Max and fulfillment options such as FBT. 


Participants share both wins and failures, highlighting the importance of targeted outreach, community-building, and careful interpretation of TikTok’s internal performance signals.

items.title: How Centurion Brands Expand Beyond Amazon Through TikTok, Community, and Multi-Channel Operations － Centurion Channel Call July 2026
items.description:
In this session, MDS Centurion members share advanced strategies for growing brands across Amazon, TikTok, and Walmart, with a strong focus on TikTok-driven awareness and profitable scaling. In this session, they trade real-world tactics on launches, community building, and fulfillment to navigate rising costs and increasing platform complexity.

  1. TikTok growth strategies, agencies, and the halo effect on Amazon.
  2. Launching and scaling products on Amazon with community and external traffic support.
  3. Pricing, retail and marketplace diversification, and optimized fulfillment (MCF, TikTok Shop, and logistics deals).
items.description_text: In this session, MDS Centurion members share advanced strategies for growing brands across Amazon, TikTok, and Walmart, with a strong focus on TikTok-driven awareness and profitable scaling. In this session, they trade real-world tactics on launches, community building, and fulfillment to navigate rising costs and increasing platform complexity. TikTok growth strategies, agencies, and the halo effect on Amazon. Launching and scaling products on Amazon with community and external traffic support. Pricing, retail and marketplace diversification, and optimized fulfillment (MCF, TikTok Shop, and logistics deals).
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS Centurion group share advanced, real-world tactics for scaling brands across Amazon, TikTok, Walmart, and DTC, with a strong focus on TikTok-driven growth and launch strategies. 


In this session, experienced operators compare what is working now versus what used to work, and they dive into the economics, community-building tactics, and fulfillment levers that affect profitable growth.

Member Introductions and Business Context

  • Participants introduce themselves and clarify that several are long-time MDS members who are new to joining Centurion calls, rather than new to the group itself.
  • Tony Brink explains that he has been selling on Amazon for about 10 years, mainly in supplements, and currently operates two supplement brands that are still roughly 99% Amazon-focused.
  • William Su shares that he is based in Taiwan and runs a multi-category business (toys, furniture, lighting, outdoor, lawn and garden) selling across the U.S., Europe, and Australia, with about 70% of revenue coming from online channels and 30% from retail.
  • William states that his company sells to Walmart, Target, Costco, and Sam’s Club, and also does OEM manufacturing for other marketplace brands, while operating five factories in Asia.
  • David Redlich describes himself as a serial entrepreneur and Wharton graduate who previously built and sold an Inc. 500 company with 200,000 SKUs on Amazon and now focuses on Thera Ice, a cold-therapy brand with products for head, shoulders, knees, back, and other body parts.
  • David notes that Thera Ice’s “headache hat” holds around 44,000 reviews and 4.6 stars on Amazon, and the brand has appeared on Good Morning America multiple times.
  • David mentions a new product line called Illo, a pillow that doubles as a sleep mask for travel and at-home use, but he notes that consumers find it confusing because they are unsure whether it is a pillow, a mask, or a companion product.
  • Participants highlight their geographic spread, with some based in South Florida, Tampa, New York, and Asia, underscoring the distributed nature of the group and the diversity of business models represented.

TikTok Strategy, Agencies, and Halo Effect

  • Tony explains that he is giving TikTok “a fifth chance” after multiple failed attempts with agencies that overpromised and underdelivered, and he now works with an agency that has a real track record.
  • He notes that the new agency sets realistic expectations by stating that the first three to six months are likely to be painful and unprofitable, which contrasts with prior agencies that promised fast revenue within a few months.
  • Tony states that the new agency actively manages creators, monitors accounts around the clock, interacts and trains creators, and does the day-to-day work that previous agencies claimed they would do but never executed.
  • He reports that the agency’s brutal honesty about timelines and uncertainty increases his confidence, even though he is only about a month into the engagement.
  • Tony shares that he sells about 50 supplement products across anti-aging, gut health, and other health categories, and that his revenue is fairly well distributed rather than dominated by a single hero SKU.
  • Prue describes her TikTok journey in skincare, noting that she scales a hero product first and then expands, and she emphasizes that TikTok only works when brands operate at real scale in terms of units seeded and content volume.
  • Prue explains that she scaled TikTok-driven revenue to around $1.1 million per month, supported by approximately 26.5 million video views and roughly 1,700 videos posted, demonstrating the volume required for meaningful TikTok impact.
  • She stresses that TikTok success relies on seeding a high number of units daily (for example, 30–40 units per day in her case) and not being “cheap” with sampling if a brand wants to reach large-scale outcomes.
  • Prue advises that brands should start with one hero product on TikTok, go all in, push ad spend behind it, and only then layer on additional SKUs once the first product reaches meaningful scale.
  • She recommends cautious adjustments to ROAS targets and warns against making large, sudden changes (e.g., dropping from 3 to 2 overnight), instead advocating for very gradual optimization to maintain performance.
  • Ershad voices skepticism about TikTok profitability and admits he knows few people who truly make money on TikTok, but Prue counters firmly that significant halo and profitability are achievable when done correctly.
  • David and Prue both highlight the “halo effect” from TikTok, where large awareness and content volume drive increases in branded search and sales on Amazon and other channels, especially for replenishable products like supplements or skincare.
  • Ershad shares that he produces roughly 400 videos per day with real creators, sees decent views, but does not observe a clear halo effect on Amazon, and he acknowledges that something seems off with his current funnel.
  • Prue suggests measuring branded search volume on Amazon and notes that in her skincare brand, branded search grew to become as large as the top category keyword, which made the TikTok halo clearly visible.
  • William asks whether high-price-point products (~$100–$200 retail) can work on TikTok, and both Prue and Ershad respond that this price point can work if the products are visually demonstrable and aligned with compelling content themes (e.g., “bedroom glow up”).
  • William explores the idea of giving away lower-cost items (e.g., smaller wooden toys) as awareness drivers for higher-ticket products like wooden toy kitchens, and Prue recommends starting with a smaller, niche product that aligns with a clear audience (e.g., “conscious moms” preferring non-plastic toys).


Brand Building, Community, and Launch Support

  • Udae Sandhu raises a key question about the current difficulty of launching new products on Amazon that do not receive external traffic or brand support from TikTok, Meta, or DTC.
  • He observes that existing, established products still perform well, but he wants to understand whether Amazon-native launches without external traffic are becoming harder across categories.
  • Tony reports that launches are indeed getting harder, as ranking and maintaining rank now take longer and require more resources, especially in competitive categories and with rising CPCs.
  • He mentions that past heavy reliance on product seeding has shifted toward more PPC, which increases launch costs and may slow momentum.
  • Tony notes that Amazon Vine Early Reviewer programs are slower and less effective for him, with some SKUs taking months to reach 15–20 reviews, forcing launches to proceed with fewer social proof signals.
  • David states that one-star Vine reviews can severely damage a launch because Vine participants often have no real need for the product and provide reviews that do not reflect the product’s intended use case.
  • Udae, who operates in supplements, explains that supplement buyers are extremely price-sensitive, and attempts to launch at a low price and later raise it often fail because demand drops sharply once the product is no longer the absolute lowest-priced option.
  • He describes how fast-moving, underpriced launches cause major inventory planning headaches and set unrealistic volume baselines that collapse when prices normalize.
  • Udae argues that most Amazon-only supplement purchases follow three main decision drivers: the brand with the most reviews by a large margin, existing brand recognition, or the absolute lowest price on the page.
  • Prue suggests that Udae build or acquire Facebook communities that closely match his target customer profile (e.g., longevity enthusiasts, supplement-focused groups) to support Amazon launches with an engaged audience.
  • She describes how BodyHealth and The Coldest (David from The Coldest) have built extremely loyal Facebook VIP communities where members buy repeatedly, respond enthusiastically to new product drops, and influence one another’s purchase decisions.
  • Prue explains that in her own brand, she created a Facebook group of about 5,000 customers by segmenting her list and inviting existing buyers, then keeps the group engaged with weekly giveaways, polls, R&D surveys, and mutual support among members.
  • She notes that a dedicated community manager (in her case, a team member based in Eastern Europe) runs this group and uses it both as a demand driver and as an R&D feedback panel for product and packaging changes.
  • Ershad shares that he successfully leverages affiliates, Facebook groups, and Instagram groups to support important launches, and he uses Monday.com forms to pre-sign up fans and hype specific product drops.
  • He reports that for the three products he launched using this approach, pre-signups and fan engagement significantly improved launch performance.
  • Ershad also describes building a Bible-reading SMS-based group linked to his Bible-related products, where participants receive daily messages and earn rewards or gift cards for consistent reading, thereby strengthening loyalty and driving Shopify traffic.
  • The group discusses Instagram Broadcast Channels as another free, effective way to notify engaged followers about launches and deals, with Ershad noting that these perform better than email or SMS in some contexts because users voluntarily check the channel.
  • Collectively, participants conclude that community-driven launches via Facebook, SMS, and broadcast tools are increasingly important to offset the rising difficulty of organic Amazon-only launches.


Amazon, Walmart, Pricing, and Retail Complexity

  • David recounts how tariffs hurt their margins when they operated heavily on Amazon 1P, because they could not raise prices easily while costs rose, even though they later received partial tariff refunds.
  • William confirms that his large and bulky 1P business also suffered during tariff hikes, as Amazon did not fully adjust pricing to pass through the 20–30% cost increases, causing sizable losses.
  • Participants agree that relying too heavily on Amazon 1P can be risky when cost structures change abruptly, and they highlight the importance of diversifying channels and having pricing flexibility.
  • David explains that he and his partner created a “Pro” version of their headache hat with slightly higher COGS (about $0.60 more) but a $10 higher price point, which now accounts for roughly 5–8% of sales and delivers very high margin.
  • He notes that they also operate additional brands such as a cosmetics brand (Aesthetica) with a beauty blender that has around 50,000 reviews on Amazon, but they have deprioritized this line because margins and box program pricing became less attractive.
  • David describes experiences with Walmart, Target, Kroger, and Costco, noting that retailers frequently charge marketing fees (e.g., $10,000 per promotion) and often deliver underwhelming results, which can lead to large chargebacks if products do not sell through.
  • He warns that getting onto retail shelves is not automatically a win, because mispriced items, poor shelf placement, and forced markdowns can result in six-figure chargebacks and erode profitability.
  • David stresses the importance of price parity planning between Amazon and brick-and-mortar, recommending that brands consider changing packaging, materials, or GTINs so that in-store items can be structurally different SKUs and priced differently.
  • He mentions using brokers and agencies who have long-standing relationships with retail buyers and understand the nuances of endcaps, sidekicks, and promotional programs, arguing that their 4–7% fees are often justified by better negotiations and fewer mistakes.
  • Jasim shares that his company operates a variety of products in home, kitchen, and outdoor use categories, and he reports strong results with Walmart marketplace advertising, especially using Walmart’s external marketing tools that push traffic from Google and other channels.
  • Jasim states that Walmart.com advertising has been surprisingly efficient and may be a lever he scales further in the coming quarters.
  • Ershad raises the challenge that Walmart fulfillment fees (WFS) can be higher than Amazon’s for small items, which forces him into unprofitable price-matching with Amazon unless he finds alternative structures or bundles.
  • The conversation touches on bundling strategies (e.g., pairing journals with pens or skincare with brushes) as a way to increase AOV, differentiate marketplace listings, and potentially break strict price comparison across channels.
  • Prue references insights from the founder of Tarte Cosmetics, who emphasizes bundling hero products with low-cost tools or accessories and using gift-with-purchase as a major revenue driver, which Prue herself plans to emulate by pairing each product with a relevant tool.


Fulfillment, Logistics, TikTok Shop, and Lives

  • Prue and Ershad discuss the strategic use of Amazon Multi-Channel Fulfillment (MCF) and Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA/FBS/FBT) to support TikTok orders more cost-effectively.
  • They mention that Amazon recently announces reduced rates (around 35–45% discounts) for MCF orders associated with TikTok traffic, and that brands can negotiate further through dedicated Amazon contacts.
  • Prue notes that at a New York Amazon Growth Summit and a related high-level dinner—apparently curated for sellers at roughly $50M+ scale—Amazon Shipping representatives promote negotiable MCF and last-mile shipping rates.
  • She provides the example of a New York–based Amazon contact (referred to as “Mike” from the Amazon Shipping office) who can negotiate lower MCF, TikTok, and Amazon Shipping rates for brands that commit to a certain number of orders.
  • Scott (joining briefly by phone) confirms that Amazon is offering about 35% off TikTok-linked MCF orders and similar discounts for regular MCF, contingent on signing volume-based agreements that currently lack strict enforcement if targets are missed.
  • Prue explains that brands with their own warehouses can also route non-Amazon shipments through Amazon Shipping for last-mile delivery, and that these arrangements can be negotiated along with MCF rates for TikTok and other channels.
  • She mentions that Amazon and TikTok are increasingly working together, and recent changes mean TikTok is more likely to recognize Amazon tracking numbers and integrate them properly into TikTok Shop order flows.
  • Ershad notes that MCF can sometimes be cheaper than standard FBA fulfillment for certain configurations, especially when discounts are applied for TikTok-related orders.
  • David shares that his company also uses FedEx One Rate from its own warehouse, which offers two-day service at a flat rate for shipments that fit within FedEx envelopes, and he highlights its reliability and negotiability via local FedEx reps.
  • Participants discuss the earlier belief that Amazon cannot scrape pricing from mobile-only apps like TikTok Shop, which might allow some sellers to price lower there than on Amazon; however, they treat this more as an anecdote than a confirmed, durable strategy.
  • Prue says she intentionally prices higher on TikTok than on Amazon because TikTok runs constant discount events, and starting higher allows her to discount without sacrificing too much margin.
  • Ershad describes experimenting with TikTok lives, including mystery box auctions built from overstock items, and he reports early results of about $1,500 in revenue per hour, which others regard as very strong performance.
  • Prue compares this to what she has heard from MaryRuth Organics, noting that their lives reportedly generate under $500 per hour, so Ershad’s $1,500-per-hour performance looks impressive by comparison.
  • The group discusses that beyond direct revenue, lives can also generate incremental followers, community engagement, and future purchase opportunities across TikTok, Amazon, and other channels.

In this session, the group converges on a shared view that TikTok, community building, and cross-channel fulfillment are now central to driving profitable growth on and off Amazon.

The discussion underscores that while Amazon remains a powerful sales engine, its economics, tariffs, and algorithmic changes make it increasingly risky to operate in isolation without TikTok, Meta, email, and community support. 


The call closes with a strong bias toward experimentation—whether through TikTok agencies, live selling, Facebook groups, or negotiated MCF rates—as members commit to testing these strategies and sharing what works in future Centurion sessions.

items.title: Reseller Strategies for Low-Price Products, Gating Risks, and Marketplace Diversification － Resellers Channel Call July 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants discuss how to profitably sell low-price products like cosmetics across Amazon and Walmart while managing shipping, packaging, and platform risk.

TOPICS:

  1. Shipping, packaging, and logistics for fragile, low-price products
  2. Managing platform risk, brand gating, and diversification across marketplaces
  3. Using documentation, seller challenges, and credit card rewards to protect margins and cash flow
items.description_text: In this session, participants discuss how to profitably sell low-price products like cosmetics across Amazon and Walmart while managing shipping, packaging, and platform risk. TOPICS: Shipping, packaging, and logistics for fragile, low-price products Managing platform risk, brand gating, and diversification across marketplaces Using documentation, seller challenges, and credit card rewards to protect margins and cash flow
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss practical strategies for selling on Amazon and Walmart with a focus on cosmetics and other low-price products. 


They explore how shipping methods platform policies and credit-card reward strategies affect margins, risk, and long-term business resilience.


Shipping, Packaging, and Logistics Strategy

  • The group discusses how the vendor ships products in master cartons containing inner boxes, and Alex wants to understand how this packaging works for Amazon and Walmart fulfillment.
  • Alex explains that Amazon does not readily accept inner boxes inside master cartons, which creates confusion about how to comply with FBA requirements without damaging the products.
  • Alex notes that the products are cosmetics and are fragile, so the foam and inner boxes provide necessary protection during transit, and removing or altering this packaging risks product damage.
  • Charles initially suggests repackaging the inner boxes but recognizes that this adds labor and cost, which can quickly erode already thin margins on low-price items.
  • The participants weigh the pros and cons of using small parcel shipments versus LTL (Less Than Truckload), and they conclude that LTL may better protect fragile shipments, but it can still pose structural and cost challenges.
  • Alex highlights that having a prep center or third party touch the inventory adds cost, and on a low-margin product, this prep cost can eliminate profits.
  • Charles recommends considering Amazon Global Logistics (AGL) to ship products directly from China into FBA, so that any in-transit damage is claimable through Amazon or AGL rather than falling fully on the seller.
  • Alex explains that the vendor can ship from existing stock in the United States or directly from China, and that going direct from China is cheaper but requires solving the master-carton and inner-box compliance issue.
  • Charles suggests asking the Chinese supplier to ship directly in reinforced inner boxes rather than master cartons, and to improve the packaging so that any damage becomes the supplier’s or carrier’s responsibility, not the seller’s.

 

Selling Low-Price Products and Margin Management

  • Alex shares that the cosmetics line will retail under $10 and that margin percentages look acceptable on calculators, but the absolute dollar profit per unit feels small.
  • Charles confirms that for sub-$10 products like candy and soap, profitability depends on high sales volume rather than on large per-unit profit, and that volume is the only way to make such products worthwhile.
  • Charles emphasizes that when selling low-price products, the main focus shifts from per-unit dollars to inventory turnover, conversion cycles, and the ability to keep product in stock.
  • The group discusses how consistent inventory in FBA appears to influence Amazon’s algorithm, and they observe that sending more units tends to result in more sales, while sending fewer units tends to produce fewer sales.
  • Alex notes that returns materially affect net margin, and they state that they typically account for around 5% returns in their cost calculations, with occasional spikes up to 8% when something goes wrong.
  • The participants highlight that competing sellers sometimes price at levels that would be a loss based on normal sourcing costs, which makes it difficult to understand how those sellers remain profitable.
  • Charles explains a case where a competitor prices at apparent cost but recoups value through credit card rewards, effectively using cash-back and points to make the economics work while driving high top-line sales.
  • Alex proposes an alternative theory that some sellers might source from liquidators, blending lower-cost liquidation inventory with regular inventory, which gives them a lower effective cost and more pricing flexibility.
  • Both agree that no one truly sells at a loss indefinitely, and that if a seller appears to be doing so, they are likely making money through hidden means such as credit card rewards, liquidation sourcing, or even, in some cases, possible money laundering.

 

Platform Risk, Gating, and Diversification (Amazon, Walmart, Timu)

  • Alex describes how friends have been suddenly gated from selling brands they have carried for years on Amazon, sometimes with only brief notice and with limited recourse, which can push resellers out of business.
  • Charles shares similar experiences of being unexpectedly gated on long-standing brands despite providing strong documentation and invoices, which underscores how unpredictable Amazon compliance decisions can be.
  • Both speakers stress the importance of diversification, and Alex explains that they are actively seeking to spread risk by adding new product lines and exploring other platforms such as Walmart and Timu.
  • Charles emphasizes that reselling differs significantly from private label in terms of risk structure and that resellers must think carefully about how much capital they tie up in inventory versus safer vehicles like T-bills or high-yield savings.
  • The participants discuss Walmart as a backup to Amazon, noting that Walmart historically has less brand gating than Amazon but that cosmetics are sometimes gated and that category-specific rules matter.
  • Charles points out that Walmart’s infrastructure is weaker in some ways, because it relies heavily on UPCs, may have inaccurate product data, and lacks robust product rank metrics, which makes listing selection and forecasting more difficult.
  • Alex explains that they chose a particular cosmetics brand for Walmart because they already have strong data from Amazon on which SKUs and colors perform well, and they estimate that Walmart sales might reach about 10% of Amazon volume in a best-case scenario.
  • The group notes that Amazon remains the most powerful and sophisticated marketplace despite its frustrations, and that no other platform currently matches its sales potential or operational capabilities.
  • Charles considers Walmart as an “insurance policy” against Amazon, stating that if Walmart ever massively expands its e-commerce footprint, having established relationships and listings there will be strategically valuable.
  • Alex mentions also attempting to sell through Timu as another diversification path, reinforcing the broader theme of not depending on a single platform for all revenue.


Seller Challenges, Account Health, and Documentation Practices

  • Alex describes using Amazon’s seller challenge mechanism to address account health issues, particularly situations where customers claim that products are fake, leading to brand gating and suspensions.
  • Alex explains that when customers allege counterfeit products, Amazon often demands extensive documentation such as a full year of invoices, bills of lading, and detailed proof of authenticity, which is time-consuming and stressful.
  • Alex recounts a successful seller challenge where a representative called from a Shanghai number to request additional documents, including the first page of a credit card statement, to confirm that the invoices truly belong to the seller.
  • The representative clarifies that they need the credit card statement not for payment details but to verify that the statement and invoices match the seller’s identity and are not fabricated from another account.
  • After Alex submits all requested documents exactly as specified, Amazon approves the challenge, which resolves the account health issue and eventually leads to the brand being ungated.
  • Alex notes that seller challenges provide a limited number of “replenishable” opportunities, and that once one is used and approved, it replenishes, so sellers effectively always have several in reserve for serious account health issues.
  • Charles reports mixed results with seller challenges, stating that even when representatives are more knowledgeable than standard support, they have not always been able to achieve ungating solely through this pathway.
  • Alex describes how some invoices from major retailers can be validated via retailer-side portals that Amazon can access; when invoice numbers and phone numbers match the retailer’s records, Amazon can quickly confirm authenticity.
  • Charles comments that some Amazon staff appear unable to access certain supplier websites, possibly due to region or network limitations, which can lead to frustrating rejections even when the seller’s documentation is valid.
  • Overall, both agree that strong, organized documentation and persistence with the right escalation channels are essential for resolving account health issues and regaining selling privileges.

 

Networking, Conferences, and Credit Card Strategy for Business Operations

  • The participants highlight the strategic importance of attending industry events such as Amazon Accelerate and Walmart conferences, not primarily for presentations but for direct access to Amazon and Walmart staff.
  • Charles explains that at events like Accelerate, booths for FBA, Amazon Global Logistics, and programs like Buy with Prime provide rare opportunities to fix stubborn issues and build relationships with decision-makers and VPs.
  • Alex shares plans to attend Amazon Accelerate for the first time, including arriving early due to long flight times from Florida and considering whether to stay until Friday in case of post-conference meetings.
  • Charles advises that the main value occurs between Tuesday and Thursday, and that by the end of Thursday most people are exhausted after days of meetings, booth visits, and evening networking events.
  • The conversation then shifts to credit card strategies, where Charles describes optimizing for cash back and points, especially on PPC (pay-per-click) ad spend, using American Express and other cards that provide high reward multipliers.
  • Charles mentions using cards that provide approximately 4x points on PPC and then converting those points at favorable rates, effectively achieving around 4.4% cash back before certain benefits are discontinued.
  • Alex explains that they use multiple credit cards with staggered due dates to maximize the effective credit period—often reaching up to 50 days of float—thereby improving cash flow for inventory purchases.
  • Alex uses points mainly for personal flights and hotels while paying for tours and incidentals with cashback, blending business rewards with personal travel benefits while still managing business liquidity.
  • Both speakers agree that annual fees only make sense if the value of the rewards significantly exceeds the cost, and Charles says they are willing to close cards when spend patterns change, such as when PPC benefits are removed.
  • They also briefly discuss preferences for hotel programs such as Hyatt and airline or travel redemptions, noting that some co-branded cards can offer attractive redemption rates when used strategically for trips.


In this session, the participants use a real-world cosmetics opportunity to explore how packaging, logistics, and marketplace rules shape the economics of selling on Amazon and Walmart. They pay special attention to the interplay between low-price products, platform risk, and the need to constantly adapt strategies in response to changing policies and competitive behavior.

The discussion also underscores how documentation, seller challenges, conferences, and even credit-card reward optimization all contribute to a resilient reseller business model. 


By diversifying across platforms, reinforcing relationships with marketplace representatives, and carefully managing both inventory and cash flow, the speakers aim to protect their businesses while positioning themselves for long-term growth.

items.title: Funding, Scaling, and Operations Strategies for Growing E-Commerce Brands － Accelerator Channel Call
items.description:
In this session, members of the Accelerator Channel Call share real-world ecommerce challenges and crowdsource solutions from fellow MDS operators. 

TOPICS:

  1. Manufacturing, sourcing, and IP protection for physical products
  2. Cash flow, funding options, and marketplace (TikTok, Amazon, Walmart, Target) strategies
  3. Operational scaling: listing optimization, Instagram growth, and global hiring/compensation approaches
items.description_text: In this session, members of the Accelerator Channel Call share real-world ecommerce challenges and crowdsource solutions from fellow MDS operators. TOPICS: Manufacturing, sourcing, and IP protection for physical products Cash flow, funding options, and marketplace (TikTok, Amazon, Walmart, Target) strategies Operational scaling: listing optimization, Instagram growth, and global hiring/compensation approaches
cliff_notes:
In this session participants in the Accelerator Channel Call share current business challenges and crowdsource practical solutions from other MDS members.

In this session the discussion covers manufacturing and IP concerns TikTok and affiliate recovery, cash flow and funding, retail expansion, listing and traffic optimization, and hiring and compensation strategies for global teams.


Product, Manufacturing, and IP Challenges

  • One founder presents Boo Boo Cooler, a combination of bandage and ice pack, and explains that the water bag component is technically complex and very expensive to produce at small size.
  • The founder states that the current manufacturer charges high prices and refuses to reduce costs even if the founder buys a semi-automated machine, so the economics currently do not make sense.
  • The group discusses the idea of the founder buying a custom machine (under $10,000) and placing it with a manufacturer, but the founder worries about trust, IP leakage, and the manufacturer using the machine for other clients.
  • Another participant recommends using an intermediary sourcing and enforcement group in China, specifically Linton Group (Linton Group, Shanghai-based sourcing and IP enforcement), which can provide vetted factory relationships and help protect IP.
  • The Boo Boo Cooler founder confirms that the product has utility and design patents in some countries, and that patents for the United States and China are still in process, which heightens their concern about knockoffs.
  • The group notes that using a trusted sourcing intermediary with IP enforcement capability can reduce risk when placing proprietary machinery or processes in Chinese factories.


TikTok, Traffic, and Cash Flow / Funding Constraints


TikTok cold start and affiliate reinstatement

  • One seller explains that they are doing a cold start on TikTok Shop, believed their products were all set for FBT (fulfilled by TikTok or equivalent), and later discovers that some orders do not ship due to a configuration issue.
  • Because of the unshipped orders, TikTok revokes their affiliate access, which prevents creators from linking to their products and undermines the momentum of existing creator content.
  • The seller describes a strategy to recover affiliate status by driving new orders that ship on time, including asking family and friends to place orders and considering reimbursing customers.
  • Another participant suggests reaching out to Facebook groups and Instagram creators in the seller’s niche (teachers and office users) and offering to reimburse or subsidize trial purchases to generate on-time orders and rebuild TikTok metrics.
  • The group discusses using discount codes—including 100% discount codes where appropriate—to lower friction for potential buyers and stimulate the order volume needed to regain affiliate privileges.


Cash flow, funding tools, and supplier terms

  • A fast-growing brand owner shares that annual revenue is on track for $2.2–2.5 million, but each larger production order ties up all available cash and increases the need for working capital.
  • The founder explains that Shopify Capital initially funds earlier rounds smoothly, but a recent expected loan of $350k is cut to $170k, leaving a $200k shortfall before a major holiday production run.
  • Several revenue-based capital providers—Wayflyer, Clearco, and others—decline financing because the brand shows firearms-related imagery on the site, even though the product is actually leather bags that can hold various items (e.g., EpiPens, trauma kits, or firearms).
  • Other founders recommend exploring QuickBooks lending, Slope, Flex, Settle, and Walmart Capital loans as non-equity funding options that can offer better APRs and structures.
  • Participants report that Slope often offers APRs in the 9–11% range for six-month payment terms, which compares favorably to many revenue-based capital offers above 18–20%.
  • Another founder reports good experiences with Walmart Capital loans, which can be quick and competitive if the brand is already selling on Walmart and can demonstrate performance.
  • The group emphasizes negotiating better terms with suppliers—such as extended payment terms or partial post-delivery payments—to treat suppliers as de facto financiers, especially when the brand is growing rapidly.
  • One founder suggests pre-orders as a cash flow lever, including offering discounted pre-orders or “reserve now” positioning so that customers finance a portion of the purchase order before inventory arrives.


Retail Expansion, Listing Optimization, and Traffic Tools


Retail expansion: Target, Shields, PGA, and brokers

  • A founder expanding into retail channels such as Target and Shields shares that this feels like “a whole new business” and asks for advice on managing inventory, supply chain, and channel balance.
  • Another participant describes joining a Retail Accelerator group (small cohort with a mentor with 25+ years of retail experience) that meets weekly to focus on pricing, packaging, terms, and retail-specific strategy (approx. $300/month).
  • Participants discuss working with brokers and consultants for retail, such as an agency that helps brands get into Target, Shields, or PGA Tour Superstores, and debate the trade-off between broker-controlled relationships and owning buyer relationships in-house.
  • One founder reports exhibiting at the PGA Show in Orlando and notes that trade shows are expensive gambles because results depend on which buyers and retailers walk by the booth.
  • Another founder offers an introduction to a holster manufacturer with a strong Shields relationship, explaining that selling into Shields involves specialized software and systems for managing POs and compliance.


Target, Walmart, and marketplace integration

  • A seller explains that Target Marketplace requires integration through a third-party connector like GoFlow or Rithum (formerly ChannelAdvisor), because Target does not allow direct self-managed listing connections.
  • The same seller notes that Target prohibits using Amazon’s MCF (Multi-Channel Fulfillment) for Target orders and may shut down the account if MCF is detected, which forces brands to solve logistics via 3PLs or other methods.
  • On Walmart, participants explain that Walmart Fulfillment Services (WFS) charges higher fees for products under $10, which harms margins for low-priced SKUs and pushes some sellers to either raise prices or move to multipacks.
  • One seller reports negotiating into a beta program where Walmart waives the sub-$10 penalty, but they still face pressure to maintain sales volume or risk losing that preferential arrangement.


Listing optimization, automation, and reviews

  • A participant with hundreds of Amazon listings asks how others handle the new 75-character title limit and whether they use tools like SQP data or automated systems to perform listing refreshes at scale.
  • Another seller explains that their team uses a Discord-based bot connected to Amazon via API, combined with Claude and Scale Insights / Scale Inset, to automatically update titles, monitor performance, and trigger workflows.
  • The bot can monitor reviews and ratings (e.g., alerting when a listing drops below 4.5 stars), check keyword rankings, and push updates through Amazon’s API after a human approves changes.
  • Some participants also use Data Dive (via MCP connection) plus Claude to generate new title recommendations based on keyword rankings and search term performance.
  • The group discusses Join Brands (sometimes called “drawing brands” in the audio) and compares it with Levanta as platforms for obtaining honest reviews and influencer content by offering discounts or free products.
  • Sellers confirm that reviews obtained through Join Brands are real purchases from real customers, which means the reviews tend to stick and comply with platform rules.


Marketing, Instagram Growth, Hiring, and Global Compensation


Instagram growth and manual “growth services”

  • One participant asks how to grow Instagram followers more systematically, beyond manual outreach.
  • Another founder recommends a service called Growth Viral (sometimes heard as “Growth Fire”), which costs about $99 per month and uses human operators who log into your account to follow and unfollow accounts manually within Instagram’s Terms of Service.
  • The founder explains that Growth Viral focuses on targeted following, then unfollows users who do not follow back after seven days, resulting in real, engaged followers instead of artificial or purchased followers.
  • Using this approach, the founder grows a brand account to ~84,000 followers in about a year and a half and grows a personal account from 2,000 to nearly 9,000 followers in roughly six months, supported by naturally viral content.
  • The group contrasts this with buying followers through services like “Twixy,” which can hurt engagement and algorithm performance because the audience is not truly engaged.


Hiring strategy, locations, and pay levels

  • A participant asks who to hire next given that many tasks now have AI or tooling alternatives, and wonders which roles remain worth hiring for.
  • Several founders recommend prioritizing higher-level roles such as brand managers and catalog managers, who can orchestrate tools and make strategic decisions, rather than filling low-level VA roles that can be mostly automated.
  • Multiple people suggest looking for talent that is “AI-native” or tool-native, i.e., people who already know how to leverage Claude, automation, dashboards, and ad tools, so that they amplify productivity rather than require constant direction.
  • Founders share that they successfully hire in Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Eastern Europe, and South America, and that each region has distinctive cultural and operational patterns.
  • Participants note that some Pakistani and Bangladeshi staff can be very skilled but may lean toward people-pleasing and saying “yes” instead of proactively flagging problems, which can lead to hidden issues and costly delays.
  • Others report that some South American hires are very capable but have, in some cases, attempted to manipulate time-tracking tools (e.g., gadgets to move the mouse or using the wrong monitor for screenshots), so they emphasize monitoring and accountability.
  • The group also talks about Philippine VAs, acknowledging both success stories and patterns like frequent family emergencies, and emphasizes the importance of clear expectations and performance tracking.

Agencies, intermediaries, and direct hiring

  • One founder explains that agencies like Cleardesk can provide highly capable Filipino VAs and handle initial screening, but may keep a very large margin (e.g., charging $2,600/month while paying the VA $800/month).
  • After discovering the disparity, the founder severs the relationship with the agency and arranges to pay the VA directly at a significantly higher rate (e.g., $1,600/month), which still saves the brand money while benefiting the VA.
  • Another founder describes a similar pattern with other agencies, such as an SEO agency in California that outsources work to Bangladesh, leading the founder to bypass the agency and hire talent directly in Bangladesh.
  • The group discusses Friends of Ecom and similar accounting or support agencies, where founders sometimes later hire their best bookkeepers or specialists directly after leaving the agency.


Compensation ranges and incentives

  • Founders share rough salary benchmarks:
    • Philippines – around $800/month as a common entry-level full-time salary, with strong performers making more (e.g., $1,600–2,000/month).
    • Bangladesh – around $400/month as entry-level, higher for more experienced or specialized roles.
    • Pakistan – around $500/month as entry-level, increasing for higher-responsibility positions.
  • Some brands pay $1,500–2,000/month for highly capable offshore brand or catalog managers, often with strong English and deep marketplace experience.
  • Participants observe that some South American candidates cost $15–25/hour, which approaches US pay levels, making the case for hiring US-based staff more compelling at those rates.
  • Several founders emphasize that paying more for “rock star” talent often produces better long-term outcomes than trying to minimize hourly rates, because those employees drive growth and reduce founder workload.
  • One founder describes adding performance-based bonuses (e.g., for exceeding ROAS targets or hitting email revenue goals), which substantially improves the quality and impact of campaigns.

In summary, the Accelerator Channel Call provides a peer-to-peer space where founders openly share practical challenges in manufacturing, cash flow, TikTok growth, retail expansion, optimization, and hiring, and receive immediately actionable suggestions from fellow operators. 


The conversation highlights how this group leverages a mix of tools, platforms, intermediaries, and global talent to solve problems in a capital-efficient way.


By the end of the session, participants leave with specific resources, intros, and tactics to test—ranging from new financing options and sourcing agents to Discord-based bots, Instagram growth services, and more strategic hiring approaches. 


Collectively, the call reinforces the value of trusted peer networks for solving complex, fast-moving ecommerce problems that no one founder can tackle alone.

TOPICS:

cliff_notes:
In this session, Ali Babul demos Trellis's new product "Core," positioning it against the current wave of "just plug an LLM into your data" approaches that most sellers in the room have already tried and found unreliable.

The Core Problem: LLMs Are Powerful but Untrustworthy

  • He argues most operators spend the bulk of their day translating between their own mental SOPs and whatever dashboard/platform they're using (ads, catalog, etc.) — repetitive, reactive work that in theory AI should absorb.
  • In practice, testing MCP-connected LLMs against real ad/catalog decisions showed frequent hallucination, skipped steps, and confidently wrong output that isn't caught until someone fact-checks it — undermining the "give back my time" promise of AI.
  • The group pushes back with real-world counterpoints: a human still has to make judgment calls AI can't infer (e.g., don't advertise a product that will stock out anyway due to a shipping delay), so full autonomy isn't realistic yet regardless of the tool.

Core's Pitch: Skills Instead of Prompts

  • Core's answer is "skills" — a defined, traceable workflow (data sources, calculations, steps) built once with a human confirming the plan, then rerun on a schedule with no hallucination and consistent output, unlike open-ended chat prompts.
  • Live in the session, Ali builds a skill from a prompt: flag top-selling products with under 4 weeks of stock remaining and auto-pause their ads — walking through how the "planner" breaks the request into sourced steps before executing.
  • He contrasts this with raw LLM usage, where an agency on Core's beta was burning hundreds to thousands of dollars in token costs rerunning the same weekly client report by hand each time something needed fixing.
  • Other examples raised: auto-notifying an inventory manager when a parent/child listing disconnects (a real cause of lost sales for a 6,000+ SKU brand), and flagging search terms with clicks but no sales for review.

Pushback: Build vs. Buy, and Does This Replace SOPs

  • A member argues he's already solving similar problems by building his own skill/database layer independent of any vendor, questioning why Core would stay differentiated as the underlying tools commoditize — Ali counters that maintaining your own scalable data lake long-term is harder than it looks, and that the "skill layer" (transparency, no hallucination, traceability) is the real differentiation, not the data pipeline itself.
  • Another concern raised: this still requires the actual ads/inventory expert to define the rules correctly — Core doesn't replace that person's judgment, it reduces their repetitive execution time.
  • Ali reframes a comment that "this forces you to actually write SOPs that get followed" as effectively the product's core value proposition, since most SOPs go stale and unused without something enforcing them.
  • Core is currently in private/invite-based beta (priced around $1,000/month in initial member offers), covers e-commerce broadly (Amazon, Walmart, Shopify, TikTok) rather than being Amazon-only, and includes prebuilt templates (price optimizer, dark-hours revenue recovery, daily pacing dashboards).

In conclusion, this session frames the current AI moment less as "AI can now run your business" and more as a case for building disciplined, transparent, non-hallucinating automation around the judgment calls a human operator already makes — with real disagreement in the room over whether that's better solved in-house or bought as a platform.

items.title: Edge vs. Core: Scaling AI Automation Across an Agency and Software Company － Adam Weiler － AI Mastermind 2026

TOPICS:

  1. The edge/core model — letting employees tinker with AI freely, then promoting only the ideas that clearly save time or money into standardized, reliable tools.
  2. Practical infrastructure choices: Claude team vs. individual plan pricing, always-on VPS/Mac Mini setups, and a "plain language query" layer for translating client jargon into database queries.
  3. Automated marketing tooling — landing pages built via Claude Design/Code, an automated Amazon image/infographic generator, and a voice-agent-run brand discovery workshop.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Adam Weiler walks through how he's structured AI adoption across two very different businesses — a 50-person agency running client money, and a 2-person software company where he can experiment freely — and shares a batch of automations built along the way.

The Edge/Core Model for Rolling Out AI

  • At the agency, employees ("the edge") get access to Claude to tinker and build quick prototypes; a small core team (one full-time US-based automator plus a couple overseas) standardizes anything that proves valuable into a reliable, production-ready tool.
  • Promotion from edge to core is judged only on time saved, revenue increase, or client retention — anything else is a "nice to have" that goes on a backlog.
  • He enforces two-week sprint limits to prevent scope creep (citing a year-and-a-half internal "pipes" project that dragged on and became outdated); one example win was automating a weekly ads-report pull that had taken each of 6-7 ads staff ~90 minutes.
  • When staff try to sneak custom variations into a standardized automation, he pushes those back to the edge (using Claude skills) rather than letting the core automation balloon into handling every one-off request.

Infrastructure and Pricing Choices

  • He built a "plain language query" (PLQ) layer that translates a client's informal question (e.g., "non-branded ad spend") into the correct underlying database table/structure — something he built independently before Claude announced native Slack/data querying, and now sees as a general need regardless of which AI vendor builds it.
  • On Claude pricing: staff default to the $25/month team plan (shared skills/docs, lower usage limits); heavy builders get bumped to a $200/month individual Max plan for experimentation, then their output gets shared back to the team account.
  • For always-on automations, he prefers a cheap VPS (e.g., Hetzner, ~$10/month) over relying on a home Mac Mini, since home setups fail more often; he deliberately constrained himself to building everything on Claude rather than evaluating every available tool.

Automated Marketing and Content Tools

  • He used Claude Design plus Claude Code to build a landing-page template and chained it into a workflow: hook → landing page → lead magnet → emails → Twitter posts, deployable in minutes when a new marketing angle comes up.
  • A separate tool automatically generates Amazon infographics and A+ content images from a brand's website URL, which he's now using as a "free image stack" outreach offer to source deal flow from brands.
  • He built a voice-agent-run brand discovery workshop (Claude + ElevenLabs) that interviews a business through ~40 standard marketing questions and outputs a usable brand/ICP brief, replacing a manual process that used to take him 90 minutes per session.

In conclusion, this session is a practical case study in scaling AI adoption without chaos — separating free experimentation from production tooling, and using that same AI stack to automate reporting, marketing content, and even the process of extracting a company's brand voice.

items.title: AI-Built Data Infrastructure & FBA Inventory Audits － William Langford － Vancouver AI Mastermind 2026

TOPICS:

  1. Building a custom product information database and running AI-driven security/data-integrity audits on it (catching a broken backup, an auth flaw, and duplicated code).
  2. Setting up automated data pipelines (via Dagster) to pull and store Amazon SP API, Ads API, and Keepa data before it disappears, while working around API throttling limits.
  3. Using Claude to audit FBA inventory reports for storage-fee waste and misclassifications, and diagnosing how inventory location/quantity — not ads or listings — can quietly crater sales.

cliff_notes:
In this session, William Langford walks through several ways he's used Claude Code to build and self-audit internal tools for managing a large Amazon catalog, plus a couple of smaller AI-driven business hacks.

Building and Auditing a Custom Product Database

  • While migrating accounting systems from NetSuite to QuickBooks, he needed to preserve historical purchase order and item data, so he had Claude Code build a PIM (product information management) database in about a week.
  • Running Claude as an auditor on its own codebase turned up real issues: an authentication system that "fails open" (no login required) rather than fails closed, a database backup function that silently omitted 10 of 20 tables, and a pattern of duplicated UI code instead of reusing shared components.
  • His takeaway: AI-built tools need a second, independent audit pass — ideally in a fresh context window — since the AI won't necessarily flag its own failures, and prompts should explicitly instruct it to reuse existing code rather than rewrite from scratch.

Data Pipelines at Scale

  • With 18,000+ active ASINs, manually pulling Amazon data doesn't scale, so he built an offline, cached database combining SP API, Ads API, and Keepa data (Keepa adds metrics SP API lacks, like homepage badges and monthly units sold).
  • He uses Dagster (open-source) as an "organizer" that pulls data from each API on a schedule, saves the raw files, and routes it into a Postgres database that Claude can query via MCP.
  • Since Amazon throttles by API key rather than by account, he splits reports (inventory, economics, financials) across separate API keys to avoid hitting rate limits, and backfills historical data since SP API only exposes a 24–27 month lookback window.

FBA Inventory Health: Beyond Ads and Listings

  • He found that a 50% sales drop on some items wasn't ads- or listing-related — it traced back to inventory quantity and how many fulfillment centers a product was distributed across, which Amazon's FBA algorithm increasingly deprioritizes for lower-velocity SKUs.
  • Feeding an FBA inventory report to Claude for a "deep audit" of storage classification and size-classification errors surfaced concrete, quantified waste: oversized/misclassified items costing roughly $700+ per month in recoverable storage fees, including one item with an $1,832/month storage fee that should have been minor.
  • He's currently running this audit manually rather than automating it, but flags it as an easy candidate for automation (e.g., via Asana + Zapier) once time allows.

Smaller AI Hacks

  • He also used AI (via Cowork) to review a year of credit card statements and bonus-category rules across multiple cards, then reallocate ~$50,000 in recurring spend to the card that would actually count toward a targeted airline status tier.

In conclusion, this session is a practical look at using AI not just to build internal tools, but to independently audit them — and at using that same AI-assisted rigor to catch inventory and fee issues that ads and listing optimization alone would never surface.

items.title: Hot Seat: Drowning in Decisions: What Should I Build － Eugene Khayman － Vancouver AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this hot-seat session, Eugene Khayman discusses where AI fits in a decision-heavy role at MDS, and the group works through the organization's real bottleneck: member churn driven by disengagement rather than dissatisfaction.

 

TOPICS:

  1. Why AI struggles with high-context, emotionally-nuanced business decisions and works better as an assistant than a decision-maker.
  2. The core retention problem — unengaged members churning despite the product working — and why "too busy" is the dominant reason.
  3. Proposed fixes: an AI-powered search/digest across community conversations, more personal onboarding touchpoints, mandatory engagement structures (squads), and doubling down on events.

cliff_notes:
In this session Eugene Khayman opens up about being a decision bottleneck and unsure where AI genuinely helps versus just adding noise, which turns into a broader group discussion about member churn and engagement.

 

AI as Assistant, Not Decision-Maker

  • Eugene uses AI mainly for writing help, trend reports, and presentations, but not for actual business decisions — when run through AI, pricing or renewal decisions come back generic because AI lacks the emotional and relationship context behind them.
  • Team-written AI messages to members are easy to spot as AI and land poorly, so he acts as a check on AI-generated content and data ("calling out bullshit") more than a builder of AI tools.
  • He contrasts himself with more automated approaches (like Constantine's), saying he's "AI-assisted" rather than running bots, partly due to limited time.

The Real Problem: Disengagement, Not Dissatisfaction

  • The group identifies that churn is concentrated among unengaged members — people who are simply too busy to log in, not people unhappy with the product; join-to-engagement rate has dropped from ~70-80% to ~50%.
  • New members who skip onboarding touchpoints (one-on-one calls, introductions) are especially likely to churn within their first 90 days without ever using the community.
  • Facebook's poor searchability is called out as a specific pain point — years of valuable conversation exist but can't be found when a member needs a past answer (e.g., a UK tax issue someone already solved).

Proposed Fixes

  • Build AI-assisted search/reference (not AI-generated answers) across WhatsApp/Facebook history so members can locate past conversations and who solved similar problems.
  • Increase personal touch in onboarding — lunches with chapter leads, one-on-one intros — and consider making engagement structures like "squads" mandatory rather than opt-in, similar to peer groups like Vistage or YPO.
  • Send curated, distilled value nuggets (top tips, digest emails) directly to unengaged members so they see ROI without needing to log in themselves.
  • Double down on events specifically, since the group agrees that's MDS's hardest-to-replicate differentiator as digital engagement gets commoditized by AI elsewhere.

In conclusion, this session is less about a specific AI tool and more about diagnosing why members disengage and testing whether AI-powered search, better onboarding, and structural engagement requirements can address it before someone churns.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Constantine describes replacing much of his internal software stack — project management, customer service, competitor research — with a single AI agent built on Discord, and extends that same AI into ad targeting and community-based marketing.

 

An AI "Company Brain" for Tasks and Customer Service

  • He moved his team's chat history from Slack/Teams to Discord specifically because it's bot-native, then built a bot with a dedicated SQL database (not just a context window) holding five years of company conversations, emails, and product knowledge.
  • The bot auto-generates tasks from conversation (e.g., detecting an action item and assigning it to the right person), sends daily briefs, and flags anything left unresolved — he found 167 stale tasks once he could finally see them all in one place.
  • It also handles customer service directly: given an email asking about a formulation change from nine months ago, it searched the archive, found the change, confirmed it wouldn't affect palatability, and drafted a reply from the company email.
  • Claude, connected via CLI to Shopify, builds and publishes landing pages directly from designs, cutting out manual dev work.

Monitoring Reddit and Facebook for Relevant Conversations

  • After Reddit ads underperformed, he built a system (via F5 Bot, an approved Reddit tool) to monitor specific subreddits for relevant keywords, flag matching posts, and draft a suggested reply grounded in product ingredients, reviews, and competitor review data — a human still posts it manually from their own account.
  • A similar scraper tool (Debbie) does the same for Facebook groups.
  • He's explicit about the legal line: unlabeled brand promotion in these communities is astroturfing, an FTC violation with fines around $50K+ per case — disclosing the brand affiliation keeps it compliant.
  • Beyond promotion, he uses this monitoring for research — pulling real customer language into product listings, ad copy, and search terms.

Amazon Ads and a TikTok UGC Funnel

  • On Amazon, he builds dedicated single-search-term ("SCAT") campaigns around search terms already converting above market average, using SQP data cross-referenced with DataDive.
  • He also runs a lead-gen "challenge" funnel (built via Claude, hosted on Shopify): Meta ads (~$0.67/lead) drive dog owners to a giveaway where entrants film before/after videos of their dog using the product, post them to TikTok, and compete for a $1,000 prize.
  • This generates roughly 100 UGC videos for reuse in ads at ~$16 each, plus an Amazon ranking/review boost from the ~1,500 entrants who get a 40%-off coupon.
  • Claude also builds and tests the resulting ad creative (stripped-audio UGC clips with text overlays), killing underperforming variants automatically.

 

In conclusion, this session is less about a single tactic and more about a broader shift — using an AI agent with persistent memory to absorb tasks, customer service, and market research that used to require separate tools and staff time.
