cliff_notes:
In this session, William Rivera shares how his brand Hashdash — a cannabis storage/accessory company — grew from a banned Amazon account into a $2M+/month DTC business, largely through organic content and a simplified paid-traffic strategy on Meta.

 

He walks through his account structure, testing cadence, and a full library of creative formats, closing with a candid account of why AI-generated ads backfired for his audience.

From Amazon Ban to $2M/Month on Shopify

  • William started Hashdash in 2020, initially selling only on Amazon; after getting banned and having inventory shipped back to his house, he pivoted to posting content on TikTok/Instagram to sell remaining units.
  • That pivot took off organically — content that took him five minutes to make generated roughly $100,000/month in TikTok-driven sales within days, before he had spent anything on paid ads.
  • He added paid spend in 2023 and scaled to $900,000 in a 10-day period that December, with sales flipping from Amazon-majority to roughly 70% Shopify / 30% Amazon (with zero Amazon ad spend — pure "halo effect").
  • By 2024 the brand hit $2.2 million in a single month ($1.6M Shopify, $600K Amazon), built almost entirely around one core product before recent expansion into new SKUs.
  • His organic social following now exceeds a million across platforms (500K Facebook, ~200K Instagram, TikTok at 275K before it was deleted).

Ad Account Structure: Broad Targeting and One-Campaign Simplicity

  • He argues the shift since roughly 2022–2023 has been away from manual audience targeting (interests, lookalikes) toward broad targeting, where the creative itself does the targeting — an ad aimed at older people should simply feature an older person.
  • His structure is one campaign per offer/country, with all creative dumped into as few ad sets as possible, letting Meta's Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) allocate spend to whichever ads perform, rather than manually splitting budget across top/middle/bottom-of-funnel ad sets.
  • He avoids the older "one angle per ad set" approach; current best practice (post the "Andromeda" update) is to load many creatives with a mix of hooks into a single ad set and let performance sort itself out.
  • Frequency and CPM are his read on funnel position: a frequency near 1.0 indicates top-of-funnel prospecting (video tends to serve this role for his brand), while higher frequency indicates retargeting/bottom-of-funnel (often static images).
  • He evaluates and cuts at the ad-set level, not the individual-ad level, using roughly a 5x AOV spend threshold to decide whether an ad set has earned enough data to judge; he rarely relaunches killed ads, trusting Meta's allocation "more often than not."
  • New batches of 30–50 creatives go into a fresh ad set weekly (he avoids dropping new ads into ad sets that have already exited the learning phase); sale-specific pushes (e.g., Black Friday) get their own dedicated campaign.

Creative Formats Mapped to Awareness Stages

  • He organizes formats using a stages-of-awareness framework (referencing Eugene Schwartz's Breakthrough Advertising): unaware audiences get educational or humor-driven content; problem-aware audiences get founder/testimonial ads; solution-aware audiences get comparison or feature-led ads.
  • Specific formats he's used successfully: press-release/blog-style ads, "us vs. them" comparison ads, feature call-outs, review-compilation "flexible ads" (one ad has run for four years and generated hundreds of thousands of dollars), social-proof/comment-reply ads, founder-talks-to-camera ads, street interviews, before/after, and statistic-led ads.
  • He deliberately keeps most creative low-polish ("ugly ads" that look native/organic) because they stop the scroll better than produced content, though he notes this specific ad's cost has risen over its four-year run even as execution improved.
  • Tools: he uses AdNova (~$200/month) to cut Facebook upload time and replace more expensive tools like Motion for creative reporting/organization.

The AI Creative Experiment and Backlash

  • He tested AI-generated animated creative (an anthropomorphized grinder/character) as an openly-labeled, stylized ("Pixar-like") ad rather than a deceptive one.
  • The response from his audience was strongly negative — comments calling it "AI slop" and saying it actively talked them out of purchasing, and influencers declining to work with the brand as a result.
  • His conclusion: for his stoner/cannabis audience specifically, authenticity matters enormously, and AI creative currently undermines trust; he now reserves AI for scripting and ideation rather than final creative, and continues investing in real, unpolished formats like street interviews and talking-to-camera ads.

In conclusion, this session lays out a simplified, creative-led approach to scaling Meta ads — broad targeting, single-campaign structures, and letting the algorithm allocate spend — paired with a real-world caution that AI-generated creative can damage trust with audiences that value authenticity, even as AI remains useful earlier in the ideation process.

items.title: Random AI Anecdotes － Wei Lin － Vancouver AI Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this session, Wei explains how he thinks about using AI strategically rather than just as an automation tool, drawing on his background in tech and strategy work.


TOPICS:

  1. Three levels of AI adoption: Automator, Centaur, and Cyborg.
  2. Why critical thinking should improve alongside AI use, not get outsourced to it.
  3. Practical rules for model selection and catching AI hallucinations, including a legal-database example.

Practical rules for model selection and catching AI hallucinations, including a legal-database example.

cliff_notes:
In this session Wei shares how he thinks about using AI effectively, drawing on his background in tech, finance, private equity, and management consulting.

He argues that most people underuse AI by treating it too restrictively, and lays out a framework for moving toward a more integrated, higher-value way of working with it.

The Three Archetypes of AI Use

  • Wei describes three levels of AI adoption: the Automator (using AI mainly to cut costs and automate low-level tasks), the Centaur (a clear division of labor where AI handles defined tasks and humans handle the rest), and the Cyborg (a fully integrated mode where human and AI thinking blend together).
  • He argues most organizations and corporations get stuck at the Automator or Centaur stage, often due to policy and data-privacy constraints that entrepreneurs and brand owners aren't bound by.
  • He frames the Cyborg model as the most effective because the interaction is fluid — you're training the AI as much as it's training you, and your thinking improves as a result.
  • He warns against "pure vibe coding," where blindly delegating to AI makes you lazier rather than sharpening how you think about problems or workflows.

Model Selection and Verifying AI Output

  • Wei recommends matching models to tasks: he uses a Gemini "Deep Think" model for double-checking logical consistency, and favors Gemini generally for large datasets because of its large context window and low cost.
  • His core rule: always assume the first AI answer may be wrong, especially if it sounds too good to be true — models are biased toward being agreeable, so pushing back two or three times often surfaces where they made something up.
  • He gives a concrete example: AI will claim to look up cases in CanLII (Canada's legal case database), but because the database uses a verification system AI can't actually read, any such claim is unreliable — he instead downloads the cases manually and converts them to PDF.
  • When a colleague suggests using Cowork/Claude to access the database directly instead of doing it manually, Wei admits he hasn't tried it and offers to test it.
  • He closes by noting that models change week to week, so answers should be periodically rechecked rather than assumed to remain correct.

In conclusion, this session makes the case that AI's value comes from sharpening critical thinking rather than replacing it, and offers concrete habits — matching models to tasks and always verifying rather than trusting the first answer — for using AI at a more integrated level.

items.title: E-commerce Ops in the AI Era － Steven Zhou － Mogul Call with StoreClaw.Ai
items.description:
In this session, MDS members hear from Steven Zhou of StoreClaw.AI about how an AI “operator” can streamline e‑commerce operations across Amazon, Shopify, and social channels. 

TOPICS:

  1. AI as an “operator” for e‑commerce (end‑to‑end workflows vs. single‑task assistants)
  2. Practical use cases: product research, Amazon listings, PPC, SEO/GEO, and social content
  3. Implementation details: pricing, rollout roadmap, security, and model integration
items.description_text: In this session, MDS members hear from Steven Zhou of StoreClaw.AI about how an AI “operator” can streamline e‑commerce operations across Amazon, Shopify, and social channels. TOPICS: AI as an “operator” for e‑commerce (end‑to‑end workflows vs. single‑task assistants) Practical use cases: product research, Amazon listings, PPC, SEO/GEO, and social content Implementation details: pricing, rollout roadmap, security, and model integration
cliff_notes:
In this session MDS members meet with the Seteven Zhou from StoreClaw.AI to explore how their AI-driven “operator” can streamline e‑commerce operations across Amazon Shopify, and social channels. 


The conversation covers StoreClaw’s capabilities, implementation approach, real‑world case studies, and practical considerations such as pricing, security, and model usage.

 

Overview of StoreClaw and the Shift from “Assistant” to “Operator”

  • Steven introduces himself as a co‑founder of StoreClaw and also an MDS member in the Centurion Club, explaining that he is both a seller and a tool builder, which grounds the product in real operator experience.
  • StoreClaw is presented as an AI “operator” rather than just an assistant, meaning it is designed to monitor, analyze, plan, generate deliverables, and execute across the full e‑commerce workflow, not just respond to prompts.
  • Steven explains that most people currently use three categories of AI: platform assistants (e.g., Amazon Seller Assistant, Shopify’s AI tools), general agents (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Hermes), and specialized point tools (e.g., Jasper, Triple Whale), and he states that these often fragment data and still leave humans as the “integration layer.”
  • He describes the traditional AI “assistant” as reactive and single‑task, operating within one platform and creating more tabs and tools for the team to manage.
  • In contrast, he describes the “operator” as proactive and continuous: it watches data streams, diagnoses issues, prioritizes actions, generates concrete outputs such as listings or creatives, routes them for human approval, executes changes, and then loops back to measure results.
  • Steven outlines an 8‑step loop—observe, diagnose, plan, generate deliverables, propose actions, get human approval, execute, and review results—emphasizing that the approval step stays human, especially for budget, pricing, and sensitive decisions.
  • He argues that most teams hoped AI would save time but instead became “AI editors” who review suggestions from multiple tools, while StoreClaw aims to produce fewer, higher‑value decisions and ready‑to‑deploy outputs.

 

Practical AI Use Cases in E‑commerce Operations

Product Research and Selection

  • Steven explains that many sellers approach product research by checking a few data points and then emotionally justifying a product they already like, which can lead to biased decisions.
  • StoreClaw’s AI screens hundreds of product candidates instead of just a small shortlist, and it evaluates each using a consistent, rule‑based playbook covering demand, competition, margin, supply, and risk.
  • The system pulls from multiple research sources and reconciles discrepancies according to predefined rules, so the AI does not stop at “interesting” but instead produces disciplined, evidence‑based recommendations.
  • He describes that each product idea becomes a small project with clear tasks, evidence attached, validated keywords, and draft listing or ad structures, which helps teams move from idea to launch more systematically.


Amazon Listings and Catalog Scale

  • Steven stresses that listing work is not just about copywriting text but about rebuilding search and conversion performance for every SKU.
  • He highlights the upcoming Amazon 75‑character title limit (effective around July 27) as a forcing function for mass edits, especially for large catalogs, and states that AI is ideal for this scale of repetitive work.
  • StoreClaw uses live Amazon search trends and competitor listing structures to generate title, bullet points, backend terms, A+ content logic, and image suggestions that align with how the algorithm ranks today.
  • He explains that most sellers heavily optimize perhaps their top 10 SKUs and then “set and forget” the remaining hundreds, while StoreClaw applies a consistent high standard across the entire catalog.
  • In a case study with Twinkle Star, an LED brand doing about $15M/year on Amazon, new SKU listing and asset creation time is reduced from roughly 5–7 days to about 1–1.5 days, and conversion rate improves due to more algorithm‑aligned content.
  • Steven notes that the real gain is that the team moves from “making assets” to focusing on strategy, because creative and listing production becomes much faster and more systematized.


Advertising (PPC) Optimization and Waste Recovery

  • Emily explains that PPC is one of the fastest payback use cases because ad spend is measurable and compounds daily, making wasted spend highly visible when analyzed correctly.
  • She warns that judging PPC performance only at account‑level ACOS can hide severe waste at the search term level, where some terms burn spend without generating orders.
  • StoreClaw continuously reads ACOS, TACOS, placement, and search term data, flags high‑spend zero‑conversion terms, estimates recoverable budget, and then proposes specific changes that require explicit user approval.
  • She describes a case with Lux Club, a home textiles brand doing over $10M/year, where manual review previously took a full day per pass and hid significant inefficiencies.
  • After implementing StoreClaw, ACOS drops from 35% to 22%, about $80K per month in spend is saved, and sales rise by 47% quarter over quarter, while around $500K in hidden traffic is surfaced in a single quarter.
  • Emily emphasizes that analysis is continuous but money decisions remain human, which is intentionally designed as a feature rather than a limitation.


SEO and “GEO” (AI‑Era Search Optimization)

  • Emily introduces the concept of GEO (sometimes called AEO), meaning optimizing for generative AI and LLM‑based search such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI overviews.
  • She explains that buyers increasingly ask AI for recommendations instead of just typing queries into Google, so being cited as a source by AI systems becomes critical for organic discovery.
  • To be cited, websites need structured data, clear quotable facts, and strong FAQ content, which AI can easily interpret and surface.
  • StoreClaw runs continuous SEO audits and can automatically fix many issues (e.g., meta descriptions, on‑page text, alt tags) when integrated with Shopify or WooCommerce, subject to user approval for certain changes.
  • In a case study with a three‑person natural fragrance brand, the team previously spent about 18 hours per week manually handling SEO and outreach, often without budget for agencies.
  • Using StoreClaw, they refresh SEO across hundreds to thousands of pages and images, cut meta production speed by about 22x, increase organic traffic by approximately 142%, and grow repeat subscribers by about 3.5x, while eliminating an $600–800/month outsourcing bill.
  • Emily encourages participants to run a simple test by asking ChatGPT for recommendations in their niche and checking if their brand appears, because absence indicates gaps in structured, AI‑friendly content.


Social Content, Creatives, and Competitor Monitoring

  • Emily explains that many teams treat every social channel as a separate content factory, which leads to fragmented brand voice and heavy workload across platforms like Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, and Reddit.
  • StoreClaw instead starts from one unified set of product facts and brand voice, then generates platform‑native content for each channel, producing a publishing calendar rather than isolated drafts.
  • The system maintains a consistent brand voice and handles reply suggestions as well, while still pushing content for human approval before publishing.
  • She shares a case with a baby and maternity DTC brand run by three people, where publishing volume increases from 2 posts per week to 8 posts per week, organic traffic share grows from 8% to 19%, and content operations labor drops by about 65%.
  • Steven and Emily describe StoreClaw’s creative engine, which can turn a single product photo into full ad sets: hero images, lifestyle shots, multi‑shot videos, and UGC‑style content, with roughly 80% of generated assets being deployment‑ready.
  • Twinkle Star uses this creative automation to produce more seasonal and promotional assets faster, reducing reliance on full‑day photo shoots and external designers.
  • For complex video work, StoreClaw has users approve storyboards and keyframes upfront, so expensive long renders are not discarded after discovering misalignment late in the process.
  • Emily adds that the same engine that watches competitors can also monitor internal metrics, tracking competitor prices, promotions, new listings, reviews, and internal stock levels, price moves, and margin shifts, and then surfacing only the most important alerts through channels like Slack, Discord, Lark, or WhatsApp.

 

Implementation Roadmap and Building an AI‑First Organization

  • Emily presents a three‑stage roadmap to implement StoreClaw and similar AI systems without overwhelming the team: Connect & Explore, Automate & Align, Extend & Customize.
  • In Stage 1 (Weeks 1–2), teams connect their Amazon, Shopify, TikTok, and social accounts, then start querying data in natural language (orders, inventory, listings, engagement) without enabling automation, so they can build understanding and trust.
  • In Stage 2 (Weeks 3–6), teams begin scheduling tasks, flagging anomalies, and reviewing AI recommendations; during this stage, humans review and approve batched actions, and KPIs shift from sheer output volume to quality of review and outcomes.
  • In Stage 3, teams extend and customize workflows by tailoring built‑in skills, creating new ones, and measuring concrete outcomes such as revenue impact, margin improvement, and hours saved, with the goal of making AI an integrated operational layer.
  • Emily emphasizes that trust must come before autonomy, and she notes that many AI rollouts fail because leaders start at Stage 3 with aggressive automation before teams see consistent, accurate results.
  • She summarizes that in an AI‑first org, people do less manual data collection and report building, and more strategic decision‑making, oversight, and exception handling, while scale no longer requires linearly increasing headcount.

 


Q&A: Pricing, Security, Models, and Integration Details

Pricing, Tiers, and MDS Offer

  • Jamie asks how much StoreClaw costs, and Emily and Steven explain that MDS members receive a special offer of one month free with effectively unlimited credits to fully test the platform.
  • After the free month, StoreClaw offers multiple pricing tiers starting around $20/month (about 6,000 credits), $40/month (about 12,000 credits), and higher tiers such as $100/month and “max” or “ultra” levels for larger teams and heavier usage.
  • Steven notes that for many medium‑to‑heavy individual users, the $40/month tier is usually sufficient, and he mentions that Twinkle Star runs well on two $40 memberships for their early months.
  • He also mentions a large team with about 30 users and over $100M annual GMV on Amazon that uses a mix of $20, $40, and $100 seats, demonstrating that pricing can scale with usage and team size.
  • Steven asserts that effective cost per usable asset or workflow outcome is typically lower than running raw LLMs like Claude or Gemini directly, because StoreClaw’s workflows are designed to produce a high percentage of deployment‑ready outputs (e.g., “seven out of ten” images usable).


Integration with Platforms and Communication Tools

  • Steven clarifies that StoreClaw connects directly to Amazon Seller Central, Shopify backends, TikTok shops, TikTok ads, and other key e‑commerce systems via APIs and connector authorizations.
  • He explains that everything then lives inside the StoreClaw ecosystem rather than relying on a user’s personal Claude or ChatGPT accounts, and that users interact through StoreClaw’s UI and integrated chat‑like interface.
  • StoreClaw can also integrate with Slack, Discord, Lark, and WhatsApp so that reports, alerts, and commands can flow inside the communication tools teams already use daily.
  • Steven confirms that StoreClaw operates as a standalone platform with its own model orchestration, not just a thin layer over Claude or ChatGPT CoWork, and that the value comes from pre‑built workflows and “skills” that encapsulate complex playbooks.
  • When asked whether the ads system makes automatic bid changes, Steven explains that StoreClaw can automate changes but generally requires human approval by default, because most mature advertisers prefer to control money‑sensitive adjustments.


Security, Permissions, and Model Strategy

  • In response to questions from June, Steven explains that StoreClaw uses token‑based authorization similar to other SaaS tools and ERPs, and it does not store user passwords for any connected platforms.
  • He states that data belongs to the customer, is not used for model training, and is never shared or sold to third parties, which aligns with industry best practices for commercial AI systems.
  • Admins in the team version can configure which team members have access to which stores and functions and at what permission levels, so access can be restricted by store and role.
  • Steven notes that StoreClaw uses multiple underlying models and rotates them depending on task complexity; for instance, it uses Sora‑style or Chinese‑market models like “CDNs 2.0” (as referenced) for video, ChatGPT‑image‑2 for images, and other LLMs for text and analysis, while always optimizing for deliverable quality and cost.
  • He confirms that StoreClaw has memory at both conversation and account levels so that the system learns brand guidelines, store details, and product context over time, but it is tuned to avoid over‑memorization that could clutter responses or reduce relevance.


Differentiation from General LLM Workflows

  • Pete asks how StoreClaw differs from building workflows in tools like Claude CoWork, and Steven responds that StoreClaw ships with over 40 pre‑built “skills” that encapsulate full e‑commerce playbooks.
  • These skills represent complete, battle‑tested SOPs for operators—such as product selection, listing optimization, SEO diagnostics, PPC analysis, and creative generation—so teams do not have to design and prompt complex multi‑step flows themselves.
  • Steven explains that many teams struggle to operationalize AI because building and standardizing these workflows across a full staff is complex, whereas StoreClaw centralizes the logic and enforcement.
  • He summarizes that StoreClaw aims to be the operating layer for e‑commerce AI, not just another chat interface, by combining connectors, workflows, approval flows, and monitoring loops into a single platform.


In this session, the StoreClaw team positions AI not as a novelty but as an operational backbone that can close loops across product selection, listings, advertising, SEO, content, creatives, and monitoring. 


Steven emphasizes a careful, staged rollout that preserves human judgment in key decisions while offloading repetitive, data‑intensive tasks to AI.


By the end of the call, participants gain a clear view of where AI can drive immediate ROI (PPC, SEO, listings, creatives), how StoreClaw integrates with their existing stack, and what safeguards exist around security, permissions, and model usage. 


The discussion, case studies, and Q&A collectively aim to help MDS members decide whether to trial StoreClaw using the MDS‑exclusive free month and evaluate it as a potential long‑term operating layer for their e‑commerce businesses.

items.title: How to Create Ads That Keep Attention － Jonathan Ramos － Expert Call with AppLovin
items.description:
In this session, Jonathan Ramos from AppLovin introduces its mobile app advertising platform for e‑commerce brands, explaining how ads run inside mobile games and how advertisers can use video, images, and dynamic product ads to drive website traffic and sales. 

TOPICS:

  1. AppLovin platform overview and audience reach
  2. Ad formats, user journey, and creative best practices
  3. Campaign setup, budgeting, and performance optimization
items.description_text: In this session, Jonathan Ramos from AppLovin introduces its mobile app advertising platform for e‑commerce brands, explaining how ads run inside mobile games and how advertisers can use video, images, and dynamic product ads to drive website traffic and sales. TOPICS: AppLovin platform overview and audience reach Ad formats, user journey, and creative best practices Campaign setup, budgeting, and performance optimization
cliff_notes:
In this session Jonathan Ramos from AppLovin presents an overview of their mobile app advertising platform and its relevance for e‑commerce and subscription brands. 


In this session Jonathan walks through audiences ad formats, creative best practices, campaign setup, and how to evaluate performance so that potential advertisers can assess whether AppLovin fits into their media mix.

AppLovin Platform Overview and Audience

  • AppLovin positions itself as a mobile app ad platform that has existed for over a decade and that more recently expands into website-focused e‑commerce advertisers.
  • The platform historically focuses on promoting other mobile games (for example, solitaire to Sudoku to crossword games) but now also sends traffic directly to advertisers’ websites.
  • AppLovin reports over 1 billion daily active users globally and about 150 million daily active users in the U.S., which makes it a large-scale channel for performance marketing.
  • The audience on AppLovin closely resembles the general U.S. population, with a skew toward ages 25–54 and especially 35–44, and with a slightly more female than male composition.
  • A Kantar study indicates that roughly 70% of AppLovin’s audience self-identifies as the primary decision maker in their household, which makes this inventory attractive for brands targeting buyers with disposable income.
  • The company highlights that many well-known brands already advertise on the platform, including Wayfair, Nectar, HelloFresh, Bombas, Comfort/Comfy, and other DTC and subscription brands.
  • AppLovin positions itself alongside major performance channels such as Google (Performance Max), Meta/Facebook (Advantage Shopping campaigns), TikTok, Snap, Reddit, and others, and claims that some advertisers spend more on AppLovin than on many of these alternative channels.
  • AppLovin offers a promotional incentive where new advertisers who sign up through a specific Million Dollar Sellers referral link and spend $5,000 within 60 days receive a $5,000 ad credit, effectively doubling initial test spend.

Ad Experience, Formats, and User Journey

  • AppLovin ads typically appear between levels in mobile games (for example, between level 41 and level 42) or as rewarded placements where users watch an ad in exchange for in‑game benefits (such as hints in a crossword puzzle).
  • The ad experience usually lasts around 30 seconds on average, which makes each impression longer and more immersive than many feed-based social formats.
  • Each impression generally includes three sequential touchpoints:
    • Step 1: A 9:16 vertical video, which is unskippable for at least 5 seconds and can be unskippable for up to 60 seconds.
    • Step 2: A 9:16 image or an “interactive” HTML asset, which functions as a closing statement and is often where most clicks occur.
    • Step 3: Dynamic product ads (DPA) that pull from a product catalog (commonly a Shopify catalog), displaying products relevant to the user.
  • Users can click a “Shop Now” or similar call-to-action (CTA) at any of the three steps to be taken to the advertiser’s landing page or funnel.
  • If users are not interested, they can skip the video after the unskippable window, skip the image or interactive, and finally click an X to exit from the DPA step and return to their game without visiting the advertiser’s site.
  • Jonathan clarifies that these three steps occur within a single impression, not as separate retargeting or follow-up impressions.
  • Internal data on click behavior indicates that most clicks occur on the second touchpoint (image or interactive), followed by the dynamic product ads, with the fewest clicks on the video itself.
  • Because of this distribution, AppLovin recommends that advertisers treat the video as the hook and brand education layer, while using the image/interactive and the DPA to drive the strongest direct response and conversions.

Creative Best Practices and Built-in Creative Tools

  • AppLovin stresses that creative quality is the main performance lever, especially given the limited in‑platform targeting options compared to identity-based platforms like Meta.
  • The platform recommends using 9:16 vertical videos longer than 30 seconds, because the optimizer tends to shift spend toward these longer videos and they often perform best.
  • The team strongly advises that all videos include captions, because most users watch with the sound off, and A/B tests with brands like Wayfair show higher click‑through rates and better performance when captions are added.
  • Advertisers are encouraged to test multiple hooks and angles, such as:
    • Audience-specific hooks (e.g., parents, women over a certain age, GLP‑1 users, frequent travelers, gut health–focused consumers).
    • Problem–solution messaging, especially for health, wellness, and functional product brands.
    • FOMO-based hooks (e.g., “selling out,” “limited stock”).
    • Social proof hooks, such as highlighting the number of happy customers or five‑star reviews.
    • Promo-focused hooks, such as “50% off,” “$4.99 per serving,” or evergreen discounts.
  • UGC testimonial videos and UGC-style content frequently perform among the best, especially when they mirror content that already works well on channels like Meta or TikTok.
  • Jonathan recommends that brands upload an abundance of creative, including many variants with minor tweaks, because the optimizer automatically shifts spend to top performers while deprioritizing weaker assets.
  • AppLovin provides an “Interactives Library” on support.applovin.com under “Advertise → Promote your website,” where advertisers can browse examples by vertical (for example, pet subscriptions, health and wellness, apparel).
  • Interactives are HTML-based assets that function like animated images or mini experiences similar to GIFs, often used to emphasize promos or social proof and sometimes to create quizzes or carousel-type interactions.
  • AppLovin offers a Gen AI tool in the media library that:
    • Allows advertisers to input a URL and an optional description and reference image.
    • Automatically scans the site and generates up to five interactive creatives within a few minutes, incorporating relevant imagery and copy.
  • The Creative Studio within AppLovin provides templates for interactives, such as:
    • Carousel templates that show a product (e.g., a hoodie) in different colors or on different demographic groups.
    • Quiz templates that mimic quiz funnels used by brands like HelloFresh, where users answer questions about preferences or dietary restrictions before being directed to a tailored landing page.
  • For full videos, AppLovin currently does not provide an in‑platform Gen AI video creator, and advertisers must upload their own videos, potentially created on third‑party AI video tools; Jonathan references one commonly used tool referred to as “Hicksfield” (a popular AI video model) as an example.

Campaign Setup, Targeting Strategy, and Budgeting

  • AppLovin describes a simple onboarding flow:
    • Create an account via the provided referral link.
    • Enter company and billing information.
    • Integrate the AppLovin Pixel either via Shopify app (for Shopify merchants) or Google Tag Manager and similar methods (for non‑Shopify sites).
  • Once onboarding is complete and the pixel is verified, advertisers arrive in the UI and can start building campaigns with a concise set of inputs:
    • Campaign name.
    • Goal type (either ROAS or Cost per Purchase/CPA).
    • Audience strategy (Universal, Prospecting, or Discovery).
    • Day‑target window (Day 0 or Day 7).
    • Primary URL/landing page.
    • Daily budget.
  • ROAS goal is typically used by brands with wide product ranges (e.g., apparel with many SKUs and variable prices).
  • Cost per Purchase (CPA/CAC) goal is typically used by hero product brands or subscription businesses that track a clear customer acquisition cost and benchmark channels against that.
  • Audience strategy options include:
    • Universal: Optimizes for new and returning customers together, seeking as many purchases as possible without restricting customer type; many brands start here to allow the algorithm to learn freely.
    • Prospecting: Optimizes only for net new customers who have not purchased previously.
    • Discovery: Optimizes for new users who have never visited the site, representing the coldest audience.
  • AppLovin recommends starting with Universal to avoid over‑restricting the model during the learning phase, and then later adding Prospecting or other audience strategies once performance data is available and new‑customer goals are clearer.
  • For day targeting, AppLovin recommends:
    • Day 0 (same‑day conversions) for most advertisers and lower to mid AOV purchases.
    • Day 7 for high AOV brands like home and furniture where purchasers often convert several days after first touch.
  • The platform charges on a dynamic CPM basis, and advertisers effectively just pay for ad spend according to their set budgets.
  • There are no monthly minimums, no contracts, and no platform fees, and advertisers can pause spend at any time.
  • The model bids higher on impressions that it deems more likely to lead to purchases, which sometimes results in higher CPMs but stronger ROAS, depending on the day and auction dynamics.
  • For starting budgets, AppLovin advises setting a daily budget that allows for a healthy number of conversions per day, such as:
    • If the target CPA is $20, a minimum budget of $100 per day is recommended so the model can drive at least around five conversions per day.
    • Budgets that are too low relative to CPA make it hard for the model to learn and optimize, while excessively high budgets early on may be inefficient during the initial learning period.

Creative Sets, Catalog Usage, Reporting, and Open Questions

  • AppLovin uses “creative sets” (similar to “ad sets” on other platforms) to organize and test creative systematically.
  • The team advises grouping creative sets by a logical framework relevant to the business, such as:
    • Products or categories (e.g., T‑shirts vs. hoodies vs. specific collections).
    • Creative hook or angle (e.g., before‑and‑after transformations, promo‑focused ads, FOMO messaging).
    • Audience persona (e.g., parents, travelers, GLP‑1 users, gut health personas, women over 40).
    • Funnel role (e.g., top‑of‑funnel intros vs. bottom‑funnel offer reminders).
  • Within a single creative set, advertisers can include multiple videos and images (for example, multiple UGC variations of the same concept), and the optimizer tests combinations to see which pairings perform best.
  • Over time, performance data at the creative-set level helps advertisers see which hooks, personas, or categories generate more spend, higher CTR, and more conversions.
  • AppLovin typically does not recommend pausing creative sets early, because the average buyer may see around eight ads before purchasing, and some creatives may work better as early‑touch or mid‑funnel assets.
  • After brands run on AppLovin for several months, and once it is clear that certain creative sets receive very little spend and few impressions, it becomes reasonable to pause those underperforming sets.
  • For dynamic product ads, Shopify-based advertisers can simply enable the Shopify catalog integration via the AppLovin Shopify app, which syncs the product catalog automatically.
  • The model then personalizes the catalog for each user, mixing user‑relevant products with bestsellers, and advertisers can optionally create item sets when they have large catalogs, high SKU counts, or widely varying AOVs (for example, a Wayfair-like assortment).
  • For landing pages, advertisers can:
    • Set a single campaign URL during campaign creation.
    • Override this at the creative-set level and drive different creative sets to different landing pages or funnels (for example, separate category pages, advertorials, or quiz funnels).
  • AppLovin currently offers a Reporting API (REST) designed for reporting and data retrieval, not for campaign or creative management.
  • There is no widely available campaign‑management API yet, and so campaign and creative uploads are manual through the UI, although:
    • Advertisers can bulk upload up to around 50 videos and 50 images at a time.
    • They can import assets from Google Drive to streamline asset management.
  • The platform integrates with third‑party analytics and attribution tools such as Triple Whale, Northbeam, and Workmagic, and supports UTM auto‑appending for these providers when building tracking parameters.
  • AppLovin notes that they collaborate with additional partners, including GeoLift study providers like Haus, and they encourage brands to validate AppLovin’s performance in these external systems.
  • Frequency reporting is not currently exposed in‑platform, and the team acknowledges concerns about ad fatigue while emphasizing that a large user base plus continuous creative refresh usually mitigates overexposure.
  • During the Q&A, participants raise questions about:
    • Format distinctions between images, interactives, and full videos.
    • AI-based interactive creation and potential future AI video generation tools.
    • Billing mechanics (CPM vs CPC), ad credit structure, and budget strategy.
    • Catalog performance and how dynamic product ads convert relative to other touchpoints.
    • Audience granularity and the perceived “black box” nature of optimization without detailed targeting controls.
  • AppLovin responds by emphasizing creative and structural testing (e.g., persona-based creative sets, product-level segmentation) as the main levers for understanding what works best on the platform.

In conclusion, this session provides a detailed walkthrough of how AppLovin operates as a mobile app performance channel for e‑commerce and subscription brands, from audience composition and ad formats to creative best practices and campaign setup. 


The discussion highlights that success on AppLovin depends largely on strong, well‑structured creative, thoughtful use of creative sets, and budgets that allow the optimizer to learn and scale.

The conversation also surfaces open questions around targeting transparency, frequency, and automation, which AppLovin addresses through its reporting API, third‑party integrations, and future plans for campaign‑management APIs. 


Overall, the call positions AppLovin as a mature, large‑scale channel with meaningful reach and tools for advertisers already investing in creative experimentation and data-driven optimization.

items.title: Who Is My Buyer and Why － Mergers & Acquisition Channel Call July 2026
items.description:
In this session, experts Scott and Bill walk through how buyers evaluate e‑commerce businesses and what owners must do to make their numbers “sellable.”

TOPICS:

  1. How buyers win: profit growth, debt paydown, and multiple arbitrage.
  2. Core metrics and benchmarks: EBITDA, margins, growth, COGS accuracy, and the “Rule of 40.”
  3. Value creation tactics: SKU-level and quintile analysis, reducing risk, and timing the exit while still growing.

cliff_notes:
In this session Scott and Bill from Northbound explain how to make an e‑commerce business financially “sellable” in the eyes of buyers. 


They focus on buyer psychology key financial metrics, and practical habits that owners should build in the 1–3 years leading up to an exit.


How Buyers Win and How They Think About Your Business

  • Scott explains that buyers win in three ways: growing profits (EBITDA), using the business’s cash flow to pay down acquisition debt, and achieving a higher exit multiple than the one they pay at purchase.
  • He clarifies that most sellers only think about profit growth, but this is only one-third of the value story from a buyer’s perspective.
  • He describes how a buyer typically finances a deal using loans (e.g., SBA for individuals or corporate financing), and how the business’s own EBITDA services that debt over 5–7 years.
  • He notes that efficient cash utilization and supplier terms influence how much of the business’s cash can be used to service debt versus funding working capital, which directly affects how much cash a buyer can pay at closing.
  • Scott introduces multiple arbitrage, where buyers aim to buy at a lower EBITDA multiple and exit at a higher multiple, sometimes by aggregating several companies to reach a larger EBITDA base and justify a premium multiple.
  • He stresses that sophisticated buyers always think about their own exit and the “buyer’s buyer,” and that sellers who can explain the future exit path for the acquirer support higher valuations.


Core Metrics, the “Rule of 40,” and What Makes a Business Sellable

  • Scott defines four core metrics: revenue, EBITDA (profit size), EBITDA margin (profitability percentage), growth rate, and the quality of addbacks or EBITDA adjustments.
  • He explains that buyers value not just current profit but also margin level and trajectory, and they assess profitability by SKU, distinguishing mature SKUs from new launches.
  • He introduces the “Rule of 40” as a benchmark, stating that a combination of EBITDA margin and growth rate totaling 40 or more represents a “great” business, while combinations in the mid‑30s indicate a “good to great” business.
  • He notes that buyers expect at least ~20% top-line and EBITDA growth to view a business as attractive, and they reward higher growth with better multiples if margins are healthy.
  • Scott clarifies that EBITDA adjustments include interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, owner expenses, and sometimes owner salary, but each addback must withstand buyer due diligence.
  • He emphasizes that clean, accrual-based financials, consistent margins, and clearly justified addbacks are foundational for a sellable and premium-valued business.


Accounting Quality, COGS Accuracy, and Contribution Margins (CM1, CM2, CM3)

  • Scott stresses that inaccurate books and inventory are among the most common deal-killers, and that financial statements must be on an accrual basis rather than cash basis for a sale process.
  • He explains that accrual accounting matches revenues with corresponding costs by recognizing inventory cost when it is sold rather than when it is purchased.
  • He highlights that accurate COGS must include full landed cost (product + shipping) and properly classified Amazon fees to reflect real unit economics.
  • Scott introduces contribution margin tiers: CM1 (after product + shipping), CM2 (after product, shipping, and Amazon fees), and CM3 (after product, shipping, Amazon fees, and advertising), and illustrates this with a $100 product example.
  • He shows how small improvements in product cost, packaging, FBA fees, or advertising efficiency can each add 1–2 points of margin, which cumulatively move a business from average to sellable and then to premium.
  • Scott recommends exporting the P&L into Excel as a percentage-of-revenue statement to quickly spot anomalies such as wildly fluctuating COGS ratios, which often indicate non‑accrual accounting.
  • He warns that hidden issues like misclassified shipping or duties (e.g., DDP shipping masking true duty costs) and missing disposal or lost-inventory adjustments can materially reduce true margins and even create large tax or duty liabilities that damage valuations or kill deals.


Growth Timing, Concentration Risk, and Making the Business “Premium” vs. Non‑Sellable

  • Scott states that selling during a growth phase is essential, because once growth plateaus, buyers often assume decline is next, which compresses multiples and makes exits harder.
  • He notes that owners frequently delay exits because the business is growing, but in practice the only viable time to sell is while the business is still growing, not after growth has stalled.
  • He lists factors that can make a business non‑sellable or very difficult to sell, including messy books, inaccurate inventory, heavy channel or product concentration, weak or questionable addbacks, and undisclosed liabilities.
  • He clarifies that high concentration (e.g., overreliance on Amazon, a single SKU, or one traffic source) increases perceived risk, and buyers discount valuations or walk away when they see such dependencies.
  • Scott encourages sellers to “answer buyer questions before they are asked” by proactively explaining anomalies such as margin dips, one‑time legal expenses, or seasonal effects, because each unresolved question effectively pushes the price down.
  • He gives examples of positive explanations, such as showing that mature SKUs are highly profitable while new launches temporarily depress margins, or documenting one‑time legal costs that are added back to EBITDA.
  • He summarizes that premium businesses combine clean, accrual-based data, diversified earnings, defensible margins, visible growth, and a well‑articulated story about future value and exit options for the buyer.


SKU-Level Analysis, Quintile Framework, Resellers, and Exit / Diligence Support

  • Bill and Scott emphasize that owners often do not know SKU‑level profitabilities, and they explain that unprofitable or marginal SKUs frequently hide within a blended margin, dragging down overall performance.
  • Scott recommends a quintile analysis where SKUs are grouped into five segments (A–E or 1–5) by revenue share, contribution margin (CM3), and return on COGS/ROI, to identify top‑performing SKUs and bottom 20% underperformers.
  • He explains that owners can often improve overall margins by raising prices or discontinuing the bottom 20% of SKUs, which may increase EBITDA margin and simplify operations, provided those SKUs are not strategically essential.
  • He advises that new product launches should be designed and selected with the goal of joining the top 20% tier, ensuring they are accretive to margin rather than dilutive.
  • For reseller businesses, Scott notes that margins are usually lower (around 5–10%), and that sellability depends heavily on factors like exclusive agreements and formal contracts with brands for specific channels (e.g., Amazon).
  • He introduces the idea of “exit to yourself” for lower‑multiple or less sellable reseller models, where the owner uses the business cash flows to buy themselves or partners out over time instead of selling to a third party.
  • Scott confirms that Northbound provides buy‑side diligence support for entrepreneurial acquirers (not large private equity firms) and also helps owners build value creation plans one to two years before exit.
  • He distinguishes a quality of earnings (QoE) report from a standard financial audit, explaining that QoE is transaction-focused, goes down to SKU level, and is often more critical than audited statements even for larger deals (e.g., $40–50M exits).
  • He outlines valuation breakpoints by EBITDA size (e.g., sub‑$500k, $500k–$1M, $1M–$2M, $2M+, $5M+), how these affect buyer universe (SBA buyers, strategic buyers, private equity, platform vs. bolt‑on), and how maintaining ~20–25% growth is crucial to sustain or increase multiples as earnings grow.


In conclusion, this session provides a structured, buyer-centric framework for understanding what makes an e‑commerce business sellable and how to prepare for a premium exit. 


It emphasizes that clean accrual-based numbers, accurate SKU‑level profitability, sustained growth, and proactive value creation planning all work together to increase both multiples and deal certainty.

items.title: Hire a C-Suite That Duplicates You － Mogul Call with Lisa De Rosa
items.description:
In this session, Lisa De Rosa, an experienced fractional COO and 10x business coach explains how founders can strategically “duplicate” themselves so the business no longer depends on them for every function. 

TOPICS:

  1. Identifying and structuring key leadership roles (Visionary, Builder, Integrator) to support scaling.
  2. Using the Model–Mimic–Master and Stop–Delegate–Continue–Start frameworks to delegate owner tasks.
  3. Building effective teams through clear job descriptions, metrics, and regular one‑on‑one meetings.

Using the Model–Mimic–Master and Stop–Delegate–Continue–Start frameworks to delegate owner tasks. Building effective teams through clear job descriptions, metrics, and regular one‑on‑one meetings.
