cliff_notes:
In this session Lisa de Rosa and the group discuss how founders and leaders can strategically “duplicate” themselves so the business can scale without relying on the owner for every function. 


The conversation centers on frameworks examples and practical tools for delegating structuring teams, and building a strong leadership layer in growing e‑commerce businesses.


Speaker Background and Business Context

  • Lisa De Rosa works at Cardone Ventures, an umbrella company that owns multiple subsidiaries including TenX Health, TenX Roofing, HRE Beauty, and Cardomax.
  • She serves as a fractional COO / integrator and now runs HRE Beauty and Cardomax from the inside, owning end‑to‑end execution across operations, growth, and systems.
  • She previously works with over 50 companies as a fractional COO, helping them grow from around $1 million to over $100 million in revenue.
  • Her earlier career focuses on property operations, metrics, and processes in a construction company and at Carvana, where she works in integrator‑type roles.
  • She also serves as a 10X business coach, currently coaches five CEOs, and speaks at various 10X events, using her experience to support business owners who feel stuck or overwhelmed.
  • Her core specialty is turning “chaos into clarity” by building systems and structures that allow business owners to step out of day‑to‑day operations and focus on growth.
  • She currently runs two e‑commerce brands, HRE Beauty (early stage, with a focus on product and supply chain build‑out) and Cardomax (with heavier emphasis on marketing).
  • HRE Beauty and Cardomax each generate about $1 million in revenue, with roughly six team members per brand (some part‑time), supplemented by agencies and shared services from Cardone Ventures.
  • Lisa explains that both brands are in growth mode, with HRE Beauty focusing on expanding product lines and Cardomax focusing on ramping up marketing.
  • She notes that she is based in the United States and primarily works with American team members, but she plans to begin hiring some overseas team members in the near term.


Frameworks for Duplicating the Owner and Building the C‑Suite

  • Lisa presents the goal of “strategically duplicating” business owners and leaders so they can step out of day‑to‑day work and move into higher‑level strategy.
  • She emphasizes that not all C‑suite hires matter equally, and owners should avoid delegating their primary strengths and instead hire to complement those strengths.
  • She explains that scaling is the art of delegating the current role so the owner can step into a new role that takes the business to the next level.
  • She introduces the “breakpoints” concept (used at Cardone Ventures), where businesses hit revenue plateaus and risk sliding backward if they lack the right executive structure.
  • She links this to the EOS (Entrepreneurial Operating System) concept of Visionary, Integrator, and Builder, noting that these three roles form a critical “rule of three.”
  • She states that by the $8–12 million revenue range (Breakpoint 3), businesses need at least a visionary, a builder, and an integrator, or they risk regressing in revenue.
  • She notes that in most cases, the owner is the Visionary, who should retain strategic direction while delegating operational and building functions.
  • She advises owners to ask whether they most need leadership in sales and marketing or in operations, people, and finance, and to prioritize C‑suite duplication accordingly.
  • She emphasizes that e‑commerce has unique tactical challenges (especially heavy marketing and Amazon‑specific know‑how), but the duplication strategy itself is fundamentally the same as in other industries.
  • She stresses that owners should focus on using their strengths to drive the business, rather than trying to be the person who does everything.

Model–Mimic–Master and the Stop–Delegate–Continue–Start Process

Model–Mimic–Master–Multiply (4M Framework)

  • Lisa introduces the Model–Mimic–Master–Multiply framework as a structured way to duplicate top performance.
  • She uses the Department of Transportation and learning to drive as an analogy: everyone models the rules, mimics them in practice, then masters them over time.
  • In a business context, she encourages owners to model top performers, either themselves or external mentors, to define what “good” looks like.
  • She suggests that if the owner is not strong in a given role (for example, integrator), they can model an external expert or mentor and bring that expertise into the company.
  • She notes that communities like MDS provide role models and best practices that owners and teams can model and then mimic.
  • She explains that mimic means taking best practices and implementing them consistently to hit targets.
  • She defines master as understanding not just what to do, but why it matters, similar to a driver who understands the logic behind road rules.
  • Once a leader or team member masters a function, she encourages them to multiply themselves by training others and building “clones” in capability (not personality) across the team.


3.2 Stop–Delegate–Continue–Start

  • Lisa presents a practical exercise: Stop, Delegate, Continue, Start, applied across the owner’s tasks.
  • Stop includes tasks that have low or no value and should not be done by anyone, such as unnecessary long meetings, overlong emails, or repeated unproductive retraining.
  • She encourages owners to identify meetings that should be shorter or replaced by an email, thereby freeing up calendar time.
  • Delegate includes tasks that are valuable but can be done by others, such as payroll, note‑taking, organizing spaces, or collecting data and information.
  • She states that many employees are only about 60% productive in a typical day, which means there is capacity to absorb additional delegated tasks.
  • She asks owners to question whether they are doing someone else’s work and to push those tasks back to the appropriate role.
  • Continue includes high‑value activities that align with the owner’s role, such as reviewing KPIs, holding one‑on‑ones with direct reports, developing leaders, and reviewing customer feedback and reviews.
  • She references a quote attributed to Richard Branson (transcribed as “Brunson”) about the risk of not training employees who stay, underscoring the importance of leadership development.
  • Start includes revenue‑generating or strategic tasks that the owner knows they should do but is not doing due to lack of time, such as creating social media content, reviewing a daily tracker, and saying yes to relationship‑building opportunities.
  • She stresses that the purpose of the exercise is to free up owner time for high‑leverage, revenue‑generating and strategic work.


Practical Tools: Duplication Sheet, Job Descriptions, Metrics, and Case Studies

Duplication Sheet and Task Quantification

  • Lisa describes a duplication sheet template that lists every task the owner does, how often it occurs, and how many minutes it takes.
  • The sheet also includes a column that calculates the total time per task and marks whether each task directly increases revenue or not.
  • Tasks are labeled as Start, Stop, Continue, or Delegate, and are associated with a department or future role (such as HR, accounting, purchasing, marketing).
  • She explains that this process helps owners see how much time they could get back and what type of role they truly need to hire.
  • She notes that some tasks are assigned to existing staff (who may be promoted), while others indicate the need to hire a new person (often labeled as TBD in the sheet).
  • She stresses that this approach is more effective than vaguely telling someone to “be me,” because it defines clear, concrete responsibilities.


Building Job Descriptions from Tasks

  • Once tasks are grouped by department or function, Lisa translates them into position summaries, objectives, and competencies to form a proper job description.
  • She recommends grouping tasks based on frequency, revenue impact, and alignment with organizational goals (for example, launching a specific number of new products).
  • She notes that this method lets owners design roles that are tied directly to real work they are currently doing, instead of inventing hypothetical positions.
  • She explains that this is particularly useful in deciding between hiring roles such as HR, accounting, purchasing, warehouse, or marketing.


Metrics, Accountability, and Abdication vs Delegation

  • Lisa emphasizes that once tasks are delegated, owners need metrics and accountability to measure whether the new person is succeeding.
  • She advises defining specific, trackable targets (for example, number of social posts per month, engagement growth, or revenue impact) for each delegated area.
  • She distinguishes abdication from delegation: abdication happens when an owner hires a “unicorn,” hands over everything, and stops paying attention.
  • She warns that abdication frequently leads to frustration or failure, because the owner does not provide clarity, coaching, or oversight.
  • She defines true delegation as sharing responsibility with clear expectations, regular check‑ins, and ongoing coaching and support.
  • She recommends biweekly one‑on‑ones as the main structure for checking metrics, removing roadblocks, and giving feedback, while keeping ownership of outcomes.


Case Studies

  • Lisa shares a case study of an IT company owner who wants to step away from day‑to‑day operations and enjoy vacations without constant work.
  • After implementing the duplication process, he delegates into COO, HR, and operations roles and reduces his email checking on a trip to only two times, while still providing high‑level strategic vision.
  • She shares another case study of a power supply distributor whose main office is in Philadelphia and who moves to Florida after building his leadership team.
  • Over about six months, he delegates into a VP, accounting, purchasing, and warehouse, while still visiting the site monthly and providing quarterly strategic oversight.
  • In both cases, she notes that strategy remains with the owner as Visionary, and certain areas (for example, marketing in the power supply company) are intentionally not fully delegated until the team is ready.


Team Structure, E‑Commerce Scaling, Leadership, and One‑on‑Ones

E‑commerce and C‑Suite Needs

  • Lisa confirms that all business owners feel their businesses are unusually complex, but e‑commerce is distinct mainly in its executional details, especially around marketing and platforms like Amazon.
  • She states that Amazon is very different from other sales channels, and e‑commerce businesses are especially marketing‑heavy.
  • For e‑commerce businesses approaching $20 million+, she highlights marketing and supply chain/inventory management as the two critical pillars.
  • She recommends hiring or building roles for marketing strategy and content creation, noting that strategists and creators are usually different people.
  • She stresses the importance of a purchasing / inventory management function that monitors stock weekly, manages shipments to Amazon, and ensures products do not go out of stock.
  • She notes that larger e‑commerce brands often benefit from in‑house marketing talent for platforms like Amazon and TikTok, especially once the economics justify moving away from agencies.


Agencies vs In‑House Teams

  • Lisa uses her own context as an example, where she hires agencies to manage Amazon ads and other marketing tasks as a bridge until she can justify in‑house hires.
  • She mentions that one of her agencies charges around $2,500 per month, which is currently cheaper than hiring a dedicated employee for the same scope.
  • She explains that she still meets agencies every two weeks and coordinates via email and Slack, maintaining oversight rather than fully abdicating responsibility.
  • She notes that she previously used one agency for multiple brands but finds better results splitting work across different agencies for different needs.
  • She recognizes that agencies are not always the best solution long term, and she continues to evaluate their performance and consider in‑house alternatives.


Middle Management and Revenue per Employee

  • The group discusses the challenge of middle managers, and Lisa agrees that hiring a middle manager should not simply add cost and communication layers.
  • She emphasizes that every leader, including middle managers, should be executing real work, not just “managing people.”
  • She suggests a practical guideline of about $250,000 revenue per employee as a target when evaluating when and how to add more staff.
  • She points out that decisions to outsource or hire internally should involve comparing cost, revenue impact, and the company’s current financials and goals.


Leadership Development and One‑on‑Ones

  • Lisa strongly advocates for one‑on‑one meetings between leaders and their direct reports as a primary tool for development and alignment.
  • She recommends 30‑minute one‑on‑ones every two weeks as a default, held virtually if needed, with weekly meetings during onboarding or intensive projects.
  • She explains that these meetings focus on metrics, goals, obstacles, and personal development, not just status updates.
  • She notes that structured one‑on‑ones reduce daily interruptions, because team members know they have a predictable forum to bring issues and questions.
  • She encourages leaders to stretch capable team members by giving extra responsibility before formally promoting them, to test whether they can handle a leadership role.
  • She acknowledges that not every high performer makes a good manager, and in such cases she recommends keeping them in an expert role and incentivizing them differently.
  • She shares an example of her social media manager, whom she coaches through one‑on‑ones to go beyond safe habits, create fresher content, and improve hooks and calls to action.
  • She stresses that clear vision and big goals (for example, aiming for $100 million in 10 years) help motivate team members to stretch beyond their comfort zones.

 

Resources Mentioned:

  • TEMPLATE - Leadership Duplication Activity (Google Sheets File)


In this session, leaders gain a detailed, practical framework for moving from overworked owner‑operator to strategic visionary supported by a capable leadership and operational team. 


Lisa’s examples, tools, and case studies show how intentional task analysis, structured delegation, and disciplined one‑on‑ones create the conditions for scalable growth.


The conversation also highlights specific considerations for e‑commerce founders, including the importance of marketing and supply‑chain roles, the use of agencies as interim support, and the decision points for building in‑house capabilities. 


Attendees leave with concrete next steps—such as completing a duplication sheet, refining their meeting structure, and designing targeted roles—that help them free up their own time while building a stronger, more autonomous organization.

items.title: Designing Robust AI Infrastructure: From Local Databases to Agentic Workflows － AI Channel Call July 26
items.description:
In this session, participants explore how to design robust AI and data infrastructure while sharing real-world implementation challenges from their own businesses. 

TOPICS:

  1. AI infrastructure choices: local vs cloud, databases (BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Supabase), and performance trade-offs
  2. Data quality, security, governance, and backup strategies for AI-driven systems
  3. Agentic workflows, skills, and planning–execution separation, plus personal goals around AI video at scale and enterprise architectures
items.description_text: In this session, participants explore how to design robust AI and data infrastructure while sharing real-world implementation challenges from their own businesses. TOPICS: AI infrastructure choices: local vs cloud, databases (BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Supabase), and performance trade-offs Data quality, security, governance, and backup strategies for AI-driven systems Agentic workflows, skills, and planning–execution separation, plus personal goals around AI video at scale and enterprise architectures
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss how to structure AI-focused community calls so members can share real problems and co-create solutions. 


In this session they also dive deeply into AI infrastructure database choices, security, agentic workflows, and personal goals for the coming month, especially around AI video and enterprise-grade architectures.

 

Call Format, Community, and Problem–Solution Approach

  • Participants frame this MDS AI Channel Monthly Call as a space where members share concrete AI or infrastructure problems so the group can collaboratively propose solutions.
  • Sam explains that he likes the “problem and solution” format used in New York boardroom meetings because it simultaneously helps the person asking the question and the wider community facing similar issues.
  • The group acknowledges that attendance may fluctuate due to seasonal and regional differences (e.g., summer in one region and winter in Argentina), but they agree the value comes from depth of discussion rather than the number of attendees.
  • Participants engage in informal rapport-building by talking about travel, weather, and living experiences in Argentina, Brazil, Berlin, and Amsterdam, which helps create trust and openness for more technical exchanges later in the call.


AI Infrastructure: Local vs Cloud, Databases, and Performance

  • June describes how she configures AI and development environments via the command line interface (CLI) so she can standardize multi-terminal and multi-machine setups across Linux-based systems.
  • She explains that a universal configuration file for cloud settings and code editors (e.g., “cloud MD file,” “codex file”) allows new machines to be added in minutes because configuration is already harmonized across the fleet.
  • June notes that modern large models are so computationally intensive that they often require multiple GPUs spread across more than one machine, so she slices GPU workloads and combines compute resources to approximate an enterprise-class setup.
  • The group discusses that when workloads run locally rather than through cloud APIs, they often experience significantly lower latency because the system avoids network round trips and token overhead.
  • June contrasts different database roles by explaining that BigQuery works better for quantitative and analytical workloads, whereas Supabase and PostgreSQL are better suited for text-heavy applications and advanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and GraphRAG setups.
  • Ramon asks whether specialized vector or RAG databases truly deliver speed or practical benefit over a well-implemented BigQuery solution for millions of keyword rows and thousands of SKUs, prompting a broader discussion on performance versus complexity.
  • June answers that the question is not only raw speed but also database capabilities and fit for purpose, especially when building GraphRAG, which standard BigQuery is not designed to support optimally.
  • Daniel explains that he migrated to PostgreSQL and largely local infrastructure because he experienced repeated reliability issues and credential-expiry problems with BigQuery and AWS, which disrupted automations.
  • He describes how running PostgreSQL locally with tools like NocoDB (an Airtable-like interface) and Metabase (a lightweight analytics and dashboard tool) allows him to plug and unplug front-end tools without ever migrating the underlying data.
  • Daniel emphasizes that local NVMe storage arrays and a local-area network substantially reduce query time, allowing even suboptimal schemas to feel fast while also reducing cloud cost and complexity.
  • Ramon highlights trade-offs of local hosting by raising concerns about remote team performance, internet outages, and the risk of local hardware failures and disasters such as fires.
  • Daniel responds that he applies a “3-2-1 backup” strategy, maintaining multiple backup formats, at least two locations, and one off-site store via Dropbox and periodic SQL backups to AWS, which mitigates data-loss risk while preserving local speed.

 

Data Quality, Security, Governance, and Backups

  • June explains that running infrastructure locally also gives teams more direct control over data migrations and schema evolution, which is crucial because data from Meta, Amazon, Shopify, Google, and other platforms uses inconsistent formats.
  • She illustrates data inconsistency problems such as varying date formats (YYYY-MM-DD vs DD-MM-YYYY) and name fields (e.g., “first name last name” vs “first name middle name last name”), which break joins and create errors in downstream AI workflows and automations.
  • She describes how large-scale RAG systems often fail not because of model limitations but because of poor schema design, unclean data, and insufficient planning around how different systems will integrate over time.
  • Daniel shares that he now stores raw input data exactly as received and uses automation workflows to normalize and transform it on output, which reduces the risk of losing source fidelity when partners such as Amazon change formats unexpectedly.
  • He explains that he uses n8n as a central workflow engine to parse, clean, and route data, and that most AI applications query the cleaned outputs rather than touching raw data directly.
  • June stresses the need for robust security, including row-level security and careful control of read, write, update, and delete permissions, especially once a company starts giving broader data access to non-technical employees.
  • She notes that some managed services such as Supabase may require paid tiers to fully implement user-level row security, which is one reason she prefers using PostgreSQL directly in many cases.
  • Daniel describes a security posture where machines do not communicate with each other via SSH; instead, they communicate only through authenticated APIs or containerized services, thereby reducing lateral movement risk if one system is compromised.
  • He notes that he deliberately refuses to store SSH credentials in AI tools or chat logs and runs automated processes that scrub tokens and secrets from logs stored in Dropbox, further limiting exposure if logs ever leak.
  • Both June and Daniel highlight that AI models are not yet safe to let them write directly to production databases, so they favor deterministic, non-AI workflows for ingestion and only allow AI to work through controlled intermediaries such as n8n or no-code APIs.
  • June mentions that point-in-time recovery is essential because both humans and AI will make mistakes, and teams must be able to roll back data states to maintain integrity.
  • Daniel reiterates that he treats core production data as immutable and only manipulates copies in auxiliary tables or views, which simplifies auditing and recovery.


Agentic Workflows, Skills, Context Management, and “Planning vs Doing”

  • Ramon describes a recurring issue where AI tools—especially Claude—try to rush into implementation before all scenarios are fully explored, prompting him to seek strategies to slow the model down and stay longer in a planning phase.
  • Sam describes his two-step agentic workflow, where he first uses a “brainstorming agent” in Claude (often a Fable-based or multi-agent setup) that is explicitly instructed not to build anything but to ask questions, research tools, and produce a clear goal for a separate “builder agent.”
  • In Sam’s approach, the brainstorming agent explores requirements, dependencies, and potential tools (e.g., APIs to find viral Instagram reels by niche) and outputs a well-structured goal description that a second, code-focused agent can then implement autonomously.
  • Daniel explains that he uses skills extensively in Claude, treating them as modular “micro-policies” to correct recurring behavior issues, such as launching too many sub-agents, misusing tools, or trying to write SQL directly against production databases.
  • He describes having separate skills for planning versus execution, as well as domain-specific skills (e.g., ClickUp, Shopify) and a “nerf skill” that activates whenever a model update appears to degrade performance or stability.
  • Daniel notes that he often loads many skills in a session because skills encode decisions and guardrails he does not want to repeat, and they function like permanent “operational memory” attached to specific tools or workflows.
  • June elaborates on a three-stage workflow for complex builds: a first session for strategy and high-level design, a second session for designing tests, edge cases, and constraints, and a third session for tactical execution guided by structured JSON outputs from the earlier sessions.
  • She emphasizes that using JSON as an intermediate blueprint reduces drift, because it forces structure and limits interpretive leeway compared to freeform Markdown, making it easier for subsequent sessions or agents to implement plans accurately.
  • June recommends clearing context between major phases and starting new sessions with only the final structured plan so that earlier, superseded ideas do not pollute the context window and confuse later decisions.
  • She proposes “hooks” and “gates” (e.g., a defined safe word or explicit approval signal) so that the model is not allowed to start coding or deploying until a specific trigger phrase appears and all preconditions are met.
  • Daniel reinforces June’s point by framing the context window as a stack of flashcards where all statements have equal weight, meaning that conflicting instructions (e.g., multiple heights or decisions) force the model to pick arbitrarily unless the user deliberately simplifies the context.
  • Participants agree that better separation of phases (plan, test, implement, verify) and well-designed skills or guardrails significantly improve reliability, reduce rework, and make AI collaboration more predictable.

 

Personal Goals, AI Video at Scale, and Enterprise-Grade Architectures

  • Ramon shares that his primary goal before the next monthly call is to figure out AI video production at scale, particularly building a full workflow that can generate and distribute large volumes of video content.
  • He explains that he is willing to work for free with agencies already doing AI video at scale in order to learn their processes, create sample videos, and then replicate or adapt the workflow for his own use.
  • Sam notes that he shares a similar goal focused on AI-powered content distribution and that he is starting to post on around ten different accounts to test a pipeline focused on copying and adapting already-proven content patterns.
  • Sam states that his focus for the next month is to debug and validate whether his pipeline actually produces tangible results in terms of performance and growth across these accounts.
  • Daniel reflects that his challenge is not a lack of ideas but an overabundance of them, accumulated over decades in e-commerce, and he needs to prioritize and reduce his reliance on high-cost or volatile models like Fable to manage tokens and complexity.
  • He describes a need to “dial back” experiments, focusing instead on fewer, high-impact projects and allowing some backlog of ideas to remain unimplemented to avoid spending more tokens organizing them than actually building them.
  • June discusses her evolving focus on “harness engineering,” where she applies rigorous logic, game theory, and systems architecture to build reliable agentic systems and legal-oriented RAG for enterprises.
  • She notes that she has experience in M&A, corporate governance, and board education, and she uses that background to reason about how AI agents should make decisions when finance, legal, marketing, and operations objectives conflict.
  • June highlights that many large enterprises struggle with AI deployment because they lack clean data, coherent schemas, and well-designed system architectures, which explains why many AI projects fail to produce sustainable value.
  • She emphasizes that technical architecture and workflow design must be integrated with legal constraints (e.g., privilege and confidentiality in legal models, such as UK requirements for running law models on confidential AWS clouds) to avoid regulatory or contractual breaches.
  • The group ends the call by reaffirming their individual goals and committing to using the next month to advance concrete initiatives—from AI video pipelines to infrastructure hardening and agentic workflow design—and to report back in future sessions.


In conclusion, this session centers on how experienced practitioners design AI systems that are not only powerful but also reliable, secure, and maintainable over the long term. 


The participants connect high-level architectural choices—such as local versus cloud infrastructure, database selection, and agentic workflows—with practical goals like AI video at scale, robust RAG implementations, and clear planning-execution separation.

files.name: Transcript - MDS SEO Channel Call
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783638887546-MDS SEO Channel Call_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session participants focus on upcoming Amazon SEO and listing-structure changes and how to prepare catalog-wide frameworks that will survive and benefit from the transition. 


The conversation also covers practical testing tactics image strategy and the use of multiple data sources and AI tools to improve indexing, click-through rate (CTR), and conversion.

 

AI Tools, Fable, Mythos, and GPT Usage

  • Participants discuss Fable as an AI tool that currently powers most of Alex’s frameworks, website builds, and app code checks, and Alex states that he is “doing everything in Fable right now” while it is still free until a certain date.
  • They explain that Fable is a wrapper around Mythos, and Ramon mentions that Mythos is currently performing better than GPT 5.6, making it one of the strongest available models for their use cases.
  • Alex notes that he still uses GPT mainly for image-related tasks, but he increasingly relies on Fable/Mythos for text, frameworks, and code validation.
  • The group references how they are moving most of their operational and SEO frameworks into these AI tools so they can standardize workflows and quickly generate or revise large volumes of listing content.

 

Amazon Title Changes, Item Highlights, and Indexing Strategy

  • Alex and Ramon clarify that Amazon is enforcing a new title structure, where the visible title is effectively constrained to around 75 characters, with an additional 125 characters becoming part of a separate “item highlights” field, for a total of approximately 200 characters handled on the backend.
  • They discuss a deadline around July 24 when Amazon will begin enforcing the new rules and potentially using AI to automatically rewrite or slice titles for sellers who do not update their listings themselves.
  • Daniel explains that Amazon’s handling of titles and highlights differs by device, and he observes that only part of the title shows on smaller mobile screens, which creates uncertainty about which elements (e.g., dosage, count, critical specs) the shopper actually sees before clicking.
  • Alex states that item highlights are 100% indexed and strongly influence voice and AI surfaces like Alexa/Cosmo, and he notes that Amazon appears to be shifting from pure keyword density to customer query–driven, audience-specific descriptions.
  • They emphasize that this change forces a shift from keyword stuffing to clear, benefit-focused copy that answers customer questions, explains what the product does, and defines the target audience.
  • Alex shares examples in supplements and automotive (e.g., a magnesium glycinate product) where the new structure keeps the core product definition and key specs in the main title but moves benefits and use-cases (sleep, digestion, stress, recovery) into the item highlights.
  • The group discusses that brand length may or may not count toward the 75-character limit, and Alex warns that if brand name characters are included in that limit, long brand names will heavily constrain what can be communicated in the title.
  • Daniel notes that Amazon’s API documentation suggests sellers still pass 200 characters and then split at 75 and 125 on their side, implying Amazon is internally operating with the existing 200-character field but surfacing it differently.

 

Framework for Rewriting Listings and Catalog-Wide SEO Overhaul

  • Alex explains that he has built a full framework for new Amazon titles and copy, including the “science” behind title structure, examples, and standard value propositions (SVPs), which he plans to share as multiple posts within the MDS community.
  • He plans to export his existing SKUs, apply the framework, and then use a third-party tool called Store Automator to push those changes automatically via API, enabling large-scale updates for thousands of SKUs.
  • Alex describes how he already tested the approach on around 360 SKUs, noting that the changes went live within a few hours and the process is essentially “two clicks away” once the framework and brand attributes are defined.
  • Daniel shares that his team is also revisiting their launch backlog and older catalogs, indicating that this change triggers a full catalog re-think rather than a partial tweak to just a few listings.
  • Alex states that this is not only a title project; anything removed from the title (for example, keywords or secondary benefits that no longer fit in 75 characters) must be reinserted into bullet points, product descriptions, attributes, and backend fields to maintain or improve indexation.
  • He argues that Amazon is moving toward a more advanced indexing and audience system (with lexical matching and “six layers” of relevance), and this forced rewrite is a good opportunity for proactive sellers to get ahead while many competitors either resist change or allow Amazon’s AI to rewrite their listings poorly.
  • Alex mentions that he has recently updated an acquired brand with over 500 listings in one go using his framework and has already seen improvements in indexing, impressions, and conversions, which reinforces the effectiveness of the methodology.

 

Mobile Display, Click-Through Rates, and Image Strategy

  • Daniel describes how mobile devices display titles and highlights inconsistently, with some phones showing only a few words or cutting off mid-number (e.g., “400…” instead of “400 mg”), which makes it hard to control what shoppers see before clicking.
  • He notes that ads on mobile often show only two lines instead of three, further constraining which parts of the title and highlights are visible in a sponsored ad context.
  • Alex responds that historically 80–90 characters were visible on mobile, which likely informed Amazon’s decision to aim for a 75-character main title, but he agrees that device variability still introduces risk for critical specs being truncated.
  • The group concludes that critical, product-defining specs (e.g., dosage like “1000 IU,” count like “120 capsules,” or key qualifiers like “sugar-free” in supplements) should still live in the main title if at all possible, while benefits and audience messaging (e.g., “high absorption,” “sleep support,” “gentle on digestion”) should move primarily into the item highlights.
  • Based on the uncertainty of text visibility, Daniel and Alex agree that primary images become even more important, because shoppers can always see the visual, whereas they may not see the entire title on small screens.
  • Alex shares that adding clear product boxes in the main image (showing fitment years, OEM replacement info, or key features) has tripled CTR overnight in automotive, even though the physical products actually ship in simple poly bags without branded boxes.
  • They recommend that important specifics—such as size, count, compatibility years, OEM references, or flavor—be visually represented on packaging or graphical elements in the primary image so that critical information is understood instantly, even if text fields are truncated.
  • Alex advises testing images live on the listing, rather than relying solely on Amazon’s A/B testing tools or third-party split-testing platforms, because he has seen split-test winners fail in the real market; he prefers to change the image on the main listing, run for about a week, then evaluate actual CTR and ad data.
  • Examples are shared from supplements and industrial hardware where simple, bold images with clear information outperform cluttered, text-heavy visuals that look cheap or dated.

 

Data Sources, Alexa/Rufus Insights, and Cross-Channel Considerations

  • Alex explains that he uses Alexa (often referred to as Rufus in the discussion) to understand how Amazon’s AI/assistant “sees” a product, including which features, benefits, and use-cases it emphasizes when describing a listing to customers.
  • He combines Alexa outputs with data from Search Query Performance, Brand Analytics, Product Opportunity Explorer, reviews, Q&A, and external tools like Data Dive and Data Rover, then feeds all of this into Claude to generate optimized titles, bullet points, and descriptions using his framework.
  • Ramon asks whether Alexa provides information that Search Query Performance does not, and Alex answers that Alexa tends to blend insights from competitors and broader audience behavior, so it may surface additional use-cases or messaging that are not directly visible just from one brand’s SQP data.
  • They discuss the practical challenge of scraping Alexa/Rufus, acknowledging that scraping can be brittle and may violate terms of service, but Alex notes that some people are building scrapers (for example, community members like “Anthony” who sell Claude skills and have created scrapers, possibly offered free if they are TOS-sensitive).
  • Alex suggests that a dedicated agent on a phone with a Prime account interacting with Alexa regularly could ingest and store Alexa descriptions into a database, which can then be merged with other data sources for richer optimization.
  • The group also briefly compares Amazon’s internal ecosystem to other platforms, noting that Amazon’s structured data and behavior patterns are largely self-sufficient, and external SEO tools often reproduce information already available through Amazon reviews, Q&A, and internal analytics.
  • June points out that platforms like Shopify and Google share similar schemas, while Meta and TikTok use different classification structures; however, the group agrees that for this particular Amazon-focused framework, cross-channel schema differences do not materially change the core listing strategy.
  • They mention tools and resources like AskThePublic.com for broader customer queries and CalO (or Halo) data for influencer/content insights on TikTok, but conclude that most of what they need to optimize for Amazon is already captured in Amazon’s own ecosystem and customer behavior.

 

In this session, the group systematically dissects Amazon’s upcoming title and highlight changes, agreeing that sellers who proactively adopt a structured, data-driven framework for titles, highlights, bullets, and images will gain a competitive edge as others struggle or allow Amazon’s AI to rewrite their listings. 


They highlight the importance of integrating Amazon-native data sources, AI tools like Fable and Claude, and strong primary imagery to create listings that both index well and convert reliably across devices.

They close by outlining next steps: Alex will finalize and share his Amazon SEO framework in Markdown form (with associated skills) to the group, they will begin testing it in controlled batches across multiple categories, and they will reconvene in a future call (likely around or after the enforcement date) to compare results and refine their joint approach.

  1. Cash flow management and forecasting (13‑week cash flow, channel‑level P&Ls, risk of inventory and ad prepayments).
  2. Entity structure and exit planning (S‑corp vs C‑corp, QSBS benefits, coordinating with CPAs and CFOs).

files.name: Transcript - MDS Mogul Call with Ecom CPA
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783557416101-MDS Mogul Call with Ecom CPA_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS community meet with Jeremy Allen of Ecom CPA to discuss practical tax strategies tailored to e-commerce businesses. 


The conversation focuses on ways to improve cash flow reduce tax liability structure entities for future exits and clarify how Ecom CPA works alongside existing tools and providers.

Jason Pratt’s Experience with Ecom CPA and the Importance of a Specialized CPA

  • Jason Pratt explains that he is deeply focused on marketing, analytics, and growth, and he openly states that financial and tax matters are not his area of strength.
  • He shares that he initially looks for the “cheapest” accounting options but learns through experience that this approach leads to mistakes and insufficient support.
  • Jason describes how he looks for a team that understands Amazon, Omni‑channel, and e-commerce models, and he emphasizes the value of people who truly understand the nuances of the space.
  • He highlights that he prefers to work with people he likes personally and notes that Jeremy is down-to-earth, approachable, and easy to connect with, even bonding over sports.
  • Jason states that Ecom CPA becomes a thought partner, not just a compliance provider, helping him think through business decisions, scaling issues, and future scenarios.
  • He explains that his “goal” with a CPA is to stay fully compliant while getting as close to the tax-optimization line as possible without crossing it.
  • He notes that working with Ecom CPA allows him not to think about taxes day-to-day, which gives him peace of mind and lets him focus on growth.
  • Jason points out that while tax is not exciting, it becomes very enjoyable when owners receive refund checks and know their numbers are correct and optimized.

Core Tax Strategies for E‑Commerce: Inventory, R&D, Depreciation, and Entity Tools

Inventory and Cash Flow Timing

  • Jeremy Allen explains that cash is the lifeblood of the business, and any strategy that generates or preserves cash provides more options for owners.
  • He introduces a key strategy whereby certain e-commerce businesses can deduct inventory when purchased instead of when sold, which accelerates tax deductions and improves short‑term cash flow.
  • He clarifies that this inventory strategy is subject to limitations, including a $32 million annual gross receipts cap, meaning larger businesses cannot use it.
  • He notes that this approach is fundamentally a timing difference, because tax is deferred rather than eliminated, and it assumes the business continues to grow and buy inventory over time.
  • He stresses that relying only on AI tools like ChatGPT for tax planning is risky because they can miss important thresholds and limitations, so an experienced professional needs to review and implement the strategy.


Bonus Depreciation, Real Estate, and Cost Segregation

  • Jeremy explains that bonus depreciation allows 100% deduction in the year of purchase for qualifying assets such as warehouse equipment, manufacturing equipment, and heavy vehicles.
  • He states that if a business owns a warehouse or manufacturing facility, performing a cost segregation study can reclassify parts of the property into shorter-life assets that qualify for accelerated depreciation.
  • He mentions that a typical cost segregation can allow 30–40% of the value of a property to be deducted in year one, depending on the specific property components.
  • Dan raises the idea of buying a warehouse (real estate) to mitigate taxes instead of over-buying inventory, and he suggests that real estate feels less risky and more likely to appreciate in value.
  • Jeremy confirms that over-buying inventory carries risk if the business underperforms later, whereas real estate is often more stable, but both approaches are tax tools that must be weighed against risk and capital needs.


R&D Tax Credits for E‑Commerce and AI

  • Jeremy clarifies that many e-commerce owners overlook R&D tax credits because they assume R&D only applies to classic tech or lab environments.
  • He explains that product formulation (e.g., supplements, cosmetics, food, pet products), packaging engineering, and new product development can all qualify as R&D in many cases.
  • He notes that AI-related development, such as building tools, using APIs, or creating internal systems, can also qualify for R&D credits if it meets the technical uncertainty criteria.
  • He highlights that R&D credits typically yield about 6–10% tax credit on qualifying spend, and that many U.S. states additionally offer state‑level R&D incentives.
  • He emphasizes that R&D wage and contractor costs must generally be U.S.-based to qualify under the current rules, since the code aims to incentivize onshoring of development activities.
  • Daniel asks about R&D lookbacks, and Jeremy explains that doing lookbacks requires amending returns, which extends the statute of limitations and thus potentially increases audit exposure.
  • Jeremy advises that whether to do R&D lookbacks is a cost–benefit and risk analysis, balancing the size of credits against compliance costs and the desire to avoid reopening closed years.
  • He recommends being as thorough as reasonably possible in documentation: even a one– to two‑page brief per project can be enough, and more documentation usually strengthens the file if the IRS audits.


Tariff Refunds, Shrinkage, and Other Deductions

  • Jeremy reminds attendees to ensure they have pursued tariff refunds, noting that posts in the MDS community indicate that some sellers still have not captured these opportunities.
  • He points out that shrinkage in the supply chain—such as lost, damaged, or missing inventory—is common as businesses grow and should be correctly recognized as a tax-deductible expense.
  • He stresses the importance of not leaving these shrinkage amounts “trapped” in inventory on the books and instead ensuring they are properly written off before year-end.


Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) and Future Exits

  • Jeremy introduces Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) as a powerful exit-planning tool for C corporations.
  • He explains that under the current rules, up to $15 million of gain can be excluded from federal tax on the sale of QSBS, with potential “stacking” strategies that may effectively shelter more in certain structures.
  • He notes that some states, such as California, do not conform to the federal QSBS rules, so state tax treatment can differ and requires attention.
  • He explains that previously the holding period for full QSBS exclusion is five years, but there are now provisions allowing 50% exclusion at three years, which is attractive in fast-changing e-commerce markets.
  • He emphasizes that QSBS requires a C‑corp structure, and the “clock” starts when the corporation first qualifies, so timing and legal setup are critical.
  • He states that Ecom CPA typically works with specialized attorneys on QSBS structuring to ensure that all requirements are met and that the structure does not “blow up” at exit.


Cash Flow Management, Forecasting, Channels, and Founder Practices

  • Jeremy recommends that e-commerce businesses use a 13‑week cash flow model to track incoming and outgoing cash, especially in relation to inventory purchases and platform payment delays.
  • He explains that a 13-week view allows founders and CFOs to see when cash will likely be tight and to plan financing, purchases, or tax payments accordingly.
  • He stresses the importance of channel‑level P&Ls for platforms such as Amazon, TikTok Shop, and Whatnot, so that owners can see whether each channel is actually profitable.
  • He notes that new channels can drive top-line growth but carry hidden fees and costs, making it critical to measure true profitability rather than only revenue.
  • Jason asks how founders should think about taxes by quarter, and Jeremy responds that proactive quarterly tax reviews are ideal for eight-figure and growing businesses.
  • Jeremy explains that effective tax planning must happen during the year, not just in November or December, so that real business decisions and “facts” can be shaped to match chosen tax strategies.
  • He notes that reviewing each quarter allows founders to estimate current-year tax liabilities, decide whether to invest, buy assets, or accelerate deductions, and coordinate with the CFO on cash requirements.

Ecom CPA’s Services, Structures (S‑Corp vs C‑Corp, PTET), and Practical FAQs

Ecom CPA Service Tiers and Collaboration with Other Providers

  • Jeremy describes Ecom CPA’s three main service tiers as Tax Planning, Tax Accounting, and Fractional CFO services.
  • He explains that tax planning focuses on strategies like those discussed in the call, tax accounting covers compliance and returns, and CFO services include forecasting, cash modeling, and higher-level financial guidance.
  • Dan asks whether Ecom CPA works alongside Moody, a bookkeeping provider, and Jeremy confirms that many MDS members use Moody for bookkeeping and Ecom CPA for tax planning and tax work.
  • Jeremy confirms that Ecom CPA can serve as the CFO layer while another firm, such as Moody, handles day-to-day bookkeeping.
  • Jason Munckton explains that their no‑cost assessment typically requires about 20 minutes to gather data and leads to a tax planning session where Ecom CPA grades current CPA work and identifies missed savings.


PTET (Pass-Through Entity Tax) and Multi-State Issues

  • Jason Munckton introduces PTET (Pass‑Through Entity Tax) as a mechanism for S corps and LLCs to have the entity pay state income tax rather than the owner paying it personally.
  • Jeremy elaborates that PTET helps owners bypass the federal SALT (state and local tax) deduction limitations by shifting state tax payments to the entity, where they are generally fully deductible.
  • He explains that PTET is especially useful for owners in high‑tax states like California, where state rates can reach 11–13%.
  • Jason notes that many sellers do not realize that when they reach $500,000 in revenue in a given state, that state often expects an income tax filing, which creates multi-state tax complexity.
  • Jason adds that when a seller’s home state has higher tax rates than the state where they are generating revenue, careful apportionment can reduce tax by shifting income to lower-tax jurisdictions.


S‑Corp vs C‑Corp, Sales, and Liability Considerations

  • Rich asks whether becoming a C corporation makes it harder to sell, and Jeremy explains that issues arise mainly with non‑sophisticated buyers or advisers who are unfamiliar with stock versus asset deals.
  • Jeremy states that for sophisticated buyers, lawyers can usually perform a reorganization (such as an F reorg) so that structure does not materially hinder the transaction.
  • He estimates that QSBS‑driven C‑corp structures start to make more sense for businesses with sale prices in the low millions (e.g., $2–5M and up), though exact thresholds depend on growth and reinvestment plans.
  • Daniel asks about liability differences between S‑corps and C‑corps, and Jeremy clarifies that S‑corp tax liability passes through to shareholders, whereas a C‑corp pays tax at the corporate level.
  • Jeremy confirms that if a large tax event occurs in an S‑corp, the owner is personally on the hook for the tax liability, whereas in a C‑corp, it is the corporation’s liability.


Inventory Deduction Elections and Exit Impacts

  • Daniel asks whether deducting inventory upfront increases the tax hit at sale, and Jeremy confirms that it does, because the business then has little or no tax basis in the inventory.
  • Jeremy explains that when a buyer pays for inventory and the seller has no basis, the seller recognizes ordinary income on that amount, whereas under capitalization, the buyer often purchases inventory near cost with little additional tax.
  • He notes that although this creates a larger taxable event at exit, it is offset by the cash flow benefits gained in earlier years when the inventory was immediately expensed.
  • Daniel confirms his understanding that the strategy does not necessarily increase total lifetime tax but primarily shifts the timing of when tax is paid, which Jeremy agrees with.

Ad Prepayments and Other Deferral Strategies

  • Jason Munckton notes that some sellers use prepaid Google Ads as a way to accelerate deductions in the current year, which can help shift tax into the future.
  • He explains that prepaid ad spend is similar in risk profile to buying additional inventory, because it assumes future demand and performance will justify the upfront outlay.
  • Jeremy categorizes tax strategies into three broad types: deferrals (timing), credits (no cash outlay), and investments (money put into assets such as insurance companies or real estate), and he emphasizes that strategy choice must match the owner’s cash and risk preferences.

In this session, the MDS community and Ecom CPA walk through a practical playbook for e-commerce tax strategy, covering inventory timing, R&D credits, depreciation, entity structure, and cash flow management.

The discussion shows how nuanced tax planning can significantly improve cash position and optionality for founders, especially when coordinated with forecasting and channel-level profitability analysis.


By the end of the call, attendees gain a clearer understanding of when to consider C‑corp and QSBS strategies, how to leverage tools like PTET, R&D credits, and cost segregation, and how Ecom CPA can complement existing providers such as Moody. 


The overall tone of the session is collaborative and solution-oriented, emphasizing proactive quarterly planning and thoughtful use of tax law as a strategic lever rather than a once-a-year compliance task.
