cliff_notes:
In this session Jordyn Levine from Euka presents a new way for brands to repurpose TikTok Shop creator content into Meta ads to scale performance efficiently. 


The discussion is organized into five key topics covering the strategic rationale, workflow changes, platform capabilities, practical use cases, and member-specific offers.


Call Context and Objectives

  • Jordyn Levine introduces herself as the person leading partnerships at Euka, with a focus on ensuring MDS members are successful using Euka’s tools.
  • Jordyn explains that Euka initially is known as a TikTok Shop affiliate outreach tool, but the company now significantly expands into Meta ads leveraging TikTok Shop creator content.
  • The primary objective of the session is to explain how brands can turn their best TikTok Shop creator videos into Meta ads in a streamlined way, and to present a special enterprise offer for MDS members.


Strategic Rationale: Why Use TikTok Shop Content for Meta Ads

  • Jordyn explains that top TikTok Shop videos already prove themselves as winners by generating conversions, engagement, and strong signals such as purchases, likes, and comments.
  • The strategy uses the idea that “your best Meta ads already exist” in TikTok Shop, because content that persuades on TikTok is highly likely to perform well on Meta as well.
  • Creator content is positioned as more relatable and higher-performing than polished brand ads, since viewers connect more with “regular people” than with idealized models.
  • Jordyn notes that creative is the new performance lever, and states that roughly 49% of sales impact on Meta comes from creative quality, not just targeting or bidding.
  • Euka observes from its 5,000+ brand base that brands using TikTok Shop content in Meta ads often see 65% higher ROAS when testing more ads per month, especially when they can launch 20+ fresh creatives regularly.
  • TikTok Shop creator videos are described as action-driven, emphasizing hooks, demos, and clear calls to action, which translates well into high-intent Meta ad behavior.
  • Jordyn emphasizes that ad fatigue on Meta is accelerating, with winning creatives often lasting only 2–4 weeks, so brands need a continuous pipeline of fresh, tested videos.
  • TikTok Shop is framed as a “pre-testing ground” where GMV Max and other data sources pre-validate what works, letting brands move proven winners into Meta rather than blindly testing.


Manual Workflow vs. Euka’s Automated Meta Workflow

  • Jordyn describes the traditional manual process as fragmented: brands scroll TikTok manually, hunt for videos that feature their product, then DM creators one by one to request usage rights.
  • The manual process typically requires negotiating terms in DMs, sending standalone contracts, chasing signatures, requesting original video files, and manually tracking rights and expiration dates in spreadsheets.
  • Payment in the manual system is often inconsistent and confusing, because teams must calculate commissions separately, remember who is owed what, and coordinate finance and marketing in a disjointed way.
  • Many brands either abandon Meta repurposing or severely limit it because this manual process consumes time across multiple team members and VAs.
  • In contrast, Euka’s new workflow allows brands to connect TikTok Shop and Meta Business one time and then see all top-performing TikTok Shop videos in a single dashboard ranked by performance.
  • Within Euka, brands can request usage rights in bulk from multiple creators with just a few clicks, removing the need for individual DMs and ad-hoc negotiations.
  • Euka lets brands launch licensed creator assets directly as Meta ads from within the platform, so there is no need to download and re-upload files or jump between multiple tools.
  • The platform auto-calculates creator commissions based on attributed Meta sales or ad spend, significantly simplifying financial tracking and payout operations.

Euka Platform Capabilities: Dashboard, Rights Management, and Payouts

  • Euka’s Meta Ads dashboard displays each video with its key metrics, including ad status, spend, sales, ROI, attributed items sold, product clicks, and ad conversion rate in one consolidated view.
  • Users can request usage rights per video or in bulk, using flexible compensation models such as percentage of Meta-attributed sales, percentage of ad spend with a cap, flat fees, or free usage.
  • Brands can configure contracts and compensation templates once (e.g., commission structure, duration, caps) and reuse them, ensuring legal and finance teams approve the templates upfront.
  • Creators receive a standardized enrollment and rights invitation through a single link that explains their commission rate, caps, and whether rights are lifetime or time-bound.
  • Once enrolled, a creator’s future videos are automatically covered under the agreed terms, so brands do not need to re-negotiate rights for every new piece of content.
  • Euka tracks rights duration and expiration, so brands can see clearly whether a video still has valid usage rights and avoid unintentionally running ads on expired rights.
  • The dashboard aggregates performance by creator, listing metrics such as number of linked videos, number of ads, total spend, total sales generated, and total commission earned by each creator.
  • The system tags every running ad back to a specific creator, ensuring transparent attribution and making it easy to identify which creators deserve more investment and which are less effective.
  • For payouts, Euka presents a payout view that shows pending payouts, number of payouts per creator, and overall payment status (e.g., negotiating, pending, active, expired, paid).
  • Finance and marketing teams can select multiple creators for payment with one click, and Euka automatically calculates what each creator is owed based on the agreed structure.
  • The platform is designed as a single source of truth across TikTok Shop and Meta, enabling CEOs, finance, media buyers, and creative strategists to all look at the same data.

Practical Use Cases, Q&A, and MDS Member Offer

  • James Thompson asks whether creators need their own Instagram/Meta accounts to participate, and Jordyn clarifies that they do not; the content typically runs from the brand’s Meta account.
  • James further asks if it is possible to run white-label ads through creator accounts when creators have Meta profiles; Jordyn notes this is a good idea and commits to checking with the Euka product team.
  • James inquires about Meta ad structures, asking whether brands plug TikTok winners directly into scale campaigns or first run ABO-style tests; Jordyn explains that approaches vary by brand and budget, with some going straight to scale and others using TikTok/GMV Max performance as a first screener.
  • Euka recommends using GMV Max performance and Euka’s “top converting videos” ranking as initial filters, then promoting those videos to Meta to reduce wasted ad spend.
  • Abdul from Yay Nuts shares a concrete use case where his team tests creatives first via TikTok Shop (especially through GMV Max) and then ports only winning creatives into Meta.
  • Abdul explains that his team focuses on Meta as a major revenue driver, uses TikTok Shop mainly as a content engine, and then directs Meta traffic to DTC (direct-to-consumer) channels.
  • Abdul describes a strategy of moving creators from TikTok Shop into a Discord community, where they are trained and nurtured, and notes that they pay commission on TikTok Shop but often use retainers instead of commission for Meta.
  • Jordyn highlights that Euka can support different compensation philosophies, whether brands prefer higher commissions on TikTok, lower or no commission on Meta, or a combined approach, as long as the overall creator relationship remains strong and fair.
  • James asks how the tool handles expiring rights, and Jordyn confirms that Euka tracks and shows rights duration so brands know when their rights end and can stop or adjust campaigns accordingly.
  • Jordyn emphasizes that Euka is built to reduce the manual workload that teams like Abdul’s currently handle through DMs, spreadsheets, and manual contract tracking.
  • For MDS members, Jordyn offers discounted pricing on the Euka Enterprise plan, specifically 25% off quarterly, 30% off semi-annual (six-month) contracts, and 40% off annual contracts.
  • Euka additionally offers one free month on every term for MDS members, along with strategy and training sessions to help teams adopt the Meta workflow effectively.
  • Jordyn encourages members to reach out directly for questions and onboarding via email at jordyn@euka.ai 
  • The company website referenced is https://euka.ai (Euka)


In this session, the group explores how to move from a fragmented, manual workflow for repurposing TikTok Shop content into Meta ads toward a centralized, data-driven system inside Euka. 


Through detailed feature walkthroughs and real-world use cases from members like Abdul, the conversation clarifies both the strategic value and the operational implications of this approach.


By the end of the call, participants understand how Euka can surface winning TikTok Shop videos, secure rights, launch Meta ads, and manage payouts in a unified interface.

items.title: PR That Works for Brands of Every Size - Mogul Call with Avaans Media
items.description:
In this session, MDS members meet with Tara Coomans from Avaans Media to learn how e-commerce brands can build visibility and authority in AI-driven environments beyond Amazon. 

TOPICS:

  1. Brand Extraction, Platform Dependency, and LLM Visibility
  2. PR, Earned Media, and Content Strategy for Authority Building
  3. Affiliate Networks, Skimlinks, and Practical Next Steps for E-commerce Brands
items.description_text: In this session, MDS members meet with Tara Coomans from Avaans Media to learn how e-commerce brands can build visibility and authority in AI-driven environments beyond Amazon. TOPICS: Brand Extraction, Platform Dependency, and LLM Visibility PR, Earned Media, and Content Strategy for Authority Building Affiliate Networks, Skimlinks, and Practical Next Steps for E-commerce Brands

files.name: Transcript - MDS Mogul Call with Avaans Media
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783022302627-MDS Mogul Call with Avaans Media_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Tara Coomans from Avaans Media explores how e-commerce brands can build authority and visibility in AI-driven environments beyond Amazon and other platforms. 


The discussion focuses on PR content strategy, LLM visibility, affiliate tools, and practical workflows that help brands reduce platform dependency and strengthen long-term brand equity.

 

Brand Extraction, Platform Dependency, and LLM Visibility

  • Tara defines “brand extraction” as the process where platforms like Amazon capture the customer relationship, purchase data, and much of the brand’s reputation, even though the brand creates the product, reviews, and trust.
  • She explains that Amazon is blocking LLMs from crawling its storefronts and reviews, which means AI systems do not “see” most of a brand’s Amazon-based reputation.
  • Tara emphasizes that AI and LLMs increasingly rely on authority signals—what other credible sources say about a brand—rather than on internal platform data or ad spend.
  • She highlights that brands are paying platform fees while also losing access to valuable customer data, such as repeat purchase behavior and customer insights that could inform marketing and product strategy.
  • Tara states that repeat purchase rates are significant (about 20–35% generally and 35–45% for consumables like supplements, pet care, and skincare), and platform dependency makes it harder to fully leverage this value.
  • She explains that LLMs do not read Amazon reviews, so brands must intentionally create off-Amazon reviews and content to build AI-recognized authority.
  • Tara notes that platforms like Amazon and TikTok are motivated to protect their own “moats”, so brands must counterbalance this by investing in owned media and independent authority building.

 

PR, Earned Media, and Authority Building for E-commerce Brands

  • Tara argues that PR has always been valuable, but LLMs have dramatically increased its upside because media coverage now acts as a primary authority signal in AI-generated answers.
  • She explains that branded content on outlets, press coverage, and thought leadership have longer-lasting impact than most social or ad campaigns and continue to work for brands over many months or years.
  • Tara clarifies that branded content (including press releases) provides strong authority signals while allowing the brand to fully control the narrative and positioning.
  • She positions press coverage as the highest level of authority, provided the coverage is highly relevant to the product category and audience (e.g., consumer products appearing in consumer-focused outlets, not unrelated verticals).
  • Tara describes a “media architecture” in which brands layer their own website content, LinkedIn presence, sponsored/native content, product reviews, and earned media to create a durable reputation profile.
  • She notes that publications are under financial pressure, so affiliate-based content (via tools like Skimlinks) helps them generate revenue while showcasing products, making this ecosystem increasingly important.
  • Tara confirms that PR delivers compounding long-term value, unlike ads that stop working when spend is paused, and she encourages brands to treat PR and authority building as strategic assets.

 

Key PR-related resources and entities mentioned:

  • Avaans Media (PR agency) – Website inferred: https://avaansmedia.com
  • Contact email: tara@avaansmedia.com 
  • PR Sprints (Avaans Media program):
    • Three-month PR and branded content program for consumer brands
    • Starts September 1 and typically focuses on fall and holiday periods
    • Accepts one brand per category for exclusivity
    • More details are accessible via a QR code Tara shares during the call or by emailing her and mentioning MDS

 

Content, SEO, LLM Strategy, and Use of Tools

  • Tara explains that LLMs have changed the ROI on content and media, because content is now the “toll” brands must pay to appear in AI answers and build trusted authority signals.
  • She clarifies that LLMs are not pulling from ads, influencer posts, or internal platform data; instead, they rely on web content, third-party reviews, and credible references.
  • Tara recommends brands build strong content on their own websites, including FAQs, product pages with rich information, and content answering high-intent, question-based queries.
  • She stresses that FAQ pages and product-page FAQs are “low-hanging fruit,” because they directly respond to the questions customers and LLMs often surface.
  • Tara advises using AI tools to assist with content ideation, structure, and optimization, while keeping actual text human-written to preserve unique voice and depth.
  • She notes that Google does not explicitly penalize AI-generated content but deprioritizes content without unique perspective, which is often a weakness of fully AI-written text.
  • Tara shares her own process of creating a brand-trained AI agent (e.g., via Claude projects) that:
    • Ingests SEM Rush, Google Analytics, and AI monitoring tools (e.g., Profound AI monitoring) reports weekly
    • Summarizes performance and gaps
    • Suggests content topics and briefs based on missing coverage and high-intent queries
  • She describes using AI tools to interview her (or a subject-matter expert) about a topic to capture authentic human voice, then using those transcripts as the basis for content drafts.
  • Tara recommends training AI agents to recognize and strip out common “AI tells” so that outputs feel more human and less formulaic.
  • She highlights the importance of Google AI Overviews and explains that even when click-through is low, recurring presence in AI Overviews strongly correlates with increases in direct traffic, as users see the source and visit the site independently.
  • Tara recommends LinkedIn as a platform with relatively strong search staying power, particularly for thought leadership and newsletters, as compared with X, Facebook, and Instagram.
  • She suggests quarterly press releases as an affordable and very effective way to feed LLMs and search with fresh, authoritative brand narratives.
  • For consumer brands, she specifically suggests a press release early September announcing Black Friday plans, followed by another release just before Black Friday to gain additional visibility and search momentum.

 

Affiliate Networks, Skimlinks, Gift Guides, and Practical Next Steps

  • Tara introduces Skimlinks as a critical, often underused tool that connects brands’ affiliate programs to large global publishers seeking products to review.
  • She explains that Skimlinks works as a bridge layer for existing affiliate programs on networks such as Impact and Commission Junction, and that brands with existing affiliate setups can usually join Skimlinks at no additional cost.
  • Tara clarifies that Skimlinks is not primarily a revenue generator; instead, it is a brand and authority generator, increasing the likelihood that journalists and editors will discover and feature a product.
  • She notes that Skimlinks gives access to about 57,000 publishers, including Condé Nast, Hearst, BuzzFeed, and HuffPost, and that editors use it as a product discovery database for review and listicle content.
  • Tara reports that when her team pitches products for review, they see about a 75% higher pickup rate when the products are available via Skimlinks, because publishers know they can earn affiliate revenue on any resulting sales.
  • In response to Jamie’s question, she clarifies that for her recommended setup, Skimlinks links should drive traffic to the brand’s own website, not to Amazon, to support DTC sales and authority building.
  • Jamie mentions using “Wayward,” an Amazon-only affiliate solution, at a 20% commission, and Tara suggests that a similar or even slightly lower commission could be workable for Skimlinks, depending on product uniqueness and category competition.
  • Tara explains that if a product is highly differentiated or has a strong story, a lower commission can still be attractive; if it competes in a crowded, commoditized category, a higher commission may be needed to stand out.
  • She gives practical guidance for pitching big publishers like BuzzFeed, advising founders to send journalist-centered, non-promotional pitches that clearly:
    • Reference the type of article the journalist writes (e.g., “time-saving desk products”)
    • Describe what makes the product unique
    • Provide the product link, price, and confirm Skimlinks availability
  • Tara emphasizes that journalists are open to pitches from business owners, not just PR professionals, as long as pitches are relevant, concise, and helpful.
  • On holiday gift guides, Tara advises brands to:
    • Use the summer months to update product pages, join Skimlinks, and strengthen on-site content
    • Prepare and schedule press releases for early September and pre–Black Friday
    • Expect journalist outreach for holiday and gift guide content to begin as early as August and early September
  • She reiterates that now is a “once-in-a-lifetime” window similar to the early days of SEO, where early movers in LLM-focused PR and authority building can achieve outsized long-term advantages.

 

AI Workflows, Monitoring, and Measurement Logic (Q&A Highlights)

  • In response to June Lai’s question about AI workflows, Tara distinguishes between automation mechanics and the human logic driving what should be measured and optimized.
  • She shares that her central process is to run weekly performance reports, feed them into a brand-trained AI agent, and obtain:
    • A top-line summary of what is working and what is underperforming
    • Content gap analysis relative to the brand’s positioning and goals
    • Specific content brief suggestions for new or updated pages
  • Tara uses tools like SEM Rush, Google Analytics, and Profound AI monitoring as inputs, then instructs AI to produce structured content briefs rather than fully finished content.
  • She asks AI to assess whether existing pages are optimized for both search engines and LLM visibility and to suggest modifications that address missing questions, intent gaps, or structural weaknesses.
  • Tara then has AI interview her (or a stakeholder) on key topics, using Q&A-style prompts to extract authentic human insights and tone, which she then edits into content assets.
  • She stresses that while automation can support monitoring and ideation, humans must still define goals, narratives, and positioning to train the workflow and interpret outputs.
  • Tara also recommends that brands audit AI results regularly (e.g., by querying ChatGPT or Claude about their brand and category), identify which questions appear frequently, and use those to shape future content and FAQ creation.
  • She highlights the importance of monitoring secondary queries such as “Would you like to see X?” in AI experiences and search, as those follow-up prompts reveal under-served but high-potential content topics.


In this session, MDS members and Avaans Media unpack how LLMs, PR, and content strategy intersect to influence brand visibility for Amazon and e-commerce sellers.

Tara emphasizes that while platforms like Amazon retain control over customer data and block LLMs from reading on-platform reputation, brands can counterbalance this by intentionally building off-platform authority through content, PR, and affiliate-enabled media coverage.

The group leaves with concrete next steps: join Skimlinks, strengthen owned content and FAQs, plan press releases for key periods such as Black Friday, and design AI-assisted monitoring workflows that inform content decisions.

By acting now—before the LLM landscape fully matures—brands can secure early, durable positioning in AI-generated recommendations and reduce long-term dependence on any single commerce platform.

items.title: Building a Secure, LLM-Agnostic AI System with Linux, CLI, and Open AI Infrastructure - APAC Chapter Mogul Call with June Lai June 2026
items.description:
In this session, APAC Chapter members learn from June Lai how to move beyond basic AI chat usage and design a more secure, scalable, and future‑proof AI setup using Linux, CLI, and multiple LLMs.

TOPICS:

  1. Designing a Linux- and CLI-based AI environment for scalability and control
  2. Building an LLM-agnostic, multi-machine architecture with shared universal configs
  3. Implementing security best practices for agents, data protection, and prompt‑injection risk
items.description_text: In this session, APAC Chapter members learn from June Lai how to move beyond basic AI chat usage and design a more secure, scalable, and future‑proof AI setup using Linux, CLI, and multiple LLMs. TOPICS: Designing a Linux- and CLI-based AI environment for scalability and control Building an LLM-agnostic, multi-machine architecture with shared universal configs Implementing security best practices for agents, data protection, and prompt‑injection risk

files.name: Transcript - APAC Chapter Monthly Call with June Lai
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783021207228-Transcript - APAC Chapter Monthly Call with June Lai.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the APAC Chapter meet with guest expert June Lai to explore how to design a robust secure and scalable AI system architecture using Linux CLI, and multiple LLMs. 


In addition to technical guidance, the group discusses security best practices, collaboration patterns, and upcoming in‑person MDS events relevant for the community.

Call Purpose, Flow, and June’s Background

  • The session serves as an APAC Chapter Monthly Call focused on helping members move beyond simple chat interfaces and start using AI in a more scalable, enterprise-grade way.
  • Participants set the tone by acknowledging that the topic may feel advanced, but they position the call as an opportunity to “get a kick” and level up their AI skills.
  • Scott shares that he attends an AI Ops meetup in Melbourne to stay exposed to how others use AI, even outside of e‑commerce, which reinforces the theme of continuous learning.
  • Jonathan introduces June as a long-standing MDS member with deep expertise across Amazon strategy, product, finance, and now AI, emphasizing that she consistently simplifies complex topics for others.
  • June presents her background as a scientist (biochemistry) who later completes an MBA and professional designations (CFA, CPA, CMA) and notes that she also has a pilot’s license, illustrating her breadth across disciplines.
  • June explains that her strength lies in going both broad and deep, then distilling complex systems into simple, understandable frameworks, which she applies to AI and system architecture.
  • The call format remains intentionally interactive, with June encouraging participants to interrupt with questions so they can tailor the depth and direction of the content in real time.


Moving from Chat Interfaces to CLI and Linux

  • June explains that most people currently use AI through chat or desktop interfaces, which limits what they can do because they treat AI as a black box instead of a programmable system.
  • She states that CLI (Command Line Interface) use is more powerful and scalable because it gives direct access to tools, systems, and configurations that are not exposed in typical chat UIs.
  • June clarifies that running AI workflows in terminal (often on Linux) offers more control and more tools than relying solely on web-based or graphical interfaces.
  • She notes that Linux—particularly Ubuntu—is the dominant operating system for enterprise software, with around 96% of large companies running their critical systems on Linux.
  • June recommends Ubuntu as an easy and stable Linux distribution that visually feels similar to Windows but is simpler, more robust, and less prone to breaking.
  • She explains that many people struggle when they try to run Linux “inside” Windows because they are effectively juggling two operating systems and running into conflicts and dependency issues.
  • June advises taking an older computer, backing up any needed files, wiping Windows, and installing Ubuntu as a native Linux machine dedicated to AI and development work.
  • She describes how Macs are generally more Linux-friendly, because macOS is designed to host Unix-like tools, so users can run Linux distributions and terminal workflows more easily without fully wiping the machine.
  • June highlights that, once Ubuntu is installed, users can simply open a terminal window and access powerful AI tooling directly, using natural language combined with a few core commands.
  • She encourages users to view AI as something they “train with their own logic,” where the job is to transfer their mental models and workflows into structured, repeatable AI processes rather than just chatting.

System Architecture: Multi‑Machine, LLM‑Agnostic Setup and Universal Configs

  • June recommends designing a multi‑machine, multi‑LLM architecture so the system is both scalable and resilient to changes in model availability or licensing.
  • She suggests dedicating one Linux machine as a core AI system and accessing it via SSH from a primary laptop (for example, through tools like VS Code or Cursor), so users can work comfortably while keeping heavy compute and configuration on the dedicated box.
  • June explains that users can install and configure multiple LLM-related tools such as Cloud Code, Claude, Codex, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Open Code on the same Linux machine to keep the setup LLM-agnostic.
  • She points out that Nvidia provides developer accounts with API access and a credit allowance for various models, enabling cheaper experimentation and model rotation compared to many SaaS tools.
  • She recommends designing workflows so that the system can easily switch models (for example, from Claude to another LLM) without rewriting the entire architecture, which makes the stack future‑proof.
  • June uses an example where Claude is the primary LLM and Codex acts as an auditor, so Claude calls Codex to review its outputs, identify logic gaps, and act as an adversarial checker on code or reasoning.
  • She encourages participants to build skills and shortcuts (for example, backslash commands) that standardize how prompts and workflows are run across LLMs, instead of improvising new structures every time.
  • June describes Shanewa (pronounced like “Shanewa” or “Shamewa”) as a tool that can clone configurations across multiple machines, ensuring that operating systems, skills, tools, and MCP configurations remain consistent.
  • She notes that in larger organizations, alternative Linux distributions like Nix (used at companies like Shopify with a large monorepo) support centralized, reproducible environments at scale.
  • June explains that a universal configuration file is critical, and she uses agents.md as the single source of truth that defines rules, logic, and operating standards for both Claude and Codex.
  • She details that Claude reads agents.md through a reference (for example, @agents.md), so both LLMs share identical rule sets, which minimizes drift, reduces hallucination, and simplifies debugging.
  • June emphasizes that the universal config should define how to organize projects, where rules live, and how AI should navigate the file tree, so the system behaves consistently no matter which LLM is active.


Security, Agents, and Risk Management (Lethal Trifecta, Docker, VPN, and Permissions)

  • June introduces the “lethal TRIFECTA” concept, where serious risk appears when AI can 1) scrape data, 2) access the internet and external instructions, and 3) see and send private data.
  • She explains that prompt injection attacks occur when hidden instructions (for example, white text or very small font inside a document or image) tell AI to exfiltrate secrets such as bank accounts, API keys, or passwords.
  • She warns that AI cannot reliably distinguish between a user’s explicit instructions and hidden instructions embedded in uploaded content, which makes agents particularly vulnerable without safeguards.
  • June illustrates how a malicious prompt could direct an agent to search a user’s machine for environment files, banking details, or credentials and then send them via email or upload them to a remote site.
  • She strongly recommends air‑gapping and ring‑fencing agents by giving them their own dedicated machine separate from the user’s main workstation and core data stores.
  • She advises treating an agent like an employee account, with a separate user, separate login, and limited permissions, so the agent cannot act with full administrative or root privileges.
  • June emphasizes that agents should run with least privilege access, such as read-only permissions where possible, explicitly avoiding write, delete, or email‑sending rights unless absolutely necessary.
  • She highlights tools like Tailscale and ZeroTier as private VPN solutions that securely connect multiple devices (laptops, Linux machines, VPS instances) on a private network, invisible to the public internet.
  • She explains that with Tailscale, each device joins a single private network under one account, so machines recognize each other, share files, and behave as if they sit side‑by‑side, even when remote.
  • June notes that users can add VPS (virtual private server) instances into this network when they need extra compute or RAM, thereby scaling without buying additional hardware.
  • She recommends Docker as a way to sandbox code and agents, so they run in containers that cannot escape into the host system, which is crucial when scraping or processing untrusted external content.
  • June cautions that there was a copy‑on‑write (copyfail) vulnerability in Linux discussed in relation to Anthropic and U.S. government concerns, and she advises participants to patch systems and understand that some bugs could allow escape from containers or escalation to root.
  • She reiterates that separating machines, users, and Docker containers—combined with careful permissions and VPN-level segmentation—is foundational to building safe agent architectures.


Practical Tools, Model Tuning, Workflows, and Next Steps

  • June highlights password managers as essential, noting that tools like 1Password help avoid storing secrets in plain text and support safer integration with AI-driven workflows.
  • She mentions that self-managed password and access control solutions can also be implemented directly in CLI-based tools (she references an approach often called Fisical/Infissal, i.e., self-managing secrets and rules per user and machine).
  • June references Hermes as the name of her own agent, which runs under a separate user account and does not receive root privileges, illustrating how to structure agent identities and access.
  • She mentions that Nvidia provides AI blueprints such as Nemo‑based “Claw”/agent architectures, where users can pull the GitHub repo and ask AI to help them adapt the secure reference design to their needs.
  • June suggests GLM 5.2 via zip.ai as a competitive model relative to Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex 5.5, especially for users who are comfortable with data being handled by a Singapore/China‑owned provider.
  • She states that configuring systems to be LLM‑agnostic makes it straightforward to rotate between models or add local models on dedicated machines as requirements or costs change.
  • June explains that temperature is a crucial parameter controlling how predictable or creative AI outputs are, where temperature 0 favors the most probable next tokens and temperature 1 introduces more randomness.
  • She recommends using lower temperatures (for example, 0) when the goal is accuracy and reduced hallucinations, especially for code, logic, or critical system instructions.
  • June introduces the concept of idempotency, where AI workflows must produce the same result each time they are run, which means they always check existing files, avoid blind overwrites, and respect established project structure.
  • She stresses that AI should first inspect existing code or documents before modifying them, ensuring it builds on prior work rather than deleting or recreating structures without awareness.
  • June highlights the use of YAML front matter at the top of config files to provide compact machine-readable summaries and high-priority rules, ideally within about 100 lines to stay under system context limits.
  • She describes that top-level config files should primarily act as indexes, telling AI where to find project-specific rules, machine-specific instructions, and other configuration details deeper in the file tree.
  • June recommends TMUX for splitting and managing multiple terminal sessions and Termius for viewing and controlling terminals from a mobile device, which helps developers monitor and manage systems remotely.
  • She mentions that users can interact with the system via Telegram bots or voice transcription tools like Super Whisper (running locally) to issue commands or review outputs without sending data to third-party clouds.
  • She clarifies that developers already working comfortably with tools like Cursor, Supabase, Vercel, Node.js, and GitHub may not need a full Ubuntu rebuild immediately, but they still benefit from understanding cloning, agent isolation, and future-proof infrastructure.
  • June summarizes recommended next steps as: setting up or repurposing a machine for Ubuntu, configuring a private network (for example, via Tailscale), creating consistent universal configs, and then slowly layering in agents and advanced workflows.
  • The group agrees that running agents directly on a primary personal machine is too risky, and that setting up a “padded room” environment where agents can operate safely without exposing all personal or company data is a best practice.
  • The call concludes with Jonathan reiterating the value of live MDS events such as the MDS Summit in Asia and the Bali event, positioning them as key opportunities to deepen learning on topics like AI architecture, DTC growth, and brand building.

In this session, participants gain a structured, high-level view of how to move from casual AI usage in chat interfaces to a robust, Linux- and CLI-based architecture that supports multiple LLMs and secure agent workflows. 


They also receive practical guidance on security, configuration design, and model tuning, helping them think more like system architects than end users.


The call closes with clear encouragement to treat AI agents like employees with constrained permissions, to invest early in consistent system architecture, and to leverage both online tools and in‑person events to continue building these capabilities.

items.title: What Breaks After $30M? Founder Insights on Scaling Ecom Brands － London Operator Room 2026
items.description:
In this video from the London Operator Room, Michael Corrigan, Luke Shelley, Saurabh Srivastava, and Eddie Latham share how they have scaled major e-commerce brands across Amazon, TikTok Shop, retail, DTC, and international markets. The conversation explores the operational challenges that come with growth, including hiring, inventory planning, profitability, brand building, and channel diversification.

 

Key Takeaways:

  1. Diversifying beyond Amazon is becoming essential for sustainable growth.
  2. Rapid scaling often exposes gaps in team structure, ownership, SOPs, and demand planning.
  3. TikTok Shop offers major growth potential but creates challenges around profitability, attribution, and inventory forecasting.
  4. Retail can improve cash flow, inventory turnover, brand credibility, and Amazon performance.

TikTok Shop offers major growth potential but creates challenges around profitability, attribution, and inventory forecasting. Retail can improve cash flow, inventory turnover, brand credibility, and Amazon performance.
cliff_notes:
What Breaks After $30M? Founder Insights on Scaling Ecom Brands - London Operator Room 2026

 

The panel brought together experienced operators who have scaled brands across Amazon DTC TikTok Shop, retail, and international markets.

The main discussion focused on diversification, profitability, hiring, inventory planning, retail expansion, and the operational challenges that appear as businesses grow.

Speakers

Michael Corrigan — Founder & CEO, TRTL
TRTL is a global travel accessories brand known for the Trtl Pillow. Michael shared insights on international growth, TikTok Shop, creator partnerships, and managing profitability across more than 100 countries.

Luke Shelley — Co-Founder, Lucky Egg
Lucky Egg is a fast-growing party game brand with strong Amazon, TikTok Shop, and retail sales. Luke discussed viral growth, inventory forecasting, operational ownership, and scaling the team.

Saurabh Srivastava — Senior Executive, Grace & Stella; Co-Founder & CEO, Gravitiq
Saurabh oversees a portfolio of 12 health, beauty, supplement, and medical support brands. He shared insights on hiring specialists, retail expansion, forecasting, delegation, and channel profitability.

Eddie Latham — Co-Founder, Majority Audio
Majority Audio grew from an Amazon-first brand into a major omnichannel audio company. Eddie discussed traditional retail, reverse logistics, brand marketing, inventory management, and the company’s Guinness World Records campaign.

Moderator: Eugene Khayman — MDS
Eugene guided the conversation around how established e-commerce brands are diversifying and scaling beyond a single sales channel.

Main Discussion Points

Diversification Is Becoming Essential

Eugene emphasized that diversification is no longer simply a growth opportunity. It is becoming necessary for brands that want to scale while reducing their dependence on Amazon.

The panel showed different approaches:

  • Michael Corrigan is focused heavily on TikTok Shop and social commerce.
  • Luke Shelley is scaling across Amazon, TikTok Shop, and retail.
  • Saurabh Srivastava is balancing Amazon, retail, and DTC.
  • Eddie Latham has shifted significantly from Amazon into traditional retail.

What Breaks During Growth

Luke shared that rapid growth created unclear ownership between departments, outdated SOPs, supplier limitations, and inventory planning issues.

Eddie added that teams can become distracted by new projects while neglecting business-as-usual work.

The group agreed that companies need:

  • Clear ownership
  • Updated processes
  • Better cross-department communication
  • Stronger operational discipline
  • Leaders who protect the core business while pursuing growth

Hiring and Team Structure

Saurabh explained that Gravitiq gradually moved from generalists to experienced specialists as the company scaled.

He recommended hiring people who have already operated at a similar level rather than relying only on academic credentials or raw talent.

Eddie acknowledged that Majority Audio relied heavily on talented but inexperienced employees and later realized that some roles needed more experienced leadership.

Michael shared the leadership principle:

“Be soft on the people, but hard on the issues.”

The panel agreed that founders must address underperformance early while still treating people respectfully.

Inventory and Demand Planning

Luke explained that TikTok Shop can create sudden sales spikes that are extremely difficult to forecast.

Lucky Egg sometimes allows products to sell out so the team can understand their true demand before placing larger seasonal orders.

Saurabh said Gravitiq uses internal forecasting tools based on:

  • Recent sales
  • Prior-year performance
  • Seasonality
  • Product-level demand

Michael explained that TRTL supports growth through supplier relationships, bank facilities, payment terms, and pre-orders.

TikTok Shop

Michael said TRTL grew from roughly $30,000 per month to around $300,000 per month on TikTok Shop after increasing its use of GMV Max.

However, profitability changed quickly due to creator commissions and unclear attribution.

Luke views TikTok Shop as both a sales and marketing channel. Lucky Egg often accepts break-even performance because TikTok can increase Amazon branded search and sales.

Saurabh warned that creator content can generate revenue while damaging the brand. Gravitiq became more selective after creators used misleading claims to drive urgency.

Retail

Eddie described retail as one of the biggest growth drivers for Majority Audio.

Benefits included:

  • Faster inventory turnover
  • Lower return rates
  • Lower storage costs
  • Better cash flow
  • Increased brand awareness
  • Stronger Amazon performance
  • Reduced dependence on Amazon PPC

Saurabh agreed that retail requires more than simply getting products onto shelves. Brands must create enough awareness and demand to ensure sell-through.

Profitability by Channel

The panel agreed that every channel should have a defined role.

Some channels are expected to generate profit, while others may operate near break-even to support awareness and sales elsewhere.

Saurabh explained that Gravitiq generates strong profit from Amazon and retail, while Shopify, TikTok Shop, Meta, and Google may be used more for acquisition and brand growth.

The group also discussed keeping payroll controlled, with several businesses targeting approximately 5% of revenue.

Protecting Amazon Profitability

Michael said Amazon has become more expensive and difficult, leading TRTL to reduce its reliance on Amazon PPC and invest more heavily in outside channels.

Saurabh focuses on brand differentiation, pricing power, and different pack sizes across channels.

Eddie protects margins by limiting FBA inventory and clearing aged stock through retail and other channels instead of discounting heavily on Amazon.

Brand Marketing

Eddie shared Majority Audio’s Guinness World Records campaign, which surpassed JBL’s previous record for the most Bluetooth speakers playing simultaneously.

The campaign generated:

  • Major press coverage
  • Retail buyer interest
  • Hundreds of thousands of YouTube views
  • Stronger brand credibility
  • An Amazon documentary opportunity

The main lesson was that some brand-building campaigns may be difficult to measure through direct ROAS but can still create substantial long-term value.

International Expansion

Michael discussed managing TRTL across more than 100 countries, while Luke, Saurabh, and Eddie addressed the complexity of expanding across Europe.

Common challenges included:

  • VAT
  • Compliance
  • Inventory distribution
  • Local entities
  • Logistics
  • Country-specific TikTok Shop requirements

Eddie noted that Majority Audio reduced its US presence to focus on markets where the company has stronger operational advantages.

Key Takeaways

  • Diversification beyond Amazon is becoming essential.
  • TikTok Shop offers major growth but creates forecasting and attribution challenges.
  • Retail can improve cash flow, inventory turnover, and Amazon performance.
  • Scaling companies eventually need experienced specialists, not only generalists.
  • Growth initiatives should not distract teams from core operations.
  • Not every channel needs to be directly profitable.
  • Strong supplier terms can significantly improve cash flow.
  • Brand marketing can create value even when direct ROI is difficult to track.
  • International expansion should be approached market by market.

items.title: Where Does The M&A Marketplace Stand Today? －Scott Deetz － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, MDS members and the Northbound Group team discuss the current state of e‑commerce M&A, focusing on what makes brands truly sellable in today’s highly selective buyer market. 
TOPICS:

  1. Current e‑commerce M&A landscape and active buyer types (aggregators, private equity, large brand operators)
  2. Key valuation drivers: EBITDA size, growth rate, margins, defensibility, and omni‑channel presence
  3. Exit readiness and planning: timelines, financial cleanup, and strategic positioning for a premium sale
items.description_text: In this session, MDS members and the Northbound Group team discuss the current state of e‑commerce M&A, focusing on what makes brands truly sellable in today’s highly selective buyer market. TOPICS: Current e‑commerce M&A landscape and active buyer types (aggregators, private equity, large brand operators) Key valuation drivers: EBITDA size, growth rate, margins, defensibility, and omni‑channel presence Exit readiness and planning: timelines, financial cleanup, and strategic positioning for a premium sale
cliff_notes:
In this MDS Mogul Call Scott Deetz from Northbound Group shares an up-to-date view of the e-commerce mergers and acquisitions market explaining who is buying brands today what makes a company attractive to buyers, and how founders should prepare for an eventual exit. 


The discussion emphasizes that the market has shifted dramatically from the aggregator boom, making preparation, profitability, and defensibility more important than ever.


Current Market Landscape and Buyer Behavior

 

The Aggregator Boom Has Ended

  • The era of aggregators aggressively acquiring Amazon brands is largely over.
  • Most aggregators are now:
    • Selling brands
    • Liquidating portfolios
    • Becoming highly selective buyers.

 

Today's Main Buyer Types

 

The active buyer pool primarily consists of:

  • Private equity firms
  • Strategic operators and brand owners
  • A small number of niche aggregators.

 

Private Equity's Playbook

 

PE firms commonly pursue a:

  1. Large platform acquisition
  2. Followed by smaller bolt-on acquisitions in the same niche.

 

Typical platform companies have:

  • $30M–$50M+ in revenue
  • Full operating teams
  • Clear category specialization.

 

Buyers Are More Selective

 

The market has shifted from a seller's market to a buyer's market.

Not every brand is sellable anymore. Buyers are focusing on:

  • Growth
  • Profitability
  • Defensibility
  • Channel diversification.


Financial Metrics That Drive Valuation

 

Three Core Metrics

Northbound evaluates businesses primarily on:

  1. EBITDA size
  2. Year-over-year growth
  3. Profit margins

 

EBITDA Matters

  • Businesses under $1M EBITDA often struggle to command premium multiples.
  • Larger EBITDA almost always leads to better valuations.

 

Growth Is Critical

Buyers are generally uninterested in:

  • Flat businesses
  • Declining businesses.

 

Since deals now commonly take 6–8+ months to close, businesses must continue growing throughout the transaction process.

 

Margin Expectations

Today's buyers generally look for:

  • 15%+ margins as a healthy benchmark.
  • Lower margins may still work if there is a clear path to improvement.

 

Additional Risk Factors

Buyers discount businesses with:

  • High SKU concentration
  • Extreme seasonality
  • Aggressive add-backs
  • Poor financial reporting.

 

Financial Hygiene Is Essential

Founders should maintain:

  • At least two years of clean financial statements
  • Accrual accounting
  • Minimal personal expenses in the business
  • Well-documented add-backs.


What Makes a Brand Attractive to Buyers

 

Defensibility Is the Top Non-Financial Factor

 

Buyers ask:

"Can someone easily copy this business?"

 

Defensibility may come from:

  • Intellectual property
  • Patents
  • Brand equity
  • Loyal communities
  • Differentiated products
  • Strong launch capabilities.

 

Omni-Channel Matters More Than Ever

Pure Amazon brands are less attractive than they once were.

 

Many buyers prefer businesses with:

  • DTC channels
  • Shopify revenue
  • Marketplace diversification
  • Customer ownership.

 

Meaningful Diversification

Having tiny amounts of revenue across many channels is usually not helpful.

Instead, buyers want channels that contribute meaningful revenue, often:

  • 20%+ of total sales.

 

Customer Ownership Is Valuable

Metrics buyers care about include:

  • Email list quality
  • Repeat purchase rates
  • LTV:CAC ratios.

 

Cohesive Brands Win

Buyers prefer brands that serve:

  • A specific customer
  • A specific problem.

A random collection of unrelated products is far less attractive.


AI's Impact on Valuations

 

AI Does Not Increase Multiples Directly

Buyers are not currently paying higher multiples simply because a business uses:

  • AI agents
  • Automation systems
  • Advanced workflows.

 

AI Helps Indirectly

AI can improve valuation by:

  • Increasing margins
  • Reducing payroll
  • Improving efficiency.

 

These improvements show up in EBITDA, which can ultimately increase enterprise value.

 

Defensibility Becomes More Important

As AI lowers barriers to entry, brands need stronger advantages through:

  • Brand strength
  • Community
  • Product differentiation
  • Customer loyalty.

Valuation Ranges and Exit Planning

 

Typical Valuation Ranges

 

Pure Amazon FBA Brands

  • Approximately 2.5x–4x EBITDA
  • Assumes:
    • $1M+ EBITDA
    • 15%+ margins
    • Modest growth.

 

Light Omni-Channel Brands

  • Roughly 3x–4.5x EBITDA
  • Exceptional businesses can approach 5x+.

 

DTC-Heavy Brands

  • Approximately 5x–6x EBITDA
  • Especially attractive when paired with manufacturing or strong customer ownership.

 

Distressed Brands

  • Often trade around 1x–1.5x EBITDA.
  • Sometimes only inventory value is realized.

 

Exit Preparation Should Start Early

 

Northbound recommends founders begin preparing:

  • 12–18 months before selling
  • Ideally 24 months in advance.

 

Preparation should focus on:

  • Cleaning up financials
  • Improving margins
  • Building defensibility
  • Expanding channels strategically
  • Strengthening operational systems.

Key Takeaways

 

The Market Has Changed

  • Buyers are highly selective.
  • Strong businesses still command attractive valuations.
  • Weak or undifferentiated brands may receive little or no interest.

 

Build for Quality

Premium exits increasingly require:

  • Growth
  • Healthy margins
  • Defensible positioning
  • Diversified revenue
  • Clean financial reporting.

 

AI Is a Tool, Not a Valuation Premium

 

AI matters because it improves operations, not because buyers currently pay extra for it.

 

Exit Readiness Is a Multi-Year Project

 

The best outcomes come from founders who prepare long before they intend to sell and deliberately build businesses that institutional buyers want to own.

This session provides a realistic look at today's e-commerce acquisition environment. The days of easy exits and aggressive aggregator valuations are largely gone. 


Buyers now prioritize businesses with sustainable growth, strong margins, defensible brands, and meaningful customer ownership.

For founders considering an exit, the message is clear: build intentionally, prepare early, and treat exit readiness as a long-term strategic initiative rather than a last-minute event.

files.name: AMAZON_DATA_EXTRACTION_STARTER
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783015550683-AMAZON_DATA_EXTRACTION_STARTER.md

cliff_notes:
In this session Ramon Gonzalez shares how he built a network of approximately 70 AI agents that automate significant portions of his Amazon business despite having no modern software engineering background.

The discussion covers data ownership infrastructure AI orchestration practical automations, and the mindset required to gradually build an AI-powered operating system for an e-commerce company.


AI Without a Coding Background

Starting as a Seller, Not a Developer

Ramon explains that he has been an MDS member since 2017 and operates a successful Amazon business selling board games.

Despite running a sophisticated AI ecosystem today, he emphasizes that:

  • He is not a professional developer.
  • His only coding experience was learning C++ decades ago.
  • Modern AI tools now handle most technical implementation work.

His core philosophy:

The most important skill is learning how to communicate with AI, not learning how to code.


Let AI Ask the Questions

Rather than trying to design everything himself, Ramon often begins projects by asking AI:

  • What information do you need?
  • What data should I collect?
  • What questions am I not asking?

For larger projects such as dashboards or reporting systems, he lets AI drive the discovery process before building anything.


Start Small and Expand

His recommended progression:

  1. Solve one small problem.
  2. Validate the outcome.
  3. Build another automation.
  4. Connect multiple automations together.
  5. Scale into a complete agent ecosystem.

He credits this iterative approach for enabling him to eventually manage roughly 70 daily agents.


Data First: The Foundation of Every Agent

Own Your Data

Ramon repeatedly stresses that sellers should prioritize extracting data rather than buying more dashboards.

Primary sources include:

  • Amazon SP-API
  • Amazon Ads API
  • Search Query Performance reports
  • Shopify
  • QuickBooks Online
  • TikTok
  • Other marketing and sales platforms

His philosophy:

Pull everything first. Decide later what is useful.


Centralizing Everything in BigQuery

After discussing options with AI, Ramon adopted Google BigQuery because:

  • His company already uses Google Workspace.
  • Storage costs are extremely low.
  • It scales easily.

He reports spending roughly:

  • ~$3/month for data storage

Once data is centralized, AI can answer business questions much more effectively.


Practical Examples

Examples of AI analysis include:

Return Analysis

AI:

  • Groups return reasons.
  • Compares recent periods to prior periods.
  • Identifies emerging customer issues.

Example:

If customers repeatedly return a left-handed product because they mistakenly believe it works for right-handed users, AI can recommend:

  • New images
  • Better copy
  • Clearer product positioning


PPC Waste Detection

AI can identify:

  • Keywords with high clicks
  • Minimal conversions
  • Poor profitability

Allowing rapid budget reductions on underperforming terms.


SQP Data Collection

Because Amazon's SQP APIs can be slow or inconsistent, Ramon built agents that:

  • Log into Seller Central
  • Generate reports through the UI
  • Download completed reports
  • Load them into BigQuery automatically

 

Agent Architecture and Infrastructure

What Is an Agent?

Ramon defines an agent as:

  1. Access to data.
  2. Access to an LLM.
  3. A clearly defined objective.

Each agent performs one focused task.


Infrastructure Setup

Core components include:

  • Mac Mini orchestrator
  • BigQuery data warehouse
  • Python scripts
  • Cron jobs
  • LLMs such as Claude and OpenClaw
  • ClickUp task management
  • Slack monitoring


Why a Mac Mini?

Ramon runs orchestration on a relatively inexpensive Mac Mini because:

  • It is reliable.
  • It is easy to manage.
  • It remains inside his own network.
  • Security and permissions are easier to control.

The Mac Mini does not store business data.

Instead it:

  • Schedules jobs
  • Triggers workflows
  • Runs automation scripts
  • Communicates with LLMs


ClickUp as Mission Control

Every agent corresponds to a task inside:

ClickUp

Agents:

  • Update tasks
  • Leave comments
  • Record results
  • Mark completion

This creates:

  • Accountability
  • Audit trails
  • Error tracking

Instead of monitoring 70 agents individually, Ramon only monitors a single ClickUp board.


Bug Half-Life

One of the more interesting concepts introduced is "bug half-life."

New agents typically generate many failures.

Over time:

  • Errors are identified.
  • Logic improves.
  • Failure frequency decreases.

Eventually agents become highly reliable and require minimal intervention.


Real-World AI Agent Use Cases

PPC Optimization

Ramon built a custom PPC engine that:

  • Runs daily
  • Analyzes advertising performance
  • Adjusts bids
  • Applies deterministic logic

Importantly, he avoids allowing AI to make purely mathematical decisions independently.

Instead:

  • AI assists analysis.
  • Business rules control execution.


Inventory and Forecasting

Agents help:

  • Forecast inventory
  • Recommend reorder timing
  • Monitor stock levels
  • Evaluate future demand


Financial Management

By integrating:

  • Amazon
  • QuickBooks Online
  • Operational data

His system can generate:

  • Daily P&L reports
  • Cash flow analysis
  • Purchasing recommendations

Without relying on third-party accounting connectors.


Listing Optimization

Agents continuously evaluate:

  • Rankings
  • Search performance
  • PPC data
  • Seasonal opportunities

Examples:

  • Mother's Day updates
  • Christmas messaging
  • Listing refresh recommendations


Content Creation

Ramon recently built:

  • AI-generated podcast summaries
  • Personalized audio content

In only a few hours because the underlying infrastructure already existed.


PR Automation

Agents also review:

  • HARO-style media opportunities
  • Press requests
  • Outreach opportunities

The system:

  • Filters opportunities
  • Drafts responses
  • Escalates only relevant items

Saving substantial manual review time.


Beyond Amazon

The same framework can be applied to:

  • TikTok
  • Meta Ads
  • Reddit Ads
  • Creative testing
  • Social content generation


Infrastructure, Security, and Costs

Treat AI Like an Employee

Ramon's security philosophy is straightforward:

  • Every agent gets its own accounts.
  • Every agent gets limited permissions.
  • Every action is logged.

For example:

  • Dedicated Gmail accounts
  • Seller Central permissions
  • ClickUp access
  • Slack monitoring

Agents are treated similarly to human team members.


Local vs Cloud Models

The group discusses:

  • Mac Mini setups
  • Linux servers
  • VPS environments
  • Local LLMs

Ramon currently prefers hosted frontier models because they outperform what he can run locally.

Local systems are mainly being explored for:

  • Image generation
  • Video generation
  • Compute-heavy workloads


AI Tool Costs

Ramon estimates monthly spending at approximately:

Tool

Approximate Cost

OpenClaw

~$100/month

Claude

~$200/month

Employee AI access

~$100/month

Total

~$400/month

The discussion notes that many advanced AI users in MDS now operate on similar budgets due to the value generated by automation.

 

Key Takeaways

  • You do not need a software engineering background to build effective AI automations.
  • Centralizing data is more important than building dashboards.
  • Start with one small automation tied to a real business problem.
  • Use AI to help design systems, not just execute tasks.
  • Treat agents like employees with controlled permissions and accountability.
  • Store data centrally (such as BigQuery) so AI can analyze the business holistically.
  • Build deterministic business logic around AI rather than letting models make uncontrolled decisions.
  • Scale gradually from simple automations into a coordinated network of specialized agents.

The overarching lesson from Ramon’s presentation is that successful AI adoption is less about advanced coding and more about creating a strong data foundation, defining clear business objectives, and continuously expanding small, useful automations into a larger operating system that compounds over time.

items.title: The $100M PPC Growth Playbook Anyone Can Apply － Daniel Lai － Expert Call
items.description:
In this session, Daniel Lai from Scale Insights shares a simple PPC blueprint for scaling Amazon brands while keeping ad costs efficient.

TOPICS:

  1. Building ranking pressure with SQP data, conversion delta, and AMC campaigns
  2. Protecting ad budgets using structured hero and variation ASIN portfolios
  3. Managing bids with tiered bidding, day parting, and automation tools
items.description_text: In this session, Daniel Lai from Scale Insights shares a simple PPC blueprint for scaling Amazon brands while keeping ad costs efficient. TOPICS: Building ranking pressure with SQP data, conversion delta, and AMC campaigns Protecting ad budgets using structured hero and variation ASIN portfolios Managing bids with tiered bidding, day parting, and automation tools
cliff_notes:
In this MDS Expert Call Daniel Lai from Scale Insights shares the PPC framework used alongside a $100M+ Amazon seller to drive growth while maintaining CPC efficiency. 


The discussion focuses on three pillars: creating ranking pressure protecting growth capital through portfolio structure and preventing overspending through disciplined bid management and automation. 


The session also explores how AI, MCP integrations, and large-scale automation are changing Amazon advertising management.

The Three-Step PPC Growth Framework

 

Daniel introduces a PPC system that helped scale a brand from roughly $35M to over $100M in annual revenue while keeping CPCs relatively stable.

 

The framework consists of:

  1. Build Ranking Pressure
  2. Protect Growth Capital
  3. Avoid Overpaying for Traffic

 

Key principles include:

  • Leveraging Amazon data rather than intuition.
  • Using high-converting traffic to strengthen organic ranking.
  • Structuring campaigns and budgets to prevent waste.
  • Automating optimization at scale.
  • Applying disciplined bid controls instead of constantly increasing bids.

 

The strategy was developed and refined with an experienced Amazon operator, Ivan, and relies heavily on Amazon advertising data, automation, and audience targeting.


Building Ranking Pressure with SQP and AMC

 

Using Search Query Performance (SQP)

Daniel recommends starting with Amazon's Search Query Performance report.

 

For each search term:

  • Calculate the market conversion rate:
    • Total market purchases ÷ Total market clicks
  • Calculate the brand conversion rate:
    • Brand purchases ÷ Brand clicks

 

The difference between the two is the conversion delta.

 

Why Conversion Delta Matters

A positive conversion delta indicates the product converts better than the average competitor for that keyword.

 

General ranking guidance shared:

  • Similar to market conversion → often ranks around positions 10–20.
  • 1–2% above market conversion → often ranks around positions 6–10.
  • More than 2% above market conversion → potential for top-ranking positions.

 

The recommendation is to identify and prioritize all keywords with positive conversion delta.

 

Leveraging Amazon Marketing Cloud (AMC)

Daniel explains that AMC audiences frequently outperform standard traffic because they represent higher-intent shoppers.

 

Examples include:

  • Cart audiences
  • Product viewers
  • Brand-engaged shoppers
  • High-intent audience segments

 

He notes that Amazon's pre-built AMC audiences often outperform custom audiences and lookalikes.

 

The objective is simple:

Drive highly converting traffic to keywords where you already have a conversion advantage.

Campaign Structure and Portfolio-Based Budget Protection

 

Single-Keyword Campaign Structure

For ranking campaigns, Daniel recommends:

  • One keyword per campaign.
  • One match type per campaign.
  • One AMC audience strategy per campaign.

 

This makes performance easier to analyze and scale.

 

AMC Bid Multiplier Strategy

The process:

  • Start with a low base bid.
  • Apply a strong AMC audience multiplier.
  • Allow Amazon to prioritize higher-value AMC traffic.

 

This reduces spend on lower-quality traffic while concentrating budget on shoppers most likely to convert.

 

Six-Portfolio Budget Framework

The account structure shared includes:

 

Hero ASIN

  • AMC campaigns portfolio
  • Non-AMC campaigns portfolio

 

Variation ASINs

  • AMC campaigns portfolio
  • Non-AMC campaigns portfolio

 

Brand Campaigns

  • Sponsored Brands portfolio
  • Sponsored Display portfolio

 

Benefits include:

  • Better budget allocation.
  • Easier performance tracking.
  • Reduced budget cannibalization between campaigns.

 

Daily Portfolio Budget Hack

Because Amazon only allows monthly portfolio budgets, Daniel shares a workaround:

  • Divide monthly budget by 30.
  • Set a daily target.
  • Refresh portfolio start dates daily via bulk updates.

 

This effectively creates a pseudo-daily portfolio budget system.

Bid Management, Day Parting & Automation

 

The Three Bid Tiers

Daniel advocates testing campaigns at:

  • Low bid tier
  • Medium bid tier
  • High bid tier

 

Rather than immediately bidding aggressively.

The process:

  1. Launch with low bids.
  2. Increase gradually until traffic appears.
  3. Clone into higher tiers only if needed.
  4. Observe before making additional changes.

 

The "No Bid Up" Philosophy

Once campaigns are receiving traffic:

  • Bids are generally not increased.
  • Optimization focuses primarily on lowering bids when performance deteriorates.

 

Examples:

  • ACOS significantly above target → larger bid reduction.
  • ACOS slightly above target → smaller bid reduction.

 

The goal is to continually find the lowest effective bid that maintains performance.

 

Day Parting

Ivan's strategy also includes:

  • Turning ads off during low-converting hours.
  • Concentrating spend during peak conversion periods.

 

This improves efficiency by allocating budget when shoppers are most likely to buy.

 

Automation at Scale

Daniel highlights that automation executes:

  • Bid adjustments
  • Day-parting actions
  • Negative keyword additions
  • Placement exclusions
  • Budget management

 

The system reportedly performs tens of millions of optimization actions monthly, enabling management of thousands of ASINs across multiple marketplaces.

AI, MCP Integration & Future of PPC Management

 

What MCP Does

Daniel explains that MCP (Model Context Protocol) acts as a bridge between AI tools and Scale Insights.

 

Workflow:

AI Tool → MCP → Scale Insights → Amazon Data → Insights Returned

Supported AI environments include:

  • Claude
  • OpenAI
  • Cursor

 

Instead of forcing AI models to process raw Amazon data directly, Scale Insights provides pre-calculated metrics and analysis.

 

Current MCP Capabilities

Examples include:

  • Wasted spend analysis
  • Campaign health checks
  • PPC diagnostics
  • Performance reviews

 

The MCP system is currently in beta, with additional trend analysis and automation capabilities planned.

 

Future Potential

Daniel notes that more advanced actions could eventually be performed directly through MCP, including:

  • Campaign creation
  • Campaign cloning
  • Optimization workflows
  • Budget management

Key Takeaways

  • Focus first on keywords where your product already converts better than the market.
  • Use AMC audiences to amplify ranking pressure through higher-converting traffic.
  • Protect budgets with a clear portfolio structure rather than mixing campaign types.
  • Find the lowest bid that generates results instead of constantly bidding higher.
  • Use day parting and automation to improve efficiency at scale.
  • AI and MCP integrations are making large-scale PPC analysis and optimization increasingly accessible.

 

The overarching message is that sustainable Amazon growth comes from combining conversion advantage, structured campaign architecture, disciplined bid management, and automation, rather than simply increasing ad spend.
