AI-driven customer service tools, Reddit automation, and a new problem-solving call format

files.name: MDS AI Channel Call June 2026 Transcript
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1781293662148-MDS AI Channel monthly Call_otter_ai_transcript-compressed.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS AI Channel share practical applications of AI across Amazon DTC finance, customer service, advertising, and operational workflows. 


The discussion focuses on real implementations rather than theory, with participants exchanging insights on AI orchestration, automation systems, DSP optimization, customer support tools, security frameworks, and future collaboration formats.

AI Agent Orchestration, Model Usage, and Cost Management

  • Participants discuss the challenge of managing token consumption and usage limits across advanced AI platforms, especially when conducting large-scale audits, coding projects, and automation workflows.
  • Sam explains that he uses Fable primarily as an orchestration layer and delegates specialized tasks such as coding and implementation to models like Claude and GPT.
  • Ramon shares that full code audits consume large amounts of AI resources, leading him to use Fable mainly for identifying issues while leveraging Opus for code fixes and refinements.
  • Guido runs much of his infrastructure through Fable's API mode, combining Ultra Code, workflows, and looping systems to continuously improve Amazon-related tools.
  • Guido uses automated loops that repeatedly test and optimize systems until completion, allowing projects to run for multiple days with minimal supervision.
  • Sam describes a workflow using "slash goal" combined with Ultra Code, where detailed objectives are defined collaboratively before allowing AI agents to build, test, and iterate toward completion.
  • Jacob relies heavily on Claude’s Cowork and Code capabilities for large-scale Amazon advertising analysis and campaign optimization.
  • Participants agree that successful AI implementation increasingly depends on effective orchestration between multiple models rather than relying on a single AI system.
  • The group emphasizes that selecting the right model for the right task is becoming a critical operational skill for AI-driven businesses.


AI-Powered Finance, PPC Management, and DSP Optimization

  • Ramon completes an internal finance system that analyzes cash flow, purchasing capacity, inventory planning, and future financing needs.
  • His custom-built solution replaces tools such as A2X and provides direct visibility into where company cash is being spent and when financing may be required.
  • Ramon also develops a content intelligence system that identifies viral social media content and analyzes patterns that can be adapted for his own brands.
  • He plans to scale content production using AI-generated content across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook.
  • Sam recommends Facebook as an important channel due to Ramon’s older target demographic.
  • Jacob uses Claude to combine data from multiple Amazon sources, including Data Rover, BSR data, Keepa, and other marketplace intelligence tools to create campaign recommendations.
  • Claude also generates Amazon bulk advertising files that can be uploaded directly into Amazon Ads, significantly reducing manual work.
  • Sam centralizes advertising and marketplace data into a unified database to improve pattern recognition and identify the true impact of PPC changes.
  • One example shared involves Amazon campaigns receiving zero impressions for six weeks despite appearing healthy; AI successfully identifies the underlying configuration issue within minutes after Amazon support fails to find a solution.
  • Guido and Jacob review a DSP management platform developed by Gigi’s team that focuses on surfacing actionable recommendations rather than presenting traditional dashboards.
  • The system automatically identifies anomalies, poor-performing placements, bid inefficiencies, and negative targeting opportunities.
  • Participants emphasize that DSP recommendations become significantly more valuable when AI systems understand brand-specific objectives and business constraints.
  • Jacob explains that Amazon DSP performs best for brands with strong lifetime customer value, recurring purchases, or higher average order values.
  • The group agrees that DSP often becomes inefficient when applied to low-ticket, one-time purchase products.
  • Jacob reports that Online Video campaigns using Amazon's Performance Plus bidding algorithm often outperform Prime Video campaigns due to lower costs and stronger conversion efficiency.
  • Participants suggest allocating DSP budgets at approximately 15% of total Amazon advertising spend to maintain efficiency.


Building AI-Powered Customer Service Systems

  • Cassidy demonstrates an AI-driven customer service platform built using Ruby on Rails and hosted on Render.
  • The system integrates with Gmail, Shopify, and Anthropic’s Claude models to automate customer support workflows.
  • Incoming emails are first screened using Claude Haiku to identify prompt injection attempts and malicious inputs before any processing occurs.
  • The platform categorizes support requests into common issue types such as shipping delays, address changes, replacements, refunds, and order inquiries.
  • Instead of providing the model with all available information, the system selectively attaches only the knowledge relevant to each request category.
  • The platform retrieves order data through Shopify’s Admin GraphQL API and automatically determines appropriate resolutions based on company policies.
  • For replacement requests, the system can generate Shopify draft orders automatically, reducing manual workload for support teams.
  • Users can edit AI-generated responses, and those edits are incorporated into future knowledge improvements.
  • Cassidy maintains version-controlled knowledge files inside Postgres, preserving revision histories and allowing continuous improvement.
  • To build the system initially, he processed years of historical customer support emails, categorized common issues, and extracted examples of successful responses.
  • Cou presents a complementary Gmail-based support system that focuses on surfacing contextual customer information directly inside Gmail.
  • His tool displays order history, subscription information, shipping status, customer lifetime value, and previous conversations in a sidebar interface.
  • Unlike Cassidy’s system, Cou’s workflow remains primarily human-driven and relies on internal documentation rather than automated response generation.
  • Both participants see opportunities to combine AI-generated responses with rich customer context to create more powerful support experiences.
  • Cassidy expresses interest in open-sourcing portions of the system so MDS members can contribute integrations and enhancements.

AI Architecture, Memory Systems, and Security

  • Cassidy explains that Ruby on Rails provides a strong foundation for combining traditional software architecture with AI-driven functionality.
  • Rails handles deterministic application behavior while AI is used for reasoning, categorization, and content generation.
  • June discusses the importance of maintaining deterministic systems when AI is introduced into operational workflows.
  • Participants note that Shopify’s ecosystem is heavily aligned with Rails, making it a natural choice for e-commerce-focused development.
  • Guido introduces concepts such as TimescaleDB, vector memory systems, and long-term AI knowledge storage.
  • Cassidy intentionally avoids self-modifying systems and instead keeps application code stable while allowing knowledge files to evolve over time.
  • Guido describes his use of persistent memory systems such as Obsidian and Hermes to maintain long-term AI context and historical knowledge.
  • June leads a discussion around prompt injection attacks and AI security.
  • She advocates for semantic circuit breakers that detect harmful intent based on meaning and patterns rather than relying solely on keywords or regex matching.
  • The group agrees that intent-based security systems are becoming increasingly important as AI agents gain access to tools, APIs, and business systems.
  • Participants discuss how recursive learning and pattern detection can stop many malicious requests before they reach sensitive workflows.
  • Guido references NVIDIA resources related to prompt-injection guardrails and plans to share them with the group.

Reddit Automation and Future MDS AI Collaboration

  • Sam shares progress on a Reddit automation system designed to warm up accounts and gradually introduce promotional content.
  • The system uses GoLogin to create unique browser profiles and realistic browsing behavior tied to specific personas.
  • During the warm-up phase, accounts focus on reading, voting, and casual participation before gradually moving into commenting and content creation.
  • Sam learns that overly aggressive promotion results in account bans, leading him to implement stricter thresholds around account age, karma levels, and promotional frequency.
  • The system now identifies relevant communities and discussions before introducing promotional content.
  • Chad discusses his own GoLogin experiments and asks questions about avoiding detection and improving account longevity.
  • Sam reports that many users engage naturally with the AI-driven personas without realizing they are automated.
  • Toward the end of the call, Sam proposes restructuring future AI Channel meetings around active problem-solving rather than open-ended discussion.
  • The proposed format mirrors MDS Boardroom sessions, where participants bring a current business problem and receive feedback from the group.
  • Cou strongly supports the idea and recommends incorporating more screen sharing, demos, and real-world examples.
  • Participants agree that solving actual operational challenges provides more value than discussing theoretical AI possibilities.
  • The group decides to experiment with a more use-case-driven format in future meetings to encourage deeper collaboration and faster implementation of ideas.

This session showcases how MDS members actively move beyond theory and apply AI to real workflows in finance, advertising, customer service, and growth channels like Reddit and DSP.


The group shares not only tools and models but also concrete architectures, security considerations, and lessons learned from both successes and failures.

 

By the end of the call, participants converge on a more problem-driven, demo-heavy format for future meetings, aiming to translate experimentation into repeatable, actionable systems. 


The conversation highlights a strong culture of open collaboration, with several members planning to share code, architectures, and guardrail resources to accelerate learning across the community.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1781292315209-MDS SEO Channel Call_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session participants in the MDS SEO Channel Call discuss Amazon compliance challenges SEO strategies Q&A optimization, AI-powered listing improvements, and PPC management. The discussion combines real-world seller experiences with advanced approaches to listing optimization, keyword indexing, and data-driven decision-making.

Made in USA Claims, Essential Oils, and Listing Suspensions

  • Participants discuss Amazon's increasing enforcement of FTC Made in USA regulations, particularly within the essential oils category.
  • Imran explains that products generally must contain approximately 95% U.S.-sourced materials to qualify for a Made in USA claim.
  • He shares that roughly 20% of his catalog, including several top-selling ASINs, is suspended due to origin claims that cannot be fully substantiated.
  • Imran notes that many U.S.-based suppliers import raw materials from overseas and are unwilling or unable to provide detailed sourcing documentation.
  • Participants agree that Amazon is actively removing unsupported origin claims across the marketplace.
  • Imran mentions that products such as shower steamers and sprays containing essential oils are also affected by these enforcement actions.
  • Alex and Imran observe that many brands may struggle to meet true Made in USA requirements because ingredients, packaging, bottles, and other components often originate outside the United States.

A+ Content, Translations, and Amazon Compliance Challenges

  • Imran explains that historical A+ Content and Amazon's automated translations can create compliance issues even when current English listings appear compliant.
  • He discovers multiple A+ Content versions dating back several years that remain active in Amazon's backend despite not appearing on live product pages.
  • Amazon automatically translates listing content into multiple languages, and some translated versions continue to contain prohibited claims.
  • Imran removes outdated A+ modules and comparison charts that contain problematic language or compliance risks.
  • He occasionally deletes listings temporarily to clear cached content and remove lingering violations.
  • Alex recommends reviewing retail contributions and listing ownership to ensure unauthorized edits do not introduce policy violations.
  • Imran confirms that these issues occur even though he only sells in the United States.
  • He notes that different Amazon internal systems often identify different violations, creating confusion during the appeal process.

Reinstatement Challenges and Seller Support Experiences

  • Imran describes the reinstatement process as inconsistent and difficult to navigate.
  • He reports receiving repeated automated responses indicating unresolved violations without specifying the exact issue.
  • Imran works with Seller Account Services (SAS) and an internal Amazon risk contact to escalate cases and secure reinstatements.
  • Some ASINs are successfully reinstated while others remain restricted, despite similar corrective actions.
  • Alex comments that SAS support quality varies significantly between representatives.
  • He shares that he has worked with approximately five different SAS representatives within a five-month period due to organizational changes and turnover.
  • Participants discuss broader layoffs across Amazon and other technology companies and the impact on support quality.
  • Alex encourages Imran to share his findings with the MDS community so other sellers facing similar compliance issues can benefit.

Using Customer Q&A for SEO and Keyword Indexing

  • Vitalina asks whether the discussion relates to A+ Q&A or the public customer Q&A section.
  • Alex clarifies that he is referring to the public customer Q&A section on product detail pages.
  • He explains that Amazon indexes customer Q&A content and that it contributes to relevancy signals used by Amazon's search algorithms, including Rufus.
  • Alex suggests encouraging friends and family to submit legitimate product questions, as Amazon focuses enforcement primarily on reviews rather than Q&A submissions.
  • He recommends using questions that naturally reference competitor brands to improve keyword relevance and competitive visibility.
  • Alex notes that certain regulated or sensitive keywords may be used more safely within customer questions and answers than in the main listing content.
  • He recommends framing these terms naturally within customer inquiries and providing accurate responses.
  • Ramon reports confusion when some questions are routed through Buyer-Seller Messaging instead of appearing directly in public Q&A.
  • Alex demonstrates that questions submitted through the "Ask a Question" feature can still become publicly visible and indexed.
  • He confirms that responses to these inquiries can contribute to searchable Q&A content despite changes in Amazon's interface.

AI, Listing Optimization, and PPC Strategy

 

AI-Based Listing Optimization

  • Alex explains that he is developing an AI-powered listing optimization framework that scores and evaluates all major ranking and conversion factors.
  • The framework analyzes SEO, copywriting, A+ Content, Q&A content, and launch strategy.
  • He plans to use tools such as Paradise and Apify to collect both front-end and back-end listing data.
  • Alex intends to share portions of the framework with the MDS community while potentially commercializing it externally.
  • Ramon describes a system that incorporates PPC performance, Search Query Performance data, return reasons, and ranking information to generate listing recommendations.
  • He clusters return reasons to identify information gaps that should be addressed through images and copy.
  • Both participants agree that AI-generated images still require significant human review and quality control.
  • Alex notes that ChatGPT image generation can sometimes outperform niche tools but still relies on human designers for final execution.

 

AI Systems, Models, and Workflow Design

  • June recommends separating reusable AI methodologies from brand-specific knowledge to prevent instruction drift between projects.
  • She suggests storing brand guidelines and domain knowledge in structured files while keeping workflows focused on repeatable processes.
  • Participants discuss newer AI models and their strengths in auditing, reasoning, and workflow management.
  • Ramon emphasizes creating deterministic workflows wherever possible to reduce variability in AI outputs.
  • June highlights the importance of separating planning and execution phases to prevent outdated assumptions from affecting later work.

 

Databases, RAG Systems, and Reliability

  • June explains that large language models can create database errors if allowed to modify schemas without safeguards.
  • She recommends implementing strict validation layers and schema controls.
  • Ramon shares that he performs routine database audits to identify inconsistencies and drift.
  • June describes rebuilding her retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system using a state-machine architecture with more structured workflow stages.

 

PPC Management and Niche Market Challenges

  • Alex asks for recommendations for reliable PPC agencies or consultants.
  • Ramon explains that he built a custom PPC platform because existing solutions did not meet his needs.
  • Alex describes challenges within highly specialized automotive niches where keyword tools often fail to identify fitment-specific searches.
  • He explains that AI can help generate long-tail keywords, but human review remains essential.
  • June recommends combining a standardized PPC framework with category-specific logic.
  • Participants agree that custom processes and human oversight remain critical for PPC success, especially in specialized markets with limited search volume.


In this session, participants share practical experiences navigating Amazon compliance, content management, SEO optimization, AI implementation, and PPC strategy. 


The discussion highlights how evolving regulations, automated translations, and changing Amazon systems create both challenges and opportunities for sellers.


The group concludes that AI and automation can significantly improve listing optimization and advertising performance, but success still depends on strong frameworks, reliable data, and human oversight.

For sellers operating in regulated categories or highly specialized niches, balancing automation with expert judgment remains essential.

items.description_text: In this session, MDS Centurion members discuss how to navigate Amazon’s evolving fee structure, global competition, and the realities of scaling beyond $20M in annual revenue. TOPICS: 1. Amazon economics and competition 2. Growth levers and risk management 3. Building scalable teams and systems

files.name: MDS Centurion Channel Call Transcript
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1781290889884-MDS Centurion Channel Call_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS Centurion channel discuss the realities of scaling e-commerce brands on Amazon and beyond with a focus on fees, competition, funding, team structure, retail expansion, and AI adoption. 

The conversation combines strategic perspectives with practical experiences from sellers generating more than $20 million in annual revenue across multiple channels.

Amazon Fees, Competition, and the Evolving Marketplace

  • Participants discuss how Amazon fee increases impact profitability but note that Amazon can still compare favorably to other channels when customer acquisition costs, logistics, and labor are considered.
  • Several sellers believe higher fees and stricter requirements create barriers to entry that remove weaker competitors and benefit well-run brands with healthy margins.
  • Members express concerns about competition from Chinese sellers who often operate on lower margins and may benefit from different regulatory and tax environments.
  • The group emphasizes that government policies and regulations, not just Amazon policies, play a major role in creating a fair competitive landscape.
  • Shinghi explains that U.S. sellers are taxed on worldwide income, while many foreign sellers do not face the same tax obligations in the United States.
  • Deepak shares examples of misleading product claims, such as inaccurate material compositions and exaggerated specifications, that distort competition and consumer expectations.
  • He explains that his company works with Amazon over several years to improve compliance within its category and sees enforcement improve through persistence and documentation.
  • Participants discuss the potential use of legal action under the Lanham Act and certain California laws to address false advertising and unfair competition.
  • The group notes that Amazon's DD+7 payout structure may make seller accounts more accessible targets for future legal enforcement actions.

Channel Strategy and Diversification

  • Several participants remain bullish on Amazon due to its traffic, conversion rates, and ability to maintain organic ranking even when advertising is reduced.
  • Others argue that owning customer relationships through email, SMS, subscriptions, and community building creates stronger long-term brand value.
  • Antonio highlights the risks of relying heavily on Amazon because the platform can change policies, fees, and eligibility requirements with little notice.
  • The group generally agrees that the strongest businesses operate across multiple channels, including Amazon, Shopify, TikTok Shop, retail, and other marketplaces.
  • Members note that off-Amazon marketing efforts such as influencer campaigns, TikTok content, and YouTube videos can strengthen brand awareness and improve Amazon performance.
  • Victor shares challenges with Amazon repeatedly classifying a skincare product containing 0.11% alcohol as hazardous despite supporting documentation proving otherwise.
  • Participants suggest resubmitting documentation, obtaining additional testing, and pursuing external validation to resolve hazmat classification disputes.
  • The group references previous discussions about balancing Amazon dependence with broader channel diversification strategies.

Prime Day, Promotions, and Pricing Compliance

  • Ozlem asks about Prime Day strategies, leading to a discussion on promotions and discounting.
  • Several sellers report better results from Best Deals than Lightning Deals due to lower discount requirements and stronger return on investment.
  • David and Matthew explain that they focus discounts on a small number of core products while maintaining healthier margins across the rest of the catalog.
  • Aiden recommends using Best Deals with modest discounts rather than deeper Lightning Deal discounts whenever possible.
  • Members discuss the legal requirements surrounding strikethrough pricing and reference prices.
  • Matthew shares a strategy of raising prices one day per week, increasing advertising spend during that period, and maintaining revenue while improving profitability.
  • Participants explain that Amazon's PED system can help sellers understand which reference prices are being used for promotional pricing.
  • Deepak raises concerns about Amazon displaying reference prices that sellers cannot easily trace or modify, creating compliance challenges.

Funding, Capital Structure, and Exit Opportunities

  • Antonio asks for recommendations on financing options after the failure of a previous funding provider.
  • Matthew recommends Settle for short-term inventory financing and discusses negotiating commercial lines of credit with banks such as Wells Fargo.
  • Participants compare traditional bank financing with fintech lenders, noting that bank financing generally offers lower interest rates but requires more documentation and longer approval timelines.
  • David suggests additional options such as Amazon Lending, home equity lines of credit, margin loans, and policy-backed loans.
  • Deepak mentions SBA-backed financing as another source of affordable capital for growing businesses.
  • Antonio notes that regional banks are often willing to lend but move more slowly than alternative financing providers.
  • The group briefly discusses IPOs and concludes that public-company compliance costs make them impractical for most mid-sized brands.
  • Members view private equity and growth equity investments as more realistic options for liquidity and future growth.

Team Building, Retail Expansion, and AI Adoption

  • Victor explains that his business has reached approximately $25 million in revenue and that he is searching for stronger senior leadership talent to support further growth.
  • Several members agree that finding experienced operators with both technical skills and ownership mentality is challenging.
  • Aiden recommends exploring high-level talent from China and mentions working with GNO Partners to identify experienced operators.
  • Matthew encourages founders to evaluate whether key roles should be filled through internal development or external hiring based on strategic importance.
  • David discusses the value of hiring an Integrator or Chief of Staff who can translate founder vision into operational execution.
  • The group highlights the difficulty of finding strong integrators, especially in remote-first organizations.
  • Members discuss recruiting talent from competitors while ensuring candidates have experience building systems, not just operating within mature companies.
  • David recommends looking outside a company's immediate product category and focusing on transferable growth and operational expertise.
  • Antonio asks about retail expansion, and participants explain the importance of specialized brokers, buyer relationships, and trade show networking.
  • David and Matthew describe retail as operationally demanding due to markdowns, chargebacks, inventory planning, and merchandising requirements.
  • Deepak shares that after spending many years in retail, he now prefers the higher margins and greater control offered by e-commerce.
  • On Amazon reimbursements, participants discuss managing claims internally versus using third-party reimbursement services.
  • Matthew shares that his team uses Sellerise to manage reimbursement-related workflows.
  • Members discuss practical AI applications, including creative generation, documentation, workflow automation, communication, and team training.
  • Tools mentioned include Chat Walrus, Claude, Notion, Adobe Firefly, and speech-to-text solutions such as SuperWhisper.
  • The group agrees that AI is becoming a valuable force multiplier when paired with structured team training and adoption programs.

In conclusion, this session brings together experienced Amazon and e-commerce operators who openly discuss the challenges of rising fees, increasing competition, financing growth, building leadership teams, and adopting new technologies. 

The overarching theme is that long-term success comes from building a strong brand, diversifying channels, maintaining operational discipline, and investing in the people, systems, and tools needed to scale sustainably.

cliff_notes:
In this session MDS members join an expert webinar with Omnisend's Deliverability and Compliance Lead Desi Zhivkova, to learn how to improve email deliverability, avoid spam folders, and maximize email marketing revenue.

The discussion also includes MDS community updates, recent industry changes, and practical strategies that founders and marketers can implement immediately.

Email Delivery, Deliverability, and Industry Changes

  • Desi Zhivkova introduces herself as Omnisend's Deliverability and Compliance Lead with more than a decade of email industry experience.
  • She explains that delivery refers to whether an email is accepted by the receiving mail server without bouncing.
  • She explains that deliverability refers to where the email ultimately lands, such as the inbox, Promotions tab, spam folder, or junk folder.
  • Major mailbox providers such as Gmail, Yahoo, and Microsoft primarily evaluate sender reputation and user engagement when determining placement.
  • Desi notes that a high delivery rate does not guarantee inbox placement.
  • She explains that traditional concerns such as spam trigger words and image-to-text ratios are much less important than engagement signals.
  • Promotional emails landing in the Promotions tab are not necessarily a problem and often reach users when they are in a buying mindset.
  • Transactional emails, such as order confirmations and password resets, should ideally reach the Primary inbox.
  • Desi reviews the sender requirements introduced by Gmail and Yahoo in February 2024 and later adopted by Microsoft.
  • She defines bulk senders as those sending more than 5,000 emails per day to these mailbox providers.
  • Bulk senders are expected to:
    • Implement SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication.
    • Maintain spam complaint rates below 0.3%, with a target below 0.1%.
    • Support one-click unsubscribe functionality.
  • Desi explains:
    • SPF authorizes approved sending servers.
    • DKIM verifies message integrity.
    • DMARC helps protect against spoofing and impersonation.
  • She warns that brands lacking proper authentication are more vulnerable to phishing attacks and deliverability problems.

List Quality, Consent, and Subscriber Engagement

  • Desi identifies poor authentication as one of the most common deliverability issues.
  • She strongly advises against purchased, scraped, or third-party email lists.
  • She recommends double opt-in because it confirms subscriber intent and reduces fake signups.
  • Single opt-in may generate more subscribers but increases exposure to bots and invalid addresses.
  • Desi explains that spam traps are email addresses created to identify senders with poor list acquisition practices.
  • She notes that spam trap hits can severely damage sender reputation.
  • Sender reputation can be damaged quickly but often takes months to repair.
  • She recommends implementing CAPTCHA protection on all signup forms.
  • Sending campaigns to inactive subscribers can hurt engagement metrics and negatively impact deliverability.
  • Desi emphasizes that quality is more important than list size.
  • Engagement signals such as opens, clicks, and meaningful interactions are major drivers of inbox placement.
  • Low complaint rates alone do not guarantee good deliverability if engagement is weak.
  • She warns against sending large promotional campaigns to an entire list, particularly during major sales events.
  • Segmentation and personalization consistently improve engagement and reputation.
  • Desi recommends implementing a sunset policy for inactive subscribers.
  • Typical sunset campaigns include:
    • A re-engagement sequence.
    • An incentive to remain subscribed.
    • A final notice before removal.
  • She advises making unsubscribe options easy to find.
  • Unsubscribe activity can provide valuable feedback about content relevance and email frequency.

Monitoring Reputation and Managing Deliverability

  • Desi emphasizes that sender reputation requires ongoing monitoring.
  • She recommends using Google Postmaster Tools to monitor Gmail reputation and spam complaint rates.
  • Google categorizes domain reputation as High, Medium, Low, or Bad.
  • Microsoft Smart Network Data Services (SNDS) provides similar visibility for IP reputation.
  • Omnisend and other ESP dashboards can provide mailbox-provider-specific performance insights.
  • Desi recommends focusing on long-term trends rather than individual campaign results.
  • She notes that Apple Mail Privacy Protection can inflate open rates and should be considered when analyzing performance.
  • Bounce reports often contain useful diagnostic information regarding authentication failures, invalid addresses, or reputation issues.
  • Gmail does not provide individual spam complaint reports and instead surfaces complaint data through Google Postmaster Tools.
  • Desi reiterates the importance of maintaining complaint rates below 0.3%.
  • For Gmail reputation issues, she recommends:
    • Pausing Gmail sends for approximately two weeks.
    • Restarting with only the most engaged subscribers.
    • Gradually increasing volume while monitoring performance.
  • Seasonal businesses should warm up their lists before peak selling periods rather than emailing dormant audiences all at once.
  • Historical engagement data can help identify the best segments for reactivation.
  • Desi explains that subdomains maintain separate reputations but can still influence the root domain.
  • She recommends separating sending domains:
    • Transactional emails from domains such as transactional.brand.com.
    • Marketing emails from domains such as marketing.brand.com.
  • She advises against sending cold outreach from the primary company domain.
  • If cold outreach is necessary, she recommends using a separate subdomain or dedicated domain.
  • Brands experiencing severe deliverability issues can work through their ESP's deliverability team or submit escalation requests through mailbox provider support channels.

AI, Omnisend MCP, and Audience Questions

  • Desi explains that mailbox providers increasingly use AI models to evaluate and prioritize email placement.
  • Gmail uses AI systems to determine which promotional emails are most relevant to recipients.
  • She advises marketers to avoid deceptive tactics such as using "Re:" or "Fwd:" in promotional subject lines.
  • Desi notes that mailbox providers can likely identify AI-generated content but do not penalize it solely because it was created using AI.
  • Performance depends on audience engagement rather than the method used to create content.
  • She encourages marketers to evaluate AI-generated content based on opens, clicks, and conversions.
  • Desi explains that both marketers and mailbox providers are increasingly relying on AI technologies.
  • Ben Anderson asks about Omnisend MCP and its ability to access deliverability data.
  • Desi explains that Google Postmaster Tools data is not yet integrated directly into MCP.
  • Omnisend plans to develop future integrations that connect Postmaster data with MCP workflows.
  • She references a recent Omnisend deliverability webinar that includes practical MCP prompts for deliverability analysis.
  • Ben shares positive feedback regarding MCP's speed and analytical capabilities.
  • In closing, Brian asks for a simple deliverability audit process.
  • Desi recommends:
    • Verifying SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and one-click unsubscribe setup.
    • Reviewing open rates and engagement metrics.
    • Analyzing performance by mailbox provider.
    • Monitoring bounce rates, spam complaints, and unsubscribe trends.

In this session, MDS members learn practical strategies for improving email deliverability from Omnisend's Deliverability and Compliance Lead, Desi Zhivkova.


The discussion highlights how modern deliverability depends on strong technical foundations, subscriber engagement, proper list management, and ongoing monitoring rather than outdated spam-filter myths.

The key takeaway is that brands that prioritize authentication, permission-based marketing, audience segmentation, and reputation monitoring will be better positioned to maintain inbox placement and drive long-term email revenue as mailbox providers continue adopting more advanced AI-driven filtering systems.

items.title: Resellers Channel Call May 2026
items.description:
In this session, Resellers Channel members discuss recent policy changes affecting ASIN creation and brand registry, and how these shifts increasingly favor authorized resellers over traditional arbitrage models.

TOPICS:

  1. Amazon policy changes on ASIN creation and brand registry requirements
  2. Abuse, counterfeits, and enforcement gaps (Transparency, catalog manipulation, black-hat tactics)
  3. Long-term strategies: building brand relationships, gaining authorization, and using effective escalation paths
items.description_text: In this session, Resellers Channel members discuss recent policy changes affecting ASIN creation and brand registry, and how these shifts increasingly favor authorized resellers over traditional arbitrage models. TOPICS: Amazon policy changes on ASIN creation and brand registry requirements Abuse, counterfeits, and enforcement gaps (Transparency, catalog manipulation, black-hat tactics) Long-term strategies: building brand relationships, gaining authorization, and using effective escalation paths
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss recent and upcoming Amazon policy changes affecting resellers with a particular focus on ASIN creation, Brand Registry, and the growing emphasis on authorized reseller status. 

The group shares practical experiences, frustrations, and tactical approaches to staying compliant and profitable in an increasingly restrictive environment.


Amazon Policy Updates and Their Impact on Resellers

  • The group discusses a new Amazon policy, effective June 1, that prevents sellers who are not designated as authorized resellers in Brand Registry from creating new ASINs for a brand.
  • Participants believe this policy may reduce sales opportunities for Amazon, brands, and resellers because unauthorized sellers can no longer create listings for products when brands are not enrolled in Brand Registry or do not actively manage reseller permissions.
  • The group notes that Amazon has recently increased enforcement around product identifiers such as UPCs and GS1 codes, giving sellers approximately 30 days to sell through inventory when identifiers do not match brand records.
  • Amazon's public guidance encourages sellers to maintain authorized reseller agreements or valid invoices, but participants report that enforcement remains inconsistent and often confusing.
  • Several attendees agree that these changes place additional pressure on traditional arbitrage models by making it more difficult for unauthorized sellers to create or maintain listings for branded products.


Authorized vs. Unauthorized Reselling and Marketplace Direction

  • Participants discuss Amazon's position that it does not officially arbitrate disputes between authorized and unauthorized resellers while simultaneously introducing tools and policies that favor brand-controlled authorization.
  • One participant suggests Amazon may eventually provide a system that allows sellers to request selling permissions directly from brands through Brand Registry.
  • The group compares Amazon's direction to Walmart, which is already viewed as a more authorization-driven marketplace.
  • Several resellers note that although Amazon does not publicly describe itself as an authorized-seller-only marketplace, recent policy changes increasingly favor brands and authorized sellers.
  • Participants recognize that brands benefit from greater control over distribution, while independent resellers face additional compliance requirements and operational risks.


ASIN Creation, Black Hat Tactics, and Listing Manipulation

  • The group clarifies that the new policy affects the creation of new ASINs and does not directly impact existing listings.
  • Participants note that Amazon is simultaneously removing listings that contain questionable or inaccurate product identifiers.
  • Several attendees share that some brands have restricted ASIN creation for years, yet unauthorized listings still appear, suggesting that loopholes or black hat tactics remain in use.
  • One tactic discussed involves repurposing inactive or abandoned ASINs by changing product details, images, and brand information rather than creating entirely new listings.
  • Examples are shared of branded products appearing under unrelated brand names due to catalog manipulation through flat files or API updates.
  • Participants express frustration that sellers following Amazon's policies often face more obstacles than bad actors exploiting catalog vulnerabilities.


Transparency, Counterfeits, and Enforcement Challenges

  • The discussion covers Amazon's Transparency program, which uses unique product codes to authenticate inventory.
  • Participants explain that Transparency officially requires codes to be applied to every manufactured unit, although many brands do not fully implement the program in this manner.
  • One attendee shares a counterfeit case where fake products were paired with legitimate Transparency codes and sent into FBA, resulting in counterfeit items appearing on a Transparency-protected listing.
  • Because Transparency inventory can be pooled across sellers, identifying the source of counterfeit units can become extremely difficult.
  • Participants note that brands sometimes respond to counterfeit incidents by removing all third-party sellers from a listing, affecting both legitimate and illegitimate sellers.
  • The group highlights the ongoing gap between Amazon's documented enforcement procedures and the inconsistent outcomes sellers often experience when working with support teams.


Practical Strategies: Relationships, Authorizations, and Escalations

  • Several participants describe moving away from pure arbitrage and toward direct relationships with brands, distributors, and licensing partners.
  • One participant recommends treating arbitrage as inherently volatile and focusing on securing authorized reseller status whenever possible.
  • Attendees share examples of leveraging relationships with licensing companies and brand owners to gain authorization for major brands, including licensed products tied to well-known franchises.
  • The group discusses how distributors and licensing partners can sometimes advocate on behalf of resellers and help them become approved sellers within Brand Registry.
  • Participants recommend attending industry events such as the Licensing Expo to build relationships with brand owners and licensing teams.
  • On the support side, attendees advise thoroughly documenting issues through standard Seller Support channels before pursuing executive escalations when necessary.
  • Some participants report better experiences when reaching Seller Support teams located in Costa Rica, which they perceive as more knowledgeable and empowered to resolve issues.
  • The group also discusses the possibility that Amazon analyzes invoice patterns, supplier templates, and ERP-generated documentation to verify supplier authenticity, meaning changes in supplier invoicing practices can create unexpected verification challenges.


Key Takeaways

  • Amazon continues to strengthen brand control and authorization requirements across the marketplace.
  • Traditional arbitrage models face increasing pressure as listing creation and compliance requirements become more restrictive.
  • Direct relationships with brands, distributors, and licensing partners are becoming increasingly important for long-term sustainability.
  • Transparency and anti-counterfeit programs provide additional protection but do not eliminate enforcement challenges.
  • Strong documentation, authorized reseller agreements, and proactive relationship-building are becoming critical competitive advantages.


In conclusion, this session provides a detailed view of how Amazon's evolving policies are reshaping the reseller landscape.

Participants emphasize that long-term success increasingly depends on building direct brand relationships, securing formal authorization, maintaining strong documentation, and developing effective escalation strategies rather than relying solely on traditional arbitrage opportunities.

items.title: Scaling TikTok Shop with Founder-Led Content and Affiliate Marketing Strategies－David Stark－TikTok Channel Call May 2026
items.description:
In this session, David Stark, CEO of Coldest, shares how he scales a TikTok- and affiliate-driven growth engine on top of an Amazon and DTC business. 

TOPICS:

  1. David’s journey from Amazon to DTC and TikTok, including Shark Tank and warehouse scaling.
  2. Building, organizing, and incentivizing a large affiliate/creator ecosystem on TikTok Shop.
  3. Content strategy with founder-led videos, volume testing, and repurposing TikTok winners into Meta ads.
items.description_text: In this session, David Stark, CEO of Coldest, shares how he scales a TikTok- and affiliate-driven growth engine on top of an Amazon and DTC business. TOPICS: David’s journey from Amazon to DTC and TikTok, including Shark Tank and warehouse scaling. Building, organizing, and incentivizing a large affiliate/creator ecosystem on TikTok Shop. Content strategy with founder-led videos, volume testing, and repurposing TikTok winners into Meta ads.

files.name: TikTok Channel Call May 2026 Transcript
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1780918763784-TikTok Channel Call May 2026_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session participants hear from David Stark CEO of Coldest, about how he builds and scales a TikTok- and affiliate-led growth engine on top of an Amazon and DTC business. 

David shares practical tactics, trade-offs, and long-term strategies around TikTok Shop, affiliates, content creation, and operations, while answering questions from other founders about applying these approaches to their own brands.

Founder Journey, Channel Mix, and Business Evolution

  • David Stark launched Coldest in 2015 on Amazon, initially operating from a one-car garage where he personally handles fulfillment, packing, and product design.
  • He explains that repeated Amazon account suspensions in 2016 and 2017 motivate him to diversify and reduce reliance on a single platform.
  • Despite generating eight figures in Amazon revenue, he remains cautious about platform dependency because of the lack of control and account-related risks.
  • He notes that similar platform risks exist on TikTok, where algorithm changes can dramatically impact daily sales performance.
  • David describes the company's growth from a garage operation to a 2,000-square-foot warehouse with 20 storage containers and eventually to a 52,000-square-foot facility that is now nearing capacity.
  • He shares that warehouse expansions are operationally challenging and expensive, making efficient use of existing space a long-term priority.
  • Coldest appears on Shark Tank Season 15, largely due to encouragement from his twin brother.
  • While the initial Shark Tank airing generates approximately $80,000 in sales in one day, David believes the greatest benefit comes from leveraging the "As Seen on Shark Tank" branding in future marketing efforts.
  • He emphasizes that Coldest remains a bootstrapped company, requiring careful management of inventory, marketing spend, and cash flow.

Early TikTok Strategy, TikTok Shop, and Affiliate Mechanics

  • David begins investing in TikTok around 2019 and 2020, before TikTok Shop launches and before the platform becomes highly structured.
  • He builds a large-scale affiliate outreach operation supported by more than 100 virtual assistants responsible for creator recruitment and relationship management.
  • Virtual assistants negotiate agreements that typically include content deliverables, a small fixed payment, and commission-based incentives.
  • The team manages contracts, sample distribution, and affiliate communications through a structured management system.
  • David estimates that maintaining this operation costs approximately $30,000 to $40,000 per month.
  • When TikTok Shop launches, Coldest is already positioned with an established creator network and can quickly capitalize on the new opportunity.
  • He explains that TikTok initially subsidizes growth by covering portions of shipping costs and offering customer incentives, creating significant early sales momentum.
  • As one of the first major water bottle brands on TikTok Shop, Coldest benefits from limited competition and strong visibility in category searches.
  • He reports that sales can reach approximately $90,000 per day during the platform's early growth phase.
  • As TikTok Shop matures, competition increases and early advantages diminish.
  • David notes that affiliates increasingly expect proof of sales performance before committing significant effort to a product.
  • He stresses that strong brand credibility and demonstrated sales history are becoming increasingly important for attracting affiliates.

Building, Organizing, and Incentivizing Affiliates

  • David recommends building a long-term affiliate community rather than relying on one-off creator relationships.
  • Coldest primarily manages affiliates through Discord while using WhatsApp for internal operational communication.
  • When launching new products, the company activates its existing affiliate network rather than starting outreach from scratch.
  • Affiliates typically purchase products at discounted rates through a dedicated DTC portal instead of receiving unlimited free samples.
  • The discounted purchasing model provides better control over inventory, pricing, and affiliate participation.
  • David describes a custom affiliate portal where creators can access approved products and launch opportunities.
  • He encourages affiliate participation and feedback during product launches to create stronger buy-in and engagement.
  • While customer and affiliate feedback is valuable, he believes founders must still rely on their own judgment when making product decisions.
  • He notes that affiliate content quality varies significantly, and only a small percentage of creator content performs exceptionally well.
  • David observes that top-performing brands succeed because they combine both quality and quantity of content production.
  • He emphasizes that strong sales performance motivates affiliates to create more content and improve content quality.
  • He describes affiliate growth as a reinforcing cycle where successful content drives sales, which in turn encourages additional creator participation.

Content Strategy, Founder-Led Marketing, and Multichannel Growth

  • David believes founder-led content provides a significant competitive advantage over larger corporate brands.
  • He continues to appear personally in content because it builds trust, authenticity, and stronger relationships with customers and affiliates.
  • Founder-led content performs particularly well on Meta platforms but also contributes value across TikTok, email marketing, and live streams.
  • Affiliates often adopt messaging, storytelling techniques, and hooks directly from founder-created content.
  • David encourages founders to experiment with different content styles, including acting as customers, characters, or product users.
  • He stresses that success on TikTok requires volume because the algorithm rewards continuous testing and experimentation.
  • His philosophy is to create numerous content variations rather than relying on a single creative concept.
  • At times, Coldest intentionally slows affiliate recruitment when inventory constraints make additional demand difficult to support.
  • David cautions that certain TikTok promotional programs can reduce profitability through heavy discounting and margin compression.
  • He notes that TikTok increasingly promotes newer brands and may incentivize affiliates to diversify beyond heavily saturated products.
  • Coldest uses TikTok as a testing platform for Meta advertising by identifying high-performing organic videos before investing in paid promotion.
  • This approach results in a high success rate when transferring winning creatives from TikTok to Meta campaigns.
  • He mentions tools that help brands secure content rights and manage creator payments more efficiently.

Long-Term Mindset, Operations, and Community Management

  • David emphasizes that TikTok success requires long-term commitment rather than short-term experimentation.
  • He advises founders to invest consistently within their risk tolerance and avoid abandoning the platform prematurely.
  • He repeatedly highlights the importance of persistence, continuous testing, and incremental improvement over time.
  • Coldest has spent nearly a decade refining its water bottle products, regularly improving functionality, design, and aesthetics.
  • He points to brands such as Stanley as examples of how sustained effort and consistency can eventually create major breakthroughs.
  • David shares that Coldest experimented with adjacent products, including the Coldest Pillow, but ultimately refocused on products that align closely with the brand's core identity.
  • Inventory management remains one of the biggest challenges in affiliate-driven growth models because successful campaigns can rapidly deplete stock.
  • He expresses skepticism about TikTok's GMV Max advertising product, believing many attributed sales would have occurred organically.
  • He argues that combining affiliate commissions with GMV Max spending can create significant pressure on margins.
  • David uses advertising budget allocation as leverage when communicating with TikTok account managers regarding platform issues.
  • While acknowledging that some brands report positive results with GMV Max, he remains cautious about its long-term value.
  • During the Q&A, he advises founders to determine how much they can consistently invest in TikTok and commit to that level of effort over time.
  • He compares e-commerce growth to calculated risk-taking, where success depends on investing aggressively while protecting the overall health of the business.
  • David recommends that founders remain visible within affiliate communities through Discord, live streams, and regular engagement.
  • He believes founder participation strengthens relationships and helps affiliates feel more connected to the brand.
  • He supports community-building tactics such as creator recognition, feedback sessions, educational content, and direct interaction.


Additional Insights from the Q&A

  • David recommends founder-led community engagement supported by staff rather than fully delegating affiliate relationships.
  • Participants discuss the value of recurring training sessions, dashboards, and performance analysis for improving affiliate success rates.
  • The group notes that experienced creators often benefit the most from education and coaching, while newer creators may require significantly more support.
  • One founder asks about targeting schools and small businesses on TikTok, and David recommends focusing first on consumer-facing content that can achieve broader reach.
  • He explains that small business owners are also consumers and are more likely to discover products through strong consumer-focused content than through direct B2B targeting.
  • David concludes that TikTok remains primarily a consumer-driven platform, making consumer virality the most effective path to broader market adoption.


In this session, David Stark provides a detailed overview of how Coldest scales through TikTok Shop, affiliate marketing, founder-led content, and community building. 


Drawing on nearly a decade of experience across Amazon, DTC, and social commerce, he emphasizes that sustained growth comes from consistent execution rather than shortcuts.


The discussion highlights that success on TikTok depends on building a strong affiliate network, continuously improving products and creative assets, maintaining close relationships with creators, and committing to long-term experimentation.

For brand operators, the key takeaway is that TikTok should be treated as a strategic growth channel that rewards persistence, operational discipline, and authentic founder involvement.

items.title: One Influencer Doubled Sales and Profits －Craig Brockie －Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Craig shares how he builds a gut‑health brand to $10M in 18 months by combining Amazon listing strategy, deep influencer partnerships, and viral X (Twitter) content. I

TOPICS:

  1. Building and exiting an Amazon toys brand, and key lessons from failed and discounted exits
  2. Creating the “Ultimate” gut‑health brand and partnering with experts like Dr. William Davis and Dr. Eric Berg
  3. Using X (Twitter) threads, celebrity features, and affiliate structures to drive traffic, sales, and audience growth
items.description_text: In this session, Craig shares how he builds a gut‑health brand to $10M in 18 months by combining Amazon listing strategy, deep influencer partnerships, and viral X (Twitter) content. I TOPICS: Building and exiting an Amazon toys brand, and key lessons from failed and discounted exits Creating the “Ultimate” gut‑health brand and partnering with experts like Dr. William Davis and Dr. Eric Berg Using X (Twitter) threads, celebrity features, and affiliate structures to drive traffic, sales, and audience growth

files.name: Mogul Call with Craig Brockie Transcript
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1780511601718-Mogul Call with Craig Brockie _otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session participants hear how Craig Brockie takes a new brand from zero to $10 million in 18 months by combining Amazon fundamentals with strategic influencer partnerships and viral X (Twitter) threads. 


He also shares lessons from a previous toys brand exit details of his gut health brand Ultimate and specific tactics for networking with high-profile experts and driving traffic through social channels.

Craig’s Background, Frisbee Brand, and Exit Lessons

  • Craig has been in e-commerce since the 1990s, starting with black hat SEO before Google existed and by gaming early search engines like Yahoo.
  • He enters Amazon in 2016 and builds a highly successful frisbee and skip ball brand that becomes a top seller in Toys & Games and Sports & Outdoors.
  • The original frisbee concept starts as a guerrilla marketing idea where he prints his investment company name on promotional frisbees and distributes them in upscale neighborhoods.
  • Customer feedback reveals that the frisbee itself is a popular toy, which prompts him to package and sell it on Amazon as a consumer product.
  • In the toys category, he positions products under multiple gifting angles, such as beach toys, Christmas gifts, and stocking stuffers, to expand keyword opportunities.
  • He uses strong, conversion-focused parent titles while creating keyword-rich child ASIN titles that target seasonal and category-specific search terms.
  • This combination helps drive significant ranking improvements and top category positions during peak seasons.
  • Craig attempts to exit the brand in 2022 and receives two offers, ultimately choosing a more speculative buyer over a lower guaranteed cash offer.
  • As post-COVID demand declines, sales soften and the speculative deal falls apart.
  • While pursuing the exit, he launches a second brand, which divides his attention and reduces focus on the sale process.
  • Weak year-over-year Q4 performance causes another buyer to walk away, cutting the value of the business significantly.
  • He eventually sells the company but allows the buyer to pay for inventory through quarterly installments.
  • When the buyer encounters financial difficulties, Craig becomes an unsecured creditor and accepts a significant loss on the remaining inventory balance.
  • His key lessons are to avoid unnecessary greed, prioritize guaranteed cash offers when appropriate, and secure any deferred payments with collateral or legal protections.


Launching the Ultimate Gut Health Brand and Product Strategy

  • After the challenging exit, Craig decides to build a business around his passion for natural health and gut health.
  • He secures the Ultimate trademark and obtains the Amazon brand URL amazon.com/ultimate.
  • The brand is built around three pillars that improve his own health: gut repair, detoxification, and peptides.
  • Craig shares how long-term antibiotic use during his youth contributes to gut issues, inflammation, anxiety, and other health challenges.
  • Through dietary changes and targeted health interventions, he restores his gut health and experiences significant improvements in overall well-being.
  • His first flagship product is a probiotic yogurt maker designed to create highly potent probiotic yogurts at home.
  • The concept is inspired by fermented dairy probiotics such as Bio K Plus, which he had used personally for years.
  • He tests the process himself and distributes yogurt makers, probiotic starters, and educational resources to friends and family who report positive results.
  • The Ultimate brand later expands into probiotic starters, probiotic capsules, prebiotics, and additional gut-health products.
  • He builds an email list through warranty registrations and lead magnets, allowing him to cross-sell new products to existing customers.
  • The brand grows beyond Amazon and expands onto channels such as Target, Walmart, Canada, and the United Kingdom.


Influencer, Author, and Expert Relationships

  • Craig's core strategy is to lean into existing fame by partnering with experts and influencers who already have trusted audiences.
  • He identifies Dr. William Davis, author of Wheat Belly and Super Gut, as a leading authority in gut health.
  • After reaching out directly, he quickly validates demand within Dr. Davis's audience for a high-quality probiotic yogurt maker.
  • Together they help popularize a product designed specifically to support the probiotic methods discussed in Super Gut.
  • The Ultimate yogurt maker becomes a category leader on Amazon through strong product performance and customer support.
  • Craig invests heavily in the relationship, including hosting Dr. Davis at personal and business events.
  • Dr. Davis becomes a major affiliate partner while Craig promotes his books and helps expand his reach.
  • Craig also develops a long-term relationship with Dr. Eric Berg through shared personal connections and community involvement.
  • After purchasing the yogurt maker himself, Dr. Berg works closely with Craig and later features the product in a YouTube video.
  • The video generates approximately 3.7 million views and contributes to a complete sellout of Craig's U.S. inventory within days.
  • Craig proactively addresses affiliate tracking issues and compensates Dr. Berg for missed commissions, helping strengthen trust.
  • He provides additional value by supporting Dr. Berg's staff, charitable initiatives, and lead generation efforts.
  • Craig also collaborates with other well-known figures such as Ben Patrick, Gary Brecka, Dr. Mark Hyman, Grant Cardone, and Alex Hormozi.
  • He emphasizes that successful influencer relationships come from creating value first rather than simply asking for promotion.


X Growth, Viral Threads, and Monetization Strategy

  • Craig views X as one of the most powerful platforms for organic reach because it remains highly text-driven and rewards strong ideas.
  • He initially works with a ghostwriter before refining his own content strategy based on performance data.
  • Early growth comes from creating threads about recognizable personalities and established brands.
  • In some cases, he coordinates directly with featured individuals and encourages them to repost the content after publication.
  • The objective is to gain impressions, attract followers, and guide readers toward products, lead magnets, and affiliate offers.
  • He closely monitors click-through rates between the first and second posts in a thread and looks for at least a 5% engagement rate before scaling distribution.
  • To expand reach, he pays large X accounts to repost high-performing content.
  • One fasting-related thread generates approximately 22 million impressions and drives significant affiliate sales.
  • Another thread about colon health exceeds 8 million impressions and becomes widely copied across the platform.
  • Craig frequently republishes successful threads and often generates millions of additional impressions from recycled content.
  • More recent algorithm changes produce fewer impressions but attract more targeted audiences that convert better into customers.
  • A niche thread about the probiotic strain Akkermansia generates approximately $5,000 in affiliate sales despite a smaller audience.
  • Some affiliate programs offer commissions as high as 90% on initial purchases because they rely on subscriptions and repeat orders for profitability.
  • Craig recommends keeping posts concise, using strong visual hooks, and including clear follow and lead magnet calls to action.
  • Through consistent publishing and distribution, he grows his X audience to more than 250,000 followers.


Health Insights, Gut Health, and Educational Resources

  • Craig believes gut health plays a major role in overall wellness, mood, and mental health.
  • He shares how repairing his own gut health significantly reduces anxiety and inflammation.
  • The Super Gut approach focuses on removing harmful bacteria, yeast, and parasites before rebuilding the microbiome with targeted probiotics.
  • He discusses specific probiotic strains such as L. gasseri and Akkermansia, which are associated with benefits related to weight management, metabolism, and overall health.
  • He explains that many beneficial probiotic strains are highly temperature-sensitive, making controlled fermentation important.
  • Customers frequently report improvements in digestion, skin conditions, sleep quality, and food sensitivities after implementing these protocols.
  • Participants discuss topics such as PANS, PANDAS, mold exposure, and immune health.
  • Craig shares his experience discovering severe mold contamination within his home's HVAC system despite regular maintenance.
  • He recommends addressing gut health first before adding detoxification strategies such as sauna use and liver-support protocols.
  • Craig also discusses his book, Ultimate Health: How to Break Free from Your Health Issues and Live Your Best Life.
  • After the book is removed from Amazon, he chooses to distribute it as a free digital resource.
  • He provides additional educational guides covering probiotics, gut repair, sleep improvement, and related health topics through his websites and email newsletter.
  • Lead magnets and educational resources help him build trust with his audience while supporting product and affiliate sales.

In conclusion, this session presents a detailed case study of how Craig Brockie combines Amazon fundamentals, strategic influencer partnerships, and X virality to build a health brand to $10 million in 18 months. 


It also highlights how authentic passion for gut health and a commitment to creating value for experts and audiences can lead to strong relationships, sustained brand growth, and diversified revenue streams.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1780507075354-MDS Expert Call with Returnstack_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Mayank Sharma and Maria Pavlovskaia from Returnstack share practical strategies for managing customer returns reducing fraud and maximizing the value recovered from returned inventory. 


Drawing on their experience building returns systems at Amazon and other large technology companies, they explain how sellers can transform returns from a cost center into a source of margin improvement and operational efficiency.

Returns Are a Major Profitability Lever

  • Returns are no longer just a customer service function—they directly impact customer retention, profitability, and cash flow.
  • According to Mayank, approximately 75–80% of customers are unlikely to return to a brand after a poor returns experience.
  • The true cost of a return extends far beyond the refund itself and often includes:
    • Shipping costs
    • Inspection and grading expenses
    • Restocking costs
    • Fraud losses
    • Portal and processing fees
    • Inventory value erosion
  • These costs can total approximately $35–$40 per returned unit.
  • With average ecommerce return rates ranging from 15–25%, returns can consume 10–15% of Gross Merchandise Sales (GMS) if not managed effectively.

Building a Strong Fraud Prevention Framework

Most Return Fraud Is a Process Problem

  • Return fraud often stems from weak processes rather than isolated bad actors.
  • Common fraud examples include customers returning damaged, incorrect, or worthless items instead of the original product.
  • Mayank explains that the most effective defense combines customer segmentation, operational controls, and evidence collection.

Segment Customers Based on Risk

  • The lowest-performing 2–3% of customers often account for 30–50% of fraud activity.
  • Sellers should segment customers using:
    • Lifetime value (LTV)
    • Purchase history
    • Return frequency
    • Product categories
    • Order values
    • Historical behavior patterns
  • Policies should be applied dynamically rather than uniformly.

Use Progressive Enforcement

  • Rather than immediately penalizing suspicious customers, Mayank recommends starting with educational or warning messages.
  • Simple notifications acknowledging unusual return behavior can significantly reduce fraud without creating customer-service issues.
  • Additional verification requirements and delayed refunds can be introduced for higher-risk segments.

Evidence Matters

  • Effective fraud management requires:
    • Consistent item grading
    • Photos and inspection records
    • Item tracking throughout the return process
    • Documentation accessible to customer service teams
  • A structured evidence trail improves chargeback success rates and supports refund disputes.

Software Is Essential

  • Manual spreadsheets and checklists do not scale.
  • Specialized returns platforms can help sellers prevent 80–90% of fraudulent return activity when combined with proper operational processes.

Designing High-Performance Reverse Logistics

Optimize the Entire Return Journey

Mayank breaks reverse logistics into three stages:

  1. Returns portal
  2. Warehouse grading and processing
  3. Recovery and resale

Many companies optimize only one step, leaving significant value unrealized.

Predict Item Condition Early

  • Customer-submitted information can be used to determine the likely condition of a return before it reaches the warehouse.
  • Useful signals include:
    • Return reason codes
    • Product photos
    • Customer risk scores
    • Purchase history

Examples:

  • A damaged bike helmet with supporting photos may not need to be shipped back.
  • A sealed, unopened product from a trusted customer may qualify for direct restocking.

At Amazon, these types of optimizations reportedly prevented 20–25% of returns from ever reaching a warehouse, reducing transportation and processing costs.

FBA vs. FBM Returns

FBA

  • Amazon controls:
    • Receiving
    • Grading
    • Matching
    • Restocking decisions
  • Sellers benefit from Amazon's infrastructure but have limited visibility and control.

FBM

  • Sellers retain more operational control.
  • Better opportunities exist to:
    • Detect fraud
    • Improve grading accuracy
    • Recover inventory value
    • File product mismatch or safety claims through Seller Central APIs

Mayank notes that FBM is where Returnstack typically delivers the greatest value.

Improving Recovery Through Better Grading

Most Returned Products Are Still Sellable

  • For apparel, approximately 80–85% of returns are still in new condition.
  • For many other categories, 60–70% remain in new condition.

Why Accurate Grading Matters

Poor grading often leads retailers to liquidate inventory unnecessarily.

Typical recovery rates:

  • Liquidation: roughly 5–10% of original value
  • Restocked as new: close to 100% of original selling value

Benefits of accurate grading include:

  • Higher margin recovery
  • Lower inventory requirements
  • Better cash flow
  • Improved in-stock availability

Product-Specific Workflows

Rather than subjective warehouse inspections, Mayank recommends:

  • Category-specific grading rules
  • Guided inspection workflows
  • Automated decision trees

He also highlights the growing role of computer vision and AI in:

  • Damage detection
  • Product matching
  • Counterfeit identification
  • Automated grading

Recovery and Resale Strategies

Prioritize Direct Channels

The speakers recommend selling returned inventory through a brand's own storefront whenever possible because:

  • Existing customers already trust the brand.
  • Margins are typically higher.
  • Condition-based pricing can move inventory efficiently.

Expand Distribution When Necessary

For brands unwilling to list open-box inventory on their primary storefront:

  • Use secondary marketplaces.
  • Utilize multiple resale channels.
  • Consider physical retail liquidation options as a final step.

The goal is to maximize the probability that each returned item finds a buyer.

Using Returns Data to Improve the Entire Business

Mayank emphasizes that returns data should influence more than warehouse operations.

Returns information should feed into:

  • Advertising decisions
  • Merchandising strategy
  • Inventory planning
  • Product development
  • Pricing decisions

Many sellers unknowingly spend heavily promoting products with poor return economics.

By connecting return-rate data to marketing and inventory decisions, businesses can significantly improve profitability.

Mayank and Maria present returns management as a strategic business function rather than a necessary expense. 

Through customer segmentation, fraud prevention, integrated reverse logistics, accurate grading, and intelligent recovery strategies, sellers can dramatically reduce return costs while recovering significant margin. 

The session demonstrates that connecting returns data across the entire customer journey—from the returns portal through final disposition—can improve profitability, inventory efficiency, and customer experience simultaneously.

items.title: Using AI to Create Amazon Imagery, Content, and Video － Kim Cruickshank － APAC Chapter Mogul Call May 2026
items.description:

TOPICS:
