files.name: The Future of Design — AI Workflows
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1783021947789-The Future of Design — AI Workflows.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS APAC Chapter meet for their May monthly call featuring a deep-dive presentation by Kimberly Cruickshanks on using AI for creative assets. 

The group explores how AI tools support product photography, Amazon listings, and video ads, and closes with community updates about upcoming events and future speakers.

 

Kimberly’s Background and Overview of Key AI Tools

  • Kimberly explains that she is a graphic designer and photographer with more than 15 years of experience, having worked with major brands such as Old Navy and Too Faced while also running a boutique agency focused on branding, packaging, and product photography.
  • She shares that she eventually launched her own brand in the gifting category around 2016 after working with hundreds of small businesses.
  • Kimberly demonstrates how far AI has progressed by showing two AI-generated images of herself: one older attempt that only loosely resembles her and a newer portrait realistic enough that even close friends struggle to tell it is AI-generated.
  • She shares her belief that the future of design is shifting from traditional photographers and designers to “AI directors” who orchestrate creative deliverables through AI tools rather than relying entirely on physical studios and equipment.
  • Kimberly states that she uses AI for product development ideation, mockups for sourcing agents, customer cards, packaging, studio photography, Amazon listing images, and video ads.
  • She introduces Magnific as her primary AI image and video generation tool and notes that she also uses ChatGPT and Claude to help build prompts and camera-angle ideas.
  • Kimberly explains that Magnific supports multiple generation models, including more creative models and more literal models, and she values the flexibility to switch between them when results are inconsistent.

 

AI Studio Photography Workflow with Magnific

  • Kimberly explains that Magnific allows users to select different generation models depending on whether the goal is photorealism, illustration, or graphic design work.
  • She demonstrates how users can upload reference images such as product photos, packaging art, style references, or personal portraits and then prompt the AI to maintain consistency while modifying specific elements.
  • Kimberly shows that Magnific supports style references and character training, allowing her to generate consistent portraits and maintain visual brand standards across outputs.
  • She notes that the platform offers control over aspect ratios and output resolution, with higher resolutions requiring more generation time.
  • Using simple iPhone photos of bamboo trays as an example, Kimberly demonstrates how prompts can generate professional-looking studio product photos on seamless white backgrounds with realistic shadows and textures in approximately 10 minutes.
  • She also demonstrates AI-generated fashion and lifestyle photography, including tote bag images with realistic fabric texture, stitching, and lifestyle scenes featuring models using the product naturally.
  • For a probiotic bottle example, Kimberly shows that AI can now maintain high label fidelity, including small typography and detailed watercolor artwork that older AI tools struggled to reproduce accurately.
  • She explains that more complex products often require several hours of iteration to build a polished and consistent image library.
  • To improve consistency in scale, angle, and color, Kimberly creates product turnaround sheets showing multiple product angles in one layout, then crops and re-uploads those images as references for higher-resolution outputs.
  • Kimberly emphasizes that users should treat AI as a capable employee that requires clear direction, iteration, and feedback rather than expecting perfect results from the first prompt.

 

Amazon Listing Creation with Pixi and Other Amazon-Focused Tools

  • Kimberly introduces Pixi, sometimes referred to as Pixie, as an AI tool specifically designed for Amazon listing images, while also mentioning alternatives such as Loveart Scalable and Listing Optimization AI.
  • She explains that Pixi generates listing images primarily from product data rather than relying entirely on detailed prompts, allowing the system to automatically create headlines, layouts, badges, and lifestyle imagery.
  • Kimberly notes that Pixi appears to be trained specifically on Amazon image conventions and naturally produces outputs aligned with Amazon’s formatting and visual standards.
  • She explains that users can create detailed brand profiles within Pixi, including brand colors, fonts, target audience details, and product information such as ingredients, benefits, and customer reviews.
  • Kimberly demonstrates how Pixi generates multiple variations of main images and secondary listing images using uploaded product photos and Amazon-style design logic.
  • She shares that Pixi supports reusable “playbooks” that allow users to reference and adapt competitor image layouts while still keeping the outputs aligned to their own brand.
  • Kimberly stresses the importance of defining fonts and brand styling early in the workflow to avoid inconsistent typography across generated images.
  • She explains that success with AI image generation comes from generating large volumes of creative options quickly and then curating the strongest outputs for testing.
  • Kimberly clarifies that the examples shown during the presentation, including text and layouts, were created entirely with AI tools and did not require manual editing in traditional design software.

 

Video Ads, Prompt Strategy, Team Skills, and Community Announcements

 

Video Ad Workflow Using AI

  • Kimberly explains her 22-second video ad structure, which consists of eight scenes lasting approximately 2.5 seconds each to maintain viewer engagement.
  • She builds storyboards around emotional hooks, product differentiation, sensory appeal, product functionality, and final product close-ups.
  • Kimberly typically generates the widest and most complete lifestyle scene first and then reuses the same characters, outfits, and settings throughout the remaining shots to maintain continuity.
  • She creates 16:9 still images in Magnific and then converts them into short animated clips using the platform’s built-in video tools.
  • Kimberly notes that AI-generated clips sometimes contain glitches, so she trims and edits them to retain only the strongest moments.
  • She estimates that producing a polished 20-to-22-second AI-generated ad usually takes around five hours, much of which is spent waiting for rendering and generation processes.

 

Prompting, Tool Comparisons, and Skill Requirements

  • Kimberly explains that she embeds text directly into AI-generated images by including typographic instructions within prompts rather than manually adding overlays afterward.
  • She recommends beginning with simple prompts, identifying what the AI misunderstands, and then progressively refining instructions to fix issues related to lighting, scale, packaging fidelity, or perspective.
  • Kimberly advises using reference photos with hands or human subjects to help AI better understand realistic product scale and proportions.
  • She emphasizes that AI amplifies existing creative skill rather than replacing it, meaning experienced designers still outperform less experienced users because they provide stronger direction and curation.
  • Kimberly describes her hiring process for designers, explaining that she focuses on workflow and final quality rather than loyalty to any specific tool.
  • Cam shares his experience using Listing Optimization AI and notes how quickly AI listing tools evolve, often adding major features within weeks.
  • He highlights that Listing Optimization AI allows users to inspect underlying prompts and camera settings, helping teams learn how effective prompts are structured.
  • Cam explains that his team prioritizes speed and scalability by getting large numbers of listings to a strong but not necessarily perfect quality level quickly.
  • He also mentions that some AI tools now generate customer avatars and market analysis insights that his team finds surprisingly accurate and useful.
  • Cam discusses experimenting with Amazon Brand Studio inside the Amazon Ads console, where entering an ASIN can automatically generate storyboard-driven video ads that can then be refined manually.

 

In conclusion, this session explores how AI dramatically accelerates the creation of product photos, Amazon listing images, and short-form video ads while still requiring strong human judgment, taste, and direction. 

 

Kimberly’s workflows demonstrate that sellers can now generate near studio-quality visuals from simple reference photos in a fraction of the traditional production time.

 

The discussion also highlights how quickly AI creative tools are evolving, especially for Amazon-focused workflows such as listing optimization, market analysis, and video ad generation. 

 

Participants leave with practical examples, recommended tools to test, and encouragement to continue experimenting while building stronger relationships within the MDS community through upcoming events in Singapore and Bali.

TOPICS:

  2. The “10x AI SOP method” to capture and scale founder judgment
  3. Product development and brand strategy in a multi‑channel e‑commerce environment
items.description_text: In this session, members of the MDS community learn from e‑commerce founder Josh Hadley how he uses AI to clone his decision-making and embed it into business processes. TOPICS: Using AI to manage advertising campaigns and hiring workflows The “10x AI SOP method” to capture and scale founder judgment Product development and brand strategy in a multi‑channel e‑commerce environment

files.name: Transcript - MDS Mogul Call with Josh Hadley
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779955272357-MDS Mogul Call with Josh Hadley_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session the MDS Mogul Call with guest Josh Hadley focuses on how to use AI to clone founder-level judgment and embed it into business systems. 

In addition the group discusses practical use cases for AI in advertising, hiring, onboarding, and product development, along with broader implications for brand strategy and team structure.

Josh Hadley’s AI Use Cases in Advertising, Hiring, and Email

  • Josh introduces himself as a man of faith, husband, father of four, and an e-commerce seller for more than a decade, generating over $20M annually across Shopify, TikTok Shop, and Amazon. He also hosts the Ecom Breakthrough Podcast.
  • Josh explains that his business has around 35 team members, including approximately 10 people focused specifically on Amazon sales, PPC campaign management, listing management, and seller support.
  • Josh describes how his team uses AI and the TikTok advertising API to adjust campaigns daily, using 7-day and 30-day performance data to modify budgets and settings according to ROI goals.
  • He clarifies that TikTok currently serves as a testing environment where they generate several million dollars per year, making experimentation manageable and easier to correct when mistakes occur.
  • Josh states that the current TikTok campaign agent always has human oversight because APIs change, rules evolve, and automations require constant monitoring and updates.
  • Josh outlines a 12-month goal to train the AI system to operate at roughly 90% autonomy for campaign management while humans continue overseeing strategic decisions.
  • He plans to replicate the TikTok automation framework on Amazon, including automated optimization of titles, listings, descriptions, and main images based on conversion and click-through rate performance.
  • In hiring, Josh explains that he previously manually invited around 1,000 candidates on Upwork, collected IQ tests, case studies, and Loom videos, and personally reviewed many applications.
  • He states that the hiring workflow is now heavily automated with AI. Bots invite candidates, AI evaluates case studies and Loom videos against predefined scoring criteria, and the system narrows candidates down to the top group for final review.
  • Josh explains that AI also evaluates communication clarity and presentation skills on video while identifying whether candidates are genuinely speaking or reading scripted AI-generated answers.
  • Josh notes that his chief of staff manages his inbox using Anthropic’s Claude, routing messages, drafting responses, and assigning tasks to team members while continuously retraining the system for different contexts.

The “10x AI SOP Method”: Cloning Founder Judgment

  • Josh argues that the real power of AI is not just automating tasks but cloning the founder’s judgment, decision-making, and communication style into scalable systems.
  • He explains that many AI and delegation failures happen because the founder’s internal context and decision logic are never properly documented.
  • Josh states that traditional SOPs often fail because they are written from memory, focus only on linear actions, and ignore edge cases, trade-offs, and escalation logic.
  • He describes the ineffective approach as simply asking ChatGPT to generate an SOP, which usually results in generic but polished documentation that lacks real-world judgment.
  • Josh presents his “10x AI SOP Method,” where AI first acts as a judgment extractor rather than only an SOP writer.
  • Step one is recording Loom videos while performing the task and narrating every thought process and decision aloud.
  • Step two is feeding the Loom transcript into AI so the model can analyze how the founder thinks and identify key decision signals and exceptions.
  • Step three involves having AI interrogate the founder by identifying missing logic and asking extensive follow-up questions, sometimes more than 200 questions, to reach roughly 95% clarity.
  • Step four is building SOPs and decision trees only after multiple iterations using the Loom transcripts, AI analysis, and Q&A responses.
  • Josh notes that he records multiple Looms for recurring processes over several months because different scenarios expose different exceptions and judgment calls.
  • He explains that AI can extract nuanced “founder judgment rules,” such as when margin profile matters more than search volume or when low-cost competitors are concerning but not automatically disqualifying.
  • Josh emphasizes that the resulting SOP memory contains confirmed rules, assumptions, unresolved questions, and decision logic that continuously improves over time.
  • Once SOPs are stabilized, Josh reuses Looms as training assets and asks AI to determine which Looms new hires should watch, in what order, and which sections are most valuable.

Training AI Agents and Human Team Members

  • Josh explains that the principles for training AI agents and onboarding employees are essentially the same and should follow structured stages with continuous feedback.
  • He outlines three phases for both AI systems and human hires:
    • Phase 1: Observance period, where the person or agent watches, learns, documents, and studies while the expert performs the work.
    • Phase 2: Independence period, where work is completed independently but remains in draft mode for review before going live.
    • Phase 3: Ownership period, where outputs go live first and are reviewed afterward through spot-checking and verification.
  • During the observance phase for employees, Josh holds daily 15-minute huddles and applies similar close oversight when training AI agents.
  • In the independence phase, no changes go live without approval, whether the work comes from an employee or AI system.
  • In the ownership phase, Josh expects employees to operate independently by days 61–90, with managers reviewing outcomes rather than every individual action.
  • Josh says this process dramatically shortens ramp-up time compared to traditional corporate onboarding where employees may need a year to fully understand their role.
  • For AI agents, his team reviews outputs daily at first and then transitions to weekly reviews as performance stabilizes.
  • When AI makes poor decisions, the team feeds back examples and explanations so the system can update its reasoning, mirroring human coaching practices.
  • Josh repeatedly emphasizes that reliable delegation depends on clearly documented judgment and decision trees.
  • He believes this framework allows new hires to become highly productive within 90 days while enabling AI agents to achieve strong autonomy without drifting away from company strategy.

Product Development, Brand Strategy, Tools, Security, and Q&A

  • Josh shares that product research and development has historically been the area he guarded most closely because it requires both creative and financial judgment.
  • He explains that his former R&D process relied heavily on tools such as Helium 10 and approaches similar to Data Dive, but his current focus is on using AI to codify his judgment through Loom recordings and transcripts.
  • Josh states that older Amazon product research formulas based mainly on search volume, review count, and price point are no longer central to his strategy.
  • Instead, he evaluates whether products can succeed across Amazon, Shopify, TikTok Shop, and eventually retail distribution, viewing Amazon as one channel within a broader brand ecosystem.
  • Josh argues that the key strategic question for the next decade is whether brands want to become true multi-channel businesses or remain dependent on Amazon alone as fees and competition continue increasing.
  • In discussion with Jamie, Josh agrees that easy Amazon opportunities are increasingly rare and that success now depends on which operational challenges a brand is willing to handle better than competitors.
  • Jamie notes that opportunities are becoming highly specific to each company’s strengths, such as product design, audience understanding, or operational capabilities, and Josh agrees with that perspective.
  • Josh describes the “10-80-10” principle inspired by Steve Jobs, where the founder provides the initial 10% vision, the team or AI executes 80% of the work, and the founder returns for the final 10% of refinement and polish.
  • During Q&A, participant Dimitri asks which AI tools Josh prefers, and Josh explains that his organization primarily standardizes around Claude and Claude Code while still experimenting with other frameworks such as Hermes and Axio.
  • Josh explains that his company deliberately standardizes around Claude for consistency across the organization, even while advanced team members continue testing alternative tools.
  • When asked about TikTok API access, Josh explains that he requested access directly through the TikTok Ads console and submitted a business use case that Claude helped draft.
  • Penina raises concerns about security and employees leaving with AI systems or knowledge, and Josh responds that while some risk always exists, he prioritizes cultural fit, trust, and centralized ownership under company-controlled Claude accounts and admin systems.
  • Josh explains that while employees may leave with some knowledge, his real competitive advantage comes from combining strong people with deeply integrated AI systems.
  • He notes that competitors sometimes question why he shares so much publicly through his podcast and MDS calls, and he responds that anything he shares publicly is already at least 12 months behind what his team is currently implementing internally.
  • Josh reiterates that founder judgment is one of the most valuable business assets and that AI now provides a practical way to capture, scale, and replicate that judgment across teams and systems.
  • Jamie closes the session by mentioning plans to invite Craig Brockie for a future Mogul Call, promoting an upcoming Omnisend email masterclass, and encouraging attendees to submit feedback through the virtual event form.

In this session, participants explore how AI can move beyond simple task automation to become a structured system for capturing and scaling founder-level judgment across advertising, hiring, onboarding, and product development. 

The discussion highlights that sustainable competitive advantage in modern e-commerce increasingly depends on combining strong human talent with thoughtfully trained AI agents, clear SOPs, and deeply embedded decision-making systems.

items.title: Corporate Structure Done Right－Mergers & Acquisitions Channel Call May 2026
items.description:
In this session, the MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel explains how to set up a company’s corporate, tax, and equity structure to support a future exit.
TOPICS:
  1. Corporate structure choices (LLC vs. C corporation) and their tax implications, including QSBS.
  2. Valuation and basis considerations for S Corp–to–C Corp conversions and future exits.
  3. Designing equity and incentive structures for key employees and investors (bonuses, phantom equity, reverse vesting).
items.description_text: In this session, the MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel explains how to set up a company’s corporate, tax, and equity structure to support a future exit. TOPICS: Corporate structure choices (LLC vs. C corporation) and their tax implications, including QSBS. Valuation and basis considerations for S Corp–to–C Corp conversions and future exits. Designing equity and incentive structures for key employees and investors (bonuses, phantom equity, reverse vesting).

files.name: Transcript - MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel Call.pdf
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779951776659-MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel Call_otter_ai_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session the MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel focuses on how to design corporate structures that are simple for today yet optimized for a future exit. 

Scott Deetz with input from Bill Sterry and participants such as Cassidy, walk through tax structures, valuation, and equity design so owners can avoid costly mistakes later.

Foundations of Corporate Structure and Exit Planning

  • The session frames corporate structure as a strategic tool that directly affects a future exit, especially for founders aiming for eight-figure outcomes.
  • Scott explains that in almost every eight-figure exit they handle, the owner does not receive 100% of the proceeds because key employees, partners, management teams, or equity investors typically share in the value created.
  • The discussion emphasizes that bringing in people who can grow the business, such as someone who can increase growth by 20% in exchange for 5% equity or upside participation, generally results in the founder earning more total value.
  • Scott outlines that a founder typically starts by owning 100% of the shares and must then decide what legal and tax structure to use as the company grows.
  • The session focuses mainly on U.S. corporate structures, especially LLCs and C corporations, and clarifies that legal structure (for example, LLC or C corporation) and tax status (for example, partnership, S corporation, or C corporation taxation) are separate decisions.
  • Scott and Bill clearly state that they are not CPAs or attorneys and that the purpose of the session is to help business owners ask better questions when working with legal and accounting advisors.
  • The discussion stresses that exit planning needs to happen early because certain tax-advantaged structures require multi-year holding periods that cannot be created retroactively shortly before a sale.

Tax Structures: LLC vs. C Corporation and QSBS (Section 1202)

  • The session compares an LLC taxed as a partnership or S corporation with a C corporation using a sample company that grows profits from $0 to $2 million annually and then sells for $10 million after five years.
  • Scott explains that with an LLC taxed as a partnership or S corporation, there is no tax at the company level. Instead, profits pass through to the owner and are taxed at individual rates, using 37% as a sample top federal rate.
  • The discussion explains that a C corporation is subject to double taxation, including 21% federal tax on company profits and approximately 20% tax on dividends distributed to owners, which can create a combined tax burden above 40% on distributed profits.
  • Scott introduces Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) under Section 1202, explaining that it can allow a tax-free exit on up to roughly $10 million per shareholder if qualifying C corporation stock is held for at least five years.
  • The session highlights that the QSBS benefit applies per shareholder, meaning multiple qualifying shareholders may each receive their own exclusion.
  • The discussion clarifies that QSBS generally requires a stock sale rather than an asset sale, although some more advanced structures may partially replicate the benefit in certain asset-based transactions.
  • Scott emphasizes that if an LLC converts to a C corporation to pursue QSBS treatment, the five-year holding period begins at the date of conversion.
  • The model demonstrates that C corporations can produce significantly higher after-tax proceeds in scenarios where the business exits at a high valuation and the QSBS exclusion applies.
  • The talk notes that QSBS rules are subject to legislative risk because tax laws may change in the future.
  • The discussion also explains that C corporations are more tax-efficient when profits are reinvested into growth initiatives, inventory, or operations because only the corporate tax applies until money is distributed.
  • The session notes that LLC owners may owe taxes on allocated profits even if no distributions are taken, which can create cash-flow strain during aggressive reinvestment periods.

Valuation, Basis, and S Corporation to C Corporation Conversion

  • Cassidy raises a practical question about converting from an S corporation to a C corporation and explains that a valuation is required at the conversion date to establish tax basis for QSBS and future calculations.
  • Cassidy shares that his company is still relatively new with low cash flow and that he prefers a lower valuation at conversion to maximize future QSBS upside if the company later sells for more than $10 million.
  • The discussion notes that some valuation firms are unfamiliar with this type of engagement and may attempt to assign high values based on future growth projections or intangible brand value.
  • Scott recommends focusing primarily on hard assets such as inventory, cash, trademarks, and conservative earnings multiples, especially for newer businesses with limited operating history.
  • The session advises using realistic market-based valuation approaches tied to actual earnings and comparable transactions rather than optimistic projections.
  • Cassidy confirms that his business currently operates entirely through Shopify and not Amazon, and Scott notes that early-stage DTC brands may reasonably argue for limited intrinsic brand value if customer acquisition still relies heavily on paid advertising and search-driven purchasing behavior.
  • The guidance recommends using conservative growth assumptions to avoid inflating valuations unnecessarily.
  • Scott notes that marketplaces such as Empire Flippers provide visibility into real transaction multiples for smaller online businesses and can help support realistic valuation assumptions.
  • The discussion acknowledges that founders technically can create their own valuation, but using a professional valuation firm is safer from a documentation and audit-defense perspective.
  • The session explains that the tax basis for LLC owners increases when profits are taxed but not distributed and decreases when distributions are taken.
  • Scotts clarify that these basis rules exist to prevent double taxation because owners should not pay capital gains taxes again on profits already taxed as pass-through income in prior years.

Rewarding Key Employees: Bonuses, Phantom Equity, and Reverse Vesting

  • The session transitions into how founders can reward key employees, such as COOs, strategists, or brand leaders, in ways that align with a future exit.
  • The simplest structure discussed is a change-of-control bonus, where a key employee receives a defined payout only if the company is sold.
  • This bonus can be structured as either a flat dollar amount or as a percentage of the exit proceeds.
  • To avoid giving away upside on value already created before the employee joined, the session recommends tying compensation to a share of the increase in company value above a defined baseline valuation.
  • Scott and Bill use the concepts of accretion and dilution to explain that giving up ownership percentage can still increase the founder’s absolute dollar outcome if the company grows significantly.
  • The discussion warns against early 50/50 partnerships where one party contributes far less than half the value, since these arrangements often create future conflict and renegotiation challenges.
  • Scott explains that phantom equity, stock options, and contractual bonuses usually provide economic participation without actual ownership, meaning payouts are typically taxed as ordinary income.
  • Because of this tax treatment, the session recommends considering actual equity grants with reverse vesting structures for key employees expected to create meaningful long-term value.
  • In a reverse vesting arrangement, the employee receives the full equity grant upfront, but the shares remain subject to forfeiture if the employee leaves before completing the vesting period.
  • The structure uses restricted shares with a defined vesting and forfeiture schedule, often releasing portions of the shares quarterly or annually over time.
  • The session explains that if the company qualifies for QSBS treatment and the employee holds qualifying shares for at least five years, the employee may also benefit from QSBS tax treatment on exit.
  • Scott clarifies that exits within the first year generally receive no special tax advantage because short-term gains are taxed similarly to ordinary income, while longer holding periods may qualify for lower long-term capital gains rates or QSBS treatment.

Investment from Key Personnel, Accretion Logic, and Strategic Takeaways

  • The session strongly encourages founders to ask key hires or potential partners to invest capital into the company when receiving equity, both as a commitment signal and as a way to reduce dilution pressure.
  • Scott notes that if someone claims to have extensive experience and successful exits but refuses to invest even a modest amount, that may reveal a lack of commitment or financial alignment.
  • The session walks through an example where a new executive both invests cash into the company and receives additional equity through a reverse vesting structure over several years.
  • The capitalization example demonstrates that raising money at a higher valuation can increase the founder’s total equity value even if their ownership percentage decreases.
  • The discussion emphasizes that founders should focus less on percentage ownership and more on the value of their shares based on company valuation and price per share.
  • The session highlights the importance of properly documented operating agreements, share classes, vesting terms, and forfeiture provisions to prevent disputes later in the business lifecycle.
  • Scott and Bill recommend that founders with informal agreements, undocumented promises, or unclear equity arrangements begin formalizing and renegotiating those structures before entering an exit process.
  • The recap stresses that early structural and legal decisions may feel unimportant initially but become extremely expensive if neglected when preparing for a sale.
  • Scott notes that future M&A channel sessions will continue building on these concepts and will focus more heavily on strategies for increasing company value.

In conclusion, this session provides a practical overview of how founders can align corporate structure, tax planning, valuation, and equity incentives with long-term exit goals. 

By comparing LLC and C corporation structures, explaining QSBS, and outlining real-world approaches to valuation and reverse vesting, Scotts equip attendees with frameworks they can take directly to their legal and accounting advisors.

The discussion consistently emphasizes that thoughtful planning done early can significantly improve after-tax outcomes, reduce future conflict, and create stronger alignment between founders, employees, and investors. 

The overall message is that building a company for exit requires not only operational growth, but also disciplined attention to structure, incentives, and long-term strategic planning.

files.name: Transcript - DTC_ Shopify Channel Call May 2026
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779391756814-DTC_ Shopify Channel Call May 2026_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Curtis Howland discusses how to scale Meta ads on Meta Platforms using a “creator group” model instead of relying solely on AI-generated ads or traditional UGC agencies. 

The conversation focuses on why creator groups act as a sustainable performance moat how to structure them how to pay and motivate creators, and how to integrate this model into a Meta media buying strategy.

Meta Ads Landscape, AI Ads, and Current UGC Agency Limitations

  • Curtis explains that they have spent around $150 million on paid ads, including more than $100 million on Meta platforms, and currently run ads for brands generating between $10 million and $500 million in annual revenue.
  • He states that AI-generated ads can scale quickly but usually fatigue rapidly because competitors can easily replicate them, causing Meta to serve similar ads to overlapping audiences.
  • He notes that AI has “raised the floor” of ad quality, allowing nearly anyone to create decent UGC-style or static ads, which increases competition and reduces the durability of individual creative concepts.
  • He explains that AI performs well at understanding brand guidelines, tone of voice, product details, and structured information, but it cannot genuinely experience a product or create nuanced, real-life use cases from lived experience.
  • He argues that because AI ads are not a durable moat, brands need a deeper system focused on creator relationships, authentic product experience, and unique brand context to sustain performance over time.
  • He explains that many UGC agencies have structural limitations because they recycle the same creators across competing brands, rely on overly scripted briefs, and often separate content creation from editing and performance analysis.
  • He acknowledges that some premium UGC agencies use stronger data analysis, open-ended creative briefs, and exclusivity arrangements, but these models are expensive and still may not create a compounding creative ecosystem for a single brand.

Creator Group Model and Strategic Benefits

  • Curtis introduces the “creator group” model as one of the most successful scaling strategies they have tested for Meta ads.
  • He states that one brand already allocates roughly 50% of its ad spend to creator-group ads while achieving strong performance at about 10% of the total creative cost.
  • He defines a creator group as a curated community of creators who both use the product and produce strong video content, organized through communication channels such as Slack, WhatsApp, or Telegram.
  • He explains that creator groups function as ongoing communities where creators receive coaching on winning messages, scalable concepts, and high-converting selling points instead of following rigid one-off scripts.
  • He states that creator-group performance compounds over time because creators become increasingly familiar with the brand, live with the product, and iterate on concepts based on shared learnings from the group.
  • He notes that major performance improvements often appear after three to four months as creators gain deeper familiarity with the product and audience.
  • He highlights that creator groups effectively operate as distributed creative strategy teams, continuously bringing in fresh ideas from daily life, trends, and platforms like TikTok.
  • He explains that creator groups create a competitive moat because the best-performing concepts are rooted in authentic product experience and nuanced brand understanding that competitors cannot easily replicate.
  • He adds that creator groups provide operational leverage during product launches because trusted creators already familiar with the brand can quickly produce launch content.

Incentives, Payment Models, and Partnership Ads

  • Curtis explains that Meta increasingly favors partnership ads, where ads run from creator handles instead of brand accounts, and notes that Meta representatives position this as a major strategic priority for 2026.
  • He states that partnership ads frequently outperform standard brand ads, with approximately 70–75% of tests producing stronger results.
  • He clarifies that creators typically do not receive built-in commission structures on Meta similar to TikTok Shop, so compensation is usually handled through direct agreements.
  • He describes a flat-fee payment structure where creators are paid fixed amounts per video, often around $200–$300 per asset in many U.S.-based campaigns.
  • He outlines a percentage-of-spend model, typically around 3%–5% of ad spend tied to a creator’s ads, which better aligns incentives between creators and brands.
  • He notes that at higher spend levels, percentage-based payouts can generate meaningful monthly income for creators while still remaining significantly cheaper than traditional agency models.
  • He explains that many creators coming from TikTok Shop are already familiar with GMV-based compensation and commission structures.
  • He emphasizes that top-performing creators deserve significantly higher compensation because a single winning ad can support large amounts of profitable ad spend.
  • He stresses the importance of rewarding top creators properly to maintain loyalty and prevent them from becoming exclusive to competing brands.

Sourcing, Evaluating, and Managing Creators

  • Curtis explains that creators can be sourced through UGC marketplaces, affiliate programs, and existing creator relationships.
  • He cites TikTok Shop as a strong source of performance-focused creators because creators who convert well there often perform effectively in Meta ads.
  • He mentions Billo as a platform where creator content typically costs around $140–$180 per ad.
  • He mentions Backstage as a source for finding actors and performance-oriented creators.
  • He mentions Insense as another marketplace for sourcing UGC creators.
  • He recommends re-engaging creators whose past content has already performed well for the brand, since those creators already understand the product and audience.
  • He advises using a pre-filtering process where new creators first produce one or two test ads before being invited into the long-term creator group.
  • He provides rough benchmarks for creator-group size by spend level, suggesting approximately 5–7 creators at $50k/month in Meta spend, 10–15 creators at around $200k/month, and 20+ creators at $500k+/month.
  • He explains that dedicated communication channels are maintained for each brand, where winning ads, creative concepts, and weekly feedback are shared publicly to encourage learning and collaboration.
  • He emphasizes that creator contracts should include perpetual ad usage rights and partnership-ad permissions so brands can continue running content indefinitely.

Workflow, Tools, and Meta Account / Media Buying Structure

  • Curtis explains that they use an internal tool called “Ad Review” to manage creator submissions, apply AI-driven checks, route content for approval, and track creator payments.
  • He states that Ad Review automatically adds captions and music, provides AI-generated feedback on common issues, and passes approved content directly to media buyers.
  • He notes that similar systems can be built using APIs from Slack, cloud automation tools, Dropbox integrations, and the Meta API, even without a large engineering team.
  • He stresses that one internal team member should own creator-group operations, including posting briefs, sharing performance insights, and maintaining engagement inside the group.
  • He advises that brands spending under roughly $50k/month on Meta may have more foundational priorities to solve before implementing a full creator-group system.
  • He notes that this strategy works best for brands already heavily invested in UGC and video-based creative.

Media buying and campaign structure

  • Curtis explains that the Meta account structure should match the complexity of the product and buying journey.
  • Simpler products can rely more heavily on automated campaign structures such as CBO (Campaign Budget Optimization) and ASC (Advantage+ Shopping Campaigns).
  • More complex products often require greater manual control through ABO (Ad Set Budget Optimization) and segmented testing structures.
  • He shares that their typical account structure is approximately 70% ABO and 30% ASC across many accounts.
  • He describes a testing process where new creatives are grouped into ad sets of roughly 6–10 ads and launched on specific testing days, such as Mondays and Thursdays.
  • He explains that Meta typically allocates most spend to two or three winning ads within each test set, which are then scaled into broader campaigns.
  • He cautions that testing spend is usually less efficient than scaling spend, so brands must balance creative experimentation with account profitability.
  • He recommends regularly auditing ad accounts to identify whether strong-performing ads were cut too early, whether poor performers are receiving too much spend, and whether a small number of ads are carrying a disproportionate share of total revenue.

This session presents a detailed framework for scaling Meta ads through a structured creator-group model centered on long-term creator relationships, coaching, and compounding creative performance rather than relying solely on AI-generated content or transactional UGC production.

The discussion explains why AI ads alone are not a sustainable moat, how to structure creator incentives and contracts, and how to integrate creator content into disciplined Meta testing and scaling systems. 

The key takeaway is that creator groups require operational commitment, ongoing management, and clear workflows, but they can significantly reduce creative costs, improve ad durability, and create a stronger competitive advantage in increasingly crowded advertising environments.

files.name: Transcript - MDS Mogul Call with Eugene Khayman
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779388208815-MDS Mogul Call with Eugene Khayman_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Eugene Khayman and members of the MDS community discuss the new Save Our Sellers (SOS) initiative in response to Amazon’s recent policy and fee changes. 

The group also explores how to use PR data and member stories to influence Amazon and educate the broader public while maintaining a professional, non-confrontational stance.

Meeting Context, MDS Community Updates, and Housekeeping

  • The call serves as a regular MDS Mogul community session hosted by Eugene in place of Jamie, who usually runs the calls.
  • Eugene introduces Megan from the PR team at Avaans Media and Belinda from the community team, explaining that Megan joins to observe the community and collect story angles and quotes.
  • Members briefly discuss recent in-person meetups, including a New York meetup with around 40 signups, and note that noisy public venues can make networking difficult.
  • Eugene and Tomi highlight ongoing MDS engagement initiatives, including a contest where members who post the most value-added content over a month and a half receive a free ticket to the Singapore Summit.
  • Tomi reminds members about the Advisory Council elections and encourages members to apply or nominate others so the council can represent member perspectives and help shape the direction of MDS.
  • The team promotes WhatsApp reminder groups and QR-code-based access to Mogul call reminder channels so members can stay informed about future calls.
  • Eugene and Tomi present AppLovin as a recommended advertising partner for brands doing more than $10M in revenue, noting that AppLovin offers MDS members a $5,000 ad credit when they spend $5,000.

Save Our Sellers (SOS) Campaign Overview and PR Strategy

  • Eugene explains that the Save Our Sellers (SOS) campaign is a three-month initiative leading up to the August 1 Amazon ads fee and credit-card removal deadline, aiming to spotlight how Amazon’s changes impact third-party sellers.
  • The campaign’s core narrative positions Amazon as the marketplace that “changes sellers’ lives” while showing how recent fee and policy shifts now threaten those same businesses.
  • Eugene outlines a planned 12-week content strategy on X and other channels, with each weekly post addressing topics such as Amazon’s early benefits, post-pandemic changes, fee expansion, Prime Day economics, and the impact on seller profitability.
  • The group clarifies that SOS is not designed to attack Amazon directly. Instead, it frames sellers as partners who want to help Amazon remain the best marketplace for building brands.
  • Megan Hanson from Avaans Media introduces herself as VP of Media Relations and explains how the agency will shape the story and pitch it to major media outlets.
  • Megan notes that there is now a dedicated Amazon media beat at outlets such as The Wall Street Journal, Reuters, CNN, and Business Insider, creating opportunities to position seller stories in front of influential journalists and Amazon leadership.
  • She explains that many reporters covering Amazon are based in Seattle or closely follow the company, increasing the likelihood that Amazon executives will see stories connected to the SOS initiative.
  • Members and Megan discuss focusing on both national media and Seattle-based publications such as Puget Sound Business Journal and The Seattle Times.
  • Megan reassures members that nothing shared will be used publicly without consent and that anecdotes, screenshots, and data will be reviewed with participating members before publication.
  • The group agrees that data-backed storytelling strengthens media outreach, so they prioritize surveys, screenshots, Profit Analytics reports, and pricing-health examples to support the campaign narrative.

Amazon Fee Structure, Policy Changes, and Financial Pressure on Sellers

  • Members describe how Amazon’s combined commissions, FBA fees, advertising costs, and surcharges can now consume 50–60% of revenue, which some participants refer to as an “Amazon tax.”
  • Abe explains that Amazon is removing credit-card payment options for ads and moving some accounts to 30-day billing terms, eliminating rewards and cashback programs many sellers rely on.
  • The group notes that extended billing terms may not immediately create cash-flow issues for every seller, but they still reduce seller flexibility and benefits.
  • Eugene and others argue that Amazon frequently introduces changes that initially appear neutral or beneficial before later shifting terms further in Amazon’s favor.
  • Members discuss BD+7 delayed disbursements and question whether Amazon’s revenue timing practices could raise concerns similar to themes discussed in How the Mighty Fall.
  • Eugene emphasizes that once fees or operational changes are introduced, they are rarely reevaluated or rolled back, even when marketplace conditions evolve.
  • The group highlights how Prime Day has become less profitable for many brands as Amazon increases deal-related costs and fee caps.
  • Several members believe that since Jeff Bezos stepped back and Andy Jassy took over, Amazon’s focus has shifted more heavily toward margin optimization and monetization.
  • Members argue that Amazon increasingly funds broader corporate initiatives through cash generated from third-party sellers.
  • Daniel suggests that messaging aimed at consumers should emphasize how rising seller costs eventually lead to higher prices and reduced product choice.
  • For policymakers and regulators, he recommends focusing on antitrust concerns, fee structures, and broader marketplace fairness issues.

Operational Pain Points, AI Enforcement, and Seller Support Gaps

  • Members describe a growing operational burden caused by Amazon’s systems and AI enforcement tools, which create additional work, lost sales, and stress for sellers.
  • June Lai notes that Amazon increasingly relies on AI-driven catalog scans and automated policy enforcement with limited human review.
  • She explains that sellers often receive only three human escalations every six months, which can be difficult for large catalogs dealing with constant automated flags and misclassifications.
  • June argues that Amazon’s low-human-oversight enforcement approach conflicts with emerging AI governance principles, particularly in Europe and the UK, where human review is emphasized for automated decisions.
  • She also raises concerns about AI-driven price scraping and cross-site price comparisons potentially contributing to antitrust concerns if Amazon uses those systems to enforce lowest-price expectations.
  • Jon Jewett describes severe issues with pricing-health and competitive-pricing flags, where listings become search suppressed due to outdated or inaccurate comparison products.
  • Jon reports that resolving a single pricing issue can require multiple support interactions lasting 45–60 minutes each, resulting in significant time loss and over $100,000 in lost sales in one quarter.
  • He explains that updated Seller Central interfaces now hide important pricing diagnostics, forcing sellers to switch back to older catalog views to access necessary information.
  • Peter Weisberg describes problems with vertical sector discounts for healthcare and education pricing, where Amazon applies incorrect legacy pricing without providing reliable reporting tools.
  • Peter says an internal Amazon SME acknowledged limitations in monitoring these prices accurately before redirecting him back to standard seller-support channels.
  • Eugene and others classify these operational issues as hidden costs rather than direct fees because they consume time, labor, and revenue.
  • Members argue that sellers would tolerate fees more easily if those fees funded meaningful improvements to seller support and marketplace systems.

Strategic Responses, Narrative Angles, and Next Steps

  • Fernando Becattini stresses that the MDS group’s official stance remains non-confrontational and focused on helping Amazon improve rather than attacking the company.
  • He notes that Amazon’s marketplace remains a major strategic asset and that SOS messaging should focus on how current policies may weaken long-term marketplace health.
  • Fernando introduces the Profit Analytics report in Seller Central as a useful tool for understanding total fee impact, including sponsored-product costs.
  • Eugene encourages members to download Profit Analytics reports and provide redacted screenshots to support SOS research and PR materials.
  • Yuriy shares that his company diversified its channels so Amazon now represents about 40% of sales instead of 60%, reducing dependence on Amazon.
  • Tony Brink highlights the “malicious competitor tax,” particularly in supplements, where competitors repeatedly attack listings and Amazon enforcement remains inconsistent.
  • Tony explains that even with documented evidence of abuse, Amazon often fails to take meaningful action against bad actors.
  • Daniel proposes tailoring SOS messaging by audience: consumers should hear about higher prices and fewer product choices, regulators should focus on antitrust and systemic concerns, and Amazon leadership should hear about long-term marketplace trust and sustainability.
  • Jon introduces the local concept of “Boeingification” in Seattle, describing how financial optimization can gradually replace engineering excellence and long-term innovation.
  • Peter asks whether sellers should also propose alternative strategies that Amazon could pursue to improve profitability without overburdening sellers.
  • Eugene acknowledges that sellers only see part of Amazon’s broader strategy but still wants survey data and testimonials to support any future recommendations.
  • Megan and Eugene agree that the SOS survey should target at least 200 responses from MDS members and broader seller communities, capturing metrics such as fee percentages, cash-flow impacts, and Prime Day profitability trends.
  • The session concludes with Eugene thanking members, confirming that all shared information remains anonymous unless members explicitly agree otherwise, and stating that the survey link and presentation slides will be distributed through follow-up posts and email.

In this session, the MDS community aligns on the goals, messaging, and strategy behind the Save Our Sellers initiative. 

The discussion combines operational pain points, policy concerns, PR strategy, and long-term marketplace trends while emphasizing a professional and data-driven approach. 

Members commit to sharing documentation, metrics, and personal experiences to help quantify the impact of rising Amazon costs and operational burdens while positioning themselves as partners who want Amazon’s marketplace to remain healthy, competitive, and sustainable for sellers and consumers alike.

items.title: Amazon Catalog Cleanup: Are Your Listings at Risk? - Expert Call with Riverbend Consulting
items.description:

TOPICS:

  2. Authorization, documentation, and AI-driven enforcement (including product safety)
  3. FBA fee increases, margin reassessment, and multichannel selling strategy
items.description_text: In this session, Brianna, Matt and Kayleigh from Riverbend Consulting explains Amazon’s major catalog cleanup and how it affects resellers and brand relationships. TOPICS: Amazon catalog cleanup, ASIN reductions, and impact on reseller listings Authorization, documentation, and AI-driven enforcement (including product safety) FBA fee increases, margin reassessment, and multichannel selling strategy

files.name: Transcript - Expert Call with Riverbend Consulting
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779219848560-GMT20260519-160253_Recording_640x360_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Brianna Matt and Kayleigh from Riverbend Consulting explains Amazon’s current catalog cleanup efforts safety enforcement trends, and fee changes, and how these shifts affect sellers, especially resellers and businesses with large catalogs. 

They focus on how proactive catalog management, strong documentation, and strategic pricing and channel decisions can help sellers remain compliant and profitable on Amazon.

Amazon’s Catalog Cleanup: Goals and Rationale

  • Amazon is undertaking a large-scale catalog cleanup initiative aimed at removing approximately 27 billion ASINs by 2026, reducing the catalog from roughly 74 billion ASINs to under 50 billion.
  • The cleanup is intended to improve buyer trust, as Amazon believes the post-pandemic marketplace has become crowded with inaccurate, duplicate, or low-quality listings that create uncertainty for customers.
  • Amazon wants product detail pages to accurately represent the actual products being sold, including correct branding, attributes, images, configurations, and supporting documentation.
  • The speakers explain that many problematic listings are created by resellers without direct brand relationships, especially listings for configurations such as 2-packs or 4-packs that the original brand does not manufacture.
  • Amazon views inaccurate or duplicate listings as harmful to both the customer experience and brand identity, particularly when products are outdated, gray-market, or parallel-imported.
  • The catalog cleanup is framed as both an intellectual property initiative and a buyer-experience initiative focused on improving catalog accuracy and trust.

Impact on Resellers, Multipacks, and Authorization

  • The cleanup impacts resellers most heavily, especially sellers listing on ASINs they did not create and that were not created or approved by the brand owner.
  • Amazon increasingly flags detail pages that do not match official brand-created configurations, particularly when resellers create bundles or multipacks from individual units.
  • Most violations related to the cleanup are classified as “no-impact violations,” meaning they may not directly damage account health scores but can still suppress or remove profitable listings.
  • Amazon now expects branded multipacks to match the exact configurations officially produced by the brand, making unauthorized reseller-created packs increasingly risky.
  • Sellers with strong brand relationships and letters of authorization may still be able to preserve non-standard configurations if the documentation explicitly lists the exact products, configurations, and titles used in Seller Central.
  • When inventory in FBA is tied to an incorrect ASIN, Amazon may allow inventory transfers through virtual moves or restickering processes, though these actions create additional operational costs.
  • Amazon is also targeting listings that intentionally misspell or obscure brand names to bypass gating systems, and the company treats these tactics as deceptive circumvention of policy enforcement.
  • Sellers who cannot obtain authorization for restricted brands or categories are advised to protect their accounts by selling those products through other marketplaces rather than attempting to bypass Amazon policies.

Proactive Catalog Management, Documentation, and AI Enforcement

  • Riverbend emphasizes that many enforcement actions are not about product authenticity but about authorization, compliance, and alignment with current catalog standards.
  • Sellers are encouraged to conduct regular listing audits to confirm that products, UPCs/GTINs, titles, and attributes accurately match the actual products being sold.
  • Documentation such as invoices and letters of authorization must support the exact products and configurations listed and must comply with Amazon’s invoice age requirements, typically within the last 365 days.
  • AI systems now continuously scan Amazon’s catalog, including dormant or inactive listings, meaning even old listings with no recent sales can still trigger enforcement actions.
  • Legacy listings that have not sold in years still create exposure because Amazon may request invoices less than 365 days old when reviewing compliance.
  • Riverbend recommends regularly deleting inactive, outdated, irrelevant, or zero-sales listings to reduce enforcement exposure and simplify future catalog audits.
  • AI-driven invoice reviews now automatically reject invoices that fail formatting or age requirements, making successful appeals more difficult than in the past when more human review was available.
  • Because human review opportunities are limited, such as through the account health assurance “seller challenge” process, sellers are encouraged to make initial appeals as complete and accurate as possible.
  • Documentation must align exactly with Seller Central account information, including names, addresses, emails, and phone numbers, and discrepancies may require updated invoices, revised authorization letters, or supporting business documentation.
  • Repeated weak or incomplete appeals may cause Amazon systems to stop reviewing a specific ASIN altogether, limiting future reinstatement opportunities.
  • Amazon may also restrict a seller’s ability to create new ASINs if the ratio of inactive listings to active listings becomes too high, making ongoing catalog cleanup strategically important.

Product Safety Investigations, Lab Central, and Compliance

  • Product safety enforcement is increasing rapidly, with safety investigations reportedly rising by approximately 40% year over year due largely to AI-driven monitoring.
  • Amazon’s AI systems flag products based on patterns such as increased returns, safety-related language in reviews or return comments, and historical issues associated with specific product categories.
  • Categories under especially high scrutiny include supplements, children’s products, toys, electronics, FCC-regulated items, and topical products such as skin-lightening products.
  • The speakers describe Amazon’s current approach as highly aggressive, where listings may be restricted or removed before any human review occurs, creating immediate revenue disruption for sellers.
  • Sellers who handle safety investigations successfully are typically those who maintain complete and current compliance documentation before enforcement occurs.
  • Amazon has introduced “Lab Central,” a system requiring some product categories to submit safety testing directly through Amazon-approved testing partners rather than through seller-uploaded documentation.
  • Categories frequently associated with Lab Central include toys, children’s products, supplements, electronics, radios, hazardous-material-related products, and products requiring ISO 17025-type testing standards.
  • The speakers explain that the new process is partly a response to past abuse where sellers manipulated or reused safety reports by altering product names or details before submission.
  • Under Lab Central, approved laboratories send testing results directly to Amazon, reducing the likelihood of forged or manipulated documentation.
  • Even when Lab Central is not mandatory, sellers are encouraged to use trusted laboratories such as Underwriters Laboratories or Eurofins and to leverage Amazon’s Service Provider Network for vetted testing providers.
  • Sellers should also recognize that older testing documents that were once accepted may no longer meet current standards when AI systems reevaluate listings, making periodic retesting and documentation updates important.

FBA Fee Increases, Economics, and Multichannel Strategy

  • The session also covers recent FBA fee increases and the significant impact these changes can have on seller profitability despite Amazon characterizing the increases as relatively minor.
  • While Amazon presents the average increase as roughly eight cents per unit, the actual impact varies significantly depending on product size tiers and price ranges.
  • Small standard-size products priced above $50 face increases of approximately $0.51 per unit, while large standard-size items above $50 increase by around $0.31 per unit.
  • Standard-size products priced between $10 and $50 generally experience increases of approximately $0.25 per unit, which can create substantial annual cost increases for high-volume sellers.
  • The speakers stress the importance of recalculating margins at the SKU level by incorporating FBA fees, receiving costs, shipping expenses, closing fees, and product costs to determine whether a product remains viable on Amazon.
  • Smaller, higher-priced products are identified as some of the hardest-hit categories under the updated fee structure, making detailed profitability analysis especially important.
  • Riverbend recommends reassessing whether some products still belong on Amazon or whether they may perform better through other channels with more favorable economics.
  • The discussion acknowledges that Amazon remains the dominant marketplace with unmatched customer reach, but sellers are encouraged to view it as one component of a broader multichannel strategy that may also include Walmart, TikTok Shop, Shopify, and other platforms.
  • The broader theme of the session is that Amazon is evolving from a volume-first marketplace into a more quality-controlled, compliance-driven, and IP-conscious platform, and sellers who adapt proactively will be better positioned for long-term growth.

In this session, Riverbend Consulting presents a detailed overview of how Amazon’s marketplace is evolving across catalog integrity, authorization requirements, safety enforcement, and fee structures. 

The discussion highlights the increasing role of AI-driven enforcement and the growing importance of accurate listings, strong documentation, and proactive compliance management.

The speakers emphasize that sellers who continuously clean up their catalogs, maintain current authorization and safety documentation, monitor SKU-level profitability, and diversify their channel strategies will be in the strongest position to remain competitive and resilient as Amazon’s standards continue to tighten.
