In this session participants discuss how they use AI and automation to drive visibility traffic, and sales across Amazon, Shopify, and other channels. 

 

They share concrete workflows, tools, and emerging ideas for collaborative AI “agents” that can learn from multiple businesses while still respecting proprietary constraints.

 

AI-Driven SEO / GEO Optimization and Content Strategy

  • Participants focus heavily on AI SEO / GEO optimization as a primary lever to increase visibility and organic traffic to both websites and Amazon listings.
  • Sam explains that purchase decisions are increasingly shifting from manual human research, such as Google and Amazon search, to AI-generated recommendations from tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, so brands need to become discoverable within those AI ecosystems.
  • Sam shares that he redesigns websites to prioritize FAQ-style, question-and-answer content that is highly readable for humans and structurally optimized for AI systems and search engines.
  • He confirms that FAQs are both visible on-page and encoded in schema so search engines and AI agents can crawl and interpret the content effectively.
  • Sam builds AI “skills” using Claude so nutrition facts and ingredient lists are rendered in real HTML rather than images, making them fully crawlable for AI models and search engines.
  • He notes that while it is difficult to isolate which specific tactic drives results, he has observed increased website and Amazon traffic over the past two months and attributes much of that growth to GEO-focused optimization efforts.
  • Participants highlight the importance of structured data and schema control, but Sam emphasizes that schema alone is not enough and that content strategy, FAQs, and crawlable data are equally important.
  • The group discusses how Amazon AI now surfaces “Top Highlights” and attribute summaries on listings, and Sam commits to researching how these are generated and how they affect visibility and AI-driven recommendations.
  • Ramon describes a process of monthly Amazon listing copy updates where AI recommends revisions based on performance, search volume, and keyword importance, with a human reviewing outputs for compliance and accuracy.
  • Ramon’s system automatically pushes updated copy through the Amazon Listing API, and if catalog updates are rejected, the system automatically opens support cases to force updates while maintaining human oversight.

 

Automated Reddit Personas and Network Strategy for GEO & Attribution

  • Sam describes a Reddit-based GEO strategy where he operates approximately 10 AI-driven personas, each with its own interests, behavior patterns, and posting style.
  • Each persona runs through dedicated IPs and cookie profiles using a service called GoLogin and its Orbiter browser to simulate realistic user behavior and reduce the risk of bans.
  • Sam explains that the workflow logs into each account, scrolls and browses naturally, checks notifications, and probabilistically decides whether to reply to posts or comments to appear more human.
  • He confirms that most activity occurs in comments rather than original posts, and that only around 10% of outputs are promotional to avoid appearing spammy.
  • Sam reports that an earlier, more aggressive account with roughly one-third promotional posts was banned quickly, leading him to prioritize anti-ban tactics and long-term account aging.
  • He shares an example where a single Reddit reply about a pasta product generated around 10 website orders within five minutes, demonstrating the direct conversion potential of Reddit traffic.
  • Sam outlines methods for making AI-generated text appear more human, including intentional imperfections, natural phrasing, and prompt structures designed to avoid common AI patterns.
  • He notes that earlier comments were identified by users as AI-generated, which pushed him to refine prompts and workflows so current outputs no longer get called out as bots.
  • Sam’s Reddit agents sometimes seed questions and indirectly reference products before naming the brand only when another user asks, reducing obvious promotional behavior.
  • He envisions scaling the system to hundreds of accounts, enabling coordinated engagement such as accounts replying to and upvoting one another to strengthen perceived authority in targeted subreddits.

 

PR, HARO/SOS Outreach, and CRM + Agentic Workflows

  • Sam and Ramon both use AI and automation to manage PR outreach through services like HARO and SOS, which provide journalist and blogger opportunities for product placements and backlinks.
  • Sam has built a workflow that identifies relevant PR opportunities, drafts customized responses, and routes them through a human review process before submission to ensure tone, compliance, and accuracy.
  • Ramon sets minimum monthly search-volume thresholds through the DataForSEO API so his system only targets websites with meaningful traffic potential.
  • He filters out low-value opportunities, such as sites with little or no meaningful search traffic, to avoid wasting outreach effort and product samples.
  • Ramon maintains a custom CRM dashboard that tracks pitches, follow-ups, placements, publishers, and publicists, and he uses an email service such as Resend to automate outreach and follow-up sequences.
  • Sam uses a Google Sheets-based tracker focused on operational metrics such as pitches sent, samples shipped, and associated cost of goods, especially for expensive sample bundles or gift boxes.
  • Sam emphasizes that even when AI drafts the majority of outreach content, human review remains critical to:
    • Ensure the messaging sounds genuinely human and aligned with the brand voice.
    • Avoid generic “AI-sounding” language that could reduce credibility with journalists and bloggers.
  • The group agrees that even small blogs and micro-influencers can provide value for GEO because they contribute additional backlinks, mentions, and authority signals that feed search engines and AI systems.
  • They acknowledge that attribution remains imperfect, but they view broad PR coverage as a long-term investment in discoverability and brand visibility within AI ecosystems.

 

Meta/Facebook Ads, Shopify Integrations, and Fast Experimentation

  • Cou shares a Meta ads workflow integrated with Shopify, AI image generation, and template-based landing pages that enables rapid avatar and creative testing.
  • He explains that Shopify AI Toolkit and Claude, along with previous use of Gemini and ChatGPT, allow him to:
    • Generate avatar-specific ad copy and creatives.
    • Build multiple landing pages tailored to different customer avatars.
    • Synchronize updates across many landing pages programmatically.
  • Cou uses Shopify pages through a third-party integration and AI tooling to create standalone, conversion-focused landing pages that still operate within the Shopify backend and reuse existing product data and assets.
  • He describes a workflow where prompts and templates generate creative briefs, images, and copy, and he only intervenes to approve or reject outputs through a structured spreadsheet process.
  • After review and approval, he uses Telegram-based automation to launch or update campaigns in Meta Ads Manager without rebuilding campaigns manually in the interface.
  • Cou emphasizes the importance of avatar-level testing, where each audience receives its own messaging and landing page, significantly increasing testing velocity compared to traditional workflows.
  • He generally keeps Meta targeting broad and relies on Meta’s optimization systems to identify the right audience based on creatives, copy, and conversion signals, while occasionally applying high-level filters such as age ranges.
  • Gary adds best practices such as excluding recent purchasers for 90 to 180 days and using audiences like “Engaged Shoppers” to avoid wasting ad spend on existing customers or low-intent traffic.
  • Participants note that Meta advertising has historically been difficult for some brands, but they are more optimistic now because AI significantly lowers the effort required to create and manage large numbers of creative variations.

 

Shared AI Agents, Skills, and Cross-Business Knowledge Networks

  • In the latter part of the call, Alex raises the concept of linking AI agents across businesses so they can share experience and strategic insights rather than only public information.
  • Alex describes how his current setup logs calls, emails, Amazon data, Slack messages, and Monday.com data into an OpenAI- or Claude-based agent that learns operational patterns across his supplement businesses.
  • He proposes connecting multiple business agents through controlled links so each agent can access anonymized and structured operational learnings from others while protecting sensitive business information.
  • Alex emphasizes that businesses would not need to expose brand identities or confidential information, but instead could share abstracted patterns, strategies, and outcomes to improve recommendations across the network.
  • Ramon notes that many founders view their AI workflows and operational data as proprietary, particularly when direct competitors are involved, which may limit willingness to participate in open sharing systems.
  • Despite those concerns, Sam and others see strong potential in a “skills pool” model where members contribute reusable AI skills, such as PR workflows or Amazon support-case automation, in exchange for access to skills built by others.
  • Sam suggests a modular structure consisting of:
    • A portable general skills layer that applies broadly across businesses.
    • A company-specific data layer grounded in each business’s own products, policies, and operational information.
  • June highlights the importance of data structure and retrieval systems, noting that combining information from multiple companies requires standardized schemas, embeddings, and table structures to prevent conflicts and confusion.
  • Sam references an existing process where he loads full course transcripts into a system, creates indexed skills from the material, and then removes the raw transcript once the skill is operational.
  • The group concludes that skills-sharing is likely the most practical near-term opportunity, while broader agent-to-agent collaboration and cross-business retrieval systems may emerge later as the ecosystem matures.

 

In this session, participants share practical ways they are using AI, automation, and structured experimentation to increase visibility, traffic, and operational efficiency across Amazon, Shopify, Reddit, PR, and Meta advertising. 

 

The discussion highlights how AI-driven systems are changing SEO, content creation, advertising workflows, and customer acquisition strategies across multiple channels.

 

The session also explores the longer-term vision of collaborative AI ecosystems, including shared skills, reusable workflows, and cross-business learning networks. 

 

Overall, the discussion presents a forward-looking view of how operators are combining AI tools, automation infrastructure, and human oversight to scale experimentation, improve discoverability, and build more adaptive digital businesses.

items.title: Scaling Large Catalog Operations with AI Imaging, Inventory Systems, and Return-Rate Optimization - Large Catalog Sellers Channel Call May 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants from the MDS Large Catalog Sellers group discuss how they manage product images, inventory systems, and returns across large Amazon catalogs.

TOPICS:
  1. AI-driven product image creation and lifestyle photography at scale
  2. Warehouse, inventory, and demand-planning systems
  3. Return rates, refund analysis, and using AI and data to investigate potential abuse or anomalies
items.description_text: In this session, participants from the MDS Large Catalog Sellers group discuss how they manage product images, inventory systems, and returns across large Amazon catalogs. TOPICS: AI-driven product image creation and lifestyle photography at scale Warehouse, inventory, and demand-planning systems Return rates, refund analysis, and using AI and data to investigate potential abuse or anomalies

files.name: Transcript - MDS Large Catalog Sellers Monthly Call
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1779217333778-MDS Large Catalog Sellers Monthly Call_transcript.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss how large catalog sellers manage product images inventory systems demand planning, and operational challenges at scale. 

They also share specific tools, workflows, and tactics used to optimize Amazon-focused businesses, especially in bedding, toys, scientific supplies, pet products, fashion, and niche products like fingerboards.

Product Image Creation and AI Tools

  • The group discusses how sellers historically spent substantial amounts on photographers and lifestyle image production, sometimes totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars over time.
  • Sohail explains that his bedding business now relies heavily on AI-generated images and that, over the last three months, his team has used photographers only for the main product image.
  • He states that his team uses Algo Fuse as a primary AI tool for generating lifestyle images, image stacks, room scenes, and different image variations. He also notes that they are experimenting with AI-generated video through Algo Fuse.
  • He mentions that his team uses another AI image tool alongside Algo Fuse and plans to confirm the exact name with his internal AI specialist.
  • William and Sohail agree that AI performs well for simple, solid-color products, but more complex prints, floral patterns, and multicolor designs still require manual prompting and human review because AI often distorts patterns or colors.
  • William explains that his catalog includes pet supplies and fast fashion products with thousands of print variations reused across multiple product categories, making scalable image generation especially valuable.
  • Matt describes using a Photoshop script to bulk-generate images for fingerboard decks by layering artwork and shadows, and he considers integrating AI into that workflow.
  • He reports success using AI tools, including one he refers to as “nano banana,” to add realistic lab coats onto human models in lifestyle photos. However, he notes weaker results with glassware and fingerboard products, likely because those categories have limited training data.
  • The group highlights that using AI to generate or refine prompts for image generation often produces better outcomes than manually writing prompts from scratch.

Catalog Strategies, Product Types, and Operational Models

  • Sohail explains that his bedding business depends heavily on lifestyle imagery because products are displayed in styled bedroom environments where visual presentation strongly impacts conversion rates.
  • William states that his catalog includes pet supplies and fashion products, many of which are manufactured overseas and printed or finished in the United States.
  • Matt describes operating two businesses: a scientific supply company selling laboratory and educational products, and a fingerboard brand focused on miniature skateboards and accessories.
  • Trevor explains that his company specializes in discontinued name-brand toys and purchases overstock inventory from licensors such as Hasbro or from retailers like Walmart after contracts end or orders are reduced.
  • He notes that his team cross-posts listings onto marketplaces such as Temu and Shein using existing Amazon content and images, minimizing the need for new creative assets.
  • He outlines a dual inventory strategy where part of the toy inventory is sold immediately while the remainder is held for one to two years to capture higher collector-market pricing.
  • Trevor mentions that his company recently purchased a warehouse and is currently managing the operational complexity of moving inventory into the new facility.
  • Matt shares an example involving a miniature fingerboard parking curb accessory that created confusion among municipal buyers. His team solved the issue by updating the main image to show the product in a person’s hand to better communicate scale.

Inventory Management Systems, WMS, and ERP Solutions

  • Matt introduces the topic of inventory systems and explains that his company is implementing a new inventory management platform that functions as a lightweight ERP.
  • Sohail states that he operates a 68,000-square-foot warehouse in Las Vegas, provides 3PL services, and is attempting to sublease approximately 20,000 square feet of excess space, including office and storage areas.
  • He explains that his business uses Opal as its warehouse management system and works with an implementation partner called Cityon Systems to configure and maintain the platform.
  • He notes that Opal manages fulfillment, shipping, scanning, and bin locations but does not include demand-planning functionality.
  • Sohail reports that implementing Opal is a large project that takes roughly six months, requires significant investment, and still needs continuous refinement after launch.
  • Trevor states that his company operates a 65,000-square-foot warehouse in Missouri and currently uses a WMS called Three Links, which he had previously used at another company.
  • He says he is evaluating ShipHero as a possible replacement and has scheduled demos to assess picking workflows, light-directed picking, and system integrations.
  • He explains that ShipHero supports direct-to-consumer shipping with carriers such as UPS, USPS, FedEx, and DHL, while allowing merchants to preserve carrier volume under their own shipping accounts.
  • Trevor points out that some platforms, including ShipStation, aggregate shipping volume under master accounts, which can reduce a merchant’s leverage and visibility with carriers like UPS.
  • Matt describes implementing Finale for his toy brand because it integrates with ShipStation, QuickBooks Online, Shopify, Amazon, eBay, and Etsy, while offering detailed accounting controls.
  • He compares Finale with a previous Acumatica ERP implementation for his scientific supply business, explaining that Acumatica required nine to ten months and roughly $150,000 to implement, whereas Finale was self-implemented in approximately six weeks.
  • Trevor notes that ShipHero includes accounting-related features, though some users find them difficult to navigate. He shares an example where another operator exports ShipHero reports into Claude to generate formatted invoices for QuickBooks automatically.
  • William explains that his operation uses ScanPower for FBA pick, pack, and ship workflows, especially for products requiring poly-bagging and FNSKU labeling.
  • He notes that ScanPower is simple for warehouse staff to learn and integrates effectively with auto-bagging equipment and label printers.

Demand Planning, Forecasting, and Use of AI

  • Sohail explains that he previously used Flieber for forecasting but found it too expensive and insufficiently responsive to short-term demand spikes across his approximately 3,500 ASINs.
  • He states that his current process involves exporting operational data from Opal into large spreadsheets, sometimes approaching 100 MB, and then using Claude to assist with forecasting and identifying unusual demand patterns.
  • He shares that historical analysis reveals strong seasonality patterns, with certain prints and product types consistently performing well during the same periods each year.
  • Trevor explains that his team uses SoStocked for forecasting because it can support both simple and advanced planning workflows.
  • He notes that SoStocked becomes significantly more reliable once products accumulate at least 12 months of sales history.
  • Matt discusses previous limitations he experienced with SoStocked when combining Amazon FBA and FBM demand, while William adds that some of those issues have improved over time.
  • William explains that his company manages roughly 30,000 ASINs through SoStocked and maintains direct communication with the founders because of the scale and complexity of his operation.
  • He clarifies that SoStocked is primarily a demand-planning platform rather than a complete warehouse management system.
  • Matt notes that his Acumatica-based business currently uses Inventory Planner for forecasting but is evaluating specialized platforms such as Netstock.
  • William offers to connect Matt’s team with a contact at Netstock and believes the company has potential to expand further into Amazon-focused forecasting workflows.
  • Sohail and William both express caution about relying entirely on AI for large purchasing decisions, especially for seasonal products and expensive inventory commitments.
  • William mentions that some sellers in the MDS AI WhatsApp group reportedly trust AI directly for purchasing and cash flow decisions, though he personally views that approach as risky without human oversight.
  • Matt explains that he prefers using AI to help build spreadsheet models and forecasting formulas rather than relying on AI to continuously generate unrestricted numeric outputs.

Returns, Refunds, and Potential Fraud Analysis

  • Sohail raises concerns that his bedding business experiences unusually high refund rates, averaging approximately 12% to 16% at the payment-SKU level.
  • He explains that return reasons are spread across many categories, including color mismatch and subjective preference issues, without one obvious root cause.
  • Matt shares comparative benchmarks from Sellerboard, stating that his toy brand typically sees refund rates around 2.5% to 2.9%, while his scientific supply business ranges from 2.7% to 4.5%.
  • Trevor reports refund rates around 2.5%, while William reports approximately 5% to 5.5%, reinforcing that Sohail’s return rates are significantly above normal levels.
  • The group discusses the sellable return percentage metric in Sellerboard. Matt reports rates between 63% and 80%, while Trevor reports approximately 55% to 57%.
  • Trevor explains that Amazon avoids reselling many used toys because of safety and regulatory concerns, which negatively impacts recoverable inventory rates in toy categories.
  • Sohail shares examples of suspicious customer behavior, including one customer purchasing multiple bedding colors and returning items gradually over several weeks from the same address.
  • Matt recommends that Sohail contact his Amazon SAS (Strategic Account Services) representative to request category benchmarks and determine whether his return rates are unusually high relative to similar bedding sellers.
  • William suggests exporting detailed sales and return data over a 24-month period and using Claude to analyze trends related to SKUs, return reasons, geographies, and time periods.
  • He recommends using highly specific prompts inside Claude, such as explicitly asking whether competitor attacks or organized return abuse may exist, to encourage deeper analytical review.
  • Matt and William suggest examining ZIP code patterns to identify potential coordinated fraud or malicious return activity.
  • William references prior MDS discussions about organized return and review fraud and believes similar analytical methods may help uncover whether Sohail’s business is being targeted.
  • He offers to collaborate directly with Sohail on analyzing exports inside Claude and cross-checking multiple AI-generated analyses to identify likely root causes.

Overall, this session provides a practical and detailed look at how large catalog Amazon sellers modernize operations through AI-generated imagery, specialized WMS and ERP systems, and increasingly sophisticated forecasting workflows. 

The participants share real-world experiences across industries including bedding, toys, pet supplies, scientific products, and collectibles.

The discussion also highlights the importance of balancing automation with human judgment. While AI significantly improves image production, forecasting support, and operational analysis, the group emphasizes that critical decisions involving purchasing, inventory commitments, and fraud analysis still require experienced human oversight. 

The session reinforces the value of strong systems, reliable data, peer collaboration, and disciplined operational processes in building scalable and resilient Amazon businesses.

items.title: Training Amazon’s AI: How Rufus Reads Listings and Increases Average Order Value － SEO Channel Call May 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants explore how Amazon’s new AI systems, Cosmo and Rufus, change the way search, personalization, and recommendations work on the platform.

TOPICS:
  1. Amazon’s evolving AI search architecture (Cosmo and Rufus)
  2. Practical listing optimization for AI
  3. Use of AI tools, scraping, and automation (Claude, Playwright, external SEO) to run deeper audits and scale improvements
items.description_text: In this session, participants explore how Amazon’s new AI systems, Cosmo and Rufus, change the way search, personalization, and recommendations work on the platform. TOPICS: Amazon’s evolving AI search architecture (Cosmo and Rufus) Practical listing optimization for AI Use of AI tools, scraping, and automation (Claude, Playwright, external SEO) to run deeper audits and scale improvements

files.name: Transcript - MDS SEO Channel Call May 2026
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1778538654957-Transcript - MDS SEO Channel Call May 2026-compressed.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session MDS SEO Channel members discuss how Amazon’s evolving AI systems particularly Cosmo and Rufus are transforming search, personalization, and listing optimization. 

The conversation explores practical frameworks, tools, and workflows that sellers can use to future-proof Amazon listings and leverage AI for deeper audits and automation.

 

Amazon’s New AI Search Architecture (Cosmo & Rufus)

  • Participants explain that Amazon search now operates with multiple AI-driven layers that go beyond exact keyword matching and instead interpret meaning, shopper intent, and behavioral patterns.
  • The group states that Amazon has evolved from a traditional keyword-focused search engine into an AI system that attempts to understand the meaning of words, phrases, images, and customer behavior.
  • They describe Cosmo as Amazon’s back-end AI system that reads titles, bullets, attributes, reviews, and images to build a deeper understanding of products and shopper activity.
  • Rufus is described as the personalized shopping assistant layer that sits on top of Cosmo and pulls answers directly from listings to respond to shopper questions.
  • Participants explain that Amazon’s growth in new Prime members in the U.S. has slowed, leading the company to focus more heavily on increasing average order value (AOV) from existing shoppers.
  • The group discusses how Amazon’s AI analyzes co-purchase behavior, time on page, frequently bought together relationships, and browsing flows to predict the next best purchase opportunity.
  • They explain that these AI systems influence which products Amazon recommends, promotes, and surfaces more frequently, especially for upsells and complementary purchases.
  • Participants note that Amazon segments customers into different shopping “modes,” such as broad discovery searches, narrowed searches, and high-intent exact searches, with rankings and recommendations changing accordingly.
  • They mention that when shoppers repeatedly narrow their search without purchasing, Amazon may assume the shopper is willing to switch brands and begin surfacing alternative products.
  • The group emphasizes that Amazon is rapidly moving toward AI-centric discovery and recommendation systems, creating urgency for sellers to adapt listings and optimization strategies quickly.


Listing Optimization for AI and Rufus

  • Participants stress that listings must now answer customer questions in natural language rather than relying primarily on keyword stuffing.
  • They explain that titles, bullets, and descriptions should clearly communicate use cases, audiences, and scenarios so AI systems can understand who the product is designed for and how it is used.
  • The group recommends structuring A+ Content and A+ Premium modules around multiple clear use cases and shopper scenarios.
  • For products with several applications or audiences, they advise dedicating separate A+ modules or layouts to each use case so Amazon’s AI can better associate the listing with different shopping intents.
  • Participants explain that Rufus and Cosmo actively analyze images and can infer demographics, environments, activities, and lifestyle contexts from listing photos.
  • They note that while AI may not fully process all A+ text in every placement, it clearly interprets image content and visual context.
  • The group strongly recommends filling out backend attribute fields as completely as possible whenever relevant to improve relevance and discoverability.
  • They explain that many sellers leave large portions of attribute fields incomplete, which weakens the signals available to Amazon’s AI systems.
  • Participants recommend building out 10 to 20 Q&A entries per listing because Rufus uses Q&A content and customer reviews to understand shopper language and intent.
  • They advise writing Q&A content using phrasing that mirrors real customer questions and search behavior.
  • Comparison charts within A+ Content are highlighted as valuable because they help Amazon understand product differentiation and feature positioning relative to competitors.
  • Participants recommend using cross-sell modules such as “Pairs well with” and “Goes well with” to strengthen AI-driven basket and relationship signals between products.
  • The group emphasizes that every section of the listing, including titles, bullets, images, attributes, Q&A, reviews, A+ modules, and Brand Story content, should actively answer customer questions and communicate product value clearly.


Use of Images, Video, and AI-Generated Media

  • Participants explain that Amazon’s AI systems now interpret images deeply, identifying demographics, settings, activities, and lifestyle cues to improve personalization and recommendations.
  • The group discusses how Amazon’s AI may infer detailed audience information from image composition and environmental context.
  • They note that many large sellers already rely heavily on AI-generated images that are later refined in tools such as Photoshop.
  • Participants explain that AI-generated images can still send strong relevance signals to Amazon as long as the images clearly communicate real-world use cases and scenarios.
  • They discuss Claude’s integration with Photoshop, allowing AI-assisted image generation and editing workflows.
  • The group recommends including complementary products or related ecosystems in listing images so Amazon better understands cross-product relationships.
  • They suggest showing compatibility with multiple brands or product ecosystems in accessory listings to expand relevance signals.
  • Participants note that visible brand logos in compatibility images may help AI associate products correctly in some categories, though certain categories may require stricter compliance considerations.
  • They discuss video content and believe Amazon’s AI is likely capable of analyzing video, although they have not yet seen strong evidence or official confirmation regarding how Rufus currently uses video data.
  • The group concludes that static images and structured A+ modules remain the most reliable and controllable tools for influencing Amazon’s AI understanding.

Data Collection, Audits, and Technical Tooling

  • Participants discuss building a framework and audit tool that evaluates listings across titles, bullets, attributes, images, Q&A, reviews, and other AI-related optimization factors.
  • The planned audit system scores listings based on intent coverage, attribute completion, Q&A depth, frequently bought together relationships, and content quality gaps.
  • Claude is described as the primary AI engine used to generate repeatable listing audits and recommendations using historic listing data and examples.
  • The group explains that their current workflows still rely heavily on manual data collection and virtual assistants to gather listing content, reviews, Q&A, and competitor information.
  • Participants note that Amazon’s official APIs do not expose all desired data, especially complete Q&A and review datasets, leading them to explore scraping tools and automation.
  • They discuss testing Apify for scraping Amazon content, though they mention limitations and inconsistencies in some review collection workflows.
  • Higgsfield is referenced as a platform for accessing advanced AI image-generation models before refining outputs inside Photoshop.
  • Participants explain that combining Claude with scraping and automation tools allows the generation of detailed listing audits with minimal manual effort.
  • The group references using Product Opportunity Explorer, Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance (SQP) reports, Data Dive, and Data Rover to identify keyword gaps and competitive opportunities.
  • They also describe copying conversations with Rufus into Claude to better understand how Amazon frames a niche and to improve listing recommendations.

Browser Automation, Playwright, and CoWork

  • Participants discuss using CoWork, Claude’s browser automation feature, to navigate Amazon listings, open Q&A sections, and gather information automatically.
  • They explain that CoWork behaves similarly to a human user controlling a browser but may operate more slowly than dedicated automation systems.
  • Microsoft Playwright is introduced as a faster and more advanced browser automation framework.
  • The group describes Playwright as significantly faster and more scalable than browser-based manual workflows when paired with advanced language models.
  • Participants explain that Playwright was originally designed for QA and browser testing, making it effective for scripted workflows involving clicking, logging in, extracting data, and navigating pages.
  • They discuss workflows where Playwright combined with AI can retrieve reports, process spreadsheets, and move data between systems with minimal human input.
  • The group recommends pairing Playwright with VS Code and Claude for more programmable and scalable automation pipelines.
  • They acknowledge that these systems require upfront setup and scripting effort but can unlock significant long-term efficiency gains once operational.

External Authority Signals, Off-Amazon SEO, and Group Logistics

  • Participants explain that Amazon’s AI increasingly evaluates off-Amazon authority signals similarly to how traditional search engines evaluate websites and brands.
  • The group recommends investing again in press releases, backlinks, and external SEO content to strengthen brand authority and relevance signals.
  • They suggest creating blog content that answers real customer questions sourced from Google and related search tools.
  • Participants reference a tool similar to AskTheCustomer.com that surfaces real-world Google questions related to a niche.
  • They explain that strong external content can influence both Google rankings and the contextual signals Amazon gathers about brands and products.
  • The group notes that Claude can significantly speed up blog and SEO content production using collected customer questions and search data.
  • They recommend featuring external authority signals such as press mentions, certifications, and media coverage visually inside Amazon listings to reinforce trust and credibility.
  • Brand Story modules are highlighted as underused but highly effective for upselling, storytelling, and cross-promoting products within a catalog.
  • Participants mention that Brand Story content may pass Amazon approval processes more easily than some A+ modules in certain situations.

Tools, Platforms, and Community Logistics

  • The Helium 10 AM/PM Podcast is referenced as a place where similar Amazon AI discussions and presentations are shared publicly.
  • Participants discuss the release of Meta’s API for advertising and analytics while noting that many large direct-to-consumer brands are reducing Meta ad spend due to regulation changes and reporting challenges.
  • The group mentions that some advertisers have significantly reduced daily Meta ad budgets compared to prior years.
  • A WhatsApp group is used to share frameworks, slides, and examples from the session.
  • Participants explain that workshop slides and materials will be distributed through the WhatsApp group after the session.
  • They also note that group invitations and links are sent individually so members can join the discussion channels.


Overall, this session presents a practical view of how Amazon’s AI systems, especially Cosmo and Rufus, are reshaping search, personalization, and listing optimization. 

The discussion connects larger strategic shifts, such as AI-driven discovery and average order value optimization, with actionable tactics involving A+ Content, attributes, Q&A, image strategy, automation, and external authority building.

By combining stronger on-Amazon content with external SEO signals and scalable automation workflows, participants outline a framework for building listings that are better aligned with Amazon’s evolving AI ecosystem. 

The session also demonstrates how tools such as Claude, Playwright, and advanced audit systems can help sellers operationalize these strategies across larger catalogs more efficiently.

items.description:
In this session, Meher Patel highlighted the benefits of using Claude over ChatGPT for PPC, emphasizing its capabilities in data analysis and agentic workflows. 
 
TOPICS:
  1. Creating scheduled tasks in Claude CoWorks
  2. Identifying high-converting search terms
  3. Setting up skills for automated bid adjustments

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1778511603100-Transcript - MDS Mogul Call with Hector_compressed.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Meher Patel focuses on how brands agencies and Amazon sellers can use Claude and Hector MCP to improve PPC and operational workflows. 

He walks through live examples, discusses data and infrastructure considerations, and answers advanced questions about scaling AI-driven advertising operations.

 

AI for PPC and Why Claude Is Recommended Over ChatGPT

  • Meher Patel frames the discussion around how brands can use AI to improve Amazon PPC and advertising workflows, with a strong focus on Claude.
  • He explains that, based on his experience and feedback from practitioners, Claude consistently performs better than ChatGPT for PPC analysis, structured reasoning, and data-heavy workflows.
  • Meher clarifies that his expertise is centered on PPC and advertising operations, and he describes Claude as a strong fit for these use cases because of its analytical capabilities and ability to handle structured datasets.
  • He notes that many MDS members already use Hector AI tools and integrations, which allows the session to focus on more advanced Claude workflows instead of introductory concepts.
  • Participants acknowledge that AI is currently one of the most active discussion areas in the MDS community, making the topic especially timely.

 

Claude Interfaces, MCPs, and Context Engineering

  • Meher explains that Claude includes several interfaces, including the Claude web chat, Claude desktop app, Co-work tab, and Claude Code, each serving different workflow needs.
  • He clarifies that scheduled and agentic workflows must be configured through the Co-work environment in the desktop app rather than the browser-based web chat.
  • He describes agents, schedules, and agentic workflows as essentially the same concept: structured sequences of tasks executed automatically based on triggers or schedules.
  • Meher explains that MCPs (Model Context Protocol connectors) act as the bridge between Claude and structured business data such as Amazon advertising reports and search query datasets.
  • He strongly advises PPC operators not to spend excessive time building their own MCP infrastructure because maintaining APIs, connectors, and data layers becomes extremely resource-intensive.
  • The session introduces the concept of context engineering, where prompts and tool outputs are intentionally designed to remain lean and relevant instead of overloaded with unnecessary context.
  • Meher notes that Amazon’s native MCP APIs provide little built-in context, meaning teams must manually structure and define context if building systems internally.
  • He encourages sellers to focus on becoming strong optimization operators rather than becoming infrastructure developers.

 

Building PPC Workflows, Skills, and Schedules with Claude and Hector MCP

  • Meher demonstrates a PPC workflow using Search Query Performance (SQP) reports where Claude, through Hector MCP, identifies search queries with stronger conversion rates than category benchmarks over a 12-week period.
  • He shows how Claude can determine whether those search terms already exist as exact match keywords in active campaigns and whether bids align with suggested bid ranges.
  • Hector MCP processes large datasets server-side and only returns filtered results to Claude, reducing token usage and improving reliability when handling large reports.
  • Meher demonstrates how Claude can identify keyword harvesting opportunities by surfacing high-converting search terms that are not yet targeted as exact match keywords.
  • He walks through Claude’s skill creation workflow, where users define trigger phrases, thresholds, conditions, and expected outputs.
  • Once created, these skills can be uploaded into Claude’s Skills manager and reused without needing to recreate prompts manually each time.
  • Meher converts one workflow into a scheduled task inside Co-work, configuring it to run automatically on specific days and trigger alerts such as Slack notifications when anomalies or opportunities are detected.
  • Another workflow compares ROAS performance between two seven-day periods and flags targets with significant changes only when sufficient spend exists in both periods.
  • He confirms that Claude, through Hector MCP, can eventually execute account actions such as bid adjustments once proper safeguards and workflows are established.
  • Throughout the session, he repeatedly emphasizes that prompt quality, filtering logic, and clean data structures are critical for reliable outputs.

 

Advanced Q&A: SQL, BigQuery, Inventory, Agencies, and Hector MCP

  • During the Q&A session, Meher confirms that users can run SQL-style analyses through Hector MCP and explains that Hector’s infrastructure is built on BigQuery.
  • He notes that Hector can support custom data migrations, dedicated reporting endpoints, and even custom MCP implementations connected to a client’s own BigQuery environment.
  • He explains that users can work with more raw datasets and multiple language models as long as Hector defines the necessary endpoints connecting the data to Claude.
  • For agencies managing many Amazon accounts, Hector is building bulk-processing endpoints that allow Claude to analyze performance across dozens of accounts simultaneously.
  • He explains that server-side grouping and filtering prevent Claude from becoming overloaded with raw account-level data.
  • On inventory workflows, Meher states that Hector MCP already includes inventory-level information and can support forecasting and replenishment analysis, although some datasets may still need more granular segmentation.
  • Jamie asks what differentiates Hector MCP from other MCP systems, and Meher explains that the advantages come from lean context design, server-side processing, specialized tools, efficient token usage, and reduced hallucination risk.
  • Meher describes how Hector builds highly specialized tools for specific PPC actions rather than one large generalized tool, which improves reliability and reduces errors.
  • On pricing, he explains that Hector offers MCP-only access plans, though pricing is still evolving because infrastructure and BigQuery costs vary significantly by usage volume.
  • He also notes that Hector provides additional services including managed PPC and DSP support.
  • Anush Shetty from Hector AI shares his contact information and invites members to reach out for custom analyses or more information about Hector services.

 

In this session, Meher demonstrate how combining Claude with a well-designed MCP like Hector’s can move Amazon PPC operations from manual spreadsheet analysis into automated, agentic workflows that run on schedules, detect anomalies, and even execute account changes. 

 

The discussion highlights that the true advantage comes not only from the AI model itself, but from the quality of the data infrastructure, context engineering, and workflow design connecting the model to Amazon advertising systems.

cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss real estate investing and deal acquisition strategies with a focus on Cleveland Ohio and several other U.S. markets. 

 

The conversation centers on how investors source deals manage marketing channels, and operate rental portfolios, especially when working remotely.

Market Focus and Investment Strategy

  • Chris Im invests primarily in Cleveland, Ohio while living in Las Vegas, Nevada. He chose Cleveland for its low purchase prices, strong rental demand, and favorable rent-to-price ratios.
  • He focuses on single-family properties, typically 3 to 4 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms, around 1,500 square feet. Many homes are older, often built in the early 1900s, and require specialized maintenance considerations.
  • Chris currently owns about 13 doors and uses a mix of flips and buy-and-hold rentals as his core strategy.
  • He is transitioning away from third-party property management and building an in-house team to gain more control and reduce costs.
  • Financing remains a constraint, but he works with lenders offering hard money and DSCR loans and is open to sharing these resources.
  • Jun Kim and others highlight that markets like Dallas, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Florida, and Boston offer different opportunities, including multifamily and student housing strategies.

Cold Calling and Direct-to-Seller Deal Sourcing

  • Chris relies on a cold calling agency as his primary channel for sourcing off-market, direct-to-seller deals in Cleveland.
  • The agency manages dialing, software, list building, and call handling, then delivers leads daily.
  • He receives approximately 8 to 10 leads per week, mostly colder leads with a smaller portion of highly motivated sellers.
  • The service costs about $2,000 per month, which he considers cost-effective since one deal can cover the expense.
  • Estimated cost per lead is $15 to $18, and cost per deal is roughly $200 to $300.
  • He prefers agencies because they filter out unqualified or hostile leads, allowing him to focus on closing motivated sellers.
  • Data quality is critical, and performance varies significantly between agencies depending on how lists are sourced.

SEO, Websites, and Digital Marketing Channels

  • Chris invests in SEO and website optimization to generate inbound seller leads.
  • He initially builds his site on WordPress using Elementor, then transitions to an AI-based tool referred to as Cloud code to improve structure, interlinking, and updates.
  • He uses Outrank to generate blog content, which improves impressions and keyword rankings.
  • His best deal to date came from an inbound SEO lead, reinforcing SEO as a high ROI channel.
  • SEO is especially valuable for reaching homeowners on Do Not Call lists who cannot be contacted through cold outreach.
  • His Cloud code plan costs about $100 per month, making SEO leads relatively low cost compared to other channels.
  • He plans to expand into Google PPC and Facebook ads, using landing pages built through his AI tools.
  • He cautions that PPC requires testing and can become expensive, so it is not ideal for someone with only $1,000 per month to spend.

Other Acquisition Channels: Direct Mail, MLS, Wholesalers, and Agent Networks

  • Direct mail and postcards
    • Carl Branker shares experience with HomeVestors, using large-scale postcard campaigns targeted by zip code and demographics.
    • Postcards previously cost about $0.12 each at scale and remain effective, though he now prefers more targeted outreach for specific deals.
  • MLS and real estate licenses
    • Dimitri Vorona has held a real estate license for about 15 years to gain early MLS access in New Jersey.
    • Early access allows him to identify opportunities before other buyers.
    • Chris confirms his partner, who is an agent, regularly finds viable deals on the MLS, including in Cleveland.
  • Wholesalers and deal platforms
    • Chris reports mixed results with wholesalers, noting they often underestimate rehab costs and overestimate ARV.
    • He recommends Investor Lift as a platform where buyers can access deal flow and filter by market.
  • Agent outreach strategy
    • Chris plans to use AI tools to scrape Zillow and Redfin for agents listing properties with keywords like “investor special” or “flip project.”
    • He intends to build a list and run SMS outreach campaigns targeting agents who regularly work with distressed properties.
    • This strategy is common in Las Vegas and appears underutilized in Cleveland.

Operations: Lead Management, Compliance, and Tenant Systems

  • Lead screening and underwriting
    • Chris reviews call recordings and notes from the agency to assess seller motivation and property condition.
    • He performs quick valuation checks on Zillow or Redfin before engaging.
    • Leads are managed in a simple Notion CRM that updates automatically for fast follow-up.
  • Compliance and outreach risk
    • Jun Kim shares that his team purchases public data from county records, such as Collin County, Texas, for low cost.
    • They clean data using AI and run SMS campaigns through Launch Control, managed by freelancers on Upwork.
    • Chris experienced a legal issue in Texas involving strict telemarketing laws, leading to a settlement by a provider.
    • He now recommends caution with SMS outreach in highly regulated states and keeping volume controlled.
  • Tenant and property management
    • Chris is building a custom tenant management system using AI tools because many existing platforms feel limiting.
    • Dimitri asks about solutions for rent collection and automation.
    • Jun recommends Innago as a free, effective property management platform after moving away from Avail, which declined after being acquired by Realtor.com.
  • Student housing strategy
    • Dimitri focuses on student housing in markets like Boston, purchasing larger units and renting by room with co-signers.
    • This approach improves payment reliability but increases wear and tear, requiring strong deposits and management.
    • Frequent lease turnover allows for regular rent increases.

In this session, the group explores a range of real estate acquisition, marketing, and operational strategies, anchored by Chris Im’s experience building a remote portfolio in Cleveland.

 

The discussion highlights how investors combine cold calling, SEO, direct mail, MLS access, and agent networks to maintain a steady pipeline of deals. 

 

Cold calling agencies and SEO-driven inbound leads stand out as the highest leverage channels, while other strategies like postcards, MLS sourcing, and student housing add diversification.

 

Participants close by sharing tools and resources and encouraging each other to implement at least one new strategy in their own markets.

files.name: MDS AI Presentation
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1777665383058-MDS AI Presentation 4-29-26 Final.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Derrek Wiedeman and MDS members break down how to move from basic AI usage into fully operational AI agents that automate real workflows—especially in sourcing procurement and internal operations. 

The discussion focuses on practical implementation tooling and how to structure agents for long-term scalability.

Core Concept: Agents vs Skills

  • Key distinction:
    • Agent = Role (e.g. sourcing manager)
    • Skill = Task/SOP (e.g. send RFQ, log quotes)
  • Derrek clarifies:
    • He does not have 74 agents, but 74 skills
    • This modular structure makes systems more scalable and maintainable
  • AI agents are defined as:
    • Models + tools + structured workflows
    • Capable of multi-step execution, not just chat
  • Critical principle:
    • Skills = SOPs translated into AI-executable steps
  • Takeaway:
    • If you can clearly document a process → you can likely automate it.

Turning Real Roles into AI Systems (Sourcing Case Study)

  • Derrek’s automation starts when he loses two sourcing/procurement team members.
  • Instead of rehiring, he:
    • Takes over the role himself
    • Documents all tasks
    • Converts each task into a skill
  • Example skills created:
    • Browse suppliers (Alibaba)
    • Post RFQs
    • Extract quote data from emails
    • Log quotes into databases
    • Generate weekly reports
  • System setup:
    • All SOPs stored in a central docs folder
    • Agents connected to:
      • Email inboxes
      • Supplier communications
      • Databases (e.g., Baserow, Supabase)
  • Advanced layer:
    • Skills include:
      • Logging
      • Error detection
      • Self-healing loops
  • Result:
    • No need to rehire staff → agents fully replace the role.

Browser Automation vs CLI Tools (Key Technical Shift)

  • Traditional approach:
    • Browser automation (clicking, screenshots)
    • Slow + expensive (high token usage)
  • Derrek’s approach:
    • Build CLI tools (Command Line Interfaces) for each platform
  • Example:
    • Custom Alibaba CLI tool can:
      • Log in
      • Search suppliers
      • Post RFQs
      • Retrieve messages
  • Benefits:
    • Faster execution
    • Lower cost
    • More reliable automation
  • Supporting tool:
    • Browser Use → enables cloud browsers + CAPTCHA handling
  • Key insight:
    • If a platform has no API → build your own CLI layer.

Tool Stack, Cost Optimization, and Multi-Model Workflows

  • Initial setup:
    • OpenClaw + Claude Opus
    • Costs reached ~$150/day
  • Optimization strategy:
    • Move development to:
      • Claude Code
      • OpenAI Codex
    • Use OpenClaw mainly for:
      • Scripts
      • Scheduled jobs (cron)
  • Cost-saving tactics:
    • Use ChatGPT subscriptions instead of heavy API usage
    • Limit real-time LLM calls
  • Infrastructure principle:
    • Everything lives in GitHub
    • Ensures:
      • Portability
      • Model-agnostic workflows
  • Standard files per project:
    • claude.md → Claude instructions
    • agent.md → Codex/OpenAI instructions
    • README.md → system overview

Multi-Model Strategy (“Model Blaster” Approach)

  • Derrek uses multiple models in parallel:
    • Claude Opus
    • GPT-5.5
    • Gemini 3.1
    • Others
  • Workflow:
    • Send same prompt to all models
    • Compare outputs
    • Merge best results
  • Benefits:
    • Higher accuracy
    • Fewer bugs
    • Better creative + logical balance
  • General positioning:
    • Claude Opus → creativity, nuance
    • GPT-5.5 → accuracy, structure

Organizing Agents Across the Business

  • Common mistake:
    • Too many fragmented channels (e.g., 70 Slack chats)
  • Recommended structure:
    • Organize by business function, not topic:
      • Sales Agent
      • Sourcing Agent
      • Website Agent
  • Each agent:
    • Owns a folder
    • Owns its skills
    • Uses shared documentation
  • Key upgrade:
    • Convert long chat histories → structured skills
  • Why:
    • Chats = fragile
    • Skills = reusable + scalable

Key Takeaways & Strategic Framework

  • Start with SOPs
    • If it’s not documented → it can’t be automated
  • Think in roles
    • Build agents as replacements for real hires
  • Break work into skills
    • Each repeatable task = one skill
  • Use GitHub as the source of truth
    • Keep systems portable across tools
  • Avoid UI-based automation when possible
    • Prefer CLI or structured integrations
  • Use multiple models
    • Don’t rely on a single AI system
  • Continuously improve
    • Add logging, feedback, and self-healing loops

Final Insight

This session marks a clear shift from “using AI tools” → “building AI systems.”

The biggest unlock is not better prompts—it’s:

  • Structuring your business into roles, SOPs, and skills
  • Then letting agents execute those workflows reliably and repeatedly

 

Resources:

  • MDS AI Presentation: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1AKkqyehD_agDYirC75fhTByVfaehZEcP/view?usp=drive_link
  • Alibaba CLI: https://github.com/gtg708q/ali-cli

items.title: Scaling Past $30M via Amazon, DTC, TikTok & Retail － Miami Operator Room 2026
items.description:
Go behind closed doors at a private, invite-only gathering of elite e-commerce founders and operators in Miami’s historic Morningside neighborhood. This wasn't a conference or a sales pitch; it was a candid, peer-to-peer exchange between leaders managing brands at the $15M to $300M+ annual revenue scale.

In this session, four industry titans discuss the raw realities of scaling, from defending the #1 Best Seller badge on Amazon to navigating the "hot potato" risks of a potential exit. 

Key Discussion Points:
• Defending the #1 Spot: Chris Kjeldsen (CGK Linens) reveals how he monitors BSR every three hours and his willingness to sacrifice $350k in monthly profit to secure a category-leading position. 

• The DTC & TikTok Pivot: David Stark (Coldest) shares the journey of taking a brand from $4M in debt to a debt-free, 130% year-over-year growth trajectory by shifting focus to community and TikTok Shop. 

• Retail Velocity at Scale: Chris Hunter (Koia) discusses the "liquid to lips" strategy that landed his brand in 35,000 stores and his approach to raising $72M in capital. 

• The "Top of Drawer" Marketing Strategy: Hyla Nayeri (437) explains her aggressive organic social strategy—posting 10 times per day—to maintain "brand cool factor" and dominate on Revolve. 

• What Breaks at $50M: The founders dive into the challenges that don't show up on podcasts, including "ghost orders" on TikTok, navigating Amazon’s changing disbursement cycles, and the debate over the 4-day workweek. 

• The AI "Cooked" Theory: A deep dive into the future of e-commerce, discussing whether AI will eventually automate brand building end-to-end and how to use it for efficiency without losing the human moat. 

Featuring:
• Chris Kjeldsen – Founder & CEO, CGK Linens ($325M+ Revenue)  
• David Stark – Founder & CEO, Coldest ($40M–$50M Revenue)  
• Chris Hunter – Co-Founder & CEO, Koia (35,000+ Retail Stores)  
• Hyla Nayeri – Co-Founder & Co-CEO, 437 (Top Activewear Brand on Revolve)

About the Operator Room: A closed-door room for high-level operators who value signal, perspective, and honest conversation over access and tactics. Hosted by Million Dollar Sellers (MDS) and ecompreneur.

cliff_notes:
I. Panelist Profiles & Success Metrics

  • Chris Kjeldsen (CGK Linens):
    • Scale: Projecting $325M in revenue for 2026 a significant increase from $250M in 2025.
    • Market Dominance: Holds multiple #1 Best Seller spots on Amazon including for sheet sets bed skirts and extra deep pocket sheets.
    • Strategy: Heavily aggressive reinvestment putting at least 90% of every dollar back into the business for the last decade.
  • David Stark (Coldest):
    • Scale: Annual revenue currently tracking between $40M–$50M.
    • Pivot: Successfully transitioned the brand from being Amazon-centric to a 20% Amazon / 80% DTC & TikTok split.
    • Recovery: Led the company from $4M in debt back to a debt-free high-growth trajectory with 130% year-over-year growth.
  • Chris Hunter (Koia):
    • Scale: Distributed in over 35,000 stores across all retail channels.
    • Capital: Has raised a total of $72M for the company through institutional and community rounds.
    • Focus: Transitioning from refrigerated-only to building a shelf-stable product line to broaden the "buyer universe" for a future acquisition.
  • Hyla Nayeri (437):
    • Scale: Projecting between $20M and $25M in revenue by the end of the year.
    • Marketing: Built a globally recognized label primarily through organic and influencer marketing, reaching $15M+ in revenue before wholesale expansion.
    • Recognition: Positioned as the top activewear brand on Revolve.

II. Tactical Deep Dives

1. Mastering Amazon & Omnichannel Defense

  • Buying the Badge: To capture a #1 Best Seller spot, Kjeldsen was willing to "kiss profit goodbye," dropping monthly profit from $500k to $150k for a three-month "war".
  • BSR Monitoring: CGK Linens receives BSR reports every three hours to ensure they can instantly react if a competitor encroaches on their rank.
  • Ranking Blitzes: They use Q1 (their slowest period) to order extra inventory and run aggressive "ranking blitzes" with heavy discounts to boost standing for the year.
  • DTC Payout Speed: Stark noted that DTC and TikTok Shop offer much faster payouts (often daily or +1 day after arrival) compared to Amazon’s two-week cycle.

2. Organic Growth & Influencer Relations

  • The "Top of Drawer" (TOD) Strategy: Hyla Nayeri focuses on sending 500–1,000 targeted gifting shipments monthly to creators so the brand remains the most recent, "top of drawer" option.
  • Content Volume: 437 saw revenue exceed projections by $300,000 in a single month after shifting to a strategy of posting 10 times per day on TikTok and Instagram Reels.
  • Influencer Gifting Ethics: 437 spends $50k–$60k per month just on the product cost for gifting.
  • The "Date" Analogy: Nayeri advises that your Instagram grid must be "attractive enough for the date" before reaching out to influencers; "small business energy" or poor branding results in low response rates.

3. Scaling Pains & "What Breaks"

  • Cash Flow Squeeze: Recent changes to Amazon’s disbursement cycle (holding funds for 7 days after delivery) and Meta/Amazon pulling the plug on credit cards for ad spend have strained cash cycles.
  • TikTok "Ghost Orders": David Stark warned that during high-volume spikes, up to 12% of orders may fail to sync from TikTok to Shopify due to a software glitch.
  • Inventory Debt: CGK Linens reported being $12M in debt post-pandemic due to massive inventory orders and $40k container prices.

III. The Future: AI & Business Philosophy

1. The AI Disruption Debate

  • The "Cooked" Theory: David Stark believes E-commerce founders are "cooked" within five years because AI will eventually create brands and manage the end-to-end process autonomously.
  • VA Headcount Reduction: Chris Kjeldsen expects his Philippines-based team to shrink from 40 to 20 or 30 people by year-end as AI takes over reporting and manual tasks.
  • AI Photoshoots: Brands are testing AI tools that can turn a mannequin photo into a full lifestyle shoot in a "Tulum villa" with realistic fabric and models.

2. Operational Culture

  • Work-Life Balance: Hyla Nayeri implements a 4-day work week and a lifestyle-first approach, though she admits this creates friction when competing against $100M+ brands.
  • The Binary Bet: Chris Hunter’s beverage business (Koia) represents a "binary" bet where they burned money for nine years to achieve a massive strategic acquisition.

3. Exit Strategies

  • The "Hot Potato" Mindset: Some sellers view Amazon brands as "hot potatoes" that must be sold before categories commoditize or algorithm changes occur.
  • Experiential Moats: The consensus was that the ultimate defense against AI is building real-life relationships and experiential retail environments that cannot be replicated by software.

Summary

The Miami gathering highlighted a stark contrast between Amazon-native operators focused on BSR defense and DTC/Retail founders focused on "brand cool factor" and community. 

While the group debated the impending threat of AI and the necessity of aggressive work cultures, they found common ground in the challenges of inventory-driven cash flow and the need to diversify beyond a single platform to ensure long-term brand survival.

cliff_notes:
In this session the group discusses advanced strategies for scaling TikTok Shop using creators affiliates, and structured incentive programs. 

 

In addition, they compare tools, pricing approaches, and operational setups across TikTok, Meta, Amazon, and other channels to build sustainable, multi-platform growth.

 

VIP & Bonus Programs = Scalable Creator Growth Engine
  • Top creators are placed into a VIP tier (e.g., ~100 out of thousands).
  • VIP perks include:
    • Access to proven winning creatives
    • Higher earning potential
    • Priority support
  • Instead of flat retainers, brands use:
  • → Performance-based bonuses (e.g., $1,000 for 20 posts/month)
  • Key structure:
    • Clear rules (quality, GMV Max on, proper setup)
    • Ongoing feedback via Discord
    • Transparent dashboards (GMV, commissions)
  • Core insight:
  • → Incentives drive behavior — top creators produce more, others push to qualify

 

Contests, GMV Max, and Inventory Alignment
  • Brands are deploying large-scale contests (e.g., reallocating $100K into prizes).
  • Best practices:
    • Multiple winners → keeps more creators engaged
    • Weighted raffle systems → balance fairness + performance
  • GMV Max strategy:
    • Requires aggressive spend and realistic ROAS
    • Conservative ROAS targets limit scale
  • Inventory alignment is critical:
    • High inventory → push volume (lower ROAS targets)
    • Low inventory → slow demand (raise ROAS targets)
  • Review generation tactic:
    • Small incentives (e.g., $15) → quickly build social proof
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Promotion without inventory = wasted momentum

 

Cross-Channel Strategy & Pricing Dynamics
  • Channel roles:
    • TikTok Shop → demand creation
    • Amazon → demand capture
    • Meta → scaling + retargeting
    • Google → search + intent capture
  • Key insight:
  • → If you're not on Amazon, you're losing conversions from TikTok traffic
  • Branded search on Amazon = 25–60% of sales for strong brands
  • Pricing strategies vary:
    • Some brands:
    • → Higher TikTok prices + heavy discounts
    • Others:
    • → Lower TikTok pricing to drive virality
  • Risks:
    • Pricing violations
    • Channel conflict
    • Google Shopping exposure
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Pricing is a growth lever, but must be controlled carefully
 
 
Creator Recruitment = Numbers + Segmentation Game
  • Outreach reality:
    • ~1% response rate is normal
    • 100+ samples/month → only a few winners
  • TikTok “sample score” (1–100):
    • 80+ = strong candidates
  • Creator segmentation:
    • Top tier (90k+ GMV): instant VIP + free product
    • Mid tier (25k–100k): nurture + upsell into VIP
    • Low tier: education + refundable samples
  • Most GMV comes from:
  • → A small % of creators (power law)
  • Coaching tactics:
    • Share scripts + hooks
    • Feedback loops
    • Tools like CapCut for better content
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Recruiting is volume; scaling is retention of top performers

 

Operations, Tools, and Live Selling Systems
  • Core ecosystem includes:
    • TikTok Shop
    • Amazon
    • Meta
    • Google
    • Klaviyo
  • Creator ops tools:
    • Outreach: Yuka / Reacher
    • Marketplace: Join Brands
    • Communication: Discord, WhatsApp, Telegram
    • Training: Loom
  • Live selling strategy:
    • Affiliates (not just brand accounts) run lives → more authentic
    • Structured playbooks:
      • First 15 min = heavy promos
      • Repeatable loop thereafter
  • Advanced ops:
    • Warehouse-based live studios
    • Real-time support teams (flash sales, inventory updates)
    • “Always-on” lives (near 24/7 rotation)
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Live + affiliate = next level of scale

 

Key Takeaways
  • VIP + bonus programs outperform flat retainers
  • Contests + GMV Max = scalable growth levers (if inventory supports it)
  • TikTok creates demand, Amazon captures it
  • Top creators drive most revenue — focus on them
  • Pricing strategy directly impacts virality and margin
  • Live selling + affiliates is a major unlock
  • Operations (tools, systems, support) = the real bottleneck at scale

 

In conclusion, this session provides a comprehensive, practitioner-level overview of how advanced brands use TikTok creators, contests, and structured bonus programs to drive scalable GMV. 

 

It also highlights the operational challenges of recruiting, training, and supporting thousands of creators across multiple tools and languages, while balancing pricing and channel strategy across TikTok, Amazon, Meta, and beyond.

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS Trading Channel discuss how to approach both crypto and traditional markets in a highly volatile macro environment. 

The conversation covers market outlooks, specific assets and protocols, yield strategies, and practical ways to balance risk, return, and mental bandwidth as busy business owners.

Purpose of the Call and Participant Goals

  • The call focuses on practical trading and investing strategies across crypto and traditional markets within the MDS community.
  • Guido Reyes explains that engagement in the trading channel has been low and that he is working to revive it.
  • Participants agree the goal is to share ideas and frameworks, not financial advice or high-risk speculation.
  • Travis Reese shares that he is shifting toward long-term investing and exploring quantitative trading strategies supported by AI.
  • The group emphasizes focusing on realistic, repeatable returns rather than chasing “home run” trades.

Macro View and Crypto Market Outlook

  • Guido shares a cautious macro outlook and states that he is currently net short the S&P 500, expecting a broader correction.
  • He believes markets may form a cycle low between mid-year and late-year, though timing remains uncertain.
  • Participants note that Bitcoin is increasingly correlated with equities and often acts as a leading indicator due to its 24/7 trading.
  • Guido suggests Bitcoin is not yet in a confirmed bull market and may revisit lower price ranges before recovering.
  • The group observes that rising BTC dominance weakens altcoins, making Bitcoin or stablecoins safer core positions in the current environment.

Crypto Platforms, Protocols, and DeFi Yield

  • Guido highlights Hyperliquid as a high-performing “picks and shovels” play that benefits from trading volume and supports 24/7 leveraged trading.
  • He maintains strong conviction in Ethereum as a core asset due to its central role in DeFi.
  • The group discusses risks in DeFi, including protocol exploits, referencing issues involving Aave and Kelp DAO.
  • Guido explains how he uses DeFiLlama to find stablecoin yields, typically targeting 4–8% returns on platforms like Morpho and Sky.
  • He emphasizes that the main risk in these strategies is smart contract failure, not price volatility, when using stablecoins.

Traditional Markets, Stocks, and Sector Themes

  • Participants shift toward long-term equity investing, favoring strong, liquid companies over fragmented copy trading strategies.
  • Guido highlights names like Goldman Sachs and Apple as durable long-term holdings.
  • The group debates Adobe, with some viewing AI as a threat while others see it as a strong long-term opportunity.
  • They discuss sector opportunities in energy (e.g., Chevron), materials (e.g., Dow Chemical), and emerging themes like AI and quantum computing.
  • Participants agree that large-cap, high-quality assets offer better compounding potential with less stress than speculative trades.

Trading Approach, Risk Management, and AI Use

  • Participants emphasize that most entrepreneurs should prioritize simple, scalable strategies over high-frequency trading due to limited time and attention.
  • They suggest targeting steady annual returns rather than chasing extreme gains, which often come with significant risk.
  • The group discusses meme coins and speculative tokens, noting they can generate outsized returns but should only be treated as small, high-risk bets.
  • Guido shares that he is integrating TradingView with Claude to assist with chart analysis, while cautioning against relying blindly on AI outputs.
  • Participants suggest using AI tools to scan sentiment sources like Reddit, but stress that these insights should support—not replace—human judgment.

The group agrees that success in trading comes from balancing opportunity with risk, while staying aligned with personal time and mental bandwidth.

They emphasize combining strong fundamentals with selective use of tools like DeFi platforms, analytics software, and AI models.

Overall, the session reinforces a disciplined approach: focus on sustainable returns, avoid unnecessary complexity, and use AI as support rather than a decision-maker.

items.description:

TOPICS:
  1. Optimizing inventory flow to prevent stockouts and protect rankings and PPC efficiency
  2. Comparing Amazon AWD, FBA placement fees, five‑way splits, and Tactical’s Split Smart program
  3. Diversifying across Amazon, TikTok Shop, and Walmart while managing rising fuel and logistics costs

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1777036838310-Mogul Call with Tactical Logistics.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session Ephraim Ausch discusses how logistics strategy inventory planning and channel diversification affect margins and sales performance for Amazon and e‑commerce brands. 

 

He also explores current Amazon policy changes geopolitical impacts on fuel and freight, and tactical ways to mitigate risk through better use of 3PLs and AWD/FBA.

 

Context: Why Logistics Matters More Than Ever
  • Ephraim Ausch (Tactical Logistics) brings both seller and operator experience, highlighting how Amazon has become significantly harder post-2018.
  • Margins are now heavily influenced by logistics decisions, not just PPC or product.
  • Sellers must actively track fees, policies, and supply chain risks to stay competitive.

 

Amazon Fees, Policy Changes, and Peak Season Planning
  • Key upcoming events:
    • Prime Day (June–July likely)
    • Walmart Deals + TikTok sales events
  • Major updates:
    • 3.5% fuel surcharge added to FBA + MCF fees (likely permanent).
    • New Prime Day deal structure:
      • $100 upfront (discounted to $50 short-term)
      • +1.5% of sales
  • Ongoing issue:
    • Amazon auto-deducting ad spend from revenue (currently paused for some sellers).
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Amazon continues increasing fees quietly, so margin awareness is critical.

 

Inventory Strategy: The #1 Driver of Performance
  • Biggest mistake: stockouts, not poor ads.
  • Impact of stockouts:
    • Ranking drops
    • Higher PPC costs
    • Lost long-term market share
  • Recommended inventory framework:
    • 2 months in FBA
    • 2 months in transit
    • 2 months in 3PL/AWD
  • Key principle:
  • → Inventory should flow, not sit (idle inventory kills margins).

 

AWD vs 3PL: Cost vs Control Tradeoff
  • AWD (Amazon Warehousing & Distribution):
    • Pros: cheap transfer into FBA
    • Cons: higher storage + slower processing
  • 3PLs:
    • Pros: flexibility, control, faster reaction times
    • Cons: potentially higher transfer costs
  • Key insight:
    • AWD becomes more expensive when holding > ~2 months of inventory
    • 3PLs are safer during Q4 congestion and delays
  • Bottom line:
  • → Use AWD for efficiency, 3PL for control + risk mitigation

 

Placement Fees vs Split Shipments (Speed = Sales)
  • Paying placement fees:
    • Inventory goes to 1 location → slowly redistributed
    • Slower availability nationwide
  • Split shipments (5-way):
    • Faster distribution across 15–40+ FCs
    • Better delivery speed → higher conversion
  • Key data point:
    • Faster delivery = ~7% average sales uplift
  • Tactical solution: “Split Smart”
    • Faster check-in (1–2 weeks improvement)
    • Live unloads vs idle trailers
    • Often cheaper than placement fees
  • Core takeaway:
  • → Speed to availability directly drives revenue

 

Channel Diversification and Fulfillment Complexity
  • Current channel mix trend:
    • Amazon = core revenue
    • TikTok Shop = demand generation
    • Walmart (WFS) = growing secondary channel
  • Operational differences:
    • Amazon → optimize fees + Prime speed
    • TikTok → handle sudden spikes
    • Walmart → focus on compliance + consistency
  • Risk:
  • → 3PLs must handle multi-channel spikes, especially in Q4
 
External Risks: Fuel, Geopolitics, and Cost Volatility
  • Middle East instability → rising fuel + freight costs
  • Approx impact:
    • +~$1,000 per container vs prior months
  • Logistics reality:
    • New cost pressures emerge every 6–12 months
    • Requires constant adjustment

 

Key Takeaways
  • Stockouts are the biggest profit killer (not ads).
  • Inventory flow = margin protection + ranking stability.
  • Speed (delivery + check-in) directly increases conversion and sales.
  • AWD vs 3PL is a strategic decision, not just cost comparison.
  • Amazon fees will continue rising → plan margins conservatively.
  • Diversification adds growth, but also operational complexity.
  • Logistics is no longer backend—it’s a core growth lever.
