1. TikTok affiliates and creator strategies for rapid customer acquisition and branded search growth
2. Meta (Facebook/Instagram) ads, whitelisting, and emotionally driven founder/creator content
3. Google, Amazon, and analytics approaches to optimize spend, attribution, and DTC vs. retail strategy
items.description_text: In this session, DTC founders and operators share how they scale brands using TikTok, Meta, Google, and Amazon while shifting from agency dependence to in‑house teams. TOPICS: 1. TikTok affiliates and creator strategies for rapid customer acquisition and branded search growth 2. Meta (Facebook/Instagram) ads, whitelisting, and emotionally driven founder/creator content 3. Google, Amazon, and analytics approaches to optimize spend, attribution, and DTC vs. retail strategy
cliff_notes:
In this session a group of DTC and e‑commerce founders and operators discuss how they grow brands across TikTok, Meta, Google, Amazon, and retail. 

 

In this session, they share specific tactics, tools, and lessons learned about content, creators, attribution, and the shift from Amazon/retail into stronger DTC and social-led growth. 

 

Founder Backgrounds and Business Context
  • Dave Stickland explains that PopSmith is primarily a DTC brand on Shopify, with Amazon as a secondary channel, reflecting a deliberate shift away from Amazon dependence.
  • He shares that his core audience consists of women aged 40–70, which is why Facebook and Instagram outperform TikTok for his brand.
  • Brandon Himmel describes how Roughliners scales rapidly across DTC, Amazon, and TikTok Shop, reaching multi-million monthly revenue.
  • He explains that he builds an internal team to reduce reliance on agencies and improve execution across social and search.
  • Other founders highlight that while Amazon and retail remain important, the biggest growth opportunity now comes from creating demand through social and capturing it across all channels.
 
TikTok Strategy, Affiliates, and Creator Programs
  • Brandon explains that TikTok drives new customer acquisition and significantly increases branded search on Amazon and Google.
  • He shares that success requires aggressive investment in creators, often sending out 100+ samples to generate initial content and momentum.
  • He emphasizes that early campaigns are often unprofitable but are necessary to build social proof and attract high-performing affiliates.
  • He explains that once a product reaches consistent GMV, stronger creators begin reaching out organically to promote it.
  • He notes that TikTok content scales because most views come from new audiences, allowing repeated messaging without audience fatigue.
  • The group agrees that for high-LTV or consumable products, it is rational to break even or lose money on the first TikTok sale.
 
Meta Ads, Whitelisting, and Emotional Creative
  • Dave emphasizes that successful Meta advertising relies heavily on founder-led content combined with diverse creator assets.
  • He explains that whitelisting allows brands to run ads from a creator’s profile, which improves performance and lowers CPMs.
  • He notes that Meta increasingly rewards creative diversity, making it important to use multiple creators and formats.
  • Brandon shares that scaling founder content is effective but time-intensive, so brands must balance it with creator-generated content.
  • Dave highlights that high-performing ads focus on emotional drivers, identity, and lifestyle rather than just product features.
  • He explains that aligning messaging with customer motivations—such as family experiences or status—significantly improves conversion rates.
 
Google, Amazon, and Attribution Strategy
  • Brandon explains that he is restructuring his Google Ads campaigns using segmented keyword strategies and dedicated landing pages.
  • He notes that Performance Max campaigns can be useful but often lack transparency and require tighter control.
  • The group observes that on Amazon, auto campaigns can still outperform manual campaigns when left properly optimized.
  • Brandon shares that switching Meta attribution to 1-day click provides a more realistic view of performance across channels.
  • Participants highlight tools like Kendall and SEMrush for tracking performance and building keyword strategies.
  • The group agrees that strict attribution models are imperfect, so decisions should be based on blended performance and overall business impact.
 
Team Building, Content Systems, and Future Growth
  • Brandon explains that scaling requires building an internal team, including roles for social media, SEO, content editing, and creator outreach.
  • He shares that VAs and tools like Yuka help manage large volumes of creators and communication.
  • The group emphasizes that social and DTC growth require a dedicated leader focused on revenue, not just content output.
  • Brandon describes using SEO-driven blog content and email marketing to attract and nurture customers beyond paid ads.
  • Tyler shares that creators can be activated through commission-based partnerships using tools like the Meta Creator Marketplace.
  • The group notes that building scalable systems for content production and creator management is the next major growth lever.
 
The group concludes that modern growth comes from integrating TikTok, Meta, Google, and Amazon into one system rather than treating them separately.
 
They emphasize that demand creation through social media is now the primary driver, while other channels capture and monetize that demand.
 
They agree that long-term success depends on strong teams, consistent content production, and disciplined measurement across channels.

cliff_notes:
In this session the MDS Retail Channel Call discusses real-world challenges and strategies related to entering and scaling in retail channels. 

 

In particular, they focus on pricing risks, EDI and logistics issues, brokers and distributors, retail outreach, and the long-term value of networking and trade shows.  

 

Entering Retail and Managing Risk
  • Participants explain that entering major retailers like Walmart, Target, or CVS is exciting, but brands must plan conservatively to avoid financial strain.
  • They emphasize that retailers prioritize pricing competitiveness, and brands that are not priced correctly risk chargebacks, fines, and margin erosion.
  • David shares that poor pricing and positioning can lead to severe financial consequences, including cases where brands face bankruptcy after retail expansion.
  • The group advises founders to validate pricing and shelf competitiveness objectively before committing to large retail rollouts.

 

EDI, Logistics, and Operational Complexity
  • Participants explain that EDI systems are critical for retail but often create operational challenges, especially during early setup.
  • Gianmarco shares that despite using TrueCommerce, his team encounters configuration issues that lead to delays and potential penalties.
  • David mentions using SPS Commerce and notes that switching providers mid-process can be difficult.
  • The group explains that many brands rely on 3PLs and retailer “collect” logistics, where retailers pick up inventory instead of the brand shipping directly.

 

Brokers, Distributors, and Deal Structures
  • Participants recommend working with specialized brokers for each major retailer rather than relying on a single generalist.
  • They explain that broker commissions of around 4–5% are standard, with performance-based incentives often layered on top.
  • The group highlights the importance of structuring retainers, milestones, and exit terms to manage long sales cycles and upfront costs.
  • They clarify that distributors typically take significant margins between brand wholesale and retailer pricing, which must be factored into profitability.
  • Participants warn that some distributors may block markets without actively growing the brand, so careful partner selection is essential.

 

Outreach Strategies and Sales Execution
  • Participants describe using a mix of brokers, distributors, internal outreach, and platforms like Faire to reach retailers.
  • Gianmarco explains that retail expansion often requires both internal sales efforts and external partners working in parallel.
  • The group emphasizes that retail growth is slower than Amazon and typically takes years to produce meaningful results.
  • Etienne shares that tools like Leo Biz Dev can support outbound efforts, but automation still requires active management.
  • Participants note that cold outreach systems can fail without strong execution and consistent optimization.

 

Networking, Trade Shows, and Long-Term Growth
  • Participants highlight events like ECRM as valuable for long-term relationship building, even if short-term ROI is unclear.
  • Gianmarco explains that connections made at ECRM eventually lead to partnerships, including brokers and distributors that unlock retail accounts.
  • The group emphasizes that trade shows deliver stronger results over time, often after repeated attendance and relationship building.
  • They recommend choosing events where established brands exhibit and using partnerships with complementary brands to expand reach.
  • Participants also suggest tracking in-store execution through low-cost audits to ensure products are properly displayed and stocked.
In this session, the group ultimately converges on a shared understanding that retail growth requires patience, careful financial planning, and a strong network of brokers, distributors, and peers. 

 

The conversation highlights that operational readiness, from EDI to logistics and store checks, is just as crucial as product quality and pricing.  

 

Participants underscore that success in retail often arrives years after the initial efforts, whether through trade shows, ECRM, or broker relationships, and that consistent presence and relationship-building pay off over time. 

 

They close by encouraging continued collaboration via WhatsApp and LinkedIn, positioning the MDS community as an ongoing support network for tackling the complexities of retail.

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS AI Channel discuss how they are using modern AI tools and infrastructure to automate e‑commerce operations, marketing, and even personal tasks like travel planning. 

 

The conversation focuses on practical implementations, architecture choices, and guardrails needed to make these systems reliable and secure.

 

AI-Driven Shopify Development and Store Architecture
  • The group explains that Shopify CLI can integrate with Anthropic’s Claude, allowing the model to read and modify store resources programmatically.
  • Sam shares that he uses an AI-assisted workflow to generate fully designed pages, including complete cart pages, from simple prompts.
  • He demonstrates that AI can automate tasks like identifying SKUs with specific attributes (e.g., red images) and applying discounts instantly.
  • He prefers starting from a minimal “skeleton” theme so AI can build a clean, modern site without legacy complexity.
  • He emphasizes that rebuilding a fast, visually strong storefront is critical for PR, partnerships, and conversion performance.
 
Cron Jobs, Workflow Orchestration, and n8n Automation
  • Ramon explains that smaller AI models often break cron workflows, so he standardizes on more capable models for reliability.
  • Sam notes that many cron-based processes should remove AI entirely and run as deterministic scripts to reduce failure points.
  • Several members use n8n as a workflow engine to handle scheduled tasks, API calls, and automation pipelines.
  • Jacob shares that he hosts n8n on DigitalOcean, where AI can help build and manage workflows efficiently.
  • Daniel highlights that n8n can preprocess large datasets and send only small, relevant outputs to AI, reducing token usage and cost.
  • The group notes that cloud providers like Amazon Web Services offer startup credits that can support experimentation.
 
Amazon Data Pipelines and Agentic Analytics
  • Members describe building pipelines from Amazon SP-API into databases like DuckDB, MySQL, or BigQuery.
  • They emphasize that data ingestion should be handled by scripts or cron jobs, while AI is used only for querying and analysis.
  • Sam shares that his AI agent can answer questions about daily performance changes by analyzing structured data.
  • The group stresses that queries should aggregate data before sending it to AI to avoid overwhelming context windows.
  • They recommend storing proven SQL queries as reusable “skills” so agents consistently return accurate insights.
 
Security, Isolation, and Customer Service Agents
  • Participants discuss building AI customer service agents for Shopify and TikTok Shop that handle support workflows.
  • They emphasize that these agents must be treated as high-risk systems due to exposure to external inputs.
  • June recommends sanitizing inputs and using intermediate layers to prevent prompt injection or malicious actions.
  • Cassidy suggests limiting permissions so agents can only create drafts and require human approval for critical actions.
  • The group agrees that agents should be isolated with restricted access, similar to employees with defined roles and permissions.
  • Daniel adds that separating environments, credentials, and systems helps prevent a single breach from affecting the entire stack.
 
Product Research and AI-Powered Travel Optimization
  • Members debate the value of Amazon Product Opportunity Explorer, with some finding it highly useful for niche and keyword insights.
  • Others note that while scraping the tool is difficult, its structured data and summaries provide valuable market intelligence.
  • The group highlights that POE often reveals hidden micro-niches and search behavior patterns.
  • Christian shares a separate use case where he builds an AI travel agent using APIs like Seats.aero and Duffel API.
  • His system compares points vs. cash pricing and applies a target valuation to recommend the best booking strategy.
  • He notes that this setup significantly reduces manual effort and produces strong travel optimization decisions.
 
The group aligns on a clear pattern: combine strong engineering systems (cron jobs, databases, workflows) with AI layered on top for reasoning and decision-making.
 
They emphasize that AI agents should be trained, constrained, and iterated like employees before being trusted in production.
 
They conclude that the real advantage comes from designing reliable systems around AI, not just using AI itself.

items.title: Getting Started with AI in Business: Tools, Setup, and Practical Use Cases－Gregg Alper－Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, participants explore how to move from basic AI usage to building practical, business-ready workflows using Claude and related tools.
TOPICS:
1. Choosing and using core AI tools (Claude, Claude Code, CoWork, and supporting IDEs)
2. Building and organizing reusable AI skills, agents, and deterministic automations
3. Strategic mindset for adapting to the fast-changing AI landscape and capturing first-mover advantages
items.description_text: In this session, participants explore how to move from basic AI usage to building practical, business-ready workflows using Claude and related tools. TOPICS: 1. Choosing and using core AI tools (Claude, Claude Code, CoWork, and supporting IDEs) 2. Building and organizing reusable AI skills, agents, and deterministic automations 3. Strategic mindset for adapting to the fast-changing AI landscape and capturing first-mover advantages
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss how to practically adopt and scale AI tools (especially Claude and related tooling) inside their businesses. 

In this session they share concrete workflows, best practices, and strategic considerations so that people at earlier stages can catch up and begin implementing AI more confidently.

Purpose of the Call and AI Adoption Levels

  • The goal of the session is to help members who feel behind on AI become more confident and practical in implementing it.
  • Participants assess their AI usage on a scale from basic prompting to advanced agent-based systems.
  • Jamie describes being at an early stage, using tools like Claude with integrations but not yet running complex agents.
  • The session is structured as a mix of short expert inputs and open Q&A to translate advanced workflows into actionable steps.

Core AI Tools and Environments

  • Participants highlight Claude (especially Claude Code with Opus) as a primary tool for building workflows and automations.
  • They explain that Claude Code offers deep file access and building capability, while GUI options like Claude CoWork make it more beginner-friendly.
  • Other environments like Visual Studio Code, Cursor, and Anti-Gravity provide flexibility depending on user preference.
  • The group notes that model performance often depends on using APIs and higher “thinking” modes rather than standard chat interfaces.
  • They also reference a broader ecosystem of models, including Gemini, Grok, and GPT variants.

Skills vs. Agents and Practical Use Cases

  • Derek defines a skill as a repeatable workflow or SOP that an AI can execute consistently once refined.
  • He recommends first running workflows manually with AI, then converting them into reusable skills after they are proven.
  • The group explains that agents are higher-level systems that can run independently, calling multiple skills and tools.
  • They emphasize that many business processes are deterministic and should be automated with simple scripts instead of AI at runtime.
  • AI is best used to design and generate these systems, while tools like n8n can handle execution.

Building and Organizing AI Projects

  • Derek explains that the real power of AI comes from combining it with structured knowledge, tools, and workflows—not just chat.
  • He recommends starting projects with a clear plan that includes architecture, data sources, and folder structure.
  • Greg warns that blindly approving AI-generated plans can create messy systems, so users should review outputs carefully.
  • The group highlights the importance of saving progress, managing context windows, and organizing files clearly.
  • They stress using GitHub for version control and backup, along with tools like Obsidian for visibility.
  • Skills should be continuously refined after each use, turning them into improving, reusable assets over time.

This session shows that effective AI adoption moves from simple prompts to structured systems like skills, agents, and automations.

It emphasizes that the biggest advantage comes from combining AI with clear workflows, proper organization, and thoughtful use of deterministic systems.

Businesses that experiment consistently and build reusable infrastructure will be better positioned as AI capabilities continue to evolve.
