cliff_notes:
In this session MDS Logistics Channel members discuss practical logistics strategies across Amazon marketplaces with a focus on FBA, 3PLs, and freight optimization. 

 

The conversation also covers current cost pressures (surcharges, shipping rate increases) and how different sellers adapt their operations and margins.

 

Direct-to-FBA Strategies, DDP, and Tax Handling
  • Members explain that shipping inventory directly to FBA reduces handling, transit time, and overall costs.
  • Ali shares that his team is testing direct-to-FBA shipments in Canada, while Mo recommends using this approach across all regions whenever possible.
  • Mo notes that AWD (Amazon Warehousing & Distribution) is now mainly used as a backup rather than a primary solution.
  • He explains that tax handling in Canada depends on Incoterms and advises comparing DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) versus non-DDP options.
  • Mo adds that DDP is often simpler and sometimes cheaper in Canada, while US imports currently face more customs challenges.

 

3PLs and Warehousing Across Regions
  • Ali shares that he owns warehouse space in Vancouver and can offer short-term overflow storage for other sellers.
  • Members emphasize the importance of choosing 3PLs with strong WMS systems and integrations, not manual processes.
  • Recommended options include Delegate in Canada, ebb and flow for consistent pricing, and RedStack in the US for large products.
  • Mo cautions that Canadian 3PL quality can vary and mentions mixed feedback on AMZ Prep.
  • Members also discuss using supplier storage or shared warehouse setups in China to reduce costs.

 

FBA Fees, Surcharges, and Shipping Economics
  • Members discuss the 3.5% surcharge on FBA fees, which increases costs significantly for higher-fee items.
  • Rising carrier rates and fuel surcharges continue to make FBM shipping more expensive, especially for small parcels.
  • Julian explains that FBA is usually cheaper for small items, while FBM is far more cost-effective for large, heavy products.
  • Ali highlights inconsistencies in FBA size measurements, which can lead to unpredictable fees.
  • The group also explores the idea of group shipping rates to reduce costs through shared volume.

 

Shipment Planning, Delivery Windows, and Tracking
  • Mo explains that Amazon assigns delivery windows to shipments, and missing them can result in inbound defects or fees.
  • He recommends setting delivery windows far in advance, then updating them once timelines are confirmed.
  • He warns that delivery windows cannot be changed after they pass, making timing critical.
  • Members note risks around the five-shipment rule, where delays can trigger penalties if shipments are not delivered within 30 days.
  • Mo advises regularly reviewing Seller Central reports and using Terminal 49 to track shipments and improve accuracy.

 

International Expansion and Returns Strategy
  • Members explain that most sellers expand into the EU starting with Germany, then move into France or Spain as volume grows.
  • Mo shares that EU markets can help offset slower growth in the US, though results vary by product.
  • Julian notes that expansion into Mexico has become easier, but priorities depend on each seller’s setup.
  • For returns, Mo prefers disposal for low-cost items, while Julian inspects and resells high-value returns to recover margin.
  • Chris uses a data-driven approach to estimate return costs and build them into pricing decisions.

 

This session provides a rich, tactical discussion of how experienced Amazon sellers and operators are adapting to rising logistics costs, new Amazon surcharges, and evolving inbound rules. 

 

The participants share concrete tactics for direct‑to‑FBA shipping, 3PL selection, return economics, and international expansion, giving practical frameworks that others can adapt to their own product types and risk tolerance.

items.title: Max Mikhaylenko, Gia Mezz & Will August  － Scaling Modern Brands － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, panelist Max Mikhaylenko, Gia Mezz & Will August share how they use TikTok, live shopping, and affiliates to scale sales across multiple channels.
TOPICS:
1. Building and scaling multi‑channel e‑commerce with TikTok Shop, Amazon, and retail
2. Designing and managing effective affiliate and creator programs as a true sales force
3. Structuring teams, agencies, and operations (including AI use) to support social commerce growth
items.description_text: In this session, panelist Max Mikhaylenko, Gia Mezz & Will August share how they use TikTok, live shopping, and affiliates to scale sales across multiple channels. TOPICS: 1. Building and scaling multi‑channel e‑commerce with TikTok Shop, Amazon, and retail 2. Designing and managing effective affiliate and creator programs as a true sales force 3. Structuring teams, agencies, and operations (including AI use) to support social commerce growth
cliff_notes:
In this session, panelists Max Mikhaylenko, Gia Mezz & Will August discuss how they build and scale multi‑channel, creator‑led businesses. 


In particular, they focus on TikTok Shop, live shopping, affiliate programs, and the team structures and tactics that make these engines work sustainably.

Business Models, Categories, and Growth Focus

Max Mikhaylenko – Supplement Brand and Multi-Channel Expansion

  • Max explains that his supplement brand focuses on men’s health and cardiovascular health and is operating at a nine-figure revenue run rate after approximately 100% year-over-year growth.
  • He shares that the brand’s hero categories include blood pressure support, cardiovascular health, testosterone support, prostate health, and men’s performance products.
  • Max notes that the company sells across TikTok Shop, Amazon (including international marketplaces), and retail channels.
  • He emphasizes that future growth comes from channel diversification rather than endlessly adding new SKUs.
  • Max repeatedly references China’s social commerce ecosystem as a leading indicator for where Western commerce platforms are heading.

Will August – TikTok Shop Agency and Global Expansion

  • Will explains that his agency, Outlandish, started in the China market before expanding into seven international markets.
  • He notes that Outlandish became one of the earliest TikTok Shop agencies in the UK in 2021 and in the US in 2022.
  • Sellers managed by the agency collectively generated roughly $500 million in TikTok Shop GMV over the last year.
  • Will describes TikTok Shop as still being early in its lifecycle, creating opportunities for brands willing to invest before the market becomes saturated.

Gia Mezz – Fashion Brand Positioning and Retail Expansion

  • Gia explains that her fashion brand focuses on “timeless investment fashion,” centered around versatile wardrobe staples and elevated basics.
  • She shares that the company launched in 2020 and reached approximately $2 million in sales within the first 18 months.
  • Retail later expanded to roughly 40% of total revenue through partnerships with channels such as Nordstrom and Urban Outfitters–style marketplaces.
  • Gia stresses that premium fashion brands must be cautious about how TikTok Shop impacts long-term brand perception and positioning.

TikTok Shop, Live Shopping, and Channel Strategy

TikTok Shop as a Demand-Generation Engine

  • Max identifies TikTok Shop as the brand’s primary customer acquisition and demand-generation channel.
  • He shares that the company was at one point the #1 top-selling TikTok Shop brand across all categories during a given month.
  • Max emphasizes that brands should think beyond Amazon and diversify across TikTok, retail, marketplaces, and direct channels.

Live Shopping and Consumer Habit Formation

  • Will explains that live shopping can become extremely powerful, but only if brands understand that conversion often happens over long time horizons.
  • He compares live shopping behavior to legacy home shopping networks, where consumers may watch repeatedly for months before purchasing.
  • Will notes that audiences build loyalty around specific hosts, making consistency in live-stream talent essential.
  • He references China’s advanced live-commerce ecosystem, including examples of billion-dollar livestream sales events during major shopping holidays.

Brand Perception and Channel Alignment

  • Gia explains that fashion brands must carefully control which products appear on TikTok Shop and how they are presented.
  • She warns that luxury or premium positioning can be damaged if the platform experience feels overly discount-driven or low quality.
  • Gia nevertheless acknowledges that ignoring emerging commerce platforms entirely can be risky because early adopters often gain outsized advantages.

Emerging Platforms and Future Positioning

  • The panel agrees that brands should think three to four years ahead when building infrastructure for live shopping, creator management, and social commerce.
  • YouTube Shopping is mentioned as a developing channel, though panelists currently view its commerce infrastructure and user experience as weaker than TikTok’s.


Affiliates, Creators, and Community Building

Affiliates as an Extension of the Sales Team

  • Max explains that his company manages more than 10,000 affiliates, though the top 10–15% generate the majority of revenue.
  • He stresses that creators require continuous coaching, communication, and relationship management just like internal sales representatives.
  • His team runs regular education sessions, product briefings, and performance conversations with affiliates.

Creator Communities and Training Systems

  • Will highlights that the US TikTok ecosystem outperforms other regions partly because brands invest more heavily in affiliate education and community infrastructure.
  • He encourages brands to use WhatsApp, iMessage, and other direct communication channels to create fast feedback loops with creators.
  • Will explains that offline events and immersive experiences dramatically increase creator loyalty and engagement.

Gifting, Seeding, and Authentic Partnerships

  • Gia describes initially resisting affiliate programs before seeing creators generate significant revenue during Black Friday promotions.
  • Her brand now relies heavily on gifting and seeding to identify creators who genuinely align with the brand aesthetic and values.
  • Gia explains that creators who authentically love the product consistently outperform purely transactional influencer partnerships.

Events, Incentives, and Creator Loyalty

  • The supplement brand hosts quarterly creator events in cities such as Austin, Miami, Los Angeles, and New York.
  • Events often include facility tours and behind-the-scenes access to help creators produce more authentic content.
  • The panel discusses using competitions, prizes, and incentive systems to motivate top affiliates and deepen long-term engagement.
  • They repeatedly caution against treating creators as anonymous metrics inside a dashboard rather than as true brand partners.

Team Structure, Agencies, and Delegation

Team Quality as the Main Growth Lever

  • Max repeatedly states that team quality is the single most important driver of long-term scale.
  • He emphasizes clear KPIs, defined expectations, and strong accountability systems during hiring and probation periods.
  • He explains that even friends or family members are held to performance standards and may be removed if they cannot execute.
  • His leadership philosophy centers on building a company where employees later view it as the most formative workplace experience of their careers.

Delegation and Creative Scale

  • Gia shares that she personally managed Meta advertising for approximately six years before finally hiring an agency.
  • She recognizes that keeping too much responsibility in-house limited testing velocity, creative refresh cycles, and overall growth.
  • Gia explains that delegation became necessary once she realized the business needed more specialized execution to scale efficiently.

Specialized Agencies vs. Generalists

  • The panel strongly recommends hiring specialized agencies rather than broad “full-service” firms.
  • They advise brands to investigate who will actually manage the account daily instead of focusing only on agency case studies or client logos.
  • Strong agency relationships are described as highly collaborative, with rapid communication and direct access to decision-makers on both sides.
  • The panel warns that under-staffed agencies or weak account managers can severely limit growth performance.

Building Dedicated Social Commerce Teams

  • Brands increasingly hire dedicated affiliate managers, live-stream coordinators, creator relationship managers, and TikTok specialists.
  • Gia notes that her small team of six is now expanding to support full-time live shopping and daily TikTok execution.

Product Strategy, Creative Systems, and AI

Hero Products and Sequential Launch Strategy

  • Max advises brands to avoid saturated “me-too” categories and instead dominate focused sub-niches.
  • He believes most brands only have a few true hero products and should avoid spreading creator attention too thin.
  • His strategy is to concentrate all creator energy behind one hero SKU until momentum builds, then rotate focus to the next launch.

Fashion Bundling and Product Expansion

  • Gia explains that fashion upsells center around “complete the look” merchandising strategies.
  • Successful silhouettes are expanded into additional colors, fabrics, and lengths to increase customer lifetime value and wardrobe depth.
  • She uses pre-orders selectively but notes operational challenges when customers need products for time-sensitive occasions.

Bundling and TikTok Shop Fulfillment

  • Max explains that fulfilled-by-TikTok bundles can become expensive when multiple picks are required.
  • To solve this, the company invested in a bundling machine that creates pre-bundled products under a single UPC to reduce pick fees.
  • His team also asks creators which product bundles they want to promote and then operationalizes successful combinations.

Creative Hooks and Content Strategy

  • Food and CPG products rely heavily on strong visual hooks and immediate social proof in the first few seconds of content.
  • Novelty products benefit from humorous creators and highly situational storytelling.
  • Travel products should dramatize the “problem versus solution” experience through realistic travel scenarios and expert validation.

AI and Automation

  • Max uses AI internally for workflow automation, customer support analysis, ERP systems, and repetitive operational processes.
  • His team uses AI to summarize call-center conversations and surface recurring customer pain points.
  • Will’s agency is actively building AI-generated bottom-of-funnel video content to replace low-value repetitive creator videos.

AI Limitations in Fashion

  • Gia explains that AI-generated fashion creatives currently struggle to accurately represent garment fit, texture, and fabric quality.
  • However, her company successfully uses AI for reporting, inventory forecasting, and operational planning.

Overall AI Perspective

  • The panel agrees that AI will not replace strong operators, but operators who effectively use AI will outperform those who do not.
  • AI literacy is framed as becoming increasingly essential for competitive e-commerce teams.

In this session, Max Mikhaylenko, Gia Mezz, and Will August explain how modern e-commerce growth increasingly depends on creator ecosystems, social commerce infrastructure, and operational specialization.


The panel presents TikTok Shop, live shopping, and affiliate programs not as short-term hacks, but as long-term systems requiring disciplined execution, strong relationships, and dedicated teams. 


Across supplements, fashion, and agency operations, the speakers consistently emphasize that sustainable growth comes from focusing on hero products, investing deeply in creators, hiring specialized talent, and using AI to enhance human creativity and decision-making rather than replace it.

items.title: Hack Contest － MDS Inspire 2026 Hack Contest
items.description:
In this session, participants share rapid “hack” presentations in a live contest format to improve profits, cash flow, operations, and marketing performance.
TOPICS:
  1. Pricing, deals, inventory, and reimbursement hacks for Amazon sellers
  2. Marketing, listing optimization, and customer retention strategies
  3. Cash‑flow optimization, AI agents, and custom software tools for scaling businesses
items.description_text: In this session, participants share rapid “hack” presentations in a live contest format to improve profits, cash flow, operations, and marketing performance. TOPICS: Pricing, deals, inventory, and reimbursement hacks for Amazon sellers Marketing, listing optimization, and customer retention strategies Cash‑flow optimization, AI agents, and custom software tools for scaling businesses
cliff_notes:
In this fast-paced MDS session Amazon and e-commerce operators participate in a friendly “hack contest,” sharing quick, tactical strategies designed to improve profitability, efficiency, customer retention, and cash flow. 

Participants present actionable ideas ranging from Amazon listing tactics and reimbursement optimization to AI tooling, Subscribe & Save growth, and credit-card-based cash flow management, while the group informally votes on the strongest hack throughout the call.

Contest Structure and Purpose

  • The session is hosted by Eugene, who frames the call as a rapid-fire “hack contest” where attendees compete by sharing the most valuable tactical ideas.
  • Eugene explains that participants can interrupt at any point with a stronger hack, and whoever maintains the longest “best hack streak” wins premium MDS merchandise.
  • The focus is on simple, high-impact tactics that members can implement quickly to improve status, margins, operational efficiency, or growth.
  • Eugene opens with a travel-status hack involving an American Airlines status match challenge, where proof of elite status from another airline can unlock temporary Executive Platinum benefits and potentially extend status for the remainder of the year.
  • Throughout the session, Eugene continually recaps who currently holds the streak, adding a competitive and entertaining structure to the discussion.

Amazon Pricing, Inventory, and Reimbursement Hacks

Aiden – Deal Control, Returns Badge Removal, and Inventory Age Reset

  • Aiden explains how sellers can selectively prevent low-stock ASIN variations from participating in Amazon Best Deals by setting minimum prices above the promotional deal price.
  • He notes that sellers can strategically toggle variations on or off during deal periods by adjusting minimum prices, helping preserve margins and ASP.
  • Aiden also shares a tactic for removing Amazon’s “frequent returns” badge by creating a new ASIN and FNSKU, slightly modifying the listing content, and then merging it into the parent variation family so reviews remain intact while the badge disappears.
  • Another tactic involves temporarily routing inventory through Woot so the inventory effectively disappears from Seller Central before returning with refreshed inventory age, potentially reducing long-term storage fee exposure.

Chris Holt – Reimbursement Optimization

  • Chris Holt explains that many Amazon reimbursement claims are processed automatically by bots based on submitted sourcing cost data.
  • He uploads revised sourcing costs at approximately 50–60% of retail price, which often increases reimbursement payouts without extensive documentation review.
  • Chris compares Amazon’s current reimbursement baseline against his target sourcing cost and updates only under-valued lines to streamline the process.
  • He estimates that roughly 90% of submissions are automatically accepted, while the remaining cases are manually supported using “master invoices” for each brand.
  • According to Chris, this process can improve reimbursement recovery rates by roughly 10–15%.

Matt and Co-Presenter – Amazon Business and Bulk Services

  • Matt highlights the scale of Amazon Business, describing it as an underutilized B2B opportunity for many sellers.
  • He explains that sellers can create multi-pack configurations tailored to business buyers and leverage Amazon Bulk Services to reduce referral fees by as much as 25%.
  • The presenters discuss configuring special pricing tiers for business segments such as government, education, and startups.
  • They also describe using linked “dummy” or single-unit SKUs to unlock bulk-service fee reductions while maintaining the desired catalog structure.

Marketing, Conversion, and Customer Retention Hacks

Charles – Buy with Prime and Amazon Attribution Abandoned Cart Flow

  • Charles explains that many abandoned-cart sequences underperform because consumers may not fully trust standalone brand websites.
  • His solution routes abandoned-cart users to hidden Buy with Prime-enabled product pages, leveraging Amazon’s trust and checkout experience to improve conversion.
  • When Buy with Prime economics are unfavorable, Charles recommends using Amazon Attribution links so customers still complete purchases on Amazon while the brand earns attribution benefits and referral fee credits.
  • He clarifies that the setup often uses hidden or duplicate product variations accessible only through abandoned-cart emails.

David – AI Listing Optimization with Scalable.so

  • David introduces Scalable.so, an AI-powered tool that analyzes Amazon listings and rapidly generates optimized image concepts and messaging.
  • He demonstrates how the platform identifies customer motivations, conversion blockers, and positioning opportunities while producing refreshed hero images and image stacks.
  • The tool emphasizes use-case imagery and emotional positioning such as gifting, convenience, portability, and family usage scenarios.
  • David notes that while premium agencies may still outperform AI-generated creative slightly in testing, Scalable.so delivers near-agency-quality work at dramatically lower cost and faster turnaround.

Jaime – Scaling Subscribe & Save

  • Jaime shares a strategy focused on aggressively acquiring high-quality Subscribe & Save customers for replenishable products.
  • The approach combines strong introductory discounts with carefully managed creator campaigns through Creator Connections.
  • Jaime reports growing from approximately 11,000 to 22,000 subscribers in one year while maintaining a 65%+ retention rate after 90 days.
  • He emphasizes that long-term customer value dramatically outweighs short-term margin sacrifice, citing subscriber lifetime values far above non-subscriber customers.
  • Jaime also recommends pausing aggressive discounts during inventory shortages to avoid cancellations and lost ranking momentum.
  • He further discusses adapting A+ content to visually communicate realistic product timelines and expectations to improve subscriber retention.

Chad – Wallet-Based Push Notifications with Blurk

  • Chad introduces Blurk, a platform that enables brands to distribute QR-code-triggered wallet passes for Apple Wallet and Google Wallet.
  • Once customers add the branded pass, brands can send unlimited lock-screen push notifications without ongoing SMS costs.
  • Chad explains that brands use these notifications for replenishment reminders, promotions, launches, and clearance campaigns.
  • Because customers voluntarily install the pass, the process operates as an opt-in loyalty or membership experience rather than relying on Amazon customer data extraction.
  • Chad ultimately wins the hack contest with this presentation.

Cash Flow and Financial Optimization Hacks

Josh – Extending the Cash Conversion Cycle

  • Josh explains that cash flow is the primary scaling constraint for many e-commerce businesses and focuses heavily on extending the cash conversion cycle.
  • He recommends maintaining multiple business credit cards with staggered billing cycles so purchases can effectively receive up to roughly 55 days of float.
  • Josh also advises increasing Amazon Ads billing thresholds to reduce billing frequency and extend working capital availability.
  • He references services such as “Plastic” and “Emilio,” which allow supplier invoices to be paid via credit card despite processing fees.
  • Josh details his team’s use of high-reward cards such as:
    • Chase Sapphire Reserve
    • American Express Gold
    • American Express Plum
  • He notes that during Q4, these strategies can significantly reduce reliance on expensive lending products while preserving margins.

Host Add-On – Negative Cash Conversion Cycle

  • Eugene adds that brands can offer delayed-fulfillment discounts on DTC websites, allowing customers to prepay for products they are willing to wait for.
  • This creates a negative cash conversion cycle where the company receives cash before inventory fulfillment occurs, improving liquidity during rapid growth periods.

AI, Automation, and Custom Software Hacks

BJ (Vijay) – “Selfware” and Internal Software Creation

  • BJ introduces the concept of “selfware,” where businesses build highly customized internal software instead of relying entirely on large SaaS providers.
  • He highlights platforms such as:
    • Radian
    • Vercel
    • Replit
    • Lovable
  • BJ explains that users can upload screenshots of dashboards from systems like Sellerboard or NetSuite and instruct AI platforms to recreate consolidated internal tools and interfaces.
  • The workflow allows teams to visually design systems first and then generate working code through iterative prompts and clarifying questions.

Connor Jarvio – Building Effective AI Agents

  • Connor Jarvio explains that truly useful AI agents require three components: “soul,” “memories,” and “skills.”
  • “Soul” refers to foundational files that define brand identity, positioning, tone, and product context.
  • “Memories” are continuously updated operational data sources such as PPC metrics, account notes, and current priorities.
  • “Skills” are reusable workflows that specify how the agent performs structured tasks such as account audits or performance reviews.
  • Connor emphasizes that combining these layers transforms AI from a generic chatbot into a practical operational assistant capable of consistent, repeatable work.

Additional AI Mentions

  • The group notes that tools like ChatGPT are useful for quickly drafting abandoned-cart flows and marketing sequences.
  • David’s Scalable.so example also demonstrates how AI-generated creative can dramatically reduce the time and cost associated with Amazon listing production.

This session delivers a wide-ranging collection of tactical e-commerce hacks covering Amazon pricing strategy, reimbursements, B2B selling, customer retention, cash flow optimization, AI automation, and custom software development. 

The rapid-fire format highlights how experienced operators continuously refine small operational advantages that compound into meaningful improvements in profitability and efficiency.

A recurring theme throughout the session is the growing role of AI and automation—not just for content generation, but for building highly customized workflows, internal tools, and customer engagement systems. 

The conversation also reinforces that operational leverage, cash flow management, and retention strategies remain some of the most important competitive advantages in modern e-commerce.

items.title: Scott Deetz － The Path to Your Biggest Payday － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Scott Deetz explains how entrepreneurs can design their “biggest payday” by planning exits strategically, structuring creative deals, and using capital efficiently.
TOPICS:
1. Strategic exit planning using lanes, levers, and timing lifts
2. Financial readiness, working capital, and investor deal structuring
3. Using acquisitions, creative financing, and team incentives to grow enterprise value
items.description_text: In this session, Scott Deetz explains how entrepreneurs can design their “biggest payday” by planning exits strategically, structuring creative deals, and using capital efficiently. TOPICS: 1. Strategic exit planning using lanes, levers, and timing lifts 2. Financial readiness, working capital, and investor deal structuring 3. Using acquisitions, creative financing, and team incentives to grow enterprise value
cliff_notes:
In this session Scott Deetz presents a structured approach to achieving an entrepreneur’s “biggest payday” through thoughtful exit planning and strategic transactions.

The discussion focuses on how different deal structures, financial preparation, and creative capital strategies can significantly increase business value over time.

Mindset and Fundamentals of Your “Biggest Payday”

  • Scott emphasizes that more than half of an entrepreneur’s lifetime financial reward typically comes from the exit, not from annual operating profits.
  • The session highlights that inventory-based businesses constantly reinvest in stock and new products, which limits take-home cash during the years of operation.
  • Scott states that every business ultimately faces one of four outcomes: the owner dies, the business fails, the owner runs it indefinitely, or the owner exits.
  • The concept of “value enablement” is introduced, which combines operational improvements with corporate development activities to produce quantum lifts in valuation.
  • Scott explains that many entrepreneurs spend less than two hours per week on exit planning despite exits representing the majority of potential earnings.

Exit “Lanes,” Payment “Levers,” and Timing “Lifts”

  • Scott categorizes exits into six “lanes,” including raising venture debt, doing preferred equity deals, bringing in minority investors, selling a majority stake while rolling equity, completing cash deals with earn-outs, and pursuing all-cash exits.
  • He explains that these lanes are not mutually exclusive and that entrepreneurs can sequence or combine them over several years to optimize outcomes.
  • The concept of “levers” describes the different ways a seller gets paid, such as cash at closing, holdbacks, seller financing, stabilization payments, earn-outs, rolled equity in their own company, and equity in the buyer’s company.
  • Scott stresses that a sophisticated exit strategy looks at the full mix of levers, not just the headline cash-at-closing number.
  • The concept of “lifts” refers to timing and scenario planning, where sellers build worst case, base case, and synergistic (best case in the right buyer’s hands) scenarios to decide when to exit.
  • Scott advises that owners aim to sell just before the peak rather than at the visible peak, because buyers become wary when growth appears to flatten.

Financial Readiness and Working Capital Discipline

  • Scott stresses that sellers must have accurate and buyer-ready financial statements, including income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement.
  • He explains that buyers often want financials presented differently from how owners currently keep them, and reclassification or recategorization can positively influence perceived value.
  • The concept of net working capital is defined as inventory investment relative to revenue, such as carrying $1 million of inventory on $5 million of revenue (20%).
  • Scott clarifies that when revenue grows, working capital requirements grow, and owners must plan for the additional cash needed to support inventory expansion.
  • He notes that understanding working capital is “table stakes” for exit readiness, because it affects both valuation and the ability to sustain growth.
  • Scott explains that his firm, Northbound Group, routinely helps entrepreneurs recast financials in a format that aligns with how sophisticated buyers evaluate businesses.

Raising Capital and Structuring Investor Deals

  • Scott presents a real case study in which Northbound Group raises $200,000 for a startup company that exists only on paper and has no current revenue.
  • The valuation for this startup is based on next year’s expected earnings (e.g., $800,000 of profit), resulting in a pre-money valuation of about $1.5 million.
  • An equity investor receives 12% ownership for the $200,000 injection, which provides the founder with capital to grow and a modest salary of about $5,000 per month.
  • Scott explains the principle of accretion, where giving up 12–15% equity is acceptable if the capital enables much faster growth and ultimately increases the absolute value retained by the founder.
  • A performance adjustment mechanism allows the investor to receive more equity (up to 15%) if the company underperforms against the $800,000 target, with a capped maximum equity allocation.
  • A strategic advisory layer gives the investor an opportunity to earn up to an additional 5% equity (to 17% total) if they help the business reach higher earnings, such as $1.6 million, by opening new channels or opportunities.
  • The deal is structured with pro rata vesting rather than cliffs, so equity increments align with performance across the earnings range.
  • An “out clause” at 12 months allows termination of the advisory contract and reduction of future equity accrual if either party is not satisfied with the relationship.
  • Scott notes that the equity is structured using restricted stock units rather than simple stock options to position the investor for capital gains treatment and potentially leverage QSBS / Section 1202 tax advantages.
  • He explains that stacking equity capital alongside debt becomes easier after raising initial equity, because lenders are more comfortable providing inventory financing when equity is already in the business.

Buying Companies, Creative Deal Structures, and Team Incentives

  • Scott states that most eight-figure exits he sees involve more than one owner, often a founder and a Chief Operating Officer or partner, underlining the importance of shared equity and team incentives.
  • He notes there are at least six ways to incentivize team members, such as equity, profit-sharing, bonuses, or structured stock units, and that choosing the right mix is critical for retention and alignment.
  • A case study shows a company with $800,000 of EBITDA and a 4x multiple (a $3.2 million valuation) being acquired with highly creative terms that minimize upfront cash.
  • In that deal, 40% of the purchase price is contingent (earn-out style), 10% is paid in equity in the combined “topco,” and 45% is structured as a seller note, leaving only about 5% payable at closing.
  • Scott explains that the buyer uses the target’s own cash flow to service the seller note, effectively financing the acquisition from the acquired company’s earnings.
  • The seller note is unsecured, with no personal guarantees, and carries 6% interest with a 12% default rate, which is still cheaper than typical acquisition financing at 14–15%.
  • The payment terms cap note payments at 50% of cash flow so that if performance is slower than expected, the note amortization extends rather than forcing immediate distress.
  • Scott stresses that understanding the math behind accretive deals is crucial, because well-structured acquisitions can pay for themselves within a couple of years and significantly increase enterprise value.
  • He highlights that the trust between buyer and seller in this case comes from a prior relationship and demonstrated operating capability, making the seller comfortable with contingent and deferred payments.
  • Scott advises buyers to position themselves as strong operators—“anti-aggregators”—who can reassure sellers that performance-based payments and earn-outs are realistic and attainable.
  • A long-term example is given where an MDS member’s company value grows from about $2 million to over $60 million in three and a half years by combining multiple transactions: mergers, partner buyouts, bringing in a partner, and raising $5 million in capital.

MDS M&A Channel and Ongoing Learning

  • Scott announces the launch of the MDS M&A Channel, a monthly 90-minute session for MDS members focused on deal structures and real case studies.
  • Each session dedicates approximately 45 minutes to structured content and 45 minutes to live discussion of real deals participants are facing.
  • Scott invites attendees to join a WhatsApp group via a QR code to receive the invite and participate in the series.
  • He mentions that the first session is scheduled for March 24 at noon Central, and subsequent sessions are planned as recurring monthly calls.
  • The goal of the channel is to give entrepreneurs a practical “deals MBA” by exposing them to diverse structures, when to use them, and which structures can create significant risk if executed poorly.
  • Scott reinforces that understanding constraints—team, cash, talent, and product development speed—allows entrepreneurs to select the right combination of capital raises, joint ventures, acquisitions, and exits to reach their biggest payday.

In this session, Scott Deetz provides a detailed, practitioner-level overview of how entrepreneurs can design exits and transactions to create their largest financial outcomes. 


The talk reframes exits as a series of strategic options—lanes, levers, and lifts—rather than a single event at the end of a company’s life.


By combining disciplined financial preparation, creative capital raising, intelligent acquisition structures, and team incentives, owners can substantially increase enterprise value while managing risk. 


The ongoing MDS M&A Channel is positioned as a forum where members can continue to deepen their understanding of these deal strategies and apply them to real-world situations.

items.title: Fernando Becattini, Matthew Greene  & Alex Yale － The Truth About Retail: Fit, Placement & Survival － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Fernanda, Matthew and Alex share how Amazon-focused businesses can expand into brick-and-mortar retail without hurting their online channels.
TOPICS:
1. Evaluating product fit for retail
2. Managing channel conflict between Amazon and retail
3. Handling retail operations and relationships
items.description_text: In this session, Fernanda, Matthew and Alex share how Amazon-focused businesses can expand into brick-and-mortar retail without hurting their online channels. TOPICS: 1. Evaluating product fit for retail 2. Managing channel conflict between Amazon and retail 3. Handling retail operations and relationships
cliff_notes:
In this session, Fernando Becattini, Matthew Greene  & Alex Yale discuss how Amazon-native brands can successfully and sustainably expand into brick-and-mortar retail. 

They share hard-won lessons about product fit, retail economics, operational readiness, and managing channel conflict, especially with Amazon.

Determining Product Fit and Entry Strategy for Retail

  • Fernando explains what retailers look for: innovation, patents, differentiation, and strong margins.
  • He discusses why big-box chains avoid “me-too” products that retailers can easily replicate through private label and overseas sourcing.
  • He advises brands to begin with independent stores or smaller regional chains to learn the retail process and reduce risk before approaching national retailers.
  • He strongly cautions against broad or long-term exclusivity agreements because they can block expansion into other major retailers for years.
  • Matt adds that brands need to use common sense when selecting both the retailer and the specific shelf location inside the store.
  • He notes that being placed in the wrong retailer or wrong aisle can significantly hurt sell-through and damage retailer relationships.
  • Alex reinforces the importance of having a differentiated product and strong marketing story before entering line reviews.

Retail Metrics, Timelines, and Growth Dynamics

  • Fernando explains line reviews, category resets, and why it often takes 12–18 months before a product appears on shelves after buyer approval.
  • He provides examples of acceptable units-per-store-per-week metrics in pet specialty and big-box retail environments.
  • He explains why proving performance in smaller chains first helps convince larger retailers to take a chance on a new product.
  • Matt reinforces that retail growth is “slow and steady,” with long testing periods and relationship-building over time.

Product Placement, Merchandising, and Relationship Building

  • Matt focuses heavily on choosing the correct retailer, aisle, and shelf location so customers naturally discover the product.
  • He shares the example of anti-chafing products performing poorly in a hair-removal aisle because shoppers do not expect to find them there.
  • He emphasizes operational trust: shipping on time, following routing guides, maintaining compliance, and avoiding quality issues.
  • He explains how retail brokers work, including typical commission structures (around 4–5%), reset timing knowledge, and the risks of expensive retainers.
  • Fernando adds that strong brokers should also help brands understand markdowns, retailer fees, and chargebacks before pricing products.
  • Alex notes that once merchandising and operational systems are fully set up, retail can become relatively predictable and low-maintenance outside of annual reviews.

Managing Channel Conflict Between Amazon and Retail

  • Alex explains the risks of channel conflict when the same product is sold at different price points across Amazon and retailers like Walmart.
  • He describes how lower retail pricing can damage Buy Box control and compress Amazon margins.
  • He outlines strategies for differentiating SKUs by size, count, packaging, and configuration (e.g., 24 oz online vs. 20 oz in retail).
  • He explains why simply changing GTINs or UPCs is not enough to avoid price matching and pricing conflicts.
  • He discusses framing cost-per-ounce or cost-per-unit economics so retail buyers see value while Amazon remains profitable.
  • Matt adds tactics such as using different scents, bundled extras, or retailer-specific variations to create more separation between channels.
  • Fernando shares that they have sometimes convinced retailers to honor MAP/IMAP policies tied to Amazon pricing for online listings.

Operational Requirements, Risk Management, and Strategic Policies

  • Alex covers vendor onboarding processes, EDI requirements, and the complexity of retailer compliance systems.
  • He explains increased insurance requirements, including examples such as needing a $10M policy for certain retailers.
  • He discusses packaging and labeling standards, including font sizes, barcode placement, net weight rules, and RFID requirements at Walmart.
  • He breaks down freight terms (freight collect vs. prepaid) and how logistics decisions directly affect margins.
  • He explains that once systems are operational, retail fulfillment can become predictable and routine.
  • He also discusses cooperative hardware groups and challenges related to franchise retailers that may resell on Amazon.
  • Fernando expands on markdown policies, retailer returns, and how slow-moving inventory is handled.
  • He explains why he prefers building his own brand equity instead of producing retailer-owned private label products.
  • He recommends tools like RangeMe and trade shows for buyer outreach while enforcing strict online listing controls.
  • Matt highlights liability and legal risks in personal care categories when entering white-label or retailer-owned product arrangements.
  • He joins the others in warning against broad exclusivity agreements that can block future retail opportunities.

In this session, Fernando, Matthew and Alex present a realistic, operationally detailed picture of what it takes for Amazon-focused brands to expand into retail without damaging their existing online business. 

The discussion highlights that success in retail depends on more than just getting shelf placement — brands must carefully manage pricing, channel differentiation, operational compliance, merchandising, and retailer relationships.

The session ultimately reinforces that sustainable retail expansion requires patience, differentiated products, disciplined execution, and a long-term strategy that balances both Amazon and brick-and-mortar growth.

items.title: Meher Patel － Amazon MCP: Hype vs. Reality － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Meher Patel explains how AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT, powered by MCP (Model Context Protocol), transform Amazon advertising workflows.
TOPICS:
1. How Amazon MCP and Hector MCP differ in context, usability, and plug‑and‑play readiness.
2. Using Hector MCP with Claude to perform advanced performance analysis and automated campaign creation.
3. Building AI agents and workflows to continuously monitor, optimize, and report on Amazon ad performance.
items.description_text: In this session, Meher Patel explains how AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT, powered by MCP (Model Context Protocol), transform Amazon advertising workflows. TOPICS: 1. How Amazon MCP and Hector MCP differ in context, usability, and plug‑and‑play readiness. 2. Using Hector MCP with Claude to perform advanced performance analysis and automated campaign creation. 3. Building AI agents and workflows to continuously monitor, optimize, and report on Amazon ad performance.
cliff_notes:
In this MDS session, Meher Patel explores how AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and MCPs (Model Context Protocols) are transforming Amazon advertising workflows and performance analysis. 

The discussion focuses on the difference between Amazon’s native MCP APIs and Hector MCP, a plug-and-play, context-rich solution designed to make conversational analytics and AI-driven campaign management accessible to advertisers and agencies.

AI Adoption and Understanding MCPs

  • The session opens with a discussion about how many participants actively use AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT and whether they connect systems such as Gmail, Slack, or Notion to these models for workflow automation.
  • Meher uses Gmail as a practical example, explaining that an MCP allows Claude or ChatGPT to access inbox data and perform actions such as summarizing emails from a specific sender or identifying unanswered messages.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) is described as a standardized framework that allows external platforms and software systems to expose data and actions directly to AI models in a plug-and-play format.
  • Meher emphasizes that the true value of MCPs is not simply API connectivity, but the addition of context, structure, and intelligence that helps AI interpret requests correctly and retrieve the right information.
  • The talk positions AI-powered workflows as the next evolution beyond traditional SaaS dashboards, replacing rigid interfaces with conversational “open canvas” interactions where users can ask questions naturally.

Amazon MCP APIs vs. Hector MCP

  • Meher explains that Amazon’s native MCP offering currently functions primarily as a set of APIs, requiring engineering work to authenticate access, build data pipelines, store datasets, and create custom logic layers.
  • In contrast, Hector MCP is presented as a ready-made, plug-and-play MCP system that already includes context, relationships, and structured resources, allowing non-technical users to interact with Amazon Ads data immediately inside Claude or ChatGPT.
  • The session clarifies that Amazon MCP APIs do not inherently contain contextual awareness. For example, they do not automatically understand that a query about “search terms” should reference a search term report rather than a keyword report.
  • Hector MCP addresses this limitation by defining entities such as search terms, campaigns, keywords, ASINs, DSP data, and sponsored ads as structured tools with rich descriptions that help the LLM select the correct dataset.
  • Meher repeatedly stresses that intelligence layered onto the data is what makes an MCP operationally valuable for advertisers and agencies.

Advanced Analytics and Context-Aware Campaign Management

  • Meher demonstrates a workflow where Claude identifies search terms that generated more than 10 orders over the last 30 days for the highest-spend ASINs and then creates single-campaign, single-ad-group, exact-match campaigns for those terms.
  • This example highlights how Hector MCP allows search term data and ASIN data to interact dynamically, enabling analyses and actions that would otherwise require significant manual effort.
  • The session explains that Hector MCP supports comparative analysis workflows, such as evaluating the last seven days against the previous seven days while interpreting “performance” through metrics like ROAS and minimum order volume.
  • Hector MCP includes predefined resources such as a “Health Check” framework so that broad performance questions automatically evaluate relevant KPIs like ROAS and order count before generating conclusions.
  • To optimize the LLM context window, the system selectively passes only the most relevant columns and metrics instead of overwhelming the model with raw report exports.
  • Meher confirms that data retrieved through Hector MCP aligns with the metrics shown in the Hector SaaS platform, ensuring consistency and reliability.

AI Agents and Automated Advertising Workflows

  • The session introduces the idea that the future of advertising operations will revolve around personalized AI agents tailored to specific optimization goals, workflows, and performance targets.
  • One example discussed is a “budget agent” that regularly checks campaigns approaching budget caps and automatically increases budgets for campaigns that exceed predefined ROAS thresholds.
  • Meher notes that similar workflows can already be built using automation platforms like n8n, especially when paired with Hector MCP data access.
  • Another example involves an AI-powered morning PPC health check that identifies the top actions required for the day and posts recommendations into a Slack channel for a PPC manager or agency team.
  • The session highlights the importance of guardrails and contextual understanding when building trustworthy AI agents. For example, DSP workflows may rely on order IDs rather than campaign-level structures.
  • Meher predicts that AI agents will soon become standard operating tools across agencies and brands, fundamentally changing how advertising teams operate.

Getting Started with Hector MCP and Broader Strategic Implications

  • The onboarding process for Hector MCP is described as relatively simple: users sign into Hector, allow approximately 90 minutes for Amazon Ads API synchronization, and then connect Hector to their Claude or ChatGPT environment.
  • Once connected, users can immediately ask natural-language questions such as:
    • “Why did ROAS drop last week?”
    • “Which search terms are under-invested despite strong conversion rates?”
  • Meher contrasts this experience with the significantly heavier engineering effort required to build workflows directly on Amazon MCP APIs.
  • Hector MCP is also positioned as a multi-channel intelligence layer capable of integrating data from Shopify, Meta, and Google alongside Amazon Ads data.
  • The session mentions an introductory pricing offer where the first 50 customers can access Hector MCP for $200 per month during the first three months before pricing is reevaluated.
  • Meher states that more than 300 global brands and agencies are already using Hector MCP to prepare for AI-driven advertising workflows.

This session argues that the next major shift in Amazon advertising will come not from dashboards alone, but from AI systems that combine APIs with context, structured resources, and agentic workflows. 

Meher positions Hector MCP as a practical bridge between raw Amazon Ads data and conversational AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT, enabling advertisers to ask deeper questions, automate repetitive analysis, and execute actions more intelligently.

The broader takeaway is that brands and agencies adopting MCPs, AI agents, and conversational workflows early will gain a significant operational advantage. 

As advertising systems evolve from static interfaces into context-aware AI environments, the ability to combine structured data, automation, and human strategy will increasingly define competitive performance in e-commerce advertising.

items.title: State of Commerce 2026 － Eugene Khayman － Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Eugene Khayman presents a data-driven state of commerce report based on census data from 139 e‑commerce brands, with a strong focus on Amazon-native businesses and emerging channels.
TOPICS:
1. Channel diversification and TikTok Shop performance
2. Growth outlook by brand size and niche (including the 5–10M “danger zone”)
3. Constraints, talent and AI adoption, and founder focus on operations vs. leadership
items.description_text: In this session, Eugene Khayman presents a data-driven state of commerce report based on census data from 139 e‑commerce brands, with a strong focus on Amazon-native businesses and emerging channels. TOPICS: 1. Channel diversification and TikTok Shop performance 2. Growth outlook by brand size and niche (including the 5–10M “danger zone”) 3. Constraints, talent and AI adoption, and founder focus on operations vs. leadership
cliff_notes:
In this session Eugene Khayman presents a data-driven “state of commerce” report based on census data from 139 brands, with a strong focus on Amazon-native e‑commerce businesses. 

The discussion centers on channel diversification, TikTok Shop performance, growth outlook by size and niche, operational constraints, AI adoption, and founder mindset, followed by a brief Q&A.

State of Commerce Overview and Audience Profile

  • Eugene presents a data-driven “state of commerce” report using census responses from 139 brands, primarily focused on Amazon-native e-commerce businesses.
  • AI tools, particularly Anthropic’s Claude, are used to analyze the dataset and dramatically reduce the time required to prepare the report.
  • Eugene emphasizes that the presentation is based on real operating data and practical observations rather than theory.
  • Most brands represented generate between $1 million and $5 million annually, while more than 40% report annual revenue above $10 million.
  • Amazon remains the dominant primary sales channel for the majority of attendees, reflecting the group’s roots as an Amazon-first operator community.
  • Approximately 78% of attendees are members of the community hosting the event, while roughly 20% are non-members, reinforcing the event’s community-driven nature.
  • The report is designed to be distributed afterward through shared slides and recap materials.

Channel Diversification and TikTok Shop Performance

“Always Be Diversifying”

  • Eugene positions channel diversification as the next major operating principle for e-commerce brands, comparing it to the long-standing “always be launching” philosophy.
  • Brands increasingly rely on multiple revenue channels instead of depending exclusively on Amazon.

Secondary Revenue Channels

  • Approximately 55% of brands now generate DTC revenue, 45% actively sell on TikTok Shop, and 35% participate in retail distribution.
  • A “real secondary channel” is defined as one generating more than 15% of total company revenue.
  • One-third of brands in the room have successfully built at least one meaningful secondary channel that contributes above this threshold.
  • Some brands operate multiple significant secondary channels simultaneously.

TikTok Shop Growth and Demand Creation

  • TikTok Shop emerges as one of the strongest-performing growth channels discussed during the session.
  • The median TikTok Shop brand in the room generates approximately $300,000 annually from the platform.
  • Top-performing TikTok brands generate roughly $3 million annually within the top 10 cohort, while the top three brands reportedly reach around $25 million per year on TikTok Shop.
  • TikTok is framed less as a traditional shopping destination and more as a demand-creation engine with significant halo effects across Amazon, DTC, and retail channels.
  • Eugene notes that even strong brands often struggle to push TikTok Shop above 10% of total revenue, but the awareness and demand generation remain highly valuable.

Growth Outlook by Brand Size and Niche

Overall Market Sentiment

  • Despite tariff pressures and broader e-commerce challenges throughout 2025, approximately 78% of brands report feeling optimistic or bullish heading into 2026.
  • Confidence levels strongly correlate with recent growth performance.

The $5–10 Million “Danger Zone”

  • Brands in the $5–10 million revenue range are identified as being in a particularly vulnerable stage.
  • This cohort shows the lowest confidence levels and the weakest expectations for aggressive growth.
  • Only around 17% of brands in this range expect rapid growth, compared with approximately 39% of the broader room.
  • Eugene suggests these businesses often become operationally cautious, psychologically stuck, or overly conservative in strategic decision-making.
  • Lower TikTok adoption among these brands may contribute to slower growth expectations and weaker momentum.

Larger Brand Optimism

  • Brands generating between $20 million and $50 million annually display the strongest optimism.
  • Approximately 57% of these larger operators describe themselves as highly bullish about future growth.

Category and Niche Trends

  • Health, supplements, and beauty categories show the strongest optimism and highest TikTok penetration.
  • Pet brands appear less optimistic than in prior years, potentially due to increasing competition and category saturation.
  • Sports and outdoors is described as an underrated or “sleeper” category with meaningful growth optimism.
  • Baby-related categories appear more distressed, with weaker TikTok adoption and lower confidence overall.

Constraints, Strategy Shifts, and AI Adoption

Team Talent Remains the Biggest Constraint

  • Despite growing excitement around AI, the largest operational constraint remains talent and team quality.
  • Founders still require capable operators, leaders, and execution-focused employees to scale effectively.

Platform Risk and Operational Pressure

  • Amazon platform risk continues to create major anxiety due to sudden policy changes and traffic volatility.
  • Brands also cite demand softness, supply-chain uncertainty, and inventory planning challenges as major concerns.

Shift Away From Spray-and-Pray Marketing

  • Many companies are reducing indiscriminate influencer sampling and focusing instead on more measurable, ROI-driven creator partnerships.
  • Heavy discounting is also becoming less popular as brands seek healthier long-term margins and stronger brand positioning.

Emerging Channels Beyond Amazon

  • TikTok Shop is repeatedly identified as the strongest outperforming emerging channel, especially when paired with creator affiliate systems.
  • Walmart is also gaining traction as an important growth opportunity for brands seeking diversification.
  • Owned retention channels such as email and SMS remain highly important, particularly for brands in the $10–20 million range looking to maximize existing customer value.

AI and Organizational Structure

  • Larger brands increasingly hire senior leaders or specialists to oversee AI initiatives strategically rather than having founders operate tools directly.
  • Smaller brands are more experimental and hands-on, often redesigning workflows or replacing junior functions using AI tools.
  • Eugene notes that overseas virtual assistants and certain repetitive junior roles may face increasing disruption if they do not provide unique operational value.
  • Strong integrators, analysts, lifecycle marketers, and operational leaders are described as highly undervalued roles in modern e-commerce organizations.

Founder Mindset, Growth Patterns, and Q&A Insights

Leadership Focus and Delegation

  • Founders are roughly divided between those who remain deeply operational and those who focus primarily on leadership and delegation.
  • The discussion highlights that growth often requires transitioning from operator to systems builder and strategic leader.

Growth Data and Confidence Correlation

  • Median year-over-year growth across respondents is approximately 18%.
  • Roughly 66% of brands are growing, while about 34% remain flat or are declining.
  • Brands that performed well in the previous year tend to report significantly higher confidence about future growth.

“Diversify or Die Slowly”

  • Eugene summarizes the session’s central lesson as “diversify or die slowly.”
  • The presentation repeatedly reinforces that channel diversification is becoming essential for long-term resilience and sustainable growth.

TikTok and Demand Creation

  • Eugene contrasts Amazon’s historically fixed-demand mindset with TikTok’s ability to actively generate and amplify consumer demand around products.
  • TikTok Shop demonstrates that strong creator ecosystems can unlock demand levels many Amazon-native operators previously underestimated.

Q&A Discussion on the $5–10 Million Plateau

  • During Q&A, attendees explore why the $5–10 million range appears particularly difficult.
  • Contributors suggest that inventory financing pressure, cautious decision-making, and weak channel diversification often trap brands in this stage.
  • Participants recommend setting significantly larger goals, reverse-engineering systems for scale, and accepting calculated short-term risks to break through the plateau.
  • One contributor advises founders to avoid chasing generic AI hype and instead focus on clearly mapping workflows, rules, and processes before implementing automation tools.


This session presents a detailed snapshot of Amazon-native brands navigating a rapidly evolving commerce landscape increasingly shaped by TikTok Shop, DTC expansion, retail diversification, and AI-driven operational changes.

The strongest-performing brands are those investing in channel diversification, creator-led demand generation, operational discipline, and high-quality talent.

At the same time, the discussion highlights that many mid-sized brands—especially those in the $5–10 million range—face unique operational and psychological challenges that can stall growth if not addressed proactively.

Ultimately, the session argues that future winners will be brands capable of combining diversified distribution, strong operators, thoughtful AI adoption, and disciplined execution into a resilient multi-channel growth strategy.

items.title: AI‑Driven SEO and Amazon Strategies for Surviving a Changing Marketplace － SEO Channel Call April 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants discuss how recent changes in Google and Amazon algorithms impact SEO, advertising, and brand growth.
TOPICS:
1. Google SEO shifts toward opinionated, expert-driven content and domain authority.
2. Amazon marketplace challenges, Prime Day economics, and the need for outside traffic.

items.description_text: In this session, participants discuss how recent changes in Google and Amazon algorithms impact SEO, advertising, and brand growth. TOPICS: 1. Google SEO shifts toward opinionated, expert-driven content and domain authority. 2. Amazon marketplace challenges, Prime Day economics, and the need for outside traffic. 3. cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss how rapid changes in Google and Amazon algorithms affect SEO advertising, and brand-building strategies. 

They also explore how AI tools and custom frameworks can optimize listings, content, and decision-making while acknowledging the complexity and risks involved.

 

Google SEO Shifts and Content Strategy

  • Google now penalizes generic AI content and rewards human opinions and unique perspectives
  • Eli uses an AI tool trained on his voice but manually approves all outputs
  • Content with expertise and opinion now outperforms purely informational content
  • Shorter, opinion-driven articles outperform long 4,000-word posts
  • SEO traffic dipped recently but is recovering with updated strategy
  • Google favors novel phrasing and original insights over recycled content
  • Domain Authority has become more important after backlink cleanups
  • Publishing around 60 articles per month is treated as a long-term investment
  • Keyword stuffing is no longer necessary as Google understands context

 

Amazon SEO and Marketplace Economics

  • Amazon increasingly mirrors Google by prioritizing customer preferences and intent
  • The platform is more pay-to-play, with $40K to $45K often needed to launch a product
  • Around 30 to 35 percent of launch budgets now go to ads
  • Launching with $10K is no longer realistic in most categories
  • Brands protect margins by raising prices and offering premium versions
  • Operators diversify into other channels, B2B, and retail to reduce Amazon reliance
  • Rising fees and costs are squeezing smaller sellers
  • Amazon currently rewards external traffic from SEO and content
  • Sending traffic back to Amazon sacrifices customer ownership but may boost ranking
  • Some brands scale by dominating one channel at a time before expanding

 

Prime Day and Promotional Strategy

  • Prime Day often requires discounts of around 30 percent
  • Deal types include Top Deals, Best Deals, and Lightning Deals
  • Lightning Deals now perform the weakest
  • Best Deals provide moderate visibility to active Prime shoppers
  • Top Deals drive the highest lift, sometimes 9 to 12 times normal sales
  • Top Deals are less exclusive but still outperform other formats
  • Prime Exclusive Discount visibility may decrease
  • Profitability is pressured by deep discounts, fees, and ad costs
  • Strong margins are required to benefit from Prime Day

 

AI Tools for SEO and Listing Optimization

  • Shopify AI helps analyze traffic, sales, and geography in one place
  • It replaces much of the need for manual Google Analytics analysis
  • AI assists with site structure but still requires developer cleanup
  • Common SEO tools include Ubersuggest, AnswerThePublic, Similarweb, and Google Trends
  • Product opportunities are identified by demand, ranking difficulty, and content gaps
  • AI search and keyword expansion reduce the need for manual keyword targeting
  • Advanced tools aggregate Amazon data including rankings, PPC, and competitor insights
  • AI can combine datasets and generate reports in minutes instead of hours
  • Image optimization tools help replicate high-performing creative patterns
  • AI tools require human validation before publishing or scaling changes

 

AI Frameworks and Amazon Playbooks

  • Sellers are building AI systems that encode years of experience into structured frameworks
  • These systems analyze accounts and identify issues like ranking drops or inventory risk
  • Inventory levels can directly impact visibility even when ads perform well
  • Relaunch campaigns require at least 16 to 21 days to be effective
  • Structured relaunch frameworks define actions by timeline and budget
  • AI can generate detailed, per-ASIN action plans for optimization
  • Knowledge bases and rule systems improve AI output quality
  • Automated listing updates require caution, especially in regulated categories
  • Human review is critical to avoid errors and compliance issues
  • Effective AI systems require clean data, strong logic, and validation layers
  • Adversarial checks help reduce hallucinations and improve accuracy

 

In this session, the group highlights how quickly search and marketplaces are evolving, forcing brands to rethink content, pricing, and channel strategies. 

Success now depends on combining human judgment with AI tools rather than relying on outdated tactics.

In conclusion, participants emphasize that external traffic, authority-driven content, and well-designed AI systems are becoming essential for success on both Amazon and Google. 

While AI increases speed and efficiency, it also introduces complexity that requires careful design, validation, and ongoing human oversight.

items.title: Why Profitable E-Commerce Brands Still Run Out of Cash and How to Fix It － Nadav Gorlicki － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Nadav Gorlicki of Capec discusses how to manage cash flow in inventory-heavy e‑commerce businesses.
 
TOPICS:
  1. Cash flow fundamentals for inventory-based Amazon and e‑commerce businesses
  2. Comparison of financing options (banks, revenue-based financing, MCAs, Amazon Lending, inventory financing)
  3. Best practices and Capec’s model for aligning financing with purchase orders and sales cycles
