files.name: MDS Mogul Call with Nadav Gorlicki - Transcript
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1775701816953-MDS Mogul Call with Nadav Gorlicki.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS community meet with Nadav Gorlicki from Capec to discuss cash flow challenges and financing solutions for inventory-heavy e-commerce businesses. 

 

The conversation focuses on structuring financing to align with real-world inventory timelines reduce risk, and support sustainable growth.

 

MDS Community Updates and Call Setup
  • Jamie Graham shares that the MDS app has recent updates and encourages members to update via the Apple App Store or Google Play Store to access improved features and recordings. 
  • He highlights the Inspire Live event and notes that booking early tickets, flights, and hotels in advance helps reduce costs. 
  • Jamie describes the MDS WhatsApp broadcast channel as a low-noise group where weekly Mogul Call topics and reminders are shared. 
  • He introduces Capec as the guest and emphasizes the importance of cash flow for inventory-based businesses such as Amazon and e-commerce brands. 
  • He also mentions that MDS members receive a 10 percent discount with Capec. The group briefly discusses real-world financing, including Jamie referencing his experience with HSBC.

 

Cash Flow Fundamentals and Inventory Challenges
  • Nadav shares that he has built six brands, has 12 years of e-commerce experience, and founded Capec four years ago to help sellers manage inventory-related cash flow.
  • He explains that 32 percent of businesses fail due to cash flow issues, even when revenue and profit look strong. 
  • Fast-growing e-commerce businesses often face negative cash flow because larger purchase orders require upfront capital before previous inventory generates returns. 
  • A typical timeline includes deposit payments, final supplier payments, shipping, and ad spend, with returns often taking 90 to 180 days. 
  • Sellers frequently need to place the next purchase order before recovering returns from the previous one. 
  • Even profitable businesses face strain due to timing mismatches between cash inflows and outflows. Inventory and advertising are the main drivers of capital needs.

 

Types of Financing for E-commerce Inventory

 

Nadav outlines several financing options including banks, revenue-based financing, merchant cash advances, Amazon Lending, and inventory financing.

 

  • Bank Loans and Lines of Credit 
    • Bank financing offers the lowest cost but is slower and less accessible for newer businesses. 
    • It typically requires a personal guarantee, exposing personal assets. It is better suited for long-term growth rather than short-term inventory cycles.

 

  • Revenue-Based Financing and Amazon Lending
    • Revenue-based financing can work well for short-term uses like advertising, where returns come quickly. 
    • It is less suitable for inventory because repayments begin before inventory generates revenue. 
    • This can create cash flow pressure. Amazon Lending, often provided through partners such as Goldman Sachs, should be evaluated similarly by carefully modeling repayment timing.

 

  • Merchant Cash Advances
    • Merchant cash advances involve fixed daily or weekly repayments that do not adjust to revenue fluctuations. 
    • This can strain cash flow during slower sales periods or account issues and may lead to a cycle of taking on new debt to repay existing obligations.

 

  • Inventory Financing
    • Effective inventory financing aligns directly with purchase orders and inventory cycles.
    • Nadav explains that Capec finances up to 80 percent of a purchase order, including production, shipping, and customs. 
    • Payments are structured according to supplier terms, with a grace period before repayment begins. 
    • Repayments are then spread over three to six months based on actual sales. Proper alignment allows sellers to finance inventory and repay it as it sells.

 

Best Practices for Cash Flow Management

 

  • Nadav emphasizes that aligning cash inflows and outflows is critical. 
  • Sellers should understand timelines for each product, including production, shipping, and sell-through. 
  • Weekly cash flow reviews are recommended instead of relying only on profit and loss statements. Improving supplier payment terms can significantly extend cash runway. 
  • Placing smaller, more frequent orders can reduce capital tied up in inventory. 
  • He highlights that internal capital has an opportunity cost and could be used for other growth initiatives. 
  • Using external financing without personal guarantees can reduce risk. 
  • Maintaining a bank line of credit provides a safety net. 
  • Sellers should secure financing before it is needed, as last-minute options are often more expensive and less flexible.

 

Capec Criteria and Support
  • Capec typically requires at least one year of selling history, six months of product history, and approximately 200,000 to 300,000 dollars in annual revenue. 
  • The company works with sellers globally who sell in the US or Europe. 
  • Capec does not rely on personal guarantees or credit scores, instead focusing on product performance and unit economics. 
  • Pricing is a fixed fee typically between 7 and 13 percent over three to six months. 
  • Capec may selectively finance only profitable products and can provide support such as logistics or advertising partner introductions. 
  • The company aims to build long-term relationships and may assist in selling inventory if issues arise.

 

In the Q and A, Gary Kane asks about costs and setup, and Nadav confirms the 7 to 13 percent range. Jamie asks about Amazon Lending, and Nadav advises evaluating repayment timing carefully. When asked about struggling businesses, Nadav notes that Capec may still support profitable products or provide guidance.

items.title: How to Prepare for a Business Exit with M&A Value Creation and Deal Structuring－Scott Deetz－Mergers & Acquisition Channel Call March 2026
items.description:
In this session, Scott Deetz and MDS members kick off the Mergers & Acquisitions Channel by explaining why most wealth is created at exit, how to plan for that exit, and what real deal structures look like for e‑commerce founders.
TOPICS:
  1. Why most wealth is made at exit (80/20 rule)
  2. How to plan and build value to increase earnings and multiples
  3. Real deal structures (LOIs, rolled equity, call options) and buy/sell strategies
items.description_text: In this session, Scott Deetz and MDS members kick off the Mergers & Acquisitions Channel by explaining why most wealth is created at exit, how to plan for that exit, and what real deal structures look like for e‑commerce founders. TOPICS: Why most wealth is made at exit (80/20 rule) How to plan and build value to increase earnings and multiples Real deal structures (LOIs, rolled equity, call options) and buy/sell strategies
cliff_notes:
This session kicks off the MDS Mergers & Acquisitions Channel focusing on how e-commerce entrepreneurs can plan and execute high-value exits. Scott Deetz and the Northbound Group team cover core M&A concepts value creation planning, and real-world deal structures.

 

1. Introductions & Purpose
  • Scott Deetz opens the session and introduces Northbound Group, an M&A advisory firm specializing in e-commerce.
  • Northbound has completed $750M+ in transactions, including $200M+ with MDS members.
  • Scott emphasizes his mission: helping founders maximize value at exit.
  • He shares his background, including improving his own exit outcome with mentorship.
  • Team introductions:
    • Bill Sterry – works with clients and active deals (LOIs)
    • Zach Luke – VP, supports clients from start to close
  • Additional participant intros include operators and M&A professionals from the MDS community.
  • Purpose of the channel:
    • Provide practical M&A education
    • Support both buy-side and sell-side opportunities
    • Share real deal structures and frameworks
  • Monthly calls + WhatsApp group will support ongoing learning.

 

2. 80/20 Rule #1 – Wealth Is Realized at Exit
  • Most founders receive 50–66%+ of lifetime after-tax wealth at exit.
  • “Me account” = personal, after-tax cash actually received.
  • Lifetime value includes:
    • Past distributions
    • Future pre-exit distributions
    • Exit proceeds (cash, earn-outs, equity, etc.)
  • Reasons exit drives wealth:
    • Constant reinvestment into inventory and growth
    • Hiring reduces distributable cash
    • Expansion into new channels/geographies requires capital
    • Exit proceeds often taxed more favorably than income
  • Key takeaway:
    • Not planning an exit = leaving significant wealth unrealized
Possible paths for founders:
  1. Run business indefinitely
  2. Business declines or fails
  3. Stay stuck operating
  4. Execute a strategic exit
  • Alternative: “Exit to yourself” (e.g., structured internal buyout)

 

3. 80/20 Rule #2 – Corporate Development Drives Value
  • ~80% of major exit value often comes from pre-exit deal activity, not just operations.
Corporate development includes:
  • Debt financing
  • Minority equity raises
  • Partner buyouts
  • Joint ventures (JVs)
  • Executive incentive structures
Key insights:
  • Many large exits follow strategic capital + partnership moves before sale
  • Poorly structured JVs are common (e.g., uneven workload in 50/50 splits)
  • Incentives (equity, bonuses, RSUs) align key team members with exit outcomes
Buyer mindset:
  • Buyers are the “end customer”
  • Businesses must be built for acquirability
  • Buyers need to see future upside (e.g., 3–5x growth potential)
Illustrative case:
  • $2M business → partner buyout → minority investment + credit line → strategic merger → $50M+ exit
  • Compared to early exit, structured growth can yield ~10x higher personal outcome

 

4. Value Creation Planning
  • A structured approach focused on increasing enterprise value, not just revenue.
Process:
  1. Establish baseline valuation
  2. Build a strategy to improve:
    • EBITDA (earnings)
    • Valuation multiple
  3. Focus on key drivers:
    • Quality of earnings
    • Diversification
    • Defensibility
    • Scalability
  4. Translate into an execution plan (tasks, owners, timelines)
  5. Enter growth phase (may include deals, hires, capital raises)
  6. Prepare for exit (“stage the business” for buyers)
Framework:
  • Value = EBITDA × Multiple
  • Goal: grow both simultaneously
Key gap identified:
  • Many founders want to exit within 2–3 years
  • Few spend meaningful time on exit planning
Solution:
  • Monthly sessions + WhatsApp discussions to drive consistent focus

 

5. Deal Structures & Execution
5.1 LOI Example (Letter of Intent)
  • Example: 4× EBITDA valuation
  • EBITDA scenarios affect final price (TTM adjustments)
  • Structure:
    • Buyer acquires 60% upfront
    • Seller retains 40% (rolled equity)
    • ~75% cash at closing
    • ~25% deferred (performance-based reserve)
Call Option:
  • Buyer can purchase remaining 40% later
  • Typically at predefined multiple (often negotiated higher)
Key insight:
  • Don’t focus only on the multiple—structure matters just as much

 

5.2 Key Terms
  • EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization
  • Adjusted EBITDA: Includes add-backs/normalizations
  • Rolled equity: Seller retains ownership for future upside
Important metrics:
  • Guaranteed value (low risk)
  • Total potential value (includes upside + contingencies)

 

5.3 Buy-Side Opportunities
Types of acquisitions:
  • Distressed businesses (near inventory value)
  • Undervalued businesses (owner fatigue or capability gaps)
  • Premium businesses (high-quality, higher multiples)
Deal sourcing:
  • Networks (e.g., MDS)
  • Direct outreach to competitors
  • Off-market opportunities
  • Not just marketplaces like Flippa
Expanded scope:
  • Agencies, service providers, and tech-enabled businesses

 

5.4 Negotiation & Strategy
  • Negotiation is a critical but underdeveloped skill
Framework:
  • Lanes: Deal types (full sale, partial, JV, etc.)
  • Levers: Terms (cash, earn-outs, equity, etc.)
  • Lifts: Performance over time
Key principles:
  • Sell while business is growing
  • Buyers discount flat or declining performance
  • Structure deals to balance risk vs. upside
Other notes:
  • AI is becoming increasingly important in M&A positioning
  • Buyers value tech-enabled and AI-leveraged businesses

TOPICS:
1. Building Mini Katana and other brands through YouTube and short‑form organic content

items.description_text: In this session, Isaac Medeiros shares how he builds and scales brands like Mini Katana by using YouTube and short‑form content as powerful discovery and distribution channels. TOPICS: 1. Building Mini Katana and other brands through YouTube and short‑form organic content 2. Using metrics like stay‑to‑watch, TAM, and outlier analysis to shape high‑performing videos 3. Practical content strategies from the Q&A, including niches, SEO vs recommendations, and ad usage
cliff_notes:
In this session, Isaac Medeiros shares how he builds and scales multiple brands using YouTube and short-form content as discovery and distribution engines. 

 

He explains practical strategies, key metrics, and frameworks to grow audience, revenue, and retail opportunities.

 

Mini Katana and YouTube as a Discovery Engine

  • Isaac explains that YouTube has massive reach and now competes with or exceeds traditional TV in audience size.
  • He starts Mini Katana in 2020 with a samurai letter opener that quickly sells out.
  • He scales using Meta ads until the account is banned, forcing a shift to organic content.
  • Early TikTok videos go viral and sell out inventory even without links.
  • By 2021, the brand reaches 1 million followers and becomes a seven-figure business using organic content only.
  • In 2022, he expands to YouTube and grows to about 30 million subscribers across channels.
  • Ad revenue eventually covers content costs, making content production sustainable.
  • He exits the business in Q4, showing the value of YouTube-driven growth.

 

Content, Distribution, and Multi-Channel Expansion

  • Content and distribution are different, and expanding distribution increases the value of content.
  • He repurposes English content into Spanish, growing a new channel to about 7 million subscribers.
  • He launches Kanpai Foods and uses YouTube for product discovery.
  • The brand secures nationwide placement in Target because of brand awareness from YouTube.
  • He partners with Going to build content studios in Europe and Japan.
  • Their travel content gains millions of views quickly and builds a strong audience.
  • His team runs multiple channels, showing that the model works across different niches.

 

Key Metrics and Frameworks

  • The most important metric in short-form content is stay-to-watch rate.
  • A rate of 70% to 78% often leads to 10 million or more views, while below 50% is weak.
  • High-performing videos can reach over 80% stay-to-watch, which is rare at scale.
  • Teams should test different hooks and improve based on this metric.
  • Content also has a total addressable market, meaning some topics have broader appeal.
  • MrBeast is an example of targeting a wide audience.
  • Outlier videos perform 10 to 20 times better than average and reveal strong ideas.
  • Creators should study outliers and adapt them to their own niche.
  • Algorithms now focus on interests, so even new accounts can go viral.

 

Audience Funnel and Short-Form Strategy

  • Audiences move from new viewers to regular viewers to loyal fans.
  • Content should target all stages of this funnel.
  • YouTube Analytics helps track audience behavior and guide strategy.
  • Short-form content can be reused across multiple platforms.
  • Key platforms include YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels, Snapchat, Pinterest, and X.
  • The main platform you focus on shapes your content style and results.
  • Peachy Babies is an example of a brand succeeding on YouTube with very high monthly views.
  • Each platform has a different audience, but YouTube offers the widest reach.

 

Practical Q&A and Execution

  • SEO-based content alone often leads to average results because it relies on search, not recommendations.
  • Strong ideas, titles, and thumbnails are key to triggering the recommendation system.
  • Creators should plan ideas first before producing content.
  • Political content performs well due to high engagement.
  • Boardwalk is an example of fast growth using this approach.
  • Tools like TubeBuddy help track trends and outliers.
  • Flyover News grows by posting daily trending content and scaling winners.
  • Some brands run ads on winning videos, while others focus on organic growth first.
  • ReSpark uses both organic content and ads for scaling.

 

YouTube and short-form content can be used to build, scale, and exit brands.

 

Success comes from strong distribution, understanding audience behavior, and consistent testing.

 

Focusing on key metrics, using outlier ideas, and aligning content with how people watch and share leads to long-term growth.

items.title: Bryce Alderson － Balancing Market Share vs. Margin － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Bryce Alderson explains how Amazon brands can shift from aggressive growth to healthy profitability using a data-driven framework.
 
TOPICS:
1. Defining when a product is in growth mode vs. profit (margin) mode  
2. Using SQP data (impression, click, and purchase share) to guide ad spend and pricing decisions  
3. Applying a five-step framework and real ASIN case study to reduce cannibalization and increase profit
items.description_text: In this session, Bryce Alderson explains how Amazon brands can shift from aggressive growth to healthy profitability using a data-driven framework. TOPICS: 1. Defining when a product is in growth mode vs. profit (margin) mode 2. Using SQP data (impression, click, and purchase share) to guide ad spend and pricing decisions 3. Applying a five-step framework and real ASIN case study to reduce cannibalization and increase profit
cliff_notes:
In this session, Bryce Alderson shares a practical framework for balancing market share and profit margins for Amazon brands. Using real data from his supplement business, he shows how to move from growth mode to profit mode at the parent ASIN level.

 

1. Overall Goal: Balancing Market Share and Margin

  • Brands must choose between maximizing market share or margin, not both at the same time.
  • This decision should be made at the parent ASIN level, not the overall brand.
  • Each product starts from zero and requires careful resource allocation.
  • Many brands fund new launches using profits from existing products.
  • Most sellers lack a clear framework for when to shift from growth to profit.
  • The goal is to make data-driven decisions instead of reactive ones.

2. Framework and Required Data

 

Who This Is For

  • Designed for Amazon-focused brands managing products at the ASIN level.
  • Not suitable for weak listings with poor conversion or low reviews.
  • Less practical for very large catalogs that rely heavily on automation.

 

Step 1: Build a Central Data Table

  • Combine key metrics like revenue, PPC spend, ACoS, price, and profit.
  • Include market share data such as impression share, click share, and purchase share.
  • Focus on top keywords that drive most revenue.
  • Build separate views for each main keyword.

 

Step 2: Define the Current Phase

  • Decide if the product is in growth mode or profit mode.
  • Growth focuses on gaining share, profit focuses on improving margins.

Step 3: Identify Pivot Triggers

  • Growth starts to slow after strong performance.
  • Ad efficiency declines and ACoS increases.
  • TACOS stays high despite strong organic ranking.
  • Impression share approaches a ceiling.
  • Competitors are close in market share, increasing risk.

 

Step 4: Choose One Lever

  • Either reduce ad spend or increase price.
  • Change only one variable at a time.
  • Make changes at the start of the week for clean data.

 

Step 5: Monitor Expected Outcomes

  • Increasing price may reduce conversion and market share but improve margin.
  • Reducing ad spend lowers visibility but improves efficiency and profit.
  • Track results to confirm the expected impact.

3. Case Study: Moving from Growth to Profit

 

Background

  • A supplement ASIN grew from about $50K to nearly $200K monthly revenue.
  • Typical months stabilized around $150K.
  • Margin stayed low at around 10 to 12 percent, below the 25 to 30 percent target.
  • The product ranked number one organically with strong badges.
  • TACOS and ACoS remained high, indicating inefficiency.

 

Signs It Was Time to Pivot

  • Purchase share reached about 50 percent.
  • Strong organic rank but no improvement in TACOS.
  • Rising ad costs with limited incremental gains.

 

Execution

  • Chose to reduce ad spend instead of raising price due to past conversion drops.
  • Ad spend reduced by about 35 percent.

 

Results

  • Revenue dropped slightly from about $146K to $143K.
  • PPC sales dropped, but organic sales increased significantly.
  • TACOS improved while ACoS increased slightly.
  • Profit increased from about $17K to $29K.
  • Margin improved from around 12 percent to 20 percent.

4. Market Share Tracking and Ongoing Optimization

  • Purchase share dropped from about 49 percent to 39 percent after the change.
  • Click share also declined, as expected.
  • The main competitor gained only a small portion of lost share.
  • Remaining share was spread across smaller competitors.
  • This confirmed the move to profit mode was safe.
  • Charts and dashboards help track competitor movement over time.
  • Revenue stayed relatively stable while profit increased significantly.
  • Ongoing adjustments can further improve margins.

 

Managing Large Catalogs

  • Use an 80/20 approach to focus on top-performing ASINs.
  • Prioritize 50 to 100 key products for deeper analysis.
  • Consider using a data analyst for reporting and dashboards.

5. Tactical Insights and Tools

 

Reducing Ad Spend

  • Focus on exact match campaigns.
  • Reduce top-of-search bids when ranking number one organically.
  • Avoid paying for traffic you would get organically.
  • Test changes instead of applying fixed rules.

 

Data and Tools

  • Use Amazon Search Query Performance data for market share insights.
  • Competitor click share must be pulled manually.
  • Tools like Helium 10 can help but do not provide full data.
  • Power BI can be used for dashboards and visualization.

 

Operations and Process

  • Use SOPs and structured workflows to manage data.
  • AI tools can help build dashboards and analyze trends.
  • Weekly tracking is important, especially for seasonal products.

 

Additional Considerations

  • Larger product variations may have higher margins but lower volume.
  • Balance unit economics with demand across variations.
  • Focus on leading indicators, not just sales and rank.
  • Always optimize based on the current goal: growth or profit.
  • Make one change at a time and monitor full impact.

In conclusion, Bryce Alderson provides a clear, data-driven approach to shifting products from growth to profit mode. 

 

By combining internal metrics with market share data, brands can make smarter decisions with minimal revenue loss.

 

By centralizing data, choosing the right lever, and tracking both performance and competition, sellers can move beyond guesswork and manage each ASIN based on its lifecycle. 

 

This approach helps balance growth and profitability for long-term success.

cliff_notes:
In this session Matt Bertrand explains how to find “cash leaks” in an e-commerce catalog by focusing on how efficiently each SKU uses cash, not just margin. 
 
The talk presents a practical framework and tool to help brands identify which products drive growth and which drain working capital.

 

Speaker Background and Purpose of the Framework
  • Matt Bertrand is an experienced e-commerce operator and CEO of Teak Tuning.
  • He manages large catalogs with thousands of SKUs across multiple businesses.
  • The goal is to identify which SKUs generate the best return on cash.
  • Most sellers focus on margin, but this ignores cash timing.
  • The framework is designed for inventory-heavy brands with limited capital.
  • It applies to any business that holds inventory and cares about cash flow.

 

From Margin to Cash Return Efficiency (CRE)
  • Traditional metrics like margin and P&L do not show how efficiently cash is used.
  • Cash Return Efficiency (CRE) measures annual profit per dollar of cash tied up.
  • “Slow cash” costs like landed cost tie up capital long before the sale.
  • “Fast cash” costs like FBA fees and ads occur near or after the sale.
  • Cash cycle days track time from supplier shipment to payment received.
  • Payment terms affect when cash actually leaves the business.
  • Cash tied up depends on sales, cost, timing, and payment structure.
  • Two SKUs with the same margin can have very different CRE.
  • Lower margin SKUs can outperform if they turn faster and use less cash.

 

Supplier, Payment Terms, and Cash Cycle Scenarios
  • China sourcing usually offers higher margin but long cash cycles of 130+ days.
  • Payment terms like 30 percent upfront create early cash outflow.
  • U.S. sourcing has lower margin but much shorter cash cycles around 60 to 70 days.
  • Credit card payments can extend terms and delay cash outflow.
  • Faster logistics and better terms can allow sales before full payment.
  • Faster turning products can generate higher annual profit per dollar invested.
  • This is critical for brands with fixed capital like $100,000.
  • Lower-priced products often have higher CRE due to faster cash movement.

 

Portfolio View: Quadrants, Sleepers, Cash Traps, and Levers
  • A catalog should be managed as a capital portfolio based on profit and CRE.
  • High profit and high CRE SKUs should be scaled.
  • Low profit and low CRE SKUs should be fixed or removed.
  • “Sleepers” have low margins but high CRE and strong cash returns.
  • “Cash traps” have high profit but low CRE and tie up too much cash.
  • Cash traps limit growth by consuming working capital.
  • Four levers improve CRE: reduce cash cycle, improve payment terms, accept higher cost for faster turns, and reallocate capital.
  • Faster logistics and tighter inventory reduce cash tied up.
  • Payment strategies can delay cash outflow.
  • Paying more can be worth it if cash turns faster.
  • Cutting SKUs frees capital for better opportunities.

 

Practical Application, Tools, and Q&A Insights
  • A Google Sheet tool helps calculate and compare CRE across SKUs.
  • It allows scenario testing for suppliers, pricing, and terms.
  • Similar margin products can show up to a 10x difference in CRE.
  • High CRE SKUs are often not the most obvious.
  • Start by analyzing a few vendors and identifying top and worst performers.
  • Improve one weak SKU and scale one strong SKU first.
  • Some low CRE SKUs may remain for strategic reasons.
  • These can be bundled or treated as loss leaders.
  • Pricing changes can improve CRE for weaker SKUs.
  • Payment tools should be evaluated based on their true cost and benefit.
  • The framework can be adapted to different business models.

 

In conclusion, the session reframes catalog management from a margin-first approach to a cash-efficiency-first approach. The framework helps brands see which SKUs multiply cash and which hold the business back.
 
By improving cash efficiency, adjusting terms, and reallocating capital, brands can grow faster with the same resources. This approach turns inventory decisions into clear capital allocation strategies and ensures every SKU earns its place in the catalog.

items.title: Bora Mutluoglu, Leo Limin & Zain Ali － Behind the Scenes of TikTok Shop － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Bora Mutluoglu, Leo Limin & Zain Ali explain why many brands struggle on the platform and what strategies actually drive sustainable sales. 

 

TOPICS:
1. Why brands fail on TikTok Shop and how to achieve product–channel fit
2. Finding, nurturing, and scaling high-performing creators and content volume
3. Using GMB Max, understanding attribution, and adapting to TikTok Shop’s future direction
items.description_text: In this session, Bora Mutluoglu, Leo Limin & Zain Ali explain why many brands struggle on the platform and what strategies actually drive sustainable sales. TOPICS: 1. Why brands fail on TikTok Shop and how to achieve product–channel fit 2. Finding, nurturing, and scaling high-performing creators and content volume 3. Using GMB Max, understanding attribution, and adapting to TikTok Shop’s future direction
cliff_notes:
In this session, TikTok Shop experts Bora Mutluoglu, Leo Limin & Zain Ali discuss why many brands fail on the platform and what it takes to build a sustainable, profitable presence. 

 

The conversation covers product fit, creator strategy, ad mechanics (especially GMV Max), AI-generated content, and where TikTok Shop is heading next.

 

TikTok Shop ≠ Amazon (Why Most Brands Fail)
  • TikTok Shop is an advertising channel first, not a pure sales channel.
  • Success depends on impulse-driven buying, not research-heavy decisions.
  • Best-performing products are typically $20–$30 — easy, fast purchases.
  • Products over $100 usually struggle due to higher consideration.
  • Most brands quit too early after burning money in the first 2–3 months.
  • Results are delayed and momentum-based (sampling → content → traction takes weeks).
  • Profitability improves later (months 4–6) after identifying winners.
  • TikTok drives customer acquisition, with strong halo effects on Amazon & Shopify.

 

Product–Channel Fit Is Everything
  • Not all products work — winning products are:
    • Visually demonstrable
    • Simple to understand in seconds
    • Emotionally engaging
  • Categories like health, wellness, and food perform well.
  • Optimize for low-friction buying decisions.
  • Don’t force products into TikTok — adapt product, price, and creative to the platform.

 

Creator Strategy: Small % Drives Most Revenue
  • ~1–5% of creators drive ~90% of GMV.
  • Top creators are defined by consistency and loyalty, not just GMV.
  • Best strategy:
    • Start wide (“spray and pray” outreach)
    • Identify winners
    • Double down on top performers
  • Response rates are low (~2–3%), but that’s expected.
  • Early-stage creators (L0–L2) often become the most loyal long-term.
  • Retain top creators through:
    • Bonuses
    • Personal relationships
    • Recognition
  • Elite creators require either:
    • Perfect product fit, or
    • Strong financial incentives (retainers)

 

Scaling Content: Volume Wins
  • Winning brands produce massive content volume.
  • Efficient model:
    • Send 200–300 samples (commission-based)
    • Cost ~$10/video for $20–$30 products
  • Better strategy:
    • Fewer creators, more output each
    • (e.g., 100 creators × 10 videos > 1,000 creators × 1 video)
  • Creators improve over time — later videos perform better.
  • Winning content can be reused on Meta (Facebook/Instagram) for more revenue.
  • AI content is rising:
    • Useful for scaling cheaply
    • TikTok is investing heavily in it
  • Expect more AI-generated content as supply of creators becomes limited.

 

GMV Max: Powerful but Misleading
  • Combines organic + paid performance into one metric.
  • Can overstate ROI due to blended attribution.
  • Attribution on TikTok Shop is messy by default.
  • Platform is shifting toward pay-to-play.
  • Most $1M+/month brands rely heavily on GMV Max.
Key tactics:
  • Focus on engagement signals:
    • ~70%+ 2-sec view rate
    • ~60%+ 6-sec view rate
  • Use creative boosting on proven content
  • Manually trigger traction (e.g., purchases through videos)
  • Expect only a small % of videos to scale
 
Platform Reality: You Can’t Game It Long-Term
  • Short-term hacks (duplicate videos, fake traction) don’t last.
  • Algorithm reallocates spend quickly if content doesn’t convert.
  • Over-manipulation risks:
    • Poor performance
    • Account issues / shadow bans
  • TikTok’s main goal = maximize ad revenue, not seller profits.
  • Brands must work with GMV Max, not avoid it.

 

Where TikTok Shop Is Headed
  • Moving toward more ads + less organic reach.
  • Attracting larger, enterprise brands (e.g., Project Horizon).
  • Trying to shift perception away from cheap/dropshipping products.
  • Will become harder for new brands to enter over time.
Future trends:
  • Live commerce expected to grow (huge in Asia, still small in the U.S.)
  • AI content will increase significantly
  • Human creators still matter (connection + authenticity)

 

Key Takeaways
  • TikTok Shop is a long-term acquisition engine, not a quick profit channel.
  • Expect early losses, delayed wins, and heavy testing.
  • Success =
  • Right product + strong creators + high content volume + smart ad usage
  • The biggest edge comes from:
    • Moving early
    • Iterating fast
    • Doubling down on what works

items.title: Fernando Campos － TikTok Shop: Scale Past $500K/Month － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Fernando Campos shares how he scales brands on TikTok Shop by focusing on one hero product, building a strong creator ecosystem, and tracking the right leading metrics. 

 

TOPICS:
1. Focusing on a hero SKU and understanding TikTok (demand creation) vs. Amazon (demand capture).
2. Building and managing creators through shoppable videos, retainers, sprints, and creator intelligence.
3. Using cross-channel economics and spillover (TikTok → Amazon/retail) to set allowable CAC and scale profitably.
items.description_text: In this session, Fernando Campos shares how he scales brands on TikTok Shop by focusing on one hero product, building a strong creator ecosystem, and tracking the right leading metrics. TOPICS: 1. Focusing on a hero SKU and understanding TikTok (demand creation) vs. Amazon (demand capture). 2. Building and managing creators through shoppable videos, retainers, sprints, and creator intelligence. 3. Using cross-channel economics and spillover (TikTok → Amazon/retail) to set allowable CAC and scale profitably.
cliff_notes:
In this session, Fernando Campos explains the strategy and systems his team uses to scale brands on TikTok Shop from tens of thousands in monthly revenue to hundreds of thousands and beyond. 

 

He focuses on product focus, creator systems, shoppable video volume, and how to think about profitability when factoring in spillover to Amazon and retail.

 

Business Context and Core Goal: Scaling on TikTok Shop

  • Fernando and his partner Nick run a portfolio projected to generate $60 to $65 million in annual revenue
  • Their brands generate about $700,000 per month on TikTok Shop, with a goal of scaling a single product to $500,000 per month or more
  • They built Hive HQ, a profit analytics and creator intelligence platform for TikTok Shop, and also run a managed services division
  • The goal is to help brands scale from about $50,000 to $500,000 per month using a repeatable system
  • Supporting resources include a launch playbook, a nine-day roadmap, KPI benchmarks, and a high-performing ad content database

Product Strategy: Hero SKU Focus and Demand Creation

  • Amazon captures demand, while TikTok creates demand through content and discovery
  • TikTok users discover products through short-form content, not search behavior
  • Scaling one hero SKU is more effective than launching many products
  • A single product can reach very high revenue if supported by strong content and creators
  • Focusing on one SKU simplifies operations, forecasting, and supply chain
  • Many sellers stall at $10,000 to $20,000 per month because they diversify too early
  • Scaling an existing product from $50,000 to $300,000 or more is often the better path
  • Creators prefer promoting products with existing traction and social proof

Content and Creators: Where Revenue Actually Comes From

  • Live streams typically drive about 10 percent of total sales
  • Branded content usually contributes 10 to 20 percent, with top brands reaching up to 40 percent
  • Some brands generate significant revenue with little to no branded content
  • Affiliate shoppable videos are the highest leverage growth driver
  • Creators bring their own audience, content style, and proven hooks
  • The most important leading metric is the number of shoppable videos posted
  • Brands often over-focus on sampling instead of building long-term creator relationships
  • Proven creators should be moved to retainers for consistent output
  • Increasing video volume strongly correlates with GMV growth

Creator Systems: Retainers, Sprints, and Retention

  • Core principle is to invest in creators so they produce and scale content
  • Retainers create consistent output, for example paying for 30 videos per month
  • Sprints are short campaigns that incentivize high output over one to two weeks
  • The market is shifting away from large contests toward structured incentives
  • GMV Max rewards both volume and quality of content
  • Brands should communicate that they are supporting creators with ad spend
  • Creator tracking systems help identify top performers, dormant creators, and growth trends
  • Re-engaging past creators can be more efficient than recruiting new ones
  • Simple issues like running out of product can stop creator output
  • Strong relationships are built through direct communication, calls, and support
  • Reinvesting 5 to 10 percent of creator-driven revenue back into creators drives continued growth

Economics, Spillover, and Profit Strategy

  • Brands that can spend more to acquire customers gain an advantage
  • TikTok profitability should be evaluated with cross-channel impact
  • Spillover to Amazon and retail increases total return on investment
  • Example: for every 100 TikTok units sold, about 30 additional units may sell on Amazon
  • A brand may lose money on TikTok but still be profitable overall due to Amazon gains
  • Break-even on TikTok can still generate meaningful profit through other channels
  • Additional Amazon revenue increases allowable CAC and supports faster scaling
  • This allows brands to invest more in creators and ads than competitors
  • Key pitfalls include scaling too many SKUs, focusing only on GMV, and ignoring cross-channel impact
  • Spillover can be estimated using branded search trends, search rank, and TikTok activity
  • For regions with limited TikTok Shop access, solving access should be the first priority


In conclusion, this session presents a clear, system-driven approach to scaling on TikTok Shop that centers on one hero product, a high-output creator ecosystem, and disciplined tracking of shoppable videos as the key leading metric. 

Fernando shows that brands can grow beyond common plateaus by investing in creator relationships, structured incentives, and creator intelligence rather than launching too many products or relying heavily on lives and branded content.

He also highlights the importance of evaluating TikTok through a cross-channel lens, where spillover to Amazon and retail, improved lifetime value, and expanded CAC thresholds matter more than short-term platform profitability. 

Brands that adopt this approach and build the right systems are positioned to scale from five-figure to mid-six-figure monthly revenue on TikTok Shop and beyond.

items.title: Alex Chiru － Amazon's AI Search Revolution Is Here － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Alex Chiru explains how Amazon’s AI systems, particularly Rufus, Cosmo, and Alexa, are transforming search, recommendations, and listing optimization. 

TOPICS:
1. Amazon’s growth constraints and the strategic role of Rufus in driving more revenue from existing customers  
2. New optimization rules focused on use cases, clear answers, and AI-readable content instead of keyword stuffing  
3. Practical AI-driven workflows and catalog audits to protect against automatic rewrites and to align with Rufus and Cosmo

TOPICS: 1. Amazon’s growth constraints and the strategic role of Rufus in driving more revenue from existing customers 2. New optimization rules focused on use cases, clear answers, and AI-readable content instead of keyword stuffing 3. Practical AI-driven workflows and catalog audits to protect against automatic rewrites and to align with Rufus and Cosmo
cliff_notes:
In this session Alex Chiru explains how Amazon’s AI-powered systems, especially Rufus and Cosmo, are transforming search, recommendations, and listing optimization on the platform. 

The discussion focuses on what these changes mean for brand-registered sellers and outlines a practical playbook to stay competitive as Amazon’s algorithms evolve rapidly.

Amazon’s Growth Challenge and the Rise of Rufus

  • Amazon’s core growth from new Prime members in the US is slowing because about 70% of US adults already have Prime, and the remaining audience is harder to convert due to geography, generation, and behavior differences.
  • Amazon is shifting focus to increasing revenue from existing customers instead of relying on new user growth.
  • Over the past six years, Amazon increased first-party retail fees by about 91%, seller fees by around 220%, and advertising costs by close to 400%, significantly raising monetization per retail dollar.
  • Amazon’s margin per retail dollar increased from about 38 cents in 2019 to around 64 cents, and this trend continues to grow.
  • Rufus is a key response to this shift, designed to increase revenue per customer through more personalized recommendations and conversational shopping.


Rufus, Cosmo, and Alexa: How the New AI Stack Works

  • Rufus is an AI shopping assistant that, by the end of 2025, has over 300 million users and generates about $12 billion in annualized sales.
  • Rufus increases engagement, including a reported 38% rise in Black Friday sessions and a 60% purchase completion rate for Rufus-driven journeys.
  • Rufus becomes agentic, meaning it can retain contextual data such as preferences, demographics, and behavior to improve recommendations.
  • Rufus can autonomously purchase products within about 30 minutes through an auto-buy feature.
  • Rufus typically recommends only 1 to 5 products, so brands not included risk losing visibility and sales.
  • Amazon pulls data from over 200,000 branded websites to support product recommendations with external validation.
  • Cosmo works in the background to evaluate listings based on clarity, use case, and problem-solving value, influencing rankings.
  • Ranking evolves from simple keyword matching to a system that includes intent, external validation, visual signals, and traffic sources.
  • Alexa integrates with Rufus to power voice shopping and usually returns only a small number of recommended products.
  • Younger shoppers, especially those under 25, are increasingly using voice search through Alexa, making top placement even more important.


New Rules of Optimization: From Keywords to Use Cases and Answers

  • Keyword stuffing in titles and bullets is no longer effective and may be penalized.
  • Listings should clearly answer customer questions and match real use cases using natural language.
  • Rufus and Cosmo evaluate whether listings explain what the product is, what it does, and what problem it solves.
  • Listings should include when and how the product is used, key features, and who it is for.
  • Customer reviews and Q&A are important signals because AI systems analyze how customers describe their experiences.
  • Sellers should review both their own and competitor listings, as well as external sources, to identify trends and gaps.
  • Visual content should show real-life use cases instead of generic product images.
  • Amazon prioritizes what is shown in images rather than relying on alt text.
  • A+ content and brand story modules are now fully scanned and used for ranking.
  • Premium A+ content with strong use cases and clear messaging can drive up to a 20% increase in sales.


Catalog Structure, Backend Data, and Project Starfish

  • Project Starfish is an Amazon initiative that automatically updates listings, including titles, bullets, backend attributes, and sometimes images.
  • If backend attributes are incomplete, Amazon’s AI fills in the gaps, often inaccurately.
  • While this improves overall marketplace performance, it can negatively affect individual listings if not managed.
  • Many sellers report unauthorized or incorrect listing changes caused by AI updates.
  • Amazon is changing how reviews apply across variation families, making incorrect variations more risky.
  • Sellers have limited time to clean up variation structures before automatic adjustments are applied.
  • The first step is to audit variation families and ensure all attributes are accurate and consistent.
  • A+ content and brand stories should be used to clearly answer customer questions, not just for design.
  • Completing all backend attributes is one of the most important steps to prevent harmful AI changes.
  • Daily monitoring is recommended to catch and fix AI-driven updates early.


AI-Driven Workflows, Self-Audits, and Practical Next Steps

  • Alex recommends using AI tools such as Claude for listing optimization and workflow automation.
  • Sellers should gather all key Amazon reports, including SQP, search term, advertising, and business reports, into one place.
  • These reports can be used with AI tools to generate optimized listings aligned with Rufus and Cosmo.
  • Alex provides an AI listing optimization playbook and a search research report to guide this process.
  • A full catalog audit is recommended at least once a month, with more frequent tracking of key metrics.
  • Teams should monitor listing performance and attribute changes regularly.
  • External traffic is becoming more important, so driving traffic from outside Amazon helps improve ranking signals.
  • Immediate action steps include auditing variations, completing backend data, updating A+ and brand content, and setting up daily monitoring.
  • Sellers can use Rufus to benchmark by asking for product recommendations and analyzing which listings appear.
  • Alex notes that potential AI issues such as hallucinations have not yet been deeply analyzed.

 

Amazon’s shift to AI systems like Rufus, Cosmo, and Alexa is changing how products are discovered and purchased.

 

Success now depends on clear, natural language content, accurate backend data, and continuous optimization using AI tools.

 

Sellers who adapt quickly and align with these systems will have a higher chance of being recommended and driving consistent sales.

items.title: Using AI to Understand CAC, LTV and Growth － Shinghi Detelfsen － APAC Chapter Monthly Call March 2026
items.description:
In this session, the APAC MDS chapter hosts guest speaker Shinghi Detelfsen on scaling Amazon profitably using data, CAC/LTV, and AI tools.
TOPICS:
  1. Subscribe & Save updates
  2. Promotion strategies

items.description_text: In this session, the APAC MDS chapter hosts guest speaker Shinghi Detelfsen on scaling Amazon profitably using data, CAC/LTV, and AI tools. TOPICS: Subscribe & Save updates Promotion strategies Community news (Bali meetup + analytics tool giveaway)
cliff_notes:
In this session the APAC MDS chapter hosts a monthly call featuring guest speaker Shinghi Detelfsen focusing on data-driven growth on Amazon. The discussion centers on customer acquisition cost (CAC) lifetime value (LTV), promotions, and how tools and AI can improve decision-making.


APAC Chapter Call, Community, and Setup

The APAC monthly call serves as a regional touchpoint for MDS members across Asia Pacific and Australia, with content tailored specifically to this audience.

Jonathan notes that while live attendance is modest, most members watch recordings, resulting in strong overall engagement. The calls are treated as exclusive APAC content, with a lighthearted tone throughout.

The session begins with an informal discussion (including AI note-taking bots in meetings), and Jonathan encourages cameras on to maintain strong energy and interaction.

The group includes participants from across APAC, with particularly strong Australian representation. The call ends with a casual “duck race” used to randomly select a giveaway winner, reinforcing the community-driven culture.


Speaker Introduction and Background

Jonathan introduces Shinghi Detelfsen as a long-time MDS contributor with deep Amazon expertise and strong industry relationships.

Shinghi previously worked at Amazon (6 years), as well as Google and Hulu, where he developed structured thinking, documentation discipline, and operational rigor.

He now co-owns Wholesome Story, a dietary supplements brand with over 1 million customers and approaching $100M in lifetime revenue.

Jonathan highlights Shinghi’s reputation for helping sellers resolve critical Amazon issues and his broader involvement in improving the seller ecosystem.


CAC, LTV, and Ad Spend Strategy

Shinghi emphasizes that common Amazon metrics (ACOS, TACOS, ROAS) are incomplete without CAC and LTV.

  • CAC is a fixed acquisition cost per customer
  • Lifetime profit (not just revenue) is the key metric
  • LTV:CAC ratio determines true profitability

Example:
A ~$10 CAC and ~$33 12-month lifetime profit → 3.3 LTV:CAC ratio.

He introduces the spend curve, showing how increased ad spend affects CAC, customer volume, and total profit:

  • More spend → more customers (but diminishing returns)
  • CAC typically rises gradually
  • Total profit can still increase despite lower margin per customer

Key insight: scale spend until CAC rises sharply.

In his case study, doubling spend significantly increased new customers while CAC remained relatively stable (~$10–$12), indicating room to scale.

Additional points:

  • Works best with strong, high-ranking products
  • Ad structure and optimization heavily impact CAC
  • Amazon CAC is often much lower than Meta/DTC CAC
  • CAC discipline is critical for low-repeat or non-subscription products


Subscribe & Save, Promotions, and Product Strategy

Subscribe & Save Changes
Amazon shifted the default Buy Box from subscription to one-time purchase (mid-2025), leading to:

  • Subscribe rate drop (~11% → ~5%)
  • Likely driven by high cancellation rates

However, many customers continue purchasing as non-subscribers, so total repeat behavior remains strong.

Customer Mix Insight
 “Returning non-subscribers” often represent the largest segment—worth analyzing closely.

Product Strategy

  • ~97% of revenue comes from mature (“heritage”) products
  • New products contribute little but consume resources
    → Focus on scaling proven products and expanding geographically (e.g., Canada, Mexico, Australia)

Promotions

  • Amazon promotions (Prime events, etc.) are generally incremental
  • Brand Tailored Promotions:
    • New/high-potential customer offers → more incremental
    • Cart abandoner offers → less incremental (use smaller discounts)

Best Practices

  • Test discount levels (often ~20% as a baseline)
  • Occasionally pause promos to measure true incrementality
  • Avoid excessive discounting unless justified by LTV

Subscribe & Save Coupons
Often highly incremental and can outperform organic subscriptions if managed properly.


Expandify, AI, and Community Updates

Expandify (Shinghi’s Tool)
An analytics platform for Amazon (with planned Shopify and TikTok Shop support) focused on customer-level and promotion-level insights.

Key features:

  • Three data layers: raw, processed, and report-ready
  • ~75 prebuilt reports (CAC, LTV, promotions, retention, etc.)
  • Data warehouse owned by the brand
  • Access via SQL, APIs, and AI tools

Addresses Amazon’s ~18-month data limit by storing long-term data (important for operations and exit value).

AI Integration (Claude)
Expandify integrates with Claude, enabling natural-language queries on business data.

Example use cases:

  • Repurchase rates by product
  • LTV:CAC by SKU
  • Promotion incrementality
  • Budget allocation decisions
  • Business valuation insights

Key principle: AI is only as effective as the operator’s understanding of core metrics.

Shinghi recommends feeding AI rich business context (e.g., via voice transcription tools like Whisper) to improve output quality.

Build vs Buy Insight
AI can quickly build 80% of a custom solution, but the final 20% (infrastructure, reliability, scale) is complex—tools like Expandify solve this.


Community Updates

  • Expandify giveaway: 3-month subscription awarded via duck race (winner: Adi)
  • Bali meetup: Planned for October (likely Ubud), limited capacity (~16 rooms), registration to follow

Jonathan shares that attending a prior Bali meetup was a transformative experience and helped inspire ongoing APAC calls.


Key Takeaways

  • Focus on CAC, LTV, and lifetime profit—not just ACOS
  • Use spend curves to scale ads intelligently
  • Double down on proven products rather than over-launching
  • Treat promotions as measurable, testable levers
  • Combine a strong data infrastructure with AI for better decisions

The session highlights how integrating first-party data, disciplined metrics, and AI tools enables more scalable and defensible Amazon growth.

items.title: How to Win the Amazon Buy Box Using Advanced Repricing and Pricing Control Strategies － Resellers Channel Monthly Call March 2026
items.description:
In this session, the MDS Resellers Channel meets with repricing experts from Feedvisor and Flashpricer to discuss optimizing the Amazon Buy Box.
TOPICS:
  1. Buy Box factors for authorized vs. unauthorized resellers
  2. Regional dynamics, FBA distribution, and pricing impact
  3. Advanced repricing strategies and multi-marketplace price parity
items.description_text: In this session, the MDS Resellers Channel meets with repricing experts from Feedvisor and Flashpricer to discuss optimizing the Amazon Buy Box. TOPICS: Buy Box factors for authorized vs. unauthorized resellers Regional dynamics, FBA distribution, and pricing impact Advanced repricing strategies and multi-marketplace price parity
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS Resellers Channel meet with experts from Feedvisor and Flashpricer to discuss advanced Amazon repricing strategies. The conversation covers Buy Box mechanics regional and multi-marketplace pricing, private label optimization, and how to test and evaluate repricers.


Introductions and Context

Charles opens the MDS Reseller Channel monthly call and introduces the topic of repricing, which was selected by the community.

He is joined by Matt Visone (Feedvisor) and Jordan (Flashpricer), both experienced in Amazon pricing strategy. Charles notes he has personally used Feedvisor for over six years (not an official endorsement).

Replay access is available via the MDS dashboard. Contact details for both tools are shared at the end of the session.


Buy Box Mechanics: Key Factors

  • Amazon does not distinguish between authorized and unauthorized resellers once a seller is eligible to list a product
  • Customers also do not see authorization status—only price, delivery speed, and seller info

Primary Buy Box factors:

  • Price
  • Fulfillment method (FBA vs. FBM)
  • Delivery speed
  • Seller performance metrics
  • In-stock availability

Additional insights:

  • Account age does not directly impact the Buy Box, but stronger metrics over time help
  • Authorized sellers often have better margins and listing control, improving competitiveness indirectly


Regional Buy Box and Inventory Strategy

  • The regional Buy Box is real—you can win in one region and lose in another
  • Driven by proximity, delivery speed, and local inventory availability

Key strategies:

  • Maintain consistent in-stock levels (critical for ranking and Buy Box share)
  • Adjust pricing as inventory declines to extend stock coverage
  • Balance inventory distribution across FBA network

Repricer considerations:

  • Sellers can only set one price across regions
  • Strategies may include blended pricing or controlled price fluctuations to maximize margin

Tools and data:

  • Regional Buy Box insights are emerging (e.g., zip-code-level analysis)
  • Tools like SmartScout can help visualize Buy Box share geographically (often manually for top ASINs)


Price Updates and Multi-Marketplace Parity

Price Update Timing:

  • Can range from ~3 minutes (high-velocity SKUs) to ~30 minutes (slower items)
  • Repricers act instantly, but Amazon controls when prices are published

Operational considerations:

  • Large catalogs require batching and API management
  • Systems must confirm when price changes are actually reflected live

Off-Amazon Pricing (Parity):

  • Amazon may suppress the Buy Box if lower prices are detected on other marketplaces (e.g., Walmart, Target)
  • Amazon provides an “off-Amazon competitive price” that acts as a pricing ceiling

Insights:

  • Perfect price parity is not required; small differences (~5%) are typically acceptable
  • Deep discounts on other platforms (especially 1P relationships) can trigger suppression
  • Using different UPCs for the same product is not a reliable workaround

Best practice:
Create differentiated bundles or pack sizes per marketplace to avoid direct price matching conflicts.


Repricing Strategies: Resellers vs. Private Label

Private Label (Demand-Based Pricing):

  • Uses data like sales velocity, conversion rate, and sessions
  • Optimizes for profit, margin, or revenue based on goals
  • Can benchmark against selected competitors

Flashpricer approach:

  • Tests multiple price points over time
  • Learns which prices maximize revenue or profit
  • Gradually converges on optimal pricing bands

Best practices:

  • Start with narrow price ranges, then expand as confidence grows
  • Use pricing to control velocity (e.g., raise prices when inventory is low)
  • Sequence goals:
    • First stabilize sales volume
    • Then optimize profitability

Hybrid accounts (resale + private label):

  • Managed at the ASIN level with different strategies per product
  • Some tools can automatically switch strategies if competition changes


Testing Repricers and Advanced Considerations

Testing challenges:

  • Performance is hard to isolate due to changing inventory, competition, and seasonality

Recommended approach:

  • A/B test similar ASINs across tools, or
  • Test the same ASIN over defined time periods
  • Ensure sufficient duration and data volume

Advanced signals:

  • Competitor inventory levels can provide context, but are not always central to pricing decisions
  • Repricers typically react after competitors stock out rather than predicting it

Critical reminder:

  • For private label, include ad spend in profitability calculations
  • True optimization = profit after advertising, not just margin


Key Takeaways

  • The Buy Box is driven by price, fulfillment, and seller performance—not authorization
  • Regional dynamics and inventory placement significantly impact results
  • Multi-marketplace pricing must be managed carefully to avoid suppression
  • Repricing should be strategic and data-driven—not just reactive price matching
  • Structured testing is essential to evaluate repricers effectively

This session highlights how modern repricing tools enable sellers to balance growth and profitability by combining pricing strategy, inventory management, and marketplace awareness.

items.title: How to Scale TikTok Shop Using Creator Outreach Bots and High-Volume Content Systems － TikTok Channel Call March 2026
items.description:
This session covers how brands use TikTok Shop, affiliates, and JoinBrands’ outreach tools to scale sales, with a focus on practical tactics, data, and creator strategy.
TOPICS:
  • JoinBrands’ outreach bot and dashboard for managing the full funnel (launch → outreach → retainers)
  • The role of video volume, data, and growth phases in scaling on TikTok Shop
  • How to find, train, and retain creators to build long-term growth
items.description_text: This session covers how brands use TikTok Shop, affiliates, and JoinBrands’ outreach tools to scale sales, with a focus on practical tactics, data, and creator strategy. TOPICS: JoinBrands’ outreach bot and dashboard for managing the full funnel (launch → outreach → retainers) The role of video volume, data, and growth phases in scaling on TikTok Shop How to find, train, and retain creators to build long-term growth
cliff_notes:
This session explains how brands can use TikTok Shop affiliates and outreach tools to scale revenue. The discussion focuses on JoinBrands’ new outreach bot data-backed insights on video volume and building a “creator army” for sustainable growth. Members also share real brand experiences common mistakes, and how TikTok can create a halo effect on channels like Amazon. The session provides practical frameworks and tactics for execution.

JoinBrands TikTok Outreach Bot & Platform

JoinBrands introduced an outreach bot that enables performance-based outreach to TikTok creators within the same platform used for social blasts and campaigns.

Ian Sells describes a three-step system:

  1. Cold start (launch)
  2. Performance-based outreach
  3. Retainers for proven creators

The outreach bot is included in a $99/month plan with:

  • Unlimited outreach
  • Lower social blast pricing
  • Additional automations and dashboards

The platform prioritizes core functionality and adds features based on user demand.

The dashboard tracks:

  • Affiliate GMV
  • Total GMV
  • Top creators and videos
  • Performance trends

Key features:

  • Targets all TikTok creators via DMs (not just JoinBrands users)
  • Filters by GMV, category, and activity
  • Captures creator's emails automatically from replies
  • Labels existing JoinBrands creators (“JB”) for easy rehiring

The bot is available as an add-on inside the “TikTok outreach agents” section. A 30-day free trial was offered to MDS members.

Growth Phases & Creator Pyramid

Leo Limin explains that many brands fail by targeting top creators too early without traction.

Brands typically progress through:

  1. Cold start
  2. Outreach
  3. Retainers

Creator pyramid:

  • Bottom: Low-cost “blast” creators (high volume)
  • Middle: Mid-tier creators ($100–$500/video)
  • Top: Elite creators (retainers + commission)

Key points:

  • Cold start requires high volume to generate initial traction
  • Outreach phase improves content quality and consistency
  • Retainers lock in proven performers

Brands cannot skip the base layer—volume is required to scale.

Success also depends on:

  • Competitive commissions
  • Strong product listings
  • Reliable creator support

Early TikTok growth often requires accepting short-term losses (similar to Amazon launches).

Video Volume & the “Law of Big Numbers”

Data from 1,000+ TikTok shops shows a strong correlation between revenue and video volume.

Insights:

  • ~1,000 videos/month is often needed to reach higher revenue tiers (~$200K+/month)
  • Top shops may produce up to 1,000 videos/day via affiliates

Core principle:

  • ~1% of videos generate ~80% of GMV

Implications:

  • Volume and diversity matter more than “perfect” content
  • Each video is a new test for the algorithm
  • Relying on a small team limits creative variation

Common pattern:

  • Many low-performing videos
  • Occasional breakout winners
  • Aggregate volume drives results

Brands must continuously test hooks, angles, and formats.

Tactical Execution (GMV Max, Inventory, Tools)

GMV Max Optimization

Alex Bonilla recommends:

  • Turn off videos with poor ROAS (e.g., <0.75 after ~$50 spend)
  • Manually select videos when volume is low (~20 videos)
  • Switch to auto mode once volume increases (50+ videos)

Affiliate videos can automatically feed into GMV Max if authorization is enabled.

Inventory Management

Stockouts severely damage momentum:

  • Product links disappear
  • Creators stop earning commissions

Best practices:

  • Avoid stockouts at all costs
  • Communicate proactively with creators
  • Compensate top performers if needed

Subscriptions

TikTok subscriptions:

  • Currently invite-only
  • Can drive strong retention and recurring revenue

Caution:

  • Subscription revenue may inflate ROAS in GMV Max reporting

Tools Mentioned

  • Fastmoss (creative research)
  • Shop analytics tools (names referenced but unclear)

JoinBrands aims to consolidate many of these functions.

Creator Sourcing, Training & Retention

Finding effective creators is difficult:

  • Many ignore briefs
  • Many are not coachable

David shared sending ~5,000 samples over 18 months to identify strong creators.

Key insight:
Top creators are often developed, not discovered.

Best practices:

  • “Home-grow” creators
  • Provide training, feedback, and structure
  • Use Loom reviews and example videos

Process:

  1. Identify creators via social blasts
  2. Rehire and test consistency
  3. Move top performers to retainers

Creator groups (e.g., Evolution):

  • Provide trained creators
  • Often require higher commissions
  • Better suited for brands with traction (not a cold start)

Additional strategies:

  • Build private creator communities (e.g., WhatsApp groups)
  • Share hooks, ideas, and incentives
  • Encourage competition and iteration

Founder-led content can work early, but scaling requires third-party creators.

Key Takeaways

  • TikTok success is driven by volume + iteration, not single viral hits
  • Brands must progress through growth phases, not skip ahead
  • A large, diverse creator base is essential
  • Top creators are trained and developed over time
  • Inventory management is critical to maintain momentum
  • TikTok growth can create a halo effect on Amazon and other channels

Scaling on TikTok requires building a system that consistently produces and tests large volumes of content through a broad creator network. Long-term success depends on combining scale with creator development, strong operations, and data-driven optimization.

items.title: Guido Reyes － Agentic Workflows On Amazon  － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Guido explains how he builds and runs a local AI‑driven “agentic” workflow to manage a large Amazon advertising account at extreme scale. 

 

TOPICS:

1. Designing the AI agentic workflow and data architecture (Neon Postgres, vectors, Python, cron, Amazon APIs).

2. Implementing large‑scale campaign restructuring with single keyword campaigns and strategic negations.

3. Measuring results, running weekly human–AI review loops, and maintaining guardrails and local control.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Guido Reyes explains how he builds an AI-driven workflow to manage Amazon advertising on his own hardware. 
 
He shares his system, results from a 30-day case study, and how he keeps AI effective but controlled.
 
Goal and Who This Is For
  • The goal is to build an AI system that works like a skilled PPC manager.
  • The system runs locally instead of relying on external tools.
  • It is designed for advanced sellers who understand key metrics.
  • Metrics include contribution margin, MER, TACOS, and ACoS.
  • This approach requires technical thinking, not just using AI as a chatbot.
  • The focus is on turning human decision-making into scalable automation.

 

System Architecture
  • The system has five parts: data, automation, decision, feedback, and human control.
  • The data layer includes PPC, revenue, and financial data.
  • A database like Neon Postgres stores and organizes data with memory.
  • Automation uses scripts and scheduled tasks to keep data updated.
  • The decision layer defines targets like TACOS and ACoS.
  • The feedback loop updates the system based on results.
  • APIs connect the system to Amazon for campaign changes.
  • The human remains central by guiding strategy and decisions.

 

Account Structure and Scaling
  • The system is applied to a large Amazon account over 30 days.
  • Existing campaigns are preserved while adding new structure.
  • AI builds keyword lists and reorganizes campaigns.
  • The strategy focuses on single keyword campaigns for control.
  • Thousands of campaigns are launched across products.
  • Large numbers of negative keywords are used to control traffic flow.
  • Broad campaigns are used for discovery, then refined into targeted campaigns.
  • Negations ensure traffic goes to the correct campaigns.

 

Performance and Optimization
  • Sales increase by around 70% after implementation.
  • Revenue grows significantly while efficiency improves.
  • TACOS and ACoS decrease while impressions increase.
  • Impressions grow rapidly after launch.
  • CPC decreases and click-through rate improves.
  • The system can quickly adjust performance when targets change.
  • Weekly reviews guide ongoing optimization.
  • Tools like Scale Insights are used for reporting.

 

Human Control and Guardrails
  • The operator reviews performance regularly and guides the system.
  • AI can be controlled or stopped at any time.
  • Changes are reviewed before full execution.
  • Reports explain actions and expected outcomes.
  • The system is not fully automated and still requires oversight.
  • Running locally provides more control and flexibility.
  • Data is stored using vector memory for better context and learning.
  • Alternatives like BigQuery and ClickHouse were considered.
  • Data should be optimized, not overloaded.
  • Delays in Amazon data require regular review and adjustments.

 

This session presents a concrete example of how a seller can turn their own Amazon PPC decision‑making into a robust, local AI agentic workflow backed by a vector database and strong data engineering. 

 

Guido shows that when an operator truly understands their KPIs, contribution margin, and account structure, AI can manage thousands of campaigns and tens of thousands of negations in a way that drives sustained, measurable gains.

 

He also makes clear that this power comes with responsibilities: maintaining tight guardrails, retaining human oversight, building proper memory and data layers, and accepting the messy realities of attribution and real‑world performance. 

 

For sellers willing to think like developers and invest in this architecture, the potential for compounding improvements over months and years is significant.

TOPICS:

cliff_notes:
In this session Adam Weiler and Shinghi Detlefsen explain how founders should approach AI and automation without losing focus on what actually grows a physical products business. 
 
They share practical lessons on where AI helps and where it becomes a distraction.
 
Background and Perspective
  • Adam runs an Amazon agency and co-founded Flat File Pro.
  • The tool manages millions of listings and requires high reliability.
  • Shinghi has worked at Amazon Google and Hulu.
  • He co-founded Wholesome Story, serving over a million customers.
  • He is also involved in the American E-commerce Business Alliance.
  • They bring experience from both brands and software tools.
 
AI, FOMO, and Real Opportunity
  • Many founders chase AI due to fear of missing out.
  • Physical product brands are less at risk because they sell real goods.
  • AI can improve marketing, analytics, and operations.
  • AI does not replace strategy or double a business on its own.
  • Founders must start with real problems, not AI tools.
  • AI works best when applied to clear constraints in the business.
 
Focus on Fundamentals and Software Limits
  • The 4 Ps, product, price, promotion, and place, should remain the priority.
  • Saving small SaaS costs is less important than growing revenue.
  • Landing major retail opportunities can create far more value.
  • AI tools can make mistakes, and founders remain responsible.
  • Many AI projects stall before completion.
  • Software requires ongoing maintenance and security.
  • Trying to replace SaaS tools can turn a brand into a software company.
  • In many cases, paying for reliable tools is more efficient.
 
What to Automate and How to Build
  • Decisions should consider technical skill, team size, and use case.
  • Small teams can use simple tools, but larger teams need reliable systems.
  • Systems should be easy for others to understand and maintain.
  • Avoid building complex integrations when existing tools can solve them.
  • Start with simple platforms like Replit and scale up gradually.
  • Use AI tools like Claude to guide setup and development.
  • Prioritize automation based on biggest problems, cost impact, or bottlenecks.
  • Work in short cycles to ensure progress and avoid overbuilding.
  • Map and simplify processes before automating them.
 
Process, Team, and Security
  • Do not automate broken processes.
  • Document systems so teams can understand and maintain them.
  • Gather feedback from users to improve tools.
  • Build on top of existing platforms instead of recreating them.
  • Larger systems require leadership, such as a CTO or architect.
  • Security and permissions must be clearly defined.
  • Protect API keys and sensitive data at all times.
  • Platforms like Vercel and GitHub must be configured securely.
  • Set clear rules for what projects are allowed and who approves them.

 

In conclusion, this session reframes AI and software as means, not ends, for physical product businesses. Adam and Shinghi show that real leverage comes from understanding the business, clarifying constraints, and then applying AI in focused, well‑scoped ways.

 

They urge founders to prioritize the 4 Ps, design robust processes, and treat software and automation as long‑term responsibilities that demand documentation, security, and architectural thinking. 

 

With this disciplined approach, teams can harness AI’s power without getting lost in FOMO or building fragile systems that create more risk than value.

items.title: Josh Hadley － The CEO Dashboard: Focus on What Matters － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Josh Hadley shares how a near–cash crisis forces him to rethink his role as CEO and build a practical “CEO dashboard” to run his e‑commerce business.
 
TOPICS:
1. Clarifying the CEO’s role and shifting from lagging metrics (profit) to leading indicators (weekly actions).
2. Implementing the Weekly High Five tracker and departmental scorecards to drive accountability and performance.
3. Using a 52‑week cash flow forecast and smarter supplier/credit terms to manage cash and support sustainable growth.

TOPICS: 1. Clarifying the CEO’s role and shifting from lagging metrics (profit) to leading indicators (weekly actions). 2. Implementing the Weekly High Five tracker and departmental scorecards to drive accountability and performance. 3.
