cliff_notes:
In this session Josh Hadley shares how a near cash crisis in his e-commerce business led him to rethink his role as CEO and build a practical “CEO dashboard” to manage people performance, and cash. 

 

He introduces three core tools: the Weekly High Five tracker, a departmental scorecard, and a 52-week cash flow forecast to help prevent running out of money while scaling.

 

He emphasizes that a CEO’s highest leverage work is setting vision, putting the right people in the right roles, and tracking leading indicators instead of only lagging metrics like profit. 

 

He shows how simple systems create accountability and improve cash management, inventory decisions, and supplier terms.

Background, Cash Crisis, and the CEO’s Role

  • Josh is an experienced e-commerce operator selling on Amazon, TikTok, and Etsy
  • He hosts the Ecom Breakthrough Podcast and shares strategies from his own business
  • In January 2024, his team almost missed payroll due to lack of cash
  • He identifies three causes: poor supply chain cash flow, wrong people in roles, and weak CEO oversight
  • This moment led him to build the systems shared in the session
  • He defines the CEO’s role as setting vision, aligning the team, placing the right people, and protecting cash
  • He and his partner send a weekly Loom update to align the team on wins, focus, and constraints

Leading vs Lagging Metrics

  • Lagging metrics show results after the fact, such as profit
  • Leading metrics are actions that drive results, such as tasks completed or tests run
  • Most businesses track revenue and profit but ignore the actions that create them
  • CEOs should focus on measuring and managing leading indicators
  • The key question is which actions, if done consistently, will drive desired results
  • This mindset is the foundation of the CEO dashboard

Tool 1: Weekly High Five Tracker

  • Each team member has 3 to 5 weekly actions that define success
  • Every Monday, team members submit a simple yes or no report on completion
  • No partial credit keeps accountability clear and objective
  • Data feeds into a central Google Sheet with green and red status tracking
  • Each role has defined KPIs and actions tied to those KPIs
  • Leaders can use AI tools to help define KPIs but must keep focus on the few that matter
  • Each role includes one highest priority task based on the concept from The One Thing
  • Weekly one-on-one meetings review results, even if all items are completed
  • Managers should have no more than 5 to 7 direct reports
  • Notes are added for missed actions to track patterns over time
  • This system creates clear accountability and supports performance reviews

Tool 2: Weekly Department Scorecard

  • Tracks leading metrics by department instead of by individual
  • Covers functions like Amazon sales, supply chain, product development, and account health
  • Focuses on the most important KPIs for each function
  • Example: tracking Amazon IPI weekly to avoid storage and inventory issues
  • Also tracks account health issues to prevent sudden problems
  • Weekly visibility allows early intervention before major issues occur
  • Helps leadership quickly see which areas are performing well or need attention
  • Template can be adapted to fit different business models

Tool 3: 52-Week Cash Flow Forecast

  • Tracks cash position weekly for a full year
  • Includes all inflows such as marketplace payouts
  • Includes all outflows such as inventory, payroll, and expenses
  • Shows how timing of payments can create cash shortages even in profitable businesses
  • Small timing changes, like delaying a purchase order, can prevent negative cash balance
  • Helps avoid reliance on expensive financing options
  • Enables proactive planning for inventory and growth

 

Supplier Terms and Cash Strategy

  • Focus on improving cash conversion cycle and extending payment terms
  • Use multiple business credit cards with different billing cycles to increase float
  • Charge expenses early in the billing cycle to extend payment timing
  • This can create up to about 55 days of additional cash flow
  • Fees can be offset by rewards and tax benefits
  • Combined with supplier terms, this can allow selling inventory before paying for it
  • Strong supplier relationships and negotiation are key to unlocking better terms
  • Payment terms are often the biggest constraint to scaling

In conclusion, this session shows how a cash crisis pushed Josh to build a simple but powerful CEO dashboard focused on people, performance, and cash. 

 

By defining clear actions, tracking leading metrics, and forecasting cash flow, he created a system that improves alignment and prevents financial surprises.

 

He highlights that the real role of a CEO is to build systems that drive consistency and visibility, not just chase growth tactics. With the right structure in place, businesses can scale more confidently, manage cash effectively, and avoid the common pitfalls that limit growth.

cliff_notes:
In this session a group of e-commerce operators shares how they launch and scale products using TikTok and Amazon. They discuss what is working what is failing, and practical lessons from real campaigns, operations, and review strategies.

 

TikTok-First Strategy and Amazon Halo Effect
  • TikTok is used as the main launch channel, while Amazon captures demand.
  • Brands create their own content and run creator campaigns at the same time.
  • Viral TikTok content drives strong sales on Amazon.
  • Amazon sales often increase one to two weeks after TikTok campaigns.
  • Strong results can happen even with weak Amazon listings and low reviews.
  • Sales can grow organically without PPC due to external traffic.

 

AI Content and Product Mismatch
  • Viral success can attract AI-generated videos that misrepresent products.
  • Some videos show higher-quality versions than what is actually sold.
  • This creates customer disappointment and negative reviews.
  • Brands need to remove misleading content from ad campaigns.
  • One solution is to offer a premium version to match expectations.
  • Showing premium versions as limited or sold out can also help positioning.

 

Launch Strategy and Product Focus
  • Some brands prioritize TikTok or their website over Amazon during launches.
  • Expanding existing products can sometimes perform better than launching new ones.
  • Traditional Amazon launch methods still rely on keywords, PPC, and discounts.
  • The idea of always launching new products is debated.
  • New launches work well on fast-moving channels like TikTok Shop.
  • Mature products may benefit more from optimization and scaling.

 

Capacity and Operational Lessons
  • Launching too many products can overwhelm teams and reduce performance.
  • Poor planning leads to weak execution and missed opportunities.
  • It is better to launch fewer products properly than many at once.
  • Over-investing in aggressive tactics without results can waste budget.
  • Decisions should be based on data, not emotion or pressure.
  • Teams should align launches with their actual capacity.

 

Amazon Vine Strategy and Risks
  • Amazon Vine can help generate early reviews but may lower ratings.
  • Vine reviewers can be more critical and less aligned with target customers.
  • Some brands use private communities to support early reviews.
  • A strategy includes seeding positive reviews before using Vine.
  • Pricing adjustments can improve perceived value during Vine campaigns.
  • Parent and child listing structures can help manage review visibility.
  • Some sellers test Vine on separate listings to reduce risk.
  • Messaging such as social impact can improve review sentiment.
  • Vine reviewers may be more sensitive to price and product value.
 
This session highlights how TikTok-first launches and Amazon halo effects can drive significant growth when paired with accurate product representation and solid operational capacity. 
 
The participants show that brands must balance the desire to “always be launching” with realistic constraints on team bandwidth, inventory, and cash. 
They also demonstrate that Amazon Vine, while powerful, carries real risk and must be approached with deliberate seeding, structural hacks, and thoughtful messaging. 
 
By learning from others’ missteps and creative tactics, brands can design launch strategies that are both aggressive and sustainable across TikTok, Amazon, and beyond.

items.title: Damon Sununtnasuk － Automated AEO Dominance for $2 / day － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Damon Sununtnasuk explains how Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) changes the way customers discover brands through AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.

 

TOPICS:
1. What AEO is and why AI-driven, zero-click search makes it critical now.
2. How to mine Reddit and other forums for questions, then turn them into AEO-optimized Q&A articles with schema.
3. How to automate content creation and publishing across multiple sites to drive traffic, conversion, and revenue uplift.
items.description_text: In this session, Damon Sununtnasuk explains how Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) changes the way customers discover brands through AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. TOPICS: 1. What AEO is and why AI-driven, zero-click search makes it critical now. 2. How to mine Reddit and other forums for questions, then turn them into AEO-optimized Q&A articles with schema. 3. How to automate content creation and publishing across multiple sites to drive traffic, conversion, and revenue uplift.
cliff_notes:
In this session, Damon Sununtnasuk explains how Answer Engine Optimization is changing how people discover products through AI tools. 

He shares a system for building an automated content engine using Reddit data, workflows, and multiple sites to increase visibility, conversions, and revenue.
 
AEO Fundamentals and Why It Matters
  • AEO means optimizing to become the answer shown by AI tools instead of a search result link.
  • Tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity AI, Claude, and Grok return only a few answers.
  • Around 65% of searches end without clicks, reducing traffic to traditional websites.
  • AI reduces visibility to only a few top answers, making competition tighter.
  • Many consumers already rely on AI for purchase decisions.
  • AEO traffic often leads to higher engagement and conversions.
  • Early adopters can gain a strong advantage.
 
How AI Chooses Answers
  • AI mainly pulls from blogs and earned media, not ads.
  • Most citations come from non-paid content like articles and research.
  • Short, clear, and direct answers perform better than long blogs.
  • Content should follow a question-and-answer format.
  • The first 40 to 60 words are critical and should answer the question directly.
  • Clear headings and structure help AI understand content.
  • Schema markup improves how AI reads and trusts content.
  • Better structure and schema can increase AI visibility quickly.
 
Using Reddit for Content Ideas
  • Customers already share questions and problems on platforms like Reddit and Quora.
  • Reddit is a major source for AI citations.
  • The system pulls posts daily from selected subreddits.
  • Posts are ranked based on engagement like upvotes and comments.
  • Top topics are summarized and shared with the team.
  • This ensures content is based on real demand instead of guesses.
 
Automating Content and Site Strategy
  • High-performing topics are turned into structured articles using automation.
  • Content includes Q&A format, schema, and images.
  • The process is fast and low cost per article.
  • Articles are stored and managed in GitHub.
  • Content is automatically published to WordPress sites.
  • Instead of one site, the strategy uses multiple sites targeting different stages.
  • Cold sites educate, warm sites explain solutions, and hot sites focus on conversion.
  • Sites are linked together to build authority and guide users through the journey.
  • Posting consistently at scale helps build visibility.
 
Influencing Content and Results
  • The system also supports engaging in Reddit discussions with helpful responses.
  • Responses are reviewed by humans before posting to avoid issues.
  • This helps shape conversations and influence AI outputs.
  • Over 90 days, the system produces hundreds of articles across multiple sites.
  • This leads to increased revenue and higher conversion rates.
  • AI visibility helps influence purchase decisions before users reach the main store.
  • The system improves both traffic quality and conversion performance.

 

This session reframes SEO around the reality that AI answer engines are increasingly deciding which brands customers see and trust. 

 

Damon shows that by mining Reddit for real questions, writing concise Q&A‑style content with strong schema, and scaling publishing across a network of targeted sites, brands can become the “default” answer that AI tools recommend. 

 

He further demonstrates that automating this system with n8n and selectively influencing Reddit discussions can produce tangible financial results, including higher conversions and significant revenue uplift. 

 

Brands that adopt AEO now and build similar automated content engines are positioned to dominate AI‑driven discovery as zero‑click search becomes the norm.

items.title: MDS Inspire Top Takeaways  —  Mogul Call with Our Community Panel
items.description:
In this session, MDS members recap key learnings from the Inspire and Prosper events, focusing on practical tactics to grow their ecommerce brands.

  1. Amazon profitability and launch strategies (reimbursements, bulk discounts, MCF/DSP, phased keyword launches).

items.description_text: In this session, MDS members recap key learnings from the Inspire and Prosper events, focusing on practical tactics to grow their ecommerce brands. TOPICS: Amazon profitability and launch strategies (reimbursements, bulk discounts, MCF/DSP, phased keyword launches). TikTok Shop growth, creator management, and GMV Max campaign tactics. AI, automation, and data foundations to support scalable marketing and operational workflows.
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS community share key takeaways from the Inspire and Prosper events, focusing on Amazon growth, TikTok Shop, AI, and automation. The discussion blends tactical hacks, strategic frameworks, and real-world examples that operators can test immediately.
 
Event Context and Format
  • The call serves as a recap of insights from Inspire and Prosper.
  • Jamie hosts, Damon is the main panelist, and other members contribute throughout.
  • Inspire recordings are being released, depending on speaker approval.
  • Members can book early for future events, with bundle pricing available (e.g., Inspire + Singapore Summit).
  • The session is positioned as a “mini mastermind,” where:
    • Tactical insights are shared
    • Internal notes are discussed
    • Unrecorded sessions are referenced
  • Hector is mentioned as a strong DSP partner with advanced API capabilities and a “Best in Show” award.

 

Amazon Profitability, Bulk, and Launch Strategies
 
Reimbursement Hack
  • Download Amazon’s bulk reimbursement file.
  • Increase suggested reimbursement values by ~15–30%.
  • This can raise payouts without triggering issues (based on current experience).
Bulk Fee Hack
  • Create a dummy SKU (e.g., single unit item).
  • This allows a multi-pack listing to qualify for bulk discounts (~25% referral fee reduction).
  • The dummy SKU does not need to be sold.
MCF + Buy with Prime
  • Enables Amazon DSP traffic to be directed to Shopify.
  • Notable because Amazon typically keeps traffic within its ecosystem.
Promotions
  • Amazon currently offers MCF discounts (e.g., ~$1 per package + additional % discounts).
Canonical URL Hack (from Matt Altman)
  • Launch with a keyword-heavy title to lock in URL.
  • Later optimize titles for conversion while keeping SEO benefit.
Launch Strategy
  • Start with long-tail keywords → scale to broader terms.
  • Use a 45-day “escape velocity” test:
    • If product fails → recall, relabel, relaunch with new ASIN
Vine + Creator Strategy
  • Send premium-packaged units to early reviewers and creators.
  • Maintain standard packaging for main inventory.
Creator Connections
  • Run campaigns at scale (thousands active).
  • Continuously tweak to stay visible to creators.

 

TikTok Shop and Creator Strategy
 
Core Principle
  • Focus on one hero product at a time for TikTok launches.
Creator Recruitment
  • Offer referral incentives for creators bringing in others.
  • Gate samples behind joining a Discord/community.
Key Insights
  • Follower count ≠ performance
  • Even new creators can produce viral content
  • Creators now vet brands, not just the reverse
Retention
  • Top creators often stick to one brand per category → early relationships matter
Content Strategy
  • TikTok prioritizes volume over perfection:
    • Target: 100–250 videos/week
  • Key metrics:
    • ~70% retention at 2 seconds
    • ~60% retention at 6 seconds
Tools
  • FastMoss, Kalodata → identify winning creatives
Creator Payment Model
  1. Pay for first 5 videos
  2. Move to performance-based
  3. Retainers for top creators (30–100 videos/month)
GMV Max Strategy
  • Start with higher ROAS targets → lower to scale
  • Test product mixes and campaign structures
  • Combine with Ads Manager + Spark ads for scaling winners

 

Offers, Customer Journey, and Revenue Expansion
 
“Grand Slam Offer” (influenced by Alex Hormozi)
  • Bundle:
    • Hero product (e.g., dog chew)
    • Sample add-ons (e.g., supplements)
    • Digital product
  • Strategy:
    • Each product introduces the next problem/solution
    • Drives cross-sells and subscriptions
Lifecycle Monetization
  • Post-purchase email flows (e.g., via Klaviyo) upsell:
    • Larger bundles
    • Subscriptions
Key Principle
  • Bundles are intentional—not random
  • Designed to guide the customer journey
Product Selection Shift (Josh Hadley)
  • Prioritize TikTok virality potential over traditional keyword research
  • Amazon becomes a profit capture channel for demand generated elsewhere
 
AI, Automation, and Data Strategy
 
AI Workflows (Damon)
  • Uses n8n to automate content creation (blogs, Pinterest, etc.)
  • Goal: influence search and discovery over time
Implementation Principle
  • Notes → SOPs → workflows
  • Execution matters more than information
“Bus Test”
  • Systems must be documented and maintainable
  • Avoid reliance on one technical “owner.”
Data Strategy (Daniel)
  • Avoid isolated “black box” automations
  • Build a centralized data foundation
  • Reuse pipelines across tools and workflows
Key Insight
  • Define core KPIs (e.g., contribution margin, MER) before applying AI

 

Traffic, Ads, and PR Insights
 
Meta Ads (advanced tactic)
  • Discussion includes domain cloaking and geo-targeting exclusions (e.g., certain ZIP codes) for compliance-sensitive products
Press Releases
  • Platforms: PR Newswire, 24/7 Press Release, Cision
  • Limited direct ROI for traffic
  • Potential impact on LLM/AI visibility and citations
TikTok Content Strategy (Rafael)
  • Entertainment-first approach
  • Example:
    • Story-driven ad where the product appears late (~45 seconds)
AI Content Systems
  • Use structured inputs:
    • Brand strategy
    • Product data
    • Personas
    • Script frameworks

 

Key Takeaways
  • The biggest gains come from implementation, not information.
  • Short-term hacks (fees, reimbursements) can boost profitability quickly.
  • Long-term growth depends on:
    • Strong offers
    • Creator ecosystems
    • Scalable content systems
  • TikTok is now a primary demand engine, not just a marketing channel.
  • AI and automation only work if built on clear data foundations and KPIs.
  • Businesses that combine Amazon, TikTok, and AI effectively are positioned for outsized growth.

items.title: Brandon Himmel － $100K a Month in 90 Days: TikTok Shop Playbook － MDS Inspire 2026
items.description:
In this session, Brandon Himmel shares how he scaled his brand Roughliners from zero to over $100,000 in GMV on TikTok Shop in under 90 days. 

 

TOPICS:
• Brand background, Shark Tank halo, TikTok Shop as brand-building
• 90-day launch: creators, GMV Max, promos
• Scale: affiliates, systems, bonuses, cross-channel growth
items.description_text: In this session, Brandon Himmel shares how he scaled his brand Roughliners from zero to over $100,000 in GMV on TikTok Shop in under 90 days. TOPICS: • Brand background, Shark Tank halo, TikTok Shop as brand-building • 90-day launch: creators, GMV Max, promos • Scale: affiliates, systems, bonuses, cross-channel growth
cliff_notes:
In this session Brandon Himmel explains how he grows his brand Roughliners from zero to over $100000 in GMV on TikTok Shop in under 90 days. 

Big Picture: TikTok Shop = Brand Engine Not Profit Channel (At First)

  • TikTok Shop should be treated as a growth and brand-building channel, not a profit center early on.
  • Success requires inventory, budget, and willingness to take losses upfront, especially for premium products.
  • The real upside comes from the halo effect:
    • Increased branded search
    • Lift in Amazon + Shopify sales
  • Brandon is willing to run break-even or negative on TikTok because total business profit increases.


Who This Strategy Is For

  • Best suited for brands already doing ~$1M+ annually
  • Requires:
    • Strong cash flow from other channels
    • Enough inventory to support scale
  • Not ideal if:
    • You need immediate profitability
    • You’re testing casually with low commitment


Core Insight: TikTok Shop Drives Branded Demand

  • TikTok content → brand awareness → branded search → conversions elsewhere
  • Key data points:
    • Branded Amazon searches jumped massively after exposure (e.g., TV + TikTok)
    • ~24% of Amazon sales were branded vs ~1% for competitors
  • TikTok affiliate content proved more powerful than:
    • In-house content
    • Even consistent organic posting alone

Takeaway:
TikTok ≠ just a sales channel → it’s a demand creation machine

The 90-Day Launch Framework

 

Phase 1: Cold Start with Creators (JoinBrands Strategy)

  • Recruit ~100 creators
  • Goal: generate initial content + GMV momentum
  • Key tactics:
    • Use discounts (e.g., 50% off) instead of full reimbursement to reduce cost
    • Ensure creators:
      • Buy from TikTok Shop (not Amazon)
      • Follow clear briefs
  • Result:
    • ~100 videos
    • ~100 reviews (4.8★ avg)
    • ~$14K–$15K GMV baseline

Phase 2: Strong Creative Briefs (Critical Lever)

  • Most brands fail here
  • Requirements:
    • Show face / human connection
    • Avoid AI voiceovers
    • Clearly demonstrate product usage (no confusion)

You’re not just sending products — you’re directing performance content

Phase 3: Launch GMV Max Ads

  • Turn on only after content is live
  • Start with:
    • ROAS target ~2.0
  • Scale by:
    • Increasing ROAS slowly (every ~90 days)
  • Key rule:
    • Budget must match goals
       (You won’t hit $100K GMV with $50/day)

Phase 4: Promotions for Momentum

  • First 60–90 days = aggressive pricing strategy
    • Month 1: ~50% off
    • Month 2: 30–50% off
    • Then return to full price
  • Purpose:
    • Drive conversion + velocity
    • Build social proof fast

Phase 5: Maximize Creative Volume

  • Feed GMV Max with:
    • Existing content (even old posts)
    • Creator content (via Spark codes)
  • Actively:
    • Remove wrongly tagged videos
    • Re-request reposts early

Scaling After $50K GMV

 

Unlock: Unlimited Creator Outreach

  • Once past ~$50K GMV:
    • Outreach scales aggressively
  • Target creators with:
    • $25K+ GMV history

Sampling Strategy

  • Use:
    • Refundable samples (3-sale threshold)
    • Auto-approval for qualified creators

Creator System = The Real Engine

 

Key Principle:

“Sell creators so they sell for you.”

 

Systems to build:

  • Outreach scripts (AI-assisted)
  • Follow-up flows
  • Performance tracking
  • Creator community (e.g., Discord)

Messaging structure:

  • Hook
  • Offer
  • Social proof
  • CTA

Power Law: Top Creators Drive Massive Results

  • Example:
    • One creator generated $114K GMV from 53 videos
  • Long tail still matters:
    • Many creators doing $4K–$10K each

Mix of:

  • High performers (high touch)
  • Long tail (scaled systems)

Bonus Program: Scaling Content Volume

  • Pay for output, not just results
  • Example:
    • 20 videos/month → $1,000 bonus
  • Target:
    • 50 creators × 20 videos = 1,000 videos/month

Why it works:

  • Volume → more chances of virality
  • Predictable content engine

Leading Metric That Matters Most

  • # of shoppable videos posted

NOT:

  • GMV
  • ROAS
  • Revenue

More videos = more chances to win

Profitability Strategy (Advanced View)

  • TikTok P&L alone can look negative
  • But total impact includes:
    • Amazon lift
    • Shopify growth
    • Brand awareness
    • LTV

Example:

  • Losing on TikTok
  • But gaining more profit across channels

Goal:

  • Reach ~break-even TikTok
  • While it acts as “free marketing”

Key Mistakes to Avoid

  • Trying to be profitable too early
  • Weak or unclear creator briefs
  • Not controlling where creators buy (TikTok vs Amazon)
  • Launching without enough budget or inventory
  • Ignoring content volume
  • Not fixing mis-tagged posts early
  • Scaling SKUs instead of focusing on one product

Final Takeaway

This playbook is about building a content-driven growth engine, not just running ads.

Winning brands:

  • Focus on one strong product
  • Build massive creator output
  • Invest heavily upfront
  • Optimize later

TikTok Shop success =
Content volume × Creator systems × Long-term thinking

In conclusion, this session presents a detailed, numbers‑driven playbook for taking a premium product from zero to over $100,000 GMV on TikTok Shop in under 90 days. 

Brandon shows that success depends on strong briefs, concentrated cold‑start campaigns, aggressive GMV Max usage, and a willingness to invest heavily in early momentum, even at a loss.

He also demonstrates how TikTok Shop can significantly boost branded search and sales across Amazon and Shopify, justifying a long‑term, brand‑building mindset over short‑term profit. 

By layering in systems for creator recruitment, retention, bonuses, and community, he builds an engine designed to scale content and GMV far beyond the initial 90‑day sprint.

items.title: TikTok Shop for Beginners Panel － Mogul Call with Alex Bonilla, Fernando Campos and Jason Pratt
items.description:
In this session, Alex Bonilla, Fernando Campos, and Jason Pratt share practical strategies for launching and scaling products on TikTok.
TOPICS:
  1. Setting up TikTok Shop, handling technical issues, and choosing fulfillment options
  2. Cold start strategies: social proof, creator content, and early ad spend
  3. Coordinating TikTok and Amazon launches, pricing, inventory, and performance metrics
items.description_text: In this session, Alex Bonilla, Fernando Campos, and Jason Pratt share practical strategies for launching and scaling products on TikTok. TOPICS: Setting up TikTok Shop, handling technical issues, and choosing fulfillment options Cold start strategies: social proof, creator content, and early ad spend Coordinating TikTok and Amazon launches, pricing, inventory, and performance metrics
cliff_notes:
In this session Alex Bonilla Fernando Campos and Jason Pratt share practical battle-tested strategies for launching and scaling products on TikTok.

The conversation covers everything from account setup and technical pitfalls to cold starts, pricing, inventory, and ad spend strategy across channels.

The panel repeatedly emphasizes the importance of compliance, social proof, and long-term brand building over short-term profitability on a single platform. TikTok activity also positively spills over into Amazon, Meta, Google, and retail.

Setting Up TikTok Shop and Handling Technical / Account Issues

  • Non-US sellers often set up TikTok Shop through a trusted US contact using their Social Security Number to complete verification.
  • It’s recommended this contact handles signup and document submission before the original owner logs in from abroad to avoid geolocation or verification issues.
  • Using attorneys, ITINs, or paying strangers for account setup is risky and unreliable.
  • For technical problems like TikTok Shop binding to the wrong Shopify instance, forcing a full Shopify sync can delay sales; manually listing priority SKUs is faster and safer.
  • Working with an approved TikTok agency partner can speed up escalations for shop management, affiliates, or live content.
  • TikTok Shop does not require a pixel for tracking, as performance is tracked natively.
  • FBT (Fulfilled by TikTok) is TikTok’s own fulfillment program. Merchants can start with self-fulfillment or Amazon MCF and move to FBT once qualified.
  • TikTok Shipping rules allow self-fulfillment with TikTok-purchased labels; FBT is favored for inventory visibility and algorithm support.
  • Brands sending FBT stock must ensure TikTok-compatible barcodes rather than Amazon-specific barcodes.

Cold Start Strategy and Building Social Proof on TikTok

  • The “cold start” phase is when a new product has little or no social proof and must generate early sales and content.
  • Compliance is the first step—products taken down for violations cannot succeed.
  • Early social proof is critical; products with higher sales and reviews perform better.
  • Tactics for early sales include friends-and-family purchases, review syncing, off-platform audiences, and Join Brands sample campaigns.
  • Use North Star metrics like “Shop-eligible videos” to measure traction (e.g., 500–1000 videos for competitive categories).
  • Avoid “fake sales” services that inflate units without generating content, as this undermines trust.
  • Initial ad spend should be conservative; focus on high-volume affiliate and Shop videos over polished branded content or live shopping at first.
  • Sequence: ensure compliance → build basic social proof → scale with creators, retainers, and ads.

Coordinating TikTok and Amazon Launches, Pricing, and Fulfillment

  • TikTok is now a primary demand channel; activity drives Amazon sales and rankings.
  • Launch products on TikTok and Amazon simultaneously; have Amazon listings live and optimized.
  • Flash sales on TikTok can kick-start the “flywheel.”
  • Use separate UPCs to reduce Amazon price-matching issues.
  • Launch on TikTok using “New Drop” campaigns with temporary discounts, then bring Amazon fully online a week later.
  • Inventory split example: 80% TikTok (FBT), 20% Amazon FBA; rebalance based on sales velocity.
  • Amazon MCF can be used initially, but TikTok increasingly favors FBT for performance.

ROAS, Spend Strategy, Lifetime Value, and Cross-Channel Impact

  • Brands can tolerate slightly negative ROAS on TikTok if incremental profits on Amazon or other channels exceed losses.
  • TikTok-native merchandising should support higher margins to cover creator commissions, discounts, and fulfillment costs.
  • Subscription orders on TikTok increase lifetime value without additional ad spend.
  • TikTok positively impacts Meta and Google campaigns by creating warmer audiences and additional content.
  • TikTok acts as a full-funnel engine, often allowing brands to 3–5x business growth compared to Meta alone.

Product Validation, Compliance, and Operational Readiness

  • Use data from Amazon and TikTok, analytics tools (e.g., KatData, Kilo Data, Fast Follows), and customer reviews to validate products.
  • Focus on meaningful product improvements rather than “me-too” versions.
  • Test product angles and emotions, not just products; fresh angles in saturated categories reduce launch budgets.
  • Compliance and account health must be in place: product compliance, shipping, customer service, and review management.
  • Maintain Shop Performance Score above ~4.0 to avoid traffic suppression.
  • Internal checklists for TikTok readiness (compliance, shipping, customer service, reporting) prevent operational delays.

TikTok Shop is a central growth engine, not just a side channel. Success depends on rigorous compliance, disciplined cold start execution, smart product development, and willingness to invest ahead of short-term profits.

By combining launch tactics, inventory strategy, ROAS planning, and cross-channel thinking, brands can leverage TikTok to drive sales, content, and brand equity across Amazon, Meta, Google, and retail. 

With the right structure and mindset, TikTok can become the “one thing” that makes every other channel easier and more profitable.

items.title: How to Scale from Amazon to Big-Box Retail with Omni-Channel Strategy － Retail Channel Call March 2026
items.description:
In this session, members of the MDS Retail Channel discuss how they scale consumer brands across Amazon and major retailers like Target, Walmart, Kroger, and Costco while also exploring new product launches, legal challenges, and the importance of brand authority.
TOPICS:
  1. Retail distribution strategies and shelf optimization across major chains
  2. New product and brand launches, including Patch RX, Mathology, and ILO
  3. Legal, regulatory, and economic considerations in scaling omni-channel brands
items.description_text: In this session, members of the MDS Retail Channel discuss how they scale consumer brands across Amazon and major retailers like Target, Walmart, Kroger, and Costco while also exploring new product launches, legal challenges, and the importance of brand authority. TOPICS: Retail distribution strategies and shelf optimization across major chains New product and brand launches, including Patch RX, Mathology, and ILO Legal, regulatory, and economic considerations in scaling omni-channel brands
cliff_notes:
In this session the participants exchange lessons learned about launching and scaling consumer products across Amazon's big-box retail and media-driven channels like Good Morning America.

 

Retail Distribution Channel Strategy and Product Placement
  • David explains that his main brand is heavily focused on cold therapy products with a hero item referred to as the “headache hat”, which is his primary product and core revenue driver.
  • David shares that his products are already in all Target stores in the United States and that he has just launched into approximately 1500–1800 Kroger stores, marking a significant expansion in grocery retail.
  • David describes the challenge of getting a second and third product into Target and other major retailers, noting that it is much harder than getting the first listing approved.
  • He contrasts the scale of online sales on Amazon, where he can sell thousands of units a day (e.g., as a top Secret Santa gift), with the relatively limited volume achievable when there are only four to six units of a product on a physical retail shelf.
  • Garland explains that his pimple patch and skincare brand Patch RX is in about 80% of all Walmart stores in the U.S., as well as Walmart Canada, where it is in roughly 377 out of about 410 stores.
  • Garland shares that Patch RX has also secured vendor paperwork with HEB and AAFES (the U.S. military commissary system), indicating strong traction with retail buyers.
  • Garland describes his toothpaste brand Mathology, which is performing very well on Amazon, where it ranks around #13 in all toothpaste at the time of the conversation and has previously reached as high as #8 before stock issues caused a temporary setback.
  • Garland notes that retailers such as Walmart Canada ask for unique SKUs and pack configurations that are exclusive to their chain so that they can offer a distinctive deal that is not directly comparable to other channels.
  • David confirms that similar expectations exist across big chains, explaining that different retailers often require exclusive pack sizes, bundles, or flavors to differentiate themselves and maintain margin and perceived value.
  • The group discusses how facing size and shelf real estate in stores like Target and Walmart are critical, with David noting that Target allocates a 10-inch facing for his product, whereas Walmart allocates a 5-inch facing, which affects visibility and revenue per inch.
  • Etienne shows his own lunchbox product “Lupa”, explaining that the packaging is optimized to stand vertically to minimize shelf space so that retailers can add multiple colors or SKUs in the same footprint.
  • Etienne explains that in some of his channels, especially outside highly standardized chains like Target and Walmart, shelf-ready packaging or PDQs are less used or not necessary, so he is considering dropping some of that added packaging cost.
  • David and Garland emphasize that “shelf-ready” or PDQ (pre‑displayed) packaging is extremely important for large retail chains, because those retailers focus heavily on maximizing revenue per inch and simplifying in-store execution.
  • David shares ongoing efforts to expand further into Costco, where he has a two-pack configuration, but he notes that Costco’s online price positioning and buyer demands make sell-through challenging.
  • The group acknowledges that each retailer has its own rules, expectations, and internal economics, and brands must align pack size, price, and margin structure accordingly to succeed.

 

Product Innovation, New Brand Launches, and Assortment Strategy
  • David describes the difficulty of expanding his cold therapy assortment due to size variations across body parts such as knees and elbows, where different customers need different sizes, making retail SKU management complex.
  • He explains that on Amazon, he can easily offer small, medium, large, and extra-large variants, but in physical retail stores, having many size variations complicates inventory and space allocation.
  • To address these challenges, David introduces a product called the “any sleeve”, a Velcro-based sleeve that can fit multiple body parts and sizes, which simplifies the assortment by reducing size-specific SKUs.
  • David notes that the “any sleeve” is slightly off-brand because his original cold therapy concept focuses on no Velcro and a simple slide-on design, but he accepts the compromise to meet retail requirements.
  • David confirms that the “any sleeve” already launches in Walmart as a second SKU alongside his main hero product, and they are working on swapping out a weaker SKU (a $9 stick) that is underperforming.
  • David shares that he and his partner have launched a new brand and product called the “ILO”, which he describes as a pillow that is also a sleep mask, made from a mulberry silk blend and designed to be large, cozy, and visually striking.
  • He explains that the ILO is conceptually similar to his “headache hat” product, but it is filled and structured differently, shifting from gel-based cold therapy to a soft sleep-focused product.
  • David mentions that despite being a new brand with no initial sales, the ILO has already been featured on Good Morning America, leveraging his existing media relationships to gain early exposure.
  • Garland explains that over the last 12–18 months, his team has launched Mathology, a toothpaste brand, and that this brand is performing strongly in terms of Amazon ranking and sales velocity.
  • Garland notes that they launched around 15 products in the Patch RX skincare and pimple patch line over the past year, but they are now in the process of selling off most of their portfolio, except for their oral care brand Mathology.
  • He clarifies that the strategy is to maintain Mathology as the primary long-term oral care brand while exiting Patch RX in a way that captures value from its strong retail presence.
  • Garland describes how they are adding multiple variants under Mathology, including whitening formulas, kids’ formulas, and a sensitivity-focused product, to broaden the line and better serve different consumer segments.
  • The participants discuss how flavors, colors, and limited editions or seasonal designs can be used strategically to create differentiation for various channels and special events (for example, different colorways or holiday designs for David’s products).
  • The conversation highlights that new brand launches are resource-intensive and risky, requiring significant up-front advertising spend, patient scaling, and a long-term view to reach meaningful revenue.

 

Legal, Regulatory, Pricing, and Competitive Dynamics
  • David and Garland discuss recent legal and regulatory challenges that arise from product claims and labeling, especially in categories like pimple patches, pain relief, and topical products.
  • Garland explains that Patch RX is caught up in a broad enforcement wave where many pimple patch brands are scrutinized for improper or overly aggressive claims on their Amazon listings.
  • He shares that his company is forced to settle a legal matter for about $200,000, down from an original demand of $500,000, which arises from just two problematic words in their listing copy.
  • Garland notes that these experiences highlight the importance of “playing by the rules” and being careful about claims, even when competitors appear to ignore regulations.
  • David shares that his own company previously experienced a serious legal scare when authorities arrived at his office in uniform, attempting to shut them down over regulatory issues in their product claims.
  • He explains that some competitors, especially China-based sellers, do not play by the same rules, and this makes it difficult to enforce fairness or rely on platforms to level the playing field.
  • David notes that his team has tried to get Amazon to crack down on non-compliant competitors, but he reports little success in achieving meaningful enforcement.
  • He cites examples where competitors use restricted terms like “migraine” or “headache” in product names or copy that his company avoids to stay compliant, indicating a disparity in rule enforcement.
  • David also mentions facing back-end “hacks” or attacks that temporarily cause their listings to be suspended or impaired, forcing his company to quickly resolve issues and negotiate to avoid further damage.
  • The participants discuss that retail buyers and chains are often cautious about Amazon-heavy businesses, preferring brands with omni-channel presence and strong brick-and-mortar performance to reduce risk.
  • Garland points out that in Costco, Walmart, and Target, brands must carefully manage price parity and channel conflict, ensuring that each retailer feels they have a special deal or unique bundle.
  • David explains that he has to manage two-pack configurations, price points, and shipping policies across Costco, his own website, and Amazon, noting that misaligned pricing can crush sales on a specific platform.
  • He also mentions that his company is exploring a second production facility in Guatemala to diversify manufacturing risk, improve lead times (seven days instead of 35), and gain advantages in tariffs and logistics.

 

Mindset, Unit Economics, Inventory Planning, and Long-Term Vision
  • David and Garland discuss how inventory planning is crucial when products can go viral suddenly, especially with media features like Good Morning America or other major outlets.
  • David explains that for his flagship cold therapy product, he often keeps around 150,000 units of black caps in stock, because he needs to be ready for spikes in demand and cannot afford to stock out during viral moments.
  • He notes that his company is developing or considering a tool for better inventory ordering and forecasting, since they historically relied on strong cash flow and a bias toward having extra stock, which may not be optimal capital allocation.
  • David shares that Good Morning America appearances used to generate up to $500,000 in sales per feature, but over time the effect has declined to around $180,000–$200,000, showing some channel fatigue even while still providing awareness and inventory movement.
  • He describes the economics of such media deals, where the customer typically gets 50% off, the show takes a share, and the brand must build offer and shipping structures (for example, free shipping or thresholds) that still preserve some margin.
  • Garland and David analyze first-order profitability versus lifetime value (LTV) in direct-to-consumer (DTC) channels, emphasizing that many brands need to stop focusing solely on profitable first orders and instead plan for profitable LTV across repeat purchases.
  • Garland explains that his team currently operates in a first-order-centric model but is actively working on shifting to an LTV-centric model for Mathology, which better aligns with the recurring nature of toothpaste purchases.
  • They agree that for recurring products like toothpaste, brands can justify losing money on the first order because customers reorder frequently, whereas for products like David’s, reorders might happen only every six months, which changes the payback horizon.
  • David reflects on purpose and motivation after achieving financial success, noting that for him and many entrepreneurs, the pursuit and the challenge of building something meaningful is more fulfilling than money alone.
  • Garland agrees and adds that happiness comes from the pursuit of a meaningful goal, such as growing Mathology or building an authoritative brand in oral care, not from hitting an arbitrary financial number.
  • They discuss building authority and expertise as a key lever, citing how Facebook began in Ivy League schools (Harvard, then Stanford, then other elite universities), which created an aura of authority and desirability from the start.
  • Garland describes how Mathology is building authority by creating a dental advisory board, which includes Cardi B’s dentist, along with other notable dental professionals, to strengthen credibility in oral care.
  • David underscores that brands should aim to “be the expert” and “be the authority” in their niche, generating content, endorsements, and educational assets rather than just pushing an Amazon product listing.
  • The conversation closes with an emphasis on long-term thinking, omni-channel strength, and personal purpose, as both David and Garland look beyond short-term revenue to sustainable brand building and meaningful work.

 

In conclusion, this session presents a rich and practical discussion about expanding consumer brands across Amazon, big-box retailers, and media channels while navigating legal, logistical, and strategic challenges. 

 

The participants openly share both wins and setbacks, making the conversation highly instructive for anyone managing omni-channel retail growth.

items.title: How to Build Secure AI Automation Systems and Data Pipelines for E-Commerce Operations － AI Channel Call March 2026
items.description:
In this session, participants share how they use Claude/OpenClaw to automate real business workflows, especially in e-commerce and analytics, with a focus on scalability and security.
  • Building and managing skills for coding, browser automation, and business processes
  • Setting up data pipelines, reporting workflows, and project management tools
  • Designing secure, resilient infrastructure and access controls for AI agents
items.description_text: In this session, participants share how they use Claude/OpenClaw to automate real business workflows, especially in e-commerce and analytics, with a focus on scalability and security. Building and managing skills for coding, browser automation, and business processes Setting up data pipelines, reporting workflows, and project management tools Designing secure, resilient infrastructure and access controls for AI agents
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss in depth how they design secure and operationalize OpenClaw/Claude‑based agents for e‑commerce and business workflows. 

 

They share concrete implementation details: from browser automation and data pipelines to security patterns and team enablement—so others can replicate and adapt these approaches.

 

Building Skills and Development Workflows in OpenClaw/Claude
  • The group actively uses OpenClaw/Claude as the main platform for building “skills” and agents that automate business processes.
  • Sam Basilio asks how others build new skills specifically whether they develop directly in OpenClaw, in cloud code/VS Code, or with tools like Cursor.
  • Gregg Alper explains that he uses a combination of Cursor with Opus/OpenClaw and sometimes works directly in OpenClaw, depending on whether he is doing larger refactors or quick tweaks.
  • Gregg notes that Cursor’s “plan mode,” “debug mode,” and “ask mode” are very helpful because they prevent unintended changes and keep the model constrained to answering questions when needed.
  • Ramon Gonzalez shares that he often builds directly inside OpenClaw, debugging and iterating there without moving to an external editor unless necessary.
  • Sam describes building a browser‑based skill using Claude code and VS Code, then describes the skill to OpenClaw so it can call it and run test flows.
  • Participants frequently refer to plan mode as a critical safeguard because it encourages the AI to outline steps before executing, which reduces errors and improves reliability.
  • Dimitri Vorona recommends writing pseudocode (logical, natural‑language steps) before asking OpenClaw or Claude to implement features, because it reduces debugging and clarifies assumptions.
  • Sam suggests a “lazy” but effective variant where the AI first writes the pseudocode in plan mode, and then the human reviews and refines it before coding proceeds.
  • Ramon emphasizes that in many e‑commerce workflows, a large percentage of logic can be hard‑coded rather than delegated to the LLM, which reduces token usage and hallucinations.
  • The group repeatedly frames the LLM as “the brain” for only those parts of the workflow that truly need reasoning, while stable structure (templates, subject lines, sign‑offs) is better hard‑coded in scripts.

 

Browser Automation, Scraping, and Infrastructure Choices (Mac Mini vs VPS)
  • Several participants heavily use browser automation in OpenClaw to drive Chrome, interact with websites, post blog articles, and navigate complex web UIs.
  • Sam shares that he builds a browser‑based skill that posts a blog to Shopify, and he is impressed by the agent’s ability to detect errors and gracefully recover.
  • Sam also has an agent perform competitive analysis on Instagram and Twitter, where it browses accounts, opens posts, and extracts insights with minimal prompting.
  • Travis Schwartz describes running browser automations through a dedicated Mac Mini, where OpenClaw uses Google Chrome to scrape data from platforms like Airbnb and log results into Slack channels.
  • Travis mentions that his agent generates many screenshots, which significantly increases credit usage, and he discovers this only when a large Anthropic charge appears.
  • Christian Verhoeven asks which browsers others use and raises privacy and security concerns about browser‑based automations.
  • Travis explains that his Mac Mini runs as an isolated “hands” machine with its own email, credit card, phone number, and a shared Google Drive and 1Password vault, which limits blast radius.
  • Dimitri discusses using both a VPS (with a headless browser) and a Mac Mini as the “hands” for browsing tasks, noting that headless browsers often struggle with certain extensions and complex interactions.
  • Danson explains that his agent uses a Mac Mini to interact with extensions like Helium 10 for Amazon analytics and to read Twitter and Facebook groups more thoroughly than services like Apify.
  • Danson notes that Apify can miss deeply nested comments in social media threads, whereas a browser‑driven agent can open all comments and read everything.
  • Ramon points out that VPS IPs are more frequently blocked for scraping, so a residential‑type machine like a Mac Mini often works better for web scraping tasks.
  • Dimitri and others stress the importance of power resilience for Mac Minis, using UPS (battery backup) and even generators so agents remain online during outages.

 

Data Pipelines, Reporting, and Project Management Automation
  • Ramon focuses on building a reliable data pipeline from Amazon’s SP‑API and ads API, after struggling with instability and long queue times.
  • He describes scheduling daily Amazon reports: for the ads API he schedules reports by email, which are routed to the agent’s email; for SP‑API he schedules report generation via API and polls hourly until reports are ready.
  • Ramon shares that using third‑party connectors like Airbyte introduces instability, so he returns to a simpler scheduled‑report approach to maximize reliability.
  • Gregg explains that he leverages long‑term data stored in Intentwise Analytics (with historical data back to 2022), connects OpenClaw to that database, and feeds it the schema documentation in Markdown.
  • Gregg notes that once the schema is available, he can query almost any metric conversationally and have the agent generate Google Sheets via the Google Drive and Sheets APIs.
  • Christian describes pulling Amazon advertising and SP‑API data into BigQuery using Cloud Run jobs and then building a custom MCP server that both reads from BigQuery and sends actions to the Amazon advertising API.
  • Gregg and Christian both highlight that agents can generate automated weekly or daily reports and then interpret those reports to produce prioritized action lists for their teams.
  • Gregg builds an overview system where reports are written to Google Sheets and indexed in Airtable (with fields for report name, date, department, and sheet link), which creates a searchable calendar view of reports.
  • Ramon uses ClickUp to manage tasks generated and executed by his agent, with each scheduled process mapped to a ClickUp task and a database connecting cron IDs to ClickUp items.
  • Ramon describes how the agent updates each ClickUp task with status (success, partial failure, or failure) and relevant outputs, allowing him to monitor all automations simply by checking overdue tasks.
  • Several participants mention using Slack and Telegram as communication hubs, with bots posting statuses, results, and files into specific channels or threaded topics to keep information organized.
  • Travis explains that Telegram topics work well but can become confusing if users reply in “All” and mix threads; he later migrates many workflows to Slack for team collaboration.

 

Security, Credentials, Networks, and Access Management
  • Security is a dominant theme, especially around agents that can browse, access APIs, and manage financial or private data.
  • Ramon emphasizes that using a Mac Mini with no open external ports greatly reduces external attack surface, since no one can easily connect in from the outside.
  • Dimitri takes further precautions by placing the Mac Mini on a completely separate network (separate IP range, potentially even a different ISP) so an agent cannot access devices on his main home network.
  • Danson describes using a travel router connected to a guest Wi‑Fi network to segregate the Mac Mini traffic, and he combines this with a VPS‑based agent for non‑browser tasks.
  • Ramon explains that he routes email commands to his Mac Mini, but restricts which domains can send authorized commands and adds additional validation logic for safety.
  • Ramon stores all API keys and passwords in a file on the Mac Mini and wraps access via OpenClaw behind a master password so that even if someone prompts the agent for credentials, it must first request and validate a master password.
  • Participants discuss encrypting the .env file (environment variables) that holds secrets, so that if an attacker somehow obtains the file, it remains unreadable.
  • Gregg mentions using Google service accounts and JSON credential files placed directly on the Mac Mini in a credentials directory, which are referenced but not moved or exposed through chat.
  • June Lai recommends using Docker secrets (for Docker MCP Toolkit or Docker Swarm) so tokens stay encrypted and never appear in CLI history or plain text on the filesystem.
  • Gregg and Ramon recognize the risk of prompt injection where a malicious webpage might instruct the agent to email the .env file elsewhere, so Gregg adds explicit security rules forbidding access to certain files or emailing credentials.
  • Christian and others note that even if the .env file is protected, an attacker could still prompt the agent to “use the keys” to perform unauthorized actions, thus they stress multi‑layered protections and least‑privilege design.
  • June reiterates least‑privilege MCP scopes for team members, so each person’s Claude/AI environment only gets the specific data sources and actions they truly need.
  • Travis and Gregg warn that giving an agent permission to read private Slack messages or handle files means you must be very deliberate about what workspaces and channels it can access.
  • Ramon advises that any highly sensitive operations—like adding credit cards or passwords—should be done locally on the Mac Mini, with instructions such as “the file is in downloads; save it and delete the source file,” rather than sending secrets via chat.

 

Knowledge Management, Courses, Team Enablement, and AI “Employees”
  • Participants repeatedly treat AI agents as virtual team members or “antennae” that monitor markets, data sources, and social channels.
  • Danson uses an agent to continuously read Twitter and Facebook groups about OpenClaw/Claude, surfacing new use cases, tools, and business models that might match his goals.
  • Ramon highlights that constant scraping of communities where a target demographic gathers (Twitter, Facebook groups, Reddit, etc.) lets businesses learn how customers talk, what they want next, and potentially build products before competitors react.
  • Sam states that he prefers using AI to do things he would not realistically do himself, such as continuous “ears on the market,” rather than only speeding up existing manual tasks.
  • Ramon and Sam both emphasize building skills on top of structured courses and proven experts, rather than starting from scratch with generic prompting.
  • Ramon cites Anthony’s PPC course (Amazon pay‑per‑click advertising) as the foundation for his upcoming PPC manager agent, noting that he wants to turn its content plus his own experience into a robust playbook.
  • Sam shares that he previously took a long course on VSLs (video sales letters), transcribed it, and loaded those transcripts into a Claude project, allowing him to query it as if he were asking the instructor questions.
  • Christian replicates Ramon’s approach by transcribing Anthony’s PPC course, distilling the content into a knowledge base, and using it to drive a detailed PPC skill inside OpenClaw.
  • Ramon recommends using transcripts from script‑writing courses (e.g., content from Callaway) to help agents write higher‑quality scripts for video content and ads.
  • The group references Adam’s “bus test” concept, where systems should be designed so that if the main AI owner is suddenly unavailable (e.g., “hit by a bus”), someone else can still access passwords and take over operations.
  • Alex Castillo asks how to give his team access to OpenClaw and Claude safely, and participants suggest that team members should have their own Claude plans and limited MCP access instead of sharing one powerful admin agent.
  • Christian notes that a Claude team plan could ease sharing projects, while June stresses that each teammate should only get the specific scopes and tools aligned with their role.
  • Travis mentions a real example where an entrepreneur gives full OpenClaw control to a trusted long‑time assistant, who buys a Mac Mini and runs everything, which illustrates both the potential and risk of deep delegation.
  • Ramon concludes that a strong knowledge base, playbooks, and course‑derived instructions are essential so AI “employees” know exactly how to operate and do not rely solely on ad‑hoc prompting.

 

In conclusion, this session centers on practical, real‑world patterns for running Claude/OpenClaw as a reliable “operations layer” for e‑commerce and analytics businesses. 

 

Participants cover the full lifecycle, from skill development and browser automation to data pipelines, security hardening, and turning expert courses into durable AI playbooks.

 

Collectively, the group treats AI agents less as experimental toys and more as junior employees who are given structured processes, constrained permissions, and carefully designed infrastructure. 

 

This approach allows them to scale automation while preserving control, security, and long‑term maintainability of their systems.

items.title: Scaling Strategies for Growing Brands － Josh Hadley － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Josh Hadley of Hadley Designs shares simple systems for scaling an e-commerce brand toward $100M.

TOPICS:
  1. Building leadership and ownership systems.
  2. Managing performance with clear KPIs, scorecards, and regular alignment check‑ins.
  3. Improving cash flow and growth via credit‑card cash conversion strategies and Creator Connections.
items.description_text: In this session, Josh Hadley of Hadley Designs shares simple systems for scaling an e-commerce brand toward $100M. TOPICS: Building leadership and ownership systems. Managing performance with clear KPIs, scorecards, and regular alignment check‑ins. Improving cash flow and growth via credit‑card cash conversion strategies and Creator Connections.
cliff_notes:
In this session Josh Hadley from Hadley Designs shares concrete tactics for scaling an ecommerce brand toward nine figures. 

 

The conversation dives into leadership systems, performance management, and cash flow optimization. 

 

Throughout, Josh uses his own brand journey, including near‑bankruptcy and recovery, to illustrate why structure, accountability, and cash discipline are critical at scale.

 

Josh Hadley’s Journey, Brand Context, and Resilience

  • Josh explains that he runs Hadley Designs, which is not an agency but a consumer brand that sells products across Amazon, Shopify, and TikTok Shop, with about 70% of sales on Amazon.
  • He notes that the brand is a multi‑million dollar seller across multiple channels, and he positions his current goal as scaling to $100 million in revenue by 2030.
  • Josh shares that he hosts the “Ecom Breakthrough” podcast, which documents his journey and the action items he is implementing to reach nine figures.
  • He frames entrepreneurship as a roller coaster in which founders experience emotional highs and lows even within a single day, and he emphasizes that success requires staying in the game.
  • Josh recounts that in 2024 he faces intense pressure from overseas competitors who copy his products within three to six months and undercut his prices, which threatens his premium‑priced position on Amazon.
  • He explains that he nearly goes bankrupt in 2024, to the point of calculating how many months of cash runway the business has left if nothing changes.
  • He describes how an agency previously tells him that TikTok Shop is not right for his brand, but he later returns to TikTok Shop on his own, which leads to viral success and renewed momentum.
  • Josh shares a crisis in June 2024, when Amazon accuses his account of review manipulation and issues a seven‑day shutdown threat, just as he attends his grandmother’s funeral and his wife’s mother passes away unexpectedly.
  • He explains that if Amazon had forced him to remove all FBA inventory, it would have cost $600,000–$700,000, which he believes would have bankrupted the business.
  • He notes that Amazon ultimately reverses the violation after seven days and admits there is no review manipulation, which he characterizes as rare and effectively a “divine intervention” moment.
  • Josh stresses that he uses this low point to rebuild the business strategically, including implementing a true leadership team rather than relying mainly on VAs executing tasks he hands them.
  • He identifies himself as a man of faith, a husband, and a father of four, and he notes that his personal values strongly influence how he builds his company and team culture.

 

The 1311 Process and Building a Culture of Ownership

  • Josh introduces “Hack #1” as the 1311 process, which he uses to transform how team members present problems and solutions.
  • He explains that the 1311 process requires team members to:
    • State the problem clearly.
    • Provide three possible solutions.
    • Recommend one solution and explain why they choose it.
    • Describe one way to prevent the issue from occurring again in the future.
  • He notes that advances in AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) allow team members to generate more thoughtful, fully fleshed‑out solution options than they could previously.
  • Josh explains that before 1311, his inbox filled with one‑line problem reports that forced him to spend 30 minutes or more per issue devising solutions.
  • After implementing 1311, he typically receives emails where the problem, three options, a recommended choice, and preventive measures are already outlined, so he only needs a couple of minutes to approve or lightly adjust the plan.
  • He describes how this process dramatically reduces his decision fatigue and allows him to spend roughly 80% of his time on growth activities such as new sales channels, scaling TikTok Shop and Shopify, and strategic planning.
  • Josh embeds 1311 into the company’s top core value of “Extreme Ownership”, explicitly stating that team members are expected to use this process and own the outcomes of their decisions.
  • He shares that his executive assistant is instructed to bounce back any “problem‑only” messages, telling the sender that Josh will not review the issue until they add three solutions, a recommendation, and a prevention plan.
  • He explains that the repeated use of 1311 allows him to identify future leaders, because he can see which team members consistently propose strong, holistic solutions that anticipate downstream impacts.
  • Josh notes that team members whose proposed solutions are misaligned more than half the time, even after feedback, are eventually exited from the company because they are not developing the needed strategic judgment.
  • Participants share that they have tried similar frameworks, and Josh stresses that the impact only appears when the system is enforced consistently and reinforced as part of the culture.

 

Performance Management, Core Values, and KPIs

  • Josh introduces “Hack #2” as the Impact Performance Analyzer, a framework to evaluate each team member on both fit (values and capabilities) and effectiveness (results).
  • He explains that fit includes alignment with the company’s core values, which for his business are:
    • Extreme Ownership
    • Relentless Innovation
    • Integrity Above All
  • He states that effectiveness is measured via quality of work, productivity, and concrete results against agreed‑upon goals.
  • He uses a 1–5 rating scale for each core value and each effectiveness dimension, which creates a combined view of where each person sits: “enable excellence” (green), “alignment and growth needed” (yellow), or “release to the market” (red).
  • Josh explains that he sends each team member an email template asking them to self‑score on core values, performance, and effectiveness before he or their direct leader completes the same scoring independently.
  • He notes that he hides the team member’s scores when he fills out his own ratings so that his assessment remains unbiased and independent.
  • He then schedules a one‑on‑one alignment meeting to compare scores, discuss differences, give specific examples, and agree on a plan for alignment and growth over the next 4–6 months.
  • He emphasizes that the process reduces surprises because team members understand exactly where they are winning or falling short, so decisions about role changes or exits rarely come as a shock.
  • Josh shares that, over the last two years, he personally has only needed to fire about three people out of a team of around 35, while several others have self‑selected out after realizing they are not meeting expectations and do not want to operate at that standard.
  • He stresses that the same system applies to overseas team members, including those in the Philippines and Mexico, because he treats them as full team members, not just low‑level “VAs.”
  • He highlights that two of his Filipino team members function at a near‑executive level, earn near six‑figure salaries (locally life‑changing amounts), and can outperform many US‑based professionals.
  • Josh underlines that no country has a monopoly on talent, and remote‑first hiring lets him poach top talent globally rather than being restricted to a local labor pool.
  • He introduces “Hack #3” as building clear role profiles and KPIs, arguing that every role must have explicit metrics or it is like playing an NBA game with no scoreboard.
  • He shares that he previously spent about four hours per role writing detailed role profiles that define:
    • The scorecard and measurable outcomes
    • What success looks like in the role
    • The 20% of activities that drive 80% of results
    • Regular work activities and key responsibilities
  • He now uses a custom GPT / ChatGPT prompt to auto-generate role profiles and KPI ideas in under 60 seconds, then manually curates the top 3–5 KPIs rather than using every metric suggested.
  • Josh notes that these role profiles and KPIs feed into his CEO Scorecard, a dashboard he reviews weekly to see if each role and person is on track, and he plans to present this CEO Scorecard in detail at the Inspire event.
  • He reiterates that regular 4–6 month performance check‑ins revisit these KPIs, evaluate progress, and update the alignment plan as needed.

 

Cash Conversion, Credit Card Strategies, and Creator Connections

 

Cash Flow and Credit Card Optimization

  • Josh introduces “Hack #4” as a method to improve cash flow without taking loans, especially around Amazon ad spend and inventory payments.
  • He instructs sellers to contact Amazon Ads support and request that their billing threshold be raised to $10,000, rather than being charged every $500.
  • He recommends paying Amazon ads with credit cards and opening multiple cards with staggered statement start dates, so ad charges always fall in the first few days of a cycle and maximize the interest‑free float.
  • He explains that by charging ads in the first 1–5 days after the statement start, sellers can often get around 55 days before cash actually leaves their bank account.
  • Josh notes that the Amex Plum Card offers net 60 terms on top of this cycle, which can create almost 90 days of float, although it does not earn traditional rewards points.
  • He stresses that the primary outcome is not just points but a shorter cash conversion cycle, where money from Amazon sales arrives before the ad spend is paid off.
  • He shares that his team maintains a spreadsheet tracking each credit card’s billing period, statement dates, and bonus limits (e.g., 3x rewards on up to $150,000 in ad spend).
  • He uses cards such as Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business (3x rewards on ad spend), various Amex Gold cards, Capital One cards with approximately 2.5% cash back, and Chase Ink Business Premier (2.5% cash back on large transactions).
  • He describes that his finance team and executive assistant coordinate a rotation schedule, and he personally logs into Amazon (as the main admin) to update the billing card because Amazon restricts that permission to the primary account owner.
  • He also applies the same strategy to supplier invoices using payment services like Melio and Plastiq, which allow him to pay suppliers via wire or ACH while funding the payment by credit card.
  • He explains that these services charge around a 2.9–3% fee, but he often earns 2.5% cash back on the card, and crucially, the fee is a business expense while the rewards are treated as non‑taxable personal income in the US.
  • He illustrates that this creates a form of tax‑advantaged arbitrage, where he may pay $580 in fees on a $20,000 invoice, receive $500 in rewards, and still benefit from the tax deduction on the $580, effectively turning part of the cost into tax‑free compensation to himself.
  • He highlights that by combining better supplier terms (e.g., negotiating to net 120 payment terms) with 55–90 days of card float, the business can reach a position where cash from product sales is collected before the inventory is fully paid for.
  • He argues that achieving a negative cash conversion cycle is a core unlock for scaling to eight and nine figures, because it lets the business grow without constant dependence on Amazon lending or external loans.
  • Participant Rich Reister confirms that he implements Josh’s strategy—using multiple gold credit cards, rotating them around statement open dates, and paying suppliers via Plastiq—and that it is a game changer for keeping more cash safely in the business.

 

Creator Connections and Affiliate Infrastructure

  • Josh introduces “Hack #5” around Creator Connections and affiliate marketing, explaining that this has been highly effective for recent product launches.
  • He shares that in one snapshot, his brand spends about $62,000 through Creator Connections and generates around $335,000 in attributable sales.
  • He states that his primary objective is to build a large, owned database of creators and affiliates, not just to drive one‑off bursts of traffic.
  • He sets up Creator Connection campaigns that direct interested creators to a survey, where they submit information and join his email list.
  • He uses automated email sequences to follow up, ensure they actually post content, and invite them to long‑term collaboration rather than just a single campaign.
  • He instructs creators to sign up through Levanta, a tracking platform that allows him to see creator‑level performance data, including which influencers truly drive conversions—data that Amazon itself does not expose per creator.
  • He refers to the current environment as a “creator gold rush”, especially with platforms like TikTok Shop and Amazon Creator Connections active, and he aims to collect thousands of creators’ emails and phone numbers.
  • He explains that once he builds a database of 5,000+ creators, he can launch new products by emailing this list directly, without needing to start from scratch with each new Amazon or TikTok campaign.
  • He notes that he shares slides, Google Docs templates, and spreadsheets via a QR code shown at the end of the presentation, which provide detailed examples of his Creator Connections workflows and outreach templates.

 

In summary, this session walks through how systems, leadership, and financial engineering can transform a stressed seven‑figure ecommerce operation into a scalable business aimed at nine figures. 

 

Josh uses vivid stories from 2024, when he nearly loses his Amazon account and faces intense personal loss—to show that resilience alone is not enough without structured processes, clear KPIs, and disciplined cash management.
