cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS TikTok Channel discuss practical strategies for growing sales on TikTok Shop, primarily through affiliates, creators, and TikTok’s internal tools. 

 

The conversation focuses on sharing wins, troubleshooting current challenges, and refining tactics around creator management, ad spend, and logistics.

 

Case Studies and Wins from TikTok Shop Campaigns
  • Ian Sells reports that he uses Join Brands and Rebate Key together to drive about $2,000 in GMV through a single GMV Max video, which allows him to unlock a new outreach bot for a seasonal product.
  • Ian explains that he repurposes a video from a creator he has worked with before, sends all Rebate Key and Join Brands purchases through that specific video link, and sees both paid and organic sales continue even after the rebate campaign ends.
  • Ian observes that once a creator sees their video start to generate sales and commissions, the creator becomes much more motivated and proactively wants to create more videos for the brand.
  • Mike shares that his Brock supplement product did $40k in GMV in the last 30 days, with 85–90% of the videos coming from content that he and Nick create themselves rather than from outside creators.
  • Mike notes that his own videos significantly outperform those from external creators, and he is trying to understand how to take the next step, particularly in explaining what the product does in a way that converts, similar to what has been done with Moringa on TikTok.

 

Cold Start, Product Cards, and GMV Max Strategy
  • Alex Bonilla explains that a classic “cold start” on TikTok Shop involves getting around 100–500 initial sales on a single product as quickly as possible, often within one to two weeks, to give that product card strong momentum.
  • Alex states that these initial sales are often driven via sampling and creator campaigns (e.g., through Join Brands and Rebate Key), and that once a product card has this early traction, TikTok’s algorithms are more likely to reward it with additional traffic and sales.
  • Ian and Alex discuss that sending purchases directly through a video link (instead of the product detail page) can help TikTok interpret that content as a highly converting video, which may unlock more organic traffic and better performance in GMV Max.
  • Alex reminds the group that when structuring a cold start using affiliates and open commissions, brands need to account for the combined percentage: TikTok’s referral fee plus creator commission can effectively add roughly 20% extra cost during the launch phase.
  • Alex recommends restarting GMV Max campaigns for older products that are not getting pushed, especially if GMV Max has been running at aggressive settings (e.g., aiming for 1x ROI with high commissions) but is no longer driving meaningful traffic.
  • Alex notes that for brand‑new TikTok Shop brands, TikTok often caps the daily order limit, so a well‑executed cold start both trains the algorithm and naturally helps unlock higher daily order capacity.
Creator Training, Retainers, and Community Building
  • Alex emphasizes that any creator being paid a retainer should already know how to make effective content, but many still need coaching on retention rate and the importance of the first six seconds.
  • Alex explains that TikTok favors videos with around 70% retention at 2 seconds and 60% at 6 seconds, and he advises creators to audit their past content analytics, identify hooks that nearly hit those numbers, and refine them, while abandoning hooks with very poor retention.
  • Anna asks how to train retained creators to produce better‑performing content, and Alex suggests focusing on teaching them how to craft strong hooks and to study their own analytics rather than relying only on generic advice.
  • Nate Taminger shares that his brand is shifting its main focus to coaching creators, especially affiliates who are not on retainers, because he believes better coaching on content will be the next major unlock for performance.
  • Nate plans to host weekly or bi‑weekly coaching calls with creators, even though he notes that he personally has not been an affiliate creator before and will rely on platform learnings and observed best practices.
  • Alex recommends Parker’s course (a paid masterclass widely discussed in the community) as an in‑depth resource on going viral on TikTok, and says that about 90% of what he teaches creators comes from that material.
  • Tracy asks how to motivate TikTok Affiliate creators who already have samples but are not posting, and Alex advises only moving proven performers (those with at least one sale and then repeated success) into retainer or closer‑support relationships.
  • Alex describes a workflow where, as soon as a creator generates their first sale, the brand sends them a congratulatory message inviting them into a community (e.g., Discord or a WhatsApp group), where they can later be considered for retainers and special opportunities.
  • Alex suggests using Join Brands’ retainer feature to keep everything clean and performance‑tied, offering modest per‑video amounts (e.g., roughly $5–$20 per video, or about $1,000 total for a serious “30 videos in 30 days” commitment once a product is proven).
  • Alex advises Tracy to reserve retainers or more generous per‑video payments only for creators who are already generating consistent sales, rather than paying high rates (e.g., $200–$400 per video) to unproven creators.

 

Funnel Strategy, Content Types, and Subscription Economics
  • Ian observes that many successful brands seem to win by having fewer creators posting a lot of content (including repeated bottom‑of‑funnel style videos) rather than by working with a huge number of creators each posting only once.
  • Ian notes that bottom‑of‑funnel content—simple, direct videos that show the product and urge viewers to “get this” because it solves a specific problem—often appears to convert better and is easier for creators to produce at scale.
  • Alex explains that product type and existing awareness matter: when there is already lots of top‑funnel content for a category (such as Moringa), brands can focus on bottom‑funnel content that captures demand and persuades people to buy a specific SKU.
  • Alex contrasts this with categories like Mike’s Brock supplement, which may require more top‑ and mid‑funnel content to educate viewers before a bottom‑funnel pitch will convert reliably.
  • Alex mentions that in some TikTok niches, “bottom‑of‑funnel” has been abused by aggressive marketers who falsely claim “2‑for‑1” or similar limited offers; he clarifies that his brands do not use these deceptive tactics.
  • Jon Jewett recommends using subscriptions on TikTok Shop, offering 20–25% off the first subscription order, because he sees a high subscription stick rate over time, which significantly improves long‑term ROI.
  • Alex reports that TikTok has recently added friction to the subscription sign‑up flow to reduce accidental subscriptions, which lowers subscription opt‑in but also reduces complaint‑driven returns and one‑star reviews.
  • Jon shares that many of his negative reviews are from customers angry about subscriptions they did not understand, and his team has an internal process with their TikTok technical account manager to have those reviews removed regularly.
  • Alex says he is testing 50% off the first subscription order on TikTok following advice from Nick Sharma’s “Limited Supply” podcast, with the goal of breaking even on the first sale while benefiting from the approximately 80% subscription retention that many DTC brands see.

 

TikTok Policies, AI Content, Fees, Shipping, and Logistics
  • Jon explains that his brand has experienced repeated TikTok violations for “non‑original content” on videos that use AI avatars or AI‑generated B‑roll, even though the content is original and specifically created for the brand.
  • Jon describes a workaround where they first post a video with no product tag, then later attach the product link inside the GMV Max > Creatives interface, which seems to allow the content to run as part of GMV Max without triggering violations.
  • Alex notes that TikTok staff have told him AI content is allowed in principle, but in practice, brands are still encountering inconsistent enforcement and unexplained flags, particularly on shop‑tagged videos.
  • Dan Stoyan shares a theory that some competitors boost videos from their front‑end accounts using cheap TikTok boosts for followers, likes, or views (e.g., $20 per video), which may cause GMV Max to see strong engagement signals and then push those videos harder.
  • Alex acknowledges that boosting from a dedicated marketing account could be an interesting test, but he is wary of asking creators to boost from their personal accounts because he has heard that accounts that pay for followers or views may later struggle to get organic reach.
  • Mike confirms that he has previously grown an account to 200,000 followers using only paid ads and that once he turned off the ads, follower growth and organic performance fell sharply, which supports the concern about over‑relying on boosts.
  • Greg Liu asks about TikTok fees, including “transaction fees” and referral fees; Alex and Jon say that in their own financial breakdowns they mainly see referral fees and affiliate commissions, and recommend checking internal financial summaries rather than relying solely on mixed online articles.
  • Greg reports that his brand sees significantly reduced shipping rates when using TikTok labels, with average costs dropping from about $13 to about $8.50 even on larger items such as shoes, suggesting TikTok has negotiated stronger carrier deals.
  • Jon highlights the performance of virtual bundles, explaining that bundling multiple products in the catalog now accounts for over 5% of his sales and is growing, and he recommends that others set up virtual bundles and include them in GMV Max campaigns to raise AOV.
  • Jon also raises the topic of FBT/CBT (TikTok fulfillment and cross‑border fulfillment) and notes that TikTok intends to enforce stricter rules around using TikTok’s own shipping labels versus a 3PL’s independent labels, although the enforcement timeline has been repeatedly delayed.
  • Alex predicts that 3PLs and OMS providers will have to adapt their systems to integrate directly with TikTok’s shipping label and fulfillment requirements, or brands may be pushed toward using TikTok’s FBT model for some or all of their inventory.

 

In this session, the group collectively refines a playbook for TikTok Shop growth that blends cold‑start strategies, creator coaching, performance marketing, and operational optimization. 

 

By sharing specific numbers, tools, and failures, they give each other a concrete picture of what is working now and what still needs testing.

items.title: Advanced Amazon Logistics Strategies Using AWD, FBA, and Reimbursement Optimization － Logistics Channel Call Feb 2026
items.description:
In this session, Logistics Channel members discuss how they manage AWD and FBA operations, deal with inventory and reimbursement challenges, and share tools and events that help them optimize their businesses.
TOPICS:
  1. AWD and FBA replenishment, reconciliation, and lost-inbound challenges
  2. Reimbursement tools, returns handling, and stuck pending orders
  3. Freight/logistics strategies and community resources (events, tools, and communication channels)
items.description_text: In this session, Logistics Channel members discuss how they manage AWD and FBA operations, deal with inventory and reimbursement challenges, and share tools and events that help them optimize their businesses. TOPICS: AWD and FBA replenishment, reconciliation, and lost-inbound challenges Reimbursement tools, returns handling, and stuck pending orders Freight/logistics strategies and community resources (events, tools, and communication channels)
cliff_notes:
In this session the Logistics Channel members discuss advanced operational issues around Amazon Warehousing & Distribution (AWD) FBA, logistics, and reimbursements. 

 

The conversation centers on sharing practical experiences, troubleshooting Amazon-related problems, and comparing tools and processes. Newer members also seek guidance on how to get up to speed with Amazon logistics and community resources.

 

Liquidating inventory and working with 3PLs / liquidators
  • Members discuss a question about how to liquidate inventory moved from AWD to a 3PL, and whether to let the 3PL liquidate or to work with dedicated liquidators.
  • One member explains that they usually bring large, heavy items back from the 3PL because liquidators in their niche do not want those products, so liquidation through liquidators is not very successful.
  • The same member sometimes tries to sell excess or unwanted inventory to competitors, especially in the office supplies and furniture category, rather than relying on generic liquidators.
  • The group notes that a meaningful part of one seller’s business (roughly 10–15%) comes from purchasing liquidation deals from others, which indicates that liquidation can be a viable sourcing model even if it is hard to liquidate one’s own slow-moving stock.

 

AWD, FBA replenishment, reconciliation, and lost-inbound issues
  • Members describe using Amazon Warehousing & Distribution (AWD) both from China (via containers) and from US-based warehouses, and then re-supplying FBA from AWD to reduce shipping costs and improve logistics.
  • One member reports that AWD is releasing inventory to FBA too early, despite a 90‑day configuration, effectively pushing six months of stock into FBA and triggering high storage fees.
  • There is confusion over how Amazon calculates “days of cover” for FBA, whether it is based on that seller’s own sales or the overall sales rank and 1P competition; this makes AWD auto-replenishment difficult to trust.
  • Multiple members explain that auto-replenishment from AWD to FBA often performs poorly, so they turn it off and rely on manual weekly replenishment, accepting slightly higher shipping costs in exchange for tighter control and avoiding overstock and long‑term storage fees.
  • AWD frequently splits shipments into many smaller ones (e.g., 5–8 sub‑shipments), which multiplies the number of inbound reconciliations and increases back-office workload.
  • Several participants mention that lost inbound from suppliers to AWD is not reimbursed reliably: AWD often shows fewer cartons received, and escalation typically fails, so they have to track discrepancies manually in Google Sheets.
  • Members track inbound containers by comparing what is supposed to be at AWD with what AWD shows and note that sometimes “missing” cases reappear later, suggesting that items are in a kind of inbound limbo.
  • One member shares that they do a full annual reconciliation for AWD (rather than monthly) to catch these late-appearing units and adjust inventory for audits, whereas others with bank covenants must close their books and reconcile discrepancies monthly.
  • A participant mentions a new AWD report that lists all FBA shipment IDs (FBA IDs) originating from AWD, which significantly improves AWD‑to‑FBA reconciliation, though it still requires cross-warehouse aggregation.
  • Another member notes that AWD to FBA transfers do qualify for reimbursement when units are lost in that leg, since Amazon is acting as the carrier, and they have had decent success getting reimbursements for AWD→FBA losses.

 

Freight, logistics strategies, and geographical warehouse considerations
  • One member explains that they never directly import from China under their own logistics, instead issuing local purchase orders to US-based manufacturers or distributors who handle importation; products from Taiwan, China, Vietnam, etc. arrive directly at their US warehouse.
  • For domestic freight, members compare Amazon Freight with Worldwide Express (a freight broker) and report that Worldwide Express often provides better service and responsiveness, especially for LTL (less‑than‑truckload) and FTL (full‑truckload) shipments.
  • High‑value shipments, such as a full truckload of toner cartridges worth approximately $2.5 million, motivate sellers to favor more reliable freight providers and to maintain transit insurance; but claims can be challenging when AWD delays or obscures loss notifications.
  • Participants discuss the difficulty of controlling which AWD warehouse receives their inventory (e.g., trying to target California or Texas locations such as IUSF or Arizona sites).
  • Members share tactics such as changing the ship-from country, adjusting the warehouse region/zone, and keeping the shipment workflow tab open while refreshing every few hours or days to wait for more favorable AWD destinations (e.g., West Coast or specific warehouses).
  • One member jokes that Amazon seems to route shipments to the furthest possible warehouse (e.g., from Wisconsin to Miami or Los Angeles to New York), speculating that Amazon may prefer to minimize its own internal redistribution costs.
  • A participant mentions that Amazon Global Logistics plans to start shipping to Canada by late in the year (Q3 or Q4), which should simplify DDP‑style imports into Canada, similar to existing support for the UK and Germany.

 

Reimbursement tools, returns, pending orders, and AI/process automation
  • Several third‑party reimbursement tools and services are discussed, including:
    • Carbon6 / Seller Investigators (referred to collectively as Carbon6 tools)
    • TrueOps (with a special 7% fee rate for MDS members)
    • Refund Hawk (offered to one seller at 7% commission)
    • Seller Investigators (again, used at 7% commission)
  • One member reports that Seller Investigators recovered about 1.3% of revenue in reimbursements (e.g., $130,000 recovered on $10 million in annual sales), which gives members a benchmark for what they might be leaving on the table.
  • Another member mentions that a fellow seller using an internal system claims to reach about 2.5% of revenue recovered via reimbursements, though the mix of business models (retail arbitrage, online arbitrage, wholesale, private label, brand ownership) may affect these numbers.
  • Many experienced sellers still do a large portion of reimbursement work in‑house, using software only as a second pass to catch missed cases, particularly since Amazon now automatically reimburses many lost/damaged FBA units except for lost inbound.
  • There is discussion of returns handling: for high volumes, a seller may need a US warehouse and low‑cost labor (e.g., students) to inspect, photograph, repack, and then reship items to FBA, especially when products have many parts that must be checked individually.
  • One member stresses the value of marking inventory with a non-removable custom sticker on the outer box and using serial numbers to confirm that returned items are truly theirs, particularly because buyers might mix inventory from multiple office supply sources (e.g., Staples or Office Depot) and return a non‑matching product.
  • The group notes that handling customer returns that never actually make it back to FBA (customer refunds without returned goods) is still fertile ground for reimbursements but is labor‑intensive to do correctly.
  • Significant concern is raised about FBA orders stuck in “pending” status for weeks or months. One member shows numerous orders pending for one to three months, including large B2B and subscribe‑and‑save orders.
  • These pending orders tie up inventory and can cause the seller to pay storage and overage fees on stock that Amazon is not actually shipping, and they are difficult to address via Seller Support, even after escalation through Seller Café and events like Amazon Accelerate and Amazon Business (AB) meetings.
  • Members suspect many of these customers have long since abandoned or forgotten the orders, yet Amazon does not release the stock, leaving the seller with distorted inventory positions and forecasting challenges.
  • On automation, one participant mentions someone in MDS who built an AI agent to handle reimbursements, but others are wary of granting deep Seller Central API access to third parties or bots, especially for large accounts.
  • Another member suggests using scraping tools or custom Chrome-based automation (rather than APIs) to continuously refresh pages and pull data—similar to their custom repricer that scrapes competitive pricing—while maintaining tighter security control.

 

In conclusion, this meeting highlights how advanced Amazon sellers manage complex logistics across AWD, FBA, and multiple freight and warehouse partners. 

 

They share concrete tactics for replenishment, reconciliation, and reimbursements while acknowledging the limitations of Amazon’s systems—particularly around lost inbound inventory and long‑pending orders.

items.title: How to Launch and Scale TikTok from Zero in 60 Days - Alex Bonilla - APAC Chapter Monthly Call
items.description:
In this session, Alex Bonilla shares a step-by-step system for “cold starting” on TikTok Shop, helping new brands quickly drive sales and creator content.
TOPICS:
  1. Using Join Brands to generate 100 real sales, videos, and spark codes for a new product
  2. Launching and optimizing GMV Max campaigns to scale to ~1,000 units and boost algorithm signals
  3. Q&A on briefs, AI tools, non-US account setup, and balancing brand content, affiliates, and live selling
items.description_text: In this session, Alex Bonilla shares a step-by-step system for “cold starting” on TikTok Shop, helping new brands quickly drive sales and creator content. TOPICS: Using Join Brands to generate 100 real sales, videos, and spark codes for a new product Launching and optimizing GMV Max campaigns to scale to ~1,000 units and boost algorithm signals Q&A on briefs, AI tools, non-US account setup, and balancing brand content, affiliates, and live selling
cliff_notes:
In this session the MDS APAC Chapter hosts Alex Bonilla, who shares a repeatable “cold start” system for brands with no traction on TikTok Shop. 

He explains why mass sampling and agencies are inefficient early, and he outlines how brands can use Join Brands and GMV Max to manufacture momentum before scaling.

Background & Context
  • Alex shares how he grew his business from a lifestyle model to nearly $10M in annual revenue.
  • He states that he built this framework to help brands avoid wasting money at the start.

Why Traditional Tactics Struggle
  • Alex explains that agencies and bots require large budgets before brands see results.
  • He states that mass sampling now often requires 500–1,000+ units per month to create impact.
  • He defines traction as a combination of units sold and visible UGC on the product page.
  • He warns that inflated sales without matching content create distrust among creators.
  • He concludes that brands must build real traction before they scale with agencies.

Cold Start with Join Brands
  • Alex instructs brands to run a 100-post Social Blast campaign to generate 100 real sales and 100 videos.
  • He explains that creators purchase the product on TikTok Shop and receive reimbursement after delivery.
  • He emphasizes that brands must secure spark codes to run ads effectively.
  • He states that brands can reuse UGC across Amazon, Shopify, and short-form platforms.
  • He estimates that brands can complete the cold start in about two months at roughly $45 per video.

Brief Best Practices
  • Alex requires creators to show their face, speak on camera, and avoid pure unboxing videos.
  • He instructs brands to focus on strong hooks and retention metrics.
  • He recommends including video examples and clear hashtag guidance.
  • He confirms that brands can use AI tools to write and refine structured briefs.
  • He suggests commissioning a few premium videos first if no strong examples exist.

Scaling with GMV Max
  • Alex advises brands to launch GMV Max once at least 50 spark codes are live.
  • He recommends manually uploading selected video IDs to control testing.
  • He suggests lowering ROI targets initially to force spend and gather data.
  • He states that brands should aim to reach approximately 1,000 units sold to establish momentum.
  • He explains that once traction exists, bots and agencies perform more efficiently.
  • He also references The 4-Hour Work Week as the inspiration that originally led him into e-commerce.

Q&A Highlights Content & AI
  • Alex explains that his briefs often span two to three pages but remain highly structured.
  • He confirms that brands can use ChatGPT and customer reviews to generate and refine briefs.
  • He treats the brief as a creator training document, not just product instructions.

Non-US Setup
  • Participants note that TikTok Shop enforces strict compliance policies.
  • Alex advises brands to avoid inconsistent logins and unstable IP activity.
  • The group acknowledges that US-based setups often perform more reliably.

Profitability & Spillover
  • Alex explains that some brands break even on TikTok but generate profit through Amazon spillover.
  • He shares that TikTok exposure has allowed him to increase Amazon prices while lowering TACoS.

Growth Priorities
  • Alex states that brands should post daily on their own TikTok page.
  • He ranks affiliates as the second growth lever after brand-owned content.
  • He describes live shopping as a later-stage strategy that requires operational support.

Done-For-You Option
  • Alex states that his team now manages cold-start campaigns for other brands.
  • He confirms that he will share a sample Join Brands brief with the APAC group.

To conclude, brands must generate 100 real sales and 100 videos, apply GMV Max to accelerate performance, and push toward 1,000 units sold before scaling further. 

 

When brands create visible traction first, every other growth lever becomes more effective.

items.title: How to Systematically Increase Your Conversion Rate & Lower Ad Spend－Dorian Gorski－Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Dorian Gorski shares a practical, data-driven approach for improving Amazon listing conversion rates and click-through rates.
TOPICS:
  1. Advanced workflow for conversion rate and click-through rate optimization
  2. Using Amazon data (SQP, PPC vs. organic, reviews, Rufus) to identify gaps
  3. Tools and tactics to implement changes, including Keplo, A+ content, and testing strategies
items.description_text: In this session, Dorian Gorski shares a practical, data-driven approach for improving Amazon listing conversion rates and click-through rates. TOPICS: Advanced workflow for conversion rate and click-through rate optimization Using Amazon data (SQP, PPC vs. organic, reviews, Rufus) to identify gaps Tools and tactics to implement changes, including Keplo, A+ content, and testing strategies
cliff_notes:
In this session Jamie hosts a Mogul Call with Dorian Gorski focused on advanced data-driven optimization of Amazon listings—especially conversion rate and click-through rate (CTR). 

 

The discussion detailed workflow for diagnosing and improving listings, and ends with practical advice on testing, tooling, and AI-driven automation. 

 

Attendees also hear how to leverage Keplo and other tools to operationalize these strategies across many SKUs.

 

Throughout, Dorian and Jamie highlight practical resources, workflows, and mindsets that seven- and eight-figure brands can implement to systematically lift performance.

 

Dorian’s Advanced Conversion and Click-Through Rate Framework
  • Dorian presents an advanced guide to improving conversion rate (CR) and click-through rate (CTR) for both small and large brands.
  • He identifies common mistakes, including guessing changes, copying competitors without context, relying on generic best practices, trusting unverified AI or experts, focusing only on reviews, making changes without a plan, and overspending on paid traffic.
  • He introduces a loop-based workflow that helps teams proactively optimize CR and CTR rather than reacting to issues.
  • The process starts with deep product knowledge so teams understand the product, audience, and purpose.
  • He stresses creating a “master product list” documenting features, benefits, specifications, and the founder’s intent.
  • He advises replacing vague critiques like “the main image is bad” with data-backed statements tied to performance and keywords.
  • The ultimate goal is to break CR and CTR down to the keyword level to identify where clicks and conversions are lost.

 

Data Sources, Gap Analysis, and Customer Insights

 

Search Query Performance (SQP) and Keyword-Level Analysis
  • Dorian emphasizes that Search Query Performance (SQP) is critical for understanding how a product performs for relevant keywords in clicks and conversions compared to the market.
  • He explains that SQP reveals which keywords have a conversion or CTR gap, highlighting clear optimization opportunities.
  • He advocates analyzing performance at the individual keyword level instead of only looking at overall conversion metrics.
  • He suggests that if a keyword gets many sessions but few conversions, teams should check whether the listing clearly communicates the benefit or use case in the title, bullets, and images.
  • He notes that SQP allows brands to estimate potential ROI by comparing a keyword’s current performance to market averages and session volume.

 

PPC vs. Organic Performance Cross-Reference
  • Dorian explains that PPC shoppers usually have higher purchase intent because they click ads, whereas organic shoppers browse more and compare options.
  • He recommends comparing PPC conversion rates to organic conversion rates for the same keywords to identify issues.
  • He notes that when PPC converts well but organic does not, the product is acceptable, but the listing’s main image, title, or initial content fails to communicate value effectively.
Review Analysis: Intent, Usage, and Purchase Barriers
  • Dorian cautions against over-relying on reviews but uses them systematically to spot patterns in intent and usage.
  • He focuses on reviews that reveal why customers bought the product and how they use it, uncovering gaps between brand assumptions and real customer behavior.
  • He explains that aligning listing content with review insights increases shoppers’ ability to recognize relevance and convert quickly.
  • He emphasizes that review analysis benefits both product development and conversion optimization.
Rufus, FAQs, and Unanswered Questions
  • Dorian calls unanswered questions a “big conversion killer” because uncertainty discourages buyers.
  • He uses Rufus questions, FAQ sections, and review-based questions to identify recurring concerns not addressed in the listing.
  • He warns that crucial information buried in infographics or long bullet points reduces effectiveness.
  • He recommends surfacing key answers clearly in titles, bullets, images, and A+ content.
Competitive Intelligence and Niche-Level Insights
  • Dorian suggests using Product Opportunity Explorer to analyze niches, demographics, keywords, and market dynamics.
  • He combines niche data with review analysis to better understand buyers and inform positioning and messaging.
  • He advises performing competitive research after internal analysis to explain why competitors may outperform on certain keywords.
  • He recommends building comparison frameworks to document competitors’ key differences, such as main images, benefit-led messaging, or clearer information hierarchy.
  • He emphasizes anchoring competitive intelligence in data, like SQP gaps and keyword performance, rather than copying competitors blindly.
Testing Strategies, Main Images, A+ Content, and Polling
Prioritization and “Fix the Leaky Bucket First”
  • Dorian prioritizes actions based on data strength, impact, effort, and speed.
  • He explains that improving conversion slightly on a high-revenue SKU often has more effect than a larger gain on a low-revenue product.
  • He encourages brands to work on top sellers carefully, changing one element at a time and monitoring results.
  • He emphasizes fixing conversion issues before CTR issues, likening it to repairing a leaky bucket before adding more water.
  • He suggests an order of operations: fix major conversion barriers, refine titles and bullets, optimize main images, then increase PPC spend.
Amazon Experiments vs. Direct Changes
  • Dorian uploads direct changes when data is strong and the team is experienced, rather than always using Amazon Experiments.
  • He notes that experienced teams can detect performance signals within days and adjust quickly, especially for high-volume SKUs.
  • He uses Amazon Experiments for less experienced teams, weaker data, or when structured A/B testing is needed.
  • He highlights the trade-off that experiments and polling can slow iteration and reduce ROI if multiple ideas could be tested directly.
Product Opinion Surveys, Polling, and Product Pinion
  • Dorian uses tools like Product Pinion, PickFu, and Intelliview for qualitative insights later in the process, not as the primary decision-maker.
  • He favors the “rank test” in Product Pinion to see which images convince buyers and why.
  • He uses these tests to determine image order, clarify confusing copy or visuals, and highlight underappreciated features or benefits.
  • He cautions that poll respondents may nitpick or be the wrong audience, so he weights results only 20–40% in final decisions.
  • He never bases ideas solely on polling but uses it to refine data-backed decisions.
  • He notes that MDS members get 10% off Product Pinion through the MDS partner program.
A+ Content and Its Growing Importance
  • Dorian explains that improved A+ content can deliver 10–20% conversion lifts, even when previous A+ is already strong.
  • He stresses that A+ content is particularly important on mobile, where users may see it before engaging with images.
  • He uses A+ to answer secondary buyer questions, reinforce benefits from reviews and Rufus, and provide structured FAQ and benefit modules.
  • He emphasizes that A+ extends and deepens messaging rather than duplicating main images.
  • He references a free A+ “master class” and Keplo stand materials, with more detailed case studies available to Conversion Club members.
AI, Keplo, and Technical Infrastructure
Keplo Scraper, Dorian AI Club, and MDS Offer
  • Jamie introduces Keplo scraper as Dorian’s tool that quickly provides listing optimization suggestions for titles, images, bullets, A+, and more by analyzing ASINs and reviews.
  • The Keplo offer includes access to Dorian AI Club with calls, recordings, and assets.
  • The offer provides credits to run ASIN analyses, such as 20 ASINs per month with 500 reviews each.
  • Subscribers can send one ASIN per month for Dorian to review via Loom, with explanations and suggestions.
  • Users also get recordings of live breakdowns and occasional Thursday “work parties” where Dorian reviews three listings live.
  • The standard price is $139, but MDS members get 30% off with code MDS30, reducing it to approximately $111 per month.
  • Dorian is building an advanced workflow that connects directly to Seller Central via APIs to integrate SQP, ads, and other data, currently in beta for larger clients.
  • He notes that this advanced version will be publicly available later in the year, but AI-savvy sellers could replicate parts of the workflow themselves.
AI Models and Their Limitations with Raw Data
  • Dorian explains that tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are excellent for generating flows, writing code, and brainstorming, but are unreliable for large-scale Amazon data analysis.
  • Internal tests show that roughly 60% of large-scale AI outputs are fabricated or “filled in” to appear plausible, even if inaccurate.
  • He emphasizes that AI often makes “best guesses,” which is risky when decisions depend on precise metrics.
  • He recommends using AI mainly to design workflows and generate code, not to directly interpret large numerical data sets.
Workflows, Automation, and Data Storage
  • Dorian uses n8n to orchestrate data flows, connect to Amazon APIs, and process data with hard-coded logic (Python or JavaScript) instead of relying on AI for calculations.
  • Teams first identify the metrics that matter (SQP gaps, CTR vs. market, PPC ACOS, keyword-level conversions) and build step-by-step workflows that filter and transform data toward a prioritized dashboard.
  • AI models like Claude help draft code for these transformations, but once implemented, the system runs deterministically and does not hallucinate.
  • Data is stored in Supabase, Azure, or AWS to keep it cleansed, structured, and reusable for forecasts or future model training.
  • Data cleanup begins with the end goal in mind, gradually filtering raw data down to prioritized SKUs and keywords while discarding noise.
In this session, Jamie and Dorian demonstrate how serious Amazon operators can move from intuition-driven listing changes to a disciplined, data-first optimization strategy. 

 

By combining Search Query Performance, PPC vs. organic comparisons, review insights, Rufus questions, and competitive intelligence, brands can pinpoint exactly where and why they are losing clicks and conversions. 

 

The conversation shows that when this analysis is paired with thoughtful testing, targeted A+ enhancements, and carefully applied AI and automation, even small percentage gains can compound into significant revenue growth—especially on high-volume SKUs.

items.title: How Amazon Sellers Can Build AI Digital Employees for Operations and Growth － AI Channel Call February 2026
items.description:
In this session, members of the MDS AI Channel share how they use AI agents (like Claude and GPT) to automate real business work, especially in e‑commerce and Amazon.
TOPICS:
  1. Using AI for content creation, SEO, and advertising automation
  2. Managing context windows, memory, and markdown‑based project frameworks
  3. Designing AI “employees,” team roles, and secure systems for e‑commerce and Amazon operations
items.description_text: In this session, members of the MDS AI Channel share how they use AI agents (like Claude and GPT) to automate real business work, especially in e‑commerce and Amazon. TOPICS: Using AI for content creation, SEO, and advertising automation Managing context windows, memory, and markdown‑based project frameworks Designing AI “employees,” team roles, and secure systems for e‑commerce and Amazon operations
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS AI Channel discuss how they are practically using AI—especially Claude/OpenAI-style agents—in their businesses, with a strong focus on e‑commerce and Amazon operations. 

 

The conversation moves from high‑level strategy (systems thinking, org design, and “digital employees”) down to concrete implementation details such as context windows, markdown frameworks, and specific advertising use cases.

 

Participants share both their excitement and anxiety about the speed of AI progress, emphasizing that real value comes from combining good business judgment with well‑structured AI workflows. 

 

They repeatedly stress that AI is best treated as a powerful teammate or executive‑level advisor, not as a magical “make me money” button.

 

Using AI Agents for Content Creation and Marketing
  • Sam describes how he is developing an automated TikTok content generator that continuously tests different hooks, learns from performance, and refines future hooks based on what performs best.
  • He explains that he deliberately focuses AI on tasks he currently does not have bandwidth for—such as consistent social media posting—rather than trying to “optimize what already works” in his business.
  • He shares that his system maintains a database of hooks that do not work and records why they fail, so that future hook generation explicitly avoids repeating ineffective patterns.
  • Travis states that his team is working on a similar self‑learning content system, where the AI becomes “PhD‑level smart” on a subject and then generates and audits content over time.
  • He notes that their approach includes asking the AI to produce audit reports on what works and what does not, and then to log insights for continuous improvement.
  • Ian explains that he uses AI as a co‑founder‑like partner to design multi‑step marketing and SEO processes, such as improving blog articles to move them from page two to page one in search results.
  • He says he connects tools like Windsor, Google Search Console, and other SEO data sources so the AI can research, rewrite, upload content to WordPress, and then track results over time.
  • Deepak reports that he uses the Get Victor app connected to Shopify, Google Search Console, Google Ads, and Meta Ads to surface low‑hanging optimization opportunities on his website and ad campaigns.
  • He explains that Victor drafts new ad campaigns directly in Google Ads, then he uses Claude to critique and improve them before sending the refined instructions back to Victor for implementation.

 

Managing Context Windows, Memory, and Architecture
  • Travis anticipates that a continuously self‑learning agent will eventually hit context window limits, leading to extremely expensive prompts if all history is always loaded.
  • Sam advises that instead of one giant agent with everything in its head, it is better to design a “team” of smaller agents, each with a narrow scope and only the context needed for its specific task.
  • He emphasizes that you should extract only the information an agent truly needs for each execution, rather than repeatedly feeding entire books, research, or full project histories.
  • Andrei explains that models like Claude Opus 4.6 are extremely powerful but can burn through huge numbers of tokens when context and memory are poorly structured.
  • He describes how misconfigured memory and file architecture can cause an agent to repeatedly load massive context, spending hundreds of thousands of tokens per message and rapidly consuming plan limits.
  • He recommends a “lazy load” approach where an agent starts with a small, critical index file and then retrieves additional context on demand via structured references and vector search.
  • He states that using vector search to retrieve only relevant chunks of knowledge lets the AI operate over large knowledge bases without exceeding context windows or token budgets.
  • June introduces the concept of “progressive disclosure,” where you break down tasks and reveal only the necessary context step‑by‑step to control context window usage.
  • June advises that markdown files should be compact, purpose‑built, and used to hold instructions, definitions, and processes, while large raw data (like Excel) is fed separately only when required.

 

Structuring AI Projects: Frameworks, Markdown, and Systems Thinking
  • June explains that AI projects work best when you use markdown files as SOPs that define terms, frameworks, output formats, and analysis rules for the AI.
  • June notes that converting data from formats such as Word or Excel into markdown saves tokens, increases effective context capacity, and reduces hallucinations.
  • June recommends workflows where you ask the AI to summarize long chats or projects and then start a new chat with the summary, so you are not reloading redundant context every time.
  • Andrei clarifies that the markdown files should not duplicate raw data from Excel; instead, they should describe what the data is, how to interpret it, what goals you have, and what outputs you expect.
  • Andrei suggests building very small, minimal markdown files (e.g., per project, per account, or per function) rather than giant documents that quickly fill the context window.
  • Andrei emphasizes that markdown files are equivalent to onboarding documentation for a new employee, describing goals, risk tolerance, resources, and where data lives.
  • Lee urges entrepreneurs to first map out processes, flows, and frameworks (often using tools like Whisper + AI for brainstorming) before building with AI, so they have clear end goals and guardrails.
  • Sam shares that he always starts with pseudo‑code and process mapping when building anything, and then uses AI to refine that structure and fill in details.
  • Ramon argues that people should think in terms of systems rather than tiny, isolated processes, balancing how much of a system can fit into a context window without being cropped or compressed.
  • Ramon says he prefers to move slowly and build layered systems that can eventually run on their own, rather than rushing in with “go fast and break things” prototypes.

 

E‑Commerce, Amazon, and Advertising Use Cases
  • Fedor asks how to orchestrate a complex listing optimization system that combines competitor data, search query performance, PPC data, and keyword rank data across multiple tools.
  • Andrei suggests that Fedor experiment with Open Claude on a separate machine and SP‑API access, allowing an agent to download reports and condense them for further human or AI analysis.
  • Sam reminds Fedor that asking AI to “make me rank” is too vague and that humans still need to act as executives, defining clear objectives and constraints for the AI.
  • Lee reinforces that the business owner remains the expert and must specify what success looks like (e.g., specific ranking outcomes and processes), instead of handing AI a vague goal.
  • Ian describes use cases where AI manages SEO tasks: analyzing which pages are close to ranking on page one, researching top‑ranking competitors, rewriting content, uploading to WordPress, and monitoring performance.
  • Ian proposes using AI as a PPC or marketing manager that checks dashboards daily, adjusts bids and budgets, adds or negates keywords, and iteratively improves campaigns based on data.
  • Dan shares that he built a dashboard in roughly two hours that triangulates Meta Ads, Amazon Attribution, Amazon PPC, and search query data to measure the true “spillover” ROI of Meta traffic on Amazon sales.
  • Dan explains that the dashboard reveals that Meta Ads often drive at least a 3x ROI when you account for halo effects via catch‑all PPC and organic search, compared to a lower ROI seen only in attribution reports.
  • Dan plans to systematically test budget changes (e.g., reducing or increasing Meta spend by fixed percentages) and track the resulting changes in total revenue to estimate ROI with high statistical confidence.
  • Ian suggests that the next step for Dan is to let AI not just measure results but also create new ads, segment by geography, adjust budgets daily, and run experiments automatically.
  • Deepak explains that by connecting tools through Victor and then looping outputs through Claude, he can quickly improve under‑attended channels like his brand’s DTC website, thus unlocking incremental revenue.
  • Participants mention other e‑commerce use cases, including inventory management, supplier ordering automation, and shipping rate comparisons, where AI agents can act like operations VAs.
Team Design, Security, and the Future of AI Work
  • Andrei argues that models such as Claude Opus 4.6 (and GPT‑5.2) are already “executive‑level” smart in many domains, especially when combined with human life experience and judgment.
  • Sam and Lee caution that while AI can be extremely smart, humans still need to act as executives by choosing objectives, constraints, and strategies rather than delegating entirely vague goals.
  • Ian describes working with AI as working with a co‑founder: he asks, “Based on all this information, what would you suggest we do?” and then selects and refines the proposed strategy.
  • Andrei believes that one powerful machine running Open Claude can easily replace several researchers and virtual assistants if it is well‑architected and properly guarded.
  • Ramon shares that he audited his entire team’s tasks and identified which responsibilities AI agents could take over or augment, with the intention of reorganizing human roles around higher‑value work.
  • Lee recounts that he offered to pay for Claude accounts and AI courses for his staff, telling them that the world is changing and that those who upskill now will be protected from future replacement.
  • Lee notes that some employees proactively requested training while others did not, and he sees that as a signal for who will likely remain essential when more workflows are automated.
  • Andrei warns strongly about security, advising never to store secrets, passwords, or API keys in markdown or chat logs and instead to rely on environment variable files (e.g., .env) and proper encryption.
  • Andrei recommends an explicit “do not delete anything without my express permission” rule as the first instruction loaded for any system agent, along with backups (e.g., iCloud or similar) to guard against mistakes.
  • Participants discuss the idea of “digital twins” of executives—agents encoded with a person’s knowledge and frameworks—that could be hired or licensed as virtual employees at a fraction of the human cost.
  • Several speakers express that they feel both excited and scared, likening the current moment to buying Bitcoin at $0.10 and warning that those who delay learning AI will face a steep disadvantage.

 

In this session, the group converges on a clear message: the real leverage from AI comes not from flashy demos, but from disciplined system design—frameworks, markdown SOPs, context management, and security. 

 

Participants show that when AI is treated like a smart partner operating inside well‑defined processes, it can meaningfully improve marketing performance, content production, analytics, and even strategic decision‑making.

 

At the same time, the conversation underscores that humans remain responsible for defining goals, ethics, and constraints. 

 

As AI capabilities multiply, those who learn to architect systems, protect data, and upskill their teams will be best positioned to benefit, while those who delay adoption may find themselves struggling to catch up in a rapidly changing landscape.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Costin Vlaic (from AC Rank) shares insights on how Amazon buyers use Rufus, how ranking campaigns work, and how to manage reviews on TikTok Shop. 

The session combines survey data, experiments, and case studies to help sellers improve visibility and conversions.

Introduction and Objectives

Costin explains that AC Rank, founded in 2018, supports brands in launching and scaling products in the US and Europe, with a focus on ranking campaigns and product imagery.

The session covers three key areas:

  • How buyers use Rufus
  • How ranking campaigns operate
  • How to manage TikTok Shop reviews

The goal is to share practical insights based on real data and testing.

How Buyers Use Rufus (Survey Insights)

A survey of 200 Amazon buyers shows:

  • 52% have never heard of Rufus
  • 48% are somewhat familiar
  • Only ~2% use it regularly

Most users either try it out of curiosity or prefer traditional reviews.

Key insights:

  • Buyers still trust reviews more than Rufus
  • Rufus is mainly used to narrow options, not make final decisions
  • Many users are unfamiliar or indifferent to the tool

Rufus Behavior and Testing

Costin tests Rufus using product queries (e.g., supplements) to understand how it generates recommendations.

Findings:

  • Rufus prioritizes Amazon data (catalog, reviews, internal signals)
  • It recommends established brands based on strong data signals
  • External sources can influence results when prompts include terms like “latest” or “trending.”
  • Rufus now accepts external inputs (e.g., articles), which can impact recommendations

Rufus is still evolving, and sellers may influence it by building presence in credible external content.

Amazon Ranking Campaigns

AC Rank uses structured ranking campaigns to improve keyword positions, often before major events like Black Friday.

Key elements:

  • Targeted giveaways to drive sales velocity and keyword relevance
  • Focus on medium-volume, high-converting keywords
  • Campaign duration is typically around 10 days

Results from a case study show multiple keywords reaching the top 5 positions.

Key takeaways:

  • Ranking campaigns still work when executed correctly
  • Success depends on keyword selection, timing, and volume
  • Strong execution can significantly improve rankings

TikTok Shop Reviews Strategy

TikTok Shop presents both opportunities and risks due to its review system.

Key challenges:

  • Higher rate of negative reviews compared to Amazon
  • High negative review rates can block access to affiliate programs
  • One customer can leave multiple reviews from multiple purchases

Important mechanics:

  • Reviews must be submitted within 30 days
  • All reviews are public and impact performance

Strategy:

  • Leverage real, satisfied customers to maintain a healthy review ratio
  • Keep negative review rates low to remain eligible for affiliate promotion

Key Takeaways

  • Rufus adoption is currently low but evolving
  • It relies heavily on Amazon data, with growing openness to external sources
  • Ranking campaigns remain effective with proper strategy and execution
  • TikTok Shop reviews require active management to protect product performance

Costin Vlaic presents a data-driven approach to improving product visibility across platforms.

By combining testing, ranking strategies, and proactive review management, sellers can reduce risk and improve performance on both Amazon and TikTok Shop.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Slavik Kivals shares a practical, real-world process for developing and validating Amazon product packaging and main images using A/B testing and polls.

The discussion focuses on systematically testing creative ideas, understanding customer preferences, and minimizing risk before launching a product.

Background and Objectives

  • Slavik has experience in B2B sales since 2010 and Amazon selling since 2016, with a strong focus on creating high-performing main images and listings.
  • He emphasizes that A/B testing—especially using the Intelli platform—is central to their process.
  • The goal is to provide a clear SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) for designers and team members to follow.
    Their five-step process includes:
  1. Initial creative testing
  2. Comparing creative vs. traditional designs
  3. Testing against competitors
  4. Refining designs
  5. Validating with marketplace polls
  • The ultimate goal is to enter less competitive niches and win through superior packaging and main images.

USPs and Initial Design Concepts

  • A key first step is identifying the product’s Unique Selling Propositions (USPs) before design begins.
    Designs must highlight one primary USP clearly, with secondary benefits still visible.
  • They test three design styles: cartoon, minimalistic, and stickman.
    Early feedback shows the cartoon style feels too childish, so it is dropped.
  • They intentionally target niches with weak competitor designs to gain a creative advantage.

Target Audience and Design Strategy

  • Understanding the target audience is critical. The team analyzes competitor reviews to identify customer preferences.
  • They favor minimalistic designs but also test themes like tribal or tattoo-inspired visuals aligned with masculine branding.
  • Color plays a key role—orange consistently attracts attention in search results, so it is used strategically.
  • To avoid bias in polls, they remove recognizable branding and sometimes change brand names so respondents focus only on design.

A/B Testing Process and Best Practices

Their testing pipeline starts with internal concept testing, then moves to competitor comparisons.

 

They aim for decisive results (at least a 2x win), since small margins are unreliable.

 

Key learnings include:

  • USP placement must be clear and readable
  • Logos/icons increase perceived product trust
  • Iteration is essential through repeated testing

  • Best practices:
  • Test one variable at a time (design, price, title, etc.)
  • Define a clear goal for each test
  • Use the right audience to ensure relevant results
  • Test ~3 options per poll for optimal feedback

This approach reduces costly mistakes before launch.

Marketplace Validation and Launch Readiness

  • The final step is marketplace-style polling that simulates real Amazon conditions, including price, title, and reviews.
  • They typically use ~100 reviews to create realistic scenarios and run separate tests for product titles.
  • In one example, their product wins ~47% of votes—about double that of competitors—indicating strong demand.
  • The goal is to outperform competitors across all key factors before launching.
  • Slavik emphasizes that validating with marketplace polls significantly improves launch confidence and accuracy.

This session demonstrates a structured, data-driven approach to Amazon product design.

By combining a clear USP definition, audience research, and disciplined A/B testing, the team reduces risk and builds a strong competitive advantage before entering the market.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Neeme Roos from Seven Minerals explains how the brand manages and improves Amazon review ratings to protect sales and long-term stability. 
 
The focus is on product adjustments, clear communication, and packaging improvements that reduce negative reviews and increase customer satisfaction.
 
Importance of Review Ratings
Seven Minerals is a US-based skincare brand generating over $30M in revenue.
Maintaining strong review ratings is critical, as even small changes significantly impact conversions.
  • Products with 4.5–4.6 stars are relatively stable
  • Products with 4.1–4.4 stars are vulnerable and require active management
Even a small increase (e.g., 4.2 → 4.3) can improve visibility and click-through rates due to star display changes.
 
Identifying Issues and Reducing Negative Reviews
The team prioritizes products in the 4.1–4.4 range and analyzes negative reviews to identify root causes.
Common issues include:
  • Product performance
  • Side effects
  • Misunderstanding of product usage
Approach:
  • Fix product issues where possible
  • Improve customer expectations through clearer communication
Even a small reduction in 1–2 star reviews can meaningfully increase overall ratings.
 
Case Study: Magnesium Spray
Challenges:
  • Customers misunderstand usage
  • Possible side effects (itching, burning, stickiness)
  • Amazon categorizes it as a supplement, limiting returns
Solutions:
  • Add clear “how to use” instructions on packaging
  • Include inserts with support contact and refund options
  • Use QR codes for additional guidance
Despite a temporary drop to 4.2 (due to a sprayer issue), improved communication helped recover ratings to 4.3.
Key insight: better education and support can offset product friction.
 
Case Study: Rice Water for Hair Growth
Market observation:
  • Competitors using aggressive claims gain short-term sales but lower ratings (4.1–4.2)
  • More conservative products maintain higher ratings (4.3–4.4)
Strategy:
  • Avoid overpromising results
  • Target informed customers with realistic expectations
Result:
  • ~40% market share over time
  • Most aggressive competitors decline or disappear
Key insight: long-term trust outperforms short-term hype.
 
Packaging and Customer Communication
Due to Amazon messaging restrictions, the brand shifted communication to packaging and inserts.
Key elements included:
  • Clear usage instructions
  • Expected results
  • Support and refund guidance
  • QR codes for additional resources
They use friendly, personal messaging to encourage direct contact instead of negative reviews.
Outcome:
  • Better-informed customers
  • Fewer negative reviews
  • Higher satisfaction rates
 
Review Management Strategy
Core principles:
  • Focus on long-term improvements, not short-term tactics
  • Monitor ratings across all products
  • Act quickly when products drop toward 4.1–4.3
Key levers:
  • Clear labeling
  • Strong customer support
  • Accurate expectations
  • Thoughtful packaging
Even small rating improvements can significantly impact performance.
 
Conclusion
Seven Minerals demonstrates that disciplined review management, honest positioning, and clear communication can significantly improve product ratings and market share.
By focusing on customer experience, expectation setting, and packaging clarity, the brand maintains strong performance in competitive categories and avoids the long-term decline seen in overhyped competitors.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Matt Dreier shares his experience buying and operating an existing Amazon business instead of starting from scratch. He covers his reasoning for the acquisition process, operational challenges, and key lessons from managing a “fixer-upper” business.
 
Background and Motivation
Matt has been selling on Amazon since 2014 and previously built and sold a business in 2022.
After a short period working with an aggregator, he decided to stay in the Amazon space but pursue a cash-flow, lifestyle business rather than building another large brand.
He chose to buy an existing business, believing it would be less risky than starting from zero—provided he could secure stable cash flow at a reasonable price.
 
Search Criteria and Marketplaces
Matt searched across platforms like Flippa and Empire Flippers.
His approach:
  • Budget up to ~€1M (but preferred lower)
  • Focus on stable, predictable cash flow
  • Open to “fixer-upper” businesses with improvement potential
Key principles:
  • Prioritize stability over growth
  • Avoid emotional attachment to deals
  • Be willing to walk away if risks are too high
He noted that while some platforms have low-quality listings, they can still offer hidden opportunities.
 
The Deal and Negotiation
Matt acquired a glass bottle business in Europe.
Key details:
  • Initial asking price: ~€800K
  • Poor financial records required independent analysis
  • Used Sellerboard to estimate real profitability
After a 6-month negotiation:
  • Estimated EBITDA: ~€140K–€150K
  • Final purchase price: €275K
He validated the deal by visiting the seller, warehouse, and operations in person.
The Seller Central account was eventually included, affecting the final structure.
 
Operational Challenges Post-Acquisition
Matt expected a relatively passive business but encountered major operational issues:
  • Warehouse and logistics complications
  • Inventory limits and delays
  • Seller Central transition challenges
  • Limited team support (became the main operator)
The business quickly became full-time and operationally intensive.
Key changes:
  • Shut down the original warehouse
  • Shifted sourcing to China
  • Moved suppliers toward handling more logistics
Result:
  • The first year produced only minimal profit due to restructuring and delays
 
Lessons Learned and Use of AI
Key lessons:
  • Low purchase multiples do not eliminate operational risk
  • Transitions are more complex and time-consuming than expected
  • Buyers must fully understand and accept inherited problems
Matt is still evaluating whether it’s better to:
  • Buy cheaper “fixer-uppers.”
  • Or pay more for stable, well-run businesses
He also explores AI tools like Accio (by Alibaba) for:
  • Product research
  • Sourcing
  • Idea generation
These tools help streamline workflows but do not replace operational execution.

 

Conclusion
Matt highlights the gap between the idea of buying a “passive” cash-flow business and the reality of managing operational complexity.
While acquisitions can offer strong opportunities, success depends on:
  • Understanding operational risks
  • Managing transitions effectively
  • Having the time and capability to fix underlying issues
Ultimately, buying a business is not inherently easier than building one. It simply shifts the type of challenges involved.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Jamie Graham explains how Lily England transitioned from a growth-focused Amazon brand into a lean, highly profitable lifestyle business. The focus is on cost-cutting, simplification, profitability, and the trade-offs of stepping away from aggressive growth.
 
Business Performance and Scaling Limits
After strong growth during COVID, the business shifted focus from revenue growth to profitability (2020–2025).
 
Key points:
  • The brand reached a natural ceiling in its category
  • Core products (e.g., hair brushes) perform well on Amazon but not off-platform
  • New product launches showed inconsistent results
 
As a result, the company focused on optimizing existing winning SKUs rather than expanding.
 
Selling the business was not attractive due to relatively low valuation multiples.
 
Cost-Cutting and Team Restructuring
Jamie aggressively reduced costs and simplified the business:
  • Cut low-volume, low-profit SKUs
  • Eliminated influencer marketing, TikTok, and DSP campaigns
  • Reduced TACoS from 18% to 16%
  • Stopped social media and email marketing
 
Team changes:
  • Reduced from 13 people to ~4
  • Removed expensive roles and external agencies
  • Simplified finance and logistics functions
 
Result:
  • Significant cost savings (£60K+ annually, plus additional reductions)
  • Leaner and more efficient operation
 
Operational Simplification and Efficiency
With fewer SKUs and a smaller team:
  • Inventory management improved significantly
  • No major stockouts during peak Q4
  • Overselling issues nearly eliminated
  • Forecasting accuracy increased
 
Cost impact:
  • Storage fees reduced from ~£100K (previous years) to under £1K
 
Other benefits:
  • Easier PPC and promotion management
  • Higher accountability within a smaller team
  • Stronger overall execution
 
Trade-offs and Risks
The business is now optimized for profit, not rapid growth.
 
Trade-offs:
  • Slower, steady profit growth
  • No clear path to a large exit
 
Key risks:
  • Heavy reliance on Amazon (platform risk)
  • Revenue concentration in a few top products
  • Dependence on a key PPC/ads specialist
 
The business is stable but not highly scalable or diversified.
 
Lifestyle and Future Plans
The business now supports Jamie’s desired lifestyle:
  • Lower stress and fewer working hours
  • Time for personal activities (e.g., jiu-jitsu)
  • Improved work-life balance
 
Financial position:
  • Strong cash reserves
  • Consistent profit target (~£500K+ annually)
 
Future plans:
  • Launch fewer products with better validation
  • Test more thoroughly before scaling
  • Explore acquiring smaller businesses
  • Leverage operational and advertising expertise for growth opportunities
 
Conclusion
Jamie Graham demonstrates how an Amazon business can transition from growth-focused to profit-focused.
 
By cutting complexity, reducing costs, and focusing on core products, the company achieves strong profitability and stability.
 
The trade-off is slower growth and continued platform dependence, but the result is a sustainable business that supports both financial goals and personal freedom.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Ida Trifonova (the Marketing Manager at Umami) explains how her team structures and scales A/B testing for Amazon listings using ClickUp as a central system. The focus is on building a repeatable workflow to test ideas, avoid errors, and make data-driven decisions across marketplaces.
 
Purpose and System Overview
Ida presents a structured A/B testing system designed for teams that are not testing enough or lack organization.
 
Key principles:
  • Build a repeatable workflow
  • Use basic metrics (clicks, impressions, conversions)
  • Log all meaningful front-end changes (images, titles, price, etc.)
 
The system is tool-agnostic but demonstrated using ClickUp.
 
Test Planning and Organization
The process starts with listing everything that can be tested:
  • Main images
  • Titles and bullets
  • Content
  • PPC creatives
 
Best practices:
  • Test one variable at a time per ASIN
  • Plan tests ~1 month in advance
  • Use a calendar view to avoid overlapping tests
 
They also account for:
  • Seasonality
  • Promotions and deal events
 
This ensures clean, reliable data.
 
ClickUp Workflow Structure
The team organizes tests into stages:
  • Hypothesis
  • Scheduled
  • Running
  • Analyzed
  • Complete
 
Workflow highlights:
  • Brainstorm ideas (including unconventional ones)
  • Assign timelines, ASINs, and marketplaces
  • Track performance during tests
  • Record results, sample sizes, and significance
 
They also log all front-end changes, even if not planned as tests, allowing retroactive analysis.
 
Data Analysis and Common Pitfalls
Evaluation includes:
  • Click-through rate (CTR)
  • Conversion rate (CVR)
  • Statistical significance
 
If results are inconclusive:
  • Extend the test duration
  • Increase sample size
 
Common mistakes:
  • Testing multiple variables at once
  • Not logging all changes
  • Ignoring seasonality or major events
  • Inconsistent testing discipline
 
Accurate logging is critical to avoid false conclusions.
 
Key Learnings from Testing
Ida emphasizes testing everything, even ideas that seem unlikely to work.
Examples:
  • A simple phone photo outperformed a professional image
  • “Ugly” creatives can generate higher engagement
 
Additional insights:
  • Competitors often copy winning designs, reducing effectiveness over time
  • Older assets can outperform newer ones when retested
  • Performance is context-dependent across markets
 
Conclusion:
  • Regularly test new and existing assets
  • Do not rely on assumptions or aesthetics alone
 
Ida Trifonova demonstrates how structured A/B testing turns scattered experiments into a scalable system.
 
By combining clear workflows, consistent logging, and disciplined analysis, teams can continuously improve performance.
 
The key advantage comes from testing broadly, learning from data, and revisiting past ideas to stay competitive across changing marketplaces.

items.description:

TOPICS:

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1774291075299-6 Things I Tried on Amazon That Didn’t Work for Me Franco Leoni Europe Chapter Ski Retreat 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session, Franco Leoni shares his experience testing popular Amazon “growth hacks” and operational tactics at the $2M–$10M revenue level. He focuses on what actually works versus what fails in practice, using a data-driven, experimental approach.

 

Background and Approach
Franco is a former mathematician and Amazon seller who applies a scientific mindset to business.

 

Key principles:
  • Form hypotheses and test them rigorously
  • Rely on data, not assumptions
  • Share both successes and failures

 

His goal is to help sellers avoid wasting time and money on ineffective tactics.

 

External Traffic and Ranking Tests
Franco tests multiple external traffic strategies, including:
  • Bot-driven traffic services
  • Paid “search suggestion” manipulation
  • Reddit ads are driving traffic to Amazon

 

Findings:
  • Effects from paid suggestion services stop immediately when spending stops
  • Q&A manipulation shows no measurable ranking impact
  • €30K in Reddit ads produces no meaningful improvement in ranking or sales

 

Conclusion:
External traffic and bot-based tactics do not reliably improve Amazon ranking.

 

Negative Review Management
Franco evaluates services that claim to remove negative reviews via policy violations.

 

Findings:
  • Automated or manual complaint methods show no meaningful success

 

Effective strategy:
  • Offer refunds to dissatisfied customers
  • Only issue refunds when customers accept

 

Results:
  • ~300 refunds issued
  • ~14.9% of negative reviews removed

 

Conclusion:
Proactive customer service is more effective than trying to manipulate review systems.

 

“Rufus/Cosmos Optimization” Skepticism
Franco challenges the idea of optimizing listings with complex semantic tricks.

 

Key insights:
  • “AI optimization” often repackages basic marketing concepts (e.g., audience targeting)
  • Clear, direct language outperforms forced or overly complex phrasing
  • Sentiment-based keyword manipulation does not produce better results

 

Conclusion:
Focus on clarity and relevance rather than trying to game AI systems.

 

AI Customer Service and Multi-Channel Strategy
Franco tests AI tools for customer support.

 

Findings:
  • AI performs well for tone (politeness, empathy)
  • AI struggles to solve real customer issues
  • Fully automated responses often frustrate customers

 

Approach:
  • Use AI as support, but keep human oversight

 

On multi-channel expansion:
  • Each channel requires different expertise
  • Expanding without focus increases risk
  • Retail channels favor strong brands and reduce seller control

 

Conclusion:
Deep focus on one channel is more effective than spreading resources too thin.

 

Franco Leoni highlights the gap between popular “growth hacks” and real-world results.

 

His experiments show that many trending tactics fail or deliver only temporary effects, while simple strategies, like strong customer service and clear communication—consistently work.

 

The key takeaway is to prioritize data-driven testing, focus, and execution, rather than chasing hype or shortcuts.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Calin Domuta shares his journey of expanding from Amazon to Shopify and the practical steps he takes to improve performance on his e-commerce site. The discussion focuses on store design, email marketing, paid advertising, and customer support systems that work together to drive growth—especially for large and extra-large products.
 
Background, Goals, and Overall Shopify Strategy
  • Calin started selling on Amazon in 2015 through the ASM4 program and sold his first brand in 2021.
  • His current brand generates most of its revenue from large, bulky products.
  • He considers his Amazon operations (PPC, listings, pricing, logistics) well optimized, so he focuses on Shopify.
  • Shopify's growth is slower than Amazon's and requires patience and a long-term mindset.
  • His approach is most relevant for sellers with multiple products in a niche looking to scale on Shopify over time.
  • He is interested in connecting with other sellers—especially those dealing with large products—to exchange insights on Shopify and team growth.

 

Store Design and Development
  • Calin worked with Audit.co, a Canadian design agency, to redesign his Shopify store.
  • The original store was basic; Audit.co provided multiple Figma concepts and redesigned all key pages.
  • The process required minimal time, about two calls, while leveraging existing brand assets.
  • After the redesign, the conversion rate increased from 1.2% to 1.9%.
  • Design cost was $5,000, which he considers good value.
  • For development, he used Xenon Labs (India-based), recommended by Audit.co, and also discovered via the MDS community.
  • Xenon Labs implemented the designs on Shopify at about $25/hour, totaling $3,000.
  • He highlights their responsiveness, Shopify expertise, and cost efficiency compared to other agencies.
 
Email Flows, List Building, and Missed Opportunities
  • Calin hired Spring Media Inc. (US-based) to set up email automation.
  • A pop-up offering 10% off is used to capture emails (effective due to $100+ product pricing).
  • Four core flows were implemented:
    • Welcome flow
    • Browse abandonment
    • Checkout abandonment
    • Post-purchase
  • These flows segment users and nurture potential customers.
  • His list currently has 2,500 subscribers, but he is not yet running ongoing campaigns.
  • He notes the agency is relatively expensive and ROI from flows alone is unclear.
  • Despite this, he sees email as foundational with strong future upside.
Google Ads and Performance Max
  • Initial Google Ads efforts (handled by a low-cost PPC resource) underperformed for ~6 months.
  • A second agency also failed to deliver results.
  • A third agency (started in November, pre–Black Friday) showed improvement.
  • All agencies used Google Performance Max campaigns (AI-driven, multi-channel).
  • These campaigns require time and data to stabilize.
  • Current setup:
    • ~$3,000/month management fee
    • ~$3,000/month ad spend (~$100–150/day)
  • Blended ROAS is improving toward break-even or slight profitability.
  • He accepts high fees relative to spending if the agency can scale effectively.
  • Performance is becoming more consistent, indicating algorithm stabilization.
  • He emphasizes gradual scaling—avoiding large spend increases (e.g., $50K/month) before data supports it.
  • At current spend levels, he does not yet see a clear lift in Amazon sales but expects it at scale.
Concepts:
  • Google Ads Performance Max – AI-driven campaign type

 

Customer Support, Returns, and QR Codes
  • Calin uses Amazon Product Lifecycle Support to add a “Get Product Support” button on the return page.
  • The button is prominent on mobile and redirects users to a custom support site.
  • Amazon reviews and approves the support page to ensure compliance (no aggressive redirects or pop-ups).
  • Support requests go directly to the team’s customer service inbox.
  • Example metrics:
    • 27 submissions in December
    • 15 submissions in January (to date)
  • This helps resolve issues (missing parts, defects, returned items) before customers leave negative reviews.
  • He also uses QR codes on packaging and manuals to direct customers to support pages.
  • These pages differ from the Amazon support flow and serve direct customer outreach.
  • Additional insight from another participant:
    • Including visible contact info on products reduces negative feedback by encouraging customers to reach out first.
Concepts:
  • Amazon Product Lifecycle Support
  • QR code-driven support pages

 

Key Takeaways:
  • Shopify's growth is slower than Amazon's, but builds over time through incremental improvements.
  • Conversion rate optimization, email systems, paid ads, and customer support must work together.
  • Selling large products requires strong customer experience and support systems.
  • Agencies can accelerate progress, but performance must be closely monitored to justify costs.
  • Long-term success depends on patience, testing, and gradual scaling.

In this session, Nacho Nachelis shares the software stack powering his e-commerce business across Amazon, productivity, operations, and finance. The goal is for each attendee to discover at least one tool that can meaningfully improve performance or scalability.
 
Background, Business Scale, and Session Goal

    • Amazon
    • Productivity
    • Operations
    • Finance
  • Core promise: each attendee should leave with at least one high-impact tool.

Amazon Tools (Sales, Research, Advertising)
  • Sellerise
    • Used for dashboards, alerts, review requests, and reimbursements
    • Generated ~$55K + $109K in reimbursements
    • Profit calculations are not fully trusted
  • 1K + Kaper(name unclear; transcription-based)
    • Used for listing optimization, CVR improvement, and research

  • Data Dive
