    • Ranking feature seen as less useful
  • mpd.io
    • Used for Google Ads to Amazon
    • ~12% adjusted ACOS
    • Chosen partly due to favorable legacy pricing
  • Combined, Sellerise + Data Dive cover many use cases of tools like Helium 10
 
Productivity Tools
  • Loom
    • Used daily for async communication instead of meetings

    • Nacho is a heavy user (top ~2%)
  • Whisper Flow
    • Voice-to-text tool for dictation
    • Converts unstructured speech into clean written content
    • Useful while walking or working hands-free
    • Works better in English than Spanish
  • Brain.fm
    • Focus and relaxation app using neuroscience-based audio
    • Used for deep work, relaxation, and sleep
    • Helpful for falling back asleep at night
 
Operations and Customer Service Tools
  • SoStocked
    • Inventory forecasting and stock management
    • Helps avoid overstock fees and stockouts
    • Strong support; widely used by the team
    • Has a learning curve and requires manual work for multi-channel setups
    • May eventually be replaced by more advanced systems like Fulfill
  • Gorgias
    • Centralized customer support platform
    • Aggregates Amazon, Walmart, email, and phone support
    • Provides performance metrics (e.g., response time)
    • AI features are limited
  • ChannelReply
    • Required to integrate marketplaces (especially Amazon) with Gorgias
  • Pricing note:

    • Mentions others paying significantly more at scale
  • Time Doctor(participant mention)
    • Tracks employee activity and screen recordings
    • Used for accountability and issue diagnosis (not micromanagement)
  • Additional tools mentioned (unclear transcription):
    • Likely security-related software; names not fully reliable
 
Finance Tools and Additional Recommendations
  • Bill.com
    • Core AP/AR automation tool
    • Integrates with QuickBooks
    • Uses AI to read and categorize invoices
  • Workflow:
    • Suppliers send invoices to Bill.com
    • System processes and categorizes
    • Ops team reviews
    • Finance lead approves
    • Final payment executed
  • Benefits:
    • Clear audit trail
    • No need to log into bank accounts
    • Scales efficiently (e.g., 463 bills totaling ~$6M with one vendor)
  • Coefficient
    • Connects Google Sheets with QuickBooks and other data sources
    • Automates reporting and financial tracking
    • Can be slow with very large datasets
  • SAS Ant(likely “SAS Inventory / accounting automation tool”; name may need verification)
    • Automates inventory adjustments and accounting entries
    • Reduced need for additional accounting hires
  • Together, these tools:
    • Reduce manual work
    • Improve accuracy
    • Minimize need for additional finance headcount
 
Additional Tools (Participant Suggestions)
  • Workable – Applicant tracking system
  • TestGorilla – Candidate assessment platform
  • Time Doctor – Employee monitoring and productivity
  • A QR code was shared with a full list of tools (no affiliate links).
Key Takeaways
  • A well-designed software stack can replace manual work and enable scaling without proportional headcount growth.
  • Tools require setup, cost, and learning curves, but provide a strong ROI when used properly.
  • No single “perfect stack” exists; tools should fit the business model and stage.
  • High-performing operators continuously test and refine their stack.
  • Even at high revenue levels, operational efficiency comes from systems, not just people.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Tyler Phillips discusses how brands can maximize the success of new TikTok Shop launches by creating exclusive SKUs, investing aggressively in product sampling, and building the operational systems needed to support rapid creator growth. He emphasizes that speed and preparation are key to determining whether a product has the potential to scale.

 

Launch With Maximum Momentum

  • Rather than spreading product samples over several months, Tyler recommends concentrating them into the first few weeks of a launch. Sending a large number of samples early generates more creator content, gives TikTok's algorithm more data to optimize, and helps brands determine much faster whether a product has the potential to succeed.
  • If a product is going to work, you'll typically know much sooner by launching aggressively. Instead of slowly testing over six months, brands can gather enough data within the first 30–60 days to confidently scale or pivot.

Build Your Systems Before You Scale

  • Aggressive sampling only works if your internal operations are prepared. Tyler highlights the importance of having creator messaging, response templates, creative briefs, approval workflows, and support processes ready before opening the floodgates to hundreds of creators.
  • Brands that scale too quickly without these systems often spend more time reacting to creator questions and operational issues than actually growing the program. A well-prepared team can manage large creator volumes much more efficiently.

Product Sampling Is One of the Best Investments

  • Compared to paying individual creators for sponsored content, product sampling is a relatively inexpensive way to generate large amounts of user-generated content. Even a few thousand dollars spent on samples can produce dozens or hundreds of creator videos while identifying which creators and content resonate most with customers.
  • Sampling should be viewed as an investment in content generation and learning rather than simply a marketing expense. Every sample increases the chances of discovering high-performing creatives that can later be amplified through GMV Max or paid advertising.

Learn Quickly and Optimize

  • Tyler encourages brands to embrace rapid testing instead of waiting for the perfect launch. Early mistakes are expected, and gathering real-world feedback allows teams to improve workflows, messaging, and creator management much faster than extended planning.
  • The objective is to shorten the learning cycle. Identifying what works—and what doesn't—within the first couple of months allows brands to allocate resources more effectively and accelerate future product launches.

Final Thoughts

Tyler's presentation highlights that successful TikTok Shop launches are driven by preparation and momentum. Brands that build strong operational systems, invest confidently in creator sampling, and optimize quickly based on real performance data are better positioned to scale than those taking a slow, cautious approach.

cliff_notes:
In this Q&A session, Abraham Wercberger and fellow TikTok Shop operators answer audience questions about pricing strategies, creator incentives, discounting, agency vs. in-house management, and how TikTok Shop is evolving. The discussion focuses on practical advice for brands looking to build a sustainable presence on the platform while balancing growth, profitability, and creator relationships.

 

Pricing and Discount Strategy

  • TikTok Shop currently rewards compelling offers, but that doesn't necessarily mean permanently lowering your prices. The panel recommends using a higher list price combined with platform discounts so the final selling price remains competitive with Amazon while creating a stronger perceived value for shoppers.
  • Pricing strategy should depend on your category. While competitive markets like supplements often require more aggressive promotions, some brands have successfully grown without frequent discounts by emphasizing product quality and unique value. As TikTok evolves, brands should continue testing rather than assuming discounts are always necessary.

Use TikTok Shop as a Customer Acquisition Channel

  • TikTok Shop should be viewed as more than just a sales channel. Many brands experience a halo effect where creator content drives customers to purchase later on Amazon or the brand's website. Although creators don't receive commissions on those external purchases, the increased brand awareness can still deliver significant value to the business.
  • Brands should balance maximizing overall customer acquisition while maintaining attractive commission opportunities for creators. Keeping creators motivated is essential for sustaining content production and long-term partnerships.

TikTok Shop Is Continuing to Evolve

  • The panel agreed that TikTok is actively working to move beyond being known as a discount marketplace. Its long-term goal is to become a product discovery platform where customers purchase because they discover great brands and products, not simply because they're heavily discounted.
  • Because the platform changes quickly, brands should avoid building strategies around temporary trends. Pricing models, promotions, and best practices will continue evolving as TikTok attracts larger brands and expands its ecommerce ecosystem.

Agency vs. In-House Management

  • Agencies can be a great way to get started, especially for brands without an internal TikTok Shop team. Month-to-month partnerships reduce risk while allowing brands to move quickly and learn from experienced operators.
  • However, Abraham and the panel recommend spending time learning the platform yourself before fully outsourcing. Understanding how TikTok Shop works makes it much easier to evaluate agency performance, manage employees, and make informed decisions as your business scales.

Building Creator Relationships

  • New brands often struggle to recruit creators when they have little sales history or few reviews. Before aggressively scaling creator outreach, focus on building initial traction through proven cold-start launch strategies and establishing social proof that gives creators confidence in promoting the product.
  • Successful creator programs combine a strong product, competitive offers, and consistent communication. Once creators begin seeing results, it becomes much easier to grow affiliate participation organically.

Final Thoughts

Abraham's Q&A highlights that long-term success on TikTok Shop comes from understanding how the platform is changing rather than chasing short-term tactics. Brands that combine smart pricing, strong creator relationships, and a willingness to adapt will be better positioned as TikTok continues to mature.

Key takeaways:

  1. Launch products with a clear problem-solving angle and use TikTok's New Arrival campaigns to build momentum from day one.
  2. Stack multiple creator outreach channels, personalize your messaging, and automate follow-ups to maximize creator participation.
  3. Plan inventory aggressively and execute quickly, as operational mistakes can limit growth even when demand is strong.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Jason Pratt shares the launch strategy his team used to generate over $130,000 in TikTok Shop sales during the first 30 days of a new product launch. He explains how combining the right product, aggressive creator outreach, launch campaigns, and rapid execution can create explosive early growth, even when inventory and operational mistakes occur.

 

Start With the Right Product

  • The biggest factor in a successful launch isn't marketing—it's choosing a product that genuinely fits TikTok. Jason recommends launching products that solve a clear problem, have a unique selling proposition, and are easy to demonstrate in video. Generic "me-too" products struggle to gain traction because creators have little reason to feature them over competitors.
  • Before investing heavily in samples or creator outreach, validate that your product has a compelling hook. In Jason's case, his dental powder stood out because it solved a common complaint about competing products by being gentle on dogs with sensitive stomachs.

Build Momentum Before Launch Day

  • Join TikTok's New Arrival or product launch campaigns whenever possible. Jason found these campaigns gave his product additional visibility and allowed his team to center all creator outreach around the excitement of a new launch. Every email, DM, and creator message highlighted the limited-time campaign to encourage creators to post quickly.
  • Seed the listing with initial reviews and content before scaling outreach. Jason recommends using services like JoinBrands or similar platforms to generate early sales, customer reviews, and user-generated content. While this content may not become your best-performing creative, it helps establish social proof and gives affiliates more confidence to promote the product.

Scale Faster by Stacking Creator Outreach

  • Instead of relying on a single outreach platform, Jason layers multiple channels together. His team combines targeted outreach through TikTok creator platforms, AI outreach tools, Seller Center collaborations, Discord communities, and creator agencies to maximize the number of creators receiving the product at the same time.
  • Personalization dramatically improves acceptance rates. Rather than sending generic outreach, Jason segments creators based on previous performance, inactivity, or similar brands they've promoted. Referencing their past work and writing messages that feel like they're coming directly from the founder significantly increased creator response rates.
  • Follow-up automation is equally important. Once creators receive a sample, Jason's team automatically sends creative briefs, reminders, and follow-up messages to encourage posting. Setting these workflows up once allows them to consistently drive more creator content without additional manual work.

Go Bigger Than You're Comfortable With

  • One of Jason's biggest experiments was dramatically increasing product sampling. Instead of gradually distributing samples over several months, his team sent more than 1,200 product samples during the first month, believing that maximizing creator volume early would increase the chances of viral content and accelerate momentum.
  • His advice is simple: if you're confident in the product, don't launch cautiously. Moving aggressively creates more opportunities for creators to produce content, which gives TikTok's algorithm more chances to identify winning videos and scale them.

Operational Execution Matters

  • Despite generating more than $130,000 in TikTok Shop sales during the first month, Jason believes the launch could have been significantly larger. Running out of inventory, shipping products late, and receiving avoidable negative reviews limited the product's full potential even though demand remained strong.
  • Jason recommends ordering far more inventory than you think you'll need and ensuring products arrive well before launch campaigns begin. A successful marketing strategy can't reach its full potential if inventory shortages or operational issues interrupt momentum.

Final Thoughts

Jason's biggest lesson is that successful TikTok Shop launches come from combining multiple growth levers rather than relying on one tactic. A strong product, aggressive creator outreach, launch campaigns, automated follow-ups, and sufficient inventory all work together to create momentum. When those pieces are aligned, brands can achieve significant sales in their first month—even without massive advertising budgets.

items.title: TikTok Shop Pricing Strategies － Sam Haddad － TikTok Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this video, Sam Haddad shares his experimental TikTok Shop pricing strategy for increasing conversions by engineering strike-through pricing, creating an everyday low price, and treating TikTok as its own pricing ecosystem rather than matching Amazon pricing.

 

Key takeaways:

  1. Treat TikTok Shop as a separate pricing channel with exclusive offers instead of mirroring Amazon prices.
  2. Create stronger perceived value by engineering strike-through pricing and maintaining a consistent everyday low price through campaigns and promotions.
  3. Continuously test pricing strategies and measure their impact on conversions, affiliate performance, and overall brand growth.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Sam Haddad shares an experimental pricing strategy designed to increase conversions and scale TikTok Shop by treating it as its own pricing ecosystem. He explains how engineering a strike-through price, maintaining an everyday low price, and creating stronger perceived value improved clicks, conversions, and unit sales without lowering Amazon pricing.

 

Treat TikTok Shop as Its Own Pricing Channel

  • Don't mirror your Amazon pricing. Sam believes TikTok Shop is a discount-driven marketplace where customers expect to see compelling offers. Rather than matching Amazon prices, he recommends creating a TikTok-exclusive pricing strategy that gives shoppers a clear reason to purchase on the platform while relying on a potential halo effect to drive additional Amazon sales.
  • Focus on the overall business, not individual channel profitability. Instead of evaluating TikTok Shop as a standalone P&L, Sam looks at how it contributes to brand awareness, affiliate content, and sales across other channels. The goal is to use TikTok as a top-of-funnel acquisition channel that benefits the business as a whole.

Create Stronger Offers With Strike-Through Pricing

  • Perceived value matters just as much as price. After noticing that his product pages looked "boring" compared to top-performing competitors, Sam realized the biggest difference wasn't necessarily a lower price—it was the visible discounts, strike-through pricing, and promotional offers that made products feel like better deals.
  • Engineer a strike-through price when launching a product. Instead of manually setting a list price, Sam first sells around 10 organic units at a higher retail price so TikTok recognizes it as legitimate. Once that sales history is established, he lowers the selling price, allowing TikTok to display a permanent strike-through price and a larger discount percentage.

Build an Everyday Low Price Strategy

  • Use campaigns and promotions to maintain the same attractive selling price. Rather than constantly changing prices, Sam keeps a consistent everyday low price by combining retail pricing with campaign discounts and flash sales. This creates the appearance of an ongoing promotion while giving customers confidence they're receiving a strong deal whenever they visit the listing.
  • Set your retail price carefully. Since campaign discounts are calculated from the retail price—not the list price—setting the retail price too low limits how attractive your discounts can appear. Planning these pricing levels correctly is critical for maximizing perceived value.

Early Results Show Higher Engagement and Sales

  • The pricing changes produced meaningful improvements across key metrics. Within roughly two weeks of implementing the strategy, Sam saw a 111% increase in units sold, a 13% increase in click-through rate, and a 19% increase in conversion rate. Product impressions also increased significantly, suggesting stronger pricing may help TikTok surface listings to more shoppers.
  • The experiment is still ongoing. While the sample size is still relatively small and the Amazon halo effect hasn't fully materialized yet, the early results suggest that stronger offers and more compelling pricing can significantly improve TikTok Shop performance.

Test, Measure, and Adapt

  • Pricing strategies on TikTok continue to evolve. Sam encourages sellers to test different combinations of list prices, campaign discounts, flash sales, and Subscribe & Save offers while monitoring how they affect conversions and affiliate performance. What works today may change as TikTok updates the platform, so continuous testing is essential.
  • The objective isn't simply to offer the lowest price. The bigger goal is to create an offer that creators want to promote, customers feel excited to purchase, and TikTok's algorithm rewards with greater visibility.

Final Thoughts

Sam's presentation highlights the importance of treating TikTok Shop differently from traditional ecommerce channels. By creating stronger perceived value through pricing, discounts, and promotional structure, brands can improve conversion rates, encourage affiliate promotion, and potentially generate a halo effect that benefits the entire business.

items.title: Live, Connect, Convert － Michael Corrigan － TikTok Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this video, Michael Corrigan shares how his travel brand scaled TikTok Shop from $34K/month to nearly $300K/month by focusing on community instead of transactions. He explains how TikTok Lives, creator relationships, and hands-on content optimization helped drive sustainable growth while also increasing DTC sales.

 

Key takeaways:

  1. Use TikTok Lives to build trust, answer customer questions, and gather valuable feedback—not just to generate immediate sales.
  2. Invest in long-term creator relationships through consistent communication, education, and community-building across multiple touchpoints.
  3. Don't rely entirely on TikTok's automation—manually identify and boost top-performing creator content to maximize advertising performance.

cliff_notes:
Michael Corrigan shares how his travel brand scaled TikTok Shop from $34K/month to nearly $300K/month by focusing on community over transactions. His strategy combines consistent TikTok Lives, strong creator relationships, and active content optimization to build trust, drive sales, and create a halo effect across the entire business.

 

Build Community, Not Just Sales

  • Treat TikTok Shop as a relationship-building platform. Instead of viewing TikTok Shop as another marketplace, Michael focuses on creating meaningful interactions with customers and creators. This long-term approach has helped grow both TikTok Shop revenue and DTC sales.
  • Think beyond the purchase. Encouraging conversations before and after a sale helps customers feel connected to the brand, creating loyalty that extends far beyond a single transaction.

Use TikTok Lives to Learn and Engage

  • Lives are valuable because they create conversations. Michael uses them to answer questions, understand customer objections, gather product feedback, and build trust. While they aren't his biggest direct revenue driver, they provide insights that improve the entire business.
  • Keep Lives simple and interactive. A repeatable script, consistent schedule, and easy engagement questions like "Where are you traveling this summer?" encourage comments and help TikTok distribute the Live to more viewers.

Build Strong Creator Relationships

  • Creators want transparency and consistent communication. Instead of relying only on outreach messages, Michael keeps creators engaged through Zoom sessions, Discord, WhatsApp, weekly calls, and in-person events. Building trust makes creators more likely to continue promoting the brand.
  • Educate creators about your brand. Brand Spotlight sessions allow creators to learn the company story, understand the products, ask questions, and become part of a larger creator community rather than feeling like just another affiliate.

Stay Involved With Creative Optimization

  • Don't rely entirely on GMV Max. Michael found TikTok wasn't always promoting the best creator content, despite having access to thousands of videos. His team achieved better results by manually identifying winning creatives, increasing spend behind top performers, and removing fatigued content quickly.

TikTok Benefits the Entire Business

  • TikTok Shop created a halo effect across every sales channel. Rather than taking sales away from Amazon or DTC, it increased overall brand awareness and contributed to an 80% year-over-year increase in website revenue during December.
  • Community, creators, and consistency drive sustainable growth. Michael's biggest takeaway is that brands that invest in relationships—not just advertising—build stronger businesses both on and off TikTok.

Final Thoughts

Michael's presentation shows that TikTok Shop is much more than a sales platform. Brands that consistently engage with customers, invest in creator partnerships, and stay actively involved in optimizing content can build a loyal community that drives long-term growth across every sales channel.

items.title: Member Hotseat with Leslie Eisen － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Leslie gets expert feedback on improving her Amazon hero listing to better convert TikTok Shop and other traffic.
TOPICS:
  1. Optimize category, title, and core keywords (Mandelic Acid)
  2. Improve main images, packaging, and UGC for higher CTR and trust
  3. Rewrite bullets for Rufus, FAQs, social proof, and pricing strategy
items.description_text: In this session, Leslie gets expert feedback on improving her Amazon hero listing to better convert TikTok Shop and other traffic. TOPICS: Optimize category, title, and core keywords (Mandelic Acid) Improve main images, packaging, and UGC for higher CTR and trust Rewrite bullets for Rufus, FAQs, social proof, and pricing strategy
cliff_notes:
In this session members discuss how to significantly improve the Amazon performance of Leslie’s hero product by reworking the category SEO, images, and listing structure. 

The group focuses on turning strong external demand (especially from TikTok Shop) into better Amazon ranking, conversion, and long‑term brand positioning. 

Several experts share tactical and strategic recommendations, including how to use AI tools and review-scraping software to guide listing optimization.

Business Context, Channels, and Inventory Challenges

  • Leslie’s brand previously relies on Amazon for about 65–70% of total sales, with the remainder coming from her DTC website.
  • TikTok Shop is now scaling quickly and is projected to become more than half of total sales once inventory stabilizes.
  • The team notes that TikTok demand is hard to plan for, and Leslie confirms they repeatedly experience stockouts as products take off and then run out.
  • Leslie explains they have placed a large order with their manufacturer that is scheduled to ship soon to reduce repeated inventory shortages.
  • Participants agree that because TikTok is driving substantial awareness, the Amazon listing must be “dialed in” to better convert both branded searches and new category shoppers.

Category, Keyword Strategy, and Title Optimization

  • Alex questions why the hero product appears in “facial peels” instead of “facial serums,” noting that most competitors and similar products sit under facial serums.
  • Leslie explains that the product uses Mandelic Acid as an exfoliating peel and that a previous agency advised against changing copy due to Amazon’s strict category and claims policies.
  • Alex recommends switching to the more accurate and competitive category (facial serums) where most search volume and competitors are found.
  • Alex advises putting Mandelic Acid and the brand name at the very front of the title, because many shoppers search directly for “mandelic acid” and the keyword currently appears too far at the end.
  • Alex explains that including “Mandelic acid treatment” in the title is likely allowed, because many competitors already use similar phrasing without issues.
  • Alex points out that “Level 1” and “Level 2” in the title are internal naming conventions and waste valuable SEO real estate, so he recommends removing them or deprioritizing them.
  • Leslie notes that their main search term right now is their brand name, with “folliculitis treatment” as the next most common search term, which reinforces the need to expose key treatment-related language more clearly in the title and front-facing copy.

Creative Strategy: Main Image, Packaging, and Visual Flow

  • Multiple experts emphasize that the main image is the primary driver of click‑through rate and that Leslie’s current main image is hard to read, especially on mobile search results.
  • Andre explains that a listing gives an immediate emotional first impression, just like meeting a person, so the main image must feel modern, volumetric, and visually appealing.
  • Andre and Alex show contrasting examples where alternative designs make the bottle, typography, and key claims much more bold, readable, and “juicy” in the search results.
  • They recommend removing the blank side panel on the box in the hero image and replacing it with large, readable callouts such as “Mandelic Acid,” “Made in USA,” natural ingredient icons, or key benefits.
  • Jaime points out that the current box side text is effectively dead space, since no one can read it in search results, and suggests bolding the main keywords and making them visually prominent.
  • Andre suggests using AI image tools (e.g., ChatGPT with image generation capabilities) to quickly generate more appealing compositions, then having a designer refine the winning concepts.
  • Leslie mentions they are already in the middle of a rebrand with a new box and design, and Alex advises ensuring “Mandelic Acid” is clearly visible on the front of the box and bottle in a larger font.
  • The group confirms that many Amazon sellers add extra copy or badges to the main image that are not literally printed on the box, and they report that typical enforcement risk is low (image suppression, not product suspension).
  • Andre recommends curating UGC-style images so they look professional and on-brand rather than like raw iPhone shots, because premium positioning requires polished but still authentic visuals.
  • The experts propose using more models with dark skin tones, since research suggests that Black customers are a key user group for this type of product, and the visuals currently over‑index on white models.

Listing Copy, Bullet Points, Customer Journey, and Rufus Optimization

  • Alex notes that the current bullets focus too much on features and not enough on benefits and customer outcomes, which weakens both conversion and AI-based recommendations.
  • He recommends rewriting bullets and description to directly answer real customer questions, especially those surfaced via Amazon’s AI assistant Rufus.
  • Alex suggests using AI tools like Claude to ingest reviews, questions, and market data in order to generate copy that is deeply aligned with what Rufus and customers are asking.
  • Andre maps each existing image to a single main message and discovers that the “psychological flow” jumps around between product benefits, differentiation, proof, and lifestyle in an inconsistent order.
  • Andre proposes a new image and message sequence such as:
    • State the problem (body breakouts, bumps, hyperpigmentation).
    • Present the science and solution (Mandelic Acid, why it works, gentle yet effective).
    • Help the customer choose the correct level (Level 1 vs Level 2 explanation).
    • Highlight ingredients and authority (key actives, dermatologist or science framing).
    • Show clear before-and-after or visible improvement evidence.
    • Provide how-to-use instructions.
    • Reinforce with social proof and reassurance (reviews, badges, press, influencers).
  • Andre explains that AI is excellent for summarizing and structuring ideas but still needs human oversight and specific brand knowledge layered on top.
  • Leslie notes that their new branding and messaging are based on expensive customer research by a branding agency, and she is impressed that AI nevertheless quickly flags a potential conflict in lifestyle imagery versus “dermatologist‑tested” trust positioning.
  • Alex emphasizes that optimizing for Rufus means answering questions such as “What is the best treatment for folliculitis on my body?” or “What is the difference between salicylic acid and Mandelic Acid?” in the bullets, A+ content, and backend keywords.
  • Because Leslie cannot use words like “fungal” or “fungus” for compliance reasons, Alex encourages her to focus on allowed language while still addressing closely related concerns through benefits-based explanations.
  • The group suggests adding an ingredients image where the ingredient list appears clearly, paired with large badges (e.g., “Dermatologist Tested,” “Made in USA,” “Fragrance-Free”) to build trust and clarity.

Pricing Psychology, Coupons, Social Proof, and Tools

  • Jaime recommends implementing a strike‑through list price (MSRP) strategy by temporarily raising the list price and selling price, capturing a few sales, and then lowering the selling price to create a visible discount while keeping the higher list price.
  • Jaime explains that a visible percentage-off badge and strike‑through price generally improve conversion rates and ad performance, because shoppers feel they are getting a deal.
  • Leslie confirms that the product already performs strongly as a Subscribe & Save item and agrees that offering a large one‑time coupon on the first Subscribe & Save order should attract high‑intent customers who are likely to remain long‑term subscribers.
  • Leslie shares that her previous advertising agency failed to set up such coupons despite repeated requests, which reinforces her concern that she allowed an underqualified partner to manage Amazon ads and promotions.
  • The experts stress the importance of ongoing testing (A/B testing images, copy, and badges) and not assuming that one creative direction works forever.
  • Andre and Alex argue that high‑performing brands treat an Amazon listing like a flagship website or business card, where every element—images, copy, social proof, and pricing—looks intentional and premium.
  • They also recommend regularly reviewing mobile search and product detail pages to ensure all text, badges, and images remain legible and impactful at small sizes.

In conclusion, the group identifies that Leslie’s Amazon underperformance stems less from product quality and more from category choice, weak hero imagery, and under-optimized copy. 

By surfacing Mandelic Acid and the brand name more clearly, tightening the psychological flow of images, and speaking directly to real customer questions and Rufus prompts, they expect both click‑through and conversion rates to rise.

They also frame the listing as a living asset that must be continually tested and refined—especially given strong TikTok-driven awareness and a growing customer base. 

With structured use of AI tools, review-scraping, and strategic pricing and coupon tactics, Leslie has significant upside to unlock on Amazon without changing the underlying product.

items.title: How Sellers Improve Amazon Operations and Transition to AI-Driven Growth － Rockies Chapter Monthly Call
items.description:
In this session, Rockies Chapter members troubleshoot Amazon listing and inventory issues, explore AI-driven automation, and plan upcoming events and meetups.
TOPICS:
  1. Amazon listing, SDS, barcode, and stranded inventory problem-solving
  2. Using AI tools and agents for reporting, PPC, customer service, and automation
  3. Planning conferences, Canton Fair travel, and strengthening Rockies/MDS community meetups
items.description_text: In this session, Rockies Chapter members troubleshoot Amazon listing and inventory issues, explore AI-driven automation, and plan upcoming events and meetups. TOPICS: Amazon listing, SDS, barcode, and stranded inventory problem-solving Using AI tools and agents for reporting, PPC, customer service, and automation Planning conferences, Canton Fair travel, and strengthening Rockies/MDS community meetups
cliff_notes:
In this session the Rockies Chapter members discuss current operational challenges in their Amazon businesses upcoming events and travel plans and how they are experimenting with AI and automation tools. 

They also explore how to build better cross-channel reporting and they close by coordinating future chapter activities and broader e‑commerce community building.

Amazon Listing SDS, and Inventory Troubleshooting

  • The group discusses an issue where Amazon listings are affected by both a possible SDS (Safety Data Sheet) problem and a listing configuration issue at the same time.
  • One seller explains that instead of providing SDS for certain battery items, he usually submits an exemption sheet, which gets approved more easily and avoids frequent problems.
  • They note that an exemption from SDS is already approved in this case, but it is still unclear whether the current issue is driven by SDS requirements or by a listing-level problem.
  • A participant recommends deleting the problematic listings, moving everything to FBM (Fulfilled by Merchant), letting things sit for a bit, and then recreating or re-uploading the listings to see if the system resets correctly.
  • They express frustration that Amazon support often provides generic answers, escalates cases, and still leaves certain issues unresolved for months or even a year.
  • One seller describes a specific ASIN where Amazon forces the use of FNSKU labels instead of the manufacturer’s UPC, which conflicts with his multi-channel setup using the same UPCs for Amazon, international sales, and Shopify.
  • He explains that Amazon previously allowed manufacturer barcodes on that ASIN, then changed it, and support now claims they cannot fix it, which forces him to keep sending inventory, getting it mis-scanned, and then having Amazon manually correct it.
  • They discuss how deleting a listing does not automatically trigger inventory removals and instead sends units into stranded inventory status for 60 days, during which sellers can try to reactivate listings or escalate support.
  • One participant suggests deleting the listing, creating a new SKU tied to the same ASIN, and hoping Amazon will move the stranded inventory over correctly.
  • Another explains that when he tries to reuse a SKU, the system blocks it and asks for a new SKU, which may differ depending on whether a seller uses manufacturer barcodes or FNSKU-based labeling.
  • They talk about using flat files to pull down listing data, delete listings, and then re-upload them as if making a listing change, in order to “refresh” the listing and sometimes clear stuck issues.
  • The group agrees that sellers often must test their own solutions—such as deleting and recreating listings, changing SKUs, and using different barcode approaches—instead of waiting for Amazon’s case system to solve everything.

Amazon Support Channels and Specialist Chat

  • A participant asks whether the account is using specialist chat or standard case management, indicating that support route may significantly influence response quality.
  • Another explains that there is often a specialist chat option in the support area that is typically staffed by North American reps who resolve issues faster and more effectively.
  • He mentions that he gained access to specialist chat after attending an Amazon conference, and that it is enabled across all his accounts.
  • They advise checking whether specialist chat is available and, if not, requesting to have it added to the account, since it can speed up resolutions.
  • Even when Amazon states that they will keep a listing active while they work on an issue, the group notes that listings still sometimes go down and support cannot clearly explain why.
  • They describe being in constant contact with support, including texting and email escalations, but they still decide to run their own experiments (deleting and recreating listings) if the escalations do not work within a short time.

Events, Travel, and Strategic Decisions About Conferences

  • The group discusses who is attending Vegas (likely for an Amazon/e‑commerce conference) and plans informal meetups there.
  • They talk about the BDSS event in Nashville, noting that while the base price is not bad, the event tries to upsell attendees into a higher-tier package.
  • One participant explains that BDSS content is heavily partnered with Titan, making it more attractive for people who like Titan’s style but less appealing for others.
  • They observe that some prominent speakers at these events, such as Kevin and Amy Wiese, reportedly no longer actively sell on Amazon, which reduces the perceived relevancy for advanced sellers.
  • They compare Titan and MDS communities, noting some tension between the two groups and explaining that most MDS members do not attend BDSS.
  • A member is considering skipping Nashville in favor of going to Canton Fair in China, partly due to time and budget constraints.
  • They describe a typical Canton Fair trip lasting two to three weeks, arriving mid‑April and staying into early May, sometimes including a side trip to Hong Kong for the Mega Show.
  • One seller covers multiple categories—electronics (Phase 1), toys and pets (Phase 2), and outdoors (Phase 3)—so he prefers to stay for all phases of Canton Fair.
  • They also discuss possibly visiting Yiwu for cheaper, low-cost items, although they note that getting there requires flying to Shanghai and then taking a train and a bus, which makes it logistically challenging.
  • They express concern about geopolitical risk, such as potential conflicts involving the US, China, and Iran, and they note that such uncertainty makes them reluctant to book travel too far in advance.
  • One participant states that he does not want to risk being stuck in China if a major conflict breaks out, so he plans to delay commitments and book closer to the dates.

AI, Automation, and Technical Experiments

  • Several participants are “hands down in AI” and are actively setting up chat agents and workflows to automate parts of their business operations.
  • One member is very new to AI but is learning by experimentation and wants to get Matt’s SOP for creating multiple TikTok accounts using AI, which was mentioned in a previous meeting.
  • They mention a WhatsApp AI chat group where people share tweets, YouTube videos, and implementation ideas related to AI and e‑commerce.
  • A participant describes using Claude’s computer-use features to control a browser and automatically log into Amazon and ad accounts, download business reports, and build a multi-tab Excel spreadsheet that audits campaigns.
  • This AI-generated audit highlights inefficient campaigns and opportunities to increase spend where returns are strong, and it impresses the participant’s PPC agency, who even asks whether they could white-label it.
  • Based on these results, the participant questions the future of agencies, suggesting that AI tools may make many of their services redundant.
  • They speculate about building a forecasting model that uses daily unit sales data, seasonality, and stock-out events to create alerts and identify 10% upside opportunities, similar to tools like SoStocked.
  • Another participant explains how he uses Notebook-style LM tools (referred to as “notebook LM”) where he collects tweets, YouTube links, and other resources into topic-specific notebooks and then generates summaries, FAQs, mind maps, and audio overviews.
  • They talk about OpenClaw as a framework to connect multiple LLMs—such as Google’s Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude—through APIs and orchestrate them into agents.
  • The group emphasizes that using AI models via API is billed per usage, so allowing an agent to “loop” or run unchecked can make costs spike, sometimes up to $100 per day for poorly controlled workflows.
  • They recommend using regular UI-based tools (like direct ChatGPT or Claude web interfaces) for tasks such as book or content summaries when API-level orchestration is unnecessary, in order to avoid extra credit consumption.
  • One participant explains that he is setting up AI agents via OpenClaw to handle customer service, downloading and uploading reports to Google Drive, and eventually to manage PPC campaigns by adjusting bids, negating keywords, and enforcing spending rules.
  • He notes that AI can also automate the creation and management of Amazon cases, which currently take his team 20–30 manual cases per day, especially for lost inventory, damaged inventory, and misallocated inventory.
  • They discuss using AI to prepare and submit return-related reimbursement cases, where they recover approximately 30–40% of the value by documenting returns, taking photos, and requesting refunds from Amazon.
  • Another member, more security-conscious, considers using a Raspberry Pi and strict access controls to host an AI agent, while someone else prefers a VPS from Hostinger because it is faster and cheaper than reconfiguring a local Mac Mini.
  • The group also mentions tools like Tailspin (for secure connections via SSH tunnels) and warns against using preconfigured solutions hosted in China due to privacy and security concerns.

Cross‑Channel Reporting, Attribution, and Executive Dashboards

  • One participant raises a key initiative: building a company-wide executive dashboard that aggregates data across Amazon, Target, Nordstrom, Walmart, and various ad platforms.
  • He highlights that in the baby products category, “add to registry” behavior creates a long attribution window—sometimes as long as five months between adding an item to a registry and the actual purchase.
  • The group notes that this delayed attribution can make ad performance look inefficient in the short term, even when it is profitable in reality.
  • The speaker explains that in the past year, the company focused on efficiency and cut or tightened ad spending, but the lack of good attribution and cross-channel visibility turned out to be a major miss.
  • They are exploring how to incorporate registry behavior and delayed conversion data into a unified view so they can manage efficiency and growth together, rather than optimizing in silos.
  • The group mentions solutions like Triple Whale and Northbeam, but several members say they do not have direct, hands-on experience with those platforms yet.
  • They also mention Sellerboard as a commonly used tool, but the speaker is looking for something more advanced and more holistic.
  • One member suggests that, in principle, an agent built with OpenClaw could pull data via API from Amazon, Shopify, and other major platforms and generate a custom dashboard tailored to the company’s needs.
  • They discuss that using Amazon’s API requires signing up for API access, configuring credentials, and linking via merchant tokens so AI agents can pull required reports automatically.
  • The group acknowledges that building this type of dashboard will likely involve many late nights of experimentation with AI tools, but they see it as strategically important for 2026 planning.

In summary, this meeting brings together experienced Amazon and multi-channel sellers who are actively solving operational issues, particularly around SDS, barcodes, and stranded inventory, while recognizing the limitations of Amazon’s traditional support pathways. 

At the same time, they are thoughtfully weighing which events and international trips provide the best return on time and risk, especially amid geopolitical uncertainty.

The group is clearly moving toward a future where AI and automation handle much of the reporting, PPC, customer service, and case work that agencies and VAs historically did. 

Parallel to that, they are investing in better cross-channel attribution and in strengthening the Rockies Chapter and local communities, so they can continue sharing tested, high-level strategies rather than relying on generic content from public sources.

items.title: How Market Cycles, AI Agents, and Amazon PPC Strategies Intersect for Modern Operators－Trading Channel Call February 2026
items.description:
In this session, the group covers the crypto market, AI tools for e‑commerce and PPC, and collaboration within the MDS community.
TOPICS:
  1. Crypto market outlook and strategies for Bitcoin and Ethereum
  2. AI adoption for Amazon PPC, dashboards, and workflow automation
