items.description_text: In this session, the group covers the crypto market, AI tools for e‑commerce and PPC, and collaboration within the MDS community. TOPICS: Crypto market outlook and strategies for Bitcoin and Ethereum AI adoption for Amazon PPC, dashboards, and workflow automation Community collaboration in MDS around AI tools, best practices, and shared resources
cliff_notes:
In this session the group discusses the current state of the crypto markets especially Bitcoin and Ethereum and how these fit into their broader investing strategies. 

 

They also explore how AI tools are reshaping e‑commerce workflows particularly around PPC (pay‑per‑click) advertising and reporting dashboards.

 

Throughout the conversation, participants share personal approaches to risk, real estate, and technology adoption within the MDS community.

 

Crypto Market Conditions and Strategy (Bitcoin & Ethereum)
  • Discussion focused on crypto trading and market conditions.
  • Bitcoin has dropped significantly from its highs and recently broke a key support level; potential further decline to around $58,900 expected between May and October.
  • Current price zone seen as a reasonable area to start buying, despite uncertainty about the bottom.
  • Ethereum offers higher upside potential than Bitcoin (~148% vs. ~100%).
  • Assets further down the risk curve are not considered attractive relative to risk.
  • Example of avoiding losses: exiting a large crypto position before a major drop saved hundreds of thousands in unrealized losses.
  • Investments in early-stage crypto projects with token generation noted; higher risk but potential upside if volumes increase.
  • Focus is on earning yield and finding good entry points while accepting market uncertainty.
Broader Investing and Economic Outlook
  • Opportunistic investing includes real estate, crypto, and business-related products.
  • Example: buying newly built homes (~2,000 sq ft, ~$200,000) in good neighborhoods for long-term investment and rental strategy.
  • Real assets, like housing, provide a hedge against market volatility and inflation.
  • Diversification in stocks (Amazon, Google, Facebook) emphasized; these are trusted, long-term holdings.
  • Market concerns: equity corrections, geopolitical developments (Iran deals, Trump’s actions), inflation, and capital moving away from the dollar.
  • Current environment described as a “crypto winter,” with expectations of improvement in sentiment by spring or summer.
AI Adoption in E‑Commerce and PPC
  • Attention shifting from crypto to AI for e‑commerce operations.
  • AI used heavily for content generation (photos, videos, product assets); not yet fully used for PPC management.
  • AI agents (e.g., using Claude) developed for Amazon PPC management and reporting dashboards.
  • AI-driven PPC agents led to significant performance improvements (e.g., doubling impressions week over week).
  • Custom AI dashboards built to improve upon tools like Scale Insights; include key metrics and guardrails (e.g., target TACOS 8–10%).
  • Direct Amazon API access planned for AI integration to reduce reliance on third-party tools like Hector AI.
  • AI can potentially outperform human teams and reduce dependency on manual labor.

 

In this session, participants blend a practical discussion of crypto markets with a forward‑looking exploration of AI’s role in e‑commerce and advertising. 

 

They highlight how Bitcoin and Ethereum fit into broader portfolios that also include real estate and blue‑chip tech stocks, all under the shadow of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty. 

 

At the same time, they showcase how AI agents and custom dashboards are beginning to transform PPC management and reporting.

items.title: How Brands Convert Trade Show Leads and Retail Displays into Omni-Channel Sales － Retail Channel Call February 2026
items.description:
In this session, the participants discuss outcomes from a recent trade show and how those insights connect to retail execution and omni-channel growth. 

 

TOPICS:

  • Trade show performance and lead follow-up strategy
  • Retail placement, end caps/sidekicks, and POS display logistics
  • Omni-channel brand growth across Amazon and major brick-and-mortar retailers
items.description_text: In this session, the participants discuss outcomes from a recent trade show and how those insights connect to retail execution and omni-channel growth. TOPICS: Trade show performance and lead follow-up strategy Retail placement, end caps/sidekicks, and POS display logistics Omni-channel brand growth across Amazon and major brick-and-mortar retailers
cliff_notes:
In this session Etienne Ameil and David Redlich discuss the outcomes of a recent trade show and how those learnings connect to broader retail and omni-channel strategy. 

 

They move from trade show visitor profiles and sourcing dynamics into very practical details about retail execution, including end caps, sidekicks POS displays, logistics, and quality control, and then finish with reflections on follow-up and long‑term brand building. 

 

The conversation provides a concise but detailed look at how trade show lead generation, retail merchandising, and omni-channel strategy all interconnect for consumer products.

 

Trade Show Experience and Visitor Demographics
  • Etienne explains that the trade show runs for five days, but he notes that the last day is typically unproductive and low value even though exhibitors are forced to stay until the final hour.
  • He states that if a show lasts five days, only four days are truly effective, and if a show lasts three days, only two days are realistically good for business.
  • Etienne shares that the most frequent visitors to his booth are Chinese manufacturers, and he specifies that out of approximately 180 contacts, 41 are manufacturers, with almost all of them coming from China.
  • He describes these Chinese manufacturers as very pushy in their business approach, and he indicates that he must repeatedly remind them that he is exhibiting to find clients, not additional suppliers.
  • Etienne acknowledges that while he already has enough suppliers, talking to new manufacturers can still be useful for challenging prices and filling remaining sourcing gaps in certain product categories.
  • David responds that such interactions can be valuable, because they sometimes lead to backup resources or alternative suppliers, which can be helpful for risk management and cost optimization.
  • Etienne indicates that he views the trade show as a place to complete his sourcing in some remaining categories and to test the market, even if not all conversations are with the ideal target (clients).

 

Retail Strategy, Accounts, and Inventory Management
  • David explains that he now has a dedicated account with Kroger, and he clarifies that his previous retail setup is complex, involving many stores and identifiers.
  • He states that he plans to remove the Walmart number (WL Mart number) from his system and instead use the same inventory across different channels because the GTIN (Global Trade Item Number) is identical.
  • He describes a strategy where he sends containers to Dot (a distributor) and allows Dot to manage distribution to different retailers, which he believes should be efficient once the initial complexities are resolved.
  • David notes that the beginning phase of this approach is problematic, because he has to properly cover the Walmart ID at Dot while also managing a new batch that is going to launch in the summer.
  • He mentions that he is still waiting for responses from other retailers, such as Dick’s (Dick’s Sporting Goods) and additional chains, indicating that his retail expansion is ongoing and depends on retailer decisions.
  • David comments that in retail, one of the key challenges is securing end caps or sidekicks during the holiday period, because those placements can significantly boost visibility and sales.
  • He compares his performance online to retail, stating that his online conversion rate at Walmart and Target is around 35%, which is notably higher than the average of about 17%, largely because he actively buys keywords and runs online marketing campaigns.
  • He explains that retail scale is limited by shelf space and store count, noting that if there are only six units on a shelf, even a good product can sell out quickly and then be unavailable, which caps growth potential in stores.
  • David emphasizes that scaling in retail requires more stores and more SKUs, and he notes that getting additional SKUs approved by major retailers can take six months, a year, or even up to 18 months.
  • He adds that, in Walmart specifically, they are removing a small “headache stick” product, but he is swapping that space for another product (he mentions an ankle product), showing how he actively manages assortment within limited shelf allocation.
  • David stresses that just because a product gets into a retailer does not mean it will succeed, because poor sales or other issues can lead to penalties or charges, and he admits he does not yet know the full financial impact of removing some inventory.

 

End Caps, Sidekicks, and POS Materials
  • Etienne asks whether, when David gets secondary placements like end caps or sidekicks, he needs to provide dedicated POS (point of sale) materials or extra shelves, or whether Walmart or other retailers supply those structures.
  • David answers that in his previous candy business, he used a different structure, such as pop‑up displays that hold a defined number of units (e.g., 36 units) and that these displays are often made of corrugated cardboard with printed branding.
  • He explains that for sidekicks and end caps, the structure can vary depending on the retailer and promotion, and he notes that the execution can be different between retailers like Kroger and Walmart.
  • David says that off‑shelf displays are very valuable because they sit in the aisle or on the side and attract shopper attention as they walk by, making them strong drivers of incremental sales.
  • He clarifies that sometimes a retailer shares an end cap with multiple products or brands, and that the retailer’s decision is often based on their estimate of expected sales velocity.
  • David notes that retailers’ willingness to offer these placements is tied both to what is available and what the brand is willing to pay, and he mentions that in Florida, Walmart operates on an everyday low price model and does not focus heavily on promotional pricing.

 

Sourcing and Production of Displays (US vs. China)
  • Etienne shares that he has created a very similar display format, but his version is produced in China and is shipped unfilled and flat, which significantly reduces volume and shipping cost.
  • He states that this Chinese‑made solution is very cost‑effective, mentioning that a unit costs him around $20, and that it can be set up in about two minutes once it arrives at the store.
  • He expresses skepticism that typical mass‑market stores will take the time to assemble these displays themselves, because he believes staff in those environments are generally not willing to do extra manual work.
  • David explains that he has his displays manufactured in the United States for his current business, but he emphasizes that the decision depends on who is assembling them and at what point in the supply chain they are packed with product.
  • He notes that in some cases, the distributor, such as Dot or another middleman, might assemble the displays for a fee, for example three or four dollars per unit, while in other cases the manufacturer or co‑packer handles assembly and filling.
  • David mentions that he has not yet created such a display for his rice product line, but he is considering production options as he moves manufacturing to Guatemala, suggesting that displays could also be produced or assembled there if he secures end‑cap or side‑cap placements at Target for the holiday season.
  • He repeatedly emphasizes that decisions about where to produce and assemble displays are driven by cost calculations, stating that “it’s all maths” and that he simply quotes different options and chooses the one that makes the most sense economically.
  • Etienne contrasts the behavior of mass retailers like Walmart, which he characterizes as “lazy” and mainly focused on moving units from point A to point B with minimal extra work, with specialty retailers in France, who he says are more hands‑on and more willing to do some manual assembly and merchandising.

 

Logistics, Shipping, and Store Execution Details
  • David highlights logistical challenges associated with fully assembled displays, noting that they need an outer protective box or a shroud for shipping so the structure and product are not damaged in transit.
  • He points out that brands must consider whether products will stay in place inside the display during shipping and how many display units can be stacked on a pallet to optimize freight costs.
  • Etienne agrees that an outer box is required, and both speakers acknowledge that the optimal solution depends heavily on the specific channel and retailer requirements.
  • David stresses that retailers and store staff do not want to take on complex set‑up tasks; he states that stores usually want very simple handling where they can remove an outer box and place the ready‑made display on the floor or in an aisle.
  • Etienne notes that in his Chinese‑made solution, the display arrives flat and must be unfolded and assembled in store, but he believes that mass retailers will not invest the time in this, whereas his targeted specialty stores in France are more inclined to assemble such units.
  • David adds that smaller execution details, such as whether a top headboard is actually attached in store, often go wrong, explaining that his headboards are not pre‑attached and must be slotted in, which leads to many displays missing the top branding.

 

Quality Control and In‑Store Compliance
  • David explains that he conducts quality checks by having suppliers send him pictures of the displays in store, but he still suspects that a significant percentage of units do not have the headboard attached.
  • He estimates that at least 20% of displays are missing the headboard, and he suggests the true number might be even higher, due to in‑store staff oversight or lack of training.
  • He points out that missing headboards reduce the effectiveness of the display, because the top panel often carries key branding or messaging, and its absence means the product loses some of its visual impact on shoppers.
  • Etienne confirms that his own display design also uses a separate plugged‑in headboard rather than a permanently attached one, so he recognizes the same risk that store staff may fail to install it.

 

Holiday Gifting, Product Positioning, and Retailer Pitching
  • David describes how he creates holiday‑themed versions of his product packaging and displays, where he shifts the focus from functional claims (such as headache relief) to more emotional or occasion‑based messaging like “makes a great gift.”
  • He explains that he uses design elements like holiday graphics to signal that the item is suitable as a stocking stuffer or Secret Santa gift, particularly around the December holiday season.
  • He mentions that on Amazon he has been very successful with this positioning, stating that his product ranks as the number one Secret Santa gift in its category, which demonstrates strong seasonal demand.
  • David notes that his challenge is to convince retailers like Target to allocate more in‑store space and features, by showing them evidence that his product can move large volumes in a short time, especially during the holiday period.
  • He says that one of his strategies is to present retailers with sales data from Amazon and other channels to prove that the product can generate millions of dollars in sales over just a few days when properly promoted.
  • David emphasizes that retailers who want to compete with Amazon must be willing to put more inventory and more eye‑catching displays in stores, especially with clear messaging that the product is a “great gift.”

 

Omni‑Channel Strategy and Brand Building
  • David insists that an omni‑channel presence is essential, explaining that if a brand exists only as a product listing on Amazon, it lacks the broader visibility and credibility that comes from being present in physical retail as well.
  • He argues that having products “everywhere” – online and in major brick‑and‑mortar retailers – helps establish a recognizable brand rather than just generating isolated online transactions.
  • Etienne agrees with this perspective and acknowledges that balancing online sales with retail presence is necessary for long‑term growth and brand recognition.
  • David reiterates that the core challenge is a “numbers game” in retail, where the primary questions are how to get into more stores and how to secure more SKUs within those stores, because those two levers drive overall volume.

 

In conclusion, this session centers on how trade show outcomes feed into retail and omni‑channel execution, with Etienne and David examining the realities of trade show traffic, sourcing dynamics, and the practicalities of converting leads into customers. 

 

They delve deeply into the mechanics of retail merchandising—from end caps and sidekicks to display production, logistics, and in‑store compliance—and connect these operational details to broader brand strategy and holiday selling opportunities. 

 

The call ends with a clear recognition that follow‑up, data‑driven pitches to retailers, and persistence in expanding store count and SKUs are critical to achieving sustained growth.

items.title: Multi-Channel Growth Strategies Using TikTok, Meta Advertising, and Retail Partnerships－Centurion Channel Call February 2026
items.description:
In this session, MDS Centurion members share how they scale e‑commerce brands using TikTok, Meta, Amazon, Shopify, and retail.
 
TOPICS:
  1. TikTok and Meta ad tactics
  2. Profitability metrics and tools
  3. Growth and risk
items.description_text: In this session, MDS Centurion members share how they scale e‑commerce brands using TikTok, Meta, Amazon, Shopify, and retail. TOPICS: TikTok and Meta ad tactics Profitability metrics and tools Growth and risk
cliff_notes:
In this session MDS Centurion members discuss how they scale and profitably manage e‑commerce brands across TikTok Meta Amazon, Shopify, and retail. 

 

The conversation focuses on how to think about paid media, LTV, retail expansion, and new opportunities while balancing risk, exits, and lifestyle considerations.

 

TikTok ads, spillover effect, and profitability measurement
  • The group describes TikTok as a channel where many brands are either at break-even or slightly losing money on-platform while relying on a spillover effect (sales attributed later on other channels) to be profitable.
  • They explain that some brands accept low or even negative ROAS on TikTok because the content and awareness drive profitable sales on Shopify, Amazon, and other platforms.
  • Participants state that calculating true TikTok profitability is difficult because current tools do not fully account for campaign boosts and shifting commission structures.
  • David mentions a TikTok campaign called “Glow for Love Bap”, which gives an additional 3% commission and significantly increases sales when brands join such promotional campaigns.
  • The group notes that these TikTok promotional campaigns can lead to strong short-term sales but also create margin compression, as TikTok repeatedly experiments with commissions and fees.
  • Prue shares that their team uses overstock or low-cost inventory as the “gift” in gift‑with‑purchase style campaigns, so the economics remain viable despite promotional pressure.
  • They emphasize that TikTok’s variable cost structure and weekly changes in how orders are charged make it feel like “flying blind” unless you have robust tracking and are comfortable with volatility.

 

Cross‑channel ad spend, blended metrics, and LTV tools
  • The group walks through one brand’s daily ad spend: about $28,000 on Meta, $700 on Vibe, $500 on AppLovin, $3,500 on TikTok, nearly $6,000 on Google, and $21,000 on Amazon, totaling roughly $59,000 in a single day.
  • They explain that instead of focusing only on channel‑level ROAS, they primarily look at blended MER (Marketing Efficiency Ratio) across all channels, which for one brand consistently sits around 3x.
  • Guido says they regard a blended MER between 2 and 2.5 as healthy for scaling, and if Meta MER hits 1 while blended MER falls near 2, they consider pulling back spend or reevaluating.
  • The group discusses how many VC‑backed brands are comfortable breaking even or losing money on initial purchases as long as LTV (Lifetime Value) supports heavy paid acquisition.
  • Antonio says they want to understand how far they can push paid spend by modeling LTV, because historically they insist on being at least break-even or slightly profitable on the first purchase.
  • For LTV analytics, the group mentions Lifetimely and native Shopify querying as tools used to compute LTV, though they note these sometimes output differing numbers.
  • Shinghi introduces Expandify, which they use to calculate LTV to CAC and lifetime profit to CAC, specifically tied to Amazon and Shopify performance.
  • They point out that, in practice, LTV is often similar across channels, while average order value (AOV) differs, so they use a unified LTV assumption across paid channels for planning spend.

 

Bootstrapped vs VC‑backed brands, exit multiples, and legal risk
  • The participants highlight a major cultural and strategic divide between bootstrapped founders and VC‑backed brands, noting that many VC‑backed companies prioritize growth over profitability and “burn every dollar they get.”
  • Shinghi advises bootstrapped founders not to compare themselves to VC‑backed brands because those companies often run at low or negative margins and take on significant risk to chase high valuations.
  • They discuss exit multiples in the supplement and consumer brands space, stating that highly desirable, profitable women’s health brands can sometimes achieve double‑digit EBITDA multiples (around 10–12x).
  • At the same time, they explain that undifferentiated brands with weak value propositions or poor diversification command far lower multiples or attract little buyer interest.
  • The group stresses that claims compliance is critical: buyers scrutinize the last five years of labels, websites, and marketing claims, and will often walk away if they find illegal disease claims or risky health statements.
  • They reference brands like Bloom and others that allegedly did aggressive or “black hat” things, which they say makes them poor role models for compliant, long‑term exits.
  • Shinghi notes that very large supplement brands (e.g., $100M+ per year) are actually hard to sell, because founders want valuations near a billion dollars, while buyers are no longer paying those multiples.
  • According to the group, the “sweet spot” for exiting a supplement brand is around $20–50M per year in revenue, where there is a broader pool of buyers and still visible upside for acquirers.
  • They emphasize the importance of having a strong M&A lawyer who understands preferential terms, pointing out that some minority investments come with 3x preference clauses where investors must get triple their money back before founders receive any proceeds.
  • The conversation includes examples of founders who took minority capital only to realize later they had effectively sold control of the company without realizing it, underscoring the need for legal sophistication.

 

Retail expansion vs Amazon and DTC, and operational lessons
  • The group compares retail and Amazon, stating that per‑unit economics in retail can often be better than Amazon because retailers buy at fixed wholesale prices and do not charge performance‑based fees in the same way.
  • Shinghi shares that their brand is in Natural Grocers and is pitching to Walmart and Target, describing these as major growth goals and highlighting the size of orders potential from such accounts.
  • They clarify that retail buyers almost always operate on payment terms, not prepayment, so brands need to manage cash flow and inventory risk carefully.
  • Ershad recounts an experience with Walmart where they obtained a roughly $100k order across 300 stores, but the products were placed as sidekick displays (which can appear anywhere in the store), making it hard for customers to find them.
  • This placement issue, combined with the founder managing everything alone, led to no reorders from Walmart despite initial interest and opportunity.
  • The group recommends attending events like the Walmart Seller Summit and using platforms like ECRM to meet retail buyers; one founder reports generating around $600k in retail orders in a year, with about $500k of that coming through ECRM.
  • They describe ECRM as a structured meeting environment where buyers are scheduled to meet brands (either in person or virtually), and they stress the value of approaching it with clear target buyers and goals.
  • Shinghi explains that to succeed in retail, brands often need a retail salesperson or agency that knows the category, has relationships with buyers, and understands how to pitch effectively.
  • They add that different retailers treat unsold inventory differently: some might return unsold stock, while others, like Costco, are known to heavily discount products in clearance, which can damage brand positioning.

 

Creative volume, TikTok Live, whitelisting, and new creator platforms
  • The participants agree that creative volume is a key growth lever, citing top brands that push around 100 new creatives per day into their ad libraries across TikTok and Meta.
  • Prue explains that hiring a head of growth, plus designers and video editors (many in Latin America / LATAM), helped them scale Shopify revenue from around $300k/month to approximately $1.3M/month.
  • David describes a strategy of posting 50–100 videos per day across TikTok, Meta, and Instagram from in‑house teams, with the mindset that if enough volume is produced, some pieces will become strong winners that can be scaled via ads.
  • They highlight TikTok Live as a major growth driver, noting that one brand has become number one in TikTok Live within its kitchen niche by running frequent, in‑house live sessions.
  • The group explains that for lives, unscripted content often works best: staff pack orders on camera, chat casually with viewers, and build a sense of authenticity rather than following rigid scripts.
  • They mention that some brands run 24/7 TikTok Live streams or operate across multiple countries (e.g., Crocs running streams in different regions) by building out global live‑creator infrastructures.
  • The participants contrast agency‑run lives with in‑house teams, saying agencies often feel disconnected from the brand and less authentic, especially in live formats.
  • On Meta, they discuss whitelisting: running ads from a creator’s page or personal account instead of the brand’s page, because “people like to buy from people, not brands.”
  • They clarify that whitelisted ads are configured inside Meta Ads Manager and can significantly outperform standard brand‑page ads due to the perceived authenticity and social proof of the creator’s profile.
  • Prue introduces Tribe (spelled T‑R‑Y‑B‑E, often referred to as “Tribe”), a platform that replicates a TikTok‑shop‑style affiliate model on Meta, allowing brands to invite creators, offer affiliate commissions, and track performance in real time.
  • They note that Lucas Paul, who owns a men’s athletic brand, founded Tribe, and that Hudson (from the apparel brand Comfy / Comfort, as referenced) has invested in the platform and uses large numbers of creators and high creative volume to win on Meta and TikTok.
  • Tribe is described as having an early access / secret sign‑up link and being in limited rollout, with features such as real‑time attribution dashboards and visibility into which creator content is working best.
  • The group acknowledges open questions around commission accuracy and attribution, especially when using third‑party platforms layered on top of sometimes unreliable native Meta attribution.

 

Risk, regulations, and campaign configuration pitfalls
  • The group discusses injectables (such as peptides and NAD), with some participants personally using them or selling them in legitimate wellness spas via FDA‑approved pharmacies, but most agree the regulatory risk is high for online expansion.
  • They compare this risk to cannabis drink brands, noting that one legal change has effectively made many of those products illegal by the end of the year, erasing entire businesses that had grown to tens of millions in revenue.
  • They recall similar patterns with brands like Four Loko, which survived by decreasing the alcohol content but lost much of their edge and cultural relevance in the process.
  • Shinghi shares a TikTok nightmare where a third party hosted a TikTok Live promising a free iPhone 17 with every purchase of their supplement, leading to a huge wave of misled customers and negative reviews when no iPhones arrived.
  • They explain that this kind of exploit is an attack vector that brands and TikTok struggle to control, because anyone can go live and make false claims tying themselves to a product.
  • The group notes that although TikTok is hard to reach, once escalated to the right people, the platform can help resolve such fraudulent situations, but the reputation and review damage can be significant.
  • On the technical side, they discuss GMV Max campaigns on TikTok and warn against setting extremely high ROAS goals (e.g., 10x), which severely restrict delivery and impressions.
  • Guido suggests that GMV Max campaigns require hundreds of videos per product to give the algorithm enough to test and learn before scaling, so they recommend isolating hero products in their own campaigns.
  • They advise setting more realistic ROAS goals (e.g., closer to 2–4x) and using a catch‑all campaign for non‑hero SKUs, rather than splitting everything into separate campaigns with unattainable performance targets.

 

In this session, the founders collectively surface the realities of running multi‑channel e‑commerce brands, showing how TikTok, Meta, Amazon, Shopify, and retail each play different roles in growth and profitability. 

 

They emphasize that success depends on accurately measuring blended performance, understanding LTV, managing legal and platform risk, and building strong creative and operational systems.

 

Ultimately, the group leans toward sustainable, bootstrapped growth rather than chasing hyper‑growth at all costs, viewing exits as optional rather than mandatory. 

 

Their experiences point toward a playbook that combines disciplined metrics, creative scale, and careful risk management to build brands that can thrive in an increasingly competitive and regulated environment.

items.title: AI-Powered Amazon SEO Strategies Using Agents, Rufus, and Smart Catalog Growth － SEO Channel Call Januray 2026
items.description:
In this session, experienced Amazon sellers discuss how new AI tools and agents are transforming SEO, content creation, and catalog growth, especially in competitive niches like bedding.
TOPICS:
  1. AI agents and LLMs for automation (OpenClaw, Claude, GPT, Gemini)
  2. Optimizing Amazon listings for Rufus/Cosmo (titles, images, variants, content)
  3. Scaling large catalogs and operations (StoreAutomator, FBA fees, packaging, tariffs)
items.description_text: In this session, experienced Amazon sellers discuss how new AI tools and agents are transforming SEO, content creation, and catalog growth, especially in competitive niches like bedding. TOPICS: AI agents and LLMs for automation (OpenClaw, Claude, GPT, Gemini) Optimizing Amazon listings for Rufus/Cosmo (titles, images, variants, content) Scaling large catalogs and operations (StoreAutomator, FBA fees, packaging, tariffs)
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS SEO Channel explore how fast‑moving AI tools are changing the way Amazon sellers approach SEO content creation and catalog growth. 

 

The group compares different AI models and “agent” setups and then connects those capabilities directly to practical listing optimization and launch tactics. 

 

Throughout, experienced operators in categories like bedding share what is working for them right now, especially around Rufus, Cosmo, and large‑catalog strategies.

 

AI agents and the current LLM landscape
  • Participants describe how new AI agents (like OpenClaw) sit on top of LLMs such as Claude, GPT, and Gemini and orchestrate tasks like coding, content creation, and reporting.
  • Andrei explains that he considers Claude the best current model for coding, while GPT sometimes reasons better on certain tasks and Gemini scores well on complex benchmarks.
  • The group notes that these agents can combine multiple models in one workflow, so different AIs handle different specialties such as coding, reasoning, or routine system checks (“heartbeat” tasks).
  • They agree that recent advances make AI agents feel like having a highly capable assistant who can build tools, write content, and automate workflows much faster than traditional teams.

 

Practical uses of AI agents in day‑to‑day business
  • Andrei explains that he uses an AI agent controlled through Telegram as a personal and coding assistant that can send screenshots, modify code, and deploy changes to servers while he is away from the desk.
  • He shares that he builds dashboards, PPC tools, and internal content systems by having the AI write and iterate code, even though he does not consider himself a traditional developer.
  • He describes creating a “content machine” that, from a simple Telegram command, writes a blog post, improves and humanizes it, checks it, creates images, and can publish it to a site like WordPress.
  • The group concludes that such setups can replace many tasks previously done by VAs, project managers, or junior developers, especially for repetitive work like listing generation and content production.

 

Cost, infrastructure, and security considerations for AI
  • Andrei warns that directly connecting agents to paid APIs like Claude or Gemini quickly drives up token costs, and he has seen setups that burn $100–$200 per day if not configured properly.
  • He explains that regular “heartbeat” checks must be pointed at cheaper or local models (for example, via Ollama) to avoid constant expensive API calls.
  • He recommends running agents on a separate machine (such as a Mac Mini) instead of a primary work computer, because open ports and misconfigured skills can expose sensitive information.
  • He highlights that many downloadable “skills” or plugins may contain malicious prompt injection designed to steal stored API keys or financial data, so they must be inspected carefully (even with GPT) before use.

 

How Amazon’s Rufus and Cosmo change SEO priorities
  • Alex explains that Cosmo is Amazon’s back‑end AI that reads listing content, attributes, and behavior data, while Rufus is the front‑end AI shopping experience that customers interact with.
  • He notes that tens of millions of shoppers have already used Rufus and that Amazon is clearly pushing toward AI‑driven, almost “human‑free” shopping journeys.
  • Because Cosmo feeds structured data to Rufus, he stresses that sellers must structure listings around benefits, product attributes, and customer questions, not just around keyword stuffing.
  • The group agrees that as Rufus becomes more prominent, sellers who optimize for clear, authoritative, and complete information will have a major advantage over those relying on older SEO tactics.

 

Keyword stuffing vs benefit‑driven, authority content
  • Deepak shares that his SEO team still pushes to insert many keywords into titles and bullets, which makes content long and hard to read, and he fears that removing them might hurt rankings.
  • Alex counters that in his experience, full rewrites focused on benefits and customer questions do not hurt rankings and often improve performance, especially when trained AI systems generate consistent, market‑aware copy.
  • David adds that Amazon now detects and disregards duplicate keywords and sometimes auto‑rewrites titles and bullets for major sellers, which reduces any benefit from traditional keyword stuffing.
  • The group converges on the view that being the authority on the topic—with specific, helpful content tied to real customer needs—is now more important than packing every possible keyword into a single listing.

 

Variants, long‑tail demand, and catalog expansion
  • Alex emphasizes that variants are a powerful SEO tool because each variant can target a different angle or query without overloading a single listing with keywords.
  • He explains that in categories like bedding, sellers can have dozens of colors and sizes per parent, and each variant’s backend data helps the brand cover more long‑tail search terms.
  • Deepak confirms that when he adds more color variations to his bed sheets, his rankings and sales improve, because customers often leave if their exact preferred color is missing.
  • Alex and Deepak both plan aggressive catalog expansion: Alex wants to grow from 800 to 5,000 SKUs, and Deepak plans to move from around 1,500–1,800 SKUs to over 3,000 SKUs, using AI to make that scale manageable.

 

Controlling bots, LLM perception, and external reviews
  • Deepak explains that he discovers massive scraper bot traffic hitting his Shopify site, which both slows the store and feeds competitor tools, so he configures Cloudflare to block certain bots while allowing beneficial ones like Amazon’s.
  • He shares that tests with ChatGPT and Gemini suggest these models often trust Walmart and Google reviews more than Amazon reviews, due to scraping and access restrictions on Amazon’s review data.
  • He concludes that he must invest in stronger review profiles on Walmart and potentially Target, so that LLMs see his brand as high quality across multiple channels, not just on Amazon.
  • Andrei adds that sellers can shape how LLMs perceive their brands by hosting an LLM index file (llm.txt) and by publishing clear, authoritative brand information on their websites and profiles such as LinkedIn.

 

Image strategy, main images, and listing structure
  • Brandon raises concerns about Amazon Rekognition misclassifying his product images as “weapons,” and Alex answers that Rekognition appears outdated and largely unused for live marketplace ranking decisions.
  • Deepak asks for feedback on his bedding listings, and Alex focuses on the main image, noting that a partially hidden box with small text is hard to read and likely suppresses click‑through rate.
  • Alex recommends making the box fully visible and front‑facing, enlarging benefit‑driven text like “100% Egyptian Cotton,” “400 Thread Count,” and size information so shoppers can understand the offer directly from the search results.
  • They discuss keeping brand elements consistent but shifting title and image emphasis away from long brand names and toward clear features, benefits, and sizes that matter for both customers and Rufus.

 

Tools and workflows for large‑catalog management
  • Alex advises moving from flat files to an API‑based tool like StoreAutomator to manage large catalogs across Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Target, and other channels.
  • He explains that with such a tool, a seller can select all or part of the catalog, make a single change (e.g., to a field in the title or an attribute), and push it through the API to update all listings quickly and reliably.
  • He notes that this approach reduces browse node and attribute errors that commonly arise from manual flat‑file uploads, which can otherwise block indexing or hurt relevance.
  • Deepak is interested in this setup because his current manual process of producing, auditing, and uploading content is slow, and he wants to support faster catalog growth and ongoing optimization with fewer people.

 

Fulfillment economics, tariffs, and staying lean
  • David stresses that small packaging changes and regular audits of FBA size and weight tiers can produce large savings, sometimes on the order of $2 per unit when moving between fee brackets.
  • Deepak and David discuss how pricing just below certain thresholds (such as $49.99 instead of over $50) can keep FBA fees lower and protect margins.
  • They also talk about tariffs and freight costs as both challenges and barriers to entry, noting that larger, established brands may withstand these better than smaller or less efficient competitors.
  • Alex summarizes that sellers now must be extremely lean and optimized across SEO, content, packaging, pricing, and logistics, because rising complexity and AI‑driven changes will punish sloppy operations.

 

In this session, the group frames AI agents and LLMs not as futuristic experiments but as immediate, practical tools that can build content, code, and internal systems at a pace no human team can match. 

 

They show how these capabilities connect directly to Amazon's strategy by shaping how Rufus and Cosmo see listings and by enabling aggressive catalog expansion with relatively small teams.

items.title: How Brands Turn Failed Creative Tests Into High-Converting Sales Assets － Peter-Paul Maan － Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Peter‑Paul Maan and Travis Klabon from Intellivy discuss how to use structured polling, consumer insights, and AI‑assisted research to improve Amazon listing performance.
TOPICS:
  1. Using consumer polls and validation frameworks (OPA) to design and test listing changes with clear hypotheses.
  2. Case studies showing how label, image, and A+ content optimization improve BSR and conversions (e.g., luxury bath pillow, coffee descaler, litter box).
  3. Combining AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, and SQP data) with human judgment and competitor analysis to guide continuous listing optimization.
items.description_text: In this session, Peter‑Paul Maan and Travis Klabon from Intellivy discuss how to use structured polling, consumer insights, and AI‑assisted research to improve Amazon listing performance. TOPICS: Using consumer polls and validation frameworks (OPA) to design and test listing changes with clear hypotheses. Case studies showing how label, image, and A+ content optimization improve BSR and conversions (e.g., luxury bath pillow, coffee descaler, litter box). Combining AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, and SQP data) with human judgment and competitor analysis to guide continuous listing optimization.
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS community meet with Peter‑Paul Maan and Travis Klabon from Intellivy to learn how to use structured polls and consumer insights to drive real sales growth on Amazon. 

 

The focus is on turning creative testing from guesswork into a repeatable data‑driven process, supported (but not replaced) by AI tools.

 

Intros and Positioning of Intellivy
  • Peter‑Paul Maan explains that he has been selling on Amazon since 2014 and now runs many done‑for‑you consumer insights and polling services at Intellivy.
  • Travis Klabon shares that he joined Intellivy about three months ago, after working at BidX and at AMZ Insiders (Jamie Davidson’s coaching program) where he helps build multiple six‑ and seven‑figure Amazon sellers.
  • Peter‑Paul and Travis position Intellivy as a polling and consumer‑insights partner with special pricing for the MDS community.
  • Travis says he looks forward to meeting many members in Las Vegas and helping them “move the needle” on their listings.

 

Why Most Creative Tests Fail
  • Peter‑Paul states that most creative tests fail because they optimize for opinions (“looks better”) instead of actual purchase drivers.
  • He emphasizes that effective testing starts from clear intent and hypotheses, not from random trying of images or colors.
  • He insists that creatives must be evaluated in a full marketplace context (against competitors, with price and reviews in mind), because customers compare offers, not isolated designs.
  • He recalls his MDS Barcelona 2023 talk on “reinventing the optimization team,” arguing that strong optimization needs multiple skills: research, competitor selection, USP definition, and design execution.
  • He notes that cheap AI tools can now generate full image sets very quickly, but warns that automating bad thinking just produces more bad creative faster.

 

Role of AI vs Human Judgment
  • Peter‑Paul explains that he uses tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and others every day for idea generation, structuring, and category understanding, but he never relies on them alone.
  • Travis gives an example where ChatGPT gets the day of the week wrong, to show that AI can make simple errors and must be supervised.
  • They describe AI as an enhancer, not a replacement, especially since real humans (buyers) are the ones making purchase decisions.
  • Peter‑Paul mentions Claude's “projects” and tools like “Coworker”, which let him upload MD files (e.g., “pull situation generator,” “report style guide”) so he can build a persistent optimization assistant on top of his own methods.
  • He stresses that founders who historically make strategic mistakes will bake those mistakes into their AI workflows if they do not fix their thinking first.

 

OPA and Validation Frameworks
  • Peter‑Paul introduces OPA – Outcome, Purpose, Action Plan – as a simple structure for any project or test.
  • He defines the Outcome for this session as having a clear, repeatable method to prioritize and validate optimization decisions with less wasted effort.
  • The Purpose is to use polls to validate optimization hypotheses instead of guessing, and to distinguish quick wins from bigger overhauls.
  • The Action Plan includes choosing the right validation track (off‑the‑shelf product vs new concept), defining the optimization phase, and setting minimum research steps before changes go live.
  • He lays out a broader validation framework that asks:
    • What frustrates the customer (from reviews and objection polls)?
    • Can the brand credibly solve those problems and communicate them?
    • Do consumers recognize and value the advantage?
    • Does the total concept beat key alternatives enough that buyers will switch or pay more?

 

Listing Optimization, Poll Design, and Competitor Context
  • Peter‑Paul presents a default listing optimization framework that starts by identifying whether problems are mainly with CTR, CVR, or the full funnel.
  • He then calls for strong diagnostics, including:
    • A detailed competitor landscape (dimensions, materials, price, capacity, etc.).
    • Full mapping of competitors’ main images and image stacks.
    • Understanding how each competitor’s listing tells its sales story.
  • He stresses that teams must do desk research first and then use polls to validate specific hypotheses; they should not expect polls to tell them what to build from scratch.
  • He recommends polls that mimic the real Amazon environment for key decisions: this can mean showing title, price, and reviews when testing main images so that results translate better to actual performance.
  • He and participants note that poll results often align with Manage Your Experiments (MYE), but MYE requires high traffic, so brands sometimes learn faster by combining polls with PPC‑driven tests.

 

Case Studies: Label, Luxury Bath Pillow, and Litter Box
Coffee Machine Descaler Label
  • Peter‑Paul shares a label optimization for a coffee machine descaler where the brand wants a more “scroll‑stopping” look in a crowded category.
  • Multiple label concepts are tested, and the winner clearly communicates “natural, safe ingredients,” “chemical-free and safe,” “made in the USA,” and effectiveness, which are the attributes respondents care about most.
  • After the winning label is selected, they plan to update the main image and rebuild the image stack so that hooks, “why” messaging, and differentiators all support the same core decision drivers.

 

$200 Luxury Bath Pillow (Gift Product)
  • A white-glove client sells a $200–220 luxury bath pillow in a high‑end gift category with relatively few direct luxury competitors.
  • They test gold vs black and other design details, plus later model vs no‑model imagery, always benchmarking options against the top competitor’s main image.
  • Iterative polls (about nine in total between Intellivy and the client) refine color, props (e.g., soap), model choice, and background to better convey luxury and “giftability.”
  • Even in A+ content, a simple, plain design surprisingly wins over a more dramatic design, based on consumer feedback.
  • The result is a move from around BSR 120 to BSR 12 during sales season (before going out of stock) and then stabilizing around BSR 50, beating the main competitor.

 

Stainless Steel Litter Box and Visual Clarity
  • In a stainless steel litter box listing, one image attempts to show hygiene but actually makes respondents think more about size and spaciousness.
  • Peter‑Paul recommends that each image must communicate its intended message even without text, so they design visuals that directly show cleaning (e.g., water and wiping) rather than relying on text about hygiene.
  • He uses a “two‑second impact poll” to check what people immediately perceive and whether the right message is landing.
  • He also warns about leading poll intros: an original description that mentions “mess, odor, and hygiene” biases respondents to mention those topics, so he rewrites it to a neutral prompt about buying a semi‑enclosed litter box on Amazon and asking what matters to them.

 

SQP Data, AI‑Assisted Research, and Process Discipline
  • Peter‑Paul presents SQP (Search Query Performance) data integration inside Intellivy, which lets users connect keywords, traffic, and conversions to specific ASINs.
  • In one example, a supplement benefits from a TikTok‑driven branded search spike, and they analyze exactly how that traffic behaves so they can tune the listing for those queries.
  • The platform allows teams to tag polls to ASINs and see how consumer insight investments correlate with CVR improvements and overall profit, giving visibility into ROI on research.
  • Using Claude projects, Peter‑Paul has Claude generate category overviews, pain points, hypotheses, and suggested poll sequences from a single ASIN, then layers this with more precise data from their own tools.
  • Jamie concludes that his team’s next step is to formalize their testing process, adopt frameworks like OPA, and track the impact of changes over longer periods, since competitors and seasons constantly shift.
In this session, the group learns that effective listing optimization relies on clear hypotheses, strong competitor research, and unbiased consumer polling, supported but not replaced by AI. 

 

Resources Mentioned

  • Product Validation Framework
  • Listing Optimization Framework

 

The case studies show how combining structured frameworks with real buyer feedback can meaningfully change BSR, conversion rates, and revenue, especially for high‑value products.

 

Peter and Travis encourage brands to move away from ad‑hoc, opinion‑driven testing and toward repeatable, insight‑driven systems that can be applied SKU by SKU. 

 

By using tools like Intellivy, SQP data, and AI assistants within frameworks such as OPA, teams can continually adapt to changing marketplaces while basing every creative decision on what truly matters to customers.

files.name: Presentation by Charles Chakkalo - Stickerless Is Dead
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1770246128366-Presentation by Charles Chakkalo - Stickerless Is Dead.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session MDS Resellers Channel members break down Amazon’s decision to end commingling (manufacturer barcode fulfillment) and what it means operationally financially and strategically for resellers.

 

Charles a long-time Amazon reseller active since 2010 leads the discussion with real-world experience ranging from small-scale van sourcing to full truckload operations. He frames the session as a practical walkthrough of the policy change taking effect March 31, with an emphasis on minimizing risk and adapting workflows quickly.

 

Key Policy Takeaways

  • Commingling ends March 31 for most resellers. Inventory shipped after that date must use Amazon barcodes (FNSKUs).
  • Ship date—not warehouse check-in date—determines compliance.
  • Only brand owners or approved brand representatives via Brand Registry can continue using manufacturer barcodes.
  • Amazon’s core goal is unit-level traceability to a specific seller for authenticity, liability, and enforcement.

Brand Registry & Brand Representative Risks

  • Resellers can only keep manufacturer barcodes if the brand assigns them a brand representative role in Brand Registry.
  • Amazon’s language implies this role is meant for internal employees, creating ambiguity and risk.
  • Charles cautions that while the role works today, Amazon may later penalize brands that misuse it.
  • Smaller brands may be flexible; large brands with legal teams are far less likely to cooperate.

Reseller Options Moving Forward

  1. Secure brand representative access (high trust, higher risk).
  2. Transition fully to Amazon barcodes (FNSKUs).
  3. Ignore rumored future reseller classifications—don’t build strategy on speculation.

 

Charles stresses that time is limited and resellers must act now by auditing SKUs, lead times, and labeling capacity.

Operational Impact & Labeling Strategies

Resellers discussed three main labeling paths:

  • Factory-level labeling (ideal but brand-dependent)
  • Prep centers / 3PLs (easy to scale, higher per-unit costs)
  • In-house warehouses (maximum control, higher overhead)

 

Common risks include:

  • Misapplied FNSKUs
  • Poor barcode quality or placement
  • Item vs. case label mismatches
  • Inbound defect fees are charged per unit

Clear SOPs and strict label controls are essential.

Why Charles Never Trusted Commingling

Charles shared that he has always used Amazon barcodes due to:

  • Inventory misattribution under commingling
  • Amazon’s algorithm-driven enforcement and reimbursements
  • Increased risk under newer automated systems

His takeaway: Amazon is consistently moving toward tighter control and automation—looser systems are becoming liabilities.

Transparency Codes Clarified

  • Transparency and commingling are separate programs.
  • Even with Transparency, non-brand resellers must still use FNSKUs.
  • Combined FNSKU + Transparency labels are valid, but don’t bypass seller traceability requirements.

IP Enforcement, GTINs & Bundling

  • Sellers reported spikes in automated IP violations (“brand bots”), often without brand complaints.
  • GTIN/GS1 accuracy is now critical—mismatches can cause mass takedowns.
  • Bundles are increasingly risky, especially under reseller-created brands.
  • Safer strategy emerging: list bundles under the original brand, even if it increases competition.

Reimbursements & Recovery

  • Amazon is becoming more proactive with reimbursements, but gaps remain.
  • Layered recovery strategies (TrueOps → Seller Investigators → internal teams) still add value.
  • Detailed return reconciliation is an overlooked recovery opportunity.

Looking Ahead

  • Brand management and exclusivity remain powerful but risky if misaligned with Amazon's roles.
  • Amazon’s Voice of the Seller program may influence future changes, though skepticism remains.
  • Advocacy is underway for a potential third reseller classification—but nothing is guaranteed.

items.title: Ershad Ganjy － Invest Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this session, Ershad Ganjy highlighted hard lessons from partnerships, financing structures, and market dynamics.
TOPICS:
  1. Investment journey and lessons from failed partnerships and due diligence.
  2. Financial structuring, refinancing, and the need for strong property-level financial controls.
  3. Structuring developer agreements, legal protections, and risk management for new build-and-sell projects.
items.description_text: In this session, Ershad Ganjy highlighted hard lessons from partnerships, financing structures, and market dynamics. TOPICS: Investment journey and lessons from failed partnerships and due diligence. Financial structuring, refinancing, and the need for strong property-level financial controls. Structuring developer agreements, legal protections, and risk management for new build-and-sell projects.
cliff_notes:
In this session, Ershad Ganjy shares lessons from his real estate investing journey, focusing on the risks of partnerships, the importance of due diligence, and the need for stronger financial controls. 


The discussion centers on structuring deals more carefully, protecting investor capital, and building sustainable long-term real estate projects.


Investment Background and Market Lessons

  • Ershad explains that he began building wealth through Amazon in 2016 and later used those profits to invest in real estate.
  • He describes purchasing Airbnb properties in New Orleans beginning in 2018 and using a buy-refinance-buy strategy to expand his portfolio.
  • He shares that the Covid-19 pandemic severely impacted the New Orleans market and made it extremely difficult to sell those properties.
  • He notes that he spent roughly a year trying to exit the New Orleans investments and ultimately concluded that the local market was too weak.
  • He presents this experience as one of his first major investment lessons and advises others to be cautious about investing in New Orleans.
  • He explains that in 2023 he shifted his focus to flipping houses at auction in Lafayette, Louisiana, alongside a partner.
  • He reports that their Lafayette operation allows them to flip approximately 10 houses per year and generate roughly $500,000 in annual profit.


Partnership Failures and Due Diligence Gaps

  • Ershad recounts attempting to replicate the Lafayette model in North Carolina with a trusted friend and a local operating partner.
  • He explains that the local partner appeared highly credible because he owned a real estate brokerage and several related service businesses.
  • He describes how the partner sourced off-market properties that were purchased for cash, renovated, and later refinanced.
  • He admits that he and his friend relied too heavily on trust and failed to independently verify titles, ownership structures, and financial controls.
  • He later discovered that the partner had purchased properties under his own name instead of under the agreed LLC structure.
  • He states that the partner refinanced multiple properties, extracted cash, and rolled the proceeds into additional deals without fully informing investors.
  • He estimates that they invested approximately $1.5 million and now expect losses of roughly $400,000, even if the remaining properties eventually sell.
  • He emphasizes that the situation ultimately reflects a failure of proper due diligence and oversight on their side.
  • He summarizes the core lesson as never blindly trusting partners and always personally verifying ownership records, title documentation, and financial flows.


Current Rental Portfolio and Financial Controls

  • Ershad shares that he recently acquired approximately 28 to 30 duplex units in North Carolina at prices around $195,000 to $200,000 per unit.
  • He notes that each unit is roughly 1,600 square feet and rents for approximately $2,000 per month when occupied.
  • He states that 16 of the units are currently leased and highlights that the properties are newly built, reducing maintenance requirements.
  • He explains that he purchased the units entirely with cash and is now pursuing refinancing to recover liquidity and redeploy capital.
  • Other participants strongly recommend establishing an in-house finance team to review numbers regularly and maintain transparency across projects.
  • They stress the importance of treating each property like a standalone business with detailed profit and loss statements and accurate bookkeeping.
  • Ershad mentions that he uses Inago for property management and financial tracking and finds the platform easy to use.
  • Participants advise him to consistently request financial records such as P&L statements, invoices, builder documentation, and contractor licensing information whenever he invests in projects.


Structuring Developer Relationships and Build-and-Sell Deals

  • Ershad introduces a new project involving 10 units on land with a total estimated cost of approximately $405,000, including land improvements.
  • He explains that he partnered with a contractor named Derek, contributing 60% of the capital while Derek contributes 40%.
  • He states that Derek serves as the general contractor and receives a 3% fee based on total project costs plus an additional 6% of the final sales price.
  • He confirms that ownership equity is intended to follow the capital structure, with Ershad holding 60% and Derek holding 40%.
  • Participants question how construction costs and subcontractor pricing will be verified to ensure no hidden profit margins or inflated expenses exist.
  • They recommend requiring complete transparency on invoices, receipts, and subcontractor payments throughout the project.
  • The group discusses constructing the units as townhomes or duplex-style connected units with approximately 1,900 square feet per unit.
  • Participants advise maintaining clear build standards and ensuring the final product matches or exceeds the quality of comparable successful developments.


Risk Management, Legal Protections, and Long-Term Strategy

  • Several participants emphasize that real estate is highly cyclical and becomes especially challenging during periods of declining prices or reduced liquidity.
  • They warn that partnerships often function smoothly during rising markets but can deteriorate when additional capital contributions become necessary.
  • They note that real estate is particularly vulnerable to fraud and therefore requires extensive controls, documentation, and verification procedures.
  • Participants recommend creating a separate LLC for each deal, supported by signed operating agreements that clearly define ownership percentages, fees, and responsibilities.
  • They stress that all legal agreements should be completed before capital is deployed or construction begins.
  • They advise pre-selling units whenever possible so projects have committed buyers and predictable revenue before full completion.
  • The group highlights the importance of understanding the local rental and resale markets in depth, including pricing trends, demand, and fallback strategies.
  • They strongly recommend maintaining a clear Plan B, such as holding units as rentals if projected sales conditions weaken.
  • Ershad shares that his broader long-term goal is to eventually pursue larger developments, including a potential 98-unit mixed-use project with residential and commercial components if the current venture succeeds.


In conclusion, this session provides a candid discussion about the realities of real estate investing, especially the importance of due diligence, legal structure, and financial oversight when working with partners. 


The group shares practical advice for protecting capital, improving transparency, and structuring development and rental projects more responsibly over the long term.

items.title: How to Invest in Rental Properties without Banks  － Jun Kim Rich Reister － Invest Mastermind 2026
items.description:
In this session, Jun Kim & Rich Reister explain the “subject to” (sub two) real estate strategy, where investors buy properties by taking over existing mortgages without using new bank financing.
TOPICS:
  1. Core concept of subject to
  2. Deal sourcing and analysis
  3. Risks, exits, and variations
items.description_text: In this session, Jun Kim & Rich Reister explain the “subject to” (sub two) real estate strategy, where investors buy properties by taking over existing mortgages without using new bank financing. TOPICS: Core concept of subject to Deal sourcing and analysis Risks, exits, and variations

files.name: How to Invest in Rental Properties without Banks  － Jun Kim Rich Reister － Invest Mastermind 2026
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1776677477054-How to Invest in Rental Properties without Banks  － Jun Kim Rich Reister － Invest Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session, Rich Reister and Jun Kim explain the real estate investing strategy known as “subject to” (often called “sub two”) and show how it allows investors to acquire properties without obtaining new traditional mortgages. 


They walk through the mechanics, benefits, risks, and real-life deal examples so that investors with some real estate background can understand where this strategy fits and how to apply it responsibly.


Core Concept of “Subject To” and Who It Is For

  • Subject to (or sub two) is a strategy where the buyer takes ownership of a property but leaves the existing mortgage in the seller’s name while the buyer agrees to make the mortgage payments.
  • Jun & Rich emphasize that title (ownership) and mortgage debt are separate. In a subject to deal, the deed transfers to the buyer, but the loan remains legally in the seller’s name.
  • The buyer typically gains access to the seller’s mortgage account and makes payments directly, becoming contractually responsible for the payments even though the loan is not in the buyer’s name.
  • This strategy is positioned for investors with a foundational understanding of real estate, not for absolute beginners buying their first rental property.
  • They state that subject to investing requires moderate risk tolerance, strong problem-solving skills, and comfort with using professional property managers rather than self-managing every property.
  • They stress that subject to is not loan assumption, not traditional seller financing, not a lease option, and not illegal when structured properly with the right documentation.


Benefits, Risks, and Legal Considerations

  • A major benefit of subject to investing is access to existing low-interest-rate mortgages, often in the 2% to 4% range, which are significantly below current market rates and improve cash flow and equity growth.
  • Subject to deals often require less upfront cash than standard purchases, especially when sellers have little equity and mainly need relief from monthly payments.
  • The strategy allows faster closings because the buyer does not need to wait for approval on a new traditional mortgage.
  • The primary legal and practical risk is the “due on sale” clause, which gives the lender the right, but not the obligation, to call the full loan due if ownership transfers.
  • Jun & Rich note that they have not personally experienced a loan being called due and reference anecdotal estimates that the risk may be around 1% to 2%, but they still treat it as the biggest structural risk.
  • They explain that if a lender does call the loan due, the investor may need to refinance, sell the property, or otherwise pay off the balance.
  • Another major risk involves the seller’s credit. If payments are missed, the late payments or foreclosure appear on the seller’s credit report, not the buyer’s.
  • They recommend thorough disclosures and strong documentation so sellers fully understand that the loan remains in their name until it is paid off.
  • They mention that some lenders evaluating the seller for future financing may accept a 12-month payment history and supporting documentation showing the property is being paid by another party.
  • To help reduce the visibility of ownership transfer, one speaker sometimes closes properties in a land trust, although they clarify this only marginally reduces due on sale risk.


Deal Sourcing, Analysis, and Negotiation

  • Typical subject to sellers often have little or no equity and are dealing with life situations such as divorce, health challenges, financial stress, or landlord fatigue.
  • Jun & Rich explain that many of these sellers would need to bring money to closing if they sold traditionally because commissions and fees would consume their limited equity.
  • Investors commonly source deals directly from distressed owners, through networking, or from wholesalers specializing in creative finance transactions.
  • Wholesalers typically secure the contract with the seller and then assign the deal to the investor in exchange for an assignment fee.
  • One speaker shares that he previously used newspaper ads promoting “I buy houses” but now relies primarily on Facebook wholesaler groups to find opportunities.
  • They stress the importance of proper underwriting, including verifying mortgage balances, confirming PITI payments, and validating realistic rent projections.
  • The “entry fee” is defined as the total upfront investment needed, including arrears, seller payments, wholesaler fees, repairs, and closing costs.
  • Investors are encouraged to negotiate aggressively with wholesalers and agents to lower fees and improve deal economics.
  • Closings should be handled by experienced title companies or attorneys familiar with creative finance and subject to transactions.
  • They strongly discourage informal closings and emphasize that experienced legal and title professionals help reduce future operational and legal issues.


Financial Modeling, Real-Life Examples, and Buy Box

  • Jun & Rich present an example of a property with a $220,000 loan balance, $1,300 monthly PITI, and $1,700 monthly rent, creating approximately $400 in monthly cash flow before improvements.
  • They clarify that true “zero money down” deals are rare because most deals still require capital for repairs, arrears, or closing costs.
  • One detailed example involves a property in Lewisville, Texas, valued at approximately $400,000 with an existing $350,000 mortgage at 4.125% interest.
  • The investor negotiates an effective $12,000 payout to the seller after accounting for repairs, deferred maintenance, and transaction costs.
  • Current carrying costs are around $2,600 per month including PMI, while the property currently generates approximately $2,700 per month through room rentals.
  • The strategy involves converting the property into a five-bedroom midterm rental expected to generate approximately $4,700 per month in rent.
  • Renovation costs are estimated at around $15,000, with closing costs around $5,000, bringing total project costs to approximately $32,000 including the seller payout.
  • The projected annual cash flow exceeds $25,000, resulting in an estimated cash-on-cash return near 78%.
  • The investor also expects to create approximately $50,000 in additional equity through improvements and market positioning.
  • They outline a preferred “buy box” that includes single-family homes in strong areas, 3 to 5 bedrooms, low repair requirements, low entry fees, interest rates between 2% and 5%, and at least $300 per month in projected cash flow.
  • One speaker notes that he is sometimes willing to acquire properties with negative equity if the monthly cash flow is strong and long-term appreciation potential exists.
  • The group emphasizes that time in the market and positive cash flow can eventually solve many temporary equity challenges.

Exit Strategies, Variations, and Learning Resources

  • Jun & Rich emphasize that long-term wealth in real estate is typically created by holding properties rather than flipping them.
  • They commonly use professional property managers, including for out-of-state investments, and sometimes use virtual assistants to help vet management companies.
  • Alternative operating strategies discussed include short-term rentals, midterm rentals, and room-by-room rentals, each offering different levels of complexity and profitability.
  • They mention partnerships with relocation and insurance-related housing agencies that place tenants needing temporary housing after events such as floods or fires.
  • Another advanced strategy discussed is “wrapping” the mortgage, where the investor creates a new seller-financed loan at a higher interest rate for a future buyer.
  • In a wrap structure, the investor earns the spread between the original low-interest mortgage and the higher-interest loan issued to the end buyer.
  • The investor effectively operates like a private lender while continuing to service the original mortgage.
  • Emergency exit strategies include refinancing, selling the property, or potentially returning the property to the seller if the agreement allows for it.
  • They stress the importance of protecting the seller’s credit and treating payment obligations with extreme seriousness.
  • As a recommended educational resource, they mention the book “Wealth Without Cash” by Pace Morby, published through BiggerPockets.
  • They also reference Robert Kiyosaki and his book “Rich Dad Poor Dad” as an early influence on their interest in real estate investing.
  • BiggerPockets is highlighted as a valuable resource for learning more about creative finance and subject to investing.

In conclusion, this session presents subject to investing as a creative way to acquire properties using existing low-rate mortgages while solving practical problems for motivated sellers. 


Rich Reister and Jun Kim explain how thoughtful underwriting, conservative cash flow assumptions, and proper legal documentation can create attractive returns with relatively low upfront capital.

 

They also make clear that subject to deals carry unique legal and ethical responsibilities, particularly around the due on sale clause and the seller’s credit profile. 

 

Overall, the session provides a practical framework for sourcing, analyzing, structuring, and operating subject to deals while emphasizing responsible execution and long-term investing discipline.

items.description:

  1. Building custom multi-unit STR properties in resort and high-demand locations
