files.key: uploads/content-archive/1774293669748-The 1 Build Luxury STRs & Tax Alpha Strategy Ted McCune Invest Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session, Ted McCune presents a detailed strategy for building and operating short-term rental (STR) properties that maximize both cash flow and tax advantages. 


The key ideas are organized into five main topics so readers can quickly understand the investment model, tax strategies, and practical execution steps.


Speaker Background and Overall Strategy

  • Ted McCune describes himself as a licensed real estate broker in California and Utah, as well as an investor, redeveloper, and builder focused on both short-term and long-term rentals.
  • He explains that he previously worked in corporate roles at Microsoft and Monster.com, eventually serving as a CEO and senior vice president based in Prague.
  • He shares that he produces and hosts a large annual New Year’s Eve event in Utah at the state capitol building, attracting around 1,000 attendees with professional lighting and DJ equipment.
  • He states that music is a major passion of his, that he plans to start a country band, and that he lives a largely location-independent lifestyle using various STRs as places to live and work.
  • He explains that his core real estate strategy is to build custom 2-4 unit homes that meet the 1% rule, generate approximately 12% annual returns, and create substantial tax savings through STR-focused tax strategies.


Short-Term Rental Model and Regulatory Considerations

  • Ted emphasizes that short-term rentals are highly sensitive to local regulations and that investors must actively study city and county STR rules.
  • He explains that STR markets can become saturated and that sudden regulatory changes, such as those in Las Vegas, can force owners to convert STRs into long-term rentals or sell at a loss.
  • He states that successful STR investing requires building relationships with mayors, city council members, planning staff, and zoning officials to understand permitting and zoning requirements.
  • He clarifies that investors cannot take a completely hands-off approach because STR investing requires ongoing involvement in guest experience, operations, and market conditions.
  • He notes that he strongly prefers areas with no HOA or weak architectural control committees because these organizations often restrict STR use or multi-unit configurations.
  • He explains that he targets jurisdictions where 1-4 units still qualify as single-family residential properties, allowing him to legally build multiple rentable units while maintaining a single-family appearance.
  • He mentions that many cities require STRs to be owner-occupied, and he structures his properties so he can legitimately qualify as an owner-occupant while renting other units within the same property.


Building and Designing STRs in High-Demand Resort Areas

  • Ted states that he prefers building STRs rather than buying existing ones because building allows him to control location, optimize layouts, and create forced equity.
  • He explains that he targets high-demand resort areas near national parks, lakes, and vacation destinations such as Zion National Park, Hurricane, Sedona, and Gatlinburg.
  • He emphasizes that investors should understand why people travel to an area and confirm that STR demand and occupancy remain strong throughout the year.
  • He describes using AI research tools to identify promising ZIP codes and regions where STR demand, occupancy, and nightly rates support his model.
  • He notes that he looks for quarter-acre or larger lots that can accommodate a large home with a walkout basement design.
  • He explains that each house is designed as three separate rentable units consisting of a main level, a casita with a separate entrance and kitchen, and a walkout basement unit with its own entrance and lockable separation.
  • He states that this setup allows him to host multiple groups simultaneously, significantly increasing revenue potential while remaining compliant with single-family zoning.
  • He mentions that he selects finishes and layouts designed specifically for resort travelers, including RV or boat parking, multiple bedrooms, and multiple bathrooms.
  • He adds that he standardizes furnishings and interior design across multiple homes to simplify operations and allow interchangeable listing photos.


Tax Strategy, Cost Segregation, and STR Loophole

  • Ted explains that cost segregation accelerates depreciation by separating building components into different depreciation schedules based on useful life.
  • He clarifies that under traditional rules, qualifying as a real estate professional generally requires meeting the 750-hour annual participation test and materially participating in real estate activities.
  • He states that current STR rules create a potential “short-term rental loophole,” where owners may not need full real estate professional status if the average guest stay is less than seven days and material participation requirements are met.
  • He explains that investors must carefully document average guest stay lengths and maintain supporting records in case of an audit.
  • He states that cost segregation specialists analyze building plans, invoices, or completed properties to classify assets such as furniture, landscaping, pools, and fixtures into shorter depreciation schedules.
  • He notes that assets with depreciation lives of 20 years or less can qualify for bonus depreciation, often representing roughly 20-25% of the total project cost.
  • He shares an example where a roughly $900,000 build includes approximately $675,000 of long-term building structure and about $125,000 allocated to furniture and furnishings, enabling substantial first-year depreciation deductions.
  • He explains that these deductions can offset active business income from e-commerce or Amazon operations, creating significant tax savings for high-income entrepreneurs.
  • He mentions strategically timing certificate of occupancy dates so depreciation benefits can be recognized in different tax years.
  • He emphasizes that this strategy is particularly useful for business owners seeking to reduce or defer taxes while building long-term real estate wealth.


Financing, Returns, Management, and Scaling

  • Ted explains that he often purchases land first, sometimes around $150,000 per lot, and waits to build until timing and cash flow align properly.
  • He notes that some lots appreciate substantially before construction even begins, sometimes increasing from approximately $150,000 to $250,000-$300,000 in value.
  • He states that one example property has an all-in cost of approximately $1.05 million, including land and construction, while retail value may reach approximately $1.4 million, creating built-in equity.
  • He describes a model where the three separate units rent independently, with projected combined revenue exceeding $11,000 per month at target occupancy rates of around 70-80%.
  • He explains that this structure helps him meet or exceed the 1% rule while targeting approximately 12% annual returns on invested capital.
  • He points out that he also drives direct bookings through his own website and social channels to reduce platform fees from Airbnb and VRBO.
  • He mentions that he uses virtual assistants in the Philippines to manage guest messaging, listings, and administrative tasks at low cost.
  • He explains that after construction and stabilization, he can refinance the property, extract 70-75% of appraised value, recover much of his invested capital, and still retain ownership and cash flow.
  • He states that while he sometimes prefers to own properties free and clear, refinancing also creates liquidity and may reduce taxable rental income.
  • He notes that some properties are held inside Roth IRA or 401(k) structures where rental income can grow tax-free, while others are held in LLCs optimized for STR operations and tax strategy.
  • He summarizes the overall strategy as “build, cost-seg, refinance, and repeat,” particularly in markets where he has strong local knowledge and operational systems.

In conclusion, this session presents a focused blueprint for using custom-built short-term rentals as both an income engine and a tax strategy, particularly for business owners with significant cash flow. 


Ted McCune demonstrates how careful market selection, multi-unit STR design, cost segregation, refinancing, and strategic timing can create strong returns while substantially reducing taxable income.


The session also highlights that successful STR investing requires more than simply buying properties.

It demands a deep understanding of local regulations, strong operational systems, disciplined financing, and thoughtful long-term planning. 

By combining these elements with tax-focused execution, investors can create scalable real estate portfolios that generate cash flow, appreciation, and meaningful tax advantages over time.

TOPICS: Momentum investing strategy using EMAs, sector selection, and disciplined entries/exits Portfolio construction, diversification across themes, and quarterly rebalancing process Algorithmic forex bot design, backtesting, and risk management for consistent returns

files.name: Algo Trading & Momentum Investing － Ashley Thompson － Invest Mastermind 2026
files.key: uploads/content-archive/1774293452446-Algo Trading and Momentum Investing Ashley Thompson Invest Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session, Ashley Thompson presents a practical overview of momentum investing in stocks and the use of algorithmic trading bots for forex. 


Participants learn how to structure systematic strategies that aim to outperform market indices while managing risk and limiting emotional decision-making.


Speaker Background and Objectives of the Session

  • Ashley Thompson explains that he has a background as a professional poker player from 2011 to 2014 before building and exiting a nine-figure Amazon business.
  • He shares that he later expanded into real estate, crypto, and stock investing, with a stronger focus on stocks and trading during 2024 and 2025.
  • He clarifies that the session is not financial advice and is based solely on his personal experience and investment approach.
  • He explains that the material is intended for investors who want to outperform the S&P 500 without spending excessive time managing investments.
  • He notes that the strategy is best suited for investors who can tolerate meaningful drawdowns, such as temporary declines of 15% or more.
  • He emphasizes that this approach is not ideal for highly risk-averse individuals, emotionally reactive investors, or people seeking guaranteed “get rich quick” opportunities.
  • He positions momentum investing as a strategy focused on capturing strong uptrends in bull markets rather than buying “cheap” value stocks that may underperform for long periods.


Momentum Investing Framework and Market Regimes

  • Ashley defines momentum investing as buying assets that consistently trend upward and continuing to hold them while momentum remains strong.
  • He explains that the strategy works best during bull markets and that investors should first determine whether the overall market is in a bullish or bearish regime.
  • He primarily uses exponential moving averages (EMAs), specifically the 50-day, 150-day, and 200-day EMAs.
  • He explains that in strong bull trends, price often respects the 50-day EMA and may occasionally retrace to the 150-day or 200-day EMAs during broader market pullbacks.
  • He states that he evaluates technical setups before fundamentals because strong company fundamentals alone do not guarantee a profitable stock chart.
  • He contrasts momentum stocks with traditional value stocks by showing that low price-to-earnings companies can still significantly underperform high-momentum names over time.
  • He explains that a bullish market phase is often confirmed when price breaks above rising EMAs, while bearish conditions are associated with price falling below key EMAs alongside lower highs and lower lows.
  • During bear markets, he prefers holding cash and waiting for technical confirmation before re-entering positions.


Stock Selection, Trade Setup, and Risk Management

  • Ashley describes using TradingView stock screeners to filter for U.S. stocks that match his technical criteria.
  • He sets a minimum market capitalization of approximately $200 million to avoid highly speculative micro-cap or meme stocks.
  • He looks for minimum daily trading volume of roughly 1 million shares and prefers cases where current trading volume exceeds the 10-day average.
  • He uses the Relative Strength Index (RSI), often targeting ranges between 40 and 70 to avoid extremely weak or heavily overbought setups.
  • He uses Finviz to apply additional filters such as earnings per share, gross margin, and net margin.
  • He uses StockCharts.com to analyze sector and industry strength, helping identify leading industries and emerging trends.
  • He organizes opportunities into color-coded watchlists: red for weak setups, yellow for risky or extended setups, and green for strong technical trends.
  • He prefers entering positions near the 50-day EMA because it often acts as support during bullish markets and offers attractive risk-reward opportunities.
  • He uses alerts within TradingView so he does not need to constantly monitor charts throughout the day.
  • He consistently uses stop losses, typically placing them below the most recent swing low after price confirms upward momentum.
  • He uses the 20-day EMA as a dynamic trailing exit reference in strong trends.
  • For more advanced setups, he occasionally uses lower time frames such as 15-minute charts to refine entries after liquidity sweeps or gap fills.
  • He emphasizes that disciplined, rule-based execution helps remove emotional decision-making and supports favorable risk-reward outcomes, often targeting returns several times greater than the initial risk.


Diversification, Rebalancing, and Behavioral Discipline

  • Ashley emphasizes diversification across industries such as metals and mining, semiconductors, software, aerospace and defense, robotics, AI, pharmaceuticals, and financials.
  • He notes that certain sectors, such as metals and mining, may act as hedges during periods when broader markets weaken.
  • He explains that smaller-cap stocks can deliver larger upside but also carry significantly higher volatility and downside risk.
  • He shares that during his first quarter using this framework, he held approximately 40 stocks and roughly matched broader market performance while learning from process mistakes.
  • In a later quarter, he reduced the portfolio to around 20 stocks and achieved approximately 50% returns over three months compared to roughly 10% for the S&P 500 and 15% for the Nasdaq.
  • He describes a quarterly research process where he spends several hours reviewing sectors, screening stocks, and building a watchlist of approximately 100 candidates.
  • Once positions are established, he spends roughly 90 minutes per week managing alerts, stop losses, entries, and exits.
  • When stopped out of positions, he usually leaves the cash unallocated until the next portfolio review rather than immediately forcing new trades.
  • He stresses that he does not become emotionally attached to any stock and instead rotates capital into the strongest technical setups available.
  • He warns against FOMO (fear of missing out) and explains that he avoids chasing stocks that have already moved too far too quickly.
  • He closely monitors macroeconomic factors such as FOMC meetings, inflation data, unemployment reports, tariffs, and regulatory announcements that may impact market volatility.
  • He notes that he is especially cautious during periods with major economic releases or significant political events that could trigger sharp market swings.


Algorithmic Forex Bot Strategy and Backtesting Approach

  • Ashley explains that he and a partner have spent approximately two and a half years building algorithmic forex trading bots.
  • He views forex as attractive because currency pairs are relatively stable, trade nearly continuously during the week, and allow access to significant leverage.
  • He explains that one strategy focuses on mean reversion, identifying large directional price moves followed by statistically likely retracements.
  • He uses Fibonacci retracement levels, particularly the 0.5 to 0.618 range, to identify potential reversal zones.
  • He combines Fibonacci analysis with RSI signals, treating RSI readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold.
  • He describes algorithmic rules such as entering short trades after overbought conditions or entering long trades after oversold pullbacks into specific retracement zones.
  • He notes that tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok can help non-programmers generate executable trading code.
  • He explains that the bots are backtested over multiple years using tools such as Flash Research to simulate historical performance.
  • He targets backtested strategies with approximately 3% to 4% average monthly returns, drawdowns around 10%, and no account liquidations during testing periods.
  • He shares historical live performance figures of approximately 35.3% return in 2023, 23.88% in 2024, and 28.82% in 2025, while stressing that past performance does not guarantee future results.
  • He highlights major risks including broker risk, offshore leverage exposure, and black swan events that can create extreme one-directional price movements.
  • He notes that highly volatile currency pairs, particularly some JPY crosses, often require smaller position sizing.
  • He explains that generating only 2% monthly returns may not justify the complexity and tax implications of active forex trading, which is why he targets approximately 4% monthly returns.
  • He mentions that they occasionally intervene manually during extreme market events, although lower-risk systems could potentially run with less oversight.

In conclusion, Ashley Thompson presents a structured and rule-based framework for momentum investing in equities alongside a complementary algorithmic approach to forex trading. 


The session consistently emphasizes disciplined risk management, systematic execution, diversification, and emotional control as the foundations for attempting to outperform broad market benchmarks over time.


The discussion also highlights the importance of adapting strategies to market conditions, using data-driven processes, and continuously refining systems through backtesting and real-world experience.

TOPICS:
  1. Designing a four-entity stack (Holding, Asset Brand, Management, Ops) to separate value from risk.
  2. Using contracts, loans, and licensing (“pipes”) to move money and assets between entities legitimately.

files.key: uploads/content-archive/1774292757778-Corporate Structure Daniel Meredith Invest Mastermind 2026.pdf

cliff_notes:
In this session, Daniel Meredith presents a framework for building multi-entity corporate structures that separate valuable assets from operational risk, particularly for e-commerce and real estate businesses. 


The discussion focuses on how to design a stack of companies so that value and cash move upward while liability and exposure remain isolated within lower-risk operational entities, all within legal and tax-compliant guardrails.


Conceptual Foundation: Working Geniuses and the Goal of Asset Protection

  • Daniel references the Working Geniuses framework as a favorite tool for understanding personalities and roles, noting that it has been implemented company-wide since around 2017.
  • He explains that the hiring process uses core values from EOS (Entrepreneurial Operating System), core competencies, and Working Geniuses as filters to ensure people are placed in the right roles and remain engaged.
  • He states that the goal of the session is to help operators understand the importance of separating assets from risk, especially after accumulating meaningful wealth or real assets.
  • Daniel clarifies that the session does not provide legal or financial advice and should be treated as a conceptual and strategic framework rather than professional counsel.
  • He explains that the structure is widely used in real estate and can also be adapted effectively for e-commerce and other industries.
  • He highlights two guiding ideas: once someone accumulates assets, others may try to take them, and businesses should be designed with contingency and protection structures in place from the beginning.


The Four-Entity Stack: Holding, Asset, Management, and Ops

  • Daniel outlines a four-layer structure consisting of a Holding Company, Asset Brand Company, Management Company, and Operations (Ops) Company.
  • The Holding Company retains excess cash, owns equity interests, and acts like an internal bank that lends funds to other entities.
  • He explains that the Holding Company can be structured as a C corporation, S corporation, LLC, or trust-owned entity depending on tax and estate planning goals.
  • The Asset Brand Company holds valuable intangible assets such as trademarks, licenses, intellectual property, product designs, and brand equity.
  • He notes that separating brand assets into a dedicated entity makes future brand or product-line sales cleaner because buyers can acquire the IP without touching cash-heavy or risk-heavy entities.
  • The Management Company employs staff, administers benefits such as health insurance and 401(k) plans, and charges management fees for services such as PPC management, operations oversight, and creative work.
  • Daniel explains that the Ops Company contains the day-to-day commercial risk, including Amazon seller accounts, inventory, supplier contracts, 3PL relationships, and customer-facing operations.
  • He emphasizes that the Ops Company is intentionally designed as the “risk bucket,” while the Holding and Asset entities serve as the “value buckets.”
  • He notes that some businesses can operate effectively with a simpler three-entity structure, but the four-entity model provides more flexibility for employment and management separation.


Money and Risk Flows: “Pipes,” Loans, and Liens

  • Daniel describes “pipes” as the legal agreements and contracts that allow money and value to move between entities in a legitimate and documented way.
  • He explains that management fees flow from the Ops Company to the Management Company in exchange for real operational services.
  • He states that royalty and licensing payments flow from the Ops Company to the Asset Brand Company for the use of trademarks, intellectual property, and brand assets.
  • He explains that loans primarily flow from the Holding Company to the Ops Company at commercially reasonable interest rates, often referencing the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR) as a guideline.
  • Daniel notes that the Holding Company functions like an internal bank that finances inventory and working capital needs while collecting interest income.
  • He explains that entities can file UCC-1 financing statements to create liens on assets, allowing upper entities to maintain secured positions ahead of outside unsecured creditors.
  • He emphasizes that in a properly structured system, the Ops Company carries the liability while most meaningful assets are leased, licensed, or financed from upper entities.
  • He explains that if the Ops Company experiences litigation or operational failure, creditors may find that the company has limited net value because assets and cash are already tied to higher entities through documented obligations.
  • He stresses that all transfers and agreements must reflect real business activity, legitimate services, and commercially reasonable arrangements rather than artificial paper transactions.


Legal, Tax, and Compliance Guardrails

  • Daniel repeatedly states that the structure is not intended as a tax loophole or tax evasion strategy, but rather as a way to balance taxes while separating value from operational risk.
  • He stresses that these structures must be established early, long before any legal dispute or financial distress arises.
  • He explains that courts examine “adequate capitalization,” meaning the Ops Company must maintain enough capital to appear legitimate and operationally viable.
  • He highlights the importance of separate bank accounts, bookkeeping, contracts, approvals, and corporate records for each entity.
  • Daniel notes that intercompany pricing must remain commercially reasonable and at arm’s length rather than artificially low or symbolic.
  • He explains that intercompany loans should follow AFR guidelines and be documented with proper notes and repayment structures.
  • He shares a personal bankruptcy experience in which a trustee reviewed the structure and ultimately confirmed that properly protected assets remained shielded.
  • He discusses how C corporations operate as separate taxpayers, which can help shield individuals from certain tax liabilities associated with failed companies or forgiven debts.
  • Daniel contrasts this with LLCs and S corporations, where pass-through taxation can expose owners to tax obligations tied to debt cancellations or operational losses.
  • He notes that operational entities should generally be formed in the states where employees and operations exist, while Holding and Asset entities may be located in more tax-efficient jurisdictions.
  • He introduces the idea of eventually placing the Holding Company into an irrevocable insurance trust for additional long-term asset protection and estate planning.


Practical Applications, Examples, and Implementation Guidance

  • Daniel uses Amazon-based businesses as the primary example, with the Ops Company holding Seller Central accounts, inventory, and supplier relationships while intellectual property and excess cash are moved into upper entities.
  • He explains that in real estate, similar principles apply by placing separate properties into individual entities to isolate liability between assets.
  • He notes that this approach is often called “ring fencing” or “asset partitioning.”
  • He references companies such as Pepsi and Pepsi Bottling as examples of layered corporate structures that separate intellectual property, operations, and ownership.
  • Daniel also references Costco as an example of operational segmentation, where separate entities can isolate liability between locations.
  • He explains that layered structures are especially useful in partnerships because partners can be attached to specific entities rather than owning every layer equally.
  • He shares that he personally prefers working as a W-2 employee of the Management Company, drawing salary and benefits while leaving investment capital inside the upper entities.
  • He notes that, based on prior IRS positions, executive compensation can reach several million dollars annually before attracting scrutiny around classification as salary versus distributions.
  • Daniel explains that owners who want to “live large” typically do so through W-2 compensation rather than dividend structures that may trigger additional taxation.
  • He reiterates a strong preference for C corporations because of liability separation and current corporate tax treatment advantages.
  • He highlights that modern AI tools such as ChatGPT can reduce administrative work by assisting with agreements, documentation, and corporate paperwork.
  • He notes that the team is currently restructuring the Holding Company into an irrevocable insurance trust as part of a longer-term estate planning strategy.

In conclusion, Daniel Meredith presents a comprehensive framework for structuring businesses so that valuable assets remain protected while operational risk stays isolated in lower-level entities. 


The model uses Holding, Asset, Management, and Ops entities connected through documented agreements such as loans, management fees, and licensing arrangements to shift value upward while containing liability.


The session emphasizes that proper implementation requires real business purpose, separate accounting and operations, adequate capitalization, and long-term planning. 


By combining strong legal and accounting guardrails with thoughtful tax and estate planning, founders can create structures that improve resilience against lawsuits, operational failures, and partnership disputes while preserving long-term wealth inside the business ecosystem.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Trevor Morris discusses a strategy for using physical precious metals to achieve both wealth preservation and liquidity. 

The session explores how business owners can hold metals as hard assets while still accessing capital through a specialized line of credit.


Strategic Purpose of Holding Precious Metals

  • Trevor explains that the core strategy is to own physical precious metals as a long-term store of value while maintaining access to liquidity.
  • He notes that cash loses purchasing power over time, so the goal is to preserve and grow wealth by converting excess cash into hard assets like gold and silver.
  • He emphasizes that physical metals act as a hedge against inflation and monetary risk because they are not dependent on a single corporation or government.
  • Trevor states that this approach is particularly aimed at business owners and investors generating at least seven figures in revenue, since they typically have excess capital available to allocate into metals.
  • He clarifies that the intent is wealth preservation and strategic flexibility, not speculation or creating a new source of income.


Mechanics of the Metals Line of Credit (“Mee Lock”)

  • Trevor describes how the metals are stored in a secure third-party vault and used as collateral to establish a metals line of credit, referred to as a “Mee Lock.”
  • He explains that Money Metals Exchange stores the metals and provides the line of credit.
  • He states that an owner can typically borrow up to 75% of the metals’ value, but he recommends limiting borrowing to around 50% to reduce the risk of liquidation during market downturns.
  • He notes that the loan is interest-only, currently at single-digit interest rates based on information available from the provider.
  • He adds that there are no credit checks, only a small application fee, no prepayment penalties, and generally a fast funding timeline of about two to three days.
  • He clarifies that as long as the collateral remains sufficient, the metals are not sold or liquidated, and the owner continues to benefit from any price appreciation.


Practical Use Cases, Tax Positioning, and Business Structuring

  • Trevor explains that the line of credit can provide quick capital for business cash flow, real estate purchases, equipment, or other investments without selling the metals.
  • He shares that he personally holds six figures’ worth of metals and is considering using this structure to help fund a warehouse and equipment for his business.
  • He states that in his setup, his Amazon business LLC owns the metals, so the metals appear as assets on the company balance sheet.
  • He explains that when the business purchases metals, it is acquiring assets rather than generating taxable income, which can support long-term tax planning.
  • He notes that borrowed money is generally not taxed as income, so using a loan against metals to acquire other assets can defer taxable events.
  • He compares this approach to how he handles crypto investments within his Amazon business, where the business buys and holds crypto as a long-term asset and only recognizes capital gains tax when assets are sold.
  • Another participant suggests that if metals are treated as inventory, certain tax rules may allow immediate deductions for inventory purchases, though this could create larger future tax obligations.
  • Trevor repeatedly stresses that this structure is intended to fund or acquire productive assets and should not be used to support ongoing personal spending or lifestyle expenses.


Physical Metals vs. Paper Metals (ETFs and Brokerage Structures)

  • A participant asks whether there is an advantage to holding physical metals instead of purchasing an ETF in a brokerage account and borrowing against it through margin.
  • Trevor responds that one concern with ETFs is that many investors may effectively be tied to the same underlying ounce of metal, creating counterparty and systemic risk.
  • He explains that with an ETF, the investor owns a financial claim rather than the actual metal, so structural or liquidity issues could negatively impact investors.
  • He notes that ETF providers can issue additional shares while the underlying supply of metal remains limited, potentially distancing investors from direct ownership.
  • He emphasizes that holding physical metals in an allocated and segregated account provides direct ownership and greater control, similar to the principle often referenced in crypto investing: “not your keys, not your crypto.”
  • In response to a question about historical failures, he states that he is not aware of major collapses that completely wiped out regulated metals holders, but he still prefers direct ownership for transparency and control.
  • He also mentions that in some countries, such as Japan, physical silver can trade at higher premiums than in the United States, creating theoretical geographic arbitrage opportunities, although he notes that this is operationally complex.


Logistics, Security, and Providers

  • Trevor explains that Money Metals Exchange handles storage and the line of credit, while he often purchases metals from SD Bullion because of more competitive pricing once annual purchase thresholds are reached.
  • He states that after purchasing around $20,000 annually from SD Bullion, buyers may qualify for VIP pricing with tighter spreads closer to spot value.
  • He describes the process where metals purchased from SD Bullion can be shipped directly to the vault facility provided by Money Metals.
  • He notes that Money Metals provides confirmation once the metals arrive and that the metals are stored in segregated form, meaning each client’s holdings are separately identified.
  • He explains that the vault is audited quarterly and that clients can request verification of their holdings.
  • He adds that clients can visit the facility in Idaho to inspect their metals and verify serial numbers or quantities against purchase records.
  • He mentions that the facility is a high-security vault insured through a major insurer such as Lloyd’s of London.
  • He confirms that clients can request physical delivery or arrange pickup of their metals at any time, although doing so removes the metals from the collateral pool supporting the line of credit.

In conclusion, this session explores a framework for combining the stability of physical precious metals with the flexibility of a revolving line of credit.

Trevor Morris positions this strategy as a way for business owners to preserve wealth in hard assets while still being able to deploy capital quickly into new opportunities.


Overall, the discussion presents physical metals as a foundational wealth-preservation tool that can also support strategic liquidity when paired with a metals-backed line of credit. 


The session highlights how providers like Money Metals and SD Bullion, combined with disciplined use of leverage and thoughtful tax structuring, can turn metals from passive holdings into a flexible part of a long-term financial strategy.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Khalid Abdulla discusses how he leverages real estate investing to reduce taxes generated from his Amazon business. 


The conversation also explores different real estate markets, property types, financing models, and tax strategies used to build a long-term portfolio focused on wealth preservation and future family benefit.

Personal Background and Motivation for Real Estate

  • Khalid Abdulla explains that he started an Amazon business about 12 years ago to help cover expenses related to raising his autistic son because his regular job income was not sufficient.
  • He describes growing up in a household where his father repeatedly struggled in business, which initially led him to believe he would never become a business owner himself.
  • Khalid now operates multiple Amazon brands along with a recruitment agency, which together generate substantial income and a significant tax burden.
  • After facing a large tax bill, he decided that minimizing taxes would become a major financial priority and turned to real estate as a primary strategy.
  • He explains that he views his real estate portfolio as a long-term asset base intended mainly for his children and future generations rather than for short-term lifestyle upgrades.
  • Khalid admits that he enjoys spending money and uses real estate investing as a disciplined way to redirect excess cash into productive and appreciating assets instead of discretionary purchases.


Real Estate Acquisition Strategy, Financing, and Markets

  • Khalid describes a strategy focused on buying smaller properties under $500,000, typically duplexes and fourplexes, using approximately 25% down payments.
  • He aims to consistently deploy capital by purchasing roughly one property every one to two months, as long as the property at least breaks even financially.
  • He emphasizes that his current goal is not maximizing short-term cash flow, but steadily building a portfolio that compounds in value over time.
  • Khalid explains that he uses DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) loans, where lenders primarily evaluate the property’s cash flow rather than the borrower’s personal income.
  • He notes that DSCR financing allows relatively quick and simple closings and shares an example of completing a transaction in about two weeks.
  • The discussion highlights that many of the properties he buys are around 15 to 20 years old, meaning major systems such as HVAC units and roofs may be nearing replacement.
  • Khalid shares that he is actively investing in Waco, Texas, because Baylor University creates stable student housing demand and consistent occupancy.
  • Participants discuss how Texas offers abundant land and ongoing new construction, which increases competition and can pressure multifamily margins.
  • Florida is discussed as a market with strong demand and limited land availability, though rising insurance and flood insurance costs reduce profitability.
  • Tennessee and Georgia are also mentioned as additional markets with mixed experiences depending on the specific submarket.
  • Khalid also discusses investing in Dubai through “off-plan” properties, where buyers make staged payments directly to developers over multiple years instead of using traditional mortgages.
  • He explains that these Dubai investments may require an initial payment of around 10% followed by scheduled payments over four or more years, sometimes continuing after project completion.
  • Khalid notes that these staged payments help him consistently channel excess cash into appreciating assets rather than lifestyle spending.

Tax Optimization, Cost Segregation, and Real Estate Professional Status

  • Khalid clearly states that his primary objective in real estate investing is to reduce or eliminate taxes generated from his Amazon and business income.
  • He shares that his CPA encouraged him to purchase real estate rather than repeatedly buying luxury vehicles solely for tax write-offs.
  • The group discusses cost segregation studies, which accelerate depreciation by separating property components such as HVAC systems, roofing, and improvements into shorter depreciation schedules.
  • One participant explains that on a $500,000 property, a cost segregation study could potentially generate approximately $100,000 in first-year depreciation deductions.
  • Participants clarify that accelerated depreciation can offset active or non-passive income when structured correctly, making it especially valuable for high-income entrepreneurs.
  • Khalid plans to replace aging HVAC systems and possibly roofs to improve depreciation opportunities and maximize tax benefits.
  • The conversation covers “real estate professional status” (REP), which generally requires at least 750 hours of material participation in qualifying real estate activities.
  • Khalid plans to acquire Airbnb and short-term rental properties to help qualify for REP treatment and convert more real estate losses into deductions against active income.
  • Participants explain that short-term rentals with average guest stays of seven days or less may qualify for more favorable non-passive treatment under current rules.
  • Khalid also mentions exploring the possibility of purchasing losses or participating in structures that could offset additional profits, though he notes he still needs further CPA guidance.
  • A participant clarifies that investors can still benefit from cost segregation even without REP status, though the deductibility treatment changes depending on whether losses are classified as passive or non-passive.

Market Selection, Asset Types, and Airbnb vs. Other Strategies

  • Khalid explains that he prefers duplexes and fourplexes over single-family homes because he believes small multifamily properties provide stronger portfolio growth and more resilient income streams.
  • The group notes that many investors begin with single-family rentals because they are easier to rent and vacancies may have less impact on total portfolio income.
  • One participant explains that larger multifamily properties eventually benefit from economies of scale that allow more efficient operations and on-site management.
  • The discussion highlights that Texas multifamily properties face significant competition and occasional oversupply because of fewer restrictions on new construction.
  • Florida is described as benefiting from strong migration and limited land supply, though insurance costs remain a major concern.
  • Tennessee and Georgia are briefly discussed as markets with varying levels of opportunity depending on location and economic trends.
  • Participants discuss trailer parks and manufactured housing communities as a specialized but potentially attractive asset class with strong returns and less operational intensity than some value-add multifamily projects.
  • Khalid admits to experiencing “shiny object syndrome,” recognizing that he is tempted by multiple asset classes such as trailer parks and self-storage facilities.
  • The group debates self-storage investing, with some participants believing the sector has become oversaturated because of rapid development and investor interest.
  • Airbnb and short-term rentals are discussed as still viable in select markets, though many areas have become saturated and increasingly expensive to operate.
  • One participant explains that some Airbnb properties maintain near-constant occupancy while others are eventually converted back to long-term rentals because of inconsistent short-term performance.
  • The discussion highlights that many investors entered Airbnb without carefully evaluating location quality or long-term demand, leading to oversupply in some markets.

Operations, Management, AI Usage, and Passive Investing Options

  • Khalid shares that he uses AI extensively for underwriting deals, researching markets, and evaluating occupancy rates, rental trends, and ZIP code-level performance data.
  • He describes using a “shotgun approach” when sourcing lenders by contacting many lenders through local Facebook communities, gathering dozens of quotes, and narrowing down to the strongest options.
  • Khalid emphasizes the importance of working with reliable lenders and service providers who understand investor needs and can close deals efficiently.
  • The group stresses the value of building strong local teams that include property managers, maintenance professionals, brokers, and trusted local contacts.
  • Khalid explains that he currently uses a property management company for his Texas portfolio and may eventually hire dedicated local staff as the portfolio grows.
  • He also plans to build a virtual assistant team to manage administrative and operational tasks related to his properties.
  • Participants discuss legal structures, explaining that properties can be held in separate LLCs while still flowing through to personal tax returns depending on entity setup.
  • The conversation highlights that multifamily investing involves significant operational responsibilities, including maintenance, renovations, evictions, and tenant management.
  • Passive investment opportunities such as multifamily syndications are discussed as alternatives for investors seeking real estate exposure and potential tax advantages with less day-to-day involvement.
  • One participant advises that passive investors should seek syndication sponsors with at least 20 to 25 years of experience and a track record of operating through multiple market cycles.
  • The group notes that some recent multifamily syndications have struggled or faced capital calls, reinforcing the importance of conservative underwriting and sponsor quality.

In conclusion, this session focuses on how Khalid Abdulla uses real estate investing as a strategic tool to reduce taxes, preserve wealth, and build long-term assets for his family. 


The discussion covers acquisition strategies, market selection, tax optimization techniques such as cost segregation and real estate professional status, and operational considerations ranging from active multifamily ownership to passive syndication investing.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Joel Gottehrer presents a framework for building long-term, tax-efficient wealth using a “buy, borrow, die” strategy. 

The discussion centers on leveraging appreciating assets, margin loans, and real estate tax advantages to minimize taxes while growing net worth over time.


Joel’s Background and Motivation

  • Joel Gottehrer is an e-commerce entrepreneur who is also involved in real estate, private loans, and investments in private businesses.
  • He explains that paying about one million dollars in taxes in the previous year became a turning point that motivated him to significantly increase his financial literacy.
  • He describes how his e-commerce business started as a side project that gradually grew without an initial grand plan or deep understanding of wealth building.
  • He shares that he enjoys basketball, has undergone two ACL surgeries, and installed a basketball hoop in his warehouse so he can shoot every morning before work.
  • He emphasizes that his current focus is systemizing his business to create more freedom while building long-term wealth and legally minimizing taxes.


Core Concept: “Buy, Borrow, Die” and Tax-Efficient Wealth

  • Joel introduces the “buy, borrow, die” model as a strategy wealthy individuals use to access cash without selling assets or triggering taxable events.
  • The strategy focuses on acquiring appreciating and cash-flowing assets such as stocks and real estate, then borrowing against those assets instead of liquidating them.
  • He explains that this approach is especially relevant for founders, operators, and investors with significant tax liabilities.
  • He stresses that the strategy works best for people who think long term, are patient, and are comfortable using leverage responsibly.
  • He clarifies that taxes are generally triggered when assets are sold or gains are realized, not simply when assets increase in value.


Use of M1 Finance and Margin Loans

  • Joel explains that he uses M1 Finance because it allows him to create “pies” of stocks with target allocations and automated rebalancing.
  • He describes how M1 automatically allocates new investments toward positions that fall below their target percentages, helping maintain desired portfolio weightings.
  • He states that he invested about one million dollars into his M1 portfolio and then borrowed approximately 30% of its value, or about $300,000, through a margin loan at roughly 4% interest.
  • He notes that margin loan proceeds are not considered taxable income, allowing him to access liquidity while his portfolio continues appreciating.
  • He shares that he uses borrowed funds to acquire additional investments, increasing his overall market exposure.
  • He explains that he intentionally limits borrowing to around 30% of portfolio value because historical drawdowns in his selected holdings rarely exceed that level, helping reduce margin call risk.
  • He mentions that M1’s margin rates are lower than some competitors, such as Charles Schwab, and that larger account holders may be able to negotiate better terms.


Investment Approach, Risk Management, and Life Insurance Integration

  • Joel states that his portfolio is concentrated in large-cap technology and established companies such as Microsoft, Apple, Tesla, Meta, and Google, along with some allocations to gold and silver as hedges.
  • He clarifies that his goal is not to chase speculative investments, but instead to hold high-quality businesses that he believes will remain strong long term.
  • He mentions that he continuously auto-invests into his M1 portfolio on a weekly basis to steadily grow his holdings.
  • He explains that he does not intend to repay margin loans during his lifetime and instead plans to maintain and roll them forward as part of a long-term wealth strategy.
  • He describes how an indexed universal life (IUL) policy or similar insurance structure can eventually be used to repay loans and obligations through the death benefit.
  • He highlights that heirs can benefit from a step-up in basis upon inheritance, resetting the cost basis of assets to current market value.
  • He explains that this combination of appreciating assets, leverage, and life insurance mirrors how many wealthy individuals preserve and transfer wealth across generations while minimizing taxes.


Real Estate, Tax Deductions, and Overall Tax Planning

  • Joel explains that he complements his stock strategy with real estate investments, particularly trailer parks, which he says can generate substantial tax deductions.
  • He states that these deductions help offset profits from his e-commerce business and reduce his overall tax burden.
  • He mentions that he uses LLCs and an S corporation structure to organize his business entities and manage cash flow.
  • He explains that his combination of entity structuring and real estate deductions significantly lowers his projected tax liability.
  • He states that his long-term goal is to grow his investment portfolio to the point where it can fund future investments and business operations without needing to sell appreciated assets.
  • He acknowledges questions about possible future legal or policy changes related to step-up in basis and other tax strategies, noting that these policies could evolve over time.


In conclusion, this session presents Joel Gottehrer’s approach to building long-term, tax-efficient wealth through a “buy, borrow, die” framework. 


By combining appreciating assets, margin loans, life insurance strategies, and real estate tax advantages, he outlines a system designed to compound wealth, improve liquidity, and reduce realized taxes over time while preserving capital for future generations.

cliff_notes:
In this session, Guido Reyes presents a practitioner-level overview of crypto market behavior, what worked during 2025, and how he is positioning for 2026. 


The discussion covers market cycles, trading psychology, self-custody, DeFi infrastructure, and practical strategies for navigating both bull and bear markets.


2025 Crypto Market Recap and 2026 Outlook

  • Guido explains that the late-2024 U.S. election results and the inauguration of President Trump helped reignite bullish sentiment across crypto markets entering 2025.
  • He notes that the launch of Trump’s meme coin in January 2025 coincided with peak meme-coin enthusiasm and marked an early local market top.
  • He describes how the Bybit exchange hack and subsequent tariff announcements triggered a sharp correction that ultimately became one of the strongest buying opportunities of the year.
  • He highlights that total crypto market capitalization surpassed $4 trillion for the first time, while Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP all reached new all-time highs.
  • He explains that perpetual decentralized exchanges (perp DEXs), particularly HyperLiquid, emerged as major winners in 2025 and became central platforms for leveraged and derivatives trading.
  • He references a major liquidation event on October 10, 2025, which reportedly erased approximately $19 billion due largely to excessive leverage in perpetual futures markets.
  • He observes that the market topped amid distraction and apathy rather than broad retail euphoria, with many retail traders heavily losing money through meme coins and leveraged trading.
  • He points out that Bitcoin dominance continued trending upward from late 2022 onward and argues that a true broad altcoin season has not occurred since roughly 2021–2022.
  • He notes that stablecoin market capitalization and dominance kept increasing throughout the cycle, signaling both broader adoption and a more defensive “risk-off” market posture.
  • Guido states that 2026 appears to resemble the early stages of a bear market similar to 2019, with likely counter-trend rallies but an expectation of lower highs overall.
  • He believes a potential market bottom could form around May or June 2026 if the traditional four-year crypto cycle continues to hold.


Investment Philosophy, Risk Management, and Lessons Learned

  • Guido describes himself as an early crypto participant who began buying Bitcoin in 2012 and later mined both Bitcoin and Ethereum.
  • He explains that his broader philosophy centers on financial sovereignty and maintaining direct control over assets rather than relying entirely on banks or custodial institutions.
  • He repeatedly emphasizes the principle “not your keys, not your crypto,” warning that assets held on centralized exchanges technically remain under third-party control.
  • He shares that some of his largest losses in 2025 came from leveraged trading and notes that even moderate leverage such as 3x can create major emotional and financial stress.
  • He strongly advises beginners to avoid leverage and meme-coin speculation because those areas produce the largest drawdowns and psychological volatility.
  • He explains that he combines multiple inputs before entering trades, including price action, market sentiment, narrative strength, technical indicators, and social “mind share.”
  • He defines “mind share” as the level of attention and discussion concentrated around a project among influential traders, communities, and key opinion leaders.
  • He encourages participants to remain active in crypto during downturns rather than leaving the market entirely because opportunities continue to emerge in selective sectors and narratives.
  • He stresses the importance of maintaining clear rules for entries, exits, position sizing, and risk tolerance to avoid giving back gains during volatile periods.
  • He advises newer investors to focus primarily on major assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum and to prioritize stablecoin yield strategies over speculative low-cap altcoins.


Exchanges, On-Ramps, and On-Chain Trading Infrastructure

  • Guido explains that centralized exchanges such as Kraken, Gemini Active Trader, and Coinbase serve as primary fiat on-ramps into crypto markets.
  • He recommends opening and fully verifying multiple exchange accounts well before a major bull cycle so withdrawal limits and account permissions are already established.
  • He notes that funding delays and withdrawal holds can prevent traders from reacting quickly during major market moves, making pre-positioned capital a strategic advantage.
  • He suggests keeping some funds on Ethereum and some on Solana because many opportunities, meme narratives, and airdrops emerge first on those ecosystems.
  • He clarifies that centralized exchanges are custodial platforms, while decentralized exchanges such as Uniswap allow users to trade directly from personal wallets.
  • He states that Uniswap is his default decentralized exchange for most swaps because of its liquidity and ease of execution across Ethereum-compatible chains.
  • He introduces Cow Swap as a preferred option for larger trades because of its MEV protection and improved trade execution.
  • He notes that advanced users can earn yield by providing liquidity to decentralized exchanges, though impermanent loss and operational complexity make this strategy riskier.
  • He highlights the growing role of cross-chain “intent” protocols that simplify movement between blockchains without manually bridging assets.


Self-Custody, Wallet Security, and Private Key Management

  • Guido strongly recommends that every crypto participant learn how private keys and seed phrases work because they are fundamental to true ownership.
  • He explains that seed phrases typically contain either 12 or 24 words and recommends 24-word phrases for larger holdings due to increased security.
  • He describes cold storage as the safest place for long-term holdings because the assets remain offline and disconnected from internet exposure.
  • He contrasts cold storage with hot wallets, which are browser-based or mobile wallets intended for active trading, DeFi participation, and smaller speculative allocations.
  • He mentions GridSeed and Ledger hardware wallets as examples of secure hardware devices used for offline key storage and transaction signing.
  • He explains that combining a hardware wallet with a browser wallet improves security because transactions must be physically confirmed on the device.
  • He recommends splitting a 24-word seed phrase into two separate 12-word sections stored in different secure locations so that no single person or location contains the entire key.
  • He advises traders to treat hot-wallet balances as acceptable-risk capital while storing the majority of long-term wealth in rarely accessed cold-storage wallets.
  • He recommends regularly moving profits from active trading wallets into long-term cold storage to reduce overtrading and support long-term wealth accumulation.
  • He also notes that certain on-chain lending systems allow users to borrow against Bitcoin or other assets without triggering taxable sales.


Research Tools, DeFi Platforms, and Stablecoin Yield Strategies

  • Guido introduces CoinGecko as his preferred market-data platform for checking token prices, liquidity, trading pairs, and exchange listings.
  • He explains that CoinGecko’s market listings help traders avoid fraudulent links or illiquid markets by identifying where assets trade most actively.
  • He presents DeFi Llama as a key analytics platform for monitoring total value locked (TVL), protocol growth, and capital flows across chains.
  • He notes that DeFi Llama reinforces Ethereum’s continued dominance in decentralized finance by showing the concentration of TVL within the Ethereum ecosystem.
  • He references additional analytics tools including DappRadar, DexScreener, Dune, DeBank, and TradingView for specialized research, wallet analysis, and technical charting.
  • He identifies Aave as his preferred “blue-chip” DeFi lending platform because of its longevity, liquidity, and institutional-level reputation.
  • He explains that users can deposit stablecoins such as USDC and PayPal USD into Aave to earn yields that frequently exceed traditional savings or treasury returns.
  • He notes that under certain market conditions, users may earn more on stablecoin deposits than they pay on borrowing costs, enabling leveraged yield strategies.
  • He mentions Morpho as another lending platform offering potentially higher yields but with greater relative risk than Aave.
  • He highlights Worldcoin as an ecosystem where stablecoin yields can be especially attractive for verified users.
  • He explains that he prefers farming stablecoin yields and immediately selling Worldcoin reward tokens into more stable assets such as Bitcoin or euro stablecoins rather than speculating on Worldcoin itself.
  • He also mentions an upcoming Aave mobile app that may offer yields approaching 9% APY on USDC with additional boosts tied to identity verification and referrals.


Example Trades and Narrative-Driven Opportunities

  • Guido identifies Ethereum as the strongest risk-adjusted major crypto trade of 2025, appreciating roughly 257% from the April lows to the August highs.
  • He compares Ethereum’s performance to Solana, which gained approximately 164%, and Bitcoin, which rose roughly 70% from its lows.
  • He concludes that Ethereum offered the best balance of upside potential and relative safety among major cryptocurrencies during the cycle.
  • He highlights HyperLiquid as one of the most successful projects of the year due to its massive airdrop distribution and strong ecosystem growth.
  • He explains that he entered HyperLiquid based on strong fundamentals, growing mind share, and the launch of its dedicated chain, ultimately realizing gains of roughly 300%.
  • He recounts entering Trump Coin near $6 shortly after launch and exiting the next day with gains of approximately 516%.
  • He describes a successful Zcash trade driven by renewed interest in privacy coins, the announcement of a Grayscale trust, and promotion by influential figures such as Naval Ravikant.
  • He notes that Zcash’s historical highs near $1,000 reinforced his confidence in the trade’s upside potential.
  • He explains that he entered Zcash at around $150 and exited just below $700, generating gains of approximately 302%.
  • He reiterates that his strongest trades typically occur when technical strength, narrative

In conclusion, this session provides a practical and experience-driven framework for navigating crypto market cycles, managing risk, and identifying narrative-driven opportunities.

Guido consistently emphasizes disciplined strategy design, self-custody, and selective participation in high-quality ecosystems as the foundation for sustainable long-term success in crypto markets.
