cliff_notes:
In this session the APAC Chapter members with Dorian Gorski, discuss both personal life updates and a deep dive into Amazon listing optimization, click-through rate (CTR), and conversion rate optimization (CRO). 

 

The call centers around how to systematically improve product images, copy, and testing processes, using both checklists and AI-driven tools to generate and validate hypotheses. 

 

Introduction of Dorian and His Expertise
  • Jonathan introduces Dorian Gorski to the group as an expert who “lives and breathes click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate optimization (CRO),” especially for Amazon listing images and detail pages.
  • Jonathan explains that Dorian works on Amazon product images, detail pages, and A+ content to make sure listings can win the click in search results and then convert visitors into customers.
  • Jonathan references a previous session with Sean Chow, who talks about preparing listings and doing the work before launching a product, and he positions Dorian’s work as strongly aligned with that philosophy.
  • He describes an example where he spontaneously shows Dorian one of his images, and Dorian immediately comes up with new angles and ideas that Jonathan has not thought about.
  • Jonathan emphasizes that image optimization and conversion-focused listing work have become one of the “80/20” levers of Amazon success, meaning a small number of critical inputs that drive the majority of results.
  • Dorian introduces himself and says he has been in the creative and e‑commerce industry for about 13 years, running a creative agency that more recently focuses heavily on conversion and optimization.
  • He explains that he works mainly with seven- and eight-figure brands, helping them develop click-through and conversion-increasing workflows across their product catalogs.
  • Dorian states that his role is to analyze brands and product catalogs, generate data-driven hypotheses, and build a pipeline of tests that can span several months to a year.
  • He notes that everyone in the industry agrees that testing is important, but many sellers struggle with what to test and how to structure those tests.
  • Dorian highlights that his company, Keplo, works with known brands and has produced strong ROI by systematically improving image assets and listing structure.
  • He mentions that Keplo runs a Conversion Club, provides software tools, and supports clients in creative content production such as main images, listing images, and A+ content.
  • Dorian underscores that optimizing conversion is fundamentally different from optimizing things like PPC, because conversion involves subjective visual and behavioral factors rather than just manipulating numbers in a dashboard.

 

Dorian’s Listing Optimization Framework and Checklist
Second Scannability Rule
  • Dorian introduces his “20-second scannability rule” as a key principle for listing images.
  • He explains that in real user behavior, customers scroll quickly through images and do not read everything in detail.
  • The rule states that within 20 seconds of scrolling through the image gallery, a shopper should understand the main benefits of the product.
  • He demonstrates this by quickly flipping through a pregnancy journal listing and noting that, at a glance, it appears to be a standard product without clearly differentiated benefits.
  • Dorian emphasizes that if a shopper cannot quickly understand why this product is special or what problems it solves, the listing loses many potential buyers.

 

Front-Loading Benefits in Early Gallery Images
  • Dorian explains that the most important benefits must be front-loaded into the first few gallery images (usually images 2–4).
  • He states that many shoppers only look at image 2 and image 3, then decide quickly whether to stay or leave.
  • Using the pregnancy journal example, he points out that some benefits like “gender neutral design” or “protective hard cover” exist, but they are not communicated strongly or clearly in the early images.
  • He notes that the differentiation of the product is not obvious, which limits the impact of the first impression.

 

“Show Me, Don’t Tell Me”
  • Dorian stresses the principle “show me, don’t tell me” as a centerpiece of CRO for images.
  • He explains that benefits should be visualized, not just written as text; customers should see what “waterproof,” “no bleed,” or “protective” means in practice.
  • As an example, he says that instead of just saying “waterproof,” an image should visually depict water droplets bouncing off the surface.
  • For “thick paper” or “no bleed-through,” he suggests showing a side angle of stacked pages or a pen writing on a page without ink bleeding through.
  • He notes that in the pregnancy journal listing, concepts like “gender neutral design” and “protective hard cover” are mentioned but not clearly illustrated, which forces the customer to interpret vague text rather than instantly understand.

 

Typography and Legibility
  • Dorian emphasizes that typography and legibility directly affect conversions because shoppers skim rather than read deeply.
  • He states that texts should be easily readable, with an appropriate font size, high contrast, and a clean layout.
  • He highlights that Western (and many global) audiences naturally read left to right, so placing key text on the left often improves quick comprehension.
  • In the example listing, he notes that some benefits are placed on the right-hand side and in lower-contrast fonts, which he personally misses on first pass, illustrating how misplaced or low-contrast text gets ignored.
  • He suggests simplifying fonts and reducing the number of different font styles in a single image to maintain clarity.

 

Information Density and Cognitive Load
  • Dorian recommends limiting each image to three to four pieces of information, noting that this is roughly the maximum people can process at a glance.
  • He explains that fewer elements per image allow benefits to stand out and prevent the viewer from feeling overwhelmed.
  • He highlights that many sellers mistakenly believe that every image needs a headline, but in reality, some images can communicate entirely through visual storytelling.
  • He suggests that when an image already demonstrates the benefit clearly, extra headline text can be removed to free up visual space and reduce clutter.

 

Bullet Points and Benefit-First Copy
  • Dorian turns to bullet points and stresses the importance of front-loading bullets with benefits, not bland descriptive text.
  • He explains that shoppers often scan bullet headings (the first words or phrases) rather than reading full sentences.
  • Using the pregnancy journal as an example, he contrasts existing bullets like “Cherish every moment” or “Thoughtful gift” with more precise, benefit-focused phrases such as:
    • “Easily capture precious moments.”
    • “Superior quality and design”
    • “Perfect baby shower gift”
    • “Preserved memories for a lifetime”
  • He links these reworked bullets directly to customer concerns (e.g., uncertainty about quality), and he shows how bullet copy can proactively address purchase barriers.

 

Main Image Optimization and Mobile Considerations
  • Dorian emphasizes that the main image is critical for click-through rate, since it appears prominently on the Amazon search results page.
  • He performs a “white space audit” to see how much of the search-result image area the product occupies, pointing out that filling more of the frame (without violating Amazon rules) usually improves visibility.
  • He notes that 3D/dynamic angles for product images typically perform better than flat, 2D representations because they convey depth, quality, and tangibility.
  • He demonstrates how to check listings on mobile using Chrome developer tools, noting that most sessions occur on mobile devices, so mobile optimization is crucial.
  • In the pregnancy journal example, he observes that the main image is reasonably strong: it uses a dynamic angle and includes a ribbon that suggests it is a giftable item.
  • However, he points out that contrast could be improved and that inner pages are not clearly visible at mobile scale, leaving an opportunity to better show the content and layout that matter to buyers.

 

Use of AI and Keplo’s Internal Software for Hypothesis Generation
  • Dorian describes how he uses a custom software/toolset (part of Keplo) to analyze listings and generate hypotheses, powered by AI.
  • He explains that the tool ingests multiple data sources, such as search queries, Amazon reviews, top customer questions, competitor information, and even external sources like Reddit forums.
  • The software identifies patterns, concerns, and purchase barriers, which he then converts into conversion-focused opportunities.
  • For the pregnancy journal, his system surfaces purchase barriers such as:
    • Uncertainty about the journal quality and page layout, given no physical preview.
    • Concerns about whether 80+ pages are enough content.
    • Fear of buying the journal too early in pregnancy.
    • Worries about being able to maintain a consistent journaling habit.
    • Questions about the value of the journal compared with free pregnancy apps.
  • The tool also surfaces top customer questions, such as:
    • What specific prompts and sections are included?
    • When is the best time to start using the journal?
    • How does this product compare to other pregnancy journals?
  • Dorian explains that conversions are not just about convincing shoppers that the product is great but also about removing purchase barriers so they feel safe and confident to buy.
  • He then uses AI to generate content ideas and image concepts that directly address these barriers, for example:
    • Emphasizing premium quality and no-bleed paper.
    • Visually showing page layouts and guided prompts.
    • Explaining when to start using the journal (e.g., at a particular stage of pregnancy).
  • He demonstrates generating multiple main-image and gallery-image layouts via AI, then curating and refining them rather than using them as final assets.
  • Dorian clarifies that AI-generated images are usually treated as creative direction and wireframes for designers, not as final production images, because they often require polish, corrections, or re-rendering.
  • He repeatedly loops between data (purchase barriers, questions), visual concepts, and listing audits to sharpen hypotheses before passing them to a design and testing phase.

 

Second Product Review: Hair Growth Spray (Fermented Rice Water & Rosemary)

 

Understanding Different Customer Types
  • Jonathan asks Dorian to review a second listing in a different niche, a hair growth spray featuring fermented rice water and rosemary.
  • Dorian introduces the idea of two customer types for this product:
    • Purists: people who already know what fermented rice water is and believe in it; they compare several competing listings and want to know why this specific product is the best option.
    • Tourists: people who are generally looking for hair growth solutions but have no prior knowledge of fermented rice water.
  • He notes that the purists need clear comparative benefits and stronger proof, while the tourists require education on what fermented rice water is and why it helps hair.

 

Issues and Opportunities in the Hair Spray Listing
  • Dorian observes that the main image and early gallery images primarily show before-and-after hair photos and aesthetic lifestyle shots, but they do not clearly explain what fermented rice water is or how it works.
  • He argues that for a “tourist” customer, the first major question is “What is rice water?” and that the listing currently fails to answer this quickly.
  • He notes that some images include many overlapping concepts like rosemary, rice water, caffeine, and other elements, but the arrangement is visually confusing and hard to decode.
  • Dorian highlights a specific ingredient-focused image (showing rice water, rosemary, and caffeine) that contains good raw content but is overloaded and poorly structured, making it a prime candidate for simplification and reordering.
  • He suggests that this ingredient-benefit image should likely be moved to an earlier position in the gallery and redesigned with cleaner segmentation: one component explaining rice water, one for rosemary, and one for caffeine, each with concise benefits (e.g., “nourishes scalp,” “boosts volume,” “supports hair strength”).
  • In the A+ content, Dorian points out that many modules are very text-heavy, particularly on mobile, which makes them intimidating and less likely to be read.
  • He stresses that statements like “helps you get fuller-looking hair in just four weeks”, supported by an independent four‑week study with 30 participants, are extremely powerful selling points.
  • He notes that this “four weeks” claim, currently buried in the A+, should be surfaced in prominent places, such as:
    • The main image (e.g., a badge or callout: “Fuller-looking hair in 4 weeks”).
    • Early gallery images and maybe even bullets.
  • Dorian also reviews a notice in the listing that says the product packaging may look different from images because of updates and experiments.
  • Brian explains that this disclaimer exists to avoid confusion or negative reviews when the physical packaging differs from older images.
  • Dorian responds that such a disclaimer effectively introduces a purchase barrier, implying that the customer may receive different ingredients or a mismatched product.
  • He recommends removing or minimizing such disclaimers unless there is truly a major brand or name change, arguing that minor packaging tweaks rarely cause meaningful review problems but can explicitly damage trust.

 

A+ Content and Mobile Experience
  • Dorian checks the A+ content for the hair spray on mobile, noting that many customers consume listings from mobile devices.
  • He sees dense paragraphs and numerous long-form explanations under headings like “Nourish your scalp” and “Rosemary blend.”
  • He recommends that the brand distill each major ingredient or cluster (e.g., rosemary blend, fermented rice water, caffeine) into three short, clear benefit phrases, such as:
    • “Promotes fuller-looking hair.”
    • “Nourishes scalp and roots”
    • “Helps strengthen strands and reduce breakage.”
  • He stresses that A+ sections should be visually segmented and quickly scannable, with stronger visual hierarchy (headlines, icons, and short supporting text), rather than large, uniform blocks of text.
  • He points again to the “fuller-looking hair in four weeks” claim and explains that this type of scientifically anchored benefit should be one of the lead messages in both the standard listing content and the A+ modules.

 

Testing Approaches: Polls, Amazon Experiments, and PPC Data

 

Ranked Poll Tests (Product Pinion and Similar Tools)
  • Dorian describes using ranked poll tests on services like Product Pinion (and similar platforms such as PickFu or IntelliVY, which are mentioned conceptually in the discussion).
  • In these tests, multiple listing images are shown to a panel of target shoppers, who are asked to:
    1. Rank the images from most to least likely to make them want to buy.
    2. Provide qualitative feedback on what they like or dislike about each image.
  • He explains that such polls serve three main purposes:
    1. They reveal which benefits and angles resonate most, informing the order of gallery images.
    2. They highlight specific issues or confusion in particular images that can be fixed in a redesign.
    3. They show which images or benefits are least compelling, guiding teams to either improve or remove them.
  • Dorian emphasizes that he never fully trusts poll results as a direct predictor of performance on Amazon, because test audiences and real shoppers behave differently.
  • Instead, he uses them as guidance and qualitative insight, not as the final decision-maker.

 

Managed Experiments in Amazon Seller Central
  • Dorian discusses using Manage Your Experiments in Amazon Seller Central (A/B tests) to scientifically compare two versions of listing elements, such as:
    • Main images
    • Titles
    • A+ content
  • He suggests that a good experiment should reach useful conclusions in about three weeks, assuming enough traffic.
  • He says he aims for at least 80% statistical significance, and if a test fails to approach this in about three weeks, he often kills the test and moves on to a different hypothesis.
  • Dorian notes that one advantage of Amazon’s managed experiments is that external factors (like a competitor dropping prices or a temporary demand shift) generally affect both variants (A and B) equally, keeping the comparison cleaner.

 

Manual Testing with PPC and Performance Data
  • When managed experiments are not available or practical (for example, on certain ASIN types or time constraints), Dorian explains that teams can still test manually.
  • He suggests updating content and then working closely with the PPC team, who monitor:
    • Click-through rates
    • Conversion rates
    • Cost per click and other performance indicators
  • Dorian warns that manual tests must be interpreted carefully, because they can be affected by external variables, such as:
    • Promotions or price changes (yours or competitors’)
    • Seasonality or demand spikes
  • He recommends checking whether any major external changes happen during a manual test window; if they do, he advises not to treat that test as conclusive and to seek a cleaner test.

 

Conversion Club, Keplo Offering, and Giveaway
  • Dorian describes his Conversion Club, an ongoing membership community where brands receive:
    • A monthly conversion report for one ASIN.
    • Access to his tools and credits (such as the listing analysis and AI hypothesis generator).
    • Weekly live sessions where they analyze listings together and discuss CRO and AI workflows.
    • Access to an AI Academy focused on AI flows and conversion strategies.
  • He states that there is an MDS discount code: MDS20 for 20% off (applied to the Conversion Club).
  • Jonathan announces that one participant will receive two free months in Dorian’s mastermind/Conversion Club as a giveaway.
  • They run a fun “Duck Race” on screen to randomly select the winner.
  • The winner is Rhett, who appears to have left the call by the time the result is announced.
  • Jonathan says he will email Rhett with Dorian’s contact details and coordinate how Rhett can redeem the two free months and get onboarded.
  • Dorian confirms he is happy to work with Rhett to help increase CTR and conversion on Rhett’s listings.

 

The Listing Xray:  https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/12aa45db-0f28-42ef-b293-6714ad7861ef

 

In this session, the group explores how visuals, copy, and data intersect to drive success on Amazon. 

 

Dorian shows that high-performing listings are not a matter of random creativity but of structured hypotheses, clear visual communication, and disciplined testing. 

 

He demonstrates how to blend a checklist-based review with AI-driven research to uncover purchase barriers, then convert those insights into actionable image and copy changes.

items.title: How Sellers Scale Large Catalogs Across Marketplaces with PIM Systems and Inventory Management － Large Catalog Sellers Channel Call January 2026
items.description:
In this session, Large Catalog Sellers channel members discuss how to better manage product data, advertising, and logistics across multiple channels.
TOPICS:
  1. Product data enrichment and PIM tools 
  2. B2B strategies and pricing on Amazon and Walmart 
  3. Inventory, Buy Box, and fulfillment challenges at scale
items.description_text: In this session, Large Catalog Sellers channel members discuss how to better manage product data, advertising, and logistics across multiple channels. TOPICS: Product data enrichment and PIM tools B2B strategies and pricing on Amazon and Walmart Inventory, Buy Box, and fulfillment challenges at scale
cliff_notes:
In this session members of the MDS Large Catalog Sellers Channel discuss the tools, tactics, and operational challenges of running very large catalogs across Amazon, Walmart, Target, Shopify, and other marketplaces. The conversation blends systems-level strategy with hands-on operational problem-solving, reflecting the reality that scale introduces complexity, fragility, and hidden failure points.

 

A recurring theme is that as catalogs grow, sellers must rely less on manual checks and more on structured data, automation, and early-warning systems to detect issues before revenue is impacted.

 

Product Data, PIMs, and AI Enrichment

 

Matt opens by discussing an evaluation of Anglera, an AI-based product enrichment tool that claims to automatically enhance product attributes at scale by ingesting Amazon data, images, and PDFs. While the promise is attractive for large catalogs, the claims feel overly optimistic, especially given the lack of transparent pricing. Matt plans to test the tool directly and report back to the group if it delivers real value, potentially exploring an MDS-specific arrangement.

 

He contrasts this with their current PIM, Salsify, which they use as a centralized product data system rather than an order or inventory tool. Salsify allows extensive custom fields, conditional logic for channel-specific content, and real-time validation against Amazon’s attribute requirements. The team pushes data to Amazon, Shopify, and Walmart, and Matt considers the annual cost of roughly $18k–$20k to be highly efficient for their scale.

 

The group explores whether sellers should buy AI enrichment tools or build their own workflows by piping PIM data into modern language models, generating multiple versions of titles and bullets, and writing them back for review. Earlier attempts at AI content failed due to weak handling of product families and limited context windows, but newer models may make large-scale enrichment more viable today.

Marketplace Management and Channel Control

 

Morris explains that his company uses Rithum (formerly ChannelAdvisor) as its primary marketplace management platform for channels like eBay, Target, Walmart, and others, while intentionally managing Amazon directly. This approach gives them full control over listing structure, flat files, variation logic, and required fields, which they consider essential at scale. Rithum is then used downstream after data is reformatted to match each channel’s requirements.

 

The group generally agrees that Amazon’s complexity makes full abstraction through third-party tools risky for large catalogs.

Target, Walmart, and Integration Risk

 

Target Plus integrations are described as fragile, with a single variation change capable of taking large portions of a catalog offline. Walmart is viewed as even more opaque than Amazon, with examples of full account termination triggered by “unusual login activity” and little recourse for appeal or reinstatement.

 

Both Walmart Business and Amazon Business are discussed, with consensus that Walmart’s B2B efforts have not meaningfully scaled, while Amazon Business works but remains operationally clunky.

Amazon B2B Advertising and Pricing Strategy

 

Matt shares strong results from Amazon’s B2B-specific ad tools, including B2B-only campaigns and placement modifiers. These campaigns behave like audience targeting and have delivered exceptionally high conversion rates, particularly for education and institutional buyers. He strongly recommends these tools for any seller with legitimate B2B demand.

 

In contrast, sector-based pricing (such as education or healthcare discounts) failed to show incremental value. Discounts appeared to simply reduce revenue rather than unlock new demand, and Amazon could not provide evidence that sector pricing increased conversion, leading Matt’s team to discontinue it.

Buy Box Monitoring at Scale

 

After implementing large price increases driven by tariffs, Matt discovered that thousands of SKUs quietly lost Featured Offer eligibility. Manual detection is not scalable, prompting a discussion on programmatic monitoring.

 

William suggests using the Keepa API to detect Buy Box loss at scale and differentiate between suppression and legitimate out-of-stock conditions. He outlines a practical approach of temporarily upgrading API access to run heavy data pulls, exporting results to CSV or Google Sheets, and scaling back once monitoring is in place.

Geographic Coverage, Fulfillment Centers, and Delivery Times

 

William describes how Amazon’s consolidation of inventory into fewer fulfillment centers can cause offers to disappear in certain geographies or extend delivery promises from two days to five or more. This often leads to sharp sales declines without obvious signals in Seller Central.

 

The group discusses the need for geographic sampling across multiple ZIP codes and regions to monitor delivery promises and detect when Amazon’s internal inventory logic is breaking down. Simple spot checks are insufficient for large catalogs.

Inventory Levels and Distribution Strategy

 

Large-catalog sellers increasingly need to hold higher inventory levels than before to maintain broad fulfillment center coverage. Some slow-moving SKUs still require large absolute unit counts to prevent Amazon from consolidating inventory into too few locations. The group discusses combining days-of-supply metrics with minimum unit thresholds to protect geographic coverage.

 

There is interest in tooling that can alert sellers when fulfillment center counts drop or inventory distribution becomes too concentrated, as these issues often go unnoticed until sales are already impacted.

FBA Anomalies and Inventory Ledger Gaps

 

William shares examples of Amazon double-receiving inventory, charging storage fees on phantom units, and failing to fulfill orders correctly. He argues that FBA still lacks a true real-time inventory ledger and that internal politics between fulfillment centers and central operations create structural blind spots.

 

These failures disproportionately affect mid-sized and large sellers, who often absorb the operational and financial cost without clear remediation paths.

Reseller Dynamics and the End of Commingling

 

The group discusses Amazon’s move away from commingled inventory and the increased requirement for FNSKU labeling, particularly for resellers. Brand-owned sellers are less affected, while authorized resellers may face increased operational burden, including potential SKU restructuring and additional warehouse handling.

 

There is concern that Amazon has underestimated how many brands prefer wholesale relationships and do not want to manage Amazon directly, making these policy shifts disruptive to the broader reseller ecosystem.

Brand Ownership, Counterfeits, and Enforcement

 

While some sellers report manageable levels of counterfeit claims and returns, others are seeing increased resistance from Amazon when responding to authenticity complaints. The group notes inconsistencies between account health signals and customer-facing metrics, suggesting that Amazon’s internal systems remain fragmented.

Company Context and Product Complexity

 

Matt provides background on his businesses, including a high-end fingerboard brand with U.S. manufacturing components and a large science catalog with complex materials, sizes, and pack configurations. Because they already generate all of their own product content, scalable enrichment tools are appealing—but only if they can handle complexity without introducing errors.

items.title: How Women Entrepreneurs Navigate Growth, Wellness, and Business Challenges － WMDS Call January 2026
items.description:
In this session, Women of MDS discuss event logistics, share strategies for standing out in competitive markets, and highlight the importance of personal health and goal setting for women entrepreneurs.

TOPICS:

  1. Competing with international and Chinese businesses
  2. Strategies for product differentiation and managing customer reviews
  3. Prioritizing health, wellness, and effective goal planning
items.description_text: In this session, Women of MDS discuss event logistics, share strategies for standing out in competitive markets, and highlight the importance of personal health and goal setting for women entrepreneurs. TOPICS: Competing with international and Chinese businesses Strategies for product differentiation and managing customer reviews Prioritizing health, wellness, and effective goal planning
cliff_notes:
In this session Women of MDS engage in a multifaceted discussion covering event logistics challenges in business due to international competition, strategies for product differentiation, managing customer reviews, goal setting, and prioritizing health and wellness. 

 

The attendees share personal experiences, best practices, and actionable advice relevant to women entrepreneurs in product-driven businesses. 

 

Integrated throughout the conversation are real-life examples, solutions to recent issues, and suggestions for both business and self-improvement.

Challenges with International and Chinese Competitors

  • Ana discusses how her apparel business faces stiff competition from Chinese sellers offering significantly lower prices, resulting in a consistent 20% annual decrease in sales since COVID-19.
  • Dana Mavros explains that certain international companies prioritize market share and revenue over profitability, enabling aggressive underpricing.
  • It is mentioned that some Chinese and South Korean businesses may receive government subsidies to help offset launch and advertising costs, with examples given from both markets.
  • Ana expresses concern over how rival companies can afford to sell below cost and discusses rumors that the Chinese government pays sellers a percentage of their sales.
  • Dana shares a specific case where the South Korean government was prepared to subsidize $30,000 for a client's Amazon product launch.

Brand Building and Product Differentiation

  • Jennifer Adams Bunkers suggests that founders focus on storytelling and brand ownership to distinguish their offerings, even if reluctant.
  • Dana encourages participants to highlight concrete differentiators such as quality of materials, thread count, manufacturing location, and health/safety aspects, especially in sensitive categories like children's apparel.
  • Ana confirms that her products are now primarily made in China and Cambodia rather than LA due to domestic manufacturing challenges.
  • Dana recommends purchasing competitor products to verify their claims and using Amazon's quality control rules and claim-submission process to address fraudulent or misleading listings.
  • Participants discuss the importance of A/B testing main and alternate product images and using demographic insights to tailor product messaging.
  • Strategies shared include using packaging to communicate key differentiators, even via imagery, and continuously iterating based on testing results.

Managing Customer Feedback and Reviews

  • Casey Morris relates her experience with launching a new product that quickly received a negative Vine review but continued to sell due to strong community and promotional support.
  • Dana explains that Amazon’s review removal policy allows appeals for inappropriate or inaccurate reviews, and that proactive management of feedback is vital.
  • There is consensus that Vine reviews can be inconsistent, and reliance on them may no longer be advisable; participants share strategies for hand-requesting reviews from verified customers for more controlled outcomes.
  • Jennifer and Dana note the importance of star ratings above 4.0 for access to promotional opportunities on Amazon.
  • The process of appealing reviews and leveraging A+ content to clarify product features or usage is discussed in detail.

Goal Setting, Planning, and Accountability

  • Jennifer introduces the concept of “goal congruency,” emphasizing the need for alignment between actual commitment and stated goals.
  • Participants share their planning tools and habits, including Google Docs, workbooks (notably the one by Mel Robbins), visual aids like full-year wall calendars, and color-coded notebooks for different life and business domains.
  • Casey describes realistic quarterly goal setting, Monday-morning reflections, and regular progress check-ins as critical to accountability.
  • Dana suggests blocking calendar time, color-coding activities, and using monthly/weekly reporting to manage strategic focus and time allocation objectively.

Health and Wellness Initiatives for Female Entrepreneurs

  • Angie Raja describes her decision to focus on health, including undergoing genetic testing and adopting a holistic wellness mindset.
  • Dana and Jennifer share their experiences with Function Health, Prevno full-body MRI scans, and Viome, noting the advantages of early, proactive health diagnostics.
  • The team emphasizes the importance of businesswomen prioritizing their well-being, asserting that personal health is foundational to business success and that medical advocacy is necessary due to systemic neglect of women's health concerns.

 

In conclusion, the Women of MDS Monthly Call delivers a broad and insightful exchange on the unique business, operational, and personal challenges faced by women entrepreneurs. 

 

The session features in-depth discussions about adapting business models amid international competition, optimizing brand impact, handling customer feedback, and the value of clear, actionable goal setting. 

 

The conversation also underscores the significance of proactive self-care and leveraging diagnostics and support systems for long-term health. 

 

Overall, the meeting exemplifies the power of peer support, resource sharing, and collective problem-solving in advancing both professional and personal growth.

items.title: How Sellers Scale E-Commerce Teams and Expand into New Markets － Rockies Chapter Hybrid Boardroom Jan 2026
items.description:
In this session, members of the Rockies Chapter discuss practical strategies for e-commerce business growth, operational challenges, and team building. 

TOPICS:

  1. Business Operations and Efficiency
  2. Marketing, Sales Channels, and Brand Building
  3. Team Building and Talent Acquisition
items.description_text: In this session, members of the Rockies Chapter discuss practical strategies for e-commerce business growth, operational challenges, and team building. TOPICS: Business Operations and Efficiency Marketing, Sales Channels, and Brand Building Team Building and Talent Acquisition
cliff_notes:
In this session, members of the Rockies Chapter gather for their monthly call to discuss key business strategies, challenges, successes, and future plans. 

 

The participants, representing various brands and roles in e-commerce and retail, share detailed insights regarding operational improvements, team building, sales channels, marketing approaches, financial management, and networking opportunities. 

 

The meeting spans a wide range of topics, and attendees provide actionable recommendations, candid lessons, and resources to help others facing similar business situations.

 

High-ROI Activities, Team Management, and Operations
  • Members emphasize focusing on high-return activities rather than low-ROI tasks, ensuring business growth and efficient plan execution.
  • They stress the importance of establishing processes and systems—such as Slack and Basecamp—to offload tasks and improve customer service.
  • There is an ongoing need to build sustainable systems and hire the right people, freeing up leadership for strategic planning.
  • Tracking financial performance accurately is a goal, involving spreadsheets and forecasting with support from the team.
  • Automation and improved reporting systems are cited as essential to streamline data collection and optimize daily performance.

 

Product Launches, Inventory, and Profitability Challenges
  • Several attendees report difficulties with delayed or weak product launches, noting losses in market share and revenue due to a lack of execution.
  • Overstock and rising PPC costs have significantly reduced profitability for multiple businesses, forcing them to consider moving operations or reducing warehousing costs.
  • There are candid accounts of managing dead inventory, lease negotiations, and mistakes like going out of stock on key products, which result in lasting loss of rankings and sales.
  • Members exchange tactical advice on dealing with dead stock, including possible donations, liquidation, and negotiating with landlords to exit expensive leases.

 

Marketing and Brand Building Strategies
  • Mass content creation, especially via AI and TikTok, is described as a primary growth driver; some brands manage thousands of TikTok accounts for broad organic reach.
  • Members share detailed approaches to sampling—giving free product samples on Amazon and via direct mail to stimulate repeat purchases.
  • Social commerce, TikTok Shop, influencer partnerships, and niche-specific Facebook/Meta ad strategies are actively deployed to reduce reliance on PPC and Amazon.
  • Companies experiment with running promotions via non-brand-specific social media pages, which yields improved conversion rates.

 

Supply Chain, Manufacturing, and Retail Expansion
  • Managing complex global supply chains presents consistent challenges, especially when securing unique ingredients or products across regulatory environments.
  • Relocating manufacturing—such as moving operations to Algeria—has dramatically reduced costs for some enterprises.
  • Businesses aim to maintain high in-stock rates to protect growth and avoid lost sales due to supply chain lapses.
  • Retail channel expansion is a common goal, with companies securing nationwide deals with outlets like Target, Kroger, Walmart, and Costco.
  • Members discuss the impact of account health on Amazon, Buy Box suppression, and strategies to address retail pricing conflicts, particularly with large chains.

 

Financial Performance and Business Scaling
  • Attendees openly share revenue, profit, and advertising spend figures, demonstrating trends such as declining reliance on Amazon in favor of brick-and-mortar channels.
  • The importance of focusing on profitability over sheer revenue is a recurring theme; aggressive cost control and cutbacks on ad spend are cited as solutions.
  • Some companies have grown to nine-figure revenues and discuss planned IPOs or buyouts, offering benchmarks and lessons for others.

 

Team Building and Talent Acquisition
  • Hiring competent, experienced team members—especially from places like Argentina—has greatly improved operational efficiency for several firms.
  • Interns and university programs offer a pipeline for motivated talent, with successful conversion rates to full-time hires.
  • The group cautions against hiring executives from companies much larger than your own, suggesting hiring for the next logical tier to ensure adaptability and impact.
  • Members relate both the successes and failures of outsourcing and executive hiring, including pitfalls when scaling too quickly without proper infrastructure.

 

Business Advice, Mentorship, and Community Networking
  • Senior members share hard-learned lessons on pacing, work-life balance, and the necessity to delegate and let go of low-leverage tasks for company growth.
  • In-person networking is fostered through recurring events, such as the ecompreneur event in Salt Lake City and plans for future retreats.
  • The value of having a business community—particularly one open to candid discussion of failures and creative solutions—is repeatedly affirmed.
  • Sound boards and advisory relationships are offered for direct-to-consumer site development and digital strategy.

 

 Notable Tools, Platforms, and Resources
  • Brands make prominent use of Slack, Basecamp, ClickUp, Sellerboard (for Amazon), and advanced analytics via ChatGPT API and Amazon Marketing Cloud.
  • Techniques like using Amazon DSP with Performance Plus metrics are discussed for scaling digital advertising efficiently.

  • Mass sampling platforms, direct mail marketing companies, and best-in-class sampling strategies (e.g., by the company "Three Ships") are highlighted.

 

In conclusion, this detailed session offers a robust examination of the challenges and opportunities facing multi-channel e-commerce businesses today, from inventory challenges and lean operations to innovative marketing and the strategic use of AI. 

 

Members are open about both their achievements and setbacks, providing a rich learning environment for peers at various stages of growth. 

 

The meeting ends with encouragement to keep the dialogue active, signaling the power of community, the necessity of adaptability, and the ongoing quest to balance growth with sustainable, profitable operations.

items.title: Common Retail Channel Pitfalls to Avoid － Josh Taekman － Retail Channel Call January 2026
items.description:
In this session, Josh Taekman discusses how DTC and Amazon-native brands can successfully enter and scale in U.S. retail channels like Costco, Walmart, Target, and the natural channel.
TOPICS:
  1. Retail readiness, operational checklists, and avoiding costly mistakes
  2. Driving in-store velocity using community, creators, and promotions
  3. Channel and retailer strategy (Costco, Walmart, Target, natural and value channels)
items.description_text: In this session, Josh Taekman discusses how DTC and Amazon-native brands can successfully enter and scale in U.S. retail channels like Costco, Walmart, Target, and the natural channel. TOPICS: Retail readiness, operational checklists, and avoiding costly mistakes Driving in-store velocity using community, creators, and promotions Channel and retailer strategy (Costco, Walmart, Target, natural and value channels)
cliff_notes:
In this session Josh Taekman shared how to approach and succeed in U.S. retail channels especially big-box and club retailers like Costco, Walmart, and Target. 

 

Josh explains how his holding company operates across multiple retail and digital channels and shares detailed advice on retail readiness, sales velocity, brokers, timelines, and channel strategy. 

 

The conversation is highly Q&A driven, with founders asking about their own categories, challenges entering retail, and how to avoid costly mistakes.

 

Overview of Josh’s Company and Channel Coverage
  • Josh’s organization operates as a holding company called PLTFRM, with specialized teams for different channels.
  • The digital agency Vendo manages brands on Amazon, Walmart.com, TikTok Shop, Google, Meta, Instacart, and other marketplaces.
  • Vendo has about 130 people working on media buying, account services, and troubleshooting, supported by ~60 overseas staff and ~127 U.S.-based staff.
  • Team Direct, based in Bentonville, focuses on Walmart and Sam’s Club across all departments except fashion and includes around 140 people.
  • The Cities team focuses on Target and Best Buy and consists of about 85 people.
  • The Amped team works exclusively with Costco, covering all 8 regions, headquarters, and business centers.
  • The Presence team manages the natural channel (e.g., Erewhon, Whole Foods, Sprouts) and natural sets in conventional grocery, and is expanding further into conventional grocery.
  • Collectively, these teams have 20+ years in business, manage over $11 billion in sales, employ around 730 people, and work with about 700 brands and founders.
  • Josh emphasizes that they specialize in moving strong DTC and social-native brands into retail and matching them with the right channels at the right time.

 

Retail Readiness: Checklists, Logistics, and Getting Off the Shelf
  • Josh stresses that getting into retail is easier than staying in retail; the real challenge is driving sell-through off the shelf.
  • His teams use a 100-point checklist to confirm retail readiness, covering UPC/PC codes, packaging, pallets, shipping, and distribution.
  • He warns that incomplete readiness leads to missed shipments, replenishment failures, chargebacks, and loss of trust.
  • He explains that retailers rarely offer a second chance, so brands must be fully prepared before they launch.
  • He highlights that logistics and operations are as critical as sales and marketing.

 

Driving Velocity: Community, Creators, and In-Store Sales
  • Josh explains that retail success depends on velocity and sales, not just on getting listed.
  • He cites Bloom as an example of a brand that leverages a strong community and content engine from TikTok and DTC to drive foot traffic to Target and Walmart.
  • He notes that Bloom’s success is driven by consistent content, creator partnerships, and a recognizable brand face (Mari) that activates their audience in specific retailers.
  • He contrasts this with a major creator-owned brand launched in Costco that did not fully activate marketing, resulting in poor sell-through and costly markdowns.
  • He explains that when velocity is weak, retailers expect brands to support markdowns and price reductions to clear products.
  • He emphasizes that shelf space is valuable real estate, and each item must meet predefined velocity and sales expectations.

 

Retailer Expectations, Velocity Windows, and Timelines
  • Josh explains that velocity review windows vary by retailer.
  • At Costco, many items are regional and rotational, often running on 12-week rotations. By week 3–4, if sales are slow, Costco pushes for more aggressive pricing to clear inventory within the rotation.
  • At Walmart and Target, brands typically receive 3–6 months to prove performance, with clear sales targets and thresholds shared in advance.
  • He notes that retailers can be good partners if brands are transparent and collaborative when sales underperform.
  • He states that, for Costco, even after a “yes” from a buyer, it usually takes 3–6 months to get on the shelf due to setup and logistics.
  • He explains that some big-box categories (like at Target) operate on long reset cycles, and he gives an example of a meeting where the reset is not until January 2027, showing how far ahead some planning happens.

 

How to Enter Retail: Assortment Fit, Differentiation, and Buyer Mindset
  • Josh emphasizes that brands must first study the retailer’s assortment and determine whether they fill a gap or offer something incremental.
  • He explains that success is not only about price; it is about quality, brand strength, differentiation, and community.
  • He notes that buyers increasingly watch social content and industry media such as Instagram talking heads, TikTok, and CBG Wire to discover emerging brands.
  • He cautions that buyer enthusiasm based on social buzz does not guarantee readiness; the brand still must pass a thorough retail readiness checklist.
  • He urges brands to clarify how they make the category “set” more exciting and deliver incremental value rather than just duplicating existing products.

 

Advice for DTC and Early-Stage Brands Entering Retail
  • For DTC brands and those just starting B2B wholesale (e.g., selling to independent apothecaries), Josh recommends obtaining explicit sales expectations from buyers (such as units per week per store).
  • He suggests asking buyers what has worked historically in that store for similar products (demos, promotions, creator pushes, etc.).
  • He encourages brands to leverage community and creator assets to drive traffic to specific locations and to consider in-store events or demos.
  • He reiterates the need to have packaging, UPCs, fulfillment, and shipping fully dialed in before launching.
  • He recommends starting with smaller or more controlled channels to learn what actually drives sell-through before scaling nationally.

 

Competition, Saturated Categories, and Channel Strategy
  • For crowded categories like pimple patches, where major brands like Hero and Starface already dominate shelf space, Josh notes that there is limited room for more near-duplicate products.
  • He explains that major retailers prefer to back category leaders with strong brand equity and buzz instead of many similar value plays.
  • He suggests that value-focused brands offering more patches at better prices consider value-driven channels like TJ Maxx and Kohl’s, and other off-price outlets where price sensitivity is higher.
  • He frames this as a strategy to capture volume and trial where shoppers seek deals, rather than trying to displace leaders in big-box sets.

 

Brokers vs Platform: Roles, Benefits, and Perceptions
  • Participants discuss using brokers to get access to retailers, and some share positive experiences where brokers improve success rates.
  • Josh acknowledges that brokers once had a mixed reputation, but modern, good brokers:
    • Know the buyers personally and understand their expectations.
    • “Know the answers to the test” and help shape pitches, pricing, and packaging accordingly.
    • Are selective about brands because their reputation with buyers is at stake.
  • Josh describes his own company as more than a broker, but confirms they function as sales agents managing retailer relationships.
  • His teams help brands become retail-ready, interact with buyers, handle operations, in-stocks, replenishment, and data, and manage the full 100-point checklist.
  • He emphasizes that such partners add value by preventing costly mistakes, which can exceed their fees.

 

Best Practices for Retail Buyer Meetings
  • Josh stresses that buyers do not want exploratory meetings where brands are unprepared.
  • He recommends that brands arrive 98–99% buttoned up on assortment, pricing, logistics, and readiness.
  • He advises that brands should teach the buyer something new about the category or consumer instead of asking the buyer to educate them.
  • He explains that only a small detail or two should require follow-up; brands should avoid leaving with a long list of missing information.
  • He shares an example of an olive oil vendor whose presentation is so educational that the buyer says they have never learned more about olive oil in one meeting, illustrating the impact of deep category expertise.

 

Channel Focus Strategy: “Inch Wide and Mile Deep”
  • Josh advises brands not to spread themselves too thin across many retailers at the start.
  • He recommends going “an inch wide and a mile deep” by focusing on a few key channels first.
  • He explains that this approach helps brands learn to drive velocity, execute promotions, and support performance in a manageable way.
  • He warns that chasing too many doors without properly supporting them leads to weak sell-through and eventual delisting.

 

In conclusion, this session presents a detailed, real-world view of what it takes to succeed in retail beyond just landing a PO. 

 

Josh underscores that operational excellence, clear velocity targets, strong community-driven marketing, and category differentiation are essential for lasting success. 

 

By focusing on being truly retail-ready, choosing channels strategically, preparing thoroughly for buyer meetings, and learning through narrower initial distribution, brands can significantly improve their chances of building a strong and sustainable retail presence.

items.title: How to Improve Margins on Amazon While Sustaining Long - Term Growth －Jasim Eisa－Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, Jasim Eisa shares how to raise margins while sustaining growth on Amazon, using real-world examples from managing tens of thousands of SKUs. He covers practical tactics in logistics, procurement, inventory, and fees, supported by a margin-improvement checklist.


TOPICS:

  1. Optimizing logistics and product density to reduce shipping and fulfillment costs
  2. Improving procurement and supplier relationships to lower cost of goods sold
  3. Managing inventory and Amazon fee structures to protect and grow profit margins
items.description_text: In this session, Jasim Eisa shares how to raise margins while sustaining growth on Amazon, using real-world examples from managing tens of thousands of SKUs. He covers practical tactics in logistics, procurement, inventory, and fees, supported by a margin-improvement checklist. TOPICS: Optimizing logistics and product density to reduce shipping and fulfillment costs Improving procurement and supplier relationships to lower cost of goods sold Managing inventory and Amazon fee structures to protect and grow profit margins
cliff_notes:
In this session Jasim Eisa dives deep into strategies for raising margins while sustaining growth on Amazon. 
 
The discussion covers practical levers across logistics procurement inventory fees, and operations, all framed around real numbers and specific tactics. 
 
The call also highlights MDS resources and ways members can stay engaged across calls and events.
 
Jasim’s Business, Scale, and Margin Focus
  • Jasim states that his team does around $90 million in revenue with about 150 people, focusing heavily on both volume and margin.
  • He explains that the business is bootstrapped, so they grow without VC funding and avoid liabilities or debt to keep a healthy balance sheet.
  • He notes they operate across roughly 16,000–17,000 SKUs, with finance and supply chain staff dedicated to constantly optimizing margin.
  • Jasim emphasizes that as an exclusive distributor for partners, both the brand and his company must make a margin, so they “squeeze” every lever possible.
  • He underlines that valuations in the current environment are primarily based on margin, not revenue, especially post-aggregator boom.
  • He argues that many brands think they have a cash flow problem when in reality they have a margin / unit economics problem that worsens with scale.
 
Data Visibility and Measurement
  • Jasim stresses that data visibility is the starting point for all margin work, and his team made this a major initiative around late 2024 and early 2025.
  • He explains that simply reviewing numbers weekly brings both direct benefits (seeing what improves) and indirect behavior change, similar to a study where people who weigh themselves daily gain less weight.
  • He describes tracking cost per pound of shipping, which reveals seasonal cost spikes (e.g., Chinese New Year freight bump) that can be preempted.
  • He shares that by moving shipments two weeks earlier before the Chinese New Year, they save roughly $24–25k in a year.
  • He notes that they sometimes use imperfect but accessible data (e.g., cost per pound instead of cost per cubic foot) to take action rather than wait for perfect systems.
  • Jasim recommends downloading Amazon business reports, pivoting by fee type, and inspecting all fee lines to uncover hidden or creeping costs.
  • He mentions that reviewing SaaS subscriptions reveals redundancies (e.g., paying for both Helium 10 and Jungle Scout), which they then consolidate.
 
Logistics and Product Density
  • Jasim states that logistics are one of the top expense buckets in e‑commerce and are often overlooked, even though they also act as a growth engine.
  • He explains that when products are same‑day or one‑day shipping for most of the U.S., conversion rates improve and marketing becomes more efficient.
  • He contrasts inbound placement fees with maximized shipment splits, explaining that better geographic spread via splits improves placement and sales velocity.
  • He summarizes logistics efficiency with the word “density”, highlighting that higher density at the product, carton, and container levels reduces cost throughout the chain.
  • He describes an AWD example where a box initially holds 4 units, making the $2.10 AWD processing fee equal about $0.52 per unit, but by redesigning cartons to hold 10 units under the 50‑lb limit, they reduce it to roughly $0.21 per unit.
  • He notes that with 10,000 units per month on such an SKU, this density change alone saves around $3,000 per month, or ~$32k per year, on one item.
  • He advocates for a dynamic shipping strategy, especially for omni‑channel and seasonal peaks, rather than a fixed pattern like “factory → 3PL → FBA” for everything.
  • He shares a case where sending inventory from the factory to AWD and then using MCD (multi‑channel distribution) to their own warehouses for Target orders proves cheaper than prior flows.
  • He emphasizes cutting distance and touchpoints, since each mile and handling event erodes margin, and he cites examples like shipping direct from factory to FBA to eliminate a 3PL.
 
Procurement, Spec Sheets, and Supplier Relationships
  • Jasim explains that procurement / COGS is usually the largest cost bucket and must be attacked systematically.
  • He describes creating spec sheets for products, listing materials, dimensions, quality levels, and other technical details.
  • He uses these spec sheets both to understand their own products better and to standardize RFQs, sending the same specs to multiple factories to get comparable quotes.
  • He recounts a case where a cheaper quote using only a product photo led to a factory using recycled plastic, causing product quality problems and negative reviews.
  • He recommends relying on manufacturers’ expertise by sharing targets (e.g., fee tier, size threshold) and asking them for packaging or design ideas, as they know the product and variants deeply.
  • He stresses going direct to factories rather than trading companies, noting that trading companies can silently add 20–30% on top of unit cost.
  • He shares a story where a supposed factory turned out to be a trading company that changed name plaques between visits to appear as multiple manufacturers.
  • He emphasizes cultivating strong relationships with suppliers, noting that during a tariff change under Trump, a Canadian factory shipped a $20k order early—before payment cleared—to beat a 25% tariff, saving around $4k.
  • He explains that good relationships also yield priority in production queues, which matters when SKUs suddenly scale and stockouts loom.
 
Inventory Management & Amazon Fee Mitigation
  • Jasim highlights how expensive FBA storage has become, including monthly storage, inventory age surcharges (formerly LTSF), and related fees.
  • He notes that they now set an internal requirement to keep FBA at <100 days of stock, with an aspirational target closer to two months while still maintaining about 98% in‑stock rate.
  • He warns against treating FBA as a storage solution, pointing out that free removal promotions and cheaper storage are largely gone as Amazon pursues profit maximization.
  • He describes cutting around 15 SKUs that sell but have poor margins or overstock issues, avoiding the sunk‑cost fallacy on prior marketing spend.
  • He compares pallet storage costs across options, stating that 3PL storage might be around $150 per pallet per year, AWD is more expensive, and FBA is dramatically more costly, even before surcharges.
  • He lists overlooked fees such as return processing fees, liquidation fees (on top of already small recovery amounts), and multiple layers of promotion-related fees (coupon clip fees, Lightning Deal fees, SAS fees, etc.).
  • He underlines the importance of verifying product dimensions and weight in Amazon’s system, since misclassification into a higher fee tier can significantly hurt margin.
  • He recommends checking whether packaging changes can move an item into a lower FBA size/weight tier, while ensuring Amazon’s measurements correctly reflect the spec sheet.
 
Operations, Processes, and AI / Automation
  • Jasim explains that operations and processes form another key cost lever, where labor, workflows, and tools can be re‑engineered for efficiency.
  • He mentions remapping warehouse and operational processes to reduce the number of touches per item, consistent with lean / Six Sigma principles that fewer touches usually mean stronger margin.
  • He highlights the role of AI and automation in boosting productivity, citing an example where a creative designer increases weekly output from 20 to 60 items by leveraging AI tools.
  • He emphasizes upskilling existing team members so they can integrate AI into their roles rather than simply cutting headcount.
 
Best Practices and Margin Checklist
  • Jasim organizes cost levers into five main buckets: logistics, procurement / COGS, inventory/forecasting, operations & processes, and marketing.
  • He explains that his presentation includes a Google Sheets checklist that participants can use with their teams to systematically work through margin levers.
  • He frames the checklist as a practical tool that helps brands begin taking action immediately, starting the next day, rather than treating the talk as theory.
 

Resources Mentioned

  • Voadera Amazon Margin Improvement Playbook 
    A step-by-step execution checklist to cut hidden costs, optimize fees, stop margin bleed and grow profit
     

 In conclusion, this session frames margin as the true “oxygen” of an Amazon business and demonstrates how small, compounding improvements across logistics, procurement, inventory, fees, and operations can add up to hundreds of thousands in annual savings. 

 
Jasim repeatedly ties each tactic back to real numbers and decision frameworks that any brand can adopt. 
 
For MDS members, the call reinforces the value of the community’s calls, tools, and checklists in turning margin optimization from an abstract goal into a structured, ongoing practice.

items.title: How Amazon Sellers Optimize Logistics and Inventory Using AWD, 3PLs, and Smart Shipping Practices － Logistics Channel Call January 2026
items.description:
This session covers key logistics strategies for Amazon sellers, focusing on cost-effective storage, shipping, and inventory management.
 
TOPICS:
  1. Comparing AWD vs. 3PL for storage and shipping
  2. Inventory strategies, including safety stock and liquidation options
  3. Best practices for FBA shipping, split shipments, and warehouse selection
items.description_text: This session covers key logistics strategies for Amazon sellers, focusing on cost-effective storage, shipping, and inventory management. TOPICS: Comparing AWD vs. 3PL for storage and shipping Inventory strategies, including safety stock and liquidation options Best practices for FBA shipping, split shipments, and warehouse selection
cliff_notes:
In this session participants discuss advanced logistics and inventory management strategies for Amazon FBA sellers. 

 

The group covers topics ranging from scheduling logistics calls to selecting between Amazon Warehousing & Distribution (AWD) and third-party logistics (3PL) providers. 

 

Emphasis is placed on practical experiences, preferred tools, and strategic decision-making for inventory flow, costs, and risk mitigation.

 

Meeting Logistics and Timing
  • The team holds a regular logistics call and addresses changing the meeting time due to scheduling conflicts.
  • Meeting timing is flexible, and participants are encouraged to give feedback in the channel chat if the new time is better.
  • The scheduling challenge is resolved by proposing to revert to the original time in future sessions if no objections are raised.

 

AWD vs 3PL (Tactical): Cost Comparison and Calculator Tool
  • A calculator created by Tactical is demonstrated, which compares AWD storage and shipping fees with those of 3PL providers, notably Tactical.
  • The calculator allows users to input their own case counts and pallet configurations for accurate cost comparisons.
  • It is shown that AWD is generally more cost-effective for short storage durations (less than two months), but Tactical becomes significantly cheaper for storage exceeding two months, mainly due to lower storage fees.
  • Tactical’s storage fees are always cheaper than AWD for long-term storage, displaying a break-even point at around 2.66 months.
  • The conversation details the criteria for choosing AWD versus a 3PL, emphasizing storage duration as the critical factor.
  • Several shipping methods are compared: AWD, Tactical storage, Tactical cross-docking, and Tactical using a partner carrier, with a discussion of their respective costs and when to use each.
  • It is noted that AWD offers more competitive transportation fees, while 3PLs provide more flexibility and control for longer-term storage or high-SKU environments.

 

Shipment Planning: Direct from China, FBA, AWD, and Multi-Warehouse Strategies
  • Direct shipments from China to FBA, AWS, or regional warehouses are frequently utilized, and timing is a major consideration due to lead times and variable international logistics.
  • The group discusses splitting FBA shipments to five locations from China to avoid inbound placement fees, noting that this approach is easier from China than within the US.
  • Shipping strategies are tailored to SKU volume, sales velocity predictability, and the supplier’s ability to manage split shipments.
  • Recommendations include maintaining a minimum of 60 days’ inventory at FBA to avoid low inventory fees and mitigate shipment delays.
  • Discussions mention “Terminal 49,” a tool for tracking shipment status and keeping delivery windows within compliance.

 

Inventory Management Strategies: Safety Stock, Over/Understock, Liquidation, and Supplier Relationships
  • Participants outline strategies for avoiding over- or under-stocking, emphasizing safety stock and maintaining a consistent replenishment rhythm.
  • The group shares various approaches to overstock, including price drops to break even, disposal, and repurposing for other channels.
  • Liquidation is described through Amazon removal orders and direct sale or destruction at 3PLs or through AWD, with tactical mentions of fees and timing delays for proceeds.
  • Suppliers in China play a key role in keeping inventory agile, and several methods for inspection and validation before shipment are discussed.
  • Employing local agents or trusted contacts in China for product and carton inspections is advised, particularly for companies with concentrated supply chains or high volume.

 

Three PL and AWD Providers, Recommendations, and Regional Variability
  • Tactical and Pattern are discussed as major 3PL providers, each with unique value propositions: Tactical is optimal for large-volume, high-moving SKUs, while Pattern offers consolidated truckloads and in-house label management.
  • AWD is used strategically – usually for fast-moving items not stored for more than two months.
  • For Canada, challenges with forecasting and cost management in 3PL selection are described, with mention of several regional providers and peer contacts for referral.
  • The conversation covers both advantages and challenges of FBA, AWD, and different 3PLs, along with storage costs in various US regions (Texas vs. California).

 

In conclusion, this session delivers practical guidance for Amazon sellers navigating complex supply chains, multiple fulfillment centers, and shifting cost structures. 

 

Participants candidly share their experiences with AWD, 3PLs, and inventory management, offering clear distinctions on when each solution provides the best value. 

 

The group’s recommendations center around understanding inventory velocity, monitoring costs with tracking tools, and cultivating reliable supplier or local partner relationships. 

 

These strategies collectively help businesses improve efficiency, minimize fees, and better forecast for seasonality and market fluctuations.

items.title: How to Manage Amazon Account Health in 2026: Compliance, Brand Protection, and Seller Best Practices－Matthew Natassi, Brianna Kipnis & Kayleigh Cockerill－Mogul Call
items.description:
In this session, experts from Riverbend Consulting discuss best practices for Amazon account health in 2026, focusing on compliance, protecting intellectual property, and addressing marketplace challenges for sellers.
 
TOPICS:
  1. Regulatory compliance and documentation requirements
  2. Brand protection and intellectual property strategies
  3. Managing listing, product, and reseller issues on Amazon
items.description_text: In this session, experts from Riverbend Consulting discuss best practices for Amazon account health in 2026, focusing on compliance, protecting intellectual property, and addressing marketplace challenges for sellers. TOPICS: Regulatory compliance and documentation requirements Brand protection and intellectual property strategies Managing listing, product, and reseller issues on Amazon
cliff_notes:
In this session the participants focus on critical Amazon account health issues and best practices for 2026 addressing challenges such as account and ASIN suspensions, intellectual property disputes, new regulations, and compliance strategies. 

 

The team discusses real-life scenarios, the impact of changing policies, and offers expert advice for Amazon sellers facing increasing scrutiny and enforcement. 

 

Industry experts from Riverbend Consulting - Brianna Kipnis, Matthew Nastasi, and Kayleigh Cockerill- share insights on regulatory compliance, protecting your brand, and maintaining a healthy seller account.

 

Account Health and 2026 Best Practices
  • The call begins with an overview of the importance of account health for 2026 goals.
  • Matt Nastasi, Director of Consulting Services at Riverbend, introduces himself and his expertise in Amazon.
  • The group emphasizes that avoiding ASIN suspension, account suspension, and intellectual property disputes are top priorities.
  • Attendees are reminded to update all documentation to avoid enforcement actions from Amazon.

 

Regulatory Updates and Identity Verification
  • Amazon enforces the Informed Consumer Act, requiring sellers with over 200 transactions or $5,000 in annual revenue to disclose business identity and documentation.
  • Sellers need valid government IDs, tax IDs, bank account details, contact information, and utility bills, all matching Seller Central records.
  • Any inconsistencies between Seller Central and official documents may result in account suspension until the mismatch is resolved.
  • The process is largely automated, so precise matching of details is crucial to avoid triggering manual reviews.
  • The Sturdy Act and CPSC regulations require compliance for large furniture sellers.
  • Stricter rules on lithium battery products take effect from 2025 and continue strict enforcement in 2026.

 

Tax Reporting and Compliance
  • The 1099-K reporting threshold drops to $600 in 2026, requiring accurate income record-keeping from all sellers.
  • Amazon, as a payment entity, is responsible for reporting revenues to the IRS.
  • Sellers must keep TINs and W-9s current to avoid withholding issues that could lead to account suspensions.
  • Misreporting due to running a business through a virtual address in the EU or UK can create significant VAT and regulatory complications.
  • It is important to provide physical documentation for a seller's actual business location.

 

Brand Protection and Intellectual Property
  • Sellers are urged to keep trademarks up to date in every country they operate to prevent hijacking and unauthorized reselling.
  • Amazon’s global unified platform means that listings can be mirrored into other countries unless explicitly opted out—failure to do so allows for unwanted duplication.
  • Sellers are encouraged to put listings on vacation in countries where they do not actively sell.
  • Opting out of global listing mirroring or enforcing brand registry practices can help protect against IP theft and unauthorized listings.

 

Dealing with Unauthorized Resellers and Invoices
  • Amazon typically sides with brands in disputes against unauthorized resellers, even if proper invoices are available.
  • The first-sale doctrine does not guarantee the ability to sell on Amazon without brand authorization.
  • Invoices need to exactly match product bundles, as discrepancies (such as "buy one get one free" packs) can jeopardize account health.
  • Working directly with brands or through authorized distributors is emphasized as the best practice.

 

Copyright, Listing Hijacks, and Countermeasures
  • Sellers must document image and listing content creation with timestamps to defend against malicious IP claims.
  • Filing a DMCA counter-notification is recommended when facing false copyright complaints.
  • Brand registry and requesting increased detail page control scores are strategies to prevent and recover from listing hijacks.
  • Using AI-generated images based on competitor content may still result in take-downs due to similarity, and only robust documentation or court orders can ultimately resolve such disputes.

 

Handling Restricted Ingredients and Medical Claims
  • Each version of a product needs specific testing documentation listing product name and details as shown on Amazon.
  • Structure and function claims in descriptions must be carefully crafted—direct medical claims are prohibited.
  • Labeling, marketing, and ingredient disclosure must be consistent to comply with Amazon’s enforcement.

 

Managing Duplicate Listings and ASIN Creation Policy
  • Products must be listed on the correct ASIN, and bundling or creating duplicates to gain market share is a policy violation.
  • UPC and GTIN registrations must match the brand or seller.
  • Amazon enforces a “one product, one product page” rule, consolidating listings to prevent unauthorized variations or duplicates.
  • Sellers are encouraged to research before creating new listings and consult with Riverbend when facing unclear enforcement.

 

Responding to Incorrect Restricted Ingredient Claims
  • Accurate and detailed testing documents with precise product descriptions are necessary to counter false restricted ingredient claims.
  • Sellers should update marketing and label information if products are flagged by Amazon bots for enforcement.

 

Addressing Competitor ASINs and Market Share
  • Other sellers offering identical ASINs are not a valid argument if your listing is restricted.
  • Sellers are encouraged to rectify any restriction-related violations and appeal if the product is wrongfully taken down.

 

Consulting, Contact Information, and Resources
  • Attendees can contact Riverbend Consulting via mds@riverbendconsulting.com for further assistance.
  • Meeting participants are invited to email questions to mds@riverbendconsulting.com and will receive one ASIN review per quarter and possible consulting discounts. 

 

This session provides Amazon sellers with an in-depth understanding of maintaining account health, navigating evolving regulations, and protecting intellectual property in 2026. 

 

Participants gain actionable strategies to avoid suspensions, handle compliance challenges, and safeguard product listings and brands. 

 

By emphasizing documentation, proper channel authorization, and proactive brand management, sellers can position themselves for sustained success and resilience against Amazon’s increasing enforcement.

items.title: Driving E-Commerce Growth Using TikTok Marketing, Off-Amazon Advertising, and AI Innovation － Centurion Channel Call January 2026

In this session, Centurion Channel members discuss strategies for boosting e-commerce growth through TikTok marketing, off-Amazon advertising channels, and the integration of AI in business operations.
TOPICS:
  1. TikTok strategy and content creation for e-commerce products
